Trump administration prepares sanctions against International Criminal Court, sources say
Targeting the entire organisation directly could severely undermine the court’s work prosecuting war crimes and genocide worldwide
US President Donald Trump’s administration has prepared sanctions against the entire International Criminal Court (ICC) and plans to announce them soon, two sources familiar with the matter said, a move that would step up its attack on the global tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and genocide worldwide.
The Trump administration has made no secret of its disdain for the court and has worked to undermine it. US officials want the court to drop its arrest warrants against Israeli leaders as well as a past investigation into American troops in Afghanistan.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in July announced a campaign to isolate the court, calling on other countries to withdraw from the tribunal. Washington has imposed sanctions on a number of ICC judges and prosecutors but has so far held off from imposing sanctions on the court itself, although the move has long been considered one of the options.
The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Bengal SIR tribunals may take 12 years to decide on appeals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:13:55 UTC
07:13:55 KST

SIR appeals pile up in WB, EC says hike number of tribunals
NEW DELHI: The innumerable voters in West Bengal who were removed from the electoral rolls after special intensive revision (SIR) may not be able to vote for more than a decade as appellate tribunals set up by Supreme Court could take more than 12 years to decide on their appeals for inclusion, going by the present pace of adjudication.An affidavit filed by Election Commission before Supreme Court says 1,26,194 applications have been decided by tribunals in the last five months since they started functioning in mid-April. So, on average, 25,238 cases are being decided by the tribunals in a month when even Saturdays and Sundays are included as working days. The total number of pending cases as of Sept 16, when the affidavit was filed, was 37,05,235. At current speed, if the tribunals work seven days a week, it would take 146 months to decide all cases.
Excessive backlog
Admitting that the present infrastructure and number of tribunals are insufficient to handle the Herculean task of adjudicating 37 lakh cases, the poll panel pleaded with the court to increase the number of tribunals in the state from 24 to 42, almost double the present strength, and allow judicial officers to work from home.
"With a view to further streamlining and expediting the disposal of the pending appeals, it is proposed that the number of appellate tribunals in the state of West Bengal may be considered for increase to correspond with the number of parliamentary constituencies in the state, so as to facilitate expeditious disposal of the pending appeals," said the affidavit, filed in response to a petition from TMC MP Derek O' Brien. Allowing judicial workers to conduct hearings and undertake other proceedings from home "would assist in expediting the disposal of pending appeals by minimising the time lost in conveyance", it said.In another affidavit filed in response to a petition on the functioning of the tribunals, the commission said they were constituted pursuant to the directives of the apex court and the standard operating procedure (SOP) governing their functioning has been formulated by the committee constituted for this purpose, comprising, inter alia, former judges of the high court at Calcutta.
"It is humbly submitted that the reliefs sought by the petitioner pertain primarily to the functioning, procedure and accessibility of the appellate mechanism and, therefore, fall within the domain of the SOP governing the functioning of the appellate tribunals and the authorities entrusted with the administration thereof. The feasibility, modalities and implementation... are matters best left to the consideration of the concerned appellate tribunal..." the affidavit said.

Qatar says mediation efforts underway to revive US-Iran talks

Hussien Elkabany and Mohammad Sio
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Qatar said Sunday that its mediation team has been discussing proposals for nearly two weeks aimed at restarting talks between the United States and Iran.
“We have been exchanging various ideas for nearly two weeks on resuming talks between Washington and Tehran,” said Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari, according to Qatari media.
Qatar, alongside Pakistan, has been mediating between the two sides.
“We are working through our mediation team with Tehran and Washington to see whether talks can resume, and our mediators are currently moving between different capitals in the hope of making progress on this track,” al-Ansari said.
He added that Qatar had heard assurances from officials in the US administration that Washington wanted to reach an agreement.
Al-Ansari said there is a need for “a regional solution that achieves stability and an international understanding that protects waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz.”
“Subjecting waterways to the sovereignty of a single state and using them as a weapon will set a dangerous precedent for all of us,” he added.
The US has recently carried out military attacks on sites in Iran amid a deadlock in negotiations over disagreements concerning navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important routes for energy supplies and global trade, despite a memorandum of understanding signed by the two sides in mid-June.
Iran responded with attacks on what it said were US military facilities and equipment in Arab countries, including Saudi Arabia. Some of the attacks caused civilian casualties and damage to civilian infrastructure, drawing condemnation from the affected countries and calls for them to stop.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28, leaving more than 3,000 people dead, according to Tehran. Iran responded with attacks that it said killed Americans and Israelis.
The remarks from Qatar came after the US State Department issued a security alert Sunday saying that “due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex, with the potential for unforeseen escalation.”
It urged US citizens in the region to exercise caution and those outside it to reconsider travel to or through the area.
Several US embassies in the region, including those in the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Jordan, issued similar warnings Sunday.
Earlier in the day, detailing his approach to the war, US President Donald Trump told US network Fox News “my question is if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They had better behave.”
Trump described his current options as wiping the country out, allowing it to “rot” economically, or negotiating a deal, adding that “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future.”

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:07:00 CST
07:07:00 KST

SARAJEVO, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- The Farmers' Association of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH) has called on cantonal governments to declare a state of natural disaster over prolonged drought, warning that the situation in the agricultural sector has become unsustainable, local news agency Fena reported Sunday.
The association said the drought had caused heavy losses to agricultural producers, with yields of some crops falling by more than 50 percent. Meanwhile, the autumn planting season is approaching, while prices of raw materials and other agricultural inputs continue to rise.
According to data from the European Drought Observatory (EDO), whose records date back to 2012, BiH was among nine European countries that experienced their driest August since the records began.
Nedzad Bico, president of the association, said the high cost of planting would affect the prices of domestic agricultural products. He said planting costs had risen amid conflicts in the Middle East, while prices of fuel, fertilizer and seeds had also increased significantly.
At the same time, purchase prices of agricultural products have continued to decline, the association said, warning that the Federation of BiH could face widespread farm closures without urgent assistance to agricultural producers.
Under the legal framework of BiH, declaring drought a natural disaster would allow the authorities to legally and rapidly mobilize emergency reserve funds to directly compensate farmers for their economic losses. ■

SANAA, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Sunday that 28 airstrikes had hit three provinces over the previous 24 hours, amid continued ground battles between the group and the Yemeni government forces across several fronts.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said in a statement that F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets operating from the Saudi air bases of Khamis Mushait and Taif carried out the strikes in Yemen's southwestern Taiz, northeastern oil-rich Marib, and northern Al-Jawf provinces.
Sarea put the cumulative number of airstrikes since the latest escalation began at 760.
Saudi Arabia has not immediately commented on the latest figures.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported earlier in the day that an airstrike struck a telecommunications tower in Al-Jawf, while areas of northern Saada province along the Saudi border came under artillery fire.
The aerial operations came as government forces and Houthi fighters remained locked in fighting in southwestern Yemen, where control of frontline positions has shifted repeatedly in recent days.
A government military source told Xinhua Sunday that government forces had retaken several positions in western Taiz, though the broader front lines remained largely unchanged amid fierce fighting.
The Houthis have recently made major gains along Yemen's southwestern Red Sea coast, seizing Taiz province's port city of Mocha on Sept. 10, then pushing south to capture Dhubab and take Mayyun Island in the heart of Bab al-Mandab Strait on Sept. 11.
Government forces are now trying to block further Houthi advances along the mountainous approaches to the strategic waterway.
Yemen's conflict began in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. The rapid Houthi advance marked the sharpest escalation since a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities. ■

Representatives from eight SMEs in sectors including artificial intelligence, commercial spaceflight and quantum technology attended the meeting.
China has strengthened support for specialized and innovative SMEs as part of broader efforts to boost industrial innovation and supply-chain resilience.
Earlier this month, China issued a plan to promote the high-quality development of SMEs during 2026-2030, setting targets for business growth, innovation, and the development environment.
By 2030, China's SMEs are expected to grow in both quality and scale, with per-capita operating revenue of major SMEs posting cumulative growth of around 15 percent over the five-year period, according to the plan. ■

07:06:37 KST

JERUSALEM, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Israel largely shut down at sundown on Sunday for Yom Kippur, the Jewish calendar's most important day, with flights and public transport suspended.
Israel's main international airport, the Ben Gurion Airport outside Tel Aviv, halted operations at 1:00 p.m. local time, the Airports Authority said in a statement, adding that departures and arrivals would resume early on Tuesday.
Trains, buses and light rail services also stopped across the country, with services due to resume gradually after the holiday ends on Monday night.
A Xinhua photographer saw large trucks blocking a major road in Tel Aviv to prevent vehicles from passing.
In central Tel Aviv, streets around Habima Square emptied of their usual buses, cafe crowds, and restaurant traffic as families, cyclists, and pedestrians took over the roads.
Yom Kippur, or the "Day of Atonement," is a time for reflection and repentance for Jews. Jews traditionally fast on this day and hold intense services in synagogues through most of the day.
The day begins on Sunday at dusk and ends on Monday at nightfall. Most businesses, restaurants, and entertainment venues close across Israel, with laws restricting employment and business openings during Yom Kippur.
Israel also imposed a general closure on the occupied West Bank for the holiday, restricting Palestinian movement into Israel and temporarily closing all crossings between the territory and Israel. ■

He said difficult access to some parts of the site made it impossible to determine the final number of missing miners, adding that a number of the injured were transported to Port Sudan, about 300 km from the mine site.
The accident came days after the collapse of the Al-Zaraa mine near Al-Nuhud in West Kordofan State, which killed dozens of miners.
Artisanal mining is a major source of income for many Sudanese, producing about 80 percent of the country's gold. The sector operates at more than 800 sites across northern and western Sudan, employing over 1.5 million miners.
Gold is one of Sudan's major sources of foreign currency. According to official statistics, Sudan produced 70 tons of gold in 2025. Accidents are frequent at mining sites, where inadequate safety measures and deteriorating infrastructure increase the risks to miners. ■

Motor neurone disease rates are rising. This new clinic hopes to stop it at the start

Key Points
- The Brain Institute and Clinic will bring together researchers and clinicians who specialise in motor neurone disease.
- MND impacts the brain and neurons that control muscles, leading to progressive weakness and eventual paralysis.
As the rates of a once-rare neurological disease increase, it is hoped Australia's first combined institute and clinic focusing on brain diseases will help find an effective treatment.
Macquarie University on Monday will launch its Brain Institute and Clinic to bring together researchers and clinicians who specialise in motor neurone disease with the aim of understanding where it comes from and how to treat it.
MND impacts parts of a person's brain and neurons that control their muscles, leading to progressive weakness and eventual paralysis.
It can affect adults of any age and most cases are not genetic.
Macquarie University deputy vice chancellor Patrick McNeil noted there was still no effective cure for the deadly disease, despite it becoming increasingly common.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The purpose of the institute was to find treatments and deliver them to patients more quickly, he said.
"It typically takes an average of 17 years between when an important research discovery is made ... and when that is implemented in the clinic," McNeill told AAP.
"When you have integrated research and clinical institutions, that journey is shortened."
Earlier in September, NSW became the first jurisdiction in the world to make MND notifiable, meaning medical professionals are now legally required to tell the government about cases.
McNeil said he hoped the decision would help researchers understand more about the cause.
"It would be good if the other states follow because that is the way that you can find if there is an environmental agent," he said.
"Because what we have been seeing anecdotally is these clusters of cases that seem to be more frequent in a particular town or region than you would expect."
Dominic Rowe, who heads up Macquarie's Neurology Clinic, said 800 Australians would die from the disease this year.
"But I actually disagree with using the term die, motor neuron disease kills you," he said.
"We need to redouble our efforts into working out why so we can fix it."
The facility will also do research and treatment around Parkinson's disease and dementia, including Alzheimer's disease.
Macquarie University professor James Burrell said he was hopeful experts could build on recent breakthroughs in dementia treatment.
He said there were therapies available that slowed the physical progression of dementia caused by Alzheimer's.
"We now have disease modifying therapies for this disease and this gives me tremendous hope that we can identify disease modifying therapies for other neurodegenerative diseases as well," Burrell said.

People with low implicit self-worth are quicker to notice subtle facial cues of anger and disgust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:00:09 UTC
07:00:09 KST

People who harbor unconscious doubts about their self-worth, or who have a large gap between their conscious and unconscious self-esteem, tend to detect subtle facial expressions of disgust and anger earlier than others. This heightened sensitivity to potential social rejection is also linked to poorer interpersonal wellbeing, according to new research published in Personality and Individual Differences.
Self-esteem is generally understood as how much a person values themselves. But psychologists separate this concept into two distinct layers. Explicit self-esteem refers to conscious feelings of self-worth that a person can easily describe, such as agreeing with the statement that they have a number of good qualities. Implicit self-esteem refers to automatic, unconscious evaluations of the self that operate beneath the surface of awareness.
Sometimes, these two layers do not match. A person might report high self-esteem on a questionnaire but harbor deep unconscious doubts about their worth, or they might report low self-worth despite having positive automatic associations with themselves. This mismatch is known as self-esteem discrepancy.
The research was led by Patrycja Korzeniowska, a lecturer in psychology at the School of Psychology, Sport Science & Wellbeing at the University of Lincoln in the UK. She and her colleagues aimed to understand how these different layers of self-evaluation shape the way people perceive the social world around them.
“We were interested in why people differ in their sensitivity to subtle social signals of acceptance and rejection, because detecting and interpreting these cues is an important part of navigating social interactions,” Korzeniowska told PsyPost.
Previous research has explored how self-evaluation alters social perception. For instance, a 2021 study demonstrated that people with lower conscious self-esteem can detect emerging expressions of anger and disgust at earlier, more subtle stages than people with high self-esteem. Building on related concepts, a 2025 study indicated that having low unconscious self-worth, or a mismatch between conscious and unconscious self-esteem, predicts a tendency to interpret ambiguous facial expressions as rejecting.
“Our aim was therefore to examine these components together, rather than treating self-esteem as a single, purely self-reported construct,” Korzeniowska explained. This led the team to test whether unconscious self-worth and self-esteem clashes directly heighten perceptual sensitivity to emerging rejection cues, and how that heightened sensitivity might affect psychological wellbeing.
To investigate this, the scientists recruited 225 adults to complete an emotion detection task. In this task, participants watched short videos of faces that slowly morphed from a completely neutral expression into a full-intensity emotional expression. The possible emotions were anger, disgust, fear, and happiness. The faces increased in emotional intensity in two percent increments, starting from a neutral state and ending at a complete display of emotion.
Participants were instructed to press a key the exact moment they recognized an emotion taking shape on the face, and then they selected which emotion they had seen. This setup allowed the researchers to measure perceptual sensitivity, or the minimum intensity level of the facial expression required for the participant to accurately detect it.
Before the computer task, participants completed several psychological assessments. They filled out a standard questionnaire to measure their explicit self-esteem and a psychological wellbeing scale to assess aspects of their life like personal growth, positive relations with others, and autonomy. To measure implicit self-esteem, the participants completed an Implicit Association Test.
This computer-based task requires people to quickly categorize words related to the self or others alongside positive and negative words. Faster reaction times when pairing self-related words with positive concepts indicate higher implicit self-esteem. By comparing the explicit and implicit scores, the researchers calculated each participant’s self-esteem discrepancy.
The results indicate that unconscious self-evaluation plays a prominent role in reading social cues. Participants with lower implicit self-esteem were able to detect expressions of disgust and anger at much lower intensities than those with higher implicit self-esteem. They were also faster to detect expressions of fear.
The gap between conscious and unconscious self-esteem also played a role. Participants with a larger self-esteem discrepancy required less emotional intensity to spot anger and disgust. This held true regardless of the direction of the gap, meaning it applied both to people who consciously felt great but unconsciously felt poorly, and to people who consciously felt poorly but had high unconscious self-worth.
Interestingly, while conscious self-esteem initially appeared to predict how quickly people spotted anger, this relationship faded when the researchers accounted for unconscious self-esteem. This suggests that previous research attributing heightened rejection sensitivity to low conscious self-esteem might have actually been picking up on the effects of unconscious self-evaluation or the clash between the two layers.
“Wang and colleagues had previously found that lower explicit self-esteem was associated with greater sensitivity to anger and disgust using closely related stimuli, whereas in our models explicit self-esteem was not a significant predictor; instead, implicit self-esteem and self-esteem discrepancy emerged more consistently,” Korzeniowska noted.
“This does not mean that explicit self-esteem is unimportant, as it was strongly associated with psychological wellbeing in our data, but it suggests that different components of self-esteem may relate differently to rapid social-perceptual processes,” she added. “The main takeaway is that how we respond to subtle social cues may be associated with aspects of self-evaluation that are not fully captured by simply asking people how they feel about themselves.”
The researchers also explored how this sensitivity to facial expressions relates to mental health and social functioning. Being highly attuned to early signs of disgust and anger was not directly related to overall psychological wellbeing, but it was linked to specific social outcomes. Heightened sensitivity to disgust, driven by low implicit self-esteem and high discrepancy, predicted poorer positive relations with others.
On the other hand, heightened sensitivity to anger predicted higher self-reported autonomy. While autonomy is generally considered a positive trait, the authors note that in the context of low implicit self-esteem and a high self-esteem discrepancy, this might indicate a defensive posture. People who are hypersensitive to anger might distance themselves from others to avoid negative evaluation and social rejection.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The primary measure used for unconscious self-esteem is widely used, but its exact psychological interpretation remains a topic of debate. Some researchers argue that the sorting task measures automatic associations that a person has learned from their environment rather than a true, unified sense of self-worth.
“One important point is that ‘implicit self-esteem’ should not be understood as a hidden or unconscious ‘true’ self-esteem that the test somehow reveals,” Korzeniowska said. Because the test measures relatively automatic associations between the self and positive or negative evaluations, she noted that the findings “are best understood as evidence concerning automatic self-evaluative associations, and they should ideally be replicated using multiple methods.”
Additionally, while the study measured how quickly people can visually detect facial cues of rejection, this is not exactly the same as feeling rejected in daily life. Spotting a faint flicker of disgust on a computer screen is an automatic perceptual process, whereas real-world rejection sensitivity involves complex emotional and behavioral reactions to social events.
“We measured perceptual sensitivity to facial cues associated with social rejection, not rejection sensitivity as a personality or dispositional construct,” Korzeniowska clarified.
She also emphasized that the effects observed were relatively small, accounting for roughly 4 to 7 percent of the variance in sensitivity to anger and disgust. “These are modest, correlational effects, so the findings should not be interpreted as showing that a particular self-esteem profile causes someone to perceive rejection differently,” Korzeniowska explained. “I see the findings primarily as evidence for an association worth investigating further, rather than something that currently supports individual-level prediction or clinical application.” A larger sample size, she added, would help confirm some of the more subtle interactive effects observed in the data.
“An important next step is to test whether these associations replicate across different measures of automatic self-evaluation and different ways of assessing responses to social rejection,” Korzeniowska said. She hopes to explore whether the same pattern generalizes to more naturalistic social situations and to other behavioral or physiological measures of responses to rejection-related cues.
“I see this study as part of an emerging rather than settled picture,” she told PsyPost. “Together with our previous work showing that lower implicit self-esteem and greater self-esteem discrepancy were associated with interpreting ambiguous facial expressions more negatively, these findings suggest that automatic self-evaluations may be relevant both to how social expressions are interpreted and to how quickly subtle cues are detected.”
The study, “Implicit self-esteem and self-esteem discrepancy: Implications for dynamic facial expression sensitivity and psychological wellbeing,” was authored by Patrycja Korzeniowska, Kun Guo, and Petra M.J. Pollux.

Specialist courtrooms to prioritise rape cases in England and Wales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:30:26 UTC
06:30:26 KST

Specialist courtrooms prioritising cases of rape and other serious sex offences are to be introduced across England and Wales, with campaigners welcoming the move as potentially transformative.
The changes, designed to encourage more survivors to come forward, will include the provision of private entrances and waiting rooms, and facilities equipped for recording evidence in advance and observing sentencing remotely.
Announcing the move, Andy Burnham said victims of rape and serious sexual offences had felt let down by the justice system for too long, adding that prosecution rates for rape remained “shamefully low”, with many victims waiting years for justice.
“These changes are long overdue and will make a significant difference, but focusing on prosecution alone will not be enough,” the prime minister said.
“So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place.”
A multimillion-pound cash injection is intended to make sure every crown court in England and Wales has at least one room set up specifically to hear rape and serious sexual offence cases within two years.
Rape and serious sexual offence cases will also be prioritised in courts more widely, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) announced. Such trials will be given a fixed date, as opposed to being placed on floating lists where they can be moved at short notice and delayed by months.
Among those welcoming the announcement was Labour’s Charlotte Nichols, who told the House of Commons this year she was raped after an event she attended as an MP and waited 1,088 days for her case to get to court.
Nichols said: “Today marks a hugely important milestone, helping to improve the experience of victims and survivors of sexual violence in the court system who are all too often retraumatised by seeking justice.
“I’m proud that substantive, meaningful change has come from waiving my anonymity to speak about my own experiences, and am hugely grateful to the prime minister and lord chancellor for taking forward these measures, as I know the difference they would have made for me and so many of the survivors I have worked with in recent years.”
The MoJ cited Nichols’ “immense strength and bravery” in its announcement.
While welcoming the announcement, there was a warning by the victims commissioner, Claire Waxman, that the crown court backlog of rape and sexual offence cases was now “significantly worse” than when she first called for specialist courts in 2021.
She said: “Tens of thousands more victims are now waiting for their cases to reach trial, and specialist courts alone will not be enough to tackle the scale of the delays or deliver the swift justice victims deserve. Indeed, court delays could prevent many rape victims from accessing the specialist courtrooms that are being set up to support them.”
Further changes announced include new trauma-informed training for court staff and a pilot scheme giving victims of sex offences a single point of contact to ensure their needs are met during the court process.
Separate from the funding for courtrooms, there will also be £43m to support survivors through the national rape and sexual abuse support fund for the next two years, including through counselling, therapy, outreach and group activities.
The new measures also include the creation of a rape justice taskforce, drawing figures from across the criminal justice system to tackle the rising rate of postponed rape trials and confront the myths that cause victims to withdraw from cases.
The Conservatives’ shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said tackling delays in rape trials was long overdue, but that the courts backlog had been “used” by the Labour as justification for controversial plans to significantly restrict the right to jury trials.
“If resources can be found to accelerate rape trials, why are they persisting in their attack on this ancient right to jury trials?” he said.
In 2022, an announcement by Boris Johnson’s government of three specialist courtrooms to prosecute rape cases was dismissed by legal blogger the Secret Barrister as a “gimmick” that did not address the chronic underfunding of the justice system.
Changes in the new provisions include many of the reforms that campaigners and charities have been calling for over many years.
“Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice,” said Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales.
“We’re particularly pleased to see measures that will improve trial efficiency and ensure survivors are better able to participate in, and observe, proceedings.”

A resolution would allow David Ellison’s $111-billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery to finalize
Bonta and Ellison have made progress in the talks in recent days, according to four people familiar with the matter not authorized to speak publicly.
However, New York’s Letitia James and at least two other attorneys general who joined Bonta’s lawsuit in July privately have expressed reservations about the proposed compromises, believing they don’t go far enough to mitigate concerns about the power Paramount-Warner Bros. would wield over the film and TV industries should the merger go through, according to the people familiar with the matter.
James isn’t on board with Bonta’s proposed settlement, two of the people said. A potential split within Bonta’s coalition could be a setback because Bonta needs the other state attorneys general who joined his legal effort to sign off on any deal.
California’s top prosecutor blasts Paramount-Warner Bros. conduct as ‘amateur hour.’
A spokesperson for Bonta did not respond Sunday to a request for comment.
Paramount maintains its deal to bring HBO, CNN, CBS, TBS, Comedy Central and two legendary film and television studios together would create a stronger company that could withstand the fierce competition from tech giants such as Apple, Netflix, Google (which owns YouTube) and Amazon. The two studios, on their own, would not be strong enough to remain viable in the streaming age, the company has said.
On Thursday, Paramount lawyers plan to demand that U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Oakland require the states and the Writers Guild of America to post a $1.88-billion bond that would cover some of Paramount’s delay-related deal costs should the company eventually prevail.
The states and the WGA, which also sued to block the merger, have balked at the request, which was designed by Paramount to create fissures within the coalition of states, which also include Minnesota, Oregon, Colorado, Connecticut, New Jersey and Massachusetts.
Los Angeles’ identity and workers’ livelihoods are at stake, say worried residents who fear that Paramount will leave the state.
Ellison wants the merger finalized by Oct. 1, when his company will be obligated to make a higher payout to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders. The company has threatened to move its Hollywood base from its historic Melrose Avenue lot to Tennessee or Texas should the antitrust battle stretch into October.
The prospective loss of an iconic California business — a century-old film studio that helped establish Hollywood — has rattled state and local politicians, who are fearful of losing more jobs at a time when Los Angeles film production levels already are at alarming lows.
Gov. Gavin Newsom, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for California governor, have publicly called on Bonta to settle the suit rather than prepare for a trial next spring. City Councilmember Nithya Raman, Bass’ opponent in the L.A. mayor race, has been one of few California politicians in support of Bonta’s fight.
Paramount’s board has approved David Ellison’s contingency plan to move headquarters from Hollywood as early as this fall, according to people familiar with the situation.
In an opinion essay Sunday, a trio of 1st Amendment and antitrust experts dismissed Paramount’s threat to leave Los Angeles as a ploy that doesn’t make business sense.
“Ellison’s threat is empty, and the AG should call that out — not give into it,” the experts — Fiona Scott Morton, Gene Kimmelman and Norm Eisen — wrote in the Contrarian.
Both Morton, an economics professor at the Yale School of Management, and Kimmelman formerly served in the U.S. Justice Department during Democratic administrations. Eisen, founder of the group Democracy Defenders Action, is helping lead the Block the Merger campaign.
“Paramount [would be] sinking the cost of moving before it knows what businesses it owns and how best to combine and organize them — which makes expensive strategic mistakes inevitable,” the trio wrote. “A company that raises its own costs while leaving behind the most valuable labor in the industry does not threaten California; it threatens itself.”
The group noted Paramount, in its regulatory filings, still lists its Times Square offices in New York as its corporate headquarters — not its Melrose Avenue campus in Hollywood.
“There is also the possibility that Ellison is planning to move Paramount to Tennessee regardless of how the lawsuit resolves,” the group wrote.
Bonta and Paramount have discussed including in any settlement a condition that Paramount would keep its operations in California for a set period, according to people familiar with the proposal but not authorized to comment.
Merger opponents planned a Sunday evening rally outside Bonta’s offices in Oakland to encourage him to stand tough. The group plans subsequent demonstrations this week outside James’ office in New York City and the Paramount lot in Hollywood.
The jockeying comes as President Trump, who favors the Ellison takeover of CNN and Warner Bros., has sought to block several prominent news organizations, including CNN and Politico, from reporting from the White House.
“Trump just locked CNN out of the White House. Now his billionaire allies want to own it,” Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) added in a Sunday post. “State attorneys general: Don’t settle. Hold the line. Block this merger.”

In early July, China fired a test missile from a nuclear submarine into the South Pacific for the first time, a weapon capable of carrying nuclear warheads. Washington and Canberra were livid. The Pacific has long been the exclusive testing ground for such long-range missiles from the United States. How dare China!
The reaction from Pacific island states was more measured. While leaders from Tuvalu, Palau and the Solomon Islands strongly criticised the test, the 18-member Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) failed to draft a united statement. Kiribati previously said singling out China was unfair when the US regularly tested such missiles near the Marshall Islands. In March, the US launched a Minuteman III ICBM from California, landing near the Marshall Islands 6,700km away; it followed a similar test in November last year. The US has test-fired at least 15 ballistic missiles into the Pacific since 2021.

UNITED NATIONS - France will summon Iran's ambassador and take appropriate measures in response after Iranian authorities sealed a French language centre affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, the Foreign Ministry said on Sept 20.
"This new attack against France’s cultural presence in Iran, following the assault on two staff members of the French embassy last July, is unjustifiable and unacceptable," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said in a statement.
Ties between the two countries have been strained for years over Iran's nuclear programme and Tehran detaining several French nationals.
Although the relationship had improved after their release and Paris distanced itself from the US war against Iran, the situation worsened over the summer after two of its diplomats were arrested and subsequently expelled. France reciprocated.

Iran cites security concerns
The centre operated for years under the cover of foreign-language teaching despite repeated warnings to obtain a licence, authorities said, accusing it of activities against Iranian culture and national security, including identifying and building networks as well as facilitating the departure of skilled Iranians from the country.
France has previously dismissed such allegations, saying there had been a pattern of intimidation in recent months as Paris sought to increase its support for, and contacts with, Iran's civil society following a crackdown on protests at the start of 2026.
Diplomats said Iran has also been irked by a recent social media post from France's foreign minister, Jean-Noel Barrot, to mark the fourth anniversary of the death of Mahsa Amini, which triggered protests across the country.

"Your silence when the U.S. massacred our schoolkids said it all," he said, referring to a strike in Iran that Tehran believes the US was responsible for.

Canada, France agree to closer ties in defense, economy

Canada, France agree to closer ties in defense, economy
September 20, 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced deeper cooperation between their countries in many areas, including defense, energy, and business.
The two leaders made the announcement on Sunday from Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a small French territory just off the Atlantic coast of Canada.
According to a statement from Carney's office, the leaders discussed aerospace, energy, critical minerals, and advanced technologies, such as quantum computing, satellites, and supercomputing.
This move is another step in Canada's accelerating turn toward Europe, as both countries are experiencing strained relations with the US.
The meeting between Macron and Carney follows up on Carney's visit to Brussels, during which the EU offered Canada "associate member" status.
What did the leaders say?
"We both believe that our countries are two great, independent nations who want to remain so," Macron said at the joint news conference, adding that France and Canada would work together for closer ties on fishing, security and energy.
"We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for free and fair trade, the science on which our decisions are based, and the strategic autonomy that we defend," Macron said. "And this is what very deeply unites Canada and France, Canada and the European Union."
Meanwhile, Carney said: "The time has come to tighten our links between Canada and France, between Canada and the European Union — links based on the values we share."
"History remembers those who... defend their sovereignty, those who stay true to their values," Carney stressed in his speech.
However, he also proposed that France, Canada, the United States and China work together on artificial intelligence.
Where is Saint Pierre and Miquelon?
Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a French overseas territory, is located off the coast of Newfoundland and has a population of fewer than 6,000 people.
It is France's only remaining possession in North America and a remnant of its former vast territories in what are now Canada and the United States. One of Canada's provinces, Quebec, has French as its sole official language.
Macron's three-day visit to Saint Pierre and Miquelon is the first by a French president in over a decade. Carney is the first Canadian prime minister to visit the territory.
The leaders' meeting comes at a time of strained relations with the US. Ottawa has strongly rejected President Donald Trump's repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st US state.
Last Monday, Trump posted a map of North America on social media. The map depicted Canada, Greenland, Mexico, much of Central America and the Caribbean, and Iceland in the colors of the US flag.
Several French overseas territories were also included in the image, such as Guadeloupe, Martinique, and Saint Pierre and Miquelon.
However, upon his arrival in the territory late Saturday, Macron reaffirmed its status as French territory and dismissed "strange ideas" on the subject.

Trump administration prepares sanctions against International Criminal Court, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Trump administration prepares sanctions against International Criminal Court, sources say
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump’s administration has prepared sanctions against the entire International Criminal Court and plans to announce them soon, two sources familiar with the matter said, a move that would step up its attack on the global tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and genocide worldwide.
The Trump administration has made no secret of its disdain for the court and has worked to undermine it. US officials want the court to drop its arrest warrants against Israeli leaders as well as a past probe into American troops in Afghanistan.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in July announced a campaign to isolate the court, calling on other countries to withdraw from the tribunal.
Washington has imposed sanctions on a number of ICC judges and prosecutors but has so far held off from imposing sanctions on the court itself, although the move has long been considered as one of the options.
The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Sanctions against the court have been prepared, the sources said, even though the exact timing of an announcement remained unclear.
The Wall Street Journal cited officials who said the decision could be finalised as soon as this week during the United Nations General Assembly meeting.
Targeting the entire organisation directly, as well as entities that cooperate with it, could severely undermine the court’s work.
Any entity-wide sanctions imposed by the US Treasury would prohibit US citizens and companies from providing funds, goods, or services to the court without a licence from the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).
Banks often over-comply with such US sanctions because they depend on access to the American financial system.
Among the court’s operations that could be affected by sanctions against the entire organisation are the purchasing of IT services and insurance, the hiring of investigators and conducting everyday financial transactions, such as paying dozens of American employees, the ICC’s registrar and president have warned.
Trump’s opposition to the court goes back to his first term. It surfaced again with a plan to penalise ICC officials, an idea developed in November 2024 when Trump was reelected and the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza conflict.
The ICC was established in 2002 by the international community to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. It asserts jurisdiction only if a member state is unable or unwilling to prosecute atrocities itself.
The United States has never been a member. REUTERS

German state elections deal a blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:20:00 UTC
06:20:00 KST

German elections deal a blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz
September 20, 2026
Two of Germany's 16 federal states, Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, have just elected new state legislatures. The results for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) represent yet another major blow in turbulent times both nationally and internationally.
In northeastern Germany, projections suggest that the CDU narrowly failed to clear the 5% threshold for representation in parliament, a historic first in the party's history.
In the German capital, the party that led the state government, lost nearly a third of its support, dropping to around 20%.
Just minutes after the first projections were released, Merz made a statement: "We can't sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — it was a disaster." As for the heavy losses in Berlin, he described the outcome there as "reasonable."
For the CDU, this marks the third electoral defeat in two weeks. In the state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, the party came in far behind the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which the Office for the Protection of the Constitution has classified as partially far-right extremist.
In the wake of this debacle, Merz, whose term began in 2025, appeared visibly shaken.
At the federal level, Merz governs in coalition with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), which saw mixed results in Sunday's state elections.
With around 36% of the vote, SPD state premier Manuela Schwesig — who has been in office since 2017 — finished just behind the far-right AfD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The AfD, on the other hand, nearly doubled its share of the vote compared to state elections in 2021, coming in first at 38%.
In Berlin, however, the SPD's share of the vote fell by a third to 12%, while the AfD became the third-largest party, winning 16% of the vote.
Meanwhile, the new frontrunner in the German capital is the socialist Left Party, with about 25%. It too was able to double its share of the vote, just as the AfD did in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. With the support of the SPD and the environmentalist Greens, the socialists — whom the CDU has labeled radical leftists and antisemites — would be able to form a coalition.
Berlin set to get a left-wing mayor
If this happens, Elif Eralp would be the first person from the Left Party to serve as mayor of Berlin. Leading up to the election, Eralp, the daughter of Turkish exiles, shared her vision in an interview with DW: "My vision for Berlin is an affordable Berlin where everyone — regardless of their background, religion, language or income — can lead a good life in dignity," Eralp said.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a coalition of SPD, the Left Party and the Greens is the most likely outcome. State Premier Schwesig said she was committed to a "stable democratic government."
Meanwhile, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel once again declared on election night that the CDU's containment strategy of refusing to cooperate with her party had failed. Speaking on the public television network ZDF, she said: "Our long-term goal, of course, is to hold coalition talks with the CDU."
The AfD and the Left Party are stronger than the CDU and SPD
Both election results reflect widespread dissatisfaction among the population with Chancellor Merz and the coalition he leads with the SPD. In nationwide opinion polls, the governing coalition no longer has a majority. Here, too, the AfD is clearly in the lead, while the SPD is only narrowly ahead of the Left Party.
Parties on the political fringes are now gaining significantly more support at both the federal and state levels than the ruling parties, which are frequently embroiled in arguments on the federal level. These disputes often arise in connection with the reform agenda announced months ago by Chancellor Merz, aimed at bringing the rapidly rising costs of health, long-term care and pension insurance under control.
Despite yet another election setback, the German chancellor intends to stay the course: "The reforms must go ahead. Of course, this puts us all in a difficult situation. But we will shoulder this responsibility. I will shoulder this responsibility," he said.
After lengthy discussions, the coalition had already reached an agreement on health care reforms. Many things, like drugs and dental prosthetics, will become more expensive, while family insurance coverage will also be scaled back. These are all measures that won't win any new support for the already unpopular government. The same goes for the ongoing debate over reforms to the pension system, which is set to be supplemented by increased private retirement savings.
'I want to move our country forward'
Merz acknowledged that these changes would bring burdens and new uncertainties for many people. Nevertheless, he remained confident: "I want to move our country forward. I am also firmly convinced that the success of our reforms will not only improve our society but also boost our self-image and our image in the world."
In foreign policy as well, Merz — and with him the federal government — is coming under increasing pressure as a result of the election results in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The AfD, which is particularly strong in eastern Germany, opposes military support for Ukraine in its fight against Russia's invasion.
'What needs to be done now requires backbone, resolve and patience'
This complex situation makes things even more difficult for the federal government — and Merz is well aware of this. Taking stock of the heavy election defeats suffered by his CDU, he said: "What needs to be done now requires backbone, resolve and patience. I will muster that — as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as the chancellor of our country."

"From today, we're changing Berlin together," she told celebrating party members in Berlin.
The Left Party took 25.3%, ahead of the CDU on 19% and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) on 16%. It also far outstripped the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) on 12.1%.
In her first remarks after the polls closed, the 45-year-old daughter of left-wing Turkish parents who fled a coup in 1980 said the increasingly difficult rental situation was "the biggest social problem" in the capital.
She promised to proceed with nationalising the housing associations and "drive speculation from Berlin," in accordance with a referendum from 2021 in which 58% backed proposals to legislate for nationalisation.
Whether the policy, which would see some 220,000 housing units transferred to state ownership, is ever adopted remains unclear. SPD general secretary Tim Kluessendorf said nationalising the housing associations would cost some €20 billion.
An Infratest Dimap poll also found only 37% of those surveyed were in favour.
Sunday's election in Berlin came on the same day the AfD followed up on its success in the September 6 Saxony-Anhalt election by taking first place in an election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state. It also recorded its best-ever result in Berlin.
But while the AfD has attracted most attention, the Left Party has also benefited from a general turn against the mainstream parties of the centre-left and centre-right.
As in the four other state elections held this year, the dire state of the German economy and uncertainty about the way ahead weighed on the election in Berlin, with the main focus fixed on rental costs.
But significant obstacles remain for Eralp.
Both the SPD and the environmental Greens signalled a willingness to join a coalition with the Left Party. But the Greens leader Felix Banaszak said accusations of antisemitism that have been levelled against parts of the Left Party in Berlin had to be addressed for a partnership to work.
"We need a clear commitment to combating antisemitism; otherwise, things won't work with us," he said.
The Left Party rejects accusations of systematic antisemitism, saying it is against all forms of "group-focused hostility" including antisemitism, racism and sexism. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Banaszak's demand. REUTERS

Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) said the attacks affected towns and areas across Tyre, Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil and Marjayoun districts.
In Tyre district, Israeli forces fired phosphorus munitions that sparked fires in olive groves and citrus orchards around the towns of Majdal Zoun and Buyout al-Sayyad.
Majdal Zoun was also hit by a series of Israeli bombings and explosions as Israeli forces carried out a sweep of the area, with a large blast later reported in the town.
Israeli artillery also struck the town of Al-Mansouri, where repeated explosions had been reported since midnight, as well as the outskirts of Buyout al-Sayyad. Israeli shelling also targeted Wadi Zibqin.
Separately, a child was injured when an unidentified object left from the war detonated in the town of Debaal. The child was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment, while authorities launched an investigation into the incident.
In Nabatieh district, Israeli artillery targeted the outskirts of Zawtar al-Sharqiyah toward Mayfadoun, while an Israeli drone dropped a stun grenade on the town.
Heavy Israeli artillery fire was also reported in Yahmar al-Shaqif.
In Bint Jbeil district, Israeli artillery struck a wooded area in Aita al-Jabal.
Four 240mm artillery shells also landed on the outskirts of Haddatha toward the town of Haris, according to the agency.
In Marjayoun district, an Israeli force comprising three Merkava tanks advanced toward Deir Mimas and blocked its entrance, disrupting residents’ movement in and out of the town.
The force searched several homes during the incursion and damaged telephone poles along the road before continuing its movements in the area.
Israeli forces also fired four artillery shells at the town of Khiam and shelled Wadi al-Salouqi and Wadi al-Hujeir.
The developments came a day after the Israeli army targeted paramedics in an airstrike and set more homes ablaze while carrying out demolitions, explosions and shelling across several areas of southern Lebanon.
During the latest war, the Israeli army advanced about 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) into Lebanese territory and established a security zone, or the “Yellow Line.”
On June 26, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-sponsored Framework Agreement in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army to areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued to carry out attacks in southern Lebanon and maintains a military presence in parts of the south, including territory it has occupied for decades and other areas seized during more recent wars and military operations.

China cultivates 14 plant species aboard space station
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
05:10:48 CST
06:10:48 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China has now cultivated more than 20 varieties spanning 14 plant species in orbit -- a milestone that lays the groundwork for large-scale crop production aboard the space station, according to the Astronaut Center of China.
The breakthrough was highlighted at an aerospace medical engineering conference in Tianjin Municipality in north China, where Zhang Hongzhang, an astronaut from the Shenzhou-21 crewed mission, shared photos and videos of a flourishing "space garden" aboard China's Tiangong space station, featuring crops such as lettuce, carrot, sunflower, potato and wheat.
China's era of long-term crewed spaceflight began in October 2021, when Shenzhou-13 crew members Zhai Zhigang, Wang Yaping and Ye Guangfu moved into China's space station core module Tianhe.
"Long-term stays in space require us to reduce the reliance on Earth resupply. Our controlled ecological life support experiments aim to build an ecosystem in space that can regenerate water, air and food in situ -- cutting dependence on Earth and eventually achieving self-sufficiency," said Bian Qiang, an expert at the Astronaut Center of China.
Controlled ecological life support technology uses an artificially built, closed and controlled ecosystem to efficiently recycle and regenerate the air, water and food astronauts in orbit need to survive, establishing a life-and-health support system suited to long-term human habitation.
According to Bian, right now, two types of plant-growing units aboard the space station -- one using substrate culture and the other aeroponics -- are running continuously. Together, they are giving researchers valuable experience in building a basic life support system that leans mainly on physical and chemical recycling, with biological regeneration playing a supporting role.
"A more efficient aeroponics unit was sent up in 2025. Wheat has since completed a full growing cycle in orbit, and a second round cultivation using seeds from that harvest is growing well and close to reaping," Bian said.
Looking further ahead, Bian said China intends to establish a "lunar vegetable garden" as its lunar exploration program advances.
China's space station, Tiangong, which means Heavenly Palace, has now entered an era of long-term human habitation. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay, while the country's 2030 crewed moon landing mission is advancing steadily. ■

China Focus: Global mayors explore sustainable development prospects at China's Wuhan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
05:10:32 CST
06:10:32 KST

WUHAN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- More than 80 city leaders and representatives from over 20 countries, along with heads of international organizations, have gathered in Wuhan, Hubei Province, central China, to discuss shared urban challenges and explore pathways to sustainable development at the 2026 World Mayors Dialogue.
Held from Sept. 18 to 21 under the theme "River City: Shared Resonance, Shared Growth," the event focuses on how technological innovation, industrial cooperation and cultural exchanges can advance urban development and improve people's lives.
Shaukat Ali, Lord Mayor of Manchester, said he was impressed by Wuhan's efforts in developing low-carbon industries and advanced manufacturing, noting that Manchester and Wuhan have jointly established the UK-China Clean Energy Forum to harness the two cities' shared industrial and technological strengths for eco-friendly development.
Manchester and Wuhan became sister cities in 1986 because of shared industrial origins, leading educational institutions, and a shared appetite for economic transformation. As the cities have grown and evolved, the partnership continues to pioneer multi-level exchanges and developmental cooperation between the UK and China, Ali said.
The dialogue comes as Wuhan continues to pursue greener urban development while transforming its traditional industrial base.
Located at the confluence of the Yangtze and Hanjiang rivers, Wuhan is home to 166 lakes and 165 rivers. Once a major industrial center known for steel and automobile manufacturing, the city has in recent years stepped up efforts to improve its environment and promote greener industrial development.
As part of its urban renewal efforts, Wuhan has transformed small plots of unused or underused land into "pocket parks," bringing green space closer to residents. By the end of May, the city had built 788 such parks.
Water quality in Wuhan's sections of the Yangtze and Hanjiang rivers has remained at Grade II, the second-highest level in China's five-tier system, for six consecutive years.
The city also showcased its experience to international participants through visits to its suspended rail transit system, a smart home appliance factory, and a Yangtze finless porpoise breeding and conservation center, offering a closer look at its infrastructure, technological innovation, and ecological protection efforts.
"Our visits have given us different perspectives on how technological innovation and industrial development are reshaping cities and their economies," said Jordi Vaquer, secretary general of Metropolis. "We have also been reminded that innovation and development must coexist with the protection of natural systems."
Vaquer said cities play an important role in keeping international cooperation channels open, as urban challenges transcend national borders.
"None of us can address them entirely alone," he said.
Beyond Wuhan's transformation experiences, the dialogue also comes as China places greater emphasis on sustainable urban development.
This year marks the start of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The outline calls for a shift in the approach to urban development and for building cities that are more innovative, livable, beautiful, resilient, culturally vibrant and smart. ■

Key Event
CBA changes rate call to September hike
Australia's largest lender, CBA, is the latest bank to bring forward its forecast for an RBA rate hike in September.
It had previously forecast a move in November.
The switch follows a similar move by the Westpac, the second biggest lender, on Friday.
CBA's head of Australian economics Belinda Allen said the context of the September meeting, recent RBA communications and market pricing were all supporting the case to move earlier than had been anticipated post the surprise July CPI print.
"The risk sits with the need to tighten monetary policy further beyond September given the inflation backdrop, but it is not an easy decision to push monetary policy further into restrictive territory," Ms Allen said in a note this morning.
On Friday, Westpac's chief economist Luci Ellis changed the bank's stance noting a recent escalation in the RBA's communications pointing to the "upside risks to inflation appeared to be materialising".
However, Ms Ellis said she expected the RBA vote for a hike would not be unanimous.
The ANZ is now the only one of the "Big Four" retail banks still forecasting the RBA's next move, a hike, in November.
Over the past week, senior RBA officials have focussed their public comments on inflation with Deputy Governor Hauser and Assistant Governor Hunter raising concerns about the entrenched nature of the problem.
But it was Governor Michelle Bullock at the House of Representatives Standing Committee on Economics on Friday that appears to have caused the CBA to bring forward their forecast.
"Given market pricing there was a chance the Governor could provide a more balanced assessment around inflation and growth given her role of balancing the views of the staff and the Board," Ms Allen said.
"But instead, the Governor noted 'some of these upside risks to inflation appear to be materialising' and commentary around inflation remained hawkish."
The market is now placing the chances of a September rate hike at 90%.
However, the CBA and Westpac are at odds over the RBA board's likely vote, arguing that it expects a unanimous decision.
"The decision arguments to hike are not one sided," Ms Allen said.
"The case to leave the cash rate on hold is expected to receive some attention.
"The economy is slowing, the labour market is shifting back into balance and home prices are falling.
"At 4.60% monetary policy is restrictive and will see those with a mortgage facing a higher mortgage rate than seen since 2011 and 25bp above the peak seen ahead of the 2025 cutting cycle."

BIG builds a temporary city for shakira in madrid with reusable structures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:07:28 UTC
06:07:28 KST

Why settle for a stadium when you can build a town? For her Madrid residency, Shakira has taken over the 185,000-square-meter Iberdrola Music venue in Villaverde, transforming it into Macondo Park, a temporary cultural landscape designed by Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG). Conceived as an alternative to the conventional concert arena, the site combines a stadium for more than 50,000 spectators with colorful pavilions, markets, food, art, fashion, cinema, and children’s spaces — an entire world constructed around the shows rather than merely behind the stage.
Unlike an existing stadium, where attention converges on a single performance, the purpose-built environment allowed the architects to choreograph the audience’s full journey. ‘The architecture is designed to not only accommodate large crowds, but also to guide people, create moments of discovery, and offer places to gather, celebrate, and find shade throughout the day,’Stefani Fachini de Araujo, Associate at BIG and Design Lead on the project, tells designboom. Shakira may remain the main attraction, but the celebration is deliberately set in motion well before she appears.
colorful paths unfold across the temporary venue | all images courtesy of BIG
COLOR-CODED PATHS LEAD THROUGH A TEMPORARY TOWN
Visitors enter through a sequence of Es Latina welcoming arches, each assigned its own color and connected to a matching route across the site. The paths lead toward 12 temporary pavilions and complementary fan, VIP, and children’s areas, with eight of the main structures dedicated to pillars of Latin American culture. ‘Each path leads visitors to a different pavilion containing a unique experience,’explains Fachini de Araujo from BIG. At the center stands the Macondo Tree, a shared landmark that gives this otherwise vast event ground something resembling a town square.
More than 500 trees and planted islands draw from Mediterranean, Spanish, and Latin American landscapes, reducing the scale of the open venue and adding pockets of shade. ‘Along the way, more than 500 trees bring human scale to the site, turning a vast event ground into a park,’ the Design Lead continues. The fictional town of Macondo, borrowed from Gabriel García Márquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude, becomes less a literal reconstruction than a spatial framework for mixing storytelling, popular culture, and collective celebration — with a little stadium logistics tucked underneath.
BIG designs macondo park for shakira’s madrid residency
BIG DESIGNS EVERY ELEMENT FOR A SECOND LIFE
Building this temporary universe meant working against both scale and time. According to Fachini de Araujo, the design process took around six months, while some of the pavilions were assembled in roughly ten days. ‘This led us to work with the components found at any large event, such as trusses, scaffolding, containers, and stage ground support systems, and to rethink how they come together,’ she shares. Wrapped in brightly colored fabric, the familiar event infrastructure becomes a family of shaded structures, each with a distinct identity but a deliberately pragmatic skeleton.
The temporary nature of Macondo Park also informed what happens after the final concert. ‘Knowing from the start that it would be dismantled, we chose every element with its next life in mind,’Fachini de Araujo tells designboom. The structures and fabrics are intended for reuse, the artificial grass can be relocated to schools and playgrounds, and the trees will return to the nursery. For a project designed around spectacle, its disappearing act has been considered surprisingly carefully.

Tehan defends opposition's fuel price proposal
Dan Tehan has rejected claims the opposition's promise to cut the fuel excise when oil prices are high would be inflationary.
The Coalition has proposed halving the tax paid on petrol every time the two-week average global oil price hits US$100 a barrel.
Speaking to ABC's Radio National Breakfast, the shadow energy minister described it as a "sensible measure" that was completely offset by the Coalition's proposed change to the tobacco excise.
"There is no inflationary pressures put on. We have the discipline to be able to do the policy work, to make sure we can offset policies like this so it won't be inflationary," he says.

Key Event
Family violence at 'unacceptable levels'
Minister for Women Katy Gallagher has said the level of family violence in the Australian community is "unacceptable" after a spate of incidents in NSW over the weekend.
Three women, including a 90-year-old grandmother, were killed over the weekend in NSW in separate alleged domestic-violence incidents.
Separately, a 5-year-old child died and two younger children and a 42-year-old woman are in a critical condition after suffering stab wounds yesterday in the Blue Mountains. Police said the matter was being treated as a domestic violence incident and the woman is a suspect.
Gallagher said her thoughts were with the loved ones impacted by the "horrible" events.
"It's hard to get your head around the level of violence across — particularly aimed towards women and children — but in families across Australia," she said.
"This is something that is on our desk every single day … it's not just something that we look at when there are terribly sad, awful, horrific stories in the media."
She said the government was making domestic violence a priority at national cabinet and through the development of a second action plan (under their broader plan to end violence against women and children), but said governments alone couldn't deal with the issue.
"There is no easy solution, if there was one, we would have already put it in place," she said.
"More money is part of it, we're doing that, but again it's a whole of community response that's needed to end violence and to stand up and talk about the level of violence in our community right now, which is at unacceptable levels."
Key Event
Fertility rates to drop but don't expect another plea to have a baby for the country
Australia's fertility rate is expected to drop faster than previously forecast over the next 40 years, according to the latest intergenerational report.
The report looks at the nation's long-term economic outlook. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher population will also be lower than previously predicted.
Gallagher is asked if the government would consider a return to a baby bonus, such as the $3000 that was on offer back in 2002 to support new parents.
At the time, then-treasurer Peter Costello declared Australians "should have one for your husband, one for your wife and one for the country".
"Our government doesn't get into sort of, you know, deciding or promoting choices for individual families but we recongise that ... people making those choices should be supported," Gallagher told ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
She pointed to investments in early education and extending paid parental leave, including allowing second parents to take it, was how the government was offering support.
Gallagher also noted Australia's ageing population would only put further pressure on the budget, especially with aged care.
Labor not considering joining Coalition with plans on fuel excise cut
It's safe to say the government aren't fans of the opposition's vow to cut tax on fuel when the global price of Brent crude oil averages $US100 a barrel over two weeks.
"It's an unfunded, uncosted promise from [Angus] Taylor," Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC's Radio National Breakfast this morning.
The opposition says it will fund the cut through an increase in tax revenue it expects to receive from the Coalition's proposed changes to the tobacco excise.
The government halved the fuel excise for a three-month period as part of its response to the Middle East war. The measure was extended until August but at a higher excise rate.
But Gallagher says it's not something the government is "currently" considering, even with the uptick in fuel prices.
"We've shifted, and including in the budget, to providing more permanent cost-of-living arrangements, including through the tax system to make sure that ongoing cost-of-living help is there permanently, not just in these-one off arrangements," she says.
Coalition wants cut to tobacco excise to fund cut to fuel prices
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor was out to spruik his plan to automatically halve the fuel excise whenever the two-week average Brent crude oil price hit $US100 a barrel.
The Coalition says it will cut $15 off a tank. It says it will be fully funded by increased tax revenue from legal cigarettes through the opposition's proposed cut to the tobacco excise.
"It's fully funded, so it won't put pressure on inflation despite what the treasurer is trying to say. He has it wrong," he told Nine.
Asked what impact the cut to the tobacco excise would have on smoking rates, Taylor says people can already buy illegal cigarettes for $15 a pack.
"We are taking money away from the criminal gangs and using it to cut the fuel price and the government should get on board with this today," he says.
Key Event
Plibersek concedes polls are 'obviously not great' but no big change needed
Tanya Plibersek has downplayed suggestions Labor needs a shake-up at the top after a fresh poll suggested support for the party has dropped to a low not seen since the Gillard era.
The latest Newspoll, published in The Australian, suggests Labor's primary vote has fallen two points to 27 per cent for the first time since 2012.

One Nation's Barnaby Joyce, who was also on the panel, was asked about the recent dip in Pauline Hanson's own numbers.

Australia launches campaign for two-year seat on UN Security Council
Anthony Albanese has officially launched Australia's campaign for a two-year term on the powerful United Nations Security Council, declaring Australia "punches above its weight" and wants to help shape the global response to issues including the rapid rise of AI.
Declaring Australia is "in a pretty strong position" to nab one of the two spots available, the prime minister released a slick campaign video to accompany the campaign in New York on Monday, where dozens of world leaders are gathering for this year's UN General Assembly.
Speaking to reporters at the UN headquarters, Albanese said having a seat at the table would enable Australia to influence the way the world responds to emerging challenges including AI.
"Australia's voice on the council matters, so we can be a part of shaping some of these biggest issues which are facing the world and our nation," Albanese said.
"Australia punches above our weight. Punches above our weight, and we can have an impact on the world, and that's what I want to see Australia do."
Pre-empting critics at home, Albanese said the campaign would be "very modest" and sought to remind voters that Australia is not immune from global crises, including the conflict in the Middle East that is hammering Australia's economy and sending fuel prices soaring.

Germany's Central Council of Jews opposes Left Party-led government in state of Berlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:04:00 UTC
06:04:00 KST

Anadolu staff
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
The head of Germany’s Central Council of Jews on Sunday voiced opposition to a Left Party-led government in Berlin and urged other parties not to open state government coalition talks with the socialist election winner.
Josef Schuster said he was concerned about the Left Party’s solidarity with pro-Palestinian demonstrators protesting the Israeli government. He accused the party of antisemitic statements—claims its officials have repeatedly and firmly denied.
“During the election campaign, the Left Party repeatedly crossed the line with antisemitic remarks,” Schuster claimed. Entering a Left Party-led coalition, he argued, would mean promoting the “ongoing normalization of hatred against Jews.”
Left Party lead candidate Elif Eralp voiced support during the campaign for Berlin’s Palestinian community and sharply condemned the war crimes in Gaza of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government. She pledged that a Left Party-led state government would end repressive police measures against peaceful pro-Palestinian protests in the capital.
In the face of the accusations, Eralp said party leaders had distanced themselves from a handful of isolated incidents. She added that the Left Party opposes all forms of racism and noted that during her career she has been involved in projects combating antisemitism.
“It is absolutely clear that we stand for the protection of Jewish life,” she said in a recent TV debate with her rival. “Just as we stand for the protection of Muslim and Palestinian life.”
Germany’s socialist Left Party looked on track Sunday for a historic first-place finish in Berlin’s state election, with Eralp hailing a result that could make her the capital’s first governing mayor from a migrant background.
German public broadcaster ARD’s latest projection put the Left Party at 25.3% — more than double its 12.2% result in the 2023 election — and more than six points ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative CDU at 19%.
The anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) followed at 16.3%, the Greens at 14.4% and the SPD at 12.1%.
Despite its clear lead, the Left Party remained far from an absolute majority and would need at least two partners to govern. After a campaign that called for a change of course and rejected CDU policy, the most viable path was a three-party coalition with the SPD and the Greens.
Coalition math remained fluid before preliminary official results. Whether the left-populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) stays above the 5% threshold would still reshape the seat distribution. In the latest projection, it stood at 4.8%.
If the Left Party cannot reach an agreement with the SPD and the Greens, the second-place CDU could try a coalition with those two parties. The three would have enough seats if the BSW fails to enter the Berlin state parliament.
