Italy to ban burqas in schools, limit foreign students per class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:02:45 UTC
06:02:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Italy to ban burqas in schools, limit foreign students per class, PM Meloni says
Italy will ban burqas and niqabs in schools and limit the number of foreign students per class, far-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said Sunday.
Italy is a frontline country for migration, and integration is a major campaign issue ahead of next year's general election.
"A measure will soon be presented to a cabinet meeting to legally establish a maximum number of foreign students per class," Meloni told a gathering of the youth wing of her Brothers of Italy (FdI) party.
"It also requires parents of foreign students facing serious difficulties integrating into the school system to learn Italian, and bans burqas and niqabs in schools," she said.
A crackdown on the use of burqas in schools was called for in July by the National Future (FN) party.
The FN, not part of the governing coalition, is further to the right than Meloni's party and has emerged as a major challenger, rising sharply in the polls since launching in February.
While Italy has no law that expressly bans burqas in schools or public places, a 1975 law prohibits helmets or garments that make identification difficult without a justified reason.
In 2008, Italy's highest administrative court clarified that full-face veils may be worn for religious or cultural reasons provided that the face is revealed when identity verification is required.
The anti-immigrant League party, which is part of Meloni's coalition, submitted a bill to the Senate earlier this year that would ban helmets or garments except in certain circumstances, such as sporting events or places of worship.
Italian law already limits the number of foreign students per class, and Meloni did not spell out how that would change.
Foreign students account for just under 12 percent of those enrolled in Italian schools, according to the National Statistics Institute (ISTAT).
Since 2010, the number of foreign students has been limited to 30 per cent of a class and of a school's enrolment.
The limit can be raised in cases involving foreign students with adequate language skills, such as foreign students born in Italy, or lowered when foreign students have a poor command of Italian.

Winless Bombers, Saints and Magpies AFLW coaches under pressure

The AFLW has passed the midway point of this year's home-and-away season, with some expected storylines and some surprises.
With all the twists and turns, here's what fans are talking about the most.
Will pressure come on coaches without a win?
It's the question fans could be heard right around the boundary fence asking on Sunday afternoon: "Will Essendon win a game this year?"
The Bombers recorded their sixth straight loss, this time against Gold Coast by 41 points, which raised some doubts about the future of head coach Natalie Wood.
Last year, Essendon finished 14th with four wins and eight losses, but escaped a lot of scrutiny due to a high injury toll taking the blame.
This year, fans expected better. Against the Suns, the only goal came off the boot of Emily Gough.
But they're not the only ones. St Kilda remains without a victory and with a percentage of just 36.5.
It's the sixth season head coach Nick Dal Santo has been at the helm, over which time he's taken the team to one finals campaign (last year, in which it lost an elimination final to Adelaide by 44 points).
This year, they lost to Geelong by 85 points in round two, North Melbourne by 92 points in round five, and managed just one goal against Sydney in round three.
Then at Collingwood, the inaugural AFLW side continue to struggle for success, with another year down the bottom end of the ladder.
Sam Wright took over as head coach ahead of the 2024 season and quietly re-signed until the end of 2027 last week. It came amid media reports of player concern about the lack of direction in the club's AFLW program.
Wood and Dal Santo are both out of contract at season's end.
In 2022, Carlton launched an independent review into its AFLW program after managing just six wins across two seasons. The club then signed Mathew Buck as coach and rose to become a genuine finals contender.
Many are now starting to ask whether it's time Collingwood, Essendon and St Kilda do the same.
North are no longer a top of the ladder
Hawthorn's Friday night win over two-time reigning premiers North Melbourne sent shock waves through the AFLW competition.
The Kangaroos were on a 32-match winning streak — the longest in AFL/VFL/AFLW history — and had gone undefeated since 2023, a total of 1,020 days.
Carlton had got close to them the week before, going down by just 10 points, and many thought Melbourne might be the ones to break the run in round seven.
But then came along the Hawks in humid Cairns, where a clutch Lucy Wales goal in the dying minutes of a hard-fought four quarters changed the narrative of the season.
The unbeatable Kangaroos were beaten and the premiership race was blown wide open.
Less than 24 hours later, Melbourne put its foot down against Carlton to remain the only team undefeated this season and take the top spot on the ladder.
Umpiring an issue
One consistency across all leagues and codes, no matter the gender or sport, is fans having a gripe with umpiring or refereeing decisions.
But AFLW fans may have a better leg to stand on than most.
Loading Twitter content
This season, Ray Chamberlain, who retired from the AFL at the end of 2024 after 389 games, returned to help officiate and mentor the next generation of umpires in the AFLW.
He wasn't alone, with the AFL putting a call out to retired umpires to make a return in the women's game, which former AFL-listed umpires such as Jordan Bannister and Chris Donlon answered.
Ahead of the season, Chamberlain said he was happy to help because there was "a need there".
"You want to do it well and you want to support what they're doing," Chamberlain told SEN.com.au.
The state leagues are still the primary pathway for umpires wanting to make into the AFL, which has its finals campaigns running concurrently to the AFLW's start of the season.
With a lot of umpires prioritising the state leagues, there was a dearth of experienced umpires to officiate the AFLW and there was a desperate need for mentoring and development.
Who saw this coming from the Dogs and Suns?
While many of the top eight were predicted by pundits at the start of the season to be finals contenders — Melbourne, North Melbourne, Geelong, Sydney, Carlton and Hawthorn — two teams on the rise that have surprised fans have been the Gold Coast Suns and the Western Bulldogs.
The Suns have lured some big-name recruits in recent years, including premiership players Anne Hatchard and Lily Mithen.
But much of their rise this year has come off the back of teenagers.
The teams has enjoyed the fruits of the Suns Academy, with graduates Ava Usher, Alannah Welsh, Sunny Lappin, Georgia Davies, Mikayla Nurse, Dakota Baron and Bronte Parker all catching the eyes of the competition. And they've helped steer their side to four wins and two losses.
Meanwhile, things have started to click at the Kennel under Tamara Hyett, with the Dogs also sitting at 4-2.
The Dogs have struggled in recent years, and they finished in 12th place last season. But, buoyed by an extremely strong pre-season, they launched into this year with gusto.
Credit to them, they stuck to the plan even when external scrutiny came. Now they pose a serious threat to the teams coming up against them. All this work has been led by captain Isabelle Pritchard, forward Emma McDonald and midfielder Jess Fitzgerald.
There is still a lot to play out in the remaining half of the home-and-away season, particularly with Richmond and Fremantle knocking on the door of the top eight.
But one thing is for sure: It's got an ending a lot less clear than when the year started out.

US prepares new sweeping Russia sanctions: Who could get hit?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:00:27 UTC
06:00:27 KST

Trump signs off on Russia sanctions ‘from hell’: Who could get hit?
US President Donald Trump has signed into law a sweeping expansion of sanctions against Russia, giving Washington new powers to target Moscow as well as major buyers of Russian energy. The legislation authorizes tariffs of up to 100% on goods from certain countries purchasing Russian oil and gas, while imports from Russia could face duties of up to 500%.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act also expands restrictions on Russian officials, financial institutions and other entities linked to the government. The White House has said the legislation is intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow over the Ukraine conflict while giving the president broad discretion over waivers and the eventual termination of sanctions.
RT examines the law’s key provisions, who could be affected and what the measures could mean for Russia’s trade partners.
What do the sanctions cover?
The legislation was approved by the Senate 86-11 in August before passing the House 262-159 on Wednesday. It originated with Republican Senator Lindsey Graham and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal.
Unlike earlier sanctions focused largely on designated companies and individuals, the law broadens restrictions covering Russian government-linked officials, financial institutions and enterprises. It also targets vessels Washington says are used to circumvent restrictions on Russian oil exports.
One of its most consequential provisions gives the president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries among the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. That is considerably below the 500% secondary tariff proposed in earlier versions of the legislation.
Who could be targeted?
China and India are among the countries most exposed to the secondary tariff provisions because of their large purchases of Russian crude.
Türkiye, a NATO member, is also a major importer of Russian energy, while EU countries continue to purchase Russian oil and gas despite the bloc’s efforts to phase out Russian supplies.
The picture is particularly significant for natural gas, where the EU remains a major market for Russia. China has also expanded its purchases, while Türkiye remains another important destination.
The law, however, does not make maximum tariffs automatic. It contains exemptions and gives the US president broad discretion over their application, meaning the eventual impact will depend heavily on how the administration implements it.
How are major buyers responding?
China and India have rejected US pressure over their energy trade with Russia and stressed that their economic and energy interests will guide their policies.
China’s Commerce Ministry has said Beijing reserves the right to take “all necessary measures” to protect its sovereignty, development interests and Chinese companies, while calling for dialogue with Washington.
India’s Foreign Ministry has reiterated New Delhi’s “firm commitment to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people,” saying it would continue diversifying supplies according to market conditions.
Could US-Russia trade grind to a halt?
The legislation retains a 500% tariff on goods imported directly from Russia into the US.
In practice, however, the legislation contains exemptions and gives the president considerable waiver authority. The White House highlighted that discretion while backing the bill, including the president’s authority to lift sanctions following a peace agreement.
Washington has used similar exemptions before. A 2024 ban on Russian uranium imports included waivers allowing purchases to continue under certain circumstances. Moscow subsequently imposed temporary restrictions of its own on enriched uranium exports to the US, while allowing exceptions.
What has Moscow said?
Moscow has criticized the legislation, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying the new restrictions would not achieve their stated objectives and could complicate efforts to reach a settlement of the Ukraine conflict.
”Clearly, this cannot have a positive effect,” Peskov told reporters on Saturday.
The Russian Embassy in Washington has argued that the measures could also have consequences for the US economy, particularly amid tight global energy supplies. It warned that additional restrictions on Russian exports could put upward pressure on fuel prices and said escalating economic confrontation with Russia and China would be damaging to all sides.

US prepares sweeping sanctions on International Criminal Court — report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:00:19 UTC
06:00:19 KST

The Trump administration is preparing to implement expansive economic sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), The Wall Street Journal reported.
The upcoming US penalties would prohibit most financial and commercial transactions with the international tribunal following a grace period of six to seven months, according to the newspaper.
The planned sanctions mark a significant escalation in the Trump administration’s punitive actions, shifting from targeting individual court personnel to imposing broad restrictions across the entire organisation.
Sources cited in the report indicated that Washington could finalise the executive measures as soon as this week during the UN General Assembly session or shortly thereafter.
Washington has already penalised numerous tribunal personnel, including ICC President Tomoko Akane, under an executive order issued in February 2025 that declared a national emergency over court proceedings.
The sustained campaign follows the ICC issuing arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
A State Department spokesman declined to preview any sanctions decisions, the Journal said.
Last month, the ICC strongly rejected new US sanctions targeting the court’s president and a senior lawyer in its prosecutor’s office, describing the measures as a “flagrant attack” on judicial independence.
The Trump administration has imposed the sanctions in retaliation for ICC investigations into US personnel in Afghanistan and for warrants the court issued against top Israeli officials.
The latest designations target ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, a senior trial lawyer at the Office of the Prosecutor, the Hague-based court said in a statement.

The project is currently facing legal obstacles and still requires final approval. Critics are also drawing attention to the future structure's proximity to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

Iran’s economy contracts by more than 10% during US war, official data shows
TEHRAN - Iran’s economy contracted by more than 10 per cent during the Middle East war, which began with US-Israeli attacks in late February.
The country’s gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 per cent year-on-year from late March to late June, a period known in Iran as the first quarter of the Persian calendar, according to the Statistical Center of Iran on Sept 20.
Iran has been at war with the United States since late February, when US-Israeli strikes killed the Islamic republic’s supreme leader and senior military officials at the start of a vast offensive.
The strikes sparked Tehran’s retaliation in blocking the Strait of Hormuz – causing global oil prices to surge – as the conflict spread in the Middle East.
Aside from this, Iran’s economy has long struggled with hyperinflation and devaluation of its currency, caused in large part by economic sanctions. AFP

The three-day voting in Russia's State Duma elections has ended. According to preliminary data from Russia's Central Election Commission, United Russia is receiving 57.02% of the vote after 23.39% of the protocols had been processed. The elections took place amid reports of ballot stuffing, problems with the work of observers, and cases in which voters said that someone had already voted in their place, UNN writes.
Details
According to the preliminary results, five parties are entering the State Duma. The Communist Party of the Russian Federation is receiving 13.96%, the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia – 9.34%, New People – 7.98%, and A Just Russia – 5.18%. The final results are expected to be announced no earlier than September 25.
The reported turnout exceeded 56%. According to data from remote electronic voting, United Russia received 49.06%, New People – 15.42%, and the Communist Party of the Russian Federation – 12.26%. At the same time, turnout on the federal electronic voting platform, according to Russia's Ministry of Digital Development, was 90.87%.
Reports of violations
Reports of possible violations came in from a number of regions. In particular, suspected ballot stuffing was recorded in Mari El, while in Perm there were reports of a security envelope without signatures or stamps in which 100% of the votes had been cast for United Russia.

These State Duma elections were the first since the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine. Reuters notes that a significant number of anti-war candidates were barred from participating, while the political environment in Russia remains under the authorities' tight control.

Crucial regional votes in Germany: What’s at stake for Merz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
20:33:03 UTC
05:33:03 KST

Crucial regional votes in Germany: What’s at stake for Merz?
German regional elections could have major implications for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s political future, with exit polls projecting a crushing defeat for his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and a weak showing in Berlin.
The CDU was languishing at just 20% nationwide as of last weekend, according to an INSA ‘Sunday Trend’ poll. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) remained the country’s most popular party, with 29% support. This comes despite pressure on the AfD from Germany’s domestic security agency over its alleged ‘extremist’ tendencies and efforts by mainstream parties to keep it out of government.
Merz himself has also faced widespread dissatisfaction, with 78% of respondents surveyed by INSA unhappy with his performance as chancellor.
The CDU therefore entered Sunday’s vote under considerable pressure, compounded by its electoral drubbing in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month.
First exit polls
The Left Party (Die Linke) is projected to top the vote in Berlin with 25.3% of the vote, according to exit polls. Its lead candidate, Elif Eralp, a first generation German of Turkish parentage, told cheering supporters on Sunday evening that “from today on, we will change Berlin together.”
Merz’s CDU is projected to take 19.1%, while the AfD is in third place with 16.2%, according to DW.
If the projections hold, the Left Party will be in pole position to lead Berlin’s next government – potentially for the first time since German reunification in 1990.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the AfD is projected to finish first with 37.9% of the vote in an extraordinary turnaround. Party co-leader Tino Chrupalla said the result showed that the AfD “clearly have the mandate to govern here.”
Merz’s CDU, meanwhile, is projected to suffer another major setback, securing just 5% and barely clearing the threshold for entering the state parliament. The result would be the party’s worst in any German state election since 1949. Merz has described his party's showing as a “disaster.”
Who is voting for what?
In Berlin, which is both a city and one of Germany’s 16 federal states, approximately 2.5 million people are eligible to elect the House of Representatives, the local legislature.
Voters have cast two votes: one for a direct candidate in one of 78 constituencies and the other for a party’s state or district list. The second determines the overall distribution of seats. The legislature normally has 130 lawmakers, although its size can increase through so-called ‘balancing’ seats.
Preliminary data suggest turnout in Berlin has surpassed that recorded in the previous regional election in February 2023.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, around 1.3 million people are eligible to elect the state parliament. They similarly voted for both a constituency candidate and a party list.
Sunday’s elections also marked the first time 16- and 17-year-olds had been allowed to vote in either contest.
The rising cost of living has been among voters’ biggest concerns. Some 67% of respondents in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and 56% in Berlin named it as their primary preoccupation in an Infratest Dimap poll conducted earlier this week. In Berlin, unaffordable housing also emerged as a major campaign issue.
Why do the elections matter nationally?
Sunday’s votes came just two weeks after the AfD won another eastern state, Saxony-Anhalt, with 43.8%, while the CDU finished a distant second with 17.2%.
That result intensified scrutiny of Merz’s future as leader of the party.
Table.Briefings reported earlier this week that he planned to convene the CDU executive committee on Sunday and put the question of confidence to a test. ZDF has also reported that talk of replacing Merz has circulated within the party for months, although no clear successor has emerged.
Reuters reported earlier this week, citing an anonymous government source, that the chancellor had canceled a planned trip to the UN General Assembly in New York to attend a special meeting in Berlin on Sunday.
A YouGov poll published on Thursday found that 48% of respondents expect Merz to be out of office by the end of the year.
Merz under pressure
Merz took over in May 2025 promising sweeping economic reforms and a stronger German leadership role in Europe. His coalition government, which also includes the Social Democrats (SPD), has struggled to revitalize the country’s economy.
Germany endured three consecutive years of economic stagnation and recession before GDP grew 0.3% in the second quarter of 2026. German industry has faced mounting pressure from high energy costs following Berlin’s move away from Russian oil and gas.
At the same time, Merz has committed billions of euros to an ambitious rearmament program and continued military aid to Ukraine, while calling on Germans to work more.
The regional results do not directly determine the composition of the federal government, but the CDU’s projected showing – particularly its 5% result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – could intensify debate within the party over Merz’s leadership and political strategy.

Eighteen suspects extradited to US over Haitian president’s 2021 killing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
20:31:15 UTC
05:31:15 KST

Eighteen suspects extradited to US over Haitian president’s 2021 killing
Federal court in Florida to try men accused of orchestrating the transnational plot to kill Jovenel Moise from US soil.
Eighteen suspects facing federal charges for the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise have been flown to the United States.
A military flight on Sunday transported the suspects from the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince, to the US state of Florida, where the defendants are set to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the transnational plot to kill the former leader.
The major development comes after federal prosecutors in the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida successfully secured convictions in May against what they called “gang leaders” and “co-conspirators” implicated in the scheme to kill Moise.
The high-profile investigation is being directed by US Attorney Jason A Reding Quinones, an appointee of US President Donald Trump.
“Today marks the next major phase in our pursuit of accountability for the assassination of President Jovenel Moise,” Quinones wrote on social media. “We will follow the evidence wherever it leads, to those who financed it, facilitated it, supported it or committed crimes to make it possible. Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished.”
Quinones did not immediately identify the suspects being extradited, but those who remain in Haiti awaiting trial include more than a dozen Colombian soldiers and a former Haitian government official.
Quinones said that the FBI and others “remain steadfast in ensuring that all individuals who allegedly sought profit from the assassination of a head of state are held fully accountable”, with FBI Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles confirming that multiple arrests in the US and abroad were made on Sunday.
Moise, 53, had been shot dead overnight at his private residence in the Pelerin 5 neighbourhood, in the hills above Port-au-Prince in July 2021, while his wife was critically injured. His killing caused a profound political vacuum that left the Caribbean nation devoid of any elected national leader. Capitalising on this institutional collapse, armed gangs have rapidly expanded their influence, ultimately consolidating control over an estimated 90 percent of Port-au-Prince.
At least 8,100 gang killings were documented in 2025, with insecurity displacing about 1.5 million people, according to the United Nations.
Legal jurisdiction was established by US federal courts in Florida, the closest US state to Haiti, because the overarching plot to assassinate Moise had been primarily engineered, financed, and staged out of the southern part of the state, according to federal prosecutors.
A fair trial inside Haiti had also grown increasingly impossible owing to the ongoing security collapse and entrenched graft stemming from intense gang violence, political chaos and overlapping humanitarian crises that have severely paralysed and hollowed out the judicial system.
In Haiti, prominent human rights activist and executive director of the National Human Rights Defense Network Pierre Esperance said that the transfer of the 18 suspects to the US was a “disgrace for the Haitian justice system”, and called for an overhaul of the judicial system to allow such complicated cases to be tried inside Haiti in the future.
In May, a jury in Florida convicted four men in the killing, and at least five others have pleaded guilty and are serving life sentences.
No national elections have been held in Haiti since Moise’s assassination.

Iran's top negotiator said Sunday that Tehran conveyed to Washington, through mediators, its conditions for ending its blockade of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
The two foes are locked in a stalemate, months into the conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
Tehran has maintained a stranglehold on the strait, a vital shipping route for the world's oil and gas, while Washington is pushing its own campaign to choke the Islamic Republic's ports and economy.
"Our messages and the explanation of our conditions have been clearly conveyed to the other party through mediators," said Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has acted as chief negotiator in talks to end the war.
"As long as the conditions are not met...and the US commitments are not honoured, it will be impossible to return to the situation from before the negotiations and to an open strait," he added, according to state television.
Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's supreme national security council, said on Saturday that the Islamic Republic had conveyed its conditions to the US via mediator Qatar.
"Our conditions are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade," he said in an interview with Al Jazeera.
He warned that the US would face an Iran that was better prepared than at the start of the war.
"We will confront America with greater force, and with more numerous and more painful strikes," he said, singling out US bases and US commercial interests in the region as targets for an Iranian military and economic response to any US strike.
"We are prepared for a decisive war."
The Iranian security chief said in the interview that Iran had increased the speed of its hypersonic missiles "from Mach 6 to Mach 10", as well as improved its air defences and developed "electronic warfare systems".
"Therefore, should war break out again, US ships, unless they withdraw from the Indian Ocean, will be subject to attack," he said.
Iranian authorities have said that mediator Pakistan's Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi will travel to Tehran on Sunday for talks.
Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya central military command, meanwhile, issued a threat against the United States on Sunday, in a statement carried by state television.
"We warn that if the US makes a mistake in dealing with Islamic Iran, all of that country's bases and interests in the region will become the target of continuous, effective and painful attacks, without any limit or restraint," it said.

More than a dozen arrested in connection with 2021 assassination of Haitian president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
20:17:44 UTC
05:17:44 KST

Eighteen people have been arrested in association with the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse, according to US officials.
Moïse, 53, was shot dead on 7 July 2021 at his private residence by a hired group of about 20 military-trained Colombian mercenaries. His security detail did not intervene to protect him.
“Today’s multi-location and international arrests underscore the FBI’s continued commitment to bringing all participants in this plot to justice,” FBI special agent Brett Skiles said on Sunday.
The suspects have been taken to Florida to stand trial.
In the same post on X, federal prosecutor Jason Reding Quinones said: “18 transported in military plane from Haiti to face American justice in the southern district of Florida.”
“Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished,” Quinones wrote, adding that 30 suspects have thus far been indicted in the killing.
In May, four men were convicted in a federal court in Miami of charges including conspiracy to kill or kidnap Moïse, conspiracy to provide material support and violating the US Neutrality Act to engage in an illicit military operation abroad.
The men face possible sentences of life in prison.
All four were linked to CTU, a private security firm based in Florida, and lured into the plot by the prospect of securing lucrative contracts in the event of Moïse’s ouster, according to federal prosecutors.
Eleven people have already been indicted in connection with the assassination in US courts, which have jurisdiction over plots hatched on American soil.
Five of them have been sentenced to life in prison, including a former Colombian soldier, a former Haitian senator, a Haitian Chilean businessman, a retired Colombian soldier and a Haitian American.
Haiti has descended into deeper chaos since Moïse’s killing, and currently has no president.
It is preparing to hold its first presidential and legislative election since 2016, as well as a referendum on the constitution, on 13 December – if security conditions allow.
Gangs control about 80% of Port-au-Prince, and violent crimes such as kidnappings for ransom, armed robbery and carjackings plague the impoverished nation.
A UN-backed armed force tasked with helping local police combat gangs will not be fully staffed by October as planned, its spokesperson said earlier this month.
Announced by the UN security council last year, the Gang Suppression Force was expected to ramp up between April and October to a planned capacity of 5,500 uniformed personnel and 50 civilian staff.
As of July, it comprised fewer than 1,000 personnel from Chad, Mongolia, Jamaica, Guatemala, El Salvador and Sri Lanka. More recent figures have not been disclosed.

Shein, Temu shoppers keep adding to cart despite environmental concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
20:00:24 UTC
05:00:24 KST

Ultra-fast fashion buyers feel a lack of personal responsibility despite environmental concerns
Shoppers of ultra-fast fashion companies, such as Shein and Temu, say despite being aware of environmental and ethical concerns other factors such as price, convenience and not feeling personally responsible keep them coming back.
A new study published in the Journal of Global Fashion Marketing this week found millennials, who frequently expressed concern about ethical and sustainability issues, often did not translate this concern into purchasing behaviour.
The study surveyed 20 Australian millennials who shopped on ultra-fast fashion sites about what informed their purchasing behaviours.
It found affordability, convenience, promotions, social media trends, novelty, variety and social validation were the biggest purchase drivers.
For some, affordability meant they were likely to purchase styles they may not usually try and make riskier choices.
❝
You can get five things for the price of one at other places.
— Study participant
❝
I can redo my wardrobe every season without hurting my bank account.
— Study participant
❝
It's perfect when I need something quick and cheap for an event.
— Study participant
The study also found the purchases were usually not spontaneous, with many shoppers saying they saved carts and waited for a sale before purchasing.
❝
When I see a 70 per cent off notification, it's almost impossible not to look. It feels like I'm losing money if I don't buy it.
— Study participant
❝
Sales get me every time. I've bought outfits I didn't even wear just because they were on sale.
— Study participant
❝
I add things to my cart and wait for payday or a discount notification.
— Study participant
Associate Professor in the School of Fashion and Textiles at RMIT University and study co-author Carol Tan said this behaviour was known as "strategic spontaneity".
"You think it's impulsive, but it's actually planned," she said.
"So what people do is they save the items, they have a wish list, and then they monitor their sales and wait for payday.
"It could be sitting in their cart for a week or a month, and then a spur-of-the-moment decision is when they actually make the purchase and it happens in minutes."
The fast and ultra-fast fashion gap
While fast fashion has been around for some time, platforms such as Shein and Temu differ in their production and distribution methods.
Traditional fast-fashion brands release a new collection every two to four weeks that can range from hundreds to thousands of styles and sell primarily through physical stores.
Ultra-fast fashion stores produce 2,000 to 10,000 new styles daily and use digital-only, mobile app-dominant sales models.
Dr Tan said the rise of ultra-fast fashion has pushed some fast-fashion brands to change their strategy.
"They are trying to not compete with the Sheins of the world and they are trying to go a bit more upmarket. So they sell better-quality stuff and they have like $400 jackets," she said.
Outside of the growing price gap between fast fashion and ultra-fashion fashion, Dr Tan said these sites often sold items you could not buy in brick-and-mortar stores.
Cognitive dissonance
Despite participants expressing concerns about the environmental and ethical impacts of ultra-fast fashion brands, many still continued to purchase on Shein or Temu.
According to the latest figures from the Australia Institute, on average Australians purchase 56 items of clothing a year.
It also reports more than 200,000 tonnes of clothing end up in Australian landfills each year.
The study found participants were more influenced by social and economic drivers than long-term ethical concerns.
❝
I know it's bad for the planet, but when I'm on a budget and need an outfit for Saturday, I just block that out.
— Study participant
❝
I try to buy sustainable brands, but they are so expensive. Shein is just there and it's easy.
— Study participant
❝
If the big brands are allowed to sell it, then it can't be all my fault for buying it.
— Study participant
❝
I feel bad sometimes, but one small top isn't going to destroy the ocean.
— Study participant
The study also found buyers would draw on explanations such as reduced feelings of personal responsibility, affordability constraints, limited access to sustainable alternatives and the belief that the individual purchases had little impact.
In some countries, different taxes have been introduced to deter buyers from ultra-fast fashion brands.
France has banned advertising from ultra-fast fashion businesses and introduced a fee that will rise to €10 ($16) per item by 2030. New Zealand has a levy of NZ$2.21 ($1.80) per package.
Australia has a scheme called Seamless that businesses can voluntary opt into, where they pay a 4 per cent per garment levy to promote clothing repair, rental and recycling. However, the scheme does not cover overseas retailers such as Shein.
Dr Tan said she believed focusing on cost per wear would be more influential in changing consumer behaviour.
"So if you are going to buy a $200 jacket, you are going to wear a $200 jacket, I don't know, 20 times, 30 times, 40 times. Whereas if let's say, for example, you buy a $20 jacket from Shein and it falls apart, you're only going to wear it once," she said.
"I think talking about cost per wear is really important to try to signal to customers.
"Thinking about durability and quality is going to be more convincing than trying to guilt a customer."

Scientists trace the nerve pathway that links digestion to memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
20:00:08 UTC
05:00:08 KST

A new small study in rats reveals that the digestive tract communicates with the brain during meals to help remember where food was found. The research, published in Nature Communications, shows that nutrients trigger a nerve pathway that releases a memory-boosting chemical in the brain. This biological process can be disrupted by eating a junk food diet early in life.
The vagus nerve acts as an expansive information highway between the body’s internal organs and the brain. It transmits metabolic data from the gastrointestinal tract to the central nervous system. This signaling system helps maintain energy balance and controls how much an animal eats.
Recent evidence suggests this gut-brain connection also influences higher-order cognitive functions. Sensory neurons within the vagus nerve might send messages that reach the hippocampus. The hippocampus is a brain structure that governs spatial navigation and the formation of episodic memories. In the wild, remembering the exact location of a nutrient-dense food source provides a massive survival advantage.
Researchers Logan Tierno Lauer, Léa Décarie-Spain, and Scott E. Kanoski at the University of Southern California led a team to investigate this pathway. They suspected that sensory signals from the stomach and intestines guide memory circuits. The researchers focused on a neurotransmitter called acetylcholine, a chemical messenger known to promote memory formation and brain plasticity.
The team conducted a series of experiments on male rats to track these gut-to-brain signals. First, they injected rats with cholecystokinin, a hormone released by the intestines during digestion that makes animals feel full. They then examined the rodents’ brain tissue to see how the cells reacted.
The hormone triggered a surge of cellular activity and acetylcholine release in the hippocampus. To see how the signal reached this brain area, the researchers used a targeted toxin to destroy a specific group of cells in a region called the medial septum. The medial septum is a small cluster of neurons located deep in the brain that connects lower brainstem regions to the hippocampus.
Without these medial septum cells, the gut hormone failed to trigger the acetylcholine release. This indicates the medial septum acts as a necessary relay station between the gut and the hippocampus. By acting as a bridge, it filters and passes along sensory information from the body.
Next, the researchers observed the animals as they ate a standard meal. They used specialized fiber optic sensors implanted in the brain to record acetylcholine levels in real time. This technique uses light to measure the activity of specific fluorescent biosensors injected into the brain, allowing researchers to monitor microscopic chemical fluctuations second by second.
As the rats actively ate their food, acetylcholine levels spiked in the hippocampus. This chemical elevation persisted even after the animals finished their meal and entered a resting state. Just like in the hormone injection experiment, destroying the medial septum cells eliminated this chemical spike.
The researchers wanted to find out exactly what part of the eating experience drove this brain response. They offered the rats different types of liquids to drink. They compared the effects of calorie-dense sugar water and liquid fat to zero-calorie artificial sweeteners.
Only the calorie-rich sugar and fat solutions caused the acetylcholine surge in the hippocampus. The artificial sweeteners produced no such response, even when the animals drank large volumes of the liquid. This shows that the brain is reacting to the presence of actual nutrients rather than the simple taste or the physical act of swallowing.
The team then tested the role of the vagus nerve itself. They surgically severed the vagus nerve in a group of rats to disconnect the gastrointestinal tract from the brain. These animals underwent the same series of tests as the healthy control rats.
Rats with severed vagus nerves no longer showed the acetylcholine spikes in response to the gut hormone or regular meal consumption. When analyzing the brain tissue later, the scientists found biological changes in the hippocampus. The rats with severed vagus nerves had fewer transport proteins needed to package and release acetylcholine.
Knowing that a highly processed diet can impair memory, the team investigated how poor nutrition affects this gut-brain pathway. They fed young rats a “Western diet” consisting of high-fat, high-sugar foods like potato chips and chocolate. This cafeteria-style feeding model mimics human junk food consumption better than standard laboratory fat pellets. After 30 days, these animals were switched back to a standard, healthy diet.
Despite the diet correction, these rats lost the sustained post-meal acetylcholine spike seen in healthy animals. They also failed to eat less when given the fullness hormone. Because their brains were no longer receiving or processing the satiation signals properly, the animals consumed larger meals overall. The results suggest that poor dietary choices during early development can cause long-lasting damage to nerve pathways.
Finally, the scientists tested how these biological changes affected actual memory performance. They placed hungry rats in a circular maze with several holes, only one of which contained a hidden food tunnel. After the animals learned the location of the food, the researchers removed it to see if the rats would remember where to look.
Healthy rats easily remembered the spot, investigating the correct hole over the incorrect ones. The brain sensors showed an acetylcholine spike precisely when the healthy rats investigated the correct location. This suggests the chemical release is tied to the act of encoding and updating the memory rather than retrieving it.
In contrast, rats with severed vagus nerves, destroyed medial septum cells, or a history of the junk food diet all struggled to remember the food’s location. They checked the wrong holes more frequently than the healthy rats. The brain sensors in the nerve-severed rats showed no acetylcholine spike when they stumbled upon the correct location.
Because this is a small study conducted entirely on male rats, the specific neurological mechanisms might differ in humans. Rodents process diets differently than humans do, and surgically severing a nerve is an extreme model that does not mimic natural biological decline. Additional research is needed to determine if this exact gut-brain memory pathway exists in human physiology.
Future studies might explore whether these findings apply to female animals, as hormonal differences often influence brain chemistry. The researchers note that Alzheimer’s disease is characterized by a deterioration of acetylcholine signaling in the hippocampus. While the connection is still theoretical, understanding how diet affects this system could inform future Alzheimer’s research and open new avenues for treating memory disorders related to metabolic health.
The study, “The vagus nerve promotes memory in rats via nutrient-induced septo-hippocampal acetylcholine signaling,” was authored by Logan Tierno Lauer, Anna M. R. Hayes, Andrea N. Suarez, Alexander Bashaw, Molly E. Klug, Alicia E. Kao, Robert Cheng, Jessica J. Rea, Keshav S. Subramanian, Anna Nourbash, Kristen N. Donohue, Lindsey A. Schier, Kevin Myers, Léa Décarie-Spain, and Scott E. Kanoski.

Russia’s secret plan to supercharge kamikaze drone production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Russia’s secret plan to supercharge kamikaze drone production
Documents obtained by POLITICO show a Russian state company blueprint for increasing drone carbon fiber production as the Kremlin escalates air war over Europe.
Satellite images captured in May (L) and July (R) show land adjacent to Rosatom's Alabuga-Volokno carbon fiber factory in Tatarstan's Alabuga Special Economic Zone being cleared for the expansion project. | Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre
Moscow is moving to expand its capacity to make tens of thousands of the killer drones it deploys in attacks on Ukrainian cities, according to plans from a Russian state company obtained by POLITICO.
The expansion of state firm Rosatom’s Alabuga-Volokno factory in Russia’s Tatarstan region would allow Moscow to make an additional 500 tons of military-grade aerospace carbon fiber each year by 2029. The strong lightweight material is key to building the drone’s airframe.
The production increase would translate to an additional 28,000 weaponized drones every year, according to one expert estimate — a 78% increase in production of weapons like the one that struck a passenger train on the Polish border this month and others that have left scores of Ukrainian civilians dead. Ukraine estimates Russia can currently produce more than 36,000 kamikaze drones, known as “Gerans,” annually.
Advertisement
The plans underscore Russia's commitment to weaponized drone technology to power its war machine, which it is increasingly turning against the rest of Europe.
The Alabuga-Volokno factory and its parent company, Rosatom’s advanced materials division UMATEX, are sanctioned by the U.K., U.S. and multiple other Western governments.
The factory is a key node in Moscow’s military-industrial supply chain and is the same one that received a disguised shipment of 46 tons of carbon-fiber chemicals from a Chinese-state corporation earlier this year, according to internal Rosatom shipping and customs documents reported earlier this month by POLITICO. Rosatom previously said the firm and its subsidiaries “operate in full compliance” with applicable laws and regulations.
Police experts examine fragments of a drone which targeted a commuter train, killing one and wounding eight people, in the Kharkiv region on September 18, 2026 amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. | Sergey Bobok/ AFP via Getty Images
The Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement that it was unaware of the Russian drone production expansion plans and “strictly controls exports of dual use items in accordance with law.”
Business, design and structural plans gathered from Russian sources by the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre — a Kyiv-based think tank close to the Ukrainian government — detail the factory’s expansion and schematics for its equipment and construction.
Rosatom declined to comment on the documents.
Advertisement
The U.S. House Select Committee on China has reviewed the documents and determined they are authentic, according to a U.S. government official familiar with their contents. The Ukrainian government has also reviewed the documents and confirmed their authenticity, a Ukrainian official said. Both officials were granted anonymity as they were not authorized to speak on the record.
Russia's drone war expands
In May, the Russian government approved Rosatom’s plans to build the new line at its Alabuga-Volokno factory “for the production of chemical fibers and threads” to produce up to 500 tons of carbon fiber per year, according to official approval for the construction project.
Satellite images between May and July show land earmarked for the expansion project adjacent to Alabuga-Volokno’s current carbon fiber factory in Tatarstan being cleared for construction, said the Ukrainian official. The images provided by the USCC show “proof that it is already growing,” this official said.
The foundation of the new factory “is being prepared,” said weapons expert David Albright, founder and president of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security think tank, who independently obtained satellite images of the site from August. The timeline for the factory’s completion in 2027, he said, “requires rapid construction.”
Drones allow Moscow to “launch these massive volleys and put pressure on deep targets within Ukraine at many different locations, and ensure that they can saturate the defenses,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a former adviser in the Office of the Secretary of Defense who researches drone warfare at the Center for a New American Security in Washington. “It's been a very good coercive tool and critical to Russia's deep strike campaign.”
Rosatom’s plans to grow its capacity to feed Russia’s demands to increase weaponized drone production isn’t just a concern for Ukraine as Moscow’s fifth year of all-out war drags into another winter.
Advertisement
“The expansion of Alabuga and its affiliated enterprises should be viewed not merely as a problem for the Ukrainian front, but as a long-term challenge to the security of the whole of Europe,” said Serhii Kuzan, head of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre.
Rosatom’s Alabuga-Volokno will aid this national effort. The three key reasons for expanding the factory include “import substitution of dual-use products” and “meeting the demand of Russian strategic sectors (aviation, defense industry) for carbon fiber,” according to the Rosatom documents.
The factory’s total capacity “could make 28,000 Shahed 136 drone airframes,” calculates weapons expert Albright, whose Institute for Science and International Security has conducted years of in-depth research on Russia’s drone production. Russia’s Geran-2 attack drones are based on the design of Iran’s Shahed.
“Without the carbon fiber, they can't make the drone,” Albright said. Russia “can't substitute for the carbon fiber in the drone and keep its weight down,” he explained, noting the material is used to strengthen the wing and internal structures, such as those for the fuel tank and engine.
Moscow is not getting enough polyacrylonitrile tow — a so-called PAN-precursor — used to make high-spec carbon fiber “for all their defense needs,” Albright said. Through the factory, Moscow is attempting to reduce its reliance on imports of the fibrous chemical essential to reinforcing its drones’ airframe.
Advertisement
The internal Rosatom plans show the firm intends to build a new “a modern PAN plant” in Tatarstan’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone factory complex. “The project's primary product will be UMT42S-3K grade carbon fiber,” the documents detail, to be “used in the aerospace industry.”
Metadata scraped from the document shows it was created by an employee of Russian state corporation Rosatom’s advanced materials division UMATEX at the end of last year.
Drones produced in the Alabuga SEZ complex have become a key part of Moscow’s strategy of targeting both the Ukrainian military and civilians.
“Monitoring, restricting the supply of critical components, sanctions enforcement, disrupting logistics chains and reducing the production resilience of this complex must be among the priorities of the joint policy of Ukraine and its European partners,” said USCC’s Kuzan.
“At this stage, the Kremlin’s hybrid aggression is increasingly shifting towards direct escalation, particularly through the conduct of so-called sub-threshold actions, aimed at gauging the reaction of European countries,” he said, pointing to documented violations by Russian drones of Polish and Romanian airspace. Moscow has now also added jet engines to Russia’s design of its Geran drones — allowing it to strike further and faster.
Drones manufactured in the Russian Alabuga Special Economic Zone, Kuzan warned, “are likely to become the main instrument of the Russian Federation’s future campaigns in Europe.”
Advertisement
The Russian embassy in Washington didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Europe at risk
With no end in sight for the Ukraine war and as Russia increases its attacks at NATO's eastern fringe, world leaders gather this week in New York City for the annual United Nations General Assembly.
In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov attends the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12, 2026. | Alexander Kazavok/ AFP via Getty Images
Early this month, Russia’s permanent representative to the U.N., Vasily Nebenzya, reportedly led an unsuccessful effort to remove an item titled the “Situation in the Temporarily Occupied Territories of Ukraine” from the upcoming UNGA agenda.
Revelations of the carbon fiber factory’s planned expansion mean Lavrov’s overtures should be approached with skepticism, said Nicholas Fenton, associate director for the Europe, Russia and Eurasia Program at CSIS.
The September drone attack on the passenger train close to the Polish border and a series of examples of hybrid warfare in Europe — like sabotage and other tactics that fall below the threshold of open warfare — show Moscow has “significant appetite” to escalate the conflict both in Ukraine and Europe, Fenton said.
Advertisement
“No matter the political outcome over some sort of diplomatic solution to Ukraine, we don't see Russia de-escalating when it comes to its military posture vis-à-vis NATO or vis-à-vis Europe,” Fenton said. “We believe that the current leadership of the regime in Russia is committed to confrontation with the West,” he said — even if a peace deal is struck.
At the start of September, President Donald Trump dispatched U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to Moscow and Kyiv to jumpstart a peace process. These visits reaped “substantive progress including movement on scheduling additional trilateral talks,” Witkoff wrote online afterward. Yet Russia killed five people in missile and drone attacks on Kyiv just a day after Trump's envoys left. Moscow has continued drone attacks on civilian infrastructure across Ukraine since.
“The Russians are gaining momentum in the air war, continuing to iterate these systems, continuing to expand production,” Fenton said. “There's significant concern over what might be coming.”
Graham Lanktree reported from London. Phelim Kine reported from Washington.

AfD makes gains in state elections, but has no government options
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
19:58:00 UTC

AfD makes gains in elections, but has no government option
September 20, 2026
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains in the elections in northeastern Germany and in the capital, Berlin, but is likely to remain in the opposition in both states.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) scored another election victory on Sunday evening, becoming the strongest party in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania with 37.9% of the vote, according to an exit poll by the polling firm infratest-dimap on election night.
That put the far-right party just ahead of the Social Democrats (SPD), whose dramatic comeback in the last few weeks, led by incumbent State Premier Manuela Schwesig, fell just short, with 35.7% of the vote on Sunday evening. The final results may vary as votes are counted.
The AfD was not short of confidence. Even before the first exit poll results were announced, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla told public TV network ARD, "We clearly have a mandate to govern here," before adding that the party would offer coalition talks to all the other parties.
Chrupalla also said he expected Chancellor Friedrich Merz to resign now. "That would truly be a relief for this country," he said.
The AfD also made gains in the Berlin House of Representatives — the state parliament of the German capital — but fell far short of its own expectations on election night. According to infratest-dimap, it took 16.2% of the vote, though it had been polling at 18% only last week.
AfD: 'We are the new people's party!'
With Merz's center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) suffering heavy losses in both state elections, AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel said she now sees her party as the successor to the CDU.
"We are the new people's party in Germany," Weidel pronounced to public broadcaster ZDF, before criticizing the Christian Democrats for refusing to entertain the possibility of entering into a coalition with AfD: "We are holding talks because we haven't erected any firewalls." But Weidel did not explain what the policy talks with other parties would look like.
After the AfD's triumph in the state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, it has become clear that the party — some of whose members are considered a threat to Germany's constitutional order by German domestic intelligence agencies — is struggling to find political allies.
In that election, the AfD narrowly missed securing an absolute majority of seats in the state parliament and thus cannot elect the state premier on its own. In the struggle to form a governing majority, no party currently appears willing to enter into a coalition with the AfD.
No majorities for the AfD
However, the AfD's leading candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, had made it clear that he would only lead a "stable" AfD government, ruling out a minority government tolerated by representatives from other parties. During the election campaign, he had gone even further, repeatedly stating that he would only serve as state premier in a single-party AfD government.
Since then, it has been unclear exactly what the AfD is aiming for. The AfD's national leadership appears to have a strong interest in seeing form any kind of government. This was underscored by Weidel, who said after the elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania that the AfD could take power "even in a minority government."
Weidel herself is said to have ambitions to succeed Merz as chancellor. She was already her party's chancellor candidate in the last federal election in 2025, and many top AfD officials also see her as the chancellor candidate next time round. A successfully formed AfD state government could potentially give those ambitions a boost.
However, the party's rise has also been accompanied by growing protests. In the elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, it was evident that many voters mobilized to keep the AfD's votes in check.
AfD scandals during the campaign
The party also made several negative headlines during the election campaigns: In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, one AfD candidate had to pull out of the race when it emerged that he was a convicted bank robber. Another candidate withdrew his candidacy for the state parliament when it was revealed he had a DUI conviction and could no longer hold a driver's license.
In Berlin, meanwhile, drugs and Nazi memorabilia were found in the possession of a staff member of the party's lead candidate.
In the past, AfD politicians have repeatedly drawn criticism for making positive allusions to the Nazi era. One AfD European Parliament member posed with his hand on his heart in front of Adolf Hitler's "Führer Bunker" in Berlin, while one Bundestag member described himself as the "friendly face of National Socialism."
The influential AfD state leader in Thuringia, Björn Höcke, was twice fined for using a slogan of the notorious Sturmabteilung (SA), the paramilitary organization of Adolf Hitler's NSDAP party.

Libyan committee meets to discuss deal towards holding national elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
19:51:13 UTC
04:51:13 KST

Muetaz Wannes and Mohammad Sio
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
Members of a Libyan committee met in Tunisia on Sunday to discuss implementing an agreement signed in the capital Tripoli last month towards holding national elections.
The meeting in Tunis, with four representatives each from the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity and from the eastern-based General Command, was chaired by UN Special Representative for Libya Hanna Tetteh, according to a statement by the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL).
Committee members reaffirmed their commitment to implementing the agreement and moving toward national elections that meet Libyans’ aspirations for stability and prosperity under unified and legitimate institutions, the statement said.
The committee, called the 4+4 committee, on Aug. 30 signed an agreement at the UN mission headquarters in Tripoli providing for elections to be held within 24 months.
At Sunday’s meeting, members reviewed public positions on the agreement, including support expressed by the UN Security Council and Libya’s Benghazi-based House of Representatives.
They also agreed to continue consultations with other Libyan parties in an effort to broaden support for the deal.
The UNSMIL said Sunday’s session was the ninth meeting of the smaller dialogue committee and the first since the parties signed an agreement to reconstitute the national elections commission and amend electoral laws.
A follow-up meeting is scheduled for the first week of October, the mission said.
The committee has held UN-sponsored talks since April in an effort to break Libya’s political deadlock and advance implementation of the UN roadmap, particularly on elections and unifying the executive authority.
During a formal session last Monday, Libya’s House of Representatives unanimously approved the agreement towards holding elections.
The High Council of State has yet to formally announce its position, although its head, Mohammed Takala, has rejected the agreement.
The committee’s talks followed Tetteh’s announcement during an April 22 briefing to the UN Security Council that she had been engaging with a smaller group of Libyan actors.
In August 2025, Tetteh unveiled a roadmap based on three pillars: establishing a technically sound and politically acceptable electoral framework for presidential and parliamentary elections, unifying state institutions through a new unified government, and launching a structured dialogue involving a broad range of Libyan groups.
The UN-led process is intended to move Libya toward elections and resolve the political division between the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh, which controls western Libya, and the government of Osama Hammad, appointed by the House of Representatives in early 2022 and based in Benghazi, which administers the east and much of the south.
Libyans hope long-delayed elections will end years of political and armed conflict and bring to a close the series of transitional periods that followed the 2011 overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi’s regime.

US, China open high-level talks ahead of Trump-Xi summit
Scott Bessent and He Lifeng meet in New York for US-China talks ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting later this week.
Top economic officials from China and the United States have begun talks in New York City aimed at clearing the way for possible agreements on trade, artificial intelligence and critical minerals ahead of a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping later this week.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng began talks at JPMorgan Chase’s Manhattan headquarters on Sunday morning, with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer also taking part.

The talks come four days before Trump is due to host Xi at the White House, with both sides looking to ease tensions between the world’s two largest economies.
“I’m looking forward to having focused, fulsome and constructive talks today that will set the stage for our leaders’ meeting,” Bessent told reporters as he arrived.
At the top of the agenda is a fragile US-China trade truce due to expire on November 10.

Washington is also pressuring Beijing over its supply of rare-earth magnets and other critical minerals, crucial to industries ranging from cars to advanced semiconductors.
China promised to restore the flow of critical minerals under last year’s truce, but a senior US official said on Friday that Beijing’s performance had “not been up to par”.
AI enters the talks
Artificial intelligence (AI) is also expected to feature prominently, adding a relatively new issue to negotiations long dominated by trade.
Bessent has said the countries could discuss AI “guardrails” aimed at addressing shared risks, including preventing powerful models from falling into the hands of malign non-state actors.
The talks are expected to cover both open- and closed-weight AI models. Chinese open-weight models have increasingly attracted US companies, in part because they can be cheaper than closed systems developed by US firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
“The United States remains the leader in AI,” Bessent said. “And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems.”
Another potential point of friction is Iran. China remains one of Tehran’s most important economic partners and buys much of its oil, making Beijing an important target of Washington’s efforts to increase economic pressure on Iran as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its seventh month.
Expectations remain low
Despite the packed agenda, analysts are not expecting a sweeping breakthrough.
“I think there will be some show of deliverables because of the fact that it’s a presidential summit coming, but I don’t feel like we’re on the verge of some sort of breakthrough,” Anna Ashton, a China trade analyst and founder of Ashton Intelligence, told Reuters.
“I think status quo is probably both sides’ general best expectation.”
Former US Deputy Secretary of State Kurt Campbell similarly said the immediate goal may simply be keeping tensions contained.
“One of the only things we can hope for in the short term is a truce, and that this will likely continue through the remainder of this year,” Campbell said.
Sunday’s negotiations are part of a series of meetings between Bessent, He and Greer over the past 16 months aimed at hammering out areas of agreement before Trump and Xi meet face to face.

Russia's 3-day State Duma election ends with turnout approaching 57%, says poll commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
19:39:23 UTC
04:39:23 KST

Russia's three-day election for the 450-seat State Duma ended Sunday with voter turnout approaching 57%, according to preliminary data from the Central Election Commission, with the vote counting continuing.
More than 111 million voters were eligible to cast ballots in the election, which ran from Friday to Sunday and combined voting at polling stations with remote electronic voting.
The turnout was above the 51.72% seen in the 2021 State Duma election, said the commission.
The commission had not yet released final nationwide results by Sunday evening.
Preliminary results were expected after the closure of the last polling stations, with the final distribution of the 450 seats to be determined after the counting of ballots from both the party-list and single-member district components.
Under Russia's mixed electoral system, 225 deputies are elected from federal party lists, with parties required to receive at least 5% of the vote to enter the Duma through this component.
Another 225 seats are contested in single-member constituencies.
Ten parties competed in the federal party-list vote. They included the five parliamentary parties — United Russia, the Communist Party, the Liberal Democratic Party, A Just Russia, and New People — as well as Rodina, the Communists of Russia, the Greens, the Pensioners' Party and the Party of Direct Democracy.
The Yabloko party was not included in the federal party-list ballot, but candidates nominated by Yabloko continued to contest single-member constituencies.
Voting system vulnerabilities were detected and filtered by security measures
Ella Pamfilova, the election commission chair, said the poll infrastructure had faced a large-scale cyberattack during the three-day vote.
According to Pamfilova, more than 100 million potentially dangerous attempts to affect election-related resources were detected and blocked, including attacks targeting the commission websites, the voting portal, and the Gosuslugi state services platform.
She said the cyberattacks had not been successful despite "a high level of impact" and that attempts to identify vulnerabilities in the voting system had been detected, with security filters put in place.
Pamfilova also said the commission had identified signs of Ukrainian involvement in attempts to interfere with telecommunications infrastructure.
She said attacks on the remote electronic voting system originated primarily from abroad, including from Ukraine and the UK, as well as from other countries and from IP addresses disguised as Russian.
She said Russian authorities expected further attempts to interfere with the election but were prepared to respond.
Pamfilova also said a representative of a political party had tried to introduce malware into the remote electronic voting system in Moscow, calling the incident an attempt to disrupt its operation.
Despite this unsuccessful sabotage, she said the election proceeded in line with Russian law and that voters showed a high level of involvement.
Drone attack on Moscow
Alongside the weekend elections, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said Russia had repelled the largest drone attack on the capital yet.
Sobyanin said more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted at different approaches since Saturday, including about 450 near Moscow.
He said several drones reached the territory of the Moscow Oil Refinery and one struck a residential building, adding that there were no fatalities in the incidents he described.
Sobyanin said the attack had been unprecedented in scale and appeared to have been planned with the aim of disrupting the election, but that the attempt had failed.
Defense Ministry reports mass drone and missile attacks
Russia's Defense Ministry said Ukrainian forces had attempted a mass attack on Russian territory on Saturday and Sunday using drones and Flamingo cruise missiles "to disrupt the State Duma election."
The ministry said Russian air defenses and military aviation had destroyed 1,951 attack drones and eight long-range cruise missiles over Russian regions during a 24-hour period. It said another cruise missile deviated from its course and fell in an uninhabited area.
According to the ministry, all Flamingo missiles launched toward the Moscow region were destroyed by Russian air defenses before reaching civilian facilities.
The ministry said the attack had failed to achieve its stated objectives and that Russian forces would continue and intensify strikes against military facilities in Ukraine’s capital Kyiv in response to attacks on civilian sites in Russia.
The election was the first parliamentary vote in Russia since 2022 and was held amid the ongoing conflict with Ukraine. Voting also took place in Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine, a move rejected by Kyiv and condemned by some Western governments.

Cuba fully restored its national electrical grid following an extensive blackout that shut down power across the island, state authorities announced Sunday.
Technicians reconnected the island's transmission infrastructure on Saturday evening at 7.56 pm (2356GMT), the National Electric Union said on US social media company X.
The utility said solar photovoltaic output reached 985 megawatt-hours during recovery operations, a lower volume than preceding days due to reconnection procedures. By early Sunday, power generation stood at 1,160 megawatts against a demand of 2,673 megawatts, leaving 1,510 megawatts affected.
Grid operators project peak evening electricity demand will reach 3,200 megawatts against 1,160 megawatts of available capacity, creating an anticipated deficit of 2,040 megawatts and affecting an estimated 2,070 megawatts of consumption during high-use hours.
The state utility reported ongoing boiler and unit breakdowns across several major thermoelectric generation plants, including unit eight at CTE (thermoelectric power plant) Mariel, the central block at CTE Guiteras, unit two at CTE Felton, and unit three at CTE Rente. Scheduled maintenance further idled unit three at CTE Santa Cruz and unit five at both Nuevitas and Rente facilities.
Cuba suffers from persistent electricity instability, fuel shortages, and recurring generation blackouts, which Havana attributes to deteriorating infrastructure and severe economic US blockades that restrict fuel imports, critical spare parts, and foreign investment.

18 suspects in killing of Haiti's president being extradited to Florida for trial
Eighteen suspects who were arrested in the July 2021 killing of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse were awaiting extradition to the U.S. on Sunday, marking the end of a drawn-out judicial process in Haiti for a killing that shocked the troubled Caribbean country.
The suspects will face trial in Florida, according to U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Reding Quiñones.
"Today marks the next major phase in our pursuit of accountability for the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse," he wrote on X. "We will follow the evidence wherever it leads, to those who financed it, facilitated it, supported it or committed crimes to make it possible. Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished."
Quiñones did not identify the suspects, but those who remain in Haiti awaiting trial include more than a dozen Colombian soldiers and a former Haitian government official.
Quiñones said 30 people have been indicted in Moïse's killing, with FBI Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles noting that there were multiple arrests in the U.S. and abroad on Sunday.
He said that the FBI and others "remain steadfast in ensuring that all individuals who allegedly sought profit from the assassination of a head of state are held fully accountable."
The extradition comes as the U.S. continues to prosecute and sentence multiple other suspects in the case.
In May, a jury in Florida convicted four men in the killing, and at least five others have pleaded guilty and are serving life sentences.
Those recently convicted include Arcángel Pretel Ortiz, Antonio Intriago, Walter Veintemilla and James Solages, all of whom pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors alleged the four men were among the masterminds behind the plot to kill the Haitian president. A jury found them guilty of conspiring to kill or kidnap Haiti's elected leader and providing material support for the plot.
Martine Moïse, the former first lady, was wounded during her husband's assassination. She testified in Miami federal court in March, giving emotional and at times graphic testimony about the attack inside the couple's bedroom at their Petionville home.
She also directly accused former Haitian President Michel Martelly and former Prime Minister Ariel Henry of having connections to her husband's killing. In 2024, a judge in Haiti indicted Martine Moïse on charges of complicity and criminal association. Her attorney described the charges as "ridiculous and unjust."
