Racquel has a ‘potential bomb’ in her brain. She says knowing is worse than the risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
19:27:48 UTC
04:27:48 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
As medical technology advances and our awareness of good mental and physical health grows, it's never been easier to get a diagnosis. But is putting a label on what's happening in our body always a good thing? Or can it lead to harm? Watch Insight episode 'Overdiagnosed?' at 8.30pm Tuesday 22 September on SBS or SBS On Demand.
Last year, Racquel Brunzlow went to her GP for a routine checkup and left dreading the MRI and CT angiogram tests she was asked to do.
She had told the GP during the appointment that her mum had a burst brain aneurysm in recent years, and he told her it may be hereditary. An aneurysm is a weakened area in the wall of a blood vessel that can bulge out and, if it bursts, can be life-threatening.
Racquel, who is in her 30s, then found out she also had a small aneurysm in her brain.
"I was a little anxious about it — it's not every day you get told you've got a potential bomb in your brain that could go off. Otherwise, I already knew the risk factors and what to look out for because of my family history."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
A neurosurgeon then recommended she undergo a cerebral angiogram, which is an invasive procedure that involves inserting a catheter into an artery and then injecting a contrast dye while taking X-rays.
The prospect of further testing overwhelmed Racquel, who was hesitant to investigate further.
She started experiencing panic attacks because of the anxiety surrounding her diagnosis and even went to hospital by ambulance in one instance.
"I woke up in the middle of the night with hot flashes and ... a sense of dread," she said.
"I thought I was having a heart attack."
After speaking to another neurosurgeon for a second opinion, Racquel was told the cerebral angiogram wasn't needed because she was asymptomatic.
"I don't think my life is any better for knowing," Racquel said.
"I'm still asymptomatic; I just get it looked at every other year now to check on it but otherwise, there's no need for me to know."
Can we test too much?
General practitioner Justin Coleman says doctors can sometimes be too quick to order simple tests and a diagnosis of a condition "isn't always helpful" and can "occasionally be harmful".
"Most of our work is on useful diagnoses that help the patient," he told Insight.
"But the concept of over-diagnosis is where there's a label applied that doesn't actually help the patient in any way now or in the future."
Overdiagnosis is not a misdiagnosis. An over-diagnosed patient has received an accurate diagnosis (often of a very early form of a disease), but the harms, such as side effects and financial costs from unnecessary treatments or worry where there is no need, outweigh the benefits.
Overdiagnosis is often a result of overdetection when screening or testing finds an abnormality that may never lead to health problems; another cause of overdiagnosis is overdefining — when the diagnostic criteria for what is considered abnormal expands.
A 2020 study in the Australian Medical Journal analysed routinely collected Australian Institute of Health and Welfare national data to estimate recent (2012) and historical (1982) lifetime risks of five cancers. The difference in lifetime risks of cancer diagnosis between 1982 and 2012 was interpreted as probable overdiagnosis — finding that about 11,000 cancers in women and 18,000 in men may be overdiagnosed each year in Australia.
Over-diagnosis is where there's a label applied that doesn't actually help the patient in any way now or in the future.
Coleman says good medical practice starts with doctors listening to the individual patient to understand their risks and concerns and considering the likelihood of disease before ordering tests.
"The quality comes from listening, a good history, knowing what you're asking for, knowing the background odds for that individual and making the decision on an individual basis."
To test or not to test
For six years, Naomi Ferstera was adamant she would not have a genetic test to find out her risk of developing Alzheimer's disease, despite having a family history of it.
The 44-year-old pondered taking the test when her late mother was first diagnosed seven years ago. But then she "shoved it into a corner" of her mind and reminded herself she was already doing "everything" she believed she could do to prevent developing the disease.
"There was no additional benefit in getting a genetic test that could potentially cause me duress and make me stress and worry about whether that was going to be my fate," she said.
"It was only a risk; it's not a definitive. So I parked it and went, 'No, I'm not gonna get that done'."
After seven years, Naomi has changed her mind. While she wants to get tested, she still finds it scary and believes a diagnosis is only worthwhile if there are potential treatments.
"Sometimes you're just lying in bed at night thinking about it and you go through your head, 'What would happen if I got that diagnosis?'"
"And I think that when you've seen dementia up close, particularly in someone you love, you're very motivated not to get it."
'It started to make sense'
Tore Robartson sees having his diagnoses for ADHD and autism as a "double-edged sword".
He was diagnosed two years ago with both conditions at the age of 57 after some conversations with his daughter who had received her own neurodivergent diagnosis at the time.
Tore was sceptical about the growing number of people saying they had ADHD, particularly on social media, but his own diagnosis changed how he understood his behaviour.
"This is why I think a certain way — and even interactions with people; it started to make sense," he said.
"But you can go down that rabbit hole, though, of getting too much information and trying to analyse yourself as well."
He believes that medication he has started taking as part of his ADHD treatment has made him more confident, ambitious, and productive.
But he also worries that a diagnosis can become somewhat of an excuse at times and can have an adverse effect on his behaviours.
"When you're freshly diagnosed, you take on that identity ... I always used to meet deadlines, and it was a real struggle for me to do so, but I would do it at the very last minute.
"But I kind of relaxed a bit, thinking, 'well, I've got ADHD and I've got to give myself a bit of a free pass', but it was more of a cop out."
Despite Tore's diagnosis and treatment, he doesn't identify as neurodivergent.
"I don't think of it as who I am," he said.
"It's not a label for me — it's just a condition."
'The main problem is underdiagnosis'
Professor Patrick McGorry, a psychiatrist from the Orygen National Centre for Youth Mental Health, raised concerns about increasing rates of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and ADHD diagnoses.
"I certainly think there's over-diagnosis happening in ADHD and ASD, very significant because it's down the mild end of the pool," he told SBS Insight.
But McGorry says the debate is complicated.
"On the other hand, it is a real thing and it's underdiagnosed," he said.
"ADHD and ASD are certainly underdiagnosed in the patients that I see ... they haven't got thousands of dollars to spend on access [to getting a diagnosis]."
Diagnosis isn't just a medical barcode; it's a sociological phenomenon.
He believes that while a diagnosis can be beneficial for someone seeking to understand why they are the way they are, there is a risk that people will make their diagnosis a part of their identity.
"Diagnosis isn't just a medical barcode; it's a sociological phenomenon," he said.
"But if you latch onto that identity in a way that some of these self-help groups actually do, it limits you … It disables you in some ways."
'Early testing saved my life'
For Ross Hillier, there is no question about whether he would want a diagnosis, as early testing saved his life.
Ross went to his GP when he was 42 for a general check-up and, despite having no family history of prostate cancer, was ordered to do a Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) test, which is usually for men over 50.
Ross' PSA level came back high, and he promptly saw a urologist, underwent an MRI and had a biopsy. He was diagnosed with stage two prostate cancer, which was later upgraded to stage three (meaning it was close to spreading to other parts of his body) after his prostate was removed.
"It was a complete and total surprise for me," Ross said.
The father of four is now cancer-free and believes waiting could have changed his outcome.
"If I'd waited, I think, even a few more months ... then it would've spread through the lymph nodes and spread to other parts of my body."
"It would've been a terminal diagnosis for me."

The bilateral summit—held in the French territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon, located just off Canada's Atlantic coast—comes against the backdrop of increasingly strained relations between the two nations and the United States.
Carney stated that the time had come to significantly strengthen ties with France and the European Union. His comments follow a high-profile visit to Brussels and Strasbourg, where the European Commission formally proposed granting Canada "associate member" status within the bloc.
Macron confirmed that Paris and Ottawa would work together to deepen cooperation across key sectors, including fisheries, regional security, and energy infrastructure.
Looking beyond bilateral ties, Carney proposed establishing a four-way collaborative framework involving France, Canada, the US, and China to oversee the development and governance of artificial intelligence.
The leaders delivered their remarks following a working lunch and a series of high-level meetings on the island earlier in the day.
Foundations of new Atlantic ties amid Trump's unpredictability
US President Donald Trump’s tariffs, demands for economic concessions, and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st US state have pushed Ottawa to reduce its dependence on its southern neighbour and pursue deeper economic, security, and political ties with Europe.
“This is an important moment,” Macron said on Saturday upon his arrival. He noted that the bilateral discussions "will allow us… to strengthen our bilateral economic ties and defence relationship."
Macron added that Sunday’s talks form part of broader European efforts to secure stable energy supplies as the war in Iran continues to disrupt global energy markets, stoking fears of sustained price increases for fuel and other essential commodities.
“Canada is a country with significant resources of critical minerals and rare earths. It is also a major oil and natural gas producer,” Macron said. “What we want to do is conclude agreements to secure more liquefied natural gas that can be shipped to Europe’s Atlantic coast.”
Carney’s office confirmed in a statement that the leaders discussed deepening the Canada-France partnership across strategic sectors, including aerospace, energy, critical minerals, and advanced technologies such as quantum computing, satellites, and supercomputing.
The meeting also comes in the wake of Trump’s announcement regarding a deal on Greenland that will expand the US military presence on the island while maintaining Danish sovereignty, ending months of threats by the US president to seize the semi-autonomous territory of a fellow NATO ally.
Macron publicly welcomed the resolution on Saturday.

Ukraine reveals new Operation Vivaldi gains in Donetsk Oblast
Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps said it has liberated a further 40 square kilometers (15.4 square miles) of territory in Donetsk Oblast, as well as retaking several villages during the ongoing Operation Vivaldi offensive.
"As promised, I am reporting good news," corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said in a statement on Sept. 20.
"During the second 'season' of 'Vivaldi,' the 3rd Army Corps reclaimed another 40 square kilometers of Ukrainian land. Shandryholove and Derylove have been liberated. Drobysheve is under full Ukrainian control," he said.
"It is worth noting that Shandryholove is a critical point for both our troops and the enemy," he added.
Operation Vivaldi, the corps' offensive operation around Lyman in northern Donetsk Oblast, was only made public on Sept. 15, although Russian pro-war Telegram channels and independent open-source intelligence (OSINT) researchers on social media had been tracking Ukrainian attacks in the area since late spring 2026.
Until Sept.20 the 3rd Corps had only released details on the first phase of the operation and said it had cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltrators and liberated a further 10 square kilometers.
Details of the operation from Ukraine have been sparse for operational security purposes, but Russian military bloggers have reported Ukraine pushed Russian forces back to the Zherebets River, potentially reversing over 18 months of steady Russian advances in the region.
"In accordance with the corps command's plan, the villages of Shandryholove and Derylove were enveloped from north to south — assault groups moved quickly and stealthily through ravines and gullies, ensuring the element of surprise," the 3rd Army Corps statement said.
"The units operated in close coordination — while some breached the defenses, others held the flanks along the demarcation lines, preventing the enemy from launching a counterattack. Assault groups were organized into mobile tactical units that dug into every tree line and strongpoint, burning out enemy pockets of resistance," it added.
"The operation is ongoing."
On Sept. 17, in an acknowledgment of broader operational success in the Lyman area, Biletskyi said that the "northern pincer" of Russia's attempt to surround Ukraine's hold on Donetsk Oblast had been "routed and destroyed."
A day later, the corps said Russia had pulled units of its elite unmanned systems formation Rubicon from the front line in northern Donetsk Oblast after suffering heavy losses.
The Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies is a sprawling Russian drone unit and the core of Russia's recently formed Unmanned Systems branch of the military.
The unit specializes in cutting off logistics, hunting Ukrainian drone teams on the ground, and intercepting high-value reconnaissance and strike drones, and is made up of detachments, each numbering several hundred personnel.
When deployed to priority areas of the front line, Rubicon and other units like it often create particular difficulties for the Ukrainian brigades facing them by making the existing "kill zone" deeper and deadlier, just as elite Ukrainian drone units do to Russian forces.
Effectively spotting and destroying the personnel and assets of enemy elite drone teams, equivalent to counterbattery fire in artillery terms, can thus create a major impact on the overall power balance in a given sector.

US Army awards $10.6 million contract for Ukrainian Raybird drones
The U.S. Army has awarded a $10.64 million contract to Skyeton Inc., the American arm of Ukrainian drone maker Skyeton, for Raybird reconnaissance drones and related services, according to a Defense Department statement issued Sept. 18.
The Raybird is a Ukrainian-developed fixed-wing reconnaissance drone designed for long-range missions and extensively used on the battlefield in Ukraine.
The U.S. Defense Department's disclosure said it awarded Skyteton Inc. a firm-fixed-price contract of $10.64 million covering the Raybird unmanned aerial system hardware and services.
The number of systems being purchased was not disclosed. Work locations and funding will be determined with each order, with completion of the contract expected by Dec. 15, 2026.
According to Skyeton, the drone is capable of remaining airborne for up to 24 hours and can travel as far as 2,500 kilometers (1,550 miles). The company says Raybird systems have logged more than 350,000 combat hours since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion. It also estimates that intelligence gathered using Raybird drones has helped to destroy billions of dollars worth of Russian military equipment.
The company has recently been a target itself. A Russian attack on Kyiv on May 14 destroyed Skyeton's office, though the company said its production had already been dispersed across facilities in Ukraine and abroad, allowing drone deliveries to the military to continue.
In August, Slovak police detained three foreign nationals over an alleged plot to set fire to a Skyeton drone factory in Slovakia. A company representative told the Kyiv Independent that Russian actors had repeatedly attempted to target its production facilities and reputation.
The U.S. purchase comes as Washington assesses how to incorporate lessons from the Ukrainian battlefield, where drone technology has evolved rapidly and changed how the war is fought.
Earlier in September, the U.S. Army ended the specialization of an approximately 600-member drone warfare unit less than a year after it was created within the Europe-based 173rd Airborne Brigade, returning it to a conventional airborne infantry role.
Lawmakers from both parties objected, warning that shutting down the experimental unit could weaken the military's ability to learn from Ukraine's experience.
The Army has continued integrating drones and related tactics elsewhere. Ukrainian personnel recently embedded with U.S. forces during the Saber Junction military exercises in Germany, where American troops used roughly 1,900 drones while practicing maneuvers shaped by what Ukraine has learned.
read also
No tanks, lone soldiers — Ukraine details new Russian assault tactics 
Russian assault tactics have changed over the past year, with troops now attacking in groups of just a few soldiers, or sometimes individually, in an effort to get through the "kill zone," Joint Forces Task Force spokesperson Viktor Trehubov said on Sept. 20.
Small groups or individual soldiers who make it past the "kill zone" hide in cove and wait for the others to follow in order to start planning how to assault further in more organized groups, Ukrainian news agency Ukrinform cited Tregubov as saying.
He said that Russian troops are reducing the number of soldiers they send on assaults each time, struggling with the "kill zone" on the northeastern front.
The statement comes as marching through the stretch of land between the rear and the front lines becomes deadlier than ever due to both sides' advancement of drones. Both sides are now trying to reduce the number of soldiers in each group to make it harder for drones to spot them.
The prevalence of drones from both sides has significantly changed assault tactics, making heavy equipment such as tanks a rare sight on the battlefield.
With the "kill zone" reaching 20 kilometers (12.4 miles), Russia has largely stopped using tanks or other heavy equipment for assault operations, according to Tregubov. Drones have replaced many of the tanks' roles for both sides, since driving a tank close to the front would be easily spotted and hit by much cheaper drones.
Ukrainian mechanized brigades also told the Kyiv Independent this spring that their tank crews rarely deploy in the current drone-dominated phase of the war.
"So, under our current conditions, tanks have gradually moved not just to the back seat, but to the third row," Ukrinform cited Tregubov as saying on television.
The only exception, he said, is when Russia can afford to provide "mass drone support" to send tanks into the "kill zone" or if the weather is unsuitable for Ukrainian drones to fly, such as during rain or fog.

Ukraine and Hungary have a rare moment of cooperation, agreeing to build fuel storage beyond Russia’s reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
19:04:17 UTC
04:04:17 KST

Ukraine’s Naftogaz has signed a memorandum with Hungarian energy company MOL to build fuel storage facilities in Hungary near the Ukrainian border, creating additional reserves outside the reach of Russian strikes.
Acting Naftogaz CEO Sergiy Fedorenko said the project will diversify fuel supply routes and provide storage capacity outside areas exposed to Russian attacks. He said this could make fuel supplies more reliable for Ukrainian consumers while also expanding cross-border energy infrastructure.
The agreement was announced during the Carpathian Economic Forum, held as part of the first summit of the Carpathian Eight regional cooperation format.
Why Ukraine needs fuel storage outside the country
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s fuel infrastructure, including oil and gas production facilities, filling stations, and other sites needed to supply fuel across the country. These attacks increase in the lead up to and during winter months, where the impacts on civilians are especially severe.
Naftogaz said Russian attacks destroyed 37 of its filling stations during the first seven months of 2026. The company said fuel availability is particularly important for emergency services, medical teams, public transport, and communities near the front line.
Russia has also attacked Ukraine’s oil and gas production facilities. In August, Naftogaz said a major Russian attack damaged seven Ukrnafta production facilities and forced some of them offline, reducing oil and gas production.
Storing fuel in Hungary would give Ukraine additional reserves beyond the reach of these attacks and another route for bringing petroleum products into the country if domestic infrastructure is damaged.
Fedorenko said the agreement could make fuel supplies to Ukrainian consumers more reliable while supporting the development of energy infrastructure connecting the two countries.
Ukraine-Hungary ties improve
The deal comes as Kyiv and Budapest have begun rebuilding relations following years of tensions under former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
Péter Magyar replaced Orbán as Hungary’s prime minister in 2026, and the new government has moved toward closer cooperation with Ukraine, although major disagreements remain.
In June, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the relationship as entering a “new page” after Kyiv and Budapest reached an agreement addressing longstanding disputes over the rights of Hungary’s ethnic minority in Ukraine.
The two countries have since continued talks on normalizing relations. In September, the relationship was showing tentative signs of improvement, including progress on minority-rights issues and preparations for a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Magyar.
Energy cooperation has already featured in the renewed dialogue. During a Ukrainian government visit to Budapest in 2025, the two sides discussed Hungarian participation in modernizing Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and agreed to continue economic cooperation.
The improvement in relations has not eliminated disagreements. Hungary continues to block progress on parts of Ukraine’s EU accession process, citing concerns over the rights of Hungary’s ethnic minority in Ukraine.
The planned fuel-storage facilities therefore mark a practical area of cooperation between the two countries at a time when Russia’s attacks are making secure fuel supplies increasingly important for Ukraine.

JOHANNESBURG, Sept 20 - South African investigative journalist Micah Reddy has gone missing in Djibouti while on a reporting trip, his family said on Sunday, adding that they have received no information from authorities about his whereabouts since he was last heard from on Saturday.

Micah was staying at the Escale International hotel in Djibouti's capital and was last known to have met Mahmoud in the hotel lobby, according to his family. Relatives said the hotel had provided little information about his movements after he was last seen.
Niall said his brother had not reported any threats before the trip and was not investigating the Djiboutian government during his visit.

Hacking this BYD was too easy. It didn't even have a password
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
19:00:56 UTC
04:00:56 KST

On a narrow country road outside Canberra, I'm driving a BYD Shark 6, the hybrid ute loved by tradies and even a cabinet minister.
But while I'm at the wheel, I'm not the only one in control; a hacker has access to the car.
As the 2.6 tonne ute rounds a bend, he gets to work.
Loading...
With the stroke of a key, he kills the headlights, plunging me into darkness.
The attack is not a total surprise. The Shark has spent the past two weeks with Dan Hreszczuk, a cybersecurity expert who specialises in cars.
His task was to hack the vehicle and find out what could be seen and done remotely by the Shark's Chinese manufacturer.
"It was easier than we were expecting," Hreszczuk says.
Modern connected cars, particularly EVs and hybrids, are increasingly run by software, giving manufacturers the power to change, update and control vehicles, like never before.
In the case of BYD and others, that software is controlled from China.
With fuel prices on the rise, EVs and plug-in hybrids like the Shark have gone mainstream this year, making up almost a third of new cars sales to date. More than half of these are from Chinese brands.
EVs, with all their sensors, cameras and microphones, hoover up and spit out vast amounts of data. Experts say that data poses a greater risk in the hands of Chinese EV makers because they can be compelled by the country's national security laws to co-operate with authorities.
To put this potential access to the test, it made sense to pick a model from China's top EV brand, BYD.
Hreszczuk, the co-founder of Fortify Labs in Canberra, was stunned by the BYD Shark's lack of cybersecurity.
"The access we took advantage of didn't even have a password," he says.
"It's a little bit scary how open … the BYD Shark is to a hacker."
This lack of a password allowed Hreszczuk to access the car's digital arteries.
From there it was a matter of unpicking the software programs which controlled different functions in the car.
After two weeks, Hreszczuk was ready.
Sitting by the side of the country road, he demonstrates what can be done with remote access to a vehicle.
First, he locks the doors while I'm inside, blasts music over the speakers and plays images on the BYD's giant infotainment screen.
Then, as I drive, he remotely switches the wipers on at top speed, sprays the windscreen with water and turns the lights on and off.
Loading...
The combination is unsettling and highly distracting.
Adding to the distraction, Hreszczuk has the speaker telling me repeatedly: "For safety, use low beam."
Fortunately, I was only travelling 30 kilometres per hour and the road was pretty straight.
Then, Hreszczuk kills the lights altogether.
Hreszczuk says he wasn't able to access more critical functions like brakes and cameras as these were well protected.
But it doesn't take much imagination to understand how dangerous, even this kind of access could be in the hands of a malicious actor, with a vehicle travelling at high speed on a winding road.
Surveillance
While sabotage is one worry, the concern most often cited is surveillance due to the array of cameras and microphones on an EV.
Last year, the UK military banned Chinese EVs, even those made with Chinese components, from parking within 3 kilometres of some of its most sensitive locations.
China itself has previously banned foreign EVs from military sites and political enclaves, aware of their surveillance potential.
In Australia, there's no blanket ban on Chinese marques by Defence, but ASIO has warned ministers and public servants not to have sensitive conversations in their cars or connect work devices.
But there's nothing to stop them owning a Chinese EV.
Trade Minister Don Farrell has a BYD Shark 6, the same vehicle that Hreszczuk hacked.
Farrell recently told a newspaper it's the "best ute I've ever owned".
ASIO's surveillance fears appear well founded, based on what else Hreszczuk is able to do to with the Shark even at a low level of access.
We devise a demonstration: I'll take the BYD for a drive around Canberra, and give my mother a call to talk her through some internet banking.
As I drive past the war memorial and down Anzac Parade, Hreszczuk has already remotely accessed the vehicle and is tracking my progress.
Then he gets to work.
"How about we turn on the microphone?" he suggests to the crew back at his lab.
At that point Hreszczuk can hear everything.
"Hey Siri," I say to my iPhone.
"Call 'mum mobile'."
When she picks up, I'm straight into the details of how I had set up her internet banking.
"I'm going to use as a temporary password, my initials, the number of my house, and then my full date of birth. And then you can go in later and change it if you want," I tell her.
Back at the lab Hreszczuk records the whole conversation.
The key is he's now got a recording of me saying, "Hey Siri".
When I pull into a service station and leave my phone unlocked in the car, Hreszczuk seizes his opportunity.
He's done a simple audio edit, stitching together me saying "Hey Siri" and his voice asking a few questions to get the personal details he needs.
Using the car's speaker system, Hreszczuk plays the voice command from his computer into the car.
"Hey, Siri, what is my home address?" the edited audio asks.
Siri replies, without questioning why I don't know where I live.
Hreszczuk repeats this process and quickly extracts my date of birth and age.
Within minutes, he's obtained the internet banking password.
Hreszczuk keeps fishing.
"Let's try and grab a few of his contacts. Let's see if he knows a prime minister.
"Hey Siri, tell me the phone number from my contacts for Malcolm Turnbull."
Once again, Siri dutifully delivers.
Hreszczuk's hacking challenge was made easier because Australia has no minimum cybersecurity standards for cars. That means BYD is not compelled to keep its software up to date or have a system for managing cybersecurity risks to its vehicles.
"I didn't need to pick the lock as BYD left the front door open," he says.
"I think people overlook a lot of these concerns for the convenience. It is a beautiful car to drive. It looks beautiful inside, but there are real security concerns."
Surprisingly, Australia has more cybersecurity regulation around connected washing machines or vacuum cleaners than cars.
Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke defends this, saying the government has started by putting regulations around connected devices in the household.
"You want to first regulate where you will get the fastest uplift and … you also want to focus first on where the cyber attacks have principally been," he says.
The government has just started consultations with industry to introduce new cybersecurity and software rules for cars in Australia, but they likely won't be in force for years.
Alastair MacGibbon, Australia's former national cyber security adviser, says there needs to be greater protections for the data collected by all connected cars, and clearer rules about what data can be sent overseas.
MacGibbon says a cabinet minister should not be able to own a Chinese EV.
"China has always shown its strong desire to steal things, to surveil," he says.
"No-one should be in any doubt that [Chinese EVs] are used in the same manner.
"The real question would come down [to]: Could they cause harm with these vehicles? The capability is definitely there.
"Is the intent? I don't know."
Opposition Defence spokesman James Paterson says Australians' data needs to be better protected.
"A connected EV vehicle from China is the highest-risk product in the marketplace. And right now, there's nothing that says to that brand what data you can collect on Australians, how it can be stored, when it can be transmitted."
BYD says the data it collects is stored in Australia. It says it has not and would not hand over the data of Australians to Chinese authorities.
Watch Four Corners' full investigation, Asleep at the Wheel, tonight from 8:30 on ABC TV and ABC iview.

Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:56:45 UTC
03:56:45 KST

Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic.
In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East.
Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that if an attack does take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”.
Iran’s leaders also pledged some of the reprisals could extend as far as US naval forces in the Indian Ocean, and accused some Gulf leaders of “double-dealing” by allegedly giving a green light to the US attacks.
The outburst of sabre-rattling appears to have been prompted by attacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The barrage on Saturday marked the first time the capital’s Aramco oil facilities had been subject to such a sustained attack since the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire broke down in June. Riyadh insisted it had intercepted the missiles, but local photographs show smoke pouring from the Aramco facility. The port of Yanbu, vital for Saudi oil exports, was also targeted.
The US largely regards the Houthis as a proxy Iranian force and argues that the group’s attacks on Riyadh would not happen without Tehran’s approval, a claim Iran denies.
Trump last week provoked profound questions about the level of US commitment to its Middle East allies when he spurned a call by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking the US to come to Saudi’s direct military help.
The Saudis wanted US aid after the Houthis suddenly captured strategic ports along Yemen’s west coast overlooking the Red Sea, giving the Houthis control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway that takes commercial shipping through the Red Sea towards Asia.
On the other side of the Arabian peninsular, the strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman is already effectively closed to western traffic and the pressure on European energy supplies is growing by the day, leading states such as France to take emergency measures to prevent fuel shortages.
In an attempt to keep the US out of its war with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis had given commitments to US officials that they would only target Saudi-related shipping in the Red Sea, a commitment that Trump appeared to regard as sufficient to ensure essential US interests would be protected and that the US need not become involved militarily.
Pressure on the Pentagon budget and dwindling munitions supplies due to the Iran conflict have also made the US reluctant to broaden the theatre of war. Successive bombing campaigns have not dislodged the Houthis, whose lighting advance to the Red Sea coast took the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces by surprise.
Trump appeared to disregard the wider security threat by telling Fox News: “The US is in constant contact with the Houthis and they have agreed not to go to war with the US.”
The Houthi government said 318 ships passed through the strait from 10-18 September.
France will summon Iran’s ambassador after Iranian authorities closed a French-language centre affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, the foreign ministry said on Sunday.
The Iranian judiciary accused the centre of conducting “illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions”.
The French foreign ministry said: “This new attack on the French cultural presence in Iran … is unjustifiable and unacceptable.”
Trump is due to meet the six member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council when he attends the UN general assembly in New York, in a meeting that is likely to cover Iran, Yemen, Gaza and the future of the US security guarantee.
Trump said he was also open to a meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York, an encounter that would probably be rejected by the Iranians, who refuse to negotiate directly with the US, operating instead largely through mediators.
Pezeshkian is one of many world leaders due to address a general assembly that is likely to be dominated, on the sidelines at least, by Trump’s Middle East crisis.
In the first sign of a potential change of White House thinking about renewing US military action, the state department issued a security alert on Saturday to US citizens across the region warning that “the security environment remains complex with potential for unforeseen escalation. American citizens in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance.”
Hizam al-Assad, a member of the Houthi political bureau, said the attacks on Riyadh are a response to “hundreds of airstrikes that Riyadh had carried out against the people of Yemen”.
In a lengthy statement to parliament on Sunday, Mohammad Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, insisted that Iran was not interested in waging a forever war with the US. But the new secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, a hardliner, told Al Jazeera that Iran’s seven preconditions for peace – which include the US lifting its blockade of Iran oil ports, the restoration of its frozen assets and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports – remained.
Rezaei also expressed his anger with the Gulf states, saying they had been invited to a meeting in Salahah in Oman last week to approve the agreed Oman-Iran plan for a new authorised shipping route through the strait of Hormuz, but Saudi Arabia rejected attendance.
He said: “We invited them to the Salahah meeting and they reciprocated with a secret meeting in Germany with US Central Command and Israel.”
Despite the Houthi victories last week, forces allied to the UN-recognised government of Yemen claimed to be pushing back against the Houthis across the country with 75 Houthi soldiers killed on Saturday alone.

SCG madness and Plugger's point: The Swans-Bombers prelim, 30 years on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:52:44 UTC
03:52:44 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
SCG madness, Lloyd taken to hospital and Lockett's point: The Swans-Bombers prelim, 30 years on
When Dale Lewis recalls being at the Sydney Swans in the 1990s, it certainly was not all about big games and big crowds.
"We're training, doing preseason out of the showgrounds next door [to the SCG] and one of the days, the Big Day Out was on at these showgrounds. We had to walk the oval, arms linked like we're in a search party checking for needles and shit in the grass before we trained," he says.
"The Swans weren't popular. We were having crowds of 5,000 people. I jumped the fence one day to get the footy for a boundary umpire.
"I've got a great mate … his brother used to come, and he used to love it because he could sit anywhere, and he cracked the shits when we started getting good because he had to go buy a ticket and couldn't get a decent seat and sit where he wanted to."
It all changed in the mid 1990s, when the Swans went from the basement to the penthouse.
With three straight wooden spoons between 1992 and 1994, they went from winning one game in 1993 to four wins in 1994 and eight wins in 1995, then a surge to 16 wins and top of the ladder in '96.
A finals win over Hawthorn put them in a home preliminary final against Essendon at a heaving SCG, 30 years ago today.
Swans utility Troy Luff had gotten his opportunity that season. Originally from Traralgon in Victoria, he grew up attached to a footy like most kids, then he and his family moved to Nelson Bay near Newcastle.
He was spotted while kicking goals for fun in the Hunter, but struggled to make a mark with the Swans under Ron Barassi.
Then new coach Rodney Eade changed everything as Luff became a permanent fixture in the side.
"It was more excitement rather than pressure," Luff says.
"If we lose, we lose. We got this far, but everyone just went out there and enjoyed themselves, and the results came our way."
Lewis agrees.
"None of us saw it coming, but by Christ it was addictive once you started to win, especially at home," he says.
"Because I think that was the year we started. We ended up winning 22 or three in a row at the SCG as the run got going. You started to get a feeling about it.
"And once we'd beaten Hawthorn in that first qualifying [final], the expectation was why not?"
In 1992-93, the Swans lost 26 games in a row.
Lewis, drafted against his preferences in 1990 by Sydney, was out the week they broke the run against Melbourne and ended up playing in 33 consecutive losses. He tried to leave Sydney in 1994, but ended up staying.
In 1995, a series of important arrivals arrived, none bigger than the famous bookends, Paul Roos and Tony "Plugger" Lockett.
The former St Kilda superstar Lockett had won his third Coleman Medal (and first in Sydney) in 1996, booting 114 goals in the home-and-away season.
Former Fitzroy key position player Roos brought skill, leadership and experience.
Now they and the Swans were a win away from a grand final.
The game
It was fierce, frantic footy early doors. Not a heap of composure was shown, with lots of scrubby kicks under pressure, aiming for territory rather than accuracy.
Early in the game, Essendon was looking for James Hird, who - along with Michael Voss of the Brisbane Bears - would win the Brownlow Medal two days later. Hird kicked long from 60, and Steven Alessio marked before converting from 20 out.
Soon after, Lewis marked, then tripped over Hird and was crunched in a tackle. Hird grabbed the ball and scored. Swans fans were livid, but Essendon led by two goals.
The Swans tried kicking to Lockett, but Essendon cleared – their movement was better, and Hird earned a free on 50. He went long, Justin Blumfield came down with it and ran around to kick Essendon's third.
Sydney could not take a trick. Lewis grabbed the ball in the centre square and quickly went long again in Lockett's direction; in the end, Jason Mooney kicked a point to make it 3.1 to 0.1.
Hird came off the ground with blood streaming from his left cheek after he and Andrew Dunkley contested a ball, the Swans defender roughing the Bombers star as he lay on the ground with Dunkley on top of him.
A Barry Young point extended the lead, then Gary O'Donnell took possession and went long to Che Cockatoo-Collins, who marked and drilled it from inside 50. Seven minutes left, Bombers by 25.
The Bombers were dominating clearances, and Damien Hardwick set up Mick Symons for a contested mark, but his kicking radar was off. The Swans' forward forays were like chaos balls compared to the Dons.
Another series of points, then Wade Chapman marked a Stuart Maxfield kick near horizontal at half-forward. His kick came, and Lewis drifted in from the side for a great mark. He kicked it, and the Swans trailed by 19 at quarter time.
"Part of your job is to kick goals and everything else, but to take a big mark," Lewis says.
"That was in front of the Ladies Stand too, I think. A mad, mad Swans house there. Always nice to do that."
Luff says the Swans had built up confidence during the season.
"There was never an attitude of, 'Oh geez, they've got three goals on us, we're going to lose this.' We were like, 'No, no, we'll get that back.'''
Tough night for Essendon's Lloyd
On the Essendon side of things, forward Matthew Lloyd was playing a prelim in game 16 of his career, at just 18 years old.
Drafted at 16, thanks to a one-off change of the rules due to draft concessions for the new Fremantle side, Lloyd was highly touted.
He kicked three on debut against the Crows in 1995 before playing a couple of finals as a schoolboy.
In 1996 he kicked another seven against Adelaide, and then just before finals he booted three against the Swans at the MCG.
"I was playing local footy in 1993, Western Jets in '94, and then suddenly I'm playing as a 17-year-old in '95. So yeah, it all happened so fast, but I was very driven," Lloyd says.
"[The focus] was all footy, footy, footy. I was 78 kilos, and I actually ended my career at 92 to 94 kilos.
"So I was out of my depth physically. I did kick three on debut, and I kicked three in the first [1995] final, so I had some good moments."
Fast-forward to the prelim in 1996; it was a different story.
"I just felt like the SCG, where I hadn't played before, the crowd was on top of you, it was loud, and it was physical," Lloyd says.
"I was a very nervous type. I had a big fear of failure. I wasn't able to get my hands on the footy; it was more the atmosphere in that stadium and some big Sydney players too that I was playing on [that was intimidating]."
In the second quarter, Sydney was trying to hit back, and narrowed the gap through goals to skipper Paul Kelly and Daryn Cresswell. The lead was four points.
Lloyd was scrambling to make an impact. Nearly halfway through the quarter, a big Mark Harvey kick was bouncing towards the boundary at half-forward.
Mark Bayes and Hird were running one way, and Lloyd was racing out of forward 50. As Lloyd recalls, what happened next was "quite innocuous" as he tried to bump Bayes.
"You bump someone, and instead my elbow came back into my side. It took my breath away, and I felt winded. I played out the rest of the second quarter, but I felt like I was deteriorating health-wise," he says.
A review of the video does not suggest there was a huge problem – Lloyd kept launching himself into packs, although if you were keeping your eye on him rather than the ball, he was taking longer to get up each time.
"It's all a bit of a blur for me because I remember I couldn't concentrate; I couldn't really take in the half-time address [from Kevin Sheedy]," he says.
"I was losing colour in my face and body. I said to the club doctor, 'I'm not feeling very well', and they decided to have me start the third quarter and see how I was feeling after five minutes.
"I'm not sure how long I was in the third quarter where I eventually came off … but they knew to get me to hospital at that point."
Lloyd went to emergency at a Kings Cross hospital.
"I just remember lying there still in my full Essendon kit of the football jumper, the shorts, socks, and boots I presume, and just pain, just in so much pain," he says.
He was given morphine, and the pain subsided a little.
"They asked me to hop, and I hopped, and I said, 'I actually feel a bit better,'" he says.
"I can't remember what they thought it could have been, but they said, 'He's right to go back to the hotel.'"
Swans making a run
Back at the SCG, things were improving for Sydney.
After those two early goals, the Swans sensed an opportunity. Derek Kickett kicked from the right pocket to the square for Lockett to mark and goal. The crowd erupted and Sydney led by two with 9:26 left in the half.
Another scrambled ball was toed toward goal by Lockett, only for Sean Denham to palm it away like a goalkeeper.
Somehow Lockett got it out to Luff, who kicked the goal and Sydney led by eight. It was pandemonium at the SCG.
"From memory, he burst through and pushed someone out of the way, then handballed it to me at the top of the square and I snapped the goal," Luff recalls.
"And you just get pumped; it helps you keep building from moments, whether it's a good tackle or a good spoil [or a goal]."
Misses by Barry Young and Hird brought the margin back to six.
The play was getting faster and more chaotic, and the ball pinged in and out of 50 for Sydney. A kung-fu style kick from Luff found Greg Stafford, who ignored a furious Plugger before Cresswell snapped his second. Swans led by 12 at half-time.
Early in the third, a Lewis kick found Lockett near the point post – he marked then stumbled and fell over. His kick hit the post.
On the ABC Radio broadcast, commentator Peter Longman said: "He's done some good things, Lockett, but if he were a racehorse they'd be checking him out behind the barriers and declaring him a non-starter, I feel sure."
Teammates knew Lockett was in pain.
"An 80 per cent Plugger is better than not having him in the side at all, even 70 per cent Plugger. He was just that good," Luff says.
The back-and-forth continued, with a kind of stalemate.
Luff snapped over his shoulder, but it bounced out 15 metres wide of the posts. Luff then got the tap to Kelly, who took two steps and snapped for a Sydney goal. Cue huge chants from the red and white faithful.
"I started in defence when Paul Roos was injured. I'd play centre-half-back. Andrew Dunkley was injured, I'd play full-back. Plugger was out, I'd play full-forward. So I just played any role the team needed [including ruck]," Luff says.
There were 41,731 at the SCG that night – and they were totally fired up, making the noise of a much bigger crowd.
"David Murphy used to tell me before that year, 50,000 people, you can just hear your teammate. [With a] 75,000 crowd, you can barely hear your teammate," Lewis says.
"Anything over 85, 95,000, you can't hear your teammate, and you can't even feel yourself get hit. Such is the noise and the adrenaline; you don't even know what's happening.
"The messaging was always, [finals are] going to be quicker, it's going to be faster, it's going to be harder. And none of it's bullshit."
Just when Swans fans might have been feeling a little confident, the Bombers had a forward 50 stoppage; the tap went to Harvey, and then O'Donnell, who kicked from 35 and the lead was 13 points.
But Sydney went down the corridor, and Lewis marked. A huge roar greeted his goal, and a fan leapt the fence and ran next to the umpire to do a tandem goal signal. He then got out of there quick-smart.
At 19 points down, the Bombers were not done. Dean Wallis marked in the pocket, then Sydney gave away 50. Dunkley was in the umpire's face – Wallis goaled, then confronted the Sydney full-back.
The Bombers won the next clearance, and Alessio found Hird in the square to score. With 3:00 left in the term, it was a seven-point game.
In the final minute, Alessio marked around 50 – and converted. A quarter to go, Sydney led by a solitary point, 8.7 to 8.6.
"I remember Rocket (Rodney Eade) just saying that we needed to shut that down at the start of the last quarter, not go out and try and kick a goal," Luff says.
"If they got the first goal, they've kicked four in a row, and they may have gone on with it. But if we just shut that momentum down, play a bit defensive to start with, then once the game settles, then we [can] go out and attack."
Only three of the 16 goals kicked had been to the left-hand end. The Bombers would be kicking to that end in the final quarter.
Early on, O'Donnell fed Che Cockatoo-Collins, who burst down the right. His kick found Hird, and the Essendon champion slowed, then raced forward and snapped. The umpire scampered around. The Bombers had their early goal.
With 18:27 left, Essendon led by five. Everyone was tiring, and play was largely stuck between the arcs. Time ticked slowly; after a series of misses it was 9.9 to 8.9.
The tension was rising. Essendon's Denham might have cracked a rib; Sydney's Michael O'Loughlin hurt his knee. He came off and returned, still limping.
From a boundary throw 40m out, Harvey handballed to a running Symons.
ABC's Peter Longman was left incredulous:
"He's put it through! The Bombers lead by 12 points! Symons, a duffer from a standing start, has a checkside kick from 35m out and he's put it through – and he might have put the Bombers into the grand final next week!"
The Bombers led by 12, 4:09 on the clock.
The final minutes
Lewis had a sick feeling, wondering if this was how it would finish.
"Something you've wanted so bad as a kid, as a senior footballer, as an AFL player, it's within your grasp, but you can't touch it … It hits you in the gut real hard. I'm not going to lie to you, that was a shit feeling when he kicked that one," he says.
The runner told Lewis to drag Hird to full-forward because Sydney needed goals.
"So I hightailed it out of there," Lewis recalls.
Essendon hacked it forward; Adam Heuskes cleared to Kelly. He found Maxfield, who was chased through the middle, taking two bounces as the roar built. A kick from 60 to Hird and Lewis – and Lewis grabbed it and kicked the goal. Six points, 2:48 left.
It got even more frantic, the ball stuck in the middle. The Swans cleared, and it went to Simon Garlick, then Chapman, then Maxfield to Lockett, who played on but didn't go for goal, opting to kick inside to Cresswell. Cresswell marked then lay down, cramping.
He got up and kicked it, and with 89 seconds left, the scores were level.
Cresswell raised his arms skywards. The Sydney Airport curfew was still half an hour from kicking in, but the roar erupting would have matched a take-off from Mascot.
The clock ticked down, a ball-up with 1:02 left, no real progress.
The play was ferocious as players collided. The ball went inside 50; Swans couldn't mark. Blumfield cleared it desperately, and Chapman marked to the right of the centre square. He back-pedalled, then kicked high to the left side of 50.
From stage right came Tony Lockett to pluck it from the sky and draw every single decibel from surrounding suburbs with 17 seconds left.
He was 52 metres from goal, with an injured groin, and no other options. The clock ran down.
"The video shows me walking past him as he's about to line up to take the shot. I've just turned around to him and said, 'All you have to do is get it over the line. Doesn't matter what it is, just get it over the line,'" Luff recalls.
The siren's gone, the crowd's collective blood pressure had spiked into the stratosphere, but Plugger had it.
Loading...
Everyone watched the ball fly towards goal. Was it there? A point was enough; out on the full or short meant extra time.
The roar gathered. The umpire fired out one finger to signal a behind, and absolute bedlam ensued at the SCG. The Bombers were distraught. The Swans were ecstatic.
It was over. Two seasons removed from the wooden spoon, the Swans were in their first grand final since South Melbourne's infamous "Bloodbath" decider against Carlton in 1945.
Lewis recalls the feeling when Lockett took the grab.
"Call it presumptuous, but the moment he marked it, I knew we were going to play in a grand final," he says.
What about Plugger's groin, the distance, the pain, the effort required?
"None of it became relevant because he's Tony Lockett," Lewis says.
"We would pick him from anywhere, any angle, any distance. Because that's what he does. Not only was it his job, but the belief we had in him when he had the ball in hand, kick a goal or convert and finish was just amazing."
The aftermath
Luff was quick to the party.
"We're like, 'That's going to score.' And then the excitement hit us. And I was one of the first ones to jump on Plugger, and then everyone else just piled on top," Luff says.
"And what I do remember is Plugger on the bottom going, 'Get off me, get off me.' He was so sore from his groin that everyone jumping on didn't help his cause.
"Then [we] got up and we're like, 'We're in the grand final. We're in the grand final.' It was ecstatic. It was fantastic."
Lewis turned to Stafford in the square to find he was already off running.
"I get in a bit late on the pile on, and all I can do is pat a few blokes … because I was too busy celebrating down the goal square looking for a bit of love from teammates who'd already done the bolt," he says.
The euphoric crowd of Swans fans surged onto the ground.
"That's the precursor to the Buddy moment [Lance Franklin's 1,000 goals] in terms of the crowd getting on the ground at the SCG," Lewis says.
"You didn't want to get off [the ground], but you wanted to get off because you wanted to get into that little room downstairs and soak it all in with each other and just go, 'F***, how good is this. We're in one.'"
Lloyd's dream turns 'nightmare'
Back at the Bombers team hotel, Matthew Lloyd was in his room with his parents. Players were coming in, but the morphine was wearing off.
Once people had gone, Lloyd asked his parents to help him to the bathroom, where he passed blood.
Essendon's Dr Bruce Reid came, and Lloyd says he was "rolling around in bed, just the worst pain of my life." Reid asked him if he had shoulder pain.
"I stopped for a second, and I said, 'Yeah, really strong shoulder pain.' I remember him saying, 'Get him an ambulance. He's got a ruptured spleen,'" Lloyd recalls.
Scans showed a large tear in his spleen, and a litre and a half of blood. It could have been fatal if left longer. As scary as this was, Lloyd had to come to terms with what it meant for his footy career.
"I knew going into this game, the reserves had qualified for the grand final," he says.
"I thought, 'Well, I'm going to play in that because I qualify for that or I'm going to play in the AFL grand final,' and then it turned into my nightmare."
Lloyd lost eight kilos, was bedridden for a time and could not do anything physical for three months. But in 1997 he burst out with a 63-goal season.
"I lived and breathed footy, no interest in going to parties," Lloyd says.
"My dad played 29 games for Carlton, and from the moment I was three or four, I had a footy in my hand, and it's all I ever wanted to do … and I was no different with my rehab; I was willing to do anything to play AFL footy."
That determination saw Lloyd finish as Essendon's top goal-kicker and eighth in VFL/AFL history, with 926 majors.
While Lloyd was suffering through a ruptured spleen, the other Bombers were dealing with a season cut short.
He says the players filing through his hotel room that night let him know coach Kevin Sheedy had exploded like never before after the game.
Lloyd was told Sheedy was pointed in his criticism of the team and of individuals, not just for the loss but for the way they lost and a perceived lack of toughness.
Three years later, a dominant Bombers team came up against Carlton and lost in the prelim. Lloyd says it still hurts today.
"In 1999, [Sheedy] was very different. He [went], 'OK, how I'm going to go to sell to these boys the hurt and what we're going to do in 2000 and this should steel us for 2000.' But in '96, he wasn't like that."
Essendon, including Lloyd, had to wait until 2000 for the flag, as they tore through the AFL going 24-1, including three finals by a ridiculous combined margin of 230 points.
For the Swans, the euphoria became a magic grand final week and a dream first quarter and a half – but then the Kangaroos put their foot down, and North ran away with it to win by 43 points. Lockett kicked six, but it wasn't enough. Sydney had to wait until 2005 for the drought to break.
Luff, Lewis and Lockett never won a flag, although Plugger made history with an untouchable 1,360 goals.
It is now 30 years, but Dale Lewis, for one, has not forgotten that night.
"I can see it now. I get a little bit emotional about it," he says with a slight crack in his voice.
"I can see that [night]. I can see the looks in a couple of guys' eyes. I know who I turned to. You look at it, and you go, 'Unbelievable'."

Saudi Arabia is nearing the point of no return – and Israel is waiting for it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:49:23 UTC
03:49:23 KST

Saudi Arabia is nearing the point of no return – and Israel is waiting for it
In the past few days, Israeli media has been actively talking about contacts between Saudi Arabia and Israel, facilitated by the US Central Command (CENTCOM). Reportedly, Riyadh is seeking intelligence from Israel to counter the Houthis. The very fact that such contacts are taking place raises a question: is Saudi Arabia preparing to take an even more significant and risky step, one that could alter the balance of power in the Middle East?
Escalating tensions with Yemen’s Houthis are compelling the Saudi leadership to seek help where it can be found. The Houthis have missiles and drones, enabling them to strike Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure and threaten shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. For Riyadh, this presents a military, economic, and reputational challenge. This new phase of the conflict jeopardizes oil facilities, maritime routes, and sabotages plans to transform Saudi Arabia into a leading global investment and logistics hub.
Israel, for its part, has amassed considerable experience monitoring the activities of the Houthis and Iran-linked groups. Its intelligence capabilities – including satellite surveillance, signals intelligence, and the analysis of troop movements across the Red Sea and Persian Gulf – could be valuable to the Saudis. The only question is, what price is Riyadh willing to pay for access to this intelligence information?
Things become even more apparent when we consider Washington’s stance. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asked US President Donald Trump for assistance in striking Houthi positions. Trump declined direct military intervention, proposing instead to expand intelligence sharing and target-selection assistance. A meeting between the Crown Prince and CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper has been confirmed by Saudi state media. Washington is prepared to provide intelligence support but does not intend to shoulder the main burden of a new campaign in Yemen – at least not now.
This raises a key question: has Riyadh decided to take a step it had long and carefully avoided? Until recently, Saudi Arabia sought to maintain cooperation with the US while preserving the possibility of normalizing relations with Israel in the long term; however, it avoided entering into a direct confrontation with Iran. This approach allowed it to maneuver between competing power centers. Even after the outbreak of a major regional war, Riyadh did not want to be viewed as a direct participant in the war and kept channels of communication with Tehran open.
Military cooperation with Israel could upset this balance. Iran might perceive the transfer of Israeli intelligence to Saudi Arabia not merely as technical assistance in fighting the Houthis, but as Saudi Arabia’s integration into an emerging anti-Iran bloc. Tehran views the Houthis not in isolation, but as part of a broader regional architecture designed to contain its adversaries.
The risk for Saudi Arabia extends beyond Iran’s potential reaction. Direct cooperation with Israel remains a highly sensitive issue for the Arab world, especially as the Palestinian issue remains unresolved. Riyadh will have to explain why military rapprochement with Israel precedes the political settlement that Saudi diplomacy had long cited as a prerequisite for normalization.
This is precisely why the mediation of CENTCOM is of fundamental importance. The US command acts as a kind of political buffer. Saudi Arabia can obtain the necessary intelligence without acknowledging the existence of a bilateral military mechanism, while Israel can defend shared regional interests without a formal agreement with Riyadh. This arrangement allows both sides to deny the formation of a coalition, even as specific elements of that coalition begin to function.
For Israel, this development is strategically advantageous. It allows for the gradual integration of Saudi Arabia into the regional security architecture even before diplomatic relations are established. Moreover, West Jerusalem gains the opportunity to demonstrate that its military and intelligence capabilities are essential for Arab states in countering threats posed by Iran. In doing so, normalization evolves from a purely political project into a matter of practical security.
Israel has long and consistently pursued a strategy aimed at forging an alliance with the Arab monarchies of the Persian Gulf. Just a few years ago, such an alliance seemed almost unthinkable, since the burden of the Arab-Israel confrontation remained too heavy, and the unresolved Palestinian issue made open rapprochement with Israel politically risky for any Arab nation.
However, Israel apparently proceeded from the idea that in order to implement this plan, it was necessary to wait for an opportune moment. Such a moment would come when the immediate threat from Iran and its associated forces proved stronger than previous political restrictions. And it seems that this is exactly what happened.
The attacks by the Houthis, the threat to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and new attacks on Saudi infrastructure have left Riyadh with an extremely unpleasant choice. Saudi Arabia must either again enter into a difficult and unpredictable war with Yemen on its own, or seek support from those nations that have the necessary capabilities. The US is not ready to get involved in hostilities, the UK limits itself to sending advisers, and Riyadh’s regional partners don’t want to get involved in a direct clash with Iran. And the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan in August, hasn’t been of any use so far. Against this background, Israel is perhaps the only country capable of providing the Saudi side with operational information about the location of the Houthis, their infrastructure, and the preparation of new attacks.
If the information provided by Israel is used in the preparation of Saudi operations, the first operational mechanism of military-intelligence cooperation between the two countries will emerge. Although such a mechanism may be initially viewed as a temporary emergency measure, if it proves effective, it will be much more difficult to dismantle.
This is a big risk for Riyadh. Most likely, Tehran won’t draw a clear line between Saudi Arabia’s fight against the Houthis and its inclusion in the Israeli strategy to contain Iran. Even if the Saudi leadership intends to solve only the issue with Yemen, Iran may regard this as a step toward the formation of a hostile bloc. Then not only Saudi military facilities will come under threat, but also oil enterprises, ports, tanker routes, and other elements of infrastructure on which Saudi Arabia’s economic stability rests.
Apparently, Israel has been waiting for such a moment. Circumstances are pushing Saudi Arabia towards cooperation with Israel, which only a short while ago had been impossible for political reasons.
If such interaction becomes permanent and goes beyond the confrontation with the Houthis, the war will take on a completely different scale. We will no longer be talking about separate fronts in Yemen, Lebanon or the Red Sea, but about the formation of two regional systems opposing each other. On one side will be Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the Western states supporting them; on the other Iran and the forces associated with it. That is why current contacts may become not just another episode of the crisis in the Middle East; they may change the entire logic of the regional confrontation. After all, ten years ago, no Middle East expert could predict the improvement of relations between the UAE and Israel – the parties were extremely hostile towards each other; but today, they maintain diplomatic relations, albeit with some reservations.
At the same time, it is too early to say that Riyadh has made a final choice in favor of an alliance with Israel against Tehran. The Saudi leadership is most likely trying to solve a specific military problem without long-term commitments. It is interested in Israeli intelligence, American support, and British advisers, but at the same time it does not want to become the front line of someone else’s war.
If Saudi Arabia really decides to enter into a stable relationship with Israel, directed not only against the Houthis, but also against Iran as a whole, the regional confrontation will move to a completely different level. This will no longer be a struggle between Israel and the US against Iran and its allies, but a clash of two coalitions encompassing the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, and the Arabian Peninsula.
For Tehran, this would mean the emergence of a single military-intelligence space from Israel to Saudi Arabia. For Riyadh, it will mean a rejection of its previous cautious balancing role in favor of direct participation in the conflict. And for the entire troubled Middle East region, it will pose a threat of a full-scale interstate confrontation, the consequences of which would no longer be limited to the territory of Yemen.
Therefore, the current contacts should not be viewed as evidence of an already established alliance; rather, they are a test of whether the sides are ready for such an alliance. Riyadh has not yet crossed the line. But for the first time in a long while, it has come extremely close to doing so.

Labor's dilemma is that Australia needs two things voters fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:49:03 UTC
03:49:03 KST

analysis
The economy needs migration and data centres. Voters hate both
The two things holding up the economy are fast becoming the two most potent and dangerous political issues confronting the federal government.
Data centres and migration are the twin issues the government needs to keep pumping to keep the country in positive economic territory, but they are also the two issues voters have the most complex and hostile relationship with.
It presents a dilemma for the government: it can't live with it, but it also can't live without it.
Migration has long been a key contributor to the economy, with international students, workers and their spending helping tip dollars into treasury coffers.
One Nation and the Coalition want to drastically cut immigration and are smashing the government on the idea that they have allowed a "mass migration" program. Labor, stung by months of relentless campaigning on this issue, finally unveiled a plan to try to cut it back too.
But figures out from today's Intergenerational Report (IGR) show just how much we need migrants for the economy to keep growing, albeit slowly.
Australia's population growth is projected to slow from an average of 1.4 per cent a year over the past 40 years to 0.9 per cent a year over the next 40 years. This is 0.2 percentage points lower growth compared with the projection period of the 2023 IGR.
The population is projected to reach 39.3 million by 2065–66. In 2062–63, the projected population is 1.8 million lower than projected in the 2023 IGR (Chart 8.2).
So while politicians from all the major, minor and yet-to-be-determined sides launch into a debate around migration, the projections are blunt — we are failing to build our own population from our own numbers.
Migrants are the ones renewing us whether we like it or not.
The data centre conundrum
And while migration is the government's perennial political headache, data centres present the same bargain: an economic boost at an unknown political cost.
Touted as the next boom, with some figures indicating they could deliver around $150 billion by 2030. For a country that has relied on revenue from selling the things we dig up, data centres have looked like the next pot of gold.
With inflation still high and economists predicting the Reserve Bank will deliver another rate rise this month, the government will be desperately relying on investment returns from both.
That both issues are the subject of furious debate not just in Canberra but across the country is inconvenient, to put it lightly.
Huawei, the Chinese-owned tech giant banned in 2018 from being involved in Australia's 5G rollout, released a report a few days ago predicting data centres could consume up to 10 per cent of the world's electricity by 2035.
The figure is staggering.
Australia is trying to thread the needle: the government's proposed standards would force new centres to generate their own renewable energy and minimise water use to offset their demand. But those standards are not yet law.
Meanwhile, increasingly dystopian stories about the toll the centres are taking on power, water and the grid are emerging from the United States.
While migration is well-traversed political ground, the emergence of data centres and the community hostility is new territory.
The PM wants to build public consensus through national standards, but it is fanciful to think laws will contain voters' anger if people feel they are competing with global big tech firms for water and power.
Anthropic has signed an agreement to use part of a $32 billion data centre proposed for a site on Queensland's Western Downs. It will be the largest facility in Australia and would draw as much power as about 1.5 million average households.
AI questions won't disappear
Not afraid of calling a spade a spade, Labor MP Ed Husic says the government has so far had a "patronising" approach to people's concerns about artificial intelligence implementation.
"I'm still concerned that we don't have a uniform approach to dealing with the risks of AI," Husic told Afternoon Briefing.
"I've seen AI firms, in fact, some operating right here out of Canberra that are developing generative AI products that are way cheaper than what you're seeing out of US tech [companies]," he said.
But Husic said he did not think Australia would back itself to go local, pointing to leaked Treasury advice "that says we should just be the quickest at adapting someone else's technology".
"That massively undermines our ambition and capability and ability to scale up our own local solutions, and I've got to say, if you want to build confidence in AI, people knowing homegrown AI is available for them that can meet the job and give them a lot more confidence.
"I am concerned that we are dragging the chain. The best thing, if we want to have AI sorted out, is to get a national approach and get it done once, get it done right."
This is a wicked problem for Labor.
Anthony Albanese has urged the United States and China, the two leading powers in the AI race, to strike a deal that ensures "humans remain in control". He has also left the door open to changing copyright laws to attract AI investment in Australia.
Albanese will speak with like-minded leaders at the United Nations General Assembly about global rules to regulate AI development, and while significant, those discussions won't fix domestic concerns over AI.
The government needs to show voters it won't leave them footing the bill for these new futuristic centres and the cash that comes with them; otherwise, the public will keep getting angrier.
Without a reckoning not just on data centres, but also on migration, the two streams the government is banking on to sustain the economy will become two of the government's biggest liabilities.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4 pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.
