Andy Burnham faces a weakened Trump – but the president remains unpredictable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:45:23 UTC
03:45:23 KST

No international relationship has more power to determine the success of Andy Burnham’s premiership. So you might imagine the stakes for the prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump on Tuesday would be high.
Yet Burnham may prove to be a lucky general. The balance of risk has shifted. Trump is unpopular at home, where inflation remains high, and is mired in an intractable conflict in Iran that has the potential to sink his midterm dreams.
When Keir Starmer first visited Trump in February 2025, the situation could not have been more different. The notoriously unpredictable president had just won the US election and was at the height of his powers – and was showing muscle on Nato and Ukraine, and with threats of tariffs.
Starmer’s “keep calm and carry on” strategy helped keep Trump on board the defence alliance and also protected the UK from the worst of his aggression over trade. But it came with a cost: he was often left looking obsequious and at odds with the national mood.
Burnham defended his predecessor’s approach but in June signalled he would take a different direction. “Obviously the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything they say,” he said. “We’ve got in trouble in the past when that happens.”
Downing Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the more combative approach of Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister.
Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama.
Early clues about how the talks might go from the White House perspective have been mixed. In June, Trump suggested Burnham was “extremely liberal” (not as a compliment) and dismissively described him as the “mayor of a town”.
The US president remains angry the UK did not join his strikes on Iran, and has attacked the country as a “dying” nation “on the edge of disaster”. More recent comments that he might not help if Argentina again tried to seize the Falklands, and that he would love to see a united Ireland, suggest his displeasure has not abated.
But that will not necessarily translate into a strained personal relationship with Burnham. The pair have spoken on the phone twice and are said to have got on. The prime minister’s laid-back, confident style is likely to go down well with Trump, who has already shown with the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, that he can warm to leftwingers.
On policy too, government insiders point to small reasons for hope: Trump responded warmly to reports the UK government was going to “open up” the North Sea (although the decision to drill at two fields has been delayed) and has – so far – been relatively restrained when asked about the UK’s planned West Bank settlement trade ban.
Their meeting will be fraught with tension over both matters, and other areas – such as defence spending and the Iran war – have potential for further clashes.
It will help Burnham that Tuesday’s talks will be held on the comparatively neutral ground of the UN, rather than at the White House. As such, he will avoid the jeopardy of an Oval Office press conference that Trump could easily derail.
Trump may also decide he has had enough fights for one day. His meeting with Burnham will follow his address to the UN. Last year Trump told world leaders their countries were “going to hell” over their immigration policies. The UK meeting may end up as just a sideshow.
Burnham’s views on Trump have also shifted since he took office. As mayor of Greater Manchester, he said the US president would not be welcome in the city, blaming his “poisonous” politics. After winning his seat as an MP in Makerfield, he warned against the “divided, dark politics” of the US.
But over the summer, Burnham appeared to shrug off potential divisions, telling reporters that “everyone says things as politicians”. The new prime minister said he would “say what I feel” to Trump but – crucially – would also try to “find a connection” with the mercurial president.
With Trump now weaker domestically, political power in the US is starting to shift to who comes next. Burnham is walking into the room with a president who is running out of time. Yet Trump is in power for two more years, and he is nothing if not unpredictable.
Burnham’s priority may be on domestic affairs, but his closest aides acknowledge that the biggest weight on the UK right now is Trump’s war in Iran. While the war continues to wreak damage on the British economy, Burnham will struggle to deliver his promises of change.
So for the time being, the power still rests with Trump, and Burnham may yet find he has to navigate a perilous path as Starmer did before him.

Danielle Wood wants to make productivity cool again

====================================================================================================

The politics of migration hides Australia's real problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:41:02 UTC
03:41:02 KST

analysis
Everyone now understands that growing the economy only by increasing the number of people, while individuals feel worse off, is a recipe for unhappiness and dissent.
Aggregate growth is a statistic, but individual decline is a vote. The political solution? Fewer people.
That's because those in focus groups and answering polling questions complain about how many people they can see, rather than the reason they are worse off: weak productivity, which they can't see.
As a result, we now have three significant political parties instead of the usual two.
The third newcomer, One Nation, is an anti-immigration party harvesting unhappiness and dissent. The other two have put on some anti-immigration clothes and have got on the grievance catwalk as well.
The starting number for the fashion parade is 300,000, roughly the current level of net overseas migration (NOM). We learnt on Thursday that population growth in the year to March was 392,700, of which 292,100 were migrants.
That is 100,000 a year more than between the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) and the COVID pandemic, and 200,000 more than in the decades before that. ABS data shows that over the past four years, population growth has averaged 400,000 a year, or 1,100 a day. The result is noticeable crowding in cities and a 23.5 per cent increase in the national median house price.
Population growth has produced average annual GDP growth since 2010 of 2.4 per cent, while GDP per capita has grown 0.5 per cent and real disposable income just 0.1 per cent and has often been negative, according to the ABC data.
Three offers to ease migration grievance
Here are the three competing bids for the migration grievance vote:
- One Nation: Negative NOM for three years followed by a cap of 130,000 a year.
- The Coalition: 170,000 a year, or roughly the number of houses being built (based on the idea that each migrant needs a house to themselves).
- Labor: 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 in 2027/28.
All agree that we need as much, if not more, skilled migration, preferably from those who can handle a nail gun or a trowel.
That means all three plans affect farmers and universities because the only flexibility to reduce NOM lies with unskilled visitors who pick fruit and vegetables. These workers are needed because Australians don't want to do this work. Students who pay higher tertiary education fees are needed because governments have cut university funding.
None of them is what you would call a promise.
One Nation is closest, offering a pledge and a commitment. The Coalition has an elastic target tied to housing. Labor has converted a forecast into a target.
In a media release to go with his National Press Club speech on Thursday, delayed six weeks while he presumably negotiated with agriculture and education ministers over the impact the changes would have on their constituents, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the plans were "designed to deliver the Net Overseas Migration forecasts in the budget of 245,000 in this financial year and 225,000 in 2027/28".
Treasury must forecast migration for the budget every year, and they are always wildly wrong because this is the first time the minister in charge of migration has taken any notice of them.
Does Canada have the answer?
Meanwhile, two days earlier, in an exquisitely uncomfortable coincidence, Canada announced a stunning set of policies designed to lift productivity.
It is a year since Canada announced a 23 per cent cut in temporary migration, that is, international students and temporary workers from 6.5 to 5 per cent of the population.
Australia's current stock of temporary residents is 10.5 per cent. Cutting that to 5 per cent would involve deporting 1.5 million people.
Maybe in a year's time the Australian government will also address productivity. If so, they could do worse than draw inspiration from Canada.
It's true that Canada is responding to an emergency: the collapse in its relationship with the United States and the imposition of a 50 per cent tariff on its exports to the US. Drastic reform is neither optional nor politically unpopular.
Australia is dealing with an emergency of a different kind: a rut of low growth and low productivity, with high inflation likely to prompt more interest rate increases starting next week.
This will make life harder for people already in such hardship that they're prepared to try Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce.
Canada has introduced what it calls a "Productivity Mega Deduction" (PM Mark Carney says they already used "super" last year) that expands the number of investments that businesses can fully write off for tax purposes in year one from 15 per cent to 65 per cent.
The qualifying investments include fibre-optic cable and data-network infrastructure, mining property, oil and gas pipelines and production-related capital, software, computer equipment and R&D-related assets, aircraft and vehicles, patents, rail track, bridges and roads and Canadian development expenses.
The Canadian government says this will reduce the overall effective business tax rate on new investment from 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent.
At the same time, Canada's Carney announced a broader plan to streamline approvals for major projects and supply chains, framed as: "One project. One review. One year."
The government's stated standard is that a project should face one coordinated assessment rather than overlapping federal processes and receive a decision within one year.
It sits alongside the new Build Canada Strong Act and extends the expedited approach beyond the projects already handled through the Major Projects Office.
So the tax package lowers the cost of investing, and "one project, one review, one year" is designed to reduce regulatory time and burden and uncertainty.
The key reason for Australia's low productivity is declining business investment.
Not only could the Albanese government copy Mark Carney's approach, but there are also many benefits to doing so.
Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That’s Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.

TRNC urges global community to reaffirm sovereign equality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:34:43 UTC
03:34:43 KST

The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) has once again called on the international community to take steps toward reaffirming its inherent right to sovereign equality and equal international status.
In a written statement on Sunday, the TRNC foreign ministry noted that the TRNC and Türkiye’s official policy on the Cyprus issue are based on the principles of sovereign equality and equal international status.
The statement underlined that, for a lasting settlement to be reached on the island, the international community must recognise the TRNC's equal status.
"The fundamental reality is that there are two separate peoples and two independent and sovereign states living side by side on the island. Policies pursued in disregard of these realities will continue to be doomed to failure," the statement said.
On a proposed "rotating presidency" between Turkish and Greek Cypriots in a hypothetical state covering the whole island, the ministry said:
"Although this issue was an element of the model negotiated for decades, that model ultimately collapsed due to the maximalist and uncompromising stance of the Greek Cypriot Administration, which refused to recognise the TRNC's equal status and rejected the sharing of governance and resources. Moreover, the concept envisages a system of governance within a unitary state and represents a policy that is fundamentally incompatible with the TRNC's position based on sovereign equality and equal international status."
The statement once again called for the TRNC's sovereign equality and equal international status to be reaffirmed and urged the international community to take steps in this direction.
Similarly, referring in the European Parliament to "the right to two seats allocated to Turkish Cypriots" and attempting to claim those seats would mean accepting the status of the so-called 'Republic of Cyprus', in which Turkish Cypriots neither participate nor are represented and whose institutions were seized by force by the Greek Cypriot side in 1963, as well as accepting its EU membership based on that status.
"While such an approach cannot be accepted, the Turkish Cypriot people should also not be expected to support initiatives pursued in this direction."
The Greek Cypriot Administration has illicitly claimed to represent the whole island as a member of the European Union since 2004.
Decades-long issue
The island has been mired in a decades-long dispute between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots despite a series of diplomatic efforts by the UN to achieve a comprehensive settlement.
Ethnic attacks starting in the early 1960s forced Turkish Cypriots to withdraw into enclaves for their safety.
In 1974, a Greek Cypriot coup aimed at Greece’s annexation of the island led to Türkiye’s military intervention as a guarantor power to protect Turkish Cypriots from persecution and violence.
As a result, the TRNC was founded in 1983.
It has seen an on-and-off peace process in recent years, including a failed 2017 initiative in Switzerland under the auspices of guarantor countries Türkiye, Greece, and the UK.
The Greek Cypriot Administration entered the EU in 2004, the same year that Greek Cypriots single-handedly blocked a UN plan to end the longstanding dispute.

Friedrich Merz vows to stay in office after CDU ‘disaster’ in German state elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:33:02 UTC
03:33:02 KST

Germany’s embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office and fight for future-proofing economic changes despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party.
Preliminary results indicated Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) tallied just over the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament in the coastal region of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, its worst-ever state score, which he called a “disaster”.
The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party extended a streak of strong showings by coming in first in the former communist region with nearly 38%, more than doubling its previous score.
In the capital, Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the far-left Die Linke looked on course to win with about 25% of the vote, ahead of the incumbent CDU by a five-point margin. The AfD made headway there too, with a clear double-digit result.
The deeply unpopular Merz has been fighting for his political survival after a humiliating series of setbacks with voters this year.
Speculation about his ability to hold on as chancellor reached fever pitch after Saxony-Anhalt state’s AfD chapter routed the CDU with a record 44% for the party in an election two weeks ago.
The Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result marked the third time the AfD has emerged as the strongest party in a region, although the party seemed likely to remain shut out of power in the state because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties.
In a rare speech on a state election night, Merz admitted the CDU had been bitterly deprived of “tailwinds from Berlin” in both of Sunday’s races. But he said he would remain chancellor and party chair and continue a reform drive on fronts including taxes, healthcare, pensions and reducing bureaucracy.
Merz said the German economy was facing “profound upheaval”, while public discourse had become “harsher and more irreconcilable”.
“Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,” he said.
But he added: “Germany is capable of reform. I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism, which is penetrating ever deeper into our society as the fascination with authoritarianism grows.”
A jubilant AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, mocked Merz before his speech, saying voters had given his own party a “very clear result” and called on the chancellor to resign.
About 2.5 million people were eligible to vote in Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The stinging blows from the latest elections had been expected to put pressure on Merz at a minimum to cede the CDU leadership, which would have in effect ruled out a run for re-election at the next national poll, due in 2029.
Merz’s eroding support has created a sense of instability in Europe’s top economy, which is struggling with deindustrialisation, sluggish growth and soaring energy costs.
If the AfD’s surge led Merz to abandon the chancellery prematurely, it would give the far right further momentum as France, Italy, Spain and Poland head into elections next year with nativist parties on the march.
Germany has high constitutional hurdles to replacing a chancellor against their will and any appointed successor would need to demonstrate a ruling majority. A failure to do so could trigger a new election.
The AfD is the biggest opposition force in parliament and is leading national opinion polls with about 30%. It has called for Germany to quit the euro, end support for Ukraine and carry out mass deportations of “irregular” migrants, while citing the “destruction” of the CDU as one of its central goals.
The CDU’s debacle in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – a small, relatively poor state – is particularly bitter for Merz as it was home to the constituency of his arch-rival, Angela Merkel. While she governed Germany for 16 years, Merz appears to be on the ropes after no more than 16 months.
Merz took office in May 2025 at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) promising to restore the German economy to strength and slash the AfD’s support.
A failure to make decisive headway on either front has produced profound disappointment in his leadership, with only one in 10 Germans saying they are satisfied with his performance. An inability to connect with voters appears particularly marked in the former communist east, where the AfD is strongest.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the Social Democratic party state premier, Manuela Schwesig, distanced herself during the campaign from a key pension change backed by her party in Merz’s coalition government.
She was expected to hold on to power in a left-leaning coalition even if the AfD came out on top when all the votes were counted. Despite leading the polls for months, the far right failed to garner enough support to govern alone and the remaining parties have ruled out working with it.
A confirmed win by Die Linke in Berlin, where the far-left party has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs, could see its candidate, Elif Eralp, become the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin.

Liam McIntyre, the next Australian Wolverine, on playing 'gruff, angry loners'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Marvel's Wolverine has new Australian lead in Liam McIntyre
Before becoming an actor, Liam McIntyre was an assistant manager at EB Games whose duties included inspecting trade-ins and selling the latest releases.
Twenty years later, he's back selling games but there's one small difference behind his throwback return: it's his face on the cover of the PlayStation 5 game Marvel's Wolverine.
"I don't think I believed it for three years," McIntyre tells ABC Arts.
As an avid gamer (and recent Pro Jank Footy enthusiast) and X-Men fan who grew up watching the cartoons, this represented a dream role.
"I filmed three-quarters of the game going, 'you're sure I'm Wolverine?'"
When he was invited to audition for "Rough Guy John", an angry man with razor-sharp knives jutting out from his knuckles, he didn't need Wolverine's superhuman senses to sniff out that he was actually auditioning to star in Insomniac Games's latest superhero blockbuster.
Marvel's Wolverine promises a more grounded, violent and combat-driven experience than the developer's quippy, webspinning Spider-Man series. McIntyre's background in ferocious gladiatorial combat in the Spartacus: Vengeance TV series was an advantage for recording Wolverine's animalistic grunts, terse dialogue and ferocious roars in a Burbank motion-capture studio.
"I don't know why I keep being picked to be these gruff, angry loners who wield violence to help people," McIntyre says. "What's that say about me?"
Wolverine's world
McIntyre has moved into voice acting in recent years, but the relentless scrutiny of providing both a comic icon's face and voice reminds him of his early theatre career at venues like Melbourne's White Whale Theatre.
"This is the weirdest blend of stage and film, because you're always in the round, you're always in a close-up. And you never know which one they're going to pick," he says.
The experience reminds him of sparse and intimate "black box theatre" venues; he had to use his imagination while performing in a tight Lycra suit dotted with reflective balls.
As the line between Hollywood and big budget video games narrow, McIntyre faces the same unusual challenges as Marvel A-listers when he pretends to crawl through burning buildings, decapitate The Hand's crimson-cloaked ninjas, or jump out of a plane sticking two middle claws up at his feral rival Sabretooth.
"You've got this giant helmet on, so if you try to hug someone you try not to Velcro onto them, which ruins the sound, and try not to clank into each other, which ruins the footage," says McIntyre.
"But I always think about regular film and television; you're still pretending there isn't a wall of cameramen and lights."
"You're used to removing segments of the reality you're in so you can act."
Why Australians play Wolverine best
Fourteen years ago, when McIntyre was asked for his favourite actor he immediately replied "Hugh Jackman". Now he's the second Australian to play a starring role synonymous with the Sydneysider superstar.
McIntyre feels unfazed by the pressure that comes with following a beloved predecessor in a storied role; his American TV breakthrough followed the tragic death of original lead Andy Whitfield.
He carries the same lessons for Wolverine. He resists the temptation to imitate, to copy how Jackman clenches his jaw, furrows his brow, or holds his claws up like a boxer (Jackman's stance was inspired by watching Mike Tyson title fights).
"I can't ever be him. I wouldn't want to copy him," McIntyre says of Jackman.
Instead, he's drawing from beyond Hollywood, including Chris Claremont's famous run on the Marvel comics series and Cal Dodd's Clint Eastwood-influenced vocal delivery on X-Men: The Animated Series.
Despite the illustrious competition, between McIntyre and Jackman there's a strong argument that Australians make the best Wolverines.
"I don't think you have to be Australian to be Wolverine. But it helps!" McIntyre says. "The Australian ethos, gruff, earthy, don't seek the plaudits, tall poppy syndrome, all align with the way Wolverine is. He keeps his head down."
The cycle of violence
Wolverine's barely suppressed rage is one characteristic neither Australia or Canada would claim. Yet Wolverine's anger is a core element of the game, with an aggressive rage system where collecting kills is rewarded with increasingly powerful attacks and graphic slaughter.
This emphasis created an odd situation familiar to any video game voice actor: the need to record an extraordinary quantity of agonising screams, roars and grunts.
McIntyre hoped to space out these strenuous non-verbal sessions. That didn't happen.
"There was one day where it [the day's recording runsheet] was 'Grunts, angry.' 'Grunts, perturbed.' "Grunts, confused.'" remembers McIntyre, who made it through with herbal remedies and some surprisingly effective vocal exercises using a straw.
"This is the most acting I'll do in my life,' he says.
A longer, broader story than the movies
Once his voice was restored to its deep and sonorous pitch, McIntyre can be grateful for opportunities that come with the game's extended run time.
Players get 15 to 20 hours to uncover the core dichotomy of a character caught between two selves: an animal who can fall prey to his worst instincts, and a man who desperately hopes to be better than the lonely screw-up he so often is.
"I love this rare opportunity to tell this longer, broader story," McIntyre says.
"It's got so much detail and time with the character to really explore that. You don't always get that, even in a movie."
Moving from movies to games came with some surprises. Screen mediums usually give the final say to the director, but games share that autonomy with players with occasional interference from a few erratic glitches.
McIntyre was surprised to see his facial animations become the subject of numerous in-jokes in Insomniac's Slack channel, especially one glitch where his character's famous yellow outfit remained in one room, while his character progressed to the next entirely naked (a stunt double's body, he swiftly adds).
"Which was fine in theory until I realised that people would save this and then share it around. That's my face! Please be gentle," laughs McIntyre, fearing what millions of players will do with his likeness. "I didn't think that through when I signed away my rights."
Despite those misgivings, McIntyre still can't believe his career has taken him to a place where he needs to worry about such a vast global audience.
"I was a kid that got bullied at school. It just wasn't my worldview to imagine I could achieve such cool things," says McIntyre, who feels his past self had a lot to learn from Wolverine's resilience. The character's superpower isn't really his adamantium claws; it's his capacity to take a beating.
"Just keep pushing. That's what I like about Wolverine the most: No matter how many times he gets kicked down, he always finds a way to dust himself off and keep going. I want to have more of that in my life."
Marvel's Wolverine is out now on PlayStation.

Striking a balance between living for the present and future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Readers on striking a balance between living for the present and future
How much time do you spend living in the future?
Jack Waters recently wrote about how a drive to "set himself up" and optimise every part of his life made it hard to enjoy the present.
This is what readers had to say about finding the balance (and joy) in their own lives.
Striving for perfection
"My whole life has been about optimisation. In my 20s, I started exercising fanatically … in my mind I had to exercise every single day, and I remember 'having to go' for a run at midnight on a family holiday in Merimbula in the 90s instead of relaxing and going to bed.
I started journalling at 17 and still do it. It's like hoarding memories. It has spread to using my phone to video things instead of just enjoying the moment during concerts and on bushwalks.
I've always been a workaholic, a habit my parents instilled in me, and I dislike taking time off. I work hard, not smart.
Five years ago, I started learning guitar and piano to fulfil a lifelong dream. That now consumes all my spare time, probably to no avail, as I'm too self-conscious to play for anyone.
But I have missed hours of watching [TV] with my wife. I'm 60 now, and I am struggling with the thought of impending retirement, and I have serious trouble just enjoying experiences. It's got to the point where I'm wondering when the life I've been setting myself up for will start."
- Marc
"I was intensely focused on optimisation in my 20s.
I turned vegan and only ate whole foods; I stopped drinking; I tracked habits and had a rigid exercise routine. It all came tumbling down and ended in an actual mental breakdown.
I've recovered, but it wasn't without [professional] help.
Optimisation is at an all-time high, and I see articles about hacks, self-help books and the like daily. But I've never been more miserable than when I was trying to track my life.
Life is messy and beautiful and uncertain, and it would be great if we could lean into that more, which is why I ocean swim and started playing rugby union to recover."
-Kathleen
Discovering balance
"Jack's story really resonates with me as I am the same; unable to enjoy the present and rushing through, always thinking about the future. I would love to learn and understand what it means to live in the present rather than rush through my life."
- Christine
"I have recently been tossing up changing electricity providers and found myself thinking, 'This plan has a lower off-peak rate than I am currently on. If I shower at five, my hot water system should have reheated before seven and I will pay less electricity.' I knew that would put more pressure on me, so I didn't switch to that one.
I particularly struggle with exercise and food; it's all in or nothing. Balance is what I am trying to learn now."
- Sally
"I received my first cancer diagnosis at 30 and second diagnosis at 52.
I'm now 55, and while I thought for many years I would die early, I'm now faced with dying of old age.
For me, I try to make sure there's something joyful in each day, do things that help the present and future like exercise and eating well, prioritise activities that require health and mobility like trekking, and don't invest a lot in activities that might need 25 years to return the investment. It's a balance."
- Tanya
Living in the moment
"I spent my 20s living life in the moment and telling myself I'll let the future me worry about it.
I have had plenty of good experiences. I'm 32 now and have spent the last two years on personal development and optimisation. I'm feeling like I'm trying to make up for lost time.
There are so many things that I'm looking back on and feel like I could have done better, but hindsight is a beautiful thing.
Finding a happy medium is hard to accomplish.
At the moment, I'm at a place where I have left my old life behind, but I haven't fully achieved my life yet."
- Joshua
"I slogged through school and four years of a mathematics degree and programming, only to find no employment with it 10 years in.
I've stopped saving and investing and learning, sick of the constant scheming to improve my future life. I went car-free, share-housed, brewed beer, avoided ticketed events, saved $200,000 while house prices went up.
Now I spend my whole pay cheque enjoying my life, going to music festivals again, and earning less than I did in 2012. If I were a teenager again, I would consider myself reckless, but I had a go at doing the right things, tried and failed the 'getting ahead' thing. Feel like I wasted 15 years of my life."
- Phillip

Macron, Carney hail new chapter in France-Canada ties at symbolic archipelago meeting
French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sunday called for stronger bilateral ties in the face of new global threats at a meeting on Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a French territory off Canada's Newfoundland. The first-ever visit by a Canadian leader to the North Atlantic archipelago came as both countries have increasingly awkward relations with the US.
French President Emmanuel Macron said France and Canada were "two great independent nations who want to stay that way" in a joint news conference with Canadian leader Mark Carney Sunday.
Carney, visiting France's tiny North Atlantic territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon just off the Canadian coast, said the moment had come to tighten links with France and the European Union.
The leaders' meeting, in the tiny overseas French territory off the coast of Canada's Newfoundland came as both countries have increasingly awkward relations with the US under President Donald Trump.
The meeting came days after Carney embraced the prospect of Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member, saying closer ties with the continent would ensure no country could control Canada’s markets or undermine its sovereignty.
Trump’s tariffs, demands for economic concessions and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have pushed Ottawa to reduce its dependence on its neighbour and pursue deeper economic, security and political relationships with Europe.
At a joint press conference in Saint Pierre and Miquelon on Sunday, Macron said the two countries would work together for closer ties on fishing, security and energy.
"We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for international law, respect for free and fair trade, science as the basis for our decisions, and the strategic autonomy that we defend," he said.

Carney called for joint action to counter new challenges. "Our societies are being shaken by new storms: the upheavals, caused by climate change, the erosion of democratic norms, and new threats to our sovereignty," he said. "The time has come to strengthen our ties."
Fuel, critical minerals and rare earths
Earlier Sunday, Macron posted a video on X of him welcoming Carney at the airport.
"In a world in crisis, our friendship is a strength," said Macron. "Together, we affirm our sovereignty, our freedom to decide and our willingness to build a future of peace and prosperity," he added.

Macron also said that Sunday’s talks are part of broader efforts to help France secure oil and gas supplies as the Iran war disrupts global energy markets and raises fears of higher prices for fuel and other essentials.
“Canada is a country with significant resources of critical minerals and rare earths. It is also a major oil and natural gas producer,” Macron said. “What we want to do is conclude agreements to secure more liquefied natural gas that can be shipped to Europe’s Atlantic coast.”
The visit came weeks after Trump posted an image that showed the US flag draped over Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean and was labelled "United States of America".
It included Saint Pierre and Miquelon and French Caribbean territories.
Sunday’s meeting followed Trump’s announcement of a deal on Greenland that would expand the US military presence there while keeping the island under Danish control. The agreement followed months of threats by Trump to seize the semiautonomous territory of a NATO ally.
Macron welcomed the agreement Saturday.
“Danish sovereignty is being respected, international law is being respected,” he said. “Anything that helps ease tensions is a good thing.”
Visit of symbolic weight
Diplomats said the visit by Macron, who was en route to the annual UN General Assembly of world leaders, had a symbolic weight following Trump's social media post.
France did not respond publicly to the post at the time.
For France, Saint Pierre and Miquelon is strategically important due to its location on the doorstep of the US and the Arctic, a French presidency official told reporters in a briefing ahead of the visit.

Houthis warn against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen's civil war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:29:18 UTC
03:29:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Houthis warn against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen's growing civil war
A senior official with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels is warning countries against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen's revived civil war, telling The Associated Press on Sunday that his group has assured the Trump administration that it won't attack US vessels in the Red Sea.
Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, said Washington reached out to the rebels after their rapid advance down Yemen's western coast to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait earlier this month.
"We confirmed that we are not targeting the United States, or any other nation, in the strait, with the sole exception of the Saudi enemy," he told the AP in a Zoom interview from the rebel-held Yemeni capital, Sanaa. "That remains the case."
US President Donald Trump last weekend said his administration has "had discussions" with the Houthis, but did not say when. "The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," he said. "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through."
The AP later reported that Oman hosted a meeting between US and Houthi representatives last weekend, citing a Houthi official and another individual familiar with the talks. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
However, al-Bukhaiti only confirmed indirect contacts with US officials through longtime mediator Oman, which brokered a 2025 ceasefire between the Houthis and the Trump administration. That ended a weeks-long US bombing campaign against the rebels in return for them ceasing attacks on US vessels in the Red Sea.
"The goal of our military operations is not to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, but rather to ensure freedom of navigation through it for everyone, including Yemen," he said.
Al-Bukhaiti said the rebels have the capacity to fight a war on multiple fronts "should any nation become implicated in the aggression against Yemen alongside Saudi Arabia."
"Today, Yemen is capable of waging battle, not merely an internal conflict, but an international one as well," he said.
He said the Houthi attacks against neighbouring Saudi Arabia will persist until Riyadh ends its decade-long blockade on rebel-held areas in Yemen and allows vessels to reach Houthi-controlled ports on the Red Sea. Then they will be ready to negotiate, he said.
Al-Bukhaiti blamed Saudi Arabia for the latest escalation of violence in Yemen, which he said erupted after an airstrike blamed on the Saudi-led coalition fighting the rebels hit the Sanaa international airport.
The strike prevented an Iranian flight carrying a Houthi delegation to land. The flight was a Houthi attempt to challenge the coalition's air and naval blockade.
The Houthis responded with missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia, including one that targeted Riyadh on Saturday before being intercepted. Saudi officials said debris from a Houthi drone also killed one civilian and injured others.
The Houthis also declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, attacking Saudi-linked vessels and oil facilities inside the kingdom, the world's top oil exporter.
The Saudis and their allies have long struggled to contain the Houthis, and may be tempted to seek a diplomatic solution to halt attacks. That might ultimately require US concessions to Iran, the only country with leverage over the Houthis. But Washington's negotiations with Tehran over their own war fell apart weeks ago.
The US, which bombed Yemen under the Biden and Trump administrations, has shown no interest in getting involved militarily this time around.
The rebels' advance inside Yemen seized the crucial port city of Mokha and key Red Sea islands that allow them to better monitor shipping traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb, through which some 12 percent of world trade normally passes.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, long divided into factions, withdrew but have vowed to regroup.
The escalation ended a 2022 ceasefire that largely ended fighting in Yemen's civil war, which started when the Houthis swept in from their mountainous heartland and seized much of northern and central Yemen, including Sanaa, 12 years ago.
The Saudi-led coalition entered the war the following year on behalf of the internationally recognised government. The civil war killed at least 150,000 people, according to UN estimates, and pushed the country to the brink of famine.
Now, with Houthis in control of Yemen's western coast overlooking the Red Sea shipping corridor, "the balance of power has shifted in favour of the Sanaa government," al-Bukhaiti said, referring to the rebels' de facto authorities there.
"Ultimately, (Saudi Arabia) lost its most critical card: the west coast," he said.

Germany's Merz remains defiant after historic state elections defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:26:21 UTC
03:26:21 KST

Germany's Merz defiant after historic state elections defeat, vows to press ahead with reforms
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz remained defiant on Sunday, vowing to press ahead with potentially painful reforms to Europe's biggest economy, after suffering a bruising electoral setback in two state elections.
Exit polls by public broadcaster ARD indicated that Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union, or CDU, came in with just 5% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – the lowest result ever since World War II for the party in any state. Meanwhile, the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany, or AfD, party made significant gains.
Merz acknowledged that the result was a "disaster" but said he would still move ahead with his government's reform agenda. He argued that Germany's economic and political problems made difficult and potentially unpopular reforms more urgent, not less so, and pledged to press ahead.
"What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience," Merz said in a statement shortly after the exit polls were announced on public television. "I will demonstrate these qualities as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country."
In Berlin, the CDU was projected to come in second with 20%, behind Die Linke (The Left Party) at 24.5%, according to ARD's exit poll.
"In our city, love and justice have triumphed over hatred," said Die Linke's lead candidate Elif Eralp, the daughter of Turkish migrants, celebrating her party's triumph over AfD.
Merz's authority was already damaged by the CDU's stinging defeat to AfD in the Sept. 6 election in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. That result shocked many Germans who had believed their country had developed an immunity to nationalism and assertions of racial superiority after confronting the horrors of its Nazi past through education and laws to outlaw persecution.
On Sunday, AfD was projected to make big gains in both states. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, it garnered 37% of the vote, and in Berlin it achieved 15.7%, according to ARD. But it was nowhere close to being able to form a regional government.
AfD's national co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, told ZDF television that "the chancellor's statement today really was more than feeble — he announced that he'd carry on as before, instead of finally drawing the consequences and resigning."
However, in an apparent reference to the far-right party, Merz said that his government's reforms would be "the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism, which is penetrating ever deeper into our society as the fascination with authoritarianism grows."
The CDU has run Germany's government off and on for the vast majority of its post-World War II history.
Merz, 70, became Germany's leader 16 months ago with promises to turn around an economy that has barely grown in years. But his government is grappling with a weak economy, and many voters who had hoped the former corporate executive would fix that have become disillusioned with delays in implementing financial and tax reforms.
While Germany is again seeing moderate growth, the labor market deteriorated last year. In August, more than 3 million people were unemployed, an increase of 36,000 from the previous year. Demand for labor remains weak, according to the Federal Employment Agency.
The strong showing of AfD in the Saxony-Anhalt election, where it has the best chance yet of forming the country's first far-right regional government since World War II, has further weakened the chancellor's standing on the national level as well.
In the past two weeks, there have been calls, even from within his own party, for him to be replaced as chancellor, although no top-level allies have called publicly for his departure, and many have warned against "personnel debates."
Apparently anticipating a tough post-election period, Merz abandoned a planned trip to New York next week to attend the U.N. General Assembly. Despite the strong headwinds, he has repeatedly said that he's determined to stay on and finish his term as chancellor.

AI, data center alarms dominate Congressional Black Caucus week in Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:05:02 UTC
03:05:02 KST

This year's Congressional Black Caucus Annual Legislative Conference, which wraps Sunday, has taken on a different feel than its usual college homecoming vibe. The event, which has drawn thousands of attendees to Washington, took on a more serious tone with briefings and conversations focused on artificial intelligence opportunities and regulation amid escalating concern about threats posed by the technology.
"I stand 100%, and so does the CBC on regulation," CBC Vice Chair Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., told CNBC. "I think we need guardrails, I think we need transparency, I think we need to prepare and protect the community from the potential ills that come with it."
Carter said at least 60 of the 62 members of the CBC would vote for a bill to regulate artificial intelligence, creating guardrails and placing guidelines on human safety. He added that competition with China should not be a factor in any legislation.
"I'm not going to run and race with China, they're not doing it the right way. They are not protecting communities," he said. "Our race should be enhanced innovation, advanced technology, while we simultaneously protect the rights of the American people."
The CBC is an influential group whose members include 29% of Democrats in the U.S. House. As Democrats aim to take control of the House in November's midterm election, the caucus's standing could rise.
The CBC's tackling of AI came amid the backdrop of Open AI becoming the latest company to report an incident where AI agents conducted what they call 'concerning model behavior,' It's one of a growing number of so called 'jailbreaks,' the slang term for when models bypass guidelines and perform unauthorized actions.
"The message they wanted me to bring is how we can do this in a way that protects our communities but do not put us in a position to lose in a national security race," said X. Eyee, an AI expert and Army veteran, who spoke with CBC members about striking a balance between putting boundaries on the technology without inhibiting innovation. "To do that, it does require addressing some of these areas where algorithms are being used with little boundaries around them."
Carter said he is talking with voters about how important the upcoming midterm elections are for AI regulation. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., this month asked that the House stay in session to find a way to legislate AI safeguards. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., after President Donald Trump called AI-safety concerns a "hoax," countered that "It's time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people."
"They're not bringing it to the floor because I'm not sure that they want the regulation that we want," Carter said of Republican House leadership. "I've heard them say pump the breaks. I've heard them say let's let innovation handle it on its own, but we can't afford to do that."
With AI skepticism high in the caucus, the AI and tech industries also showed up for the CBC's Washington gathering.
Meta President and Vice Chair Dina Powell McCormick touted the economic benefits of data centers and the AI buildout they power. Meta is building the Hyperion data center project in Louisiana, and its hyperscaler rivals, including Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft, are all also in the data center expansion race.
"Technology and AI are the economic revolution of our generation," Rep. Steven Horsford, D-Nev., a former CBC chair who now leads its technology committee, told CNBC. "That means that as Black Americans, we cannot allow this innovation to pass us by."
Horsford spoke about the importance of helping shape the energy-intensive AI buildout on a panel with Exelon CEO Calvin Butler.
Exelon provides power and grid services for the Philadelphia, Chicago, Baltimore, and Washington areas, and Butler said he is having continuing conversations with lawmakers about the potential impact on energy prices and residents' quality of life.
"AI is a real conversation because people are trying to figure out where they fit in and can have a voice," Butler told CNBC. "What they are saying is we can't sit on the sidelines and let our constituents be impacted, and you as energy companies have a role in helping us solve this problem."
Data centers, the CBC and redistricting
The debate over AI regulation and data centers took on greater urgency because congressional redistricting could affect CBC members. The Supreme Court's ruling in Louisiana v. Callais will make creating "minority-majority" districts difficult and have major ramifications for the 2028 election and 2030 census, according to the Harvard Kennedy School.
CBC Chair Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., estimated earlier this year that as many as 19 seats held by CBC members are at risk due to redistricting.
Carter said that while that number is lower now after court challenges to redistricting plans, the impact on the Black community remains.
"This is not just about congressmen," he said. "This is about school boards. This is about legislative seats."
Horsford echoed concerns about threats to minority representation in Congress.
"This has never been about protecting any one district, and it is absolutely not about protecting one party or another," he said. "It's about protecting the voters' right to pick their representatives, and not the representatives being able to pick which voters they serve. And as long as we keep that at the center of the work, then we're honoring what our democracy is supposed to be about."

Climbing the party-branded stairs of the Brighton Centre with a Liberal Britain tote bag over his shoulder, Cody Butler looks quite at home at the Liberal Democrats’ annual jamboree.
But asked how he is finding it, the 21-year-old replied: “Odd.” The former Tory activist resigned as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network and left his old party in July, arguing that centrists, remainers and members worried about the climate crisis and conservation were no longer welcome in the party. A week ago, he joined the Lib Dems.
“There is no easy way to describe joining a new political party, because it’s like finding a new family,” he said. “I was brought up in a Conservative association. I was the local Tory boy. So it’s great, but odd.”
Butler is one of several youthful former Tories who have publicly defected to Britain’s third party and are in the process of setting up a new group: the One Nation Liberals. It’s a growing group, with other potential defectors believed to be waiting to see if they can survive in Kemi Badenoch’s increasingly rightwing party.
Butler has been joined by Josh Bancroft, a former Tory councillor on Cannock Chase council, who left the party to join the Lib Dems earlier this month. “Moderates like me have been forced out of the big tent over the past few years,” he said. “My politics haven’t changed, but the party has.”
The 26-year-old said moderates looking for the exit have grown in number since Badenoch embarked on a purge of the Conservative parliamentary party.
In July, the Tory leader warned that anyone who supported net zero targets or Britain’s membership of the European convention on human rights would be blocked from standing as a candidate in the next election. The former minister Gavin Barwell lost the whip, and another former cabinet member, Grant Shapps, was blocked from standing again for the party.
“The Conservatives have taken leaps to the right and left me and millions of voters behind,” Bancroft added. “The Liberal Democrats can be and should be their new political home.”
Bancroft and Butler have been welcomed with open arms into the Liberal ranks, with one MP joking that Badenoch had become the Lib Dems’ most effective recruiter. During a Q&A on the first full day of the conference, party leader Ed Davey repeatedly mentioned Badenoch, referencing her decision to freeze out members and MPs who support net zero policies.
“Unlike Kemi Badenoch, who thinks there wasn’t a problem with this summer’s heatwaves, we actually realise you have to take action on climate change and we’re leading that debate,” he said.
Despite being stuck at about 11% in national polling, many Liberal Democrat activists and MPs in Brighton are talking with atypical swagger about cementing the foundations of the so-called orange wall. They point to the 72 seats they won in the last election, making them the largest third party in British politics for over a century. And of the 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024, 20 were taken by the Conservatives.
When asked if reaching 100 seats by taking those targets was the aim, Davey insisted there was “no ceiling” to the Liberal Democrats’ ambitions. “If we have great local councillors, great local candidates and great local campaigners, we can beat Reform, the Tories, Labour, Green, the SNP, anyone. We can win anywhere where there’s a multiparty fight.”
On Sunday, Davey explicitly ruled out any future pact with the Tories. But when asked about an arrangement with Labour, he said maximising the number of Lib Dem MPs would give his party a stronger hand in any future negotiations. “That means you have to box really smartly,” he said.
While that prospect may have some pure-blood Tories running for the hills, it could lure others into the Liberal Democrat ranks, argued Butler.
“It used to be that if you wanted power you could only join the Conservatives or Labour, but that reality doesn’t exist any more in a five-party system,” he said. “My message to other One Nation Conservatives is: you can be true to what you believe, and if you back the Liberal Democrats, you’re actually backing the future kingmakers of government. They will write the budget. The Conservatives won’t.”

Why do people protest? Six decades of research points to social connections over personal grievances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:00:07 UTC
03:00:07 KST

A massive review of six decades of research provides evidence that people who participate in protests are driven more by social connections and political interest than by personal grievances or mistrust of the government. The meta-analysis, published in Science Advances, indicates that while millions of people might hold strong opinions about social issues, specific variables like organizational memberships and digital media use are what tend to translate that sentiment into physical action at marches and demonstrations.
Social movements and protests are primary ways people voice dissatisfaction and push for political change. Understanding what motivates a person to leave their home and join a march is a major focus in sociology and political science, a concept known as micromobilization. Micromobilization focuses on the individual decision to participate in collective action. A persistent puzzle in this field is the gap between having a grievance and actually protesting. Many people might feel wronged or agree with a movement’s goals, but only a fraction actually show up to a demonstration.
For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that higher levels of partisan animosity toward an opposing political party reliably predicted a higher likelihood of protest participation, whereas strong identification with one’s own party had little effect. While that specific research measured affective polarization rather than the general political ideologies or institutional grievances evaluated in broader studies, it highlights the ongoing quest to pinpoint exactly what pushes a person from passive agreement to active engagement.
The research was conducted by Shelley Boulianne, a full professor and the R. Klein Research Chair in Communication Studies at Mount Royal University and a visiting professor at Lund University, alongside Jennifer Earl, chair and professor in the Department of Sociology and Criminal Justice at the University of Delaware. They focused strictly on physical marches and demonstrations, ensuring they were comparing similar types of actions rather than mixing in lower-effort activities like signing petitions or posting online.
“In 2017, I collected survey data about two protest events: the Women’s March and March for Science,” Boulianne explained. “I was looking for a way to organize this large body of literature to write about it succinctly.”
“Prior scholarship on micromobilization, or what predicts participation in social movements or specific protests, has not built on itself in the way that one might expect for such an absolutely fundamental question,” Earl told PsyPost. “After almost 50 years of studying this question in a focused way, divergence in methodologies and focus (are you explaining movement participation, participation in specific events, or agreement/motivation to participate) has meant that there are a large number of smaller conversations about micromobilization and a large number of theoretical approaches to micromobilization, but far less synthesis and stock-taking.”
The authors aimed to identify the factors that consistently separate those who act from those who stay home by looking specifically at surveys that included both protesters and non-protesters. They conducted a meta-analysis, which is a statistical technique that combines the results of many past studies to identify overarching trends. The researchers gathered 181 survey-based studies published between 1965 and 2023. These surveys included data from hundreds of thousands of respondents across various countries, though mostly from Western democracies.
The team analyzed more than 1,800 different statistical estimates from these surveys. They categorized the relationships between different personal characteristics and protest participation, noting whether each factor had a positive or negative association and whether the mathematical links were robust enough to be considered reliable.
“The symmetry between different lines of evidence was surprising,” Boulianne said. “When we wove together the qualitative interviews with the quantitative survey, we found a consistent storyline about who participates in protests.”
The analysis provides evidence that several factors consistently predict whether someone will attend a march or demonstration. A high level of general political interest is one of the strongest predictors. People who already pay attention to politics are much more likely to show up at protests. Political ideology also plays a large role, with individuals leaning to the left of the political spectrum consistently showing higher rates of protest participation in the reviewed data.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that higher political extremism on both the far-left and far-right was associated with a greater likelihood of participating in collective action across ideological movements. However, the current meta-analysis synthesized general population surveys regarding broad political ideology and march participation, rather than testing ideological extremism within specific protest movements.
Beyond internal beliefs, social and organizational ties are major drivers of protest attendance. Belonging to a voluntary association, such as a labor union or a community group, strongly increases a person’s likelihood of marching. The researchers suggest that these organizations might provide direct invitations to protest, or they might simply connect people to politically engaged social networks. In many cases, social embeddedness acts as a direct pathway to activism.
Digital and social media use also emerged as a consistent predictor of mobilization. People who regularly use digital platforms are more likely to protest, likely because social media functions as an efficient way to distribute information and mobilize social networks.
Relying on traditional media like television or print newspapers did not consistently predict protest behavior. The authors suggest that social media platforms are distinct because they combine logistical information about an event with direct social connections. “The role of social media in protest is to help identify and sustain these social connections,” Boulianne noted.
Demographic factors also shape who protests. The data indicate that younger people, individuals with higher levels of education, and those living in urban areas are more likely to attend demonstrations. The authors explain these demographic trends through concepts like biographical availability and supply and demand. Biographical availability refers to having the free time and a lack of restrictive obligations, which allows people, often younger individuals, to engage in time-consuming activism.
Meanwhile, urban environments offer a higher supply of protest events and organizational infrastructure. This high supply easily meets the demand of city residents who want to participate. Urban areas also reduce the physical costs and travel time required to join a march compared to rural areas.
“Scholars, media, and politicians make assumptions about who the protesters are and what motivated them to participate,” Boulianne told PsyPost. “The common explanation is that they are angry or frustrated people who bypass regular methods of political participation.”
However, the evidence does not show this emotion to be a consistent explanation of who shows up to these events. Interestingly, the researchers found weak or inconsistent support for the idea that personal grievances drive protest. Factors like low income, unemployment, dissatisfaction with personal finances, or a general distrust of government did not consistently predict who would march. Many surveys showed results that were not statistically significant when looking at these variables.
“I think many people get stuck on the issues – or what social movement scholars would call the grievances – because if you ask people why they participated, that is what they will say,” Earl explained. “But, if you compare people who did participate and people who did not, a lot of people who didn’t participate share the same concerns or grievances.”
This makes grievances a weak predictor of action, which Earl noted is “hard for a lot of people to swallow because they think it is either a precondition for participation (empirically, it’s not) or enough to generate support (empirically, it’s not).” This suggests that feeling deprived or angry about a situation is rarely enough to prompt action without the necessary social connections and political interest.
“Instead, the consistent predictors are political interest and social connections,” Boulianne said. “If one thinks of these people as groups of engaged citizens who want a voice, then the reaction to these protests might differ.”
“For example, the police might view protesters as community members demonstrating their democratic rights, rather than disrupters,” she continued. “Politicians might view these protesters as committed citizens who show up on election day, despite the time and effort required to vote. The media might view these protesters as well-connected members of the community, rather than loners or deviants.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The meta-analysis relies heavily on survey data from Western countries, particularly the United States and European nations. The dynamics of protest might look very different in authoritarian regimes or other parts of the world where demonstrating carries severe physical or legal risks.
The studies reviewed are observational, meaning they rely on people reporting their own behaviors and characteristics. This makes it difficult to completely untangle exactly how certain factors cause protest participation. For instance, digital media use is linked to protesting, but it is not immediately apparent whether social media usage directly prompts people to protest, or if politically active people just tend to use social media more to coordinate their efforts.
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding how certain ideas were measured. The review found that general dissatisfaction does not reliably predict protest, but this does not mean emotions are irrelevant. The authors suggest that future research could explore how sudden, shared grievances might act as a catalyst for people who are already socially connected, shifting the focus from personal deprivation to collective concern.
Additionally, the authors recommend that future surveys ask participants specifically about whether they received a direct invitation to protest. Being personally asked to attend by a friend or organization seems to be a potent motivator in smaller studies, yet it is rarely measured in standard, large-scale political surveys.
“If you want people to participate, specifically invite them to – it’s simple but very powerful,” Earl advised. “Don’t expect that convincing someone of your goals, concerns or arguments is the most important thing – some people participate without knowing much about the protest (especially when they are invited) and many who agree with you on the issues won’t translate that agreement into action.”
This gap in the literature highlights a need to update methodologies across the field. Earl pointed out “the divergence in how much some survey questions are asked, even if there is not great evidence for them, but how infrequently other questions are asked even though they have elicited really strong evidence when asked.”
To help address these gaps, Boulianne is expanding on the study’s framework. “I am writing a book about protest participation across the globe,” Boulianne said. “I compare the findings from this evidence synthesis article to findings from the World Values Survey (66 countries) and four-country survey data that I gathered in 2025.”
“We really hope that future survey research looks at this article and improves and changes the questions that are asked in response to the findings so that research on the topic continues to advance,” Earl concluded.
The study, “Most people who agree with you won’t protest predictors of marches and demonstrations from six decades of research,” was authored by Shelley Boulianne and Jennifer Earl.

Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus urges global communitıy to reaffirm sovereign equality, equal international status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
17:59:45 UTC
02:59:45 KST

Sercan İrkin and Esra Tekin
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) on Sunday once again called on the international community to take steps toward reaffirming its inherent right to sovereign equality and equal international status.
In a written statement, the TRNC Foreign Ministry noted that the TRNC and Türkiye’s official policy on the Cyprus issue is based on the principles of sovereign equality and equal international status.
The statement underlined that, for a lasting settlement to be reached on the island, the international community must recognize the TRNC's equal status.
"The fundamental reality is that there are two separate peoples and two independent and sovereign states living side by side on the island. Policies pursued in disregard of these realities will continue to be doomed to failure," the statement said.
On a proposed "rotating presidency" between Turkish and Greek Cypriots in a hypothetical state covering the whole island, the ministry said: "Although this issue was an element of the model negotiated for decades, that model ultimately collapsed due to the maximalist and uncompromising stance of the Greek Cypriot Administration, which refused to recognize the TRNC's equal status and rejected the sharing of governance and resources. Moreover, the concept envisages a system of governance within a unitary state and represents a policy that is fundamentally incompatible with the TRNC's position based on sovereign equality and equal international status."
The statement once again called for the TRNC's sovereign equality and equal international status to be reaffirmed and urged the international community to take steps in this direction.
"Similarly, referring in the European Parliament to 'the right to two seats allocated to Turkish Cypriots' and attempting to claim those seats would mean accepting the status of the so-called 'Republic of Cyprus,' in which Turkish Cypriots neither participate nor are represented and whose institutions were seized by force by the Greek Cypriot side in 1963, as well as accepting its EU membership on the basis of that status.
"While such an approach cannot be accepted, the Turkish Cypriot people should also not be expected to support initiatives pursued in this direction."
The Greek Cypriot Administration has illicitly claimed to represent the whole island as a member of the European Union since 2004.
Decades-long issue
Cyprus has been mired in a decades-long dispute between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots despite a series of diplomatic efforts by the UN to achieve a comprehensive settlement.
Ethnic attacks starting in the early 1960s forced Turkish Cypriots to withdraw into enclaves for their safety.
In 1974, a Greek Cypriot coup aimed at Greece’s annexation of the island led to Türkiye’s military intervention as a guarantor power to protect Turkish Cypriots from persecution and violence. As a result, the TRNC was founded in 1983.
It has seen an on-and-off peace process in recent years, including a failed 2017 initiative in Switzerland under the auspices of guarantor countries Türkiye, Greece, and the UK.
The Greek Cypriot Administration entered the EU in 2004, the same year that Greek Cypriots single-handedly blocked a UN plan to end the longstanding dispute.

Far-right tops another German state vote as Merz’s conservatives routed in worst result since 1949
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
17:52:46 UTC
02:52:46 KST

Far-right AfD leads as Merz rues ‘disaster’ in worst state election result in postwar Germany
SCHWERIN, Germany - The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) took first place in state elections in north-eastern Germany on Sept 20, voting projections showed, delivering the worst result for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s mainstream conservative party since 1949.
“It’s a disaster,” Merz said after exit polls were published, although he signalled he would fight on as chancellor and continue his reform agenda after speculation that a bad result could prompt him to resign.
The AfD was set to win 38.3 per cent in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, ahead of the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) at 35.4 per cent, according to projections on ARD public television.
Both parties were far ahead of Merz’s conservatives, who at the latest count had fallen to 4.9 per cent, below the 5 per cent threshold needed to enter the state parliament and indicating they may be excluded altogether.
The result on Sept 20 has given the AfD its second top-place finish this month at the state level. The party leads in national opinion polls but has been kept from power by the other main parties’ refusal to work with it.
In another election on Sept 20 in the capital Berlin, the far-left Linke party was at 25.3 per cent while the vote share of Merz’s conservatives, who currently govern the state in a coalition with the Social Democrats, tumbled to 19 per cent.
The AfD also gained in strength in the typically liberal city, hitting 16.3 per cent. It is the first time Linke has topped polls in the state, where it wants to nationalise housing from corporate landlords and cap rents.
Merz vows to continue with reforms
The results on Sept 20 may not prove a knock-out blow for Merz, but his low approval ratings, unpopular reforms and the triumph of the AfD in an earlier state election in Saxony-Anhalt have left his future in the balance.
“It will now become even more difficult for the federal government to muster the courage and political support for a fundamental reform programme,” Marcel Fratzscher, president of the Berlin-based DIW research institute, told Reuters.
If the ruling coalition parties stick to their red lines, he said, “political paralysis will become entrenched, economic weakness will persist, and the likelihood of an AfD election victory in 2029 will rise further.”
The SPD’s popular state premier in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Manuela Schwesig, had climbed in the polls ahead of Sept 20’s vote by openly criticising both the AfD and the Merz-led federal government’s reforms.
Schwesig also said the AfD had won votes by criticising Germany’s support for Ukraine. She had at one time supported the Nord Stream pipeline project carrying Russian gas through her state into Germany before they were blown up in 2022, but later changed her position.
“First, in my state, many people oppose support for Ukraine, both financial and military,” she said.
“And a second point: many people also wish to see energy flowing through Nord Stream again.”
German Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil, who is also the SPD leader, signalled he wanted a change of course, noting voters’ concerns over pension reforms.
“As the federal government, we need to analyse why there is such great uncertainty in the country,” Klingbeil told the ARD.
But Merz instead doubled down on a reform agenda he says will revive sluggish growth in Europe’s largest economy.
“What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience,” he said. “I would go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that is penetrating ever deeper into our society, driven by the allure of authoritarianism.”
The elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural state in the formerly communist east, and the capital Berlin follow the Sept 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD came close to the rare feat of winning an absolute majority.
In just over a decade, the party, which wants to take tough action to deport foreigners with no right to stay in Germany, restore energy ties with Russia and quit the euro, has transformed itself from a fringe eurosceptic movement to the country’s most popular party.
Sept 20’s results underscore the advances the AfD has made in recent years and raise fresh questions over the “firewall” strategy, under which the other main parties refuse to enter coalition agreements with it.
Merz has struggled
Elected in 2025 on a promise of reforms to return Germany’s stagnant economy to growth, Merz has struggled to win over voters, as a stream of communication missteps served to compound resentment over unpopular pension, tax and healthcare reforms.
Disillusion with his government has hung over the campaigns in both Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, where voters have focused on issues including soaring energy and housing costs. Merz presented a consumer relief package on Sept 18 that included tax cuts on gas and diesel.
Several people who voted in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania said living costs were a major concern.
“Here in Schwerin, with these wages, you can hardly afford anything anymore,” voter Carlotta Heick told Reuters in the state capital.
One elderly man criticised funding for foreign aid. “We need our money here, for our country, for children and pensioners,” he said, asking not to give his name. REUTERS
