German Chancellor Merz calls state election a 'disaster' for his party but vows to stay on
- Published
Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party.
In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was initially projected to scrape through with its worst ever election result. But a few hours later, it dipped below the 5% threshold needed to stay in parliament. Merz called it "a disaster" for his party.
Meanwhile the far-right AfD was on track to win the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, but it is unlikely to govern as other parties refuse to work with it.
In Berlin, the ruling CDU was expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).
Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.
Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Echoing comments he made after that defeat, Merz told reporters at the party's Berlin headquarters on Sunday that he would forge ahead with his coalition government's plans to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms.
"The reforms have to come," he insisted. "I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward".
"What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness and patience," Merz said. "I will demonstrate this as CDU party chairman and, above all, as chancellor of our country."
"I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society," Merz added.
The AfD's national co-leader Alice Weidel said: "We are the strongest force and have reached the mainstream of the population."
Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.
But its anti-immigration, German-first, and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.
As the projected results came up on the screen at the CDU's election night gathering in Berlin, there were no cheers or celebration.
This is a party that knows it's in trouble, and its leader quickly went on the offensive, declaring that he is going nowhere.
Merz has long coveted the top job in German politics, and likely won't give it up easily.
Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected later on Sunday night, or even Monday morning.
Public broadcasters ZDF and ARD put the AfD slightly ahead in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
The party was projected to take 38% of the vote share in the state, followed in second place by the centre-left SPD, on 36%.
For Berlin, the broadcasters put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke - which has never topped polls in the capital before - on nearly 26%.
The AfD also looks set to increase its vote in Berlin, with a projected 16% of the vote.
Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved.
Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only been chancellor for 16 months.
On Sunday, Burkard Dregger from the CDU in Berlin, told the BBC it was right that Merz should stay on. "He has a lot of work to do and we don't have time to waste to form new government in the federal level".
He described the electorate as "impatient", adding that it was "not realistic to expect that every issue has been solved within one year.
"He has got four years and we have to give him the four years," Dregger said.
While his backers have argued that many of the problems the nation faces are inherited, Merz himself is deeply unpopular.
The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support, while also alienating people further to the left.

European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:47:50 UTC
01:47:50 KST

European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”.
The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented”, and on Friday summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting in Paris, where they discussed – among other topics – intelligence of a growing threat from Russia.
The escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine. Kyiv hit Moscow and other Russian regions with hundreds of drones and missiles in the early hours of Sunday, in one of its biggest air attacks of the war.
In separate interviews with the Guardian over the past week, in different locations, three European intelligence leaders discussed their views of the potential threat from Moscow.
Michal Koudelka, the head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, said that as well as increased drone activity, a small-scale invasion of Nato territory that bordered Russia could be part of the Kremlin’s plans. “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said, in a rare interview at the agency’s headquarters in Prague. He said this scenario could play out in a matter of “months, not years” but added that “a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn’t happen”.
Officials in the three Baltic countries, which border Russian territory, have been more cautious about the prospect of an invasion or other serious escalation, citing Moscow’s stretched resources in Ukraine and warning that playing up the prospect of an attack might play into the Kremlin’s hands.
“We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” said Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service, in an interview at the agency’s headquarters in Riga. He conceded there were signs that Moscow was making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans were simply part of a destabilisation strategy.
“It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said.
Baltic politicians, who for many years criticised western Europe for being soft on Russia, now find themselves in the strange position of telling some western leaders to calm down in their public messaging, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could prove damaging to their societies and economies.
On Saturday, the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, decried “panic on social media” in recent days about a possible attack. “If there is reason to fear an attack, rest assured: we will make that clear. Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine,” he wrote on X.
Mežviets said that, overall, it was good that western Europe had woken up to the threat from Russia. “Before 2022, we constantly warned our western European partners about the threat from Russia, but most of the time our voices were not listened to. In 2022, the approach of our partners changed. They said it turns out the Balts and the Poles had been right,” he said.
Neither Mežviets nor Koudelka would discuss what specific intelligence might have been obtained about Russia’s supposed planning for the coming months, nor would they comment on whether a surprise trip by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to Moscow last month – during which he stopped off in Riga – was partly to warn the Kremlin about the dangers of launching an attack on Nato.
After that visit, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed rumours of a Russian attack on Nato. “It has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation,” he said.
However, many in Europe will have the build up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in the back of their minds, when US officials repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invade and the Kremlin repeatedly denied it.
As the full-scale war that ensued approaches its fifth winter, US-led efforts to bring about peace in Ukraine show no signs of success, with Russia and Ukraine intensifying their drone and missile strikes on each other. Ukraine has destroyed much of Russia’s oil infrastructure, targeting refineries and other facilities over recent months.
Moscow has frequently said the provision to Ukraine of weaponry, intelligence and military advisers makes western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets, but has so far avoided action that might provoke a coordinated response from Nato. Instead, it has launched what western agencies describe as a campaign of sabotage against targets in countries that are the loudest backers of Ukraine, and one-off incidents apparently meant to test boundaries, such as when more than a dozen drones, flying without ammunition, veered into Polish airspace a year ago.
Koudelka said the current Russian tactic was “escalate to de-escalate”, with the Kremlin keen to push at weak points in western societies to tamp down their support for Ukraine’s war effort. “They believe if they escalate enough, then European countries will decide not to support Ukraine,” he said.
In recent weeks the Trump administration has made another attempt to kickstart peace negotiations in Ukraine. As well as the Ratcliffe visit to Moscow, the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made another trip to Moscow, as well as a first-time trip to Kyiv. While Donald Trump has frequently claimed the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, is interested in a deal, there is scepticism in Europe that the Kremlin has any interest in good-faith negotiations.
“I haven’t seen any signs that there is a serious consideration in Moscow about real negotiations,” said Thomas Nilsson, the head of Sweden’s military intelligence and security service, in an interview on the sidelines of a conference in Riga. “My assessment is that they are still thinking that they could achieve their strategic objectives, so they are just playing negotiation theatre,” he added.
All three intelligence bosses said that whatever else happened, Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe is likely to intensify in the coming months. Nilsson described as a “gamechanger” the recent armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, which German authorities have attributed to Russian intelligence.
“To have an armed UAV drone sent in to a busy airport in the middle of Europe … If you have attacks that could result in losses of life or losses of very critical infrastructure that have a huge implication for society, I think that is a gamechanger,” he said.
Mežviets said Russia was moving from randomised targeting of sabotage and arson attacks intended to sow panic to specific targets linked to western backing for Ukraine. “We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure. Right now we see a move towards defence industry targets,” he said. “If you do this then the psy-op effect is reached anyway, so you get both things in one,” he added.
Nilsson said there were several goals behind the recent intensification of Russian sabotage activity: to reduce support for Ukraine, to introduce splits in Nato and to alarm European populations. “I think Moscow would love Nato to have endless discussion about article 4 consultations, but coming up with no actions,” he said.
Koudelka said another effect of the sabotage campaign is the stretch on resources of intelligence services, as doubts often linger even when incidents are caused by other factors. “Now every fire or every malfunction needs to be investigated by intelligence services as a potential terror attack, and that is a good result for them,” he said.

Central Colombia forest fire threatens tourist town of Villa de Leyva
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:47:33 UTC
01:47:33 KST

Central Colombia forest fire threatens tourist town of Villa de Leyva
The country has battled multiple wildfires amid record-breaking temperatures fueled by El Nino and intense drought conditions.
A massive wildfire has broken out in central Colombia, threatening the popular tourist town of Villa de Leyva, according to local officials.
The forest fire is near the Andean town in the Boyaca department, with flames engulfing the San Marcos hillside above the colonial architecture and cobblestone streets that attract more than a million visitors annually. 
The blaze has already consumed 40 hectares of native forest, sending massive plumes of smoke that are visible from the town’s central square, according to Colombian authorities.
On Saturday night, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella posted on X that “Villa de Leyva is not alone”, pledging to mobilise all state resources to fight the fire and protect “this historical jewel” and “beautiful city that is the pride of Colombia”.
To combat the flames, the Boyaca department government said it is dispatching two aircraft. A military helicopter will also join the effort, along with firefighters from the capital, Bogota, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said.
The mayor of Bogota, Carlos Fernando Galan, will be sending a team of firefighters to join local crews from Tunja and Boyaca, reinforcing containment efforts and securing the urban centre, Lara said.
In the equatorial Andes, forest fires peak during the dry season, but this year they are fuelled by a severe El Nino weather pattern. Record high temperatures and lack of moisture have turned vast expanses of the Andean vegetation into tinderboxes. That has intensified a crisis that has already started 18 active wildfires across the country, according to the latest official data from Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD).
The impacts of El Nino, a natural weather pattern, are felt globally and do not affect the entire South American continent in the same way, inducing extreme droughts in some regions and torrential flooding in others. This year, it comes supercharged by the effects of climate change, which is worrying many scientists, governments and aid workers.
The warming of the adjacent Pacific has triggered catastrophic flash floods and landslides in countries such as Peru and Ecuador.
Unlike in the southern part of the continent, where countries including Argentina, Chile and Uruguay have been expecting unseasonably heavy rainfall, El Nino has the opposite effect in the northern part of the continent. A significant reduction in rainfall leads to severe drought conditions which can suppress cloud formation and displace normal rain patterns, driving average temperatures well above normal.
The soaring heat rapidly evaporates moisture from the ground and water basins, leaving countries such as Colombia with extended periods of drought and critically low precipitation.
“El Nino can bring devastating climate extremes on its own, but it’s unfolding today on a much warmer planet, increasing the likelihood that heat, drought, floods and fires will push communities and ecosystems beyond anything they have experienced before,” said Stephanie Roe, lead climate scientist with the World Wildlife Fund.

How the great gas crisis  of 2030 could play out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:20 UTC
01:37:20 KST

It is October 2030. In hindsight, the vulnerabilities that triggered the third great natural gas crisis in eight years seem painfully obvious.
After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine cut off Europe from two-fifths of its gas in 2022, importers reassured themselves that the Persian Gulf and the US had plenty to spare.
When the war with Iran similarly knocked out 20 percent of the global liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply, the US’ booming fossil-fuel industry again promised to fill the gap.
Illustration: Kevin Sheu
That confidence now seems shockingly naive. US natural gas prices have been caught in a perfect storm: Growth in shale output has been faltering. Season upon season of extreme weather has hit a power sector crippled by former US president Donald Trump’s war on clean energy. Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) labs, racing to beat a technological singularity they are warning is finally just months away, are sucking up fossil fuels to power data centers. Meanwhile, LNG terminals are allowing foreign buyers to compete with the US’ habituated to rock-bottom prices.
With storage tanks at record lows amid a polar vortex cold snap in February, US benchmark Henry Hub prices rose above US$10 per million British thermal units for the first time since 2008. Summer heatwaves repeatedly drove them back there. The ripples spread quickly through the economy.
In Iowa, a tripling in the price of gas-derived fertilizer caused farmers to plant their smallest spring corn crop in two decades. In June, China’s Fuyao Glass Industry Group Co blamed gas prices in announcing the closure of an iconic glass factory outside Dayton, Ohio, with the loss of 2,000 jobs. A month later, Ford Motor Co eliminated the second shift at its Wayne, Michigan, assembly line, citing rising energy and supply chain costs. Another 2,000 workers were put on indefinite layoff.
What began as an energy shock was becoming a political hot potato. Much as how a backlash against data centers erupted from nowhere, calls to “keep American energy for Americans” quickly became deafening. With midterms approaching, Democratic lawmakers in the northeast who had long sought restrictions on LNG exports found unlikely allies among Republicans watching one of the country’s great competitive advantages — cheap energy — disappear.
Then came July’s heat dome. New Orleans recorded 70 heat-related deaths. Many were suburban retirees who had switched off air conditioners as electricity bills devoured half of their Social Security payments.
On the day a new poll showed Louisiana Republican gas-export advocate Steve Scalise trailing a populist primary challenger by 11 points, Fox News broadcast footage of four LNG tankers departing the Gulf Coast bound for China.
Within days, protestors carrying “It’s OUR gas” placards were outside Congress.
After demurring for weeks, the president signed the bipartisan Secure American Fuel for Everyone Act, declaring a gas supply emergency and ordering the Department of Energy to curtail exports within 30 days.
That is when all hell broke loose. European gas storage was already running dangerously low after the same torrid El Nino summer, leaving importers heavily dependent on US shipments. Japan and South Korea were even more exposed. After a bruising trade fight with Washington, both had restricted Chinese clean-energy imports in return for preferential access to US LNG. That slowed deployment of the technologies that might have insulated them from the crisis.
Russia was in no position to come to the rescue. Eight years of war in Ukraine, an economy approaching Venezuela-style degeneration and incessant hybrid-warfare attacks on its petroleum infrastructure had decimated its capacity to respond.
The situation in the Gulf offered little reassurance. Relations between Qatar and Iran’s increasingly lawless government were deteriorating over the management of their vast shared offshore gas field, threatening the uneasy truce in Hormuz brokered after the 2028 US election. Then Iran’s Revolutionary Guards boarded a QatarEnergy LNG tanker and turned it back.
Australia offered no respite either. The world’s biggest LNG exporter as recently as 2022 had imposed US-style export restrictions to shield domestic supplies.
How did the world fail to see what seems so inevitable now? It was hardly unprecedented. In the 1970s, the US banned exports of soybeans and crude oil to protect consumers from rising prices. The oil ban lasted four decades before being lifted in 2015, sparking a production boom that eventually hardened into hubris about a new era of US energy dominance.
The mistake was to believe the petroleum industry’s bromides about the stability of LNG — what Shell PLC described as the fuel’s “flexible and reliable energy security.” The poorer Asian countries hit hardest by the 2022 and 2026 crises look best-placed right now. Rather than betting their power systems on a fuel for which rich countries could always outbid them, countries from Pakistan to the Philippines accelerated investment in solar, batteries and domestic energy.
In contrast, developed Asia and Europe conflated flexibility with security, and were slower to pivot. That was a disastrous choice. LNG can be shipped halfway around the world, but Russia, Qatar and the US each demonstrated how quickly politics can disrupt those flows.
After three gas crises in eight years, perhaps the remarkable thing is not that countries are finally learning this. It is that anyone still needed the lesson.
David Fickling is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering climate change and energy. Previously, he worked for Bloomberg News, the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Yet the carefully crafted 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration (NDD), the longest BRICS declaration so far, reveals a subtle, but important shift. BRICS is moving from a loose grouping toward a more substantive platform for the global south, giving developing countries greater voice and bargaining space

US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng (何立峰) were set to meet yesterday to try to set up potential agreements on artificial intelligence (AI), tariffs and critical minerals for a summit in Washington this week between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
The meetings at JPMorgan Chase & Co’s headquarters in Manhattan, which included US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, were due to start at about 10:30am on Sunday morning and were expected to run all day.
Key topics would be the status of a US-China trade truce that is set to expire on Nov. 10, flows of Chinese rare-earth magnets and critical minerals that US officials say are insufficient and guardrails for AI after reports of key security breaches involving AI models.
Photo: REUTERS
The most likely outcome, analysts say, would be for Washington and Beijing to agree on small steps to show they are continuing to avoid escalating tensions in a delicate trade relationship that has major consequences for the global economy.
“I think there will be some show of deliverables because of the fact that it’s a presidential summit coming, but I don’t feel like we’re on the verge of some sort of breakthrough,” said Anna Ashton, a China trade analyst and founder of Ashton Intelligence. “I think status quo is probably both sides’ general best expectation.”
Many of the issues that He, Bessent and Greer would have to work through for Trump and Xi are holdovers from the two leaders’ meeting in Beijing in May, including an effort on both sides to cut tariffs on non-strategic goods and Chinese pledges to increase purchases of US agricultural goods by US$17 billion a year and to purchase more than 200 Boeing Co aircraft.
Under the truce reached in Busan, South Korea in November last year, China promised to restore the flow of critical minerals to US and global users. A senior US official said on Friday that China’s performance on that front “has not been up to par” and would be a topic for discussion ahead of the Trump-Xi summit.
The discussions on AI are significant because the US and China are the two major forces driving development of advanced AI tools and the global adoption of the technology. Rare earths play a crucial role in the manufacturing of advanced semiconductor technology powering AI.
Bessent said on Friday he expected the discussions to cover “both open and closed-weight models.” Open-weight models are AI systems with publicly accessible core elements where users can download and fine-tune them for specific tasks.
Chinese open-weight models are becoming more popular with US companies because they can be cheaper than closed-weight AI tools such as those developed by Anthropic PBC, OpenAI and other US companies.
“The United States remains the leader in AI. And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems,” Bessent said in a statement regarding the China talks.
The US and China agreed in May to launch discussions to reduce tariffs for non-strategic goods under a so-called “Board of Trade” mechanism along with a similar forum to deal with specific investment issues.
While the Trump administration has tightened restrictions on US companies investing in some industries in China, Reuters reported on Friday that it is working on rules that would likely allow US pharmaceutical firms to invest in promising Chinese drugs and strike licensing deals for them.
The Chinese Ministry of Commerce said on Saturday that He would also lead a delegation of Chinese companies to the US that would participate in economic and trade consultations ahead of the summit.
The business delegation was announced as Trump expressed openness to Chinese automakers building US factories. US auto industry groups on Friday urged Trump to maintain an effective ban on Chinese vehicle sales in the US on national security grounds.

Hokuto apples perfect for Mid-Autumn gifting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:16 UTC
01:37:16 KST

The Taichung Agricultural Tourism Industry Development Association yesterday encouraged people to purchase Hokuto apples grown in Taichung’s Lishan (梨山) area, which it said are in season and ideal for a Mid-Autumn Festival giftbox.
The Lishan area is famous for its Megumi apple production, commonly known as Lishan honey apples in Taiwan.
Lishan honey apples convert starch into fructose for storage to protect themselves from frost damage in the alpine climate of the Lishan area.
Photo courtesy of Lo
The fructose forms a translucent water core inside the apples, making them taste sweet and juicy with a crisp texture.
However, Lishan honey apples are usually harvested from late October until December and might not be available until next month.
While honey apples have a concentrated harvesting season, the Hokuto apples cultivated in the Lishan area are a good alternative, association chairman Lo Ching-yu (羅進玉) said yesterday.
The Hokuto apple is an heirloom variety that was introduced to Lishan for cultivation more than three decades ago, he said.
It is a hybrid of Mutsu and Fuji apples developed by Japan’s Aomori Apple Experiment Station in 1983, Lo said.
The Hokuto apple features large fruits, each weighing from 300g to 400g, he said.
Its flesh tastes smooth, juicy, sweet and tangy, with a strong aroma after ripening, Lo said, adding that some Hokuto apples also have water cores.
The Lishan area’s high altitudes and sharp day-night temperature changes are the key to the Hokuto apple’s exquisite flavor, he said.
The Hokuto apple’s harvesting period runs from mid-September to early-October, making it ideal for a giftbox during the Mid-Autumn Festival this week or the Double Ten National Day holiday next month, Lo said.

Taiwan continues to supply safe and high-quality agricultural and fishery products to Japan and has earned recognition from the Japanese market, he said.
To meet Japanese consumers’ strong demand for quality, freshness and safety, Taiwan will continue to improve its agricultural production, quality management and related techniques, Chen said.
Taiwan’s promotional efforts for its agricultural and fishery products in the Japanese market used to focus on the Kanto region, he said.
The MOA would actively assist Taiwan-grown produce in expanding into more local markets of Japan such as Nagoya, he added.
Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa said that Taiwan’s specialty foods such as braised pork rice and fruit such as bananas, pineapples and mangoes are widely popular in Japan.

Former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet on Saturday withdrew her candidacy for the position of UN secretary-general, weeks after a straw poll showed her in second to last place among eight candidates.
“Today I announced that I have decided not to continue with my candidacy for the position of secretary-general of the United Nations,” Bachelet, who served as Chile’s first female leader, said in a video posted on her social media accounts.
“Some may believe that the time was not right for a candidacy like the one I sought to represent. I do not regret having taken on this great challenge,” she said.
Photo: Bloomberg
Bachelet stressed that by running for the top UN position, she had helped spark debate “that the next secretary-general should be a woman from Latin America.”
Chile’s government said in a statement that it had withdrawn its support for Bachelet’s candidacy in March.
Since then, it has not backed any of the candidates in the running.
The government also “reaffirmed its commitment to multilateralism and to reform of the United Nations.”
So far, in three polls as part of the informal process to choose the next UN chief, the 15-member Security Council twice placed former Costa Rican vice president Rebeca Grynspan in the lead.
Guyanese former minister of foreign affairs Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett placed first in the third poll.
Bachelet was initially nominated in February last year by the administration of then-president Gabriel Boric, and supported by the leftist leaders of Mexico and Brazil.
However, the left-leaning 74-year-old’s candidacy lost momentum after Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast withdrew his backing.
Earlier this month at a university event, Bachelet had appeared to recognize her underdog status, joking about her slim chances of leading the global body.
No woman has led the UN in its 80-year history, and only one Latin American has served as secretary-general: Javier Perez de Cuellar of Peru, at the helm from 1982 to 1991.
According to unwritten practice — one that is not always followed — the top position rotates among geographic regions. This time, it would be Latin America’s turn.
Bachelet’s withdrawal leaves four women and three men in the race to succeed 77-year-old UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres of Portugal, who completes his second five-year term on Dec. 31.

EDITORIAL: Why bother with Twin City Forum?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:13 UTC
01:37:13 KST

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) last month said the Taipei-Shanghai Twin City Forum was expected to be held in Taipei in December, but the Mainland Affairs Council’s (MAC) rejection of a Shanghai official’s application to enter Taiwan last week reignited the debate: “Why hold the Twin City Forum?”
The MAC rejected Shanghai Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) Deputy Director Li Xiaodong’s (李驍東) application to visit Taiwan last year, saying that the other approved personnel were sufficient. Separately, it has cited what it said was the Shanghai TAO’s obstruction of Taiwanese businesspeople returning to Taiwan for government-related events and that Beijing’s so-called “22 guidelines to penalize Taiwanese independence separatists” as reasons for tightening security on TAO officials.
Chiang said that the more difficult cross-strait relations become, the greater the need for communication and dialogue, and that the forum is a long-standing platform for “purely municipal exchange,” which his administration has conducted under the principles of equality, mutual dignity, goodwill and mutual benefit.
MAC Deputy Minister and spokesman Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) said they receive and review applications from local governments for cross-strait exchanges every day.
“People don’t need to treat the Taipei-Shanghai Twin City Forum as such a big deal, because in reality, it doesn’t do anything to promote peace,” he said. “The Taipei City Government should not view its exchanges with Shanghai as something more important than it really is.”
The forum was first held in Taipei in 2010 under then-Taipei mayor Hau Lung-bin (郝龍斌) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), and continued to be held under former Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲), who later founded the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP). The forum has since rotated between the two cities. Every year before the forum, whether it should be held or attended becomes a political issue across party lines.
The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and its supporters have often argued that amid China’s hostility, coercion and military threats against Taiwan, along with Taipei’s failure to uphold parity and dignity, the forum becomes a platform for China’s “united front” propaganda. Examples include Ko’s controversial “two sides of the Taiwan Strait are one family” and “community of common destiny” remarks in his 2017 speech at the forum.
The KMT and the TPP defend the forum, saying that cross-strait communication is important, and blaming the DPP government for tensions with China.
The biggest problem is not Taiwan, but China and its peremptory attitude — after the DPP government took office in 2016, Beijing has suspended all official communication channels with Taiwan. As a result, opposition parties that communicate with China do so without authority or legitimacy to negotiate on Taiwan’s behalf in an attempt to improve cross-strait relations. They blame the DPP for limiting Taiwan’s exchanges, while the ruling party criticizes the opposition for belittling the nation and kneeling to China.
Looking at the outcomes of the past forums, 49 memorandums of understanding (MOUs) have been signed, although Taipei officials this month acknowledged that not all have been implemented.
A report in 2024 said that nine of 19 MOUs signed under Hau’s administration, 17 of 23 under Ko and all three MOUs under Chiang in 2023 had not been executed as of June that year. The ones that were implemented included “fluff content,” such as municipal policies that were already in place, or promising more mutual visits in competitions or events.
Although many MOUs are nonbinding expressions of intent to cooperate, the low implementation rate is a good reason to re-examine a forum that delivers such poor results.
The principles of “equality, dignity, goodwill and mutual benefit” cited by Chiang do not seem to get through to Beijing, nor does the forum help promote peace. The day after Chiang left last year’s forum in Shanghai, the Chinese People’s Liberation Army announced joint military exercises around Taiwan.
Chiang had announced “three preconditions” for holding the forum during his 2022 mayoral bid — China stops harassing Taiwan, shows goodwill toward Taiwan, and the two sides engage on equal footing. He seems to have forgotten his promise after taking office.
A forum held only for the sake of “exchanges” and wishful thinking that “communication brings peace and prosperity” is not enough, especially when it delivers very few substantial outcomes, has not been accompanied by greater cross-strait peace and comes amid continued Chinese military pressure on Taiwan. Taipei deserves to have better exchanges with more trustworthy international cities that can provide real benefits to people, with no political preconditions.
At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, people will remember less what China achieved and more what the global south attained. China did not lose face: President Xi Jinping (習近平) was an honored guest in India, was endorsed as the chair of BRICS for next year, and China is to host the next summit. Yet the carefully crafted 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration (NDD), the longest BRICS declaration so far, reveals a subtle, but important shift. BRICS is moving from a loose grouping toward a more substantive platform for the global south, giving developing countries greater voice and bargaining space

Doctor encourages awareness of ADHD in adults
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:12 UTC
01:37:12 KST

Adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) could experience procrastination or forgetfulness in daily life, a psychiatrist said.
Although it is not unusual for people to procrastinate while dealing with the stresses of daily life, those who regularly avoid completing tasks until the last minute might have ADHD, psychiatrist Yang Tsung-tsai (楊聰財) said, calling on people who tend to procrastinate to seek medical attention.
Adult ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder, he said.
Photo: Liao Hsueh-ju, Taipei Times
Adults with ADHD have difficulties with attention and self-regulation, leading to persistent inattention, hyperactivity or impulsivity that significantly impairs work, learning, relationships and daily activities, Yang said.
They might experience discomfort and restlessness when under-stimulated, experience racing thoughts and say whatever comes to mind, he said.
Adults with ADHD might also reply before others finishing speaking, make rash decisions, feel unable to sit still during meetings or constantly bounce their leg while seated, Yang said.
They are highly likely to show behavior such as forgetting appointments, missing tasks, being late, misplacing things, interrupting others, or forgetting to pay bills, as they remain chronically busy due to misdirected attention, he said.
Such symptoms could make adults with ADHD feel frustrated in daily life, resulting in severe self-doubt or feelings of worthlessness, Yang said.
People with ADHD do not entirely lack attention, he said, adding that they just have difficulty with attention regulation and executive function.
Some patients can sustain high levels of attention when they engage in hobbies or activities with immediate feedback, strong stimulation or tight deadlines, Yang said.
Chronic procrastination due to ADHD could also make “working against the clock” a habit for sufferers, he said.
Yang listed six major symptoms of adult ADHD: limited attention span, difficulties with organization and time management, forgetfulness, impulsivity, internal or external agitation, and emotional dysregulation.
However, people with such symptoms do not necessarily have ADHD, he said.
Other mental or physical conditions, such as anxiety, depression, sleep deprivation, stress, substance use or thyroid disorders could also lead to such symptoms, Yang said.
Those who are concerned that they might have ADHD should not rush to label themselves with the disorder, he said.
They should instead seek professional medical help for evaluation of their symptoms, development history, current conditions and other possible causes, Yang said.
Even if they are diagnosed with adult ADHD, they can still significantly improve their life with proper medication, therapy and lifestyle adjustments, he said.

The US is considering postponing the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after November’s APEC summit in Shenzhen, the South China Morning Post reported on Saturday.
The potential delay comes as Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) prepares to travel to Washington on Thursday for a state visit, it said.
Xi and US President Donald Trump are expected to discuss topics such as trade, rare earths, artificial intelligence (AI) safety and Taiwan, it said.
Photo: Screen grab from the Kongsberg Defence and Aerospace Web site
Chinese officials have requested the US not announce new arms sales for Taiwan ahead of Xi’s visit, the report quoted a source as saying.
There was a “strong possibility” Trump could extend the delay through to the end of the year, the report said, citing multiple sources.
The possible postponement is related to a planned Trump-Xi meeting at the APEC summit and Xi’s expected visit to Florida for the G20 summit in December, it said.
Sources described the timing of an announcement as a compromise between Trump, supporters of a tougher China policy and Taiwan lobbyists, the report said.
Trump had at one point considered deferring the arms sales decision until late 2028 or January 2029, but faced strong resistance from hardline China skeptics, it said.
There is also a possibility that the US government may opt to approve a smaller-scale arms sale to Taiwan in the period between the US-China meeting and the APEC summit, sources said.
However, the likelihood of a large, multibillion-dollar arms deal being approved is not high, they added.
Some China hawks have advocated a phased approach, approving smaller arms sales first to reassure Taipei, the report said.
Washington could notify Beijing in advance to avoid catching Chinese officials offguard or violating any mutual understanding between the two sides, a source said.
While Beijing would still likely protest publicly, it might reluctantly accept such sales without taking major retaliatory measures, they added.
China understands that the US cannot indefinitely postpone new arms sales decisions related to Taiwan, the report said.
Beijing made a similar request prior to Trump’s visit to China in May, and Washington at that time had reportedly withheld approval for an arms sale to Taiwan, it said.
After his trip, Trump called arms sales to Taiwan a useful “bargaining chip” in negotiations, it added.
US Representative John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the US and the Chinese Communist Party, on Friday last week urged Trump to take a firm stance at the summit with Xi.
He called on Trump to reject Chinese demands to halt arms sales to Taiwan and security cooperation with US allies in Asia, and warn Beijing against providing assistance to Iran.
He also called for tighter controls to prevent China from obtaining US AI and semiconductor technologies, and urged continued pressure for the release of detained US citizens.
Meanwhile in Taipei, former US deputy national security adviser Matt Pottinger during the Resilient Taiwan for Sustainable Democracy International Forum on Saturday said he does not expect the Trump-Xi summit to yield any major breakthroughs on trade or Taiwan, nor does he anticipate any significant agreement that would come at Taiwan’s expense.
Xi is likely to make a lengthy case to Trump, but just as then-US president Joe Biden rejected Xi’s demands at their summit in San Francisco several years ago, Trump is unlikely to take the bait, he said.
Additional reporting by Chen Cheng-yu

Ukraine launches attack on Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:10 UTC
01:37:10 KST

Ukraine yesterday launched what Moscow’s mayor called the biggest drone attack yet on the Russian capital, as Russians voted on the final day of a parliamentary election that Russian President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for the war in Ukraine.
The drone strikes killed two people in the Moscow region and two more in the Russian-held part of Ukraine’s Kherson region, including an election official, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin and election authorities said.
A facility at Moscow’s oil refinery, which has been targeted before, was also damaged.
Photo: AFP
“The biggest attack by enemy drones has been repelled,” Sobyanin said on Telegram. “This unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed.”
The State Duma vote, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, is expected to see the ruling United Russia party easily retain its dominance in a political system critics say does not tolerate dissent.
The Kremlin is likely to present the outcome as evidence of public backing for Putin’s policies and for the war, now in its fifth year with no sign of ending soon.
The election authorities say the three days of voting have proceeded smoothly despite cyberattacks reported on Saturday.
Turnout was more than 50 percent by early afternoon in Moscow, Interfax news agency reported, citing the Russian Central Election Commission.
Most anti-war candidates have been barred from the ballot.
Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in the past few years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict.
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news is punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
In an act of defiance, Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party’s name and the slogan “for peace.”
The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its special military operation in Ukraine. It casts the conflict — Europe’s deadliest since World War II — as part of an existential struggle with a hostile West.
Moscow says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia.
Russian electoral officials on Saturday said that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack. Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a “pseudo election.”

Culture spending to hit NT$65.9bn: Lai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:08 UTC
01:37:08 KST

The government’s overall culture-related funding would reach NT$65.9 billion (US$2.07 billion) next year, President William Lai (賴清德) said yesterday, as he outlined four priorities for the development of nation’s cultural sector.
Taiwan’s economy has expanded rapidly in the past few years, with economic growth expected to exceed 11 percent this year, while average per capita national income is projected to reach US$46,000, giving Taiwan an opportunity to become one of the world’s 20 largest economies, Lai said at the National Cultural Conference in Taipei.
“While a strong economy makes a country powerful, culture is what makes a country great,” he said. “Technology allows Taiwan to move fast, while culture enables it to go far.”
Photo: Screen grab from the Presidential Office’s Flickr page
Referring to his presidential campaign proposals for cultural sustainability and a “global Taiwan,” Lai said his administration would continue to increase cultural spending.
While the Ministry of Culture’s budget has been substantially cut or frozen by the legislature over the past two years, the Executive Yuan would not reduce its support for cultural development, he said.
The government has allocated NT$28.8 billion to expenditures overseen by the ministry next year, Lai said.
The total reaches NT$32 billion, an increase of about 7.9 percent from the previous year, when general-purpose subsidies are included, he added.
Factoring in special funds and related expenditures from other ministries and agencies, overall cultural spending would reach NT$65.9 billion, demonstrating the government’s resolve to support culture, he said.
Lai outlined four priorities for the nation’s cultural development amid challenges posed by artificial intelligence, digital transformation and changing global environment: cultivating future generations, strengthening local cultural identity, promoting technology innovation while safeguarding human dignity and helping the world better understand Taiwan.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) and Minister of Culture Li Yuan (李遠) also attended the opening ceremony of the conference.
The government would continue to support culture, particularly efforts to bring Taiwanese culture to international audiences, Cho said in his speech.
“The government’s support for culture will never retreat. We will continue moving forward,” he said.
Taiwan faces two major challenges in promoting its culture domestically and internationally, he said.
Domestically, the nation must resist “cultural killers” and protect cultural industries, he said, referring to legislative cuts to the Ministry of Culture’s budget.
Internationally, as foreign cultural influences are spreading through film and television, and the use of certain words and social media, such as Douyin (抖音) — the Chinese version of TikTok — Taiwan must guard against the erosion of cultural subjectivity, he said.
“If we cannot protect the subjectivity of Taiwan’s local culture, the encroachment of foreign cultures will erode the fundamental spirit of our democratic constitutional order and damage the hard-won foundations of our local culture,” he said.
The recommendations that emerged from the National Cultural Conference would be discussed by the Cabinet’s cultural affairs board, he said.

Festival celebrating Taiwanese culture with bubble tea rocks Maryland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:08 UTC
01:37:08 KST

The annual Taiwan Bubble Tea Festival was held in Rockville, Maryland, on Saturday, celebrating Taiwanese culture through the island’s iconic beverage.
According to the organizers, Taiwan Sister Cities (TSC) and the Rockville Sister Cities Corporation, visitors were able to sample Taiwanese specialties and enjoy themed performances at the festival.
In addition to bubble tea, the eighth edition of the celebration featured minced pork rice and gua bao buns as well as Taiwanese songs and dance.
Photo: CNA
The event was attended by officials from Taiwan and the United States, including Taiwan’s representative to the U.S. Alexander Yui, his deputy Yang Yi-shan (楊懿珊), American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) Washington Office Managing Director Ingrid Larson, and Rockville Mayor Monique Ashton.
Speaking at the festival, Ashton said Taiwan and the US are countries that share the values of democracy, inclusivity and cooperation.
Taiwan’s iconic beverage is now commonplace in her city, and if bubble tea can become so easily accepted, then so can love, acceptance and partnerships, Ashton said.
TSC Director Minze Chien (簡明子) said the weather Saturday was the best the festival had experienced since its inception, helping draw 18,000 visitors to its 43 booths that showcased not only Taiwan but also Hong Kong and Ukraine.
The good weather was in stark contrast to one year when there was heavy rain and only 3,000 people attended, Chien said.
Of the stalls, Chien said 22 were dedicated to food and beverages, of which five, including Taiwan’s popular bubble tea brand 50 Lan, sold bubble tea specifically.
The bubble tea festival, Chien said, is the largest of its kind in the US and features not just food and drinks but also singing and dancing.

Buyers snap up fruit after farmer refuses China sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:07 UTC
01:37:07 KST

A Hualien pomelo farmer refused to sell to China after the country announced it would permit more Taiwanese pomelo imports, prompting widespread support from Taiwanese consumers, who rallied to buy his fruit.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office last month said that China’s General Administration of Customs registered an additional 79 Taiwanese pomelo orchards and packing facilities in Hualien County, allowing more Taiwanese producers to export pomelos to China.
“I am a Hualien fruit farmer and I refuse to sell to China,” Liu Tzu-hao (劉子豪) from Ruisui Township (瑞穗) said in an online post.
Photo courtesy of Liu
Liu is a well-known farmer in the community and has served for years as head of the Ruisui fruit farmers’ marketing group.
His post was flooded with supportive comments from people praising his courage, with many buying boxes of pomelos to support him.
However, the post garnered negative comments when it was reposted on Chinese social media platforms, with Chinese users saying that they do not need Taiwan’s fruit.
Liu has frequently voiced his views at local Hualien forums, including supporting the recall of Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅?萁) and publicly backing Hualien County Council Speaker and independent county commissioner candidate Chang Chun (張峻).
“I am just being myself, thank you for all your support,” Liu said on Friday last week.
Liu said he is not a member of any political party and referred to himself as a small fruit farmer.
“I love my little, mountainous Taiwan,” Liu said, emphasizing that Taiwanese people do not need to grovel to anyone.
Liu grows more than 10 hectares of pomeloes, with this year’s harvest reportedly totaling hundreds of thousands of kilograms and filling the entire packing facility.
With support from Taiwanese, he announced yesterday that his pomelos had sold out, and that lots of orders are still waiting to be shipped.
Farmers should be able to stand on their own, Liu said, adding that he remains cautious about selling pomelos to China because “a box sells for less than NT$200 or NT$300 there.”
He sells directly to customers online and has built his own brand with a reputation for quality, allowing him to sell for much higher prices, he said.
The quality of his pomeloes and a loyal customer base give him the confidence to not sell to China, he said.

Philippine indigenous group in limbo over tech hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:06 UTC
01:37:06 KST

Indigenous leader Petronila Munoz walked across the sweeping Philippine grasslands her people called home for generations, uncertain about its future, as a sprawling tech hub for a US-led initiative takes shape.
With little information and no prior consultation, the indigenous chieftain said the Aeta Hungey people were uncertain how much of their land could be affected or what would become of the livelihood it provides.
“There’s still no clarity,” Munoz said inside the Aetas’ traditional meeting hall. “What will happen to us? That’s our biggest question.”
Photo: AFP
The US in April announced that the Philippines had joined Pax Silica, a US-led effort to bolster supply chains for semiconductors and rare earth elements and reduce participating countries’ dependence on China.
The Philippines has designated a 1,620-hectare site in New Clark City in Tarlac province, north of Manila, for a manufacturing hub aimed at producing high-end components for use in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.
The government estimates the initiative could attract up to US$70 billion in investment and create about 190,000 jobs, a major boost to a country with more than 3 million unemployed people.
The project has a long timeline. No tenants have been confirmed.
Plans to domestically process the country’s mineral resources could be even further away.
However, for about 1,000 Aetas, the prospect of displacement is already here.
In July, they received a letter from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) warning that the project “could affect your occupied lands.”
Visiting BCDA employees told them to leave by December and relocate to an area about 16km from their current home, without providing a master plan showing which parts of their ancestral domains would be affected, Munoz said.
The BCDA has offered them just 30 pesos (US$0.48) per square meter for their lands, an offer all declined, she said.
“Our lives, our livelihood and our culture are tied to this ancestral land,” Munoz said. “Land is more important. Money runs out.”
The BCDA declined to address specific questions about the Aetas’ situation and rejected a freedom of information request for the site’s official boundary map and geospatial data.
It said the information was being “withheld temporarily until the official action is finalized or published.”
At a Philippine Senate hearing last month, BCDA president Joshua Bingcang said the Aetas were living on government land.
Like many indigenous groups in the Philippines, they hold no land title.
Civic groups have also raised concerns about the project’s environmental impact, particularly the demand for water and electricity in a country plagued by droughts and rotational power outages.
The US Department of State said that “environmental, water, energy and community-impact studies” would inform the project’s design.
“Before any major development happens, we expect rigorous stakeholder impact assessments will take place,” a spokesperson said.
Bingcang told the Philippine Senate that investors would be required to build their own power and water systems.
Alvin Camba, research director at an AI firm focused on supply chains and risk assessment, said Manila’s close relationship with the US could motivate investors to set up shop despite the power concerns.
Last month, reports said Washington planned to warn countries they could be excluded from Pax Silica if they joined a rival framework backed by Beijing.
“This is where the advantage of the Philippines comes in. The Philippines is the least affected by Chinese capital in Southeast Asia,” Camba said, adding that the Philippines would offer foreign companies the ability to “disentangle” from China.
Political economist Calixto Chikiamco said that Pax Silica represents a “historic opportunity” for the Philippines to move beyond its traditional wheelhouse of microchip testing and packaging.
“We have to open up to foreign investment so that technology transfer [to the Philippines] will happen,” he said.
The BCDA has been conducting public consultations in Tarlac and nearby provinces, but the agency has yet to hold talks with Aeta Hungey, Munoz said.
The Aetas remain uncertain if the government would help them build new homes or provide land to cultivate for income if they are moved.
“I wish they would listen to us. They’re just talking among themselves,” she said, adding that she worried her people would not be qualified for the sort of new jobs Pax Silica promised.
While a proponent of the initiative, Chikiamco said the government was doing “a terrible job” explaining the benefits and tradeoffs it represented.
Camba agreed.
“I would actually advise the Philippine government to be very transparent about what’s happening. A big problem is transparency,” he said.
Still, the benefits outweigh the risks, he said.
“Every country that has ... jump-started development has had to make sacrifices,” Camba said.
However, 63-year-old Munoz, who hopes to be buried in her people’’s traditional burial ground, said she would not leave, even if a backhoe flattened her home.
“Why do we have to be the ones to sacrifice for the kind of development they want?” she asked.

However, the operation was called off after officials determined that an AI chatbot used by an analyst had misidentified the material the ship was carrying. The report was “entirely false,” but “almost started a war,” CNN quoted one source

Inside data center monitoring hubs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:04 UTC
01:37:04 KST

Steady attention is crucial when keeping watch over hundreds of data centers worldwide, facilities essential to online banking, messaging and artificial intelligence (AI) services that society uses.
Analysts are surrounded by digital maps and dashboards at the Singapore operations center of US firm Digital Realty Trust Inc, a global operator of the warehouse-like sites filled with whirring servers.
The goal is not simply to react when something breaks, but to detect warning signs, such as a sudden rise in temperature, early enough to prevent disruption.
Photo: AFP
Daniel Naing, 37, and his colleagues at the center in Singapore handle thousands of system alerts flagging signs of trouble each week.
The operations center and its two sister hubs, in Europe and the US, provide round-the-clock oversight of more than 300 data centers across six continents.
Digital Realty rents its server space to about 6,000 companies, with power loss and equipment failure the most common issues.
There are procedures for earthquakes and typhoons, and an approaching storm thousands of kilometers away is enough to put the team on standby.
Demand for data centers is a political hot potato in many places, as tech companies race to develop AI tools that require massive amounts of computing power.
Without them “nothing works” in our high-tech world, Digital Realty managing director and Asia Pacific head Serene Nah said.
Data centers are essential infrastructure — a matter “almost like national security,” she said.
“We need to be up running all the time.”
However, Nah said that “our business is very misunderstood” and has little support from the public, who believe data centers emit “a lot of carbon or heat” or “use up a lot of water.”
“Yet everyone’s scrolling their phones every day,” and for each swipe “the data needs to go somewhere.”
The company is prioritizing renewable energy such as solar panels and closed-loop server cooling systems that continuously recycle water, Nah said.
Data centers operate 24 hours a day, so the Singapore center takes the 7am to 7pm shift before hand-off to Europe.
Engineers must respond to an alert within minutes. The teams liaise with on-site staff and call on a global network of experts to help, while keeping clients updated.
The company’s operations center in Singapore is housed inside one of three data centers that the company runs in the city-state.
Most areas of the data center, whose roof is lined with solar panels, are off-limits for security reasons.
AFP was shown a room where rows of black server cabinets formed long, narrow corridors, with bundles of yellow cables running overhead and the computer servers’ high-velocity fans emitting a soft hum.
AI is accelerating the growth and complexity of data centers, but for the operations center, humans remain indispensable, said Terence Tang, head of the Asia Pacific global command center.
“We still need human intervention to really look at whether or not those are genuine outages, genuine alerts and alarms, because sometimes AI or automation can give you false positives,” Tang said.

Rupert Hammond-Chambers On Taiwan: The Fourth Taiwan Arms-Sale Freeze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:37:04 UTC
01:37:04 KST

Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China.
A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from the hegemonic Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
Given these circumstances, we must ask why US President Donald Trump’s second-term administration has now initiated the fourth Taiwan arms-sale freeze since 2005.
RECENT HISTORY OF TAIWAN ARMS-SALE FREEZES
US policy toward Taiwan has long suffered from a central failing: the belief that it cannot engage Beijing in meaningful and substantive dialogue while also maintaining a robust and lawful relationship with Taiwan. This position has manifested itself in many different ways — from the failure to consistently send senior US political appointees to engage with the democratically elected leadership on Taiwan, through to ignoring US law, via the TRA, requiring that America provide Taiwan with weapons of a defensive nature (highly subjective language in today’s world) to deter aggression from an expansionist CCP.
Including the current freeze, we have seen four major arms-sales freezes in the past 21 years, two under former US president George W. Bush from 2005-2007 and 2007-2008, and one under former US president Barack Obama from 2011-2015. These freezes retarded Taiwan’s force modernization, weakened deterrence across the Taiwan Strait, played havoc with Taiwan government budgeting processes, emboldened the CCP, and violated the TRA.
The first Taiwan arms freeze was the result of a refusal by the KMT to pass a defense budget during the presidency of Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁) of the Democratic Progressive Party. Chen had submitted budget requests to the Legislative Yuan to pay for a large package of weapons green-lighted by the Bush Administration in 2001. The KMT’s objections to funding the package sound remarkably like the narratives presented earlier this year, post President William Lai’s (賴清德) initial US$41 billion special budget submission. Over 70 attempts were made to move the budget forward over two years, with some programs finally breaking free in 2006.
In Bush’s second term, while launching the surge in Iraq, his administration sought to reduce tensions on the Korean Peninsula by prioritizing negotiations with relevant parties — including the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) and the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The China hawks from Bush’s first term, such as Ambassadors Paul Wolfowitz and Richard Armitage, had moved on. That left Bush Administration leadership without a dominant voice in Asian affairs. In 2001, the Bush administration wanted to accelerate arms sales to Taiwan and made a good start. But internal Taiwan politics and a hostile US National Security Council (NSC) unwittingly conspired to undermine these efforts, leading to a halt in sales. It wasn’t until 2006 that arms sales started to move through the US Foreign Military Sales (FMS) system with any urgency, and 2007 saw a series of four tranches of Taiwan arms sales notified to Congress.
Yet the progress faltered on the false premise that the US couldn’t both support Taiwan and engage with China on regional priorities such as negotiations with the DPRK. The administration believed that support for Taiwan would undermine or even scupper Chinese willingness to lean on the DPRK. In late 2007, with three Taiwan arms sales awaiting congressional notification (CN), the word came down from the White House that Taiwan CNs should be put on indefinite hold. From November 2007 to October 2008, the Bush Administration froze Taiwan arms sales. By the time the dam broke, nine programs were stuck awaiting notification to Congress.
Even then, the Bush Administration refused to notify all nine CNs at once over concerns that the total US dollar value would cause an issue with the CCP. They therefore notified a group of six programs for an arbitrary amount of US$6.4 billion, leaving the remaining programs untouched. The PAC-3 program was split in two, merely because it was deemed too provocative to notify the total dollar amount at once. The remaining programs were notified on Jan. 29, 2010, by Obama’s government, including what remained of the PAC-3 program. This significant freeze resulted in years-long delays, along with lost Taiwanese budget dollars and a steeper total cost. Meanwhile, China’s force modernization continued apace.
America’s accommodationist policies toward China reached a high point during the Obama Administration. It saw China engagement as a deliverable unto itself, and rather than producing substantive progress on bilateral issues, the policy came down to a never-ending series of engagements intended to give the relationship the optics of partnership and progress. This approach suited important constituencies, including the US business community, which saw a future in China of never-ending record profits, along with an increasingly powerful environmental lobby looking to engage China on curbing pollution and to globalize climate regulations. Obama’s government was rarely willing to entertain initiatives with the potential to get in the way of smooth China relations, including any engagement with Taiwan or selling it weapons.
The Obama Administration believed that making unilateral concessions on issues of importance to the CCP would lead to reciprocity. There was not. It was this mistaken belief that led America to halt arms sales to Taiwan for four years. There were no CNs since the Taiwan F-16 upgrade program in September 2011 — pushed through under heavy pressure from Congress led by Senator Cornyn (R-TX) — until a small and modest package in December 2015.
By this point, Xi Jinping (習近平) was general secretary of the CCP and China’s military modernization was accelerating rapidly. A halt in US support for Taiwan only increased the pace at which the military resource gap widened. Critical vulnerabilities in cross-Strait deterrence started to emerge. The arms-sale freeze was catalyzing the progress China was making in its efforts to dominate in Asia.
THE 1982 COMMUNIQUE & CHINA’S STANCE ON TAIWAN ARMS SALES
The 1982 Communique between the US and China sought to bound American arms sales to Taiwan while providing a pathway towards ending support. That commitment was conditional on the threat to Taiwan from the CCP being reduced and then halted. In essence, America agreed to stop selling weapons to Taiwan when China posed no military threat to the island and its people.
China sees only the American obligation in the 1982 communique while ignoring its own responsibility to cease threatening Taiwan. The two are inexorably intertwined, and the failure by China to follow through on its commitment to a peaceful resolution of cross-Strait differences also negates the US commitment to stop selling weapons to Taiwan.
It is essential to understand that China’s central issue with arms sales isn’t necessarily the platform or system being sold, or even the dollar value of the program(s). Rather, it’s the sovereignty conferred in the government-to-government sales process that underpins America’s security relationship with Taiwan. The sale could be a 7.62mm bullet or a fully loaded F-16 Block 70 Viper; the CCP objects equally.
The notion that appeasing China will result in a quid pro quo concession is false, as the CCP rejects outright any responsibility to change its behavior. It sees the obligation as America’s alone, and therefore devoid of any Chinese deliverables in exchange — whether to reduce the cross-Strait threat or to make a concession in another area.
This is how you get hollow promises to lean on the DPRK in 2008 and outright lies about island-building and militarization in the South China Sea during Obama’s term. There is no evidence that appeasing China on Taiwan arms sales results in improved behavior in other areas of US-China relations.
AMERICA FIRST ARMS TRANSFER STRATEGY
On Feb. 6, 2026, Trump signed an executive order to highlight the importance of foreign military sales in driving the expansion of America’s defense industrial base. The president is quite right to see the importance of foreign sales as an action that can support high-paying American jobs, lower unit costs for America’s own defense procurement, expunge Chinese companies from the defense supply chain, and urge partners and allies to accelerate their own force modernization efforts in the face of threats from China, Russia and other hegemonic powers.
Leveraging foreign military sales to bolster these efforts is wise. Taiwan defense procurement over the next three years, 2026 through 2028, including special budgets, could top US$55 billion to US$60 billion. The freezing or disruption of significant weapons buys undermines a well-calibrated Trump administration policy that is good for jobs and the American economy.
THE ONGOING TAIWAN ARMS-SALE FREEZE
In 2017, Trump assembled a serious and experienced Asia policy team with deep exposure to Taiwan. At the NSC, the State Department, and the Department of Defense, leadership were aware of how badly the arms sales process had been politicized and broken from 2006-2017. It took 12-18 months, but they got the system back up and running properly and managed to depoliticize US considerations. By 2019, CNs were starting to flow to Capitol Hill on a regular basis.
The first Trump administration demonstrated that the best course of action is to regularize arms sales, and US president Joe Biden continued to do so through his term. Given the expanding demands of Taiwan force modernization, keeping up a steady cadence of arms sales ensures no disruption to the process of enhancing deterrence. It supports Taiwan while also strengthening America’s own Indo-Pacific Command.
China continued to object, but the objections became increasingly rote and had little material impact on bilateral relations. Indeed, note that Chinese announcements of associated “sanctions” do not disrupt core Chinese interests; they’re designed primarily for domestic optics.
Trump’s meeting with Xi in Beijing this past May appeared to be mostly a non-event. There were photo opportunities and a general agreement that the trade truce should continue. However, when Trump boarded Air Force One back to the US, he started to talk about Taiwan. Xi’s entreaties over the prior 48 hours had clearly had some impact on Trump’s thinking, as he noted, “I’m not looking to have somebody go independent,” which mirrors China’s position on Taiwan’s status. Note that long-standing US policy states that America takes no position on Taiwan sovereignty, instead insisting only that all parties commit themselves to a peaceful resolution of their differences.
Trump went on to note that arms sales to Taiwan are a “very good negotiating chip for us.” That is emphatically not what the TRA says, but it is the third time over four administrations that a sitting US president has seen arms sales to Taiwan as a fungible commitment.
The last tranche of Taiwan arms sales was announced in December of last year. Media reports indicate that Taiwan has requested more PAC-3 launchers and missiles and more NASAMS, among other items, but CNs have now been stacking up at the Department of State over the past 10 months. In early April 2026, the administration was apparently ready to move forward with new sales. However, the process was frozen at that point, not coincidentally after a telephone call between Trump and Xi.
The threat posed by China toward Taiwan is acute, and still the CNs continue to stack up at the State Department. Taiwan is budgeting increasing sums of money to modernize its forces, and new FMS requests continue to arrive. This is exactly what Trump has demanded from partners and allies, and yet his government is actively blocking Taiwan’s efforts to move to 5 percent of GDP on defense (by 2030) in the mistaken belief that a freeze will improve his bargaining position with Beijing. It hasn’t in the past and it won’t now. Beijing will pocket the concession and maintain its position.
WHAT’S COMING NEXT
The growing stack of pending CNs at State is unlikely to be sent to Capitol Hill all at once but will likely be broken into smaller packages. Some may be notified as early as late September/early October after the Trump-Xi meeting in Washington, but it is possible that the freeze may be extended through the end of the year.
The Trump Administration has let the fox in the henhouse. Telegraphing sensitivity to the Chinese position on Taiwan this past spring, Trump has empowered China to affect his decisions. This rather than considering American national interest and his responsibility, embedded in law, to assist Taiwan in maintaining peace and security in the Taiwan Strait.
Trump will meet with Xi later this month, at APEC in November, and at the G-20 meeting in December. This makes for a calendar packed with reasons not to move forward with arms sales to Taiwan: the “tyranny of the calendar.” China’s sense of agency in Trump’s considerations also means that an arms sale could come with some cost to bilateral relations — we can expect a tantrum from Beijing. Trump reopened this door, and China will walk through it seeking to capitalize and spook him into further freezes and delays.
There is strong global demand for American weapons and when there’s a delay, even when resulting in an eventual sale, a customer country will end up further down the queue. Taiwan has an urgent need for weapons now, and delays result in deliveries over longer periods.
This irregular approach creates political and military uncertainty for Taiwan, and all the while the military balance across the Taiwan Strait remains precarious and Taiwan remains in need of further fortification.
Rupert Hammond-Chambers is the president of the US-Taiwan Business Council (USTBC), a senior advisor at Bower Group Asia and sits on the board of the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security.
At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, people will remember less what China achieved and more what the global south attained. China did not lose face: President Xi Jinping (習近平) was an honored guest in India, was endorsed as the chair of BRICS for next year, and China is to host the next summit. Yet the carefully crafted 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration (NDD), the longest BRICS declaration so far, reveals a subtle, but important shift. BRICS is moving from a loose grouping toward a more substantive platform for the global south, giving developing countries greater voice and bargaining space

Leaders return to UN amid wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
