01:37:03 KST

World leaders gather in New York this week for the UN General Assembly, bracing for US President Donald Trump’s return to the rostrum for a second year running, with talks centering on the widening conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine and the risks of artificial intelligence (AI).
Nearly 130 heads of state meet with the post-World War II order under strain and with the UN itself struggling to remain relevant and weathering attacks from Trump, who has slashed the US’ contributions and withdrawn from dozens of UN bodies.
Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), who last addressed the diplomatic jamboree via video in 2021, would skip New York in favor of one-on-one talks with Trump in Washington on Thursday, fueling debate about the UN’s relevance in addressing global crises.
Photo: Reuters
Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organization: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres completes his term at the end of this year, with no clear frontrunner in the race to replace him.
The 15-member UN Security Council might hold high-level meetings on Ukraine, AI and the Middle East, including talks with Arab leaders, diplomats said.
More than a year into Trump’s second term, “we would no longer say that the UN is in freefall, but we would say that it’s stuck in an open-ended crisis,” International Crisis Group global issues and institutions program director Richard Gowan said.
“The UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it seems to be trapped in a trauma center for the foreseeable future,” Gowan said.
The US avoided losing its vote at the assembly by paying US$725 million in contributions to the regular budget this week, but it still owes the organization more than US$1 billion dollars and makes ongoing demands for cuts and reforms.
The assembly meets shortly after several AI industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and escape human control.
Guterres has said that AI would be a major topic, adding that countries pushing its frontiers should set up “common guardrails in order to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level.”
The secretary-general has long proposed global governance of AI. In 2023, the UN created an advisory body on the technology, with members including tech executives, government officials and academics.
The warning has put Guterres at odds with Trump, who dismissed AI risks as a “hoax,” saying there is a “sick conspiracy” against it and that China would benefit from the doubt being cast on its development.
The Middle East would again be a focus of discussions, as the US-Israeli war on Iran continues to drive global inflation and destabilize the region. Gains by Houthi militants threaten shipping in the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and could further spike energy prices.
“It’s very difficult to have a military solution for that problem, and the experience of fighting in Yemen demonstrated how complicated it is to have successful interventions,” Guterres said, adding that the UN’s envoy on Yemen was making a “huge effort” to advance talks.
However, peace talks remain stalled, as Iran and the US continue to exchange strikes and Trump threatens a major escalation of the war.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the assembly on Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza that Israel denies — is to speak on Thursday.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas would for the second consecutive year not attend the gathering in person. The US, a close Israeli ally, again denied him a visa.
On Thursday, the General Assembly voted to allow Abbas to appear by video.
There is likely to be a high-level meeting on the conflict in Sudan on the sidelines, although a diplomatic breakthrough is unlikely, diplomats said.
Also on the agenda is Russia’s more than four-year-old war in Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergei Lavrov are to address the General Assembly.
Zelenskiy would likely seek to shore up Ukraine’s position ahead of what is expected to be another tough winter, diplomats said.
The UN Security Council has been unable to take action to end the conflict because permanent member Russia holds a veto.
Trump has at times appeared frustrated that he has been unable to broker an end to the war, a goal he declared a priority when he began his second term in January last year. Trump spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier this month, but it was unclear whether he plans to meet Zelenskiy in New York.
Guterres highlighted the impact the war was having on civilians, but also on food security and energy prices.
“The effective blockade existing in the Black Sea is creating enormous problems that add to the problems generated by the Middle East crisis, and I think it would be very important to find a way to allow Ukrainian exports and Russian exports of food, fertilizers and energy to take place in a safe way through the Black Sea,” he said.

Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
The first are those who clearly linked to China and building grassroots networks in Taiwan, it said.
For example, Labor Party candidate Chen Chu-ying (陳竹音) has publicly expressed support for unification with China, and said she hoped to give up her Taiwanese household registration to obtain a Chinese ID.
Chen plans to run for a New Taipei City council seat in the city’s 11th electoral district, and has maintained close contact with borough wardens in Sijhih, participated in temple activities and produced local videos to build her profile, the department said.
That approach is similar to that of China Unification Promotion Party founder Chang An-le (張安樂), who has long cultivated ties with neighborhoods, farmers’ and fishers’ associations and temples, it added.
The second are Chinese spouses, it said.
This year, 26 Chinese spouses registered to run for office, seven more than in the previous election and an increase of nearly 37 percent, the department said.
Nineteen are running for village or neighborhood chief, while two are seeking seats on municipal councils, two on county or city councils, one is running for township or city mayor, and two are seeking seats as township or city representatives, it said.
The participation of Chinese spouses in politics face many issues, such as nationality, loyalty obligations and eligibility for public office, the department said, adding that it is also necessary to determine whether such people are attempting to challenge existing laws.
Their eligibility to run, sources of campaign funds and political connections must all be strictly scrutinized, it said.
The third are politicians who have long maintained close ties with China’s “united front” and Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO), it said.
The department expressed concern over the eligibility of Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) candidate Xu Gong-fan (徐功凡) to run for Miaoli County Toufen Township (頭份) mayor, after reports said he had led delegations to China several times and been received by TAO officials.
The trips were also publicly praised on the official Web site of an official from China’s Sichuan Province.
“If these were ordinary city-to-city exchanges, why were the people receiving the delegations so often from the TAO?” the department asked. “If these were simply visits, why would China’s united front agencies continue to devote personnel and resources to engaging with local political figures, neighborhood chiefs and grassroots organizations in Taiwan?”
There are the questions that Taiwanese must ask, it said.
The government must investigate the matter in accordance with the law, the department said, adding that all candidates have a responsibility to clearly explain to voters their backgrounds and connections.
It called on the authorities to strictly scrutinize candidates’ eligibility, nationality status, political donations and overseas resources, saying that Taiwan’s grassroots democratic safeguards must be protected.

Notes from Central Taiwan:  Immigration: are we on the cusp?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:58 UTC
01:36:58 KST

Apetition on the Web site of the National Development Council (NDC) arguing that non-citizens receiving National Health Insurance (NHI) should make up payments from their birth to their current age has reached 5,000 signatures last week, the threshold requiring a response. The comments under the petition are predictably odious, proving once again that the Venn diagram of racism and idiocy is a perfect circle.
Also last week, the Ministry of the Interior proudly announced that the 400th “high-level professional” was approved for citizenship on Aug. 26. Four hundred carefully selected dual citizens! At that rate, sometime around the year 2600, Taiwan will finally have permitted enough dual citizens to make up for its current immigration deficit.
The suicidal immigration policies (remember that Venn diagram cited above?) are easy to see. But for all the frustration foreigners of every type experience with racism, it is easy to forget that things are much better than they used to be. I am old enough to remember being removed from two different cram school classrooms around 1990 at a parent’s request because I did not have blue eyes, hence my English clearly wasn’t good enough. Many old-timers can recount similar stories.
Photo courtesy of the National Immigration Agency
CHANGING ATTITUDES
The changes show up in the data. Every few years, the Taiwan Social Change Survey (TSCS) has a question about attitudes toward immigration. In 2003 it asked about what should happen to the number of immigrants using a scale of 1 (increased greatly) to 5 (reduced greatly). Less than 5 percent wanted increased immigration, while 66.1 percent wanted reductions. Since 2010, however, positive attitudes have outweighed negative, though negative attitudes have risen. Increased immigration seems to have modified Taiwanese attitudes somewhat.
It is easy to root out the response in racism and xenophobia. Yet the nation faces a massive external threat. One way the Taiwanese cope with that is resorting to economic nationalism. “In this light,” as Minjin Choi put it in a PhD thesis on welfare chauvinism in East Asia: “the fruits of economic growth are portrayed as strategic assets that must be reserved for the Taiwanese people to maintain sovereignty.”
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Labor
Hence, to the people on the inside of that dynamic, outsiders may appear as plunderers of hard-won gains.
At the same time, as much research shows, migrant groups are busy reshaping attitudes. The most obvious marker is language. It is one thing to see multiple languages in government-mandated domains like department offices or trains. It is quite another to marvel at the scrolling displays at 7-11 displaying beverage menu choices in several languages. That was unthinkable 30 years ago, and not just because the technology did not exist.
‘PERCEPTUAL BIAS’
Photo: Yang Ya-min, Taipei Times
A team led by Timothy S. Rich of Western Kentucky University explored attitudes towards southeast Asians in Taiwan (“All Are Not Equal: Taiwanese Public Opinion on Southeast Asian Immigration”, International Journal of Taiwan Studies). Although Taiwanese often claim to want skilled immigrants, Rich found that racism remained a problem.
“In sum, the results show a clear perceptual bias against Southeast Asian immigration, even when skills are taken into consideration,” they wrote.
Their survey also revealed that the strongest biases were against Indonesians, who were the largest group of migrant workers when the survey was performed.
As the researchers point out, Indonesian migrant workers are disproportionately women employed in caregiving (another cohort represents fishers in the distant water fleet, who Taiwanese seldom interact with). They are also Muslims, while Thais and Vietnamese are Buddhists or Christians, religions Taiwanese are more familiar with. In fact, a decade ago the Thai-style Four-Faced Buddha (四面佛) became popular, “with shrines popping up all over the place,” as Josh Ellis, the popular photo blogger, observed at the time. Many of my students reported visiting them to resolve personal problems.
Further, Thai and Vietnamese foods are ubiquitous, while Indonesian food remains a niche cuisine of migrant workers. Still, acceptance of religion and food augurs the possibility of acceptance of people.
CITIZENSHIP FOR MIGRANT WORKERS?
Although many of these migrant workers would make excellent citizens, the issue of “skills” remains a stumbling block. The Choi thesis suggests the reason: the demand for “skills” on the part of immigrants is a response to the perception that outsiders are plunderers and raiders of precious Taiwan economic development. If immigrants arrive with “skills” they evade the nationalist perception that they are plunderers.
The government’s pride in the tiny dribble of 400 high-level professionals is thus a distortion created by the shaping effect of economic nationalism. It is the wrong response, catering to rather than confronting the problem. It is also a dead end: Many of the economies from which Taiwan hopes to recruit skilled professionals are themselves aging and will increasingly compete for talent.
In two decades the global competition for skilled workers is going to be fierce, and countries with less brutal work cultures and higher salaries are going to easily out-compete Taiwan. The only solution is to do it the hard way: import couples with small children and train up the children.
The stumbling block is that many can’t imagine a world where children are vital economic assets whose potential is fostered by enculturation and education. Instead, they live in a mental world where children of outsiders are eternally parasites who never grow up to become productive citizens.
This year the number of foreigners in Taiwan broke 1 million. As Taiwanese age, this number will continue to rise. The policies to smooth this transition need to be implemented as soon as possible, and as they are implemented they will change the way Taiwanese think about migration. As dim as the prospects look at the moment, we may actually be sitting on the cusp of profound change. Much will depend on the leadership from above.
First, the government needs to directly address how economic nationalism distorts views of potential immigrants. Ironically, the very public investments of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) in Arizona (and Japan) may help change the possessive attitudes of Taiwanese toward their economic champions.
Another thing the government must do is raise the status of both children and motherhood. This is a moral action that relies on authority’s bully pulpit.
It should also begin by permitting migrants with children under three to bring them to Taiwan and raise them here. If handing out citizenship to migrant workers proves too radical, the government can grant the workers permanent residency and their children citizenship provided they are schooled in Taiwan. That first generation will encounter much racism, but their children will be Taiwanese.
As Taiwan ages and more migrant workers come in, change is inevitable. There is still time to choose the right direction.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

More than 21,700 swimmers from 38 countries took part in this year’s Sun Moon Lake International Swimming Carnival in Nantou County yesterday, organizers said.
A total of 451 swimmers from overseas and 197 swimmers with disabilities participated in the 44th edition of the event, the Nantou County government said in a statement.
The first swimmer to complete the about 3km course from Chaowu Pier on the lake’s northern side to Ita Thao Pier on the southern side was a 43-year-old man from Spain who registered under the Chinese name Chao Wei-shin (趙偉信), the statement said.
Photo courtesy of the Nantou County Government via CNA
He finished in a time of 56 minutes and 27 seconds.
Participating in the event for the first time, Chao described the swim as pleasant and Sun Moon Lake (日月潭) as beautiful.
Chao said that he would take part again if given the opportunity.
The first swimmer with a disability to reach the finish line was Chang Wei-chieh (張維捷) of Taipei, who swam the butterfly to sprint through the final stretch, the statement said.
A longtime participant in the event, Chang encouraged people with disabilities to exercise and enjoy themselves without being constrained by their condition.
“What everyone else is capable of, we are also capable of doing,” he said.
On Sunday morning, Nantou County Commissioner Hsu Shu-hua (許淑華) released 10,000 topmouth culter fry into the lake’s waters near Shuishe Port as a gesture to promote the protection of the lake’s ecosystem.
She then went to Chaowu Pier to fire the starting pistol and cheer on the swimmers, the statement said.
Hsu said participants were equipped with a chip on their wrists and another on their buoy boards this year for the first time to improve swimmer safety.
The system was aimed at making it easier to locate and identify swimmers who need assistance, she said.

AI expected to help ease inflationary pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:56 UTC
01:36:56 KST

Inflationary pressure driven by artificial intelligence (AI) remains manageable in Taiwan, the central bank said on Thursday, adding that wider adoption of AI is expected to boost productivity and eventually help ease inflationary pressure.
In a document released after its quarterly policymaking meeting on Thursday, the bank said massive investment in AI infrastructure by major cloud service providers worldwide had driven up memory prices, making technology products such as PCs more expensive.
In the US, personal consumption expenditures rose 3.7 percent in July from a year earlier, while electricity prices and prices for information processing devices increased 4.0 percent and 15.5 percent respectively, the bank said.
Photo: CNA
Electricity and information processing equipment contributed to overall inflation only 0.05 and 0.24 percentage points respectively, it said.
In Taiwan, prices of PCs, other computer-related products and computer software and consumables rose 7.51 percent, 16.94 percent and 1.66 percent respectively year-on-year in the first eight months of this year, the bank said.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.04 percent last month, while electricity rates increased an average of 4.47 percent from a year earlier in the same month, it said.
Electricity rates and information processing equipment together contributed only 0.16 percentage points to CPI growth during the January to August period, indicating that AI-driven inflationary pressure remained under control, it added.
The bank said technological innovation driven by AI is expected to improve productivity and lower unit labor costs through an increase in the supply of goods and services, helping ease inflationary pressure in the long term.
On Thursday, the bank raised its CPI growth forecast from 1.91 percent to 2.03 percent, above the 2 percent alert threshold, citing a surge in international crude oil prices amid geopolitical tensions and rising service costs.
Its core CPI forecast, which excludes vegetables, fruits and energy, was raised from 1.90 percent to 2.16 percent, also above the 2 percent threshold.

Taiwan to crack down on deepfakes ahead of voting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:53 UTC
01:36:53 KST

The Ministry of Justice yesterday said authorities would crack down on deepfake election content ahead of the year-end local elections.
Law enforcement agencies would step up forensic tracing, take down deepfake content promptly, and strictly investigate and hold perpetrators accountable in accordance with the law, the ministry said.
The agencies would track emerging deepfake trends, enhance intelligence analysis and cooperate with national security forces to counter foreign cognitive warfare, it said, adding they would also streamline cross-agency emergency response and collaborate with news outlets, major digital platforms and messaging apps to enable the fast removal of false content.
Photo: Reuters
The Civil Servants Election and Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法) mandates that people who disseminate deepfake audio or video misinformation targeting election candidates may face a maximum penalty of seven years in prison, and social platform operators who fail to comply with removal orders also face penalties, the ministry said.
The ministry issued the reminder as the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rendered the adage “seeing is believing” increasingly outdated.
There have been reports of deepfakes of politicians, casting a shadow over Taiwan’s democratic system.
For example, an AI-generated deepfake video showed Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Changhua County commissioner candidate Chen Su-yueh (陳素月) saying that she can easily “win [the election] hands down.”
In response, Chen’s campaign headquarters held a news conference to clarify the situation, filed a report and demanded that the platform take the video down.
Meanwhile, former Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) New Media Department director Wei Chun-yu (韋淳祐) was questioned by the Criminal Investigation Bureau for allegedly using AI to fake President William Lai’s (賴清德) voice in a party video when a cooking oil scandal broke out earlier in the summer.
When former Taipei mayor Hau Lung-bin (郝龍斌) last year ran in the KMT chairperson election, he was falsely depicted in an AI-generated video kissing Taipei City Councilor Liu Tsai-wei (柳采葳).
Liu, accompanied by Broadcasting Corp of China chairman Jaw Shaw-kong (趙少康), reported the incident to the police.
Jaw at the time called it a national security issue, accusing China of interfering in the KMT chairperson election.
In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, several media outlets on Aug. 16, 2023, received an e-mail with an audio file of someone claiming to be Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) founder and presidential candidate Ko Wen-je (柯文哲).
The fake Ko said “Lai’s US trip received significant fanfare, as everyone who went could earn NT$800.”
The TPP said the voice was not Ko’s and filed a report with the Investigation Bureau’s Taipei City Field Division.
In November the same year, a deepfake video of Lai commenting on the KMT-TPP alliance circulated on social media.
“The KMT and the TPP represent the mainstream public opinion in Taiwan, and both their candidates are suitable national leaders, so regardless of who serves as president or vice president, they make the right team,” the fake video said.
Technical analysis confirmed that the video was created using deepfake technology, with a manipulation probability of more than 98 percent, and was likely an attempt to influence voter judgement and turnout.

Ed Sheeran is wrong about his fans’ political engagement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:52 UTC
01:36:52 KST

It must have come as a surprise to Ed Sheeran when all of his support acts withdrew from the remainder of the US leg of his tour. The US rapper Macklemore had triggered the walkout when he gave an impassioned speech calling for a “free Palestine” on stage and was dropped for doing so. The decision by the remaining acts to drop out in solidarity exposed a deep divide in the modern music industry. Some artists still insist on keeping politics out of music, while others expect music to speak to our perilous times.
After he was dropped, Macklemore wrote that Sheeran’s “typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before,” to which Sheeran responded: “I am not complicit” and “those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum.”
I think that the concept of expectation is worth probing. The idea that artists should make their political sentiments known is often dismissed as a parasocial delusion, one particularly rampant among young people on social media who “call out” musicians for their silence (indeed, young people are far more likely to be in favor of musicians using their concerts to make political statements).
Artists are not politicians, the criticism goes, and to consider them as such distracts from, even compromises, the purpose of art as a forum for personal expression and of escapism. In other words, why not just enjoy the music instead of expecting activism from musicians, too?
The problem with that idea is that it treats a separation of art and politics as natural rather than something determined by historical convention. It was not so long ago that expectations were quite different. There used to be a neater division between countercultural musicians who were relegated to the periphery and mainstream artists who would be disciplined if they spoke up.
The MTV era of music in the 2000s prioritized blockbuster, spectacle and glamor, while avoiding political, social and economic controversies. Artists were generally expected to keep politics out of their music. When Madonna challenged that idea in 2003 with her single American Life, which opposed US foreign policy and jingoism at the onset of the Iraq war, the backlash was heavy: She was forced to dump its “un-American” music video, and faced heavy radio blacklisting. It took years for the Chicks, then known as The Dixie Chicks, to recover commercially from the backlash they faced to their criticism of the Iraq War and former US president George W. Bush around the same period.
Today, the expectations that audiences have of artists are different from two decades ago. Partly, this is because the economics and the technology behind the music industry has changed. In the age of streaming, it is harder to silence artists who have made politically problematic statements — radio station blacklisting is far less fatal than it was before people discovered music through their phones and algorithms.
Interestingly, this greater political autonomy also means that the biggest artists take less of a commercial hit in their worst moments. After Kanye West’s anti-Semitic rants (which the rapper apologized for), his album Vultures still reached No. 1 on the Billboard charts in 2024. On his most recent tour, he performed at AT&T stadium in Arlington, Texas, one of the venues that banned Macklemore from performing.
In any case, this greater autonomy pushes young fans to ask: Why not take the risk? Why not speak? Particularly in the case of Palestine, it has often been smaller and less influential artists who have done so. Think of how the scale of Sheeran’s commercial reach, by contrast, dwarfs that of the artists around him who have risked more by speaking out.
Artists, alternative and mainstream, have also set this expectation for each other. The stances a musician has taken on pressing issues are no longer just cudgels used against them. Rather, silence on these matters has become a source of shame.
Billie Eilish rebuked her fellow celebrities for not taking a stance against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the US and its killing of civilians. The Irish singer-songwriter CMAT, who I saw at Glastonbury last year leading a “free Palestine” chant on the Pyramid Stage, had this to say while receiving the award for best album at the Ivor Novello Awards this year: “I have a very specific idea of what songwriting is supposed to be for, and I think it is to reflect the times through your own personal view so that everybody can have something to connect to and something to learn from years later. And now I would compel my fellow artists in the room, it is not the time to sit on the fence.”
The political shift in music also reflects a tonal shift. Artists have become more emotionally intimate with their audiences. I was struck by an analysis published earlier this year by the music data company Musixmatch for The Economist, which assessed lyrics from the Billboard charts to conclude that pop music has become “gloomier.” The most popular songs increasingly invoke sadness, angst and heartbreak.
A study in The Times also found that the musical mood has become more downbeat. This is in itself not surprising — listeners increasingly want authenticity from musicians and depend on it for a sense of connection. Think of the music of Eilish and CMAT, both of whom are popular with young audiences and praised for filterless emotion. They invoke that gloom, vulnerability and emotion — in other words, they communicate pain as a central tenor of their sound.
As CMAT said of her music, which muses on isolation, capitalism and disillusionment: “Everyone has the same wants and desires, and if you’re really honest as an artist with your pain, it will always connect.” For many young people, part of the pain they have felt in the past few years has been in witnessing the events in Gaza, as well as the rising global tide of far-right populism, the climate crisis and instability. So for a generation that is increasingly accustomed to having their despair made audible through gloomier music, why would they not increasingly expect artists to draw connections between their personal pain and what is causing it?
Artists, then, cannot assume that the old bargain still holds. Sheeran’s insistence on an apolitical arena of music is increasingly anachronistic — a position that has exposed the faultlines of modern music. Many listeners increasingly seek emotional clarity as well as moral clarity. Whether popular music has risen to that moment would be judged by history. However, for now, as the expectation changes, it is down to artists to decide if they change with it.
Jason Okundaye is an assistant opinion editor at The Guardian.

China did not lose face: President Xi Jinping (習近平) was an honored guest in India, was endorsed as the chair of BRICS for next year, and China is to host the next summit. Yet the carefully crafted 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration (NDD), the longest BRICS declaration so far, reveals a subtle, but important shift. BRICS is moving from a loose grouping toward a more substantive platform for the global south, giving developing countries greater voice and bargaining space

Warren Buffet’s son to ensure firm’s ‘culture’ continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:49 UTC
01:36:49 KST

Berkshire Hathaway Inc has been synonymous with Warren Buffett. It falls to his oldest son, Howard Buffett, to keep the conglomerate’s “culture” alive.
Friday’s announcement that Warren Buffett, 96, stepped down as chairman means the longtime investor would no longer have a management role at the company he took over in 1965, or be a regular sounding board for Greg Abel, who succeeded him as chief executive officer in January.
Howard Buffett, 71, is assuming a different role as non-executive chairman, focused on preserving Berkshire’s culture and values. It is the latest move in a years-long leadership transition.
Photo: Reuters
“This one is really about continuity,” University of Notre Dame business school management professor Michael Withers said. “The test moving forward will be whether Abel and Howard can honor [Warren Buffett’s] legacy while still giving Berkshire room to adapt to a market that looks very different from the one Buffett mastered.”
Their longtime presence could assure investors and analysts who do not expect, or want, big changes at the approximately US$1.1 trillion conglomerate, which owns the BNSF railroad, car insurer Geico Corp, and a slew of energy, industrial and retail companies, along with a stock portfolio that includes American Express Co, Apple Inc and Coca-Cola Co.
Abel joined Berkshire in 2000 when it bought the former MidAmerican Energy, and became part of Berkshire’s leadership team in 2018. Howard Buffett has been with Berkshire even longer, as a director since 1993.
“Howie’s there as a watchdog,” said James Armstrong, president of Henry H. Armstrong Associates in Pittsburgh, and a longtime Berkshire investor. “Minimize bureaucracy, stay focused on long-term goals, put the shareholders first, no self-dealing, no corruption and widen the moat that protects Berkshire’s businesses.”
Warren Buffett wrote on Friday in a shareholder letter that Abel has exceeded his “sky high” expectations.
“Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against,” Buffett wrote.
Buffett still controls more than 13 percent of Berkshire’s stock and about 30 percent of its voting power. These percentages would decline as his shares get distributed to foundations overseen by his children.
CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert called Howard Buffett’s lack of management experience a shortcoming in Berkshire’s succession plan.
“Compared to other family dynasties, typically when you have the heir apparent’s son he’s usually involved in day-to-day operations,” she said. “Howard Buffett doesn’t have that.”
Berkshire’s board has several directors with management experience who could act as guides.
“New managers do not have the same intuition that only time and experience can bring,” Zacks Investment Management chief market strategist Brian Mulberry said. “Buffett’s son and Abel have been in the Berkshire ecosystem for long enough that this lag should be minimal but not nothing.”
Gardner, Russo & Quinn LLC partner Tom Russo, a longtime Berkshire investor, recalled Warren Buffett telling him and other Stanford Business School students in 1983 that “you couldn’t make a good deal with a bad person.”
He said Abel and Howard Buffett should respect that thinking. Time will tell how.
“This is new territory,” Russo said.

Hermit crabs under threat: experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:42 UTC
01:36:42 KST

The Hengchun Peninsula’s (恆春半島) coastal ecosystems are facing a severe ecological crisis, with invasive yellow crazy ants, overfishing and regulatory loopholes endangering terrestrial hermit crabs, Conservation researchers have warned.
While efforts to protect terrestrial hermit crabs saw success in the early 2000s after a public campaign to provide them with discarded shells, surveys conducted in 2024 and last year found that large hermit crabs had almost completely disappeared from coastal forests, Taiwan Academy of Ecology chairman Liu Hung-chang (劉烘昌) said last week.
Commercial catching has intensified as larger crabs command higher prices in the market, while invasive yellow crazy ants kill many land crabs and other native species for protein, Liu said.
Photo: Tsai Tsung-hsien, Taipei Times
A 2023 survey of the protected coconut crab, a giant land hermit crab, found that only one of nearly 100 crabs weighed more than 1kg, raising concerns about reproduction among the population, he said.
Protecting land crabs is essential to restoring the coast’s ecosystem as they break down fallen leaves and accelerate microbial activity in the soil, Liu said, urging people not to catch, buy or harm them.
Land hermit crabs are an evolutionary “orphan group,” as their animal family, the Coenobitidae, is the only one within the Anomura animal group that has fully adapted to life on land, Kenting National Park land crab researcher Li Jheng-jhang (李政璋) said.
They rely on the microenvironment inside their shells to retain enough moisture to survive on land, making habitat conservation a top priority, Li said.
While the coconut crab is a protected species, other common land hermit crabs that are often sold are not, marine biologist Chiu Yu-wen (邱郁文) said.
People selling them often claim they are bred in captivity, but this is not possible, Chiu said.
Current technology is unable to breed them in captivity on a commercial scale, meaning that 100 percent of the land hermit crabs sold on the market are caught in the wild, Liu said.
Authorities should first verify that any animals being sold are legally sourced under the Act on Wildlife Conservation (野生動物保育法), Chiu said.
They should also require sellers to provide the appropriate documents as required under the Regulations Covering Commercial Wildlife Raising and Breeding (營利性野生動物飼養繁殖買賣加工管理辦法), he added.
Authorities should enforce the Environmental Education Act (環境教育法) and animal welfare standards to prevent illegally collected wild animals from being passed off as legally sourced, he said.
The Kenting National Park Headquarters launched a campaign calling on people to return crabs to nature, warning that wildlife protection laws are inadequate and that greater public awareness is needed to protect the Hengchun’s Peninsula’s coastal ecosystem.
Hermit crabs are difficult to keep in captivity and their natural habitat is the best place for them to live, park headquarters director Hsu Shu-kuo (許書國) said, adding that people should learn about them through wildlife observation and environmental education rather than buying them.
While hunting wild animals within a national park is illegal under the National Park Act (國家公園法), there are disputes over what regulations apply to the sale of such animals outside national parks, Han said.
Enforcement under the Act on Wildlife Conservation is challenging because local governments have often not designated protected areas as required, leaving loopholes that illegal traders can exploit, he said.

Aerospace Industrial Development Corp (AIDC, 漢翔航空工業) has finished production of the nation’s T-5 Brave Eagle (勇鷹) advanced jet trainers, with the final aircraft scheduled to be formally delivered at a ceremony on Thursday.
The delivery of the trainer jets marks the end of the program, which dates back to 2017, with the first prototypes completed in 2019. Fifty-six of the 66 trainers had been delivered as of May.
The Brave Eagle was developed and produced by AIDC and the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology.
Photo: Taipei Times
The program has provided a foundation for the development of a domestically produced next-generation primary trainer and main combat aircraft, and contributed to the development of Taiwan’s domestic aerospace supply chain, AIDC said.
The Brave Eagle has taken over as the air force’s advanced trainer, a military source said yesterday.
The AT-3 advanced jet trainer, which had been in service for more than 40 years, was retired at the end of July, while the F-5E/F jets previously used for operational training have also been phased out.
The air force’s three-stage pilot training program has been reduced from three aircraft types to two. The first student pilots to transition directly from the T-34C primary trainer to the Brave Eagle, bypassing the intermediate stage, have also completed their solo-flight tests and entered service.
In addition to routine training, the air force’s Thunder Tigers Aerobatics Team has transitioned to the Brave Eagle. Several aircraft were modified by AIDC with colored smoke-generation systems.
The aircraft are expected to be used for formation aerobatics at major national celebrations and air force open-house events.
The Brave Eagles are deployed mainly with the Flight Training Command at Gangshan Air Base (岡山基地) in Kaohsiung and at Chihhang Air Base (志航基地) in Taitung County.
The jets’ logistics support and serviceability have remained stable, military sources said.
The Brave Eagle shares design elements and a development lineage with the Indigenous Defense Fighter (經國號) and has space for weapons in its basic design. The air force plans to use air-to-air and air-to-ground weapons for the Brave Eagle, which could allow it to be used as a light attack aircraft during wartime.

Asian Games open with glitzy ceremony
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:39 UTC
01:36:39 KST

The 20th Asian Games on Saturday opened in Nagoya with a glittering ceremony of dance and fireworks following a buildup marred by operational gaffes and logistical problems.
Five years after the Tokyo Olympics played out at empty venues due to COVID-19 restrictions, Japan welcomed fans to the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium for a curtain-raiser that was initially subdued before bursting into a festival of color and sound.
Japanese Emperor Naruhito declared the Games open after watching the parade of 45 nations and regions at a dignitaries’ table along with International Olympic Committee president Kirsty Coventry.
Photo: Reuters
Naruhito’s visit with royal family members was accompanied by a heavy security operation. Organizers had said up to 10,000 police were deployed for the ceremony.
“While the world is too often divided by conflict, they [the Asiad athletes] remind us that sport remains a powerful force for peace, understanding and friendship among nations,” Olympic Council of Asia President Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad al-Thani said in a speech.
Japan’s father-and-son duo of Shigenobu and Koji Murofushi, former Asian Games champions in hammer throw, jointly lit the cauldron after climbing a set of stairs at the end of the torch relay.
Photo: AP
Organizers would hope the ceremony can draw a line under a rocky buildup laden with complaints from athletes and officials involving accommodation and transport.
Japan’s reputation for precision and efficiency has been under scrutiny as the nation welcomes more than 11,000 athletes competing for 369 gold medals in a whopping 43-sport program.
Instead of building a dedicated Games village, organizers have housed the athletes and officials in a mix of hotel rooms, temporary wooden containers and a cruise ship docked in the bay as a cost-cutting measure.
Several national team delegations, including hosts Japan, have found the arrangements below par, complaining of mix-ups and double-bookings, while South Korea said the containers at Garden Pier were too cramped for their basketballers.
India’s powerful cricket board took matters into their own hands, arranging for the men’s star-studded cricket team to stay in a separate hotel due to a tight allocation of beds from organizers.
Delegations have also lamented long waits for the athletes registering on arrival and have found buses turning up late or sending their athletes to the wrong venues.
The Olympic Council of Asia, which runs the quadrennial Games, on Saturday acknowledged the problems, but played them down as teething difficulties.
Directed by Yukihiko Tsutsumi, the opening ceremony made a low-key start, with classical music and dance on a heart-shaped stage before the parade of nations which featured a delegation from reclusive North Korea.
The spectacle ramped up later though, with dancers in boiler suits marking Nagoya’s manufacturing tradition and a fireworks display closing the night.

BOOKMAN BILINGUAL 雙語書林： Chinglish or Natural English? 中式英語或道地英語？
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:38 UTC
01:36:38 KST

1. 請你給我介紹一本好詞典好嗎？
ˇ Would you recommend a good dictionary for me?
χ Would you introduce me a good dictionary?
Photo: AdobeStock l 照片：AdobeStock
註︰把某甲介紹給某乙，使他們相識，或把某物、某種風俗習慣傳到另一地方，用introduce。把某物介紹、推薦給某人，或把某人推薦給某人，應用 recommend，例如：
Can you recommend a good dentist to me?
2. 他在這次生病以前一向洗冷水澡。
ˇ He used to take cold showers before his recent illness.
χ He was used to take cold showers before his recent illness.
註︰be used to 作「對……已習慣」解，used 是形容詞，to 後面接名詞或動名詞。如：He was used to cold showers. 或 He was used to taking cold showers.。若表示過去常做，而現在不如此，應該用 used to 接動詞原形。例如：
He used to take a walk before breakfast.（現在早餐前不散步了。）
He is not what he used to be.（他跟以前不一樣了。）
3. 史達林利用特務來剷除政治對手。
ˇ Stalin made use of the secret service to get rid of political rivals.
χ Stalin took advantage of the secret service to get rid of political rivals.
註︰to take advantage of something 作「利用」、「趁」解。例如：
Taking advantage of my spare time, I read widely.
to take advantage of someone 作「用手段欺騙人家」解。「利用某人而自己得利」應該用 to make use of。
4. 我懷疑他騙了你。
ˇ I suspect that he tricked you.
χ I doubt that he tricked you.
註︰suspect 和 doubt 都可以作「懷疑」解，但 suspect 是「有點感覺到」、「覺得可疑」、「有點發覺（危險、陰謀、犯罪行為）」，可能有其事的意味較多。例如：
I suspect that he had something to do with this.（我懷疑他與此事有關。）
I suspect him to be seriously ill.（我懷疑他病得很厲害。）
doubt 是「懷疑」、「不確定」，除了在否定句和疑問句裏可接 that 外，後面常接 if, whether, what 等疑問連接詞。試比較：
? I don’t doubt that he was there.（我相信他真的在場。）
I doubt whether he has lost the package.（我懷疑他真的丟了包裹。）
5. 他拒絕回答我的問題。
ˇ He refused to answer my question.
χ He rejected to answer my question.
註︰refuse to do something 表示「拒絕做某事」；reject 通常表示拒絕接受某物、某人的提議或申請，後面不能接不定詞。
She refused to help us.
They rejected his proposal.
Exercises:
A. 他老是佔我便宜。
He always takes __________ of me.
1. advantage
2. using
3. profit
4. cheap
B. 我懷疑這個故事是否真實。
I __________ whether the story is true.
1. suspect
2. dread
3. doubt
4. consider
Answers:
A. 1
B. 3
文章由書林出版公司提供：
www.bookman.com.tw

2026-09-20
16:36:38 UTC

Two of Taiwan’s international carriers, EVA Airways and Starlux Airlines, secured prestigious five-star airline ratings at this year’s Skytrax World Airline Awards held in London on Friday.
EVA Air also won three world No. 1 honors, while Starlux was named the world’s cleanest airline.
EVA Air said in a statement on Saturday that it was honored to have the world’s best premium economy class and the best premium economy class amenities while also being recognized as the world’s most family-friendly airline.
Photo: CNA
The carrier also retained Skytrax’s five-star airline rating for the 11th consecutive year.
The five-star rating is considered one of the airline industry’s highest honors and is awarded following professional audits of airline product and frontline service standards, according to the international airline review organization Skytrax.
EVA Air received a total of 18 top 10 rankings in this year’s awards, it said.
Executive vice president Liao Chi-wei (廖至維), who accepted the awards in London on behalf of the airline, said that the recognition belonged to the airline’s entire workforce.
The airline also said it would launch five weekly nonstop flights between Taoyuan and New Delhi beginning Dec. 1, further expanding its Asian network and bolstering Taiwan’s role as a regional transit hub.
Starlux said it retained its five-star airline certification for a second consecutive year after first earning the distinction last year. The airline made its commercial debut in January 2020.
Starlux also ranked first in the world’s cleanest airline category, which evaluates cabin cleanliness, including seats, tray tables, carpets and lavatories.
Starlux CEO Glenn Chai (翟健華) said the awards recognized the company’s commitment to service quality and the dedication of its employees to maintaining high standards across every aspect of the passenger experience.
In terms of airline rankings, EVA Air ranked 11th in the world, up from 12th last year, Starlux ranked 13th, up from 18th last year, and Taiwan’s other major international carrier, China Airlines, ranked 30th, up from 37th last year.
Nine of the top 10 airlines in Skytrax’s ratings were Asian-based, led by Singapore Airlines, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific Airways and ANA All Nippon Airways. The only non-Asian airline in the top 10 was Air France, which ranked seventh.
Dubbed the “Oscars of the aviation industry,” the annual Skytrax World Airline Awards have been held since 1999. The awards are based on global passenger satisfaction surveys evaluating airlines’ products and services.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:36 UTC
01:36:36 KST

Germans yesterday began voting in two state elections where far-right and far-left gains could send fresh shock waves through Berlin and rock the government of embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Merz, 70, has scheduled a crisis meeting of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party leadership to discuss the first results as they come in from the regional polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The chancellor, in power for 16 months, has also cleared his calendar for the following days and skipped a trip to the UN General Assembly to deal with potential aftershocks from the votes.
Photo: Reuters
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party dealt a stunning defeat to the CDU two weeks ago in Saxony-Anhalt, fueling speculation that internal party support for Merz is wobbling.
“I’d be in favor of the AfD winning, because then they’ll have to prove themselves: Either something will happen, or it’ll be the last time they get any votes,” retiree Peter Sommer said outside a polling station in Schwerin, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s state capital.
The election debacle came as Merz’s approval ratings have nosedived and he has struggled to push through promised economic and social welfare reforms with his coalition partners the Social Democratic Party (SPD).
Polls suggested that the AfD would make fresh gains yesterday, although it is unlikely to come within reach of power in either state — unlike in Saxony-Anhalt where it fell just a few seats short of an absolute majority.
Outside a polling station in the south of the capital, Moritz Lembke-Oezer, 43, said that although he fears that the vote could benefit the AfD, he hopes “the CDU will be punished” by this election.
“Maybe then Friedrich Merz will be gone,” the Berlin native said, adding that he plans to vote for Die Linke because of the far-left party’s promise to tackle the capital’s dire housing crisis.
Merz received some badly needed support from CDU powerbrokers on Wednesday, when eight state premiers declared jointly that Germany needs “stability now more than ever” rather than “discussions about personnel.”
However, they did not issue a personal endorsement for Merz.
The CDU yesterday faced different challenges unique to those regions.
In the northeastern coastal state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Merz’s party is an onlooker to the main battle between the SPD of popular state Premier Manuela Schwesig and the AfD.
While the AfD was polling at 36 percent against the SPD’s 37 percent, according to public broadcaster ZDF, Merz’s CDU, at just 6 percent, was dangerously close to missing the five percent hurdle needed to stay in the state parliament.
A CDU crash below that line would be a historic first and heap enormous pressure on Merz.
In Berlin, the ruling CDU is running a neck-and-neck race against Die Linke, which promises drastic steps to solve the housing issue and is popular with young people.
A CDU defeat there would be another black eye for Merz — especially at the hands of Die Linke, which wants to curb corporate power and leans toward Moscow.
“In personal terms, the situation is quite dramatic” for Merz, Infratest Dimap pollster Roland Abold said.
“In our last survey in September, 13 percent were still satisfied with his political performance. These are the lowest figures we have ever recorded for an incumbent chancellor,” Abold said.

16:36:35 UTC

Taiwan will experience partly cloudy to sunny weather this week, with favorable conditions for moon-gazing during the Mid- Autumn Festival on Friday, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.
CWA forecaster Cheng Chieh-jen (鄭傑仁) said that generally cloudy to sunny conditions with relatively little moisture are expected across Taiwan through Saturday.
Cheng said seasonal northerly to northeasterly winds are expected today and tomorrow, bringing isolated brief showers to southern Taiwan and mountainous areas in central Taiwan early in the morning.
Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
More rain is possible in mountainous areas in southern Taiwan in the afternoon on both days, while isolated brief showers are also expected along the northern coast and in northeastern Taiwan tomorrow, he said.
From Wednesday to Saturday, winds are forecast to shift to an easterly direction, with isolated brief showers expected along the northern coast, in eastern Taiwan and on the Hengchun Peninsula.
Meanwhile, localized brief showers are possible in mountainous areas in southern Taiwan in the afternoon, while isolated brief showers are expected in southern Taiwan and mountainous areas in the northern half of Taiwan, Cheng said.
With weather conditions on Friday and Saturday expected to remain generally stable, with only occasional clouds in eastern Taiwan, most areas across Taiwan will have good opportunities to view the full moon, he said.
Taiwan celebrates the Mid-Autumn Festival, also known as the Moon Festival, on the 15th day of the eighth month of the lunar calendar, which falls on Friday this year.
Beginning Sept. 27, however, weather conditions are expected to become unstable as tropical systems develop and change course, bringing localized brief showers to eastern Taiwan and the Hengchun Peninsula in the south, Cheng warned.
Temperatures are expected to remain relatively stable over the week, Cheng said, with highs of around 29-32°C in northern and eastern Taiwan and 32-34°C in central and southern Taiwan.
In addition, Cheng reminded people traveling to Japan to pay attention to Typhoon Dujuan, which remained over waters south of Japan yesterday and had begun shifting its track toward the northeast.
Wind and rain are already affecting Japan’s Kanto region, with the typhoon’s most significant impact expected from this afternoon through tomorrow, he said.

Chinese prodigy wins first gold at Asian Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:34 UTC
01:36:34 KST

China’s 13-year-old swimmer Yu Zidi yesterday smashed the Asian Games record as she won gold in Japan, two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics.
Yu, who turns 14 next month, romped home in the women’s 200m butterfly in 2 minutes 05.08 seconds to shave almost half a second off the time set by China’s Zhang Zufei three years ago in Hangzhou, China, of 2:05:57.
Her time in winning her first major gold medal was 3.36 seconds faster than China’s Chang Mohan, who took the silver.
Photo: AFP
It was the first of three individual events Yu is scheduled to compete in at the Asian Games, where swimming events are being held in Tokyo.
Yu became the youngest swimming world championships medalist in history last year when she won bronze as a 12-year-old as part of China’s 4x200m freestyle relay team.
She also finished a whisker outside the medals in fourth in three world individual events.
She has embellished her growing reputation this year, notably with a victory over multiple US Olympic champion Regan Smith in March.
The schoolgirl with the pixie haircut is expected to be a serious contender at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
However, she has spoken of struggling to deal with the heavy load placed on her.
During the build-up to China’s National Games last year she said the pressure to win the 400m medley nearly became too much.
Her coach told her to persevere and “believe in yourself,” she said. Yu went on to win four medals at the National Games.
Some in the swimming world have questioned the mental and physical impact of high-level training and competing on Yu at such a young age.
Under World Aquatics rules, the minimum age for international championships is 14, but exceptions can be made for younger swimmers if they are fast enough.

Man sentenced to prison for killing temple fish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:34 UTC
01:36:34 KST

A 30-year-old man surnamed Chen (陳) has been sentenced to 40 days imprisonment and fined NT$200,000 after dumping acrylic resin beads into a temple fish pond, which killed the fish.
Prosecutors said the incident occurred at Tianmei Fude Temple (田美福德宮) in Taichung’s Shalu District (沙鹿), resulting in the deaths of 20 koi.
The Taichung District Prosecutors’ Office alleged Chen went to the pond on the evening of Dec. 8 last year and dumped the beads into the water. The koi, which were worth about NT$45,000 in total, all died within a week, the indictment said.
Photo: Taipei Times
Prosecutors cited a 2024 case at the National Taiwan University Hospital Hsinchu Branch in which an 18-month-old girl was rushed to the emergency department after accidentally swallowing resin beads. She was discharged after receiving rapid treatment.
The hospital warned the highly absorbent material can rapidly expand after entering the gastrointestinal tract and potentially cause an intestinal obstruction. Severe cases can require emergency surgery and can be fatal.
Police said Chen admitted to the offense when questioned, but failed to appear when summoned by prosecutors. Prosecutors said surveillance footage and the results of police questioning are sufficient grounds to establish that he had committed the offense, and charged him with violating the Animal Protection Act (動物保護法) and damaging property.
The Shalu Summary Division of the Taichung District Court found Chen guilty of violating Article 25, Paragraph 1 of the Animal Protection Act. It sentenced him to 40 days in detention and fined him NT$200,000. The ruling can be appealed.

Myanmar win first Asian Games teqball gold medal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:33 UTC
01:36:33 KST

Myanmar’s Wai Khin Hnin yesterday became the first Asian Games gold medalist in teqball, an acrobatic soccer-table tennis hybrid making its debut at this year’s event in Japan.
Watched by Barcelona and Spain soccer legend Carles Puyol, Wai Khin Hnin beat Indonesia’s Sumaya, who goes by one name, 2-1 in the final to capture the inaugural women’s singles title.
Teqball was invented 14 years ago in a garage in Hungary and features players kicking a ball over a curved table, incorporating elements of the southeast Asian sport sepak takraw.
Photo: AP
The sport has grown quickly and featured at the 2023 European Games.
Wai Khin Hnin lost the first set of the final, but came back to win 10-12, 12-8, 12-9 and claim gold.
“I’m delighted, I’m thankful to my head coach for believing in me and selecting me to play in the women’s singles. I believed that I could do it,” she said. “My next goal is to win the gold medal for Myanmar at the 2027 SEA [Southeast Asian] Games.”
The competition has seen a diverse range of players vying to become the Asian Games’ first teqball medalists.
The Philippines men’s team featured three 14-year-olds including Prince Agustin, who lost in the singles bronze-medal match.
Japan were represented by Takahiro Nodomi, who also works as a comedian.
“I played football until high school, gave up, started teqball in my late 30s, and made it to this big stage at 40,” he said. “If the message that even old guys can work hard reached everyone, then I feel I was able to release some old guy power.”
Indonesia’s Husni Uba represented his country in sepak takraw at four previous Asian Games.
“After I was done with the sepak takraw competition at the 2018 Asian Games I didn’t expect to be back again, especially for teqball,” the 44-year-old said.

Iran win Asian Games men’s basketball bronze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:28 UTC
01:36:28 KST

Iran yesterday withstood a late fightback to beat China 79-70 and win Asian Games men’s basketball bronze, an achievement that left their players “speechless” after months of war back home.
China led 31-29 at half-time in Nagoya, but Iran took charge in the third quarter to lead 55-46 going into the fourth and held on to spark wild celebrations and an emotional place on the podium.
“To be honest with you I’m just speechless,” said 202cm power forward Arsalan Kazemi, who in 2013 was the first Iranian to be drafted in the NBA by the Washington Wizards, but never made a regular season appearance.
Photo: AFP
“The pressure that we had on us is just out of this world,” he added. “Not a lot of athletes can say that, with the way that it has been since almost six months ago, what we have been through, what our families have been through.
“I just congratulate the people of Iran because they deserve much better,” he said. “And I think my teammates and I put our hearts out on the court today just to get this win and make them happy.”
Teammate Arman Zangeneh said the squad had been through a lot but it was worth it.
“If you get the medal at the Asian Games you don’t need to go to the army any more, so it’s huge for some players,” the 203cm tall forward said.
“We had a very tough two months. We went to the Philippines to play the qualifiers, then immediately we came here,” he said.
“It was really difficult. And living in a container, with the food and everything, it was hard, very hard,” he said. “At the end, we get to the point that we go home with a medal, and it means a lot.”

Fuel prices stay stable this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:27 UTC
01:36:27 KST

CPC Corp, Taiwan (CPC, 台灣中油) announced on Saturday that it would leave its domestic gasoline and diesel prices unchanged this week, while Formosa Petrochemical Corp (台塑石化) yesterday said it would maintain its fuel prices at the same levels despite higher crude oil purchasing costs.
The decisions came after the two companies increased their gasoline prices by NT$0.7 per liter and diesel prices by NT$0.6 per liter last week.
State-run CPC said its floating price mechanism, based on a weighted average of 70 percent Dubai and 30 percent Brent crude, showed that the average international crude oil price rose to US$125.76 per barrel last week from US$115.61 per barrel a week earlier.
That increase, and a weaker New Taiwan dollar, which averaged NT$31.827 against the US dollar last week compared with NT$31.556 the previous week, pushed CPC’s purchase price for crude oil higher by 7.76 percent in the week, the company said.
The company’s decision not to raise prices at the pump was made despite rising crude oil prices after Saudi Arabian pipelines were attacked, in an effort to curb local inflationary pressures and keep Taiwan’s domestic fuel prices lower than in neighboring markets, CPC said.
Retail gasoline prices this week would remain at NT$31.2, NT$32.7 and NT$34.7 per liter for 92, 95 and 98-octane unleaded gasoline respectively at CPC and Formosa stations, while prices of premium diesel would stay at NT$29.9 per liter at CPC stations and NT$29.7 per liter at Formosa pumps, the companies said.

Unknown Publisher

Chien Hui-hsuan (簡慧萱) yesterday won a bronze medal in the women’s individual kata event in karate, earning Taiwan’s first medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, while Taiwan’s men’s and women’s soft tennis teams each won silver medals.
Chien defeated Iran’s Fatemeh Sadeghi 4-1 in the bronze medal bout to secure her first medal in Asian Games competition.
Chien thanked her friends and family for their support, adding that it was a difficult journey to the Games.
Photo: AP
“Even though there were times when a breakthrough was hard to achieve, I pushed through,” she said.
After losing to Sadeghi in a Karate World Championships qualifying event in October last year, Chien switched to a kata she was more familiar with, she said.
That paid off, Chien said, adding that she was glad to have earned recognition from the judges.
Photo: Reuters
Chien, who turns 35 on Sunday, said she was happy to win a medal and hoped the result would encourage Taiwan’s karate team, including two younger members who are to join her in the women’s team kata event tomorrow.
The karate veteran narrowly missed out on a bronze medal at her first Asian Games in 2023, finishing just 0.6 points short.
Over the past six months, she has traveled abroad, often at her own expense, to compete and train, visiting Japan’s Okinawa, Oita and Tottori, as well as Spain, where she trained with Olympic gold medalist Sandra Sanchez, Chien said.
In soft tennis, the men’s doubles duo of brothers Chen Po-yi (陳柏邑) and Chen Yu-hsun (陳郁?) were swept 5-0 in the first match of their final, while singles player Chang Yu-sung (張祐菘) lost 4-1 in the second match.
The 2-0 loss to Japan in only 54 minutes mirrored the result of the sides’ previous finals matchup at the Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, in 2023.
In the women’s team finals, Taiwan lost 2-1 to a Japanese team that had won gold in the past three Asian Games.
Taiwan’s one win in the matchup was by 22-year-old Asian Games newcomer Chiang Min-yu (江旻育), who defeated Ayaka Iwakura 4-1 in their singles match.
The silver medal finish tied the women’s soft tennis team’s best-ever performance at the Asian Games.
Team member Lo Shu-ting (羅舒婷), who previously said this would be her “last dance” before retirement, she said she was proud of the result.
“I think we did great. I don’t have any regrets in my career,” Lo said, adding that going home with a medal “made it all worthwhile.”
Soft tennis is a variety of tennis that originated in Japan. It is played on a standard tennis court, but with a soft rubber ball that flies slower and bounces lower than a tennis ball.
In the Asian Games, team soft tennis follows a best-of-three format, in which the first national team to win two matches win.

Stephanie Cole obituary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:25 UTC
01:36:25 KST

Stephanie Cole, who has died aged 84, was a skilful actor with a powerful voice. She was also an exemplar of the strong, no-nonsense characters that she played with layers of vulnerability, humour and kindness.
She made her television debut in a 1968 episode of Z Cars and maintained a solid screen career before coming to prominence as a leading member of a strong female ensemble in the BBC series Tenko (1981-84, and Tenko Reunion, 1985), as the stoic Dr Beatrice Mason, doing her best to maintain the health of her fellow internees in a Japanese prison camp during the second world war.
Convincingly realised and well-drawn, Tenko offered three-dimensional characters and tackled morally complex storylines – regularly achieving more than 14 million viewers.
Thereafter she was rarely off our screens, particularly popular as irascible senior citizens in TV comedy, despite being 48 when cast as the most enduring of these – the acerbic Diana Trent in the retirement home sitcom Waiting for God (1990-94). The role won her a 1992 British Comedy award for best TV comedy actress.
She was born in Solihull, Warwickshire, the daughter of June (nee Sheldon), an art student, and, Stephanie believed, Leslie Cole, an RAF airman, wartime lovers who split before she was born. She later learned that she was in fact the progeny of an affair between June and a man called Charles Wilson, whom she encountered only briefly in adult life (although she became close to her half-sister, his daughter).
Stephanie soon moved with her mother and great-aunt Peg to Croyde, north Devon, and she was sent as a weekly boarder to a local school aged five, where she fell in love with literature, poetry and theatre: she discovered that she had a gift for different voices and accents.
When June remarried, Stephanie moved with her to Bitton, Gloucestershire, but she did not enjoy her time at Clifton high school for girls, in Bristol and, after throwing a Latin book at a teacher who had scoffed at her acting aspirations, she was told she would not be welcome back after completing her O-levels.
She subsequently got a secretarial qualification from the College of Commerce in Bristol before enrolling at the Bristol Old Vic drama school: among her first roles there – aged 17 – was Madame Arcati in Blithe Spirit, an early indication of her tendency to be cast older than she was (she later played the role professionally at the Savoy theatre at the more sensible age of 63).
Upon graduation she joined the Old Vic as an acting assistant stage manager before repertory theatre beckoned in Lincoln, Canterbury, Hornchurch and Salisbury (where, among many roles in her six-year tenure, she played the Nurse in Romeo and Juliet, and Martha in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?).
Continually told that her career would take off when she was older, and beset with depression, she quit the profession in 1972 and worked briefly as a bookbinder and drama teacher before being invited to star in Tina at the Orange Tree theatre, Richmond (1975). She appeared in Noises Off (Savoy theatre, 1982) Steel Magnolias (Lyric theatre, 1989), Kay Mellor’s A Passionate Woman, directed by Ned Sherrin (Comedy theatre, 1994), The Shell Seekers (national tour 2003) and as Mrs Higgins in Pygmalion (Chichester, 2010).
It was TV, though, that made her a household name. Concurrent with Tenko she showed her aptitude for comedy in Roy Clarke’s Open All Hours (1982, 1985) as the gloomy “Black Widow” Delphine Featherstone, reprising the role in the 2013-19 revival Still Open All Hours. She was good value in David Nobbs’s social function comedy A Bit of a Do (1989) as the gossipy, and often inebriated, Betty. She was an addled matriarch in Keeping Mum (1997-98), and a potty-mouthed aunt opposite Greg Davies in Man Down (2014-17).
In 2011 she joined Coronation Street as Sylvia Goodwin, crotchety mother of the amiable Roy Cropper (David Neilson). Continuing that programme’s fine tradition of amusing and formidable northern women, Sylvia garnered Cole a British Soap award for best comedy performance in 2012.
Her other notable television roles included Muriel, a widow with a can-do attitude, in Soldiering On, one of Alan Bennett’s acclaimed Talking Heads monologues (1988), Dame Lettie Colston in the BBC’s excellent adaptation of Muriel Spark’s Memento Mori (1992) and Martin Clunes’s aunt Joan in ITV’s popular series Doc Martin (2004-09). Her apparent on-air suicide in the groundbreaking, meta and live Inside No 9 episode Dead Line (2018) was unforgettable event television, and more recently she was in Gentleman Jack (2019-22).
She also made her mark on radio, featuring in two BBC Radio 4 comedies: from 2005 to 2021 she played the ostensibly sweet but trouble-making Olive, a creative writing student of Christopher Douglas’s misanthropic writer in Ed Reardon’s Week, and was Carolyn Knapp-Shappey, former owner of the world’s smallest airline – crewed by Roger Allam and Benedict Cumberbatch – in John Finnemore’s much-loved Cabin Pressure (2008-14).
Her autobiography, A Passionate Life, was published in 1998 and she was appointed OBE in 2005.
Her 1973 marriage to the writer and stage combat teacher Henry Marshall ended in 1988, and in 1998 she married the actor Peter Birrell after meeting him at a reunion event decades after they had last seen each other as colleagues at Bristol. Peter died in 2004 and she is survived by her daughter, Emma, from her first marriage.

Hong Kong holds state funeral for 1st postcolonial leader

Hong Kong yesterday held a state funeral for its first postcolonial leader, Tung Chee-hwa (董建華), who led the territory through the initial years of its transition from British rule after it was returned to China in 1997.
Chinese officials from Beijing joined Hong Kong political leaders for the service in what was the third state funeral in the territory since the handover.
Tung, a shipping magnate handpicked by Beijing to serve as the territory’s chief executive from 1997 to 2005, died on Sept. 8 at the age of 89. The staunch conservative oversaw a rocky eight-year tenure, grappling with the Asian financial crisis and the SARS epidemic until he resigned in 2005, following widespread protests.
Photo: Reuters
Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference Vice Chairman Shi Taifeng (石泰峰), the former head of the Chinese United Front Work Department, referred to Tung in a eulogy as a close friend of the party and a renowned patriot, the state-run Xinhua news agency reported.
He said Tung was an outstanding contributor to the “one country, two systems” framework that governs Hong Kong and Macau.
Flower wreaths lined the wall outside the Hong Kong Funeral Home and Tung’s casket was draped in a Chinese flag when it was brought out after the service. The media were not allowed inside.
Other visiting officials included Chinese Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office Director Xia Baolong (夏寶龍).
About 200 people were invited to the service, the South China Morning Post reported.
Members of the public paid condolences at three venues set up around Hong Kong.
Cheung Kwok-lik, an 89-year-old retired renovation worker, said he had traveled an hour by bus to pay his condolences to the former leader.
During his tenure, Tung weathered the Asian financial crisis and the SARS epidemic in 2003 that killed nearly 300 people and dealt another blow to the economy, which “was by no means easy,” Cheung said.
Tung’s leadership also coincided with record unemployment and the 1997 avian flu outbreak.
In 2003, an estimated 500,000 people took to the streets to protest the government’s plan to enact an anti-treason law that was seen as a threat to civil liberties. The government shelved the plan, and Tung resigned in 2005, citing health reasons.
That protest marked the start of years of pro-democracy protests that came to a head in 2019 and were followed by a crackdown and the Beijing-imposed National Security Law in 2020.
Tung was later elected to the post of vice chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference. He was among 42 people who received national medals and honors in 2019 for their contributions to the country.

Photos: Nepal flood survivors find little trace of former lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:03 UTC
01:36:03 KST

In Pictures
Photos: Nepal flood survivors find little trace of former lives
Nepal’s floods displace thousands, with survivors mourning loved ones and searching for belongings amidst the debris.
When Anusa Thapa Magar rushed home from her job in the Maldives after hearing of Nepal’s devastating floods, she clung to the hope that her grandmother had somehow survived.
Instead, when she reached Betrawati, the small riverside town where her family lived, she found only a flat expanse of hardened grey silt.
There was no house, and no Betrawati.
“If my house is buried underneath, that means my Aama is still here underneath too, right?” the 23-year-old said quietly, standing where the family’s two-storey home once stood. Her grandmother, who could barely walk, was last seen resting on her bed.
Last month’s torrent of mud, rock and water, triggered by a glacial collapse in the mountains along the Nepal-China border, tore through settlements along the Trishuli River, killing at least 1,386 people on the Nepal side. Authorities say 5,130 are still missing, and while searches continue, it has been days since anyone was found alive.
To reach what used to be Betrawati, survivors now climb a steep hillside, cross a narrow ridge and descend into a wasteland. Along the route lie scattered shoes, school ties and children’s backpacks – “silent evidence”, residents say, of the panic as people scrambled to flee the surging floodwaters.
Garment business owner Kalpana Thapa Magar, 43, recalled the moment a friend phoned from upstream. “Run! Run!” she was told. “I just ran. When I looked back, everything was gone, even the people who had been running behind me,” she said.
Downstream in Devighat, shattered shells of houses still stand. Some residents pick through the rubble for belongings, but many say there is no reason to return; the land itself has vanished beneath debris.
For many here, the disaster reopens wounds from Nepal’s 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people. Teacher Sita Thapa Magar, 45, Kalpana’s older sister, said that after the quake, families were at least able to rebuild on their plots. “This time, we have lost everything,” she said. “Our houses, our land, our future.”
On a single broken floor tile – the last visible trace of her home – 61-year-old Shanti Dangol clutched a photograph of the three-storey lodge she once ran for pilgrims and trekkers.
“Economically, people here had started doing well,” she said. “Now, nothing remains.”

Exit polls show Merz’s party suffering heavy losses in 2 German state elections

Merz’s centre-right Christian Democratic Union is projected to fall to 5.5% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. That would be its worst result there since World War II. The CDU is projected to come in second with 20%, behind the Left party at 24.5%, according to the exit poll by public broadcaster ARD
Exit polls showed Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party suffering heavy losses in two German state elections on Sunday.
Merz’s centre-right Christian Democratic Union is projected to fall to 5.5% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural state in Germany’s formerly communist east. That would be its worst result there since World War II.
In Berlin, the CDU is projected to finish second with 20% of the vote, trailing the Left Party at 24.5%, according to an exit poll by the public broadcaster ARD.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains in Sunday's regional elections. The vote came two weeks after the AfD finished just short of an absolute majority in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, marking its best chance yet of forming the country’s first far-right regional government since the Second World War.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz, 70, assumed leadership of Germany 16 months ago, pledging to revitalise an economy that has stalled for years. However, he has failed to lift a sullen national mood and has seen his personal popularity plunge.
The AfD's strong showing in Saxony-Anhalt has further damaged the chancellor's standing nationally, sparking calls from within his own party over the past fortnight to replace him. Although no top-level allies have publicly demanded his resignation, many have warned against opening divisive internal personnel debates.
Apparently anticipating a challenging post-election period, Merz abandoned a planned trip to New York next week to attend the UN General Assembly.
Speaking after the publication of the exit polls, Merz stated that he intends to remain leader of the CDU and chancellor until the end of his term.
"The reforms have to come," 70-year-old Merz said. "I am taking on this responsibility because I want to move our country forward."
