====================================================================================================

Europe gave Russia years to perfect its aerial killing. Ukraine is paying the price. Europe may be next.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:27:38 UTC
01:27:38 KST

For years, Ukraine’s air defenses blunted Russia’s attempts to terrorize its cities from the sky. Now, after four years of adaptation, Moscow is fielding faster drones, massing ballistic missiles, and finding new ways to overwhelm a Ukrainian air-defense network running short of the interceptors needed to stop them.
Russia’s aerial campaign is becoming harder to contain just as its attacks are killing more Ukrainian civilians. July recorded at least 437 civilian deaths, the highest monthly toll since the early months of the full-scale invasion, with UN monitors pointing to Russian missile and drone attacks as a key factor.
That shift is visible most clearly in Russia’s rapidly expanding use of jet-powered Geran drones. These drones can exceed 400 km/h, making them significantly harder to intercept than the slower, propeller-driven Shaheds Ukraine has spent years learning to counter. Russia reportedly launched as many as 2,850 jet-powered drones in August alone.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Russia’s escalation with the new drones is becoming “increasingly terrorist” and called for urgent efforts to develop defenses against them.
While Ukraine’s Western partners have taken steps to strengthen its air defenses, Russia has spent the same period adapting and expanding its ability to attack from the air. The gap is becoming increasingly visible in the skies over Ukrainian cities.
Ukrainian civilians are already paying the price
Russia has increasingly turned its ability to strike deep inside Ukraine into a weapon against civilian life itself: hitting residential areas, fuel stations, railways, energy infrastructure and other sites across cities far from the front.
Since late August, Kyiv has faced near-continuous Russian drone attacks, with Russia increasingly sending waves of drones against the capital throughout the day and night. The shift has made air-raid alerts, explosions and disruptions to daily life a near-constant reality.
For Ukrainians, Russia’s evolving aerial campaign is measured in destroyed homes, injuries, deaths, and lives permanently changed.
In Kyiv, it has also changed everyday life: explosions interrupt sleep and work, people run for shelter as strikes unfold overhead, and the threat of another attack is never far away.
And the pressure is no longer confined to Kyiv. Kharkiv, Odesa, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia are all facing increasingly sophisticated combinations of drones and missiles.
The danger is not simply that Russia is launching more weapons. It is that Moscow has spent years learning which weapons can penetrate Ukraine’s defenses, how to combine them, and how to force Ukraine to spend its most valuable interceptors.
Zelenskyy’s warning captures the urgency: “You cannot simply wait for Russia to perfect its repertoire of killings.”
Russia is adapting faster than Ukraine can rebuild its shield
The jet-powered Geran is only one part of the problem.
Russia has also dramatically increased its use of ballistic missiles. Reuters reported that 228 ballistic and hypersonic missiles were launched in July and the first eight days of August, with more than half being inaccurate RM48U training missiles repurposed for combat.
Ukraine has virtually exhausted its US-made Patriot interceptors, the only systems in its arsenal capable of reliably intercepting Russia’s ballistic missiles, while Moscow continues launching them at a high tempo.
The result is a more complex aerial threat: fast drones that are difficult to intercept, ballistic missiles that are extremely difficult to stop, and large waves of cheaper weapons that can force Ukraine to expend scarce defensive ammunition.
Trending Now
Ukraine is developing new ways to counter them, including interceptor drones specifically designed to hunt down the jet-powered Gerans. But Ukraine is developing these systems as Russia is already deploying its new weapons at scale.
Western countries have continued providing air-defense assistance. Canada, for example, announced a C$350 million package for interceptors earlier this month. But Ukrainian officials continue to say that deliveries remain far below what is needed to protect the country from Russia’s expanding aerial campaign.
Russia has spent years expanding the weapons it can use against Ukraine, while Ukraine and its partners are still racing to develop and supply the systems needed to stop them.
The threat Europe helped Russia develop
Some of Ukraine’s Western partners are now confronting a threat Russia has spent years developing over Ukraine: an increasingly sophisticated aerial arsenal that could eventually be turned against them.
European officials and defense analysts are increasingly warning that NATO countries themselves lack enough air and missile defenses to deal with a large Russian attack.
Latvia’s President Edgars Rinkēvičs recently said Europe is not sufficiently prepared for the kind of drone and aerial warfare Russia has developed in Ukraine, including because of delays in supplying Ukraine with critical air-defense systems.
Those concerns are no longer hypothetical. On 14 September, an Italian NATO fighter jet shot down a Russian-made Geran-2 drone over Lithuania after it entered the country from Belarus. Poland and Romania have also faced Russian drone incursions since 2025.
This creates a problem that is partly of Europe’s own making. Russia has had more than four years to refine its drones, missiles, production lines and tactics while Ukraine’s partners have often been too slow to provide enough weapons to counter those systems as they were developed and deployed at scale.
In that same period, many European countries continued trading with Russia, particularly in fossil fuels, allowing Moscow to keep generating revenue from European markets even as those same governments were providing military aid to Ukraine.
The result is a Russian aerial arsenal that is more capable than the one Ukraine faced in 2022 – while some of the countries now worried about a future Russian threat lack the air defenses needed to protect themselves.
Western governments helped Ukraine fight Russia’s air war, but not at a scale or speed sufficient to prevent Russia from adapting.
Ukrainian civilians are paying the price for the time Russia was given to expand and refine its aerial warfare. Now, Europe is having to prepare for the possibility that those capabilities could one day be used against it.

The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, travels this Monday, 21 September, to New York, where he begins his participation in the 81st High-Level Week of the United Nations General Assembly, to which he will take Spain's proposals for the defence of international law and the reform of multilateral institutions. 
Albares begins a week with an intense agenda in which he will convey Spain's commitment to ending the war in the Middle East and Ukraine. 
The Minister will highlight Spain's commitment to the defence of a renewed, effective, and inclusive multilateralism, with the United Nations at its core, capable of guaranteeing an international order based on international law, human rights, cooperation, and dialogue. He will also convey Spain's support for the election of the first female Secretary-General of the United Nations. 
Ibero-American Summit in Madrid 
The Ibero-American Summit in Madrid will occupy a prominent place on the agenda during the High-Level Week due to its imminent celebration on 4 and 5 November. The traditional working breakfast of Ibero-American Foreign Ministers (Thursday 25), which Spain chairs this year, and the EU-CELAC Ministerial meeting (Wednesday 24) are the main events in this regard. Also noteworthy is the event co-organised by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs together with the United Nations Development Programme entitled "Democracy, Development and Shared Futures: Ibero-America heading towards the Madrid Summit" (Tuesday 22). 
Among the meetings organised by Spain, it is also worth mentioning the High-Level Roundtable jointly convened with Brazil (Wednesday 23), which will emphasise the fight against hunger and poverty and the goal of leaving no one behind. 
Situation in the Middle East 
The situation in the Middle East will also be prominently addressed through participation in the Ministerial Meeting for the implementation of the two-state solution, and the Ministerial Meeting in support of UNRWA on Thursday 25, co-chaired by Spain, Jordan, and Brazil. Spain's priorities at the UN 
Throughout this week, Albares will reaffirm Spain's priorities for this 81st session, including support for the reform process of the United Nations system through the UN80 Initiative, to achieve a more effective, efficient, and agile Organization, with greater transparency and accountability. He will do so in high-level meetings and side events of interest to Spain regarding democracy and development, human rights, gender and diversity, climate change, social justice, artificial intelligence governance, food security, conflict prevention and resolution, and non-proliferation.

The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists is gravely concerned for the safety of our colleague Micah Reddy, ICIJ’s Africa coordinator, and local journalist Mohamed Willo Ismael (“Kooki Mahmoud”).
Contact with the pair was lost in Djibouti City on Saturday, September 19, at approximately 1 p.m. local time, and neither has been in contact or reachable since.
Reddy was not reporting on Djiboutian affairs when he went missing. He was staying at the Escale International Hotel in Djibouti City.
ICIJ does not yet know the circumstances behind Reddy’s sudden loss of contact.
The Committee to Protect Journalists said Sunday it is “deeply concerned” by reports that the pair can no longer be reached, and has called on Djiboutian authorities to urgently establish their whereabouts and confirm their safety.
ICIJ echoes that statement without reservation.
We are calling on the government of Djibouti to:
- Immediately clarify Reddy and Ismael’s whereabouts and confirm their well-being;
- Launch a prompt, transparent investigation into their disappearance;
- Keep their families, colleagues and employers fully and promptly informed.
Reddy is both a citizen of the U.K. and South Africa. ICIJ alerted both London and Pretoria shortly after the pair went missing.
Authorities in Djibouti have not responded so far to ICIJ requests for information.
Before joining ICIJ, Reddy was an investigative reporter at South Africa’s amaBhungane Centre for Investigative Journalism, known for his reporting on governance, corruption and regional affairs across the continent.
Journalists must be able to travel without fear of disappearance or obstruction.

Former Kremlin political prisoner Mykola Karpiuk killed at the front
Kyiv • UNN
Mykola Karpiuk was killed at the age of 62 in a Russian drone strike. He was a co-founder of UNA-UNSO and returned from Russian captivity in 2019.
At the front, former Kremlin political prisoner and one of the founders of UNA-UNSO Mykola Karpiuk was killed in a Russian drone strike: he was 62. The death was reported by another well-known UNSO member, Armed Forces of Ukraine serviceman Ihor Mazur, known by the call sign "Topol", reports UNN.
Details
As Mazur noted, Karpiuk was killed on the birthday of another well-known member of UNA-UNSO, Oleksandr Muzychko, better known as "Sashko Bilyi." He was killed in March 2014 while being detained by officers of the Sokol special unit of Ukraine's Interior Ministry.
Yesterday (September 19 — ed.), on Sashko "Bilyi's" birthday, Mykola Karpiuk was killed by an enemy drone. Two men from Rivne, both had been members of the UNA-UNSO Leadership since the 1990s
Who was Mykola Karpiuk
Mykola Karpiuk was one of the leaders of Ukraine's nationalist movement in the early 1990s. He stood at the origins of the Ukrainian National Assembly — Ukrainian People's Self-Defense (UNA-UNSO), as part of which he took part in hostilities in Transnistria (against Moldova — ed.) and Abkhazia (on Georgia's side — ed.).
He was also one of the leaders of UNA-UNSO and headed its Rivne branch. He actively participated in the "Ukraine without Kuchma" campaign (for which he served 4.5 years in prison), the Orange Revolution, and the Revolution of Dignity.
In March 2014, he was abducted by Russian special services and taken to the russian federation. He was charged with a completely fabricated allegation of supposedly participating in the First Russian-Chechen War of 1994–1996.
In 2016, he was sentenced to 22.5 years in prison. According to human rights activists, confessions were extracted from Karpiuk and another defendant, Stanislav Klykh, through brutal torture.
In September 2019, as part of a major prisoner exchange, Karpiuk returned to Ukraine.
We remind you
At the front, serviceman and television professional Volodymyr Tyrtychnyi, who had been considered missing for more than two years, was killed.

Germany’s far right secures another win in key regional election, exit poll says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:11:44 UTC
01:11:44 KST

Merz vows to stay on as chancellor despite ‘disaster’ in another German regional vote
The embattled chancellor’s conservative party suffered its worst result in postwar German history as the far-right AfD won its second regional election in two weeks.
AfD party co-leader Tino Chrupalla reacts to preliminary results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state elections following the closure of polling stations on September 20, 2026 in Schwerin, Germany. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
BERLIN — Germany’s embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservatives suffered a second major defeat to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in a regional vote Sunday — a result Merz conceded was a “disaster.”
But the chancellor moved to quickly quell a rising storm of speculation that he would move to step aside following the loss, which comes only two weeks after another historic defeat to the AfD in a regional contest. He appeared before cameras just minutes after the polls closed Sunday to say he would continue to push through his reform agenda and act as an anchor of stability in turbulent times.
“These reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism,” he said. “What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience. I will demonstrate these qualities as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country.”
The AfD won around 38% of the vote in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — the second-best result in its history, just ahead of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) on 35%, according to preliminary results.
Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) suffered its worst result in a state or national election since the end of World War II, coming in near 5%, according to a preliminary count, hovering at or below the vote threshold required to make it into the state parliament.
If the party falls below the 5% threshold in the final count, it would deal an even more painful blow to the chancellor, who is already struggling to maintain support among his party’s rank and file.
Advertisement
AfD leaders hailed their victory — party national co-leader Tino Chrupalla called the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result a “sensation” — while also putting the pressure on a profoundly weakened Merz to step aside and abandon his party’s policy of maintaining a “firewall” around the far right.
“Friedrich Merz is the wrong chancellor for the CDU and is dragging the CDU down with him,” national co-leader Alice Weidel told German public television. “So the CDU must ask itself, above all else, does it want to continue with this chancellor and with these left-wing policies?”
Merz took the unusual step of convening CDU leaders at the party’s Berlin headquarters on Sunday night in an effort to rally their support ahead of what he knew would be another humiliating election defeat. Merz’s approval ratings are among the lowest ever recorded for a German chancellor at this point in their tenure, prompting internal CDU discussions about a possible change at the top—Kanzlertausch.
“Of course, the mood isn’t exactly lighthearted,” Ines Claus, a CDU politician who took part in the leadership meeting, told ARD. “If you ask me now whether one might prefer to just pull the covers over one’s head, well, that might be the case. But that’s not what responsibility is about; stability is what’s required now.”
Just 1% of voters — and 1% of CDU supporters — said Chancellor Merz had helped his party’s election performance in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, according to a poll by public broadcaster ZDF.
“We can’t sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania,” Merz said after the polls closed Sunday. “It’s a disaster.”
The CDU also saw its support decline in a separate regional vote in Berlin, finishing second with around 19%, according to a preliminary count, behind the Left party, a far-left force which won 25.5% and is now poised to take over the capital’s mayoralty from Merz’s conservatives in coalition with center-left parties.
But as Germany’s export-oriented growth model continues to suffer amid increased competition from China and U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff wars, German voters don’t appear to be giving him the benefit of the doubt.
The chancellor’s agenda includes raising the retirement age to shore up the pension system, cutting some health-insurance benefits to curb rising premiums and making it harder for workers to take sick leave in an effort to boost growth.
Many of those reforms impose clear costs on ordinary voters, giving the far right and far left ample opportunity to exploit public discontent.
Schwesig is now likely to lead a new coalition government in the state with a coalition of left-wing parties.
CDU leaders blamed Schwesig’s approach for effectively turning the election in her state into a two-party race that has greatly weakened Merz’s conservatives. “The CDU fought hard, but in the end, it was crushed in the escalating confrontation between the SPD and the AfD,” Merz said.
But Schwesig blamed Merz and the CDU for failing to connect with voters and was able to gain on the AfD late in the race in great part because she attacked Merz as out of touch with ordinary people and his reform drive as punishing some of the most vulnerable.
“The issue of the cost of living is a very significant one, and it’s important for the federal government to take a stand in favor of greater economic development to create jobs, but also to provide relief,” she told a public television broadcaster after the vote.
Still, trying to stabilize the situation, Philipp Amthor, a CDU politician from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the chancellery’s federal-state affairs chief, said it was time to end the Kanzlertausch discussion.
“We have seen that what we have experienced over the past two weeks since the state election in Saxony-Anhalt has done more harm than good — namely, ongoing discussions about personnel that have completely overshadowed the discussion of the issues at hand,” he said.
“In that regard, it is right to put an end to these personnel discussions now and refocus on the issues.”

The actor Cheryl Hall certainly made an impression as a Kent county councillor when I served with her as a Labour member. Lib Dems use conference to set out £2bn plan to cut fuel duty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:09:11 UTC
01:09:11 KST

The Liberal Democrats say they will tax big tech to finance a new online crime agency, as they try to address concerns that not enough voters know what the party stands for.
The plan, to be announced at the party conference on Monday by the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, would create a new Online Crime Agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images.
The planned budget of £250m a year would be paid for by an “online crime levy” on large AI and technology companies. Wilkinson is to tell the conference it is “time they picked up the bill” for offences they had enabled.
Ed Davey, the party leader, on Sunday set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies.
The party is increasingly concerned that, although it won its best election result in a century in 2024, it does not have a distinctive enough message to reach voters in an increasingly fragmented and noisy political landscape.
Polling conducted to coincide with the conference in Brighton, released on Sunday, showed Lib Dem policies are less well known than those of Restore Britain, which launched as a political party only in February and has one MP – Rupert Lowe – compared with the Lib Dems’ 71.
The research by More in Common, which was presented at the conference, showed widespread uncertainty among voters about what the Lib Dems stood for. Just 39% said they had an idea, lower than for every other major party, including Restore Britain, which was formed by Lowe after he split from Reform UK.
Other parts of the research showed just 16% of voters said they had heard from the Lib Dems in recent months, against 66% for Reform, while 3% said they had seen Davey on social media, compared with 20% for the Reform leader, Nigel Farage.
In a round of media interviews on Sunday morning, Davey pushed back against the idea that the Lib Dems, who are static in national polling at about 12%, risked being forgotten in the political conversation amid the rise in prominence of Reform and the Greens.
His party, Davey insisted, was making a genuine difference, and not just generating coverage without substance.
“I’m talking about real change, not just talking about the bubbles,” he told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show. “We have been winning council elections for eight years in a row. That has never happened before – it’s the most successful period that we’ve had.”
While there is no talk among Lib Dem MPs about a challenge to Davey, some say they are frustrated the party’s message is too vague and its support too reliant on tactical voting in a limited number of places, mainly in the south of England.
One Lib Dem MP told a conference fringe event, at which More in Common’s findings were presented, that the party needed to expand the geographical and social range of its influence.
“If we want to be a party of government, then we need to have a message for the whole country, not just parts of it,” said Tom Gordon, the MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, one of just four Lib Dem-held seats in the north of England, against 58 in the south.
Party figures see the conference as a chance to set out a more coherent and striking policy platform, including on the economy and immigration.
But there is worry among some MPs that the problem is wider. “We already have quite a lot of policies, if people look at them,” one said. “It’s less about what you get if you vote Lib Dem than why you should – about what we represent. And people don’t really know that.”
One longtime party activist said: “The voters only seem to properly notice us once every four years, when there’s an election. It’s a bit like being curling at the Winter Olympics – the rest of the time we’re forgotten. It would be good if we had a more distinctive message, and that needs boldness.”

Meloni announces ban on burqa and niqab in Italian schools, cap on foreign students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:08:34 UTC
01:08:34 KST

Italy’s government is preparing new school measures, including a ban on niqabs. Meloni is facing competition from retired general Roberto Vannacci, who has called for tougher measures on migration.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has announced that the government is preparing a bill that would ban burqas and niqabs in schools and introduce a limit on the number of foreign pupils in each class.
Several European countries, including France and Belgium, already ban face coverings in public places. Austria has also introduced restrictions in schools. Elsewhere, including Spain and Poland, freedom of conscience and religion is protected by the constitution.
Meloni said a package of measures will soon go before the Italian cabinet, including a ban on burqas and niqabs in schools, a requirement for parents of pupils facing “serious difficulties integrating” into the national school system to learn Italian, and a limit on places for foreign pupils.
Italy heads to the polls next year, with competition intensifying to the right of Meloni’s party following the entry of retired general Roberto Vannacci, who has called for even tougher measures. Migration is a highly political and divisive issue in Italy.
“It is unacceptable that in an Italian classroom the children who end up feeling pushed into a corner are Italian children because they have become the minority. That cannot be allowed,” she said during a rally organised by Gioventù Nazionale, the youth wing of her Brothers of Italy party.
“Calling all this integration is yet another lie, a convenient lie for those who live off ideology, for those who preach to us from their living rooms and then send their own children to schools where this problem does not exist.”
Previous initiatives and legislative proposals
Meloni’s announcement comes after several related initiatives in recent months.
In early August, Education and Merit Minister Giuseppe Valditara proposed action on the full-face veil through an amendment to the security bill.
At the end of July, Futuro Nazionale — the party founded by far-right MEP Roberto Vannacci, who has backed Meloni’s proposal — tabled a resolution against the full-face veil in the Chamber of Deputies’ Culture Committee. It was approved with centre-right votes after being redrafted at the government’s request.
In March, the League introduced a bill in the Senate to amend Article 5 of the 1975 Reale law, which was introduced by then-Justice Minister Oronzo Reale during the Years of Lead to ban face coverings in public places.
The proposed amendment would create a new offence of forcing someone to conceal their face, punishable by one to two years in prison and fines of between €10,000 and €30,000. It would also bar those convicted from obtaining Italian citizenship.
Full-face veils in Europe
Meloni referred specifically to a ban on burqas and niqabs. A burqa traditionally covers the entire body and includes a mesh over the eyes, while a niqab covers the face, leaving only the eyes visible. A hijab, by contrast, covers the hair and neck but leaves the face uncovered.
Several European countries have introduced restrictions on face coverings in public spaces.
France imposed a nationwide ban on concealing the face in public places in April 2011, a measure later upheld by the European Court of Human Rights.
Belgium approved a nationwide ban in July 2011, with fines and prison sentences for violations. Bulgaria has prohibited full-face veils in state, administrative and educational institutions since September 2016.
Austria passed an anti-mask law in October 2017 requiring faces to remain visible in public spaces. From September 2026, girls up to the age of 14 will also be prohibited from wearing at school any veil that “covers the head according to Islamic traditions”.
Denmark introduced a nationwide ban in August 2018, with financial penalties increasing for repeat offences. The Netherlands introduced a partial ban in August 2019 covering schools, hospitals, government offices and public transport.
Switzerland introduced a federal ban on face coverings in public spaces following a national referendum, with the implementing legislation coming into force in 2023. Portugal completed its legislative process in August 2026 with a law banning face coverings in public spaces and imposing financial penalties.
Germany has no nationwide ban, but federal legislation prohibits public employees, judges, members of the armed forces and motorists from covering their faces while driving. Several Länder also restrict full-face veils in schools and universities for students and teachers.
Foreign pupils in the classroom
If Italy introduces a statutory maximum for foreign pupils in each class, it would become the first European country to adopt such a rule, according to the proposal.
Italy already has a 30% limit on non-Italian pupils, set out in a 2010 ministerial circular issued by then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini. The limit has often gone unenforced because of local demographic conditions and a lack of flexibility, particularly in urban outskirts.
Other European countries use different approaches.
Denmark has some of the most restrictive policies. The government has allowed upper secondary schools to introduce caps of up to 50% for pupils of “non-Western origin” or from disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Schools can also organise classes based on parents’ income, with the aim of encouraging social and ethnic mixing — a model the Italian government is watching with interest.
In France, quotas based on origin would be unconstitutional because the state does not collect statistics based on ethnic or religious identity. Instead, authorities use “zoning” to redesign school catchment areas, linking working-class and wealthier neighbourhoods. In areas with high concentrations of migrants, the state also reduces the number of pupils per class.
Criticism of Meloni’s proposal
Meloni’s announcement has received support from members of the governing coalition but has also drawn criticism from the opposition and legal experts.
Speaking to ANSA, Salvatore Curreri, a professor of constitutional law at the University of Enna, pointed to Article 34 of the Constitution, which states that “school is open to everyone”, including foreign children.
“If the measure were so restrictive as to uproot minors and their families to other areas, far from where they live, it could prove excessive precisely because it conflicts with the overriding functional aim of integration, with the risk of infringing a right recognised by the constitution,” Curreri said.
Angelo Bonelli, an MP for the Green and Left Alliance (AVS) and co-spokesperson for Green Europe, also criticised the proposal.
“Yet again, instead of dealing with schools, she is chasing the neo-fascist right of AfD and Vannacci, who has proposed separate classes for students with disabilities,” he said. “The truth is that the prime minister is not at all interested in how schools work. Our teachers’ salaries are among the lowest in Europe.”

UN chief calls for global financial reform, permanent Security Council seats for Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:03:46 UTC
01:03:46 KST

Yasin Gungor
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Sunday called for sweeping reforms to global governance structures, urging permanent African representation on the UN Security Council and an overhaul of multilateral financial institutions.
"We must reform the international financial architecture that was created by the rich for the rich, and we must make it more representative of the needs of developing countries, especially in Africa," Guterres told attendees at the Unstoppable Africa 2026 forum, held on the margins of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York.
The UN chief emphasized that the continent was a "double victim of colonialism," explaining that historic subjugation prevented African nations from having a seat at the table when post-World War II international institutions were established.
Guterres argued that both the UN Security Council and international financial institutions fail to reflect Africa's demographic presence and interests, asserting that the continent must be granted permanent seats to participate directly in global decision-making.
Addressing economic transformation, Guterres noted that global markets are undergoing a fundamental structural transition from simply doing business in Africa to "doing business with Africa."
Despite global disruptions stemming from wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, Guterres said Africa's economy expanded 4.4% last year, with trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area on track to reach $230 billion this year, creating an opportunity to retain economic value domestically rather than relying on raw exports.
Critical minerals, renewable transition
Turning to natural resources, Guterres warned against ongoing exploitation amid intensifying geopolitical competition. "We must ensure that Africa's vast natural resources, particularly critical minerals, create local value and decent jobs, rather than simply being shipped overseas."
He highlighted significant advances in renewable energy and digital technology across the continent, pointing to Kenya generating more than 90% of its electricity from renewable sources, Morocco advancing plans for a submarine power cable to Europe, Tunisia competing internationally in artificial intelligence, and Rwanda developing nationwide drone logistics.
Guterres urged multilateral development banks to scale up concessional lending, match climate pledges with concrete adaptation financing, and direct capital to female entrepreneurs, who represent more than half of the continent's business owners.
Linking economic progress to sustainable peace, the UN chief praised African-led mediation efforts in regional conflicts, including in Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, reiterating that durable development cannot exist without political stability.

Women show greater willingness to interact with creative individuals experiencing schizophrenia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:00:27 UTC
01:00:27 KST

A study published in the EvoS Journal: Evolutionary Studies and Higher Education presented results of an online experiment that asked participants how much they would like to interact with a social media profile of a creative individual who also suffers from schizophrenia. Results showed that women were more interested in such interactions than men, particularly in the condition when the creative expression of the target person was unsuccessful. When it was successful, there were no differences between men and women.
Mental health stigma refers to negative stereotypes and prejudice directed toward people with mental health conditions. Individuals with mental illness are often perceived as dangerous, unpredictable, weak, or socially incompetent, even when these assumptions are unsupported. Such stigma can contribute to social rejection, difficulties in employment and relationships, and reluctance to seek professional help. It can also be internalized by affected individuals, reducing self-esteem and worsening social and psychological outcomes.
That said, psychological disorders often do involve characteristics that interfere with everyday functioning. On the other hand, there tend to also be positive traits associated with mental health conditions. From an evolutionary perspective, genetic properties that predispose individuals to certain mental health conditions persist in the population precisely because they come in combinations of traits that can sometimes provide situational advantages, particularly if the mental health condition manifests in milder, subclinical forms.
Anxiety, for example, may heighten vigilance toward threats, while social withdrawal may sometimes reduce exposure to harmful or overwhelming social situations. Psychotic traits (such as delusional thinking or disorganized behaviors) are associated with substantial cognitive difficulties and a strong social stigma, but are also linked to creativity, novel thinking, and heightened emotional sensitivity.
Lead author A. Hicks and colleagues wanted to explore how much the potential benefits of creativity protect individuals with psychotic traits from mental illness stigma. More specifically, they wanted to know how much learning that an individual is successful in creative work and/or that they suffer from schizophrenia would affect participants’ willingness to interact with such a person.
They conducted an online study. Participants were 308 individuals recruited through Prolific Academic. Of these, 167 were women. Their average age was 35 years. Study authors paid them $1.50 for their participation in the study.
Participants viewed a hypothetical Facebook post and were tasked to evaluate the person presented in the post. The posts differed in two ways: whether the person in the post spoke about suffering from schizophrenia or not, and whether the person was successful in their creative work or not (i.e., whether a poem they wrote was accepted for publication or not).
This was done in the form of a post to a writers group made by a person named Taylor Ross. In the post, Taylor Ross says that they want to give a life update and that they are working on their poetry. They also note (depending on the condition) that they are doing well or that they are struggling with schizophrenia, and that one of their poems was published or that it was denied publication. The study specifically utilized a gender-neutral silhouette for the profile picture to prevent gender bias from influencing the results.
Participants rated how much they would like to interact with Taylor Ross by liking or commenting on their post, considering them as a friend, or as a romantic partner. They also completed an assessment of stereotype endorsement by rating how much an individual with schizophrenia differs (in their view) from the general population on 11 positive and 11 negative traits.
Results indicated that women showed a greater interest in interacting with the target (Taylor Ross) than men, regardless of the study condition. Whether Taylor Ross was presented as successful in publishing the poem or not did not have an effect on how much participants wanted to interact with them overall.
When study authors looked only at the variant where Taylor Ross suffered from schizophrenia and was not successful in having their poem published, women showed a greater desire to interact with them than men. In the condition when Taylor Ross was successful, men and women did not differ in their desire to interact.
The average desire to interact with Taylor Ross was closer to the negative pole of the scale (not wanting to interact). Participants who reported having friends with mental illness were more interested in interacting with the Taylor Ross version that was creatively successful and not suffering from schizophrenia, than with the version that was both not successful and not suffering from schizophrenia.
The study contributes to scientific knowledge about the social desirability of people with mental health conditions. However, it should be noted that participants evaluated the target individual (Taylor Ross) only based on a short post, without any background information. This is unlike how people make social judgments in most real-world situations. Results of studies providing a more comprehensive set of information about an individual may differ.
The paper, “Salience of the Benefits of Psychotic Traits Buffers Against Mental Illness Stigma,” was authored by A. Hicks, D. F. Sacco, K. N. Boykin, O. Olabegi, Z. Buckner, and M. Brown.

Why have US prosecutors labelled China’s Huawei a criminal enterprise?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:57:48 UTC
00:57:48 KST

Why have US prosecutors labelled China’s Huawei a criminal enterprise?
Huawei faces a landmark US trial, accused of theft, fraud and sanctions violations in a high-stakes legal battle.
Chinese technology giant Huawei is facing a landmark criminal trial in the United States amid Washington’s long-running tech rivalry with Beijing.
The trial began in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, on September 9, with US prosecutors portraying Huawei as a criminal enterprise that spent two decades stealing technology from US companies, deceiving banks and circumventing sanctions on Iran.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump and Xi: The history of encounters between two superpower leaders
- list 2 of 3How Chinese, Iranian companies profit in Russia-occupied Ukrainian regions
- list 3 of 3China’s secret weapon in AI race with US? Lots of cheap energy
Huawei has pleaded not guilty and says the US government is attempting to turn ordinary business disputes and the actions of individual employees into evidence of a company-wide conspiracy.
The trial is expected to last about three months and overlaps with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s September 23-25 visit to Washington, where trade, artificial intelligence, tariffs and access to critical technologies are likely to be on the agenda.
Here is what you need to know:
What are the allegations against Huawei?
US prosecutors have accused the company of racketeering, money laundering, bank and wire fraud, sanctions violations, obstruction and conspiring to steal trade secrets from five US technology companies.
Prosecutors say the alleged wrongdoing stretched from about 1999 to 2020.
“Theft, lies, cover-up,” Justice Department lawyer Taylor Stout said in his opening remarks.
Prosecutors allege Huawei stole technology, including internet-router source code from Cisco and a robotic arm used by T-Mobile to test phones.
They also accuse Huawei of concealing the nature of its operations in Iran to move US dollars through the financial system despite US sanctions.
The government also alleges that Huawei supplied equipment that could help Iranian authorities monitor protesters during demonstrations in 2009.
How has Huawei responded?
Huawei, a major manufacturer of telecommunications equipment, denies any wrongdoing.
The tech giant’s lawyer Brian Heberlig told jurors the case was about “competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”
Heberlig accused prosecutors of “cherry-picking isolated events” to construct a conspiracy that did not exist. Huawei’s defence says some incidents involved individual employees whose actions were dealt with internally, rather than reflecting company policy.
He told jurors that prosecutors will describe routine activities by global tech companies “but will twist those ordinary activities to try to make them look criminal”.
Huawei separately described the broader prosecution as an attempt to undermine its competitiveness, saying the US government’s “overarching narrative is demonstrably false” and that it had “the utmost respect for intellectual property”.
The case originated during Donald Trump’s first presidency. His administration placed Huawei on a US trade blacklist in 2019 and pushed allies to exclude the company from 5G networks, arguing its equipment could present national security and espionage risks.
Huawei has repeatedly denied that its technology is used for spying.
What has China’s response been?
Beijing has strongly criticised the prosecution, which has come weeks ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US.
On Thursday, a Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson said “the Chinese government firmly opposes the US side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises”, when asked about the case and the American prosecutor’s “criminal enterprise” description.
China “firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests”, the spokesperson said at a regular news conference.
What is Huawei, and has the tech giant faced investigations before?
Huawei is one of the world’s largest telecommunications equipment manufacturers. It also produces smartphones and has become increasingly important to China’s semiconductor and AI industries.
Its activities have drawn scrutiny well beyond the current US trial.
Belgian prosecutors launched an investigation in 2025 into suspected bribery involving the European Parliament allegedly for Huawei’s benefit.
The European Parliament subsequently suspended access for Huawei lobbyists. Huawei said it had “zero-tolerance” for corruption and would cooperate with authorities.
Huawei chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou made worldwide headlines in 2018 when she was arrested on a US warrant after landing in Vancouver, straining both US-China and China-Canada relations.
The warrant was filed after a sealed indictment accused her and the company of bank fraud for misleading HSBC and other banks about Huawei’s business in Iran.
She returned to China in 2021 under a deferred prosecution agreement, and the charges against her were later dismissed.
Admissions Meng made as part of that agreement can, however, be presented as evidence in Huawei’s current trial after a US judge ruled them admissible in June.
Are these issues related to the US-China trade war?
They are legally separate but form part of a much wider economic and technological competition between Washington and Beijing.
Huawei became one of the most prominent targets of US restrictions during Trump’s first term.
Since then, the rivalry has expanded from telecommunications and 5G into semiconductors and AI, with Washington restricting China’s access to advanced US chips and chipmaking technology.
Last week, Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, warned that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world” and urged Washington to maintain restrictions on cutting-edge AI tech. He also called for action against alleged “distillation” of US models by Chinese AI laboratories.
China’s Foreign Ministry on September 14 accused the US tech giant of “fearmongering”.
“Fomenting various threats, engaging in confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt the process of global governance of artificial intelligence and is not in the interests of any party,” said ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun.
The state-backed Global Times newspaper went further, describing Amodei’s proposal as a “Cold War playbook” whose real purpose was to curb Chinese AI development and preserve US technological dominance.
China and the US were engaged in a tit-for-tat tariff war at the beginning of Trump’s presidency in 2025. The trade war ended in a truce, but the world’s two largest economies have failed to strike a trade deal.
Beijing, meanwhile, has used its dominance of critical minerals as leverage and accelerated efforts to build domestic alternatives to American technology.
Currently, China controls most of the world’s rare earth minerals, including metals that are necessary for the manufacture of many technological items, from smartphones to fighter jets. The world’s second-largest economy has 60 percent of these minerals and processes 90 percent of the world’s supply.
In October, Beijing announced plans to require foreign companies to obtain permission to export Chinese rare earth equipment or material.
This meant companies anywhere in the world would need a licence to export rare earth magnets and certain semiconductor materials that contain even trace amounts of minerals sourced from China or produced using Chinese technology.
China’s Ministry of Commerce said its export controls on rare earths, which Trump had labelled “surprising” and “very hostile”, were introduced in response to a series of US measures.

Traditional Chinese medicine supports China's crewed space missions: experts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
23:54:27 CST
00:54:27 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has played a significant role in supporting China's crewed space missions over the past decade and could offer comprehensive health protection for astronauts in the future, experts said at an aerospace medical engineering conference in Tianjin Municipality in north China.
The conference, held from Saturday to Sunday, brought together experts and scholars from fields including aerospace medicine, human factors engineering and life sciences to discuss the medical engineering challenges of future deep space exploration.
Zhang Boli, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and a renowned TCM master, said the unique conditions of spaceflight -- where astronauts face altered breathing, digestion and mobility in microgravity -- make TCM's holistic approach particularly well-suited for maintaining crew health.
"TCM uses a comprehensive approach to regulate the body, such as adjusting qi, or vital energy, and blood imbalances with herbal medicine and using acupuncture to improve unstable heart rates, indigestion and poor sleep," Zhang said.
Wu Bin, an expert at the Astronaut Center of China, highlighted specific applications of TCM in space. Acupuncture can help regulate sleep and prevent muscle atrophy, while Chinese patent medicines can improve cardiovascular function and help astronauts adapt to microgravity.
"In the future, we will continue to use the national space laboratory as a unique platform to conduct TCM research -- not only to address health protection for low-Earth orbit flights, but also to seek TCM technologies and methods for medical challenges in crewed deep space exploration," Wu said.
Astronaut Zhang Lu, who has flown on both the Shenzhou-15 and Shenzhou-21 missions, said TCM has been closely linked to mission success. During the Shenzhou-21 mission, which lasted nearly seven months in orbit, the crew used TCM equipment to stimulate nerves and muscles in the mid-to-late stages of flight to counter muscle atrophy, he said.
The space station is stocked with TCM medicines, including the space heart-nourishing pills and functional drinks that help with radiation protection and immune support, Zhang Lu added.
Zhang Boli noted that research shows TCM approaches can also counter orthostatic intolerance, cardiovascular dysfunction and space motion sickness, enriching the toolkit for astronaut health protection from physical and mental conditioning to disease prevention.
China's space station, Tiangong, which means Heavenly Palace, has now entered an era of long-term human habitation. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay, while the country's 2030 crewed moon landing mission is advancing steadily. ■

Our understanding of the slave trade is still evolving | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:43:17 UTC
00:43:17 KST

William Pettigrew’s book, Britain’s Slave Traders: A Forgotten History, adds a further dimension and depth to our understanding of how entrenched and significant Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade was. The landmark University College London’s Legacies of British Slavery project previously documented the “compensation” payments to 46,000 persons who, at the time of its abolition in 1834, had a financial interest in slave ownership – the £20m paid out is generally reckoned to be worth around £17bn at 2019 prices, or 40% of total government expenditure in 1834 – a vast national debt that was only fully amortised in 2015.
The earlier study thus highlighted the extensive involvement of sections of the British public in profiting from slavery, and the further financial benefit from “compensation”. The recent study tracks back into the prior history from the beginning of the transatlantic slave trade through the 18th century, and shows how its tentacles throughout that time reached out deep into the economy and society. The economic impact over this whole period should not be underestimated. As Pettigrew observes (Slavery was not a footnote to British history. It helped shape the nation, 14 September), the slave trade provided some of the seed funding for the Industrial Revolution. The flow of income back from the Caribbean sugar plantations provided capital surpluses to fund new industries, through an expanded banking system, not to mention personal wealth. Defending these assets in turn stimulated the growth of the British navy, and its eventual control of the seas.
Until American independence in 1776, the colonists relying on enslaved people for their cotton and coffee plantations were British settlers, paying taxes to the British exchequer. In the 19th century, “compensation” payouts fed into investments in the new railways; into banking; and into the funding of stately homes and the arts. Taken together, it could therefore be reasonably argued it was the slave trade that made Britain the cradle of the Industrial Revolution. 
Chris Hendry
Emeritus professor, City, University of London
William Pettigrew is right that slavery was not a footnote to British history. His account powerfully demonstrates how the slave trade was entangled with the state, finance, politics and culture. But there is a further question: what about class? Pettigrew speaks of “Britain” and says “we are all – in some way – connected to it”. Yet Britain was never a single social actor. The slave owner, merchant and investor had a fundamentally different relationship to slavery from the growing cotton-mill proletariat whose labour helped turn slave-grown cotton into commodities.
The danger is that “we are all connected” obscures the asymmetry of accumulation between those who owned capital and accumulated wealth from the system, and those who possessed only their labour and received wages. The question is not simply how slavery shaped Britain, but how its wealth entered an expanding capitalist economy – and was distributed through profoundly unequal class relations.
David Eaton
Sunderland
The Guardian’s excellent presentation of the findings of the Register of British Slave Traders (What is the Register of British Slave Traders and whom does it identify?, 14 September) highlighted what has been long known. It is also timely if it persuades anyone to question the thinking that underlies the philosophy shared by most western leaders that “western democracy” shines out in a challenging world, representing the best of humanity.
Historians know that this is based on contradictions. The world’s first known democracy, the dazzling civilisation of ancient Athens, was based both on slavery and on a thoroughly undemocratic empire, the Delian League. Slavery has been practised across history by all types of government from despotic monarchies to republics and democracies. Put this alongside the fact that the democratic rights we now enjoy had to be extracted, sometimes by force, from the ruling class, and we might have a more humble evaluation of the place of our civilisation in the world. As Gandhi famously said when asked what he thought of western civilisation, “It would be a good idea”.
Dr Peter Purton
Southall, London
 As slavery was abolished, poor laws were enacted across England. A distinction began to be established between those deemed to be worthy of charity and those who were not. The workhouse consolidated the form and substance of these differences. Distinctions established then persist today in ideas about the undeserving and deserving poor, scroungers and strivers, immigrant and indigenous labour. 
Rod Earle
Guildford, Surrey

It’s not just young people who need jobs | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:38:46 UTC
00:38:46 KST

I am now in my 61st year, haven’t worked for more than two years and have stopped applying for jobs (‘I feel invisible’: over-50s reveal harsh realities of trying to get a job, 17 September). The bulk of my career was as an advice worker, specialising in debt, housing and energy advice.
Some years ago I worked with a client in her late 50s who had been a hospital cleaner. She had expected to retire earlier, but the changes to women’s state pension age meant that she faced several more years before retirement. She could no longer do the physical work of cleaning, yet starting a new career while managing her physical health seemed a daunting prospect. At the time I was looking at this situation from the other side of the desk. Now my perspective is rather different.
There quite rightly needs to be an emphasis on young people who are out of work, but I have felt for some time that there also needs to be an alternative route for people who find themselves out of work when they are approaching state pension age. Our current social security and pensions system has roots in the reforms of the early 20th century, developed through the Beveridge report of 1942 and the postwar reforms of the Attlee government.
Since then, the system has been adapted and tweaked many times. But perhaps we have reached the point where tweaking isn’t enough. What we need is Beveridge for the 21st century.
Peter Wade
Leeds

Poland expands siren network amid intensified Russian border strikes
Poland's eastern Lubelskie province will have over 1,000 automated alarm sirens by the end of the year, up from nearly 350 currently, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said on Saturday, following a wave of close-range Russian attacks along the frontier.
Kierwinski told a briefing in Lublin that Russia has altered its strategy, frequently targeting border crossings on the Polish-Ukrainian frontier with jet-powered drones and missiles. "We are increasingly turning to tools designed to counteract these threats," he said, adding that the region had only 30 operational sirens at the beginning of 2024.
The security upgrade follows severe recent disruptions. On Thursday, civilian airports in Lublin and Rzeszow temporarily suspended flight operations while Polish and NATO fighter jets were scrambled to protect regional airspace during a "very brutal" Russian aerial assault on western Ukraine. Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed that a massive explosion occurred just hundreds of metres from the Polish border crossing at Dorohusk after a Russian strike hit a Ukrainian petrol station.
On September 13, a Russian drone struck a passenger train's locomotive at a railway station in western Ukraine located around two kilometers from the Polish border. The attack near the border also affected regional logistics and occurred shortly after a diplomatic train carrying international figures departed the station.
Polish authorities said that while domestic airspace was not breached during these specific incidents, the proximity of the strikes presents a recurring threat to the eastern flank. Kierwinski said that the province has prepared nearly 3,500 civilian shelters for emergency use, warning that "time is very short" to reinforce public readiness. Lubelskie and southeastern Podkarpackie provinces organised civil defence readiness drills on Saturday to test the coordinated response of emergency services and local governments. (PAP)

The 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA 81) High-level Week is taking place from September 18 to 28 at the UN Headquarters in New York, featuring the core General Debate from September 22 to 28.

Middle East escalation
Tensions in the Middle East have heightened after the US and Israel launched large-scale attacks on Iran in February, prompting Tehran to launch missile and drone strikes against US bases across the region.
Pakistan acted as a mediator to defuse tensions, helping reach an agreement between Washington and Tehran in June to end their hostilities.
The deal later faltered amid disagreements between the two rivals over the Strait of Hormuz.

Thousands march in France against ‘licence to kill’ draft law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:18:16 UTC
00:18:16 KST

Thousands march in France against ‘licence to kill’ draft law
PARIS – Thousands of people marched in Paris and other French cities on Sept 20 against a proposed law on the legitimate use of violence that critics say would be a “licence to kill” for police and gendarmes.
In July, deputies in the National Assembly approved the Bill, which says that any law-enforcement official who uses force is assumed to have acted legally in using their weapon. It now faces a vote in the Senate.
Politicians, rights groups and other activists joined others marching at the protest, among them Mathilde Panot of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party.
“The police kill already,” Panot told the crowd, calling for the Bill to be voted down in the Senate.
“In the Republic, there can be no organised police impunity,” she said. “In the Republic, there cannot be a category of citizens who have the right of life or death over other citizens.”
Amal Bentousi, the sister of Amine, a robber who was shot in the back by police in an incident in 2012 at Seine-Saint-Denis, just north of Paris, was among the marchers.
What she described as a “licence to execute” was intended to “reverse the burden of proof” in such incidents, she said.
Amnesty International, France’s magistrates’ union and the country’s League of Human Rights also took part in the protest.
Scores of other marches to protest against the Bill were organised in cities around France over the weekend.
A petition against the Bill on the National Assembly website gathered 730,000 signatures, but the Parliament’s law committee dismissed it in July.
Defenders of the Bill say it would avoid law enforcement officers automatically coming under suspicion or being detained when using armed force.
But in the Marseille protest, Cedric Picard, of Amnesty International, said that “we are afraid that police violence would only grow with this law”.
“In a country where police abuse is among the worst, this law risks worsening the situation,” said one protester, a high school student who gave his first name as Hugo.
On Sept 19, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called on police to be “particularly vigilant” during the protests, fearing incidents.

Trump says monumental arch in Washington, DC will also be military complex

Trump says monumental arch in Washington, DC will also be military complex
Plans for the arch had been met with opposition along with other projects by the US president to reshape capital city.
A planned “triumphal arch” near some of the most iconic landmarks in Washington, DC, will also be a military complex used to store drones and other military equipment, according to United States President Donald Trump.
The changes were made at the request of the military and for “National Security purposes,” Trump posted on his social media platform on Sunday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump asks US Supreme Court to allow $400m ballroom project to proceed
- list 2 of 3Trump’s threats to demolish Kennedy Center sparks protest
- list 3 of 3Demonstrators in US form human chain to protest Kennedy Center closure vote
The project would now be used to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage,” Trump said. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World.”
Trump first proposed building a monumental arch last year to mark 250 years of US independence, saying it would be akin to other famed arches like the Arc de Triomphe built in Paris after World War Two, but “the biggest one of all”.
On Sunday, the US president did not provide details on the new design, which was previously planned to be a lofty 76-metre-high (250-foot) arch that would tower above many other landmarks in the capital. By law, the height of new construction in the city is generally restricted.
Trump’s arch project has faced criticism ever since then for its size and location, and for potentially obscuring views of the Arlington National Cemetery, the country’s famed resting place for war veterans.
In February, three veterans of the Vietnam War filed a lawsuit against the plan, saying it would block the view between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial, erected to honour the US president who oversaw the Civil War. The view from the monument, the veterans said in a court filing, was “carefully designed to symbolise the unification of the country after the Civil War and the strength of a united nation”. Any major monument around the capital, the lawsuit also argued, would need approval from the US Congress. A judge ordered the Trump administration to provide notice of any work on the monument, but courts have not ruled on the larger challenge yet.
“The President’s belated efforts to manufacture a national security justification for this project do nothing to cure its fundamental illegality,” Nicolas Sansone, one of the attorneys representing the litigants, said Sunday. “Congress has not authorized the arch and unless and until Congress does so, the project should not be permitted to move forward.”
The Trump-appointed US Commission of Fine Arts, a key agency involved in the project, approved a design in April that featured statues of golden lions at the base of the arch, and golden eagles and a winged angel atop a baroque arch resembling the one in Paris.
The Federal Aviation Administration said last week the arch would not be a hazard to the nearby Reagan Washington National Airport, but would need a warning beacon on top.
Democratic Congressman Don Beyer of Virginia, who represents the area, noted a drone launching facility there would be directly in the flight landing path of the airport, which he called “a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea,” in a post on X. “Trump clearly expects to lose a lawsuit and therefore wants to set up a pretext to argue that the arch is tied to national security. Which is obviously idiotic.”
The monumental arch is one of several Trump projects in the capital to receive public pushback.
On Saturday, thousands rallied, and some protesters formed a human chain around the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, the landmark along the Potomac River waterfront built to honour the 35th US President John F Kennedy. Trump has threatened to demolish the venue if he is not allowed to add his name to it, saying that is the only way to ensure it gets enough funding to survive.
Trump is also overseeing a $400m controversial project at the White House, where the East Wing of the complex was demolished to make way for an 8,400sq m (90,000sq ft) ballroom with an impenetrable underground bunker. Historic preservation groups filed a lawsuit to stop that project, but last month the US Supreme Court allowed construction to continue.
Like the triumphal arch, Trump has also justified the need for the new ballroom on national security grounds and has referred to it as a “military complex”.

Lee’s spring/summer 2027 show took place in the unusual setting of a north London school sports hall. Starmer wore a bright turquoise knitted midi dress with a high neckline, pleated detailing and short, sculptural sleeves, paired with white block-heeled shoes, with her hair worn in loose waves.
Rather than preparations for the show taking place backstage in the usual way, in Lee’s unique show, models were fitted and adjusted in full view of the audience, dancers rehearsed beside the catwalk, while a drone followed proceedings from the high ceiling of the gymnasium.
Starmer was photographed having her makeup done beside the catwalk, against a backdrop of a football net, with makeup and hair products spread out over a table in front of her. Ballerinas stretched beside the catwalk and synchronised swimming-inspired dancers performed in bright red costumes as part of the show, in the school in Chalk Farm.
The collection was based on the Greek myth of Sisyphus, in which a man is condemned to push a boulder uphill, only for it to roll back down again each time he reaches the top.
“There’s a general feeling right now of relentlessness, a sisyphean cycle,” Lee said. “I was already thinking about the ballet – dance is incredibly transporting, but the work behind it is so intense, the way dancers train for years, the endless repetition, for one ecstatic moment of performance, and then they’re back in the studio.

Throughout Keir Starmer’s time in office, Lady Starmer kept a low public profile, but her “political chic” and “modern British” sense of style was often admired. She has favoured contemporary British brands, including ME+EM, Needle & Thread, and Edeline Lee, whose main creative design studio is based in east London.
At London fashion week’s spring/summer shows in 2024, when her husband was prime minister, Lady Starmer took a front-row seat at Edeline Lee’s show, which took place at Millbank Tower, a former campaign HQ of Labour and the Conservatives, where Reform UK’s central office is now based.
She wore a borrowed £615 cream pussy-bow blouse with a navy polka dot print and matching £715 wide-leg trousers.
It came amid a row over free clothes for Lady Starmer, with Keir Starmer facing an investigation at the time over a possible breach of parliamentary rules around gifts.

A Climate Week (source in Portuguese) began in New York this Sunday, with a series of events across the city, and runs until the 27th. Over the coming days, business and political leaders from around the world will discuss solutions for a more sustainable society with lower carbon emissions.
The event is an initiative of the non-governmental organisation Climate Group (source in Portuguese), organised in coordination with the United Nations General Assembly, which takes place at the same time in the same city.
The first day, Monday, features contributions from the Prime Minister of Australia, Anthony Albanese, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Milliband, and the Icelandic prime minister Kristún Frostadóttir.
This is the largest event in the world dedicated to climate change. It includes more than a thousand events at various locations in New York, bringing together on average more than one hundred thousand people.
This year's debates will focus on three aspects:
Energy and the changes taking place in this field,
The impact those changes are having,
The joint action that is needed.
This series of debates comes at a time when the impact of climate change is highly visible, with tragedies such as the one that recently hit Nepal and the heatwaves that have been battering many parts of the world in recent weeks.
Climate Group has been in existence for around 20 years and aims to help create a world with zero carbon emissions by 2050.
According to the description Climate Group gives on the event website, "the context is changing rapidly. Energy systems are being redesigned, supply chains are under pressure and demand for electricity is rising, driven by electrification, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure. At the same time, the transition is opening up new sources of long-term growth, investment and competitiveness."
The organisers also say that "the current challenge is not ambition but implementation". "Progress is being held back by outdated regulation, infrastructure constraints and misaligned markets. The priority is to remove these barriers and deliver change quickly and at scale. Climate Week exists to accelerate that progress," they add.
This year's conference is taking place against a backdrop of the rapid expansion of AI and the revolution that implies, but also of the strongly climate-sceptic actions and policies pursued by the Trump administration.
The last global climate summit, COP30, held in Belém do Pará, Brazil, ultimately delivered results that fell short of expectations. While a plan was agreed to help the countries most affected by the climate crisis, no precise timetable was set for the phase-out of fossil fuels.
