The Central Paradox of Stoicism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:07:50 UTC
00:07:50 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Throughout our lives we live by the rubric of principles we’ve absorbed, inherited, or deliberately embraced. We consider these ideas foundational. We follow their direction in our plans and our actions, they guide us through our ups and downs.
But occasionally these foundational ideas come to a point where they collide. This leaves us flummoxed — do we disregard one idea and follow another? Do we reconsider all our beliefs altogether? It can lead to private crisis.
The central paradox within Stoicism is one that even Stoics struggle with. It’s ignored for the most part in modern Stoic literature. Embedded within the ancient Stoic texts, there’s a black hole that threatens to break Stoicism’s internal coherence.
On the one hand, we possess a faculty of choice. It is so fundamental that it cannot be touched by circumstance or coercion. And yet, there is another idea within Stoicism, an idea that is no less insistent and forceful. When somebody commits a wrong, they are not to blame. The Stoics tell us not to punish them.
The first idea is what Stoics call prohairesis, we can translate this into modern English as “will”. It is in our power to judge, to assent to the impressions that flood through our consciousness, and to set actions in motion with our intentions.
These three faculties are ours alone, and, according to Epictetus, this tripartite structure is both the core of our being and where our absolute freedom lies. You can choose. You have moral agency. Always. This is a central force in Stoic thinking.
The second idea is that moral evil has no essence. Just as darkness is absence of light, and error is the absence of knowledge, moral evil is simply a mistake.
Everybody wants what is beneficial to them, but they become confused about what exactly is beneficial. This is ultimately an idea the Stoics inherited from Socrates. For Socrates there is no human good and evil, there is wisdom and ignorance. The good is the lodestar for all of us. Those who commit evils are simply mistaken about what is good.
It’s hard to think of good and evil in this way because for two thousand years, Western thinking has largely defined good and evil as two sides of a cosmic conflict manned by human souls.
In the Socratic view, evil is simply the absence of good, not a self-standing existing thing with an essence.
Marcus even quotes Socrates in Book 7 of the Meditations:
“‘No soul’, [Socrates] said, ‘is willingly deprived of the truth’; and the same applies to justice too, and temperance, and benevolence, and everything of the kind. It is most necessary that you should constantly keep this in mind, for you will then be gentler towards everyone.”
This seems strange — people are, after all, cruel, deceitful, lazy and so on. But somebody being deceitful to get a promotion, for example, is taking their own well-being to be more important to them than the well-being of the community.
If that person understood that the well-being of the community is paramount to the good of everybody — including themselves, and that fulfilling self-centered desires doesn’t make you truly happy, then they wouldn’t use deceit to get a promotion.
In the Discourses of Epictetus, this is made clear:
“Philosophers say that people are all guided by a single standard […] If all this is true, then what grounds do we have for being angry with anyone? We use labels like ‘thief’ and ‘robber’ in connection with them, but what do those words mean? They merely signify that people are confused about what is good and what is bad. So should we be angry with them, or should we pity them instead?” (Discourses 1.18)
Marcus repeats the idea at the start of his famous first paragraph of Book 2 of his Meditations.
“Say to yourself at the start of the day, I shall meet with meddling, ungrateful, violent, treacherous, envious, and unsociable people. They are subject to all these defects because they have no knowledge of good and bad”. (Meditations 2.1)
Those people, Marcus implies, are innocent because their thought is defective. In the Gregory Hays translation, the middle part is rendered as, “They are like this because they can’t tell good from evil” (My emphasis).
So we have the collision of two ideas:
- 
You are in absolute control of your judgements, your desires, and your intentions.
- 
You are ignorant when you commit a wrong.
It’s easy to see the questions that would arise from this paradox.
If somebody has full control over their beliefs, desires, and intentions, then how could they not be responsible for a crime they commit? If virtue is a matter of dispelling ignorance, then doesn’t luck play a role in becoming virtuous? If you’re ignorant, how can you climb out of ignorance, if your ignorance is what pulls you away from virtue?
How do we unravel this knot? How do we reconcile those two ideas? How can a person possess full control over their will, and yet be blind to what is good? How can you be wholly responsible for your choices and yet at the same time be blameless for your actions?
How We Solve a Paradox
We’re trapped between two seemingly impossible positions. Either the sinner had the power to choose correctly and failed to make use of it — and therefore deserves condemnation — or they were unable to know the difference between good and evil, which robs them of the agency — the will / prohairesis — that Stoicism takes as real.
Condemning evil in other people is in itself evil in the Stoic view of the world. Theft, violence, and insults affect only what the Stoics call “indifferents” — the externals of our property, our bodies, and our reputation — things that are neither good nor bad in themselves. We have no moral right, as far as Epictetus was concerned, to be displeased with these transgressions, let alone punish them. He wrote, “As long as you honour material things, direct your anger at yourself rather than the thief or adulterer.” (Discourses 1.18).
Epictetus is suggesting that while we cannot blame others for moral failings, we can blame ourselves. It’s clear in his own words that self-directed condemnation is permissible.
We can therefore say that Stoicism isn’t a moral system for the world — it’s a moral system for you.
The focus is inward, and the Stoic must be always watchful of moral lapses and errors that arise from misunderstanding their place in the Cosmos, and what is good in respect to that.
Other people’s ignorance may impinge on our lives, but we must handle those wrongdoings as we’d handle other externals such as natural and social evils like sickness, injury, and misfortune: with the Stoic “indifference”, choosing to see them as neither good nor bad, since only our own actions in response to them can be good or bad.
It is not incumbent on you to judge others; it’s incumbent on you to set an example to others, and to teach those who are willing to learn.
But if good is a matter of knowledge, how do we know that we’ve correctly identified the good?
Epictetus explains in the Enchiridion that “just as targets are not set up in order to be missed, so neither does the nature of evil exists in the world.” (27)
This metaphor can be interpreted as either relating to cosmology or the human condition. In the cosmological sense, Epictetus could be saying that we live in a providential universe that’s oriented toward the good. When we act badly, when we fail to be morally excellent, we “miss” the goals intended for us.
This reading may well be the one that Epictetus intended, but we can read it in another, more secular, sense that is just as compelling. We could say that all life aspires to what is good for it, and avoids what is bad.
Natural targets such as abundance, the greater good, love, and happiness, are “set up” within all of us. We strive and aim for what is good, and we miss when we misunderstand the good.
Against this background, we can see that agency and blamelessness are not in tension. The fault at stake here is a correctable error of understanding.
We all aspire to the good, but an insufficient understanding of what good is leads to moral evil. If I were to think that my own gratification at the cost of somebody else’s well-being were a good, I would simply be wrong about what is good — I’d be deficient in my understanding of the good. I’d miss the target set up for me.
But the targets for good are supplied by nature. They are enduringly there as surely as the ground beneath our feet. Nature has given us reason, and guides us with happiness, contentment, compassion, and love. We err from good, but it insistently waits for us.
Thank you for reading.

Sudan gold mine collapse kills 10, injures 21, survivors say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:07:31 UTC
00:07:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Sudan gold mine collapse kills 10, injures 21, survivors reveal
A gold mine collapsed in northern Sudan, killing at least 10 people and injuring 21 others, two survivors told AFP on Sunday after overnight rescue efforts.
Since war erupted in April 2023 between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the war efforts of both sides have been largely funded by the country's billion-dollar gold trade, in addition to foreign backers.
Shafts of the Awny mining area near Sudan's border with Egypt collapsed on Saturday.
By Sunday morning, "10 bodies had been recovered, and 21 injured miners pulled out", said one of the survivors who was working at the mine when it collapsed, requesting anonymity for security reasons.
Another survivor, also requesting anonymity, told AFP the rescue operation was "being carried out by the miners themselves" with little equipment available.
More miners were feared dead under the rubble, and survivors said the search for the missing was ongoing.
Many young Sudanese have joined a dangerous gold rush, working in unregulated mines with their hands and rudimentary tools for meagre daily wages.
They face chemical poisoning and regular mine collapses.
Last week, at least 82 people were killed and dozens injured in a collapse in the southern Kordofan region.
Artisanal and small-scale mining, which takes place in unofficial zones or decommissioned mines, accounts for most of the gold extracted in Sudan.
According to Sudanese officials and mining industry sources, nearly all of the gold produced by both sides of the war flows to the United Arab Emirates, which denies reports that it arms the RSF.
Even before the war pushed nearly 20 million Sudanese into severe hunger, artisanal mining employed more than two million people, according to industry figures.
Africa's third-largest country is one of the continent's top gold producers, and recorded a "five-year high" of 70 tonnes of production last year, the government said.
But officials say most of the gold is smuggled across Sudan's borders, including through Chad, South Sudan and Egypt before reaching the UAE, the world's second-largest gold exporter.

No tanks, lone soldiers — Ukraine details new Russian assault tactics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:04:06 UTC
00:04:06 KST

Russian assault tactics have changed over the past year, with troops now attacking in groups of just a few soldiers, or sometimes individually, in an effort to get through the "kill zone," Joint Forces Task Force spokesperson Viktor Trehubov said on Sept. 20.
Small groups or individual soldiers who make it past the "kill zone" hide in cove and wait for the others to follow in order to start planning how to assault further in more organized groups, Ukrainian news agency Ukrinform cited Tregubov as saying.
He said that Russian troops are reducing the number of soldiers they send on assaults each time, struggling with the "kill zone" on the northeastern front.
The statement comes as marching through the stretch of land between the rear and the front lines becomes deadlier than ever due to both sides' advancement of drones. Both sides are now trying to reduce the number of soldiers in each group to make it harder for drones to spot them.
The prevalence of drones from both sides has significantly changed assault tactics, making heavy equipment such as tanks a rare sight on the battlefield.
With the "kill zone" reaching 20 kilometers (12.4 miles), Russia has largely stopped using tanks or other heavy equipment for assault operations, according to Tregubov. Drones have replaced many of the tanks' roles for both sides, since driving a tank close to the front would be easily spotted and hit by much cheaper drones.
Ukrainian mechanized brigades also told the Kyiv Independent this spring that their tank crews rarely deploy in the current drone-dominated phase of the war.
"So, under our current conditions, tanks have gradually moved not just to the back seat, but to the third row," Ukrinform cited Tregubov as saying on television.
The only exception, he said, is when Russia can afford to provide "mass drone support" to send tanks into the "kill zone" or if the weather is unsuitable for Ukrainian drones to fly, such as during rain or fog.

In a separate attack, Israeli forces fired several artillery shells at the Bir Ajam woodland west of the village of Zubaida in the central Quneitra countryside, the broadcaster added.
No information was immediately available on casualties or damage from the attacks.
Southwestern Syria has seen repeated Israeli incursions involving raids, arrests, land clearing and shelling, which Damascus denounces as violations of its sovereignty and the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
Syria has repeatedly demanded the withdrawal of Israeli forces from its territory and called on the international community to press Israel to fully withdraw from southern Syria.
Despite the Syrian government posing no threat to Israel, Israeli forces have repeatedly carried out incursions into Syria and launched airstrikes that have killed civilians and destroyed military sites, vehicles, weapons and ammunition belonging to the Syrian army.
During a visit to Syria in July, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said violations of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity were “unacceptable,” calling on Israel to abide by the 1974 disengagement agreement.

The kindness of strangers: I was a ball of stress taking my four children on an international flight – then a passenger tucked a blanket around my sleeping son
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:00:20 UTC
00:00:20 KST

I won’t lie – I was having nightmares before the trip. When my family immigrated to Australia from Europe, my husband travelled ahead to organise a place for us to live. I followed him seven weeks later with our four children, all aged under seven. I was a ball of stress for weeks in the lead-up.
Walking on to the plane with four kids in tow, I could almost hear people think, “Oh my God, I don’t want to be seated next to them!” And I completely understand.
I had booked a window row and a seat in the middle row, thinking that I could put all the kids in the window row and then myself in the middle, where I could keep an eye on them. But when we got into the plane, the flight attendant told me that for security reasons we couldn’t do it that way. We had to rejig, my five-year-old son taking the middle-row seat alone, for what was to be a nearly 24-hour flight broken up into two legs.
There was a man seated next to my son. He didn’t display any of the annoyance he must be feeling about being seated next to a small child – a very kind act in itself, and one that brought me great relief. But his kindness didn’t end there.
At some point during the flight, after the cabin lights dimmed, the other three kids and I dozed off. When I woke up, I looked over to see my five-year-old had fallen asleep as well. The man next to him was pulling his blanket up and gently tucking him in. It was an unguarded moment of care and compassion.
I don’t think the man had any idea I saw him do that. We arrived safely and I never saw him again. But it was such a generous thing to do that, 20 years later, the memory remains magical.

Adults with severe mental illness die 15 to 20 years earlier from diseases such as cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:00:19 UTC
00:00:19 KST

Adults with severe mental illness are nearly five times more likely than their peers to die from serious physical diseases before the age of 75, according to research.
The analysis of NHS data by the Rethink Mental Illness charity reveals that people with severe mental health problems die 15-20 years earlier than the wider adult population, largely due to preventable physical conditions.
Rethink’s calculations show that adults under 75 with serious mental ill health – defined as those referred to specialist secondary mental health services – are 6.3 times as likely to die from liver disease, 6 times more likely from respiratory illness, 3.8 times more likely from cardiovascular disease and 2.3 times as likely from cancer. They are also 14.6 times as likely to die due to suicide, compared with those who were not referred. Overall, they are 4.8 times more likely to die before the age of 75 than the general population.
For some conditions, these health inequalities are the starkest to date. For working-age adults living with a mental illness, the number of deaths from cardiovascular disease and cancer are at their highest levels since records began, each with more than 24,000 deaths in the 2022-2024 reporting period, the charity calculated.
Cancer, cardiovascular disease, liver disease and respiratory disease accounted for more than half (56.5%) of deaths for 18 to 74 year olds with severe mental health problems in England during this period. Cancer and cardiovascular disease each accounted for just under 19% of all deaths, respiratory disease 11%, and liver disease 8%. During the same period, suicide comprised 7% of these early deaths.
The report identifies a number of factors driving this excess mortality, including poverty, poor housing, higher rates of smoking, weight gain from medication, physical inactivity, and fragmented care. But the authors conclude that “diagnostic overshadowing” – where physical symptoms are wrongly attributed to mental illness – means potential illnesses are not always properly investigated and treated.
The findings come before the government’s independent review of mental health, autism and ADHD, which is expected to be published this week and recommend a more holistic approach to supporting patients with these conditions.
Mark Winstanley, the chief executive of Rethink, said: “It is a scandal that people living with severe mental health problems are so much more likely than the rest of the population to die from often preventable physical health conditions.
“Given that many are in frequent contact with health services throughout their lives, it is clear that opportunities to identify and treat physical health problems are being missed.
“These early deaths are not inevitable. The new cross-government mental health strategy … must prioritise physical health checks, improve access to mental-health informed interventions and bolster peer support, if it wants to reduce these terrible health inequalities.”
Responding to the findings, Prof Subodh Dave, the president of the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said: “Having a severe mental illness shouldn’t be an early death sentence. This stark inequality is unacceptable. People with severe mental illness deserve the same opportunity to live long, healthy lives as everyone else. We know that evidence-based solutions to close this gap exist – from smoking cessation to routine physical health checks. But what is lacking is concerted action to prevent these premature deaths.”
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “People living with severe mental illness face stark health inequalities, and too many continue to experience poorer physical health outcomes.
“This government is taking immediate action to transform services for people with severe mental illness. We’re developing a new modern service framework to look at what action is needed to help people live healthier and longer lives through high-quality care, opening 100 new community mental health centres, and our mental health strategy will go further, outlining how we plan to build a more integrated system that responds earlier and reduces waiting times for support.”

‘The fears begin to fall away’: why Britain’s mosques are opening their doors to public
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:00:18 UTC
00:00:18 KST

At one mosque in north London, a woman shouted at worshippers that more of their children should be killed, as children had been in Gaza. On another occasion, gas pipes were ripped from the building and reconfigured so leaking gas built up inside it.
These are among a series of incidents the London Islamic Cultural Society has faced in the past three years. But rather than retreat behind closed doors, the mosque has opened them wider. It is one of more than 100 across the UK, including in London, Birmingham, Sheffield, Manchester, Glasgow, Southend and Cardiff, that have invited in members of the public this weekend to learn more about Islam and British Muslims.
As part of Visit My Mosque, they have offered tea, cultural food, talks, multi-faith activities and art exhibitions as well as workshop discussions with members. The event, hosted by the Muslim Council of Britain, is now in its 11th year and organisers say it has taken on added importance amid rising anti-Muslim hatred.
Dr Wajid Akhter, the secretary general of the Muslim Council of Britain, said: “In the current climate, far too many people are getting their information about British Muslims and their neighbours from an algorithm and foreign-funded billionaires fuelling toxic hate towards faith communities, both online and on our streets in Britain.”
Sufia Alam, the head of the Maryam Centre at the East London mosque and the London Muslim Centre, said their mosque was taking part to show that friendship and solidarity were stronger than hate. “We cannot allow hatred to define the relationship between Muslims and their neighbours,” Alam said.
“At a time when Islamophobia is becoming more visible and more normalised in parts of our public discourse, initiatives like this matter deeply. When people walk through the doors of a mosque, meet Muslim families, volunteers and worshippers, and simply have a conversation, many of the stereotypes and fears begin to fall away.”
The event comes amid heightened concerns about the safety of Muslim places of worship. One mosque is attacked in Britain every five days, according to the British Muslim Trust, the government’s partner for monitoring anti-Muslim hatred. Attacks included acts of intimidation, violence, property damage, harassment, anti-Muslim hate speech, online abuse and vandalism.
At Cheadle mosque in Greater Manchester, Farooq Rafiq described the Visit My Mosque day as an “invitation to experience a space and faith that are often misunderstood”, adding: “We have seen over the past year this manifest in the rise of Islamophobia.”
Mohammed Kozbar, the chair of Finsbury Park mosque, said the best way to respond to rising anti-Muslim hatred was with “openness, dialogue and solidarity”.
At the London Islamic Cultural Society on Saturday afternoon, people of all faiths walked in as it opened its doors. The north London mosque is run by Bibi Khan, the first woman to become president of a mosque in the UK.
“In this day and age, we see things in the media that don’t reflect what’s going on in our community. It’s so important for us to reach out and to be able to communicate exactly what’s happening with us in terms of our faith, the people we serve, what do we do and what we believe in,” said Khan.
There was a heavy police presence, with officers greeting people attending the open day. About two dozen people sat down for a roundtable discussion, speaking about their association with the mosque or, for those who didn not practise Islam, why they wanted to learn more.
Among those in attendance was Judith Prinsley, the deputy for Muswell Hill United synagogue who also serves as the vice-chair of the security, resilience, and cohesion division for the Deputies of British Jews. Khan and Prinsley, who are both part of the Haringey Multi-Faith Forum, have a close bond.
Anti-Muslim and antisemitic incidents have risen sharply in the UK since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel and Israel’s war in Gaza. Haringey, where the London Islamic Cultural Society is located, has large Muslim and Jewish communities.
Khan said: “In Haringey, especially with brothers and sisters from the Jewish community, it’s really important that we understand each other and stick together, even where there are times when we don’t agree with each other.”
Prinsley said there had been antisemitic graffiti near her synagogue and that some worshippers were scared to attend. She said she was “shocked” by the gas pipe incident and how little attention it had received outside the Muslim community: “I thought, how come we hadn’t been made aware of it? Why wasn’t it on the television?”
For Khan, social media is a big concern in terms of escalating incidents. She mentioned a false conspiracy theory, spread online, that “Albanians” were supplying mosques in the UK with guns. “Think about it. Somebody comes outside demonstrating and they’re going to automatically carry a weapon because they think we’ve got one,” she said.

Xinhua Headlines: China-Africa cooperation in vocational education builds skills, opens opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:58:22 CST
23:58:22 KST

* The skills that carried African competitors to skills competitions like the World Vocational College Skills Competition are among the everyday subjects in classrooms that China and Africa run together. For some, success in competition has opened the door to employment.
* Young Africans across the continent are gaining practical skills as China-Africa cooperation in vocational education continues to grow. For many, mastering a skill is ultimately about finding a job, or even starting a business. The longer game is not training one class of students, but enabling African schools to train their own.
by Liu Jie and Lin Jing
WINDHOEK, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- In a workshop in Ongwediva, northern Namibia, fabric rustles as Wilhemina Amadhila measures, cuts and stitches.
"Each stitch comes together to form a stunning outfit," said the 22-year-old woman who will take the craft to the 48th WorldSkills Competition to be held on Sept. 22-27 in Shanghai, China.
Amadhila and 16 other young Namibians will compete in different categories of the competition. Besides Namibia, other African countries such as Kenya, Egypt, South Africa and Morocco are also taking part in the contest to showcase their technical and vocational skills.
This is not the first time African competitors have taken part in skills competitions in China. Their active participation offers a glimpse of growing China-Africa cooperation in vocational education, which has helped endow many Africans with practical skills and opportunities.
LEARNING THROUGH PRACTICE
At the 2025 World Vocational College Skills Competition held in north China's Tianjin, Angolan student Massak Ventura Noquena Eduardo took silver on the strength of industrial robotics and automated production-line skills learned from Chinese teachers. "I hope to apply what I have learned to Angola's industrialization," he said.
The skills that carried him to the podium are among the everyday subjects in classrooms that China and Africa run together. At the Angola-China Institute of Technology, students study mechatronics, industrial robotics and automation.
Guo Xiaoyu, a teacher from Baotou Vocational and Technical College in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, remembers students who were at first hesitant to even use a multimeter or an oscilloscope.
"Vocational education cannot be based on theory alone. Students have to do things with their own hands," Guo said. After a semester of practice in circuit assembly and fault diagnosis, more than 90 percent of them met the required standard.
At Ethiopia's Holeta Polytechnic College, Chinese instructor Ma Yujie demonstrated surgical suturing as animal science students gathered around the table, taking turns practicing on training pads.
"We are now participating in practical demonstrations," Lemi Abera, 22, said. "With our Chinese instructors linking classroom concepts to practical animal health practices."
Ma is one of 20 Chinese teachers working at six vocational colleges across Ethiopia. "The students really cherish the opportunities to practice on training models, to the extent that some are willing to spend extra time in the laboratory after class," she said.
In Cameroon, the classroom has moved onto the construction site.
In early August, China First Highway Engineering Co., Ltd. teamed up with Cameroon's Ministry of Higher Education and the National Advanced School of Public Works to run the country's first certification course for surveyors.
Cameroon's Minister of Higher Education Jacques Fame Ndongo said the program turns construction sites into "open-air classrooms" and builds a direct bridge between universities and major projects.
This cooperation is not just about building roads; it is about training people, and about the future of Cameroon's workforce, the minister added.
According to an action plan released at the 2024 Beijing Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, China will continue vocational education with Africa, build with African countries schools of engineering technology, set up or upgrade 10 Luban Workshops, and offer 60,000 training opportunities aimed chiefly at African women and youth.
China has established 17 Luban Workshops in 15 African countries and trained tens of thousands of professionals.
FROM SKILLS TO LIVELIHOODS
For many young Africans, mastering a skill is ultimately about finding a job, or even starting a business.
At the end of 2025, 30 Rwandan students came home from a year of advanced training at Jinhua University of Vocational Technology in east China's Zhejiang Province.
Aimable Tuyishime, a 23-year-old e-commerce graduate who studied logistics, warehouse management and data analysis there, is now building an online shopping platform for Rwandan consumers.
"This is the right time to put all the skills and experience I gained into practice," he said.
In Tanzania, the Kilimanjaro Institute of Technology and Management launched a Chinese culinary program early this year, combining video lessons from chefs in China with practice in local kitchens.
"These are skills that make you different, and I can even start my own restaurant one day," said hospitality student Ruth Washima Seni.
For some, success in competition has opened the door to employment. At last year's Namibian national skills contest, the gold medalists in cooking and restaurant service also won three-month apprenticeships with a local hospitality group.
SEEDS THAT STAY
The longer game is not training one class of students, but enabling African schools to train their own.
In Cote d'Ivoire, seven modern vocational schools built by Chinese contractors opened last September. Spanning some 83,000 square meters, they can take about 5,600 students in 15 trades, from machining to auto repair and agro-processing.
Moreover, 184 Ivorian teachers and administrators from the schools spent four months in China learning to use and maintain equipment, while 15 school managers studied school management there. Two Chinese vocational institutions now help operate five of the schools.
In Kenya, China-supported vocational education cooperation is entering a new phase: 69 institutions will receive equipment for 70 training workshops, and 1,190 instructors and technicians will be trained in both countries.
"A trained instructor can train many generations of trainees; (and) a modern workshop can continuously produce skilled workers," said Esther Thaara Muoria, principal secretary of the State Department for Technical and Vocational Education and Training in Kenya's Ministry of Education.
Wu Jiashun, who heads the central Africa regional center of China First Highway Engineering, put it more plainly: a young person trained today will work for 30 years, and will bring up more young people along the way. "That is how a country learns to build its own roads."
For Amadhila and her teammates, Shanghai will be more than a place to compete. It will serve as a global classroom where they can test their skills, learn from their peers and bring new ideas home.
Behind these young Africans are more classrooms like these, where young people across the continent are gaining practical skills as China-Africa cooperation in vocational education continues to grow.■

Ukraine Launches Retaliatory Strikes on Moscow Refinery Supplying 40% of Region’s Petroleum Product Demand
In response to the Russian military aggression, Ukrainian strike drones and cruise missiles hit the Moscow Oil Refinery in Kapotnya overnight on September 20, sparking a large-scale fire at the plant.
Footage of the strike was published by the monitoring channel Exilenova+, which Militarnyi cited on September 20. The attack ignited a blaze on the refinery grounds, with further consequences still being assessed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Monitoring resources logged a drone-danger alert at 3:19 a.m. By 3:51, Russian channels reported air defenses engaging over the capital region, and interceptor activity continued past 5:27 a.m., according to Militarnyi.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed on social media that Russian air defenses had destroyed 151 drones overnight, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Emergency crews were working at sites where debris had fallen, he added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the operation in a post on X. He wrote: "Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night. One of Russia's key oil industry facilities and the aggressor's logistics facility were hit. These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine."
Zelenskyy added that "the systems used included FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sichen, and Pelican." He did not tie individual systems to specific targets. The president also noted the strike affected a facility in the Voronezh region.
Geolocation of the footage indicated the strike damaged installations at the refinery:
- a combined crude-oil processing unit, known as the KUPN;
- the ELOU AVT-6 primary distillation installation.
A separate fire broke out at the "Sofyino" logistics technopark, matching the logistics facility Zelenskyy referenced.
Among the systems Zelenskyy listed was the FP-5 Flamingo, a Ukrainian long-range missile. Near the refinery, local residents recovered debris from an unidentified missile visually resembling the FP-5, and one video captured the sound of a jet engine, Militarnyi reported. Its use at the site remained unconfirmed.
The Kapotnya plant ranks among Russia's ten largest refineries and supplies roughly 40% of the Moscow region's petroleum products, per Militarnyi. It processes up to 11 million tons of crude annually across more than 30 technological units, including catalytic and thermal cracking and reforming lines.
The facility produces AI-80EK, AI-92EK, and AI-95EK gasolines, diesel, aviation kerosene, bitumen, sulfur, and polymers, the outlet noted.
The strike extends a sustained Ukrainian campaign against Russia's military aggression. On August 28, FP-1 drones set fires at the Slavneft-YANOS refinery in Yaroslavl, the largest oil-processing site in Russia's Central Federal District, in an attack that killed one person and injured 27. Weeks earlier, on August 5, a drone raid ignited a blaze at Rosneft's Bashneft-UNPZ refinery in Ufa, more than 1,400 kilometers from Ukraine.

Forced Deportation of Ukrainian Children Now Explicitly Triggers US Sanctions Under Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:56:37 UTC
23:56:37 KST

- Category
- World
Forced Deportation of Ukrainian Children Now Explicitly Triggers US Sanctions Under Law
The US president, Donald Trump, signed H.R. 5334 into law on September 18, making the forced deportation of Ukrainian children an explicit statutory ground for sanctions against Russia. The measure covers knowing involvement in the removals, whether direct or indirect.
This was reported by Bring Kids Back UA on September 19, a day after the signing of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Among the grounds for sanctions, the law expressly names forcible transfers and the forced deportation of children as serious human rights abuses against citizens of Ukraine, the initiative noted. The list also includes enforced disappearances, unjust detainment, and torture, and is not exhaustive.
The measure reaches not only those who physically remove children but also the officials, institutions, and intermediaries who organize or enable the transfers, according to Bring Kids Back UA. Its threshold is knowing involvement, direct or indirect, and the law treats a person as liable if they should have known the consequences of their conduct.
Foreign persons—both individuals and legal entities such as guardianship structures, foundations, and transport operators—can be named, alongside senior Russian officials designated by virtue of their posts. The initiative reported that the designation carries two sets of restrictions.
The first is a full asset block, freezing all property and interests held in the United States or controlled by US persons, and barring transactions in such property and interests. The second is a visa bar that strips the right to enter the country and revokes any visas already issued.
The deportation of children now carries a price written into US law, not only into political statements
Maksym Maksymov
Head of Bring Kids Back UA
Because the law covers indirect involvement, it reaches those who processed and financed the removals—guardianship bodies, transport operators, and officials who signed the paperwork, Maksymov added. It places the deportation of children in the same statute as sanctions on Russian oil, banks, and the defense industry, he explained.
That turns the issue into a full instrument of pressure rather than a separate humanitarian track.
The bill was introduced in Congress in September 2025, with the sanctions text added in the summer of 2026, the initiative noted. It expands mechanisms targeting Russia's officials and its financial and energy sectors, as well as those who help Moscow evade existing restrictions, and extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 through 2031.
What sets the decision apart is its level, Bring Kids Back UA emphasized. The ground for sanctioning the deportation of Ukrainian children is now written into statute rather than an executive order, meaning it cannot be undone by a change of administrative policy.
The law designates no one automatically. It builds the mechanism, and decisions on which individuals and organizations are added to the lists rest with the US administration.
The statute lands amid a widening Western push to make the removal of Ukrainian children personally costly, for Russia, as the European Union had adopted an initial package in May, targeting 16 Russian officials and seven entities tied to the systematic deportation, indoctrination, and illegal adoption of Ukrainian children.

Israeli public broadcasting icon, journalist Prof. Gideon Kutz dies at age 78
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:48:56 UTC
23:48:56 KST

Journalist Prof. Gideon Kutz, 78, died in Paris on Sunday.
Kutz served for four decades as Voice of Israel's correspondent in Paris and was one of the most recognizable voices of Israeli public broadcasting in the French and European arena.
In recent years, Kutz also wrote for Maariv, having published reports and commentary from France and Europe.
Beginning in 1986, he broadcast on Voice of Israel, and later served as Channel 1's correspondent in Europe.
Following the establishment of the Israeli Public Broadcasting Corporation (KAN), he continued in his role as a correspondent and commentator on European affairs.
During his long career, Kutz covered some of the major events that shaped Europe and the world, including the fall of the Berlin Wall and the revolutions in Eastern Europe, the wars in Yugoslavia and Chechnya, the Middle East peace process, the Arab Spring, terrorist attacks in Europe, the crisis in Ukraine, and the nuclear talks with Iran.
Kutz researched history of Hebrew, Jewish journalism in Europe
Alongside his journalistic work, Kutz was a researcher and historian specializing in the history of the Hebrew and Jewish press in Europe.
He was a full professor of communications and culture at the University of Paris 8, and edited the journal Kesher, which researches the history of the Jewish and Hebrew press and media.
Kutz served five years as president of the Foreign Press Association in France and later as its honorary president.
He is survived by his wife, journalist and photographer Yaffa Eiron-Kutz, and his two children.
KAN News, in an article regarding Kutz’s death, remembered him as “the ultimate envoy for public broadcasting in Europe.”
"We mourn the death of Gideon Kutz, who for four decades was a symbol of Kol Yisrael and the Israeli Public Broadcasting Corporation's foreign broadcasts in Europe. Kutz, with his abilities, qualities, and rich experience, was the ultimate envoy for public broadcasting in Europe - curious, knowledgeable, thorough, and adventurous,” KAN stated.
“He covered every major theater of war in Europe and around the world, did not hesitate to go into the field and bring stories from Arab countries and Iran, and left behind a long list of journalistic achievements that became part of the journalistic history of public broadcasting in Israel."

ITIM demands equal conditions for women in upcoming Chief Rabbinate exams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:48:55 UTC
23:48:55 KST

ITIM has demanded that the Chief Rabbinate guarantee women equal conditions in its upcoming certification exams, warning that it may return to court after the Rabbinate again announced that the tests would be divided between two Jerusalem venues.
The demand comes less than a month before the next exam session, and follows the historic first sitting for women in April, when three female candidates waited approximately four and a half hours after the men began before receiving their exam papers.
In a September 17 letter, ITIM asked the Rabbinate to ensure that women’s exams begin and end on time, are graded anonymously and are held under the same physical conditions as men’s.
It also demanded qualified staff to answer questions during the tests, arrangements to protect candidates from outside disruption, and clear accommodations for pregnant and nursing women, reservists, and reservists’ spouses.
The Rabbinate published the dates for each exam subject on September 16 and said the tests would be held at the Jerusalem International Convention Center and the Religious Services Ministry.
Separating the venues between men and women could equal improper exclusion
It has not been established which candidates will be assigned to each site. ITIM said that, based on the previous session, it expects men to sit the exams at the convention center and women at the ministry.
The organization argued that separating the venues would itself amount to improper exclusion. At a minimum, it said, the Rabbinate must prove that the arrangement will not leave women with inferior conditions.
ITIM first approached the Rabbinate on August 3, seeking advance clarification of the venues, procedures and available accommodations. It sent a reminder on September 3. According to the organization, neither letter received a response.
The latest letter asks for a detailed answer “as soon as possible” but sets no specific deadline. ITIM said it would consider legal action if the Rabbinate did not provide timely assurances.
The dispute is the latest stage of an eight-year fight over women’s access to the state examinations.
Rabbinate does not ordain women
Six female Torah scholars first sought to register in 2018 but were rejected because the Rabbinate does not ordain women. They petitioned the High Court of Justice the following year alongside ITIM, the Rackman Center and Kolech.
In July 2025, the High Court unanimously ruled that women could not be barred from the exams. The justices distinguished between ordination, which was not at issue, and access to a state-administered examination system carrying professional and financial consequences.
The Rabbinate’s certificates can affect eligibility and salary scales for some public-sector positions and, under specified conditions, may be treated as equivalent to an academic degree. The certificates can also increase the salaries of some teachers of religious studies.
That makes the dispute more than symbolic. The state attaches economic value to success in the exams, while the women now entitled to sit them are still seeking assurances that they will receive conditions equal to those provided to men.
The ruling also rejected a proposed alternative examination track for women, finding that a separate system would not provide genuinely equal recognition.
Women were eventually permitted to register in February. But when the first three candidates arrived for an exam on the laws of mourning on April 27, they were sent to the Religious Services Ministry while the men sat the exam at the convention center.
According to ITIM, the women began shortly before 3 p.m. following an urgent approach to the High Court. The organization said no professional staff member was present to answer questions and that they placed their completed booklets in a box marked “women’s classroom,” raising concerns that graders could identify their gender.
“We expect the Chief Rabbinate to come to its senses and ensure fair and equal examination conditions,” said attorney Timna Guttel of ITIM’s legal department.
ITIM founder Rabbi Seth Farber said the uncertainty was particularly serious because candidates still had no clear information about their conditions or available accommodations less than a month before the exams.

Israeli father killed in Slovenia while rescuing seven-year-old son from ravine fall

A 44-year-old Israeli, Gail Hillel, a member of Kibbutz Yizrael, was tragically killed in Slovenia on Saturday while trying to rescue his 7-year-old son, who had fallen into a ravine during a family trip.
The accident occurred near the Slap Savica waterfall, a popular natural site in the Bohinj area of northwestern Slovenia.
According to the Kranj District Police, the family had stopped at a nearby rest area with picnic tables and benches after visiting the waterfall. During this stop, the boy wandered away from his family. Soon after, they heard his cries for help.
Hillel immediately searched for his son and fell into the ravine while trying to reach him.
Rescue teams later found Hillel in the Savica River channel, suffering from fatal injuries, and pronounced him dead at the scene, while his son was also located by the rescue team.
The child received initial treatment at the scene for serious injuries before being evacuated by helicopter, operated by the police aviation unit, to the University Medical Center in Ljubljana.
Rescue teams locate Israeli Father and son
The Bohinj Mountain Rescue Service stated they had initially received reports indicating that only a child had fallen into the ravine but upon their arrival, they discovered that Hillel had also fallen.
Several members of the rescue unit were conducting a training exercise nearby at the time of the incident, which enabled them to reach the accident scene quickly. The team descended nearly 60 meters into the river channel below and was able to assist both Hillel and the child, preparing them for evacuation.
After the child was airlifted to the hospital, Hillel’s body was recovered from the steep terrain using ropes.
“We sincerely hope the child recovers quickly and in the best possible way, and that one day he and the rest of his family will be able to cope with this tragedy,” local rescuers expressed in their condolences to the family.
Slovenian police have stated that they are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the accident. Once their findings are complete, a report will be submitted to the relevant district prosecutor’s office.

Breadcrumb
Iran warns against new escalation by US and allies
Iran warned on Sunday against any big new attack by the United States and its allies, saying it had information that such a move was being prepared, adding to the anxiety in a region already on edge after drone and missile strikes on Saudi Arabia.
Iran's military central command said on state media that any new attack would trigger sustained retaliation against US bases and interests, and that Washington's regional allies would be considered parties to the conflict. It did not elaborate on the information it said it had about a coming US attack.
The US State Department issued a security alert on Saturday saying there was potential for unforeseen escalation in the Middle East and Americans should exercise more vigilance and be aware of possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.
Nearly seven months into the US-Israel war on Iran, neither side has looked ready to make major concessions needed to end the fighting, and with global energy markets already stretched, the conflict continues to spill over into other crises around the region.
On Saturday, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, who made major advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast after the country's civil war reignited this month, said they had carried out strikes in the Saudi capital Riyadh and on a major oil facility in the kingdom's Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Reuters video showed a massive plume of black smoke billowing from the area of Riyadh's main international airport after booms were heard in the Saudi capital overnight.
Saudi Arabia did not comment on the incident or the Houthi claims, though a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had foiled other attacks on the kingdom. The US State Department alert cited Houthi hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports.
Recent escalation by the Houthis has forced Riyadh into a painful dilemma: continue airstrikes on the group to stop it seizing more Yemeni territory or step back in the hopes of averting drone strikes on critical infrastructure.
Strikes on Saudi Arabia
The Houthi gains along the coast mean the group's forces now sit on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, giving them easier control over shipping travelling between the Red Sea and Asia and the ability to blockade the crucial waterway.
With Iran already having blockaded most shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the oil-rich Gulf's energy exports are now almost entirely cut off from global markets, adding to pressure on global oil prices.
A US blockade of Iranian ports is meanwhile stopping Iran from selling its own oil, contributing to major problems in the Islamic Republic's economy.
With the war inflicting painful damage on all sides, however, there is little sign of a return to the interim ceasefire agreement that was struck in June, but that fell apart in July amid disputes over its terms.
Iran reiterated on Sunday that it would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the terms of that June agreement, as it interpreted them, were met.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said Iran would have to keep fighting as well as negotiating to push back its enemies and consolidate any gains through diplomacy.

nick cave’s soundsuits bring the stage into the crowd
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:45:51 UTC
23:45:51 KST

nick cave’s soundsuits: when the body becomes the stage
Imagine a sculpture that does not sit on a plinth, but moves through a train station, a street, or a crowded hall. Its surface rattles with every step, its scale alters the silhouette of the person inside, and its elaborate construction makes the wearer almost impossible to identify. This is the basic proposition of Nick Cave’s Soundsuits: the garment becomes an environment, and the body becomes its architecture.
Cave made the first Soundsuit in Chicago in 1992, following the Rodney King beating and the acquittal of the police officers involved. The event left him thinking about racial profiling, vulnerability, and what it meant to be perceived as a Black man in public. While walking through Grant Park, he found a twig and began gathering hundreds of them, eventually assembling them into a full-body sculpture.‘The moment I put it on and started to move, it made sound,’ Cave recalled. ‘Sound at that moment was my call for protest. It was a way of being heard.’
The garment functioned as what Cave describes as an ‘emotional shield’, a form of armor that concealed the wearer’s race, gender, class, and other visible markers of identity. But the discovery of the sound it made also shifted the work beyond protection. The suit could move, perform, attract attention, and occupy space.
image by Dayson Roa
A second skin that changes the body
Soundsuits are wearable sculptures that completely envelop the human figure. They can incorporate fabric, wire, raffia, feathers, beads, buttons, sequins, plastic toys, ceramic objects, synthetic fibers, rugs, quilts, and other found materials. Their surfaces are often densely assembled, turning ordinary objects into highly elaborate bodies.
The materials have changed considerably since the original twig suit, but the principle of accumulation remains. Cave gathers discarded and everyday objects and reorganizes them into forms that are difficult to classify. A suit made from hundreds of small plastic figures, for example, can become something closer to a moving landscape than a conventional garment.
Cave has described the suit as a ‘second skin’ that hides the identity of the person inside. ‘When I was inside a suit, you couldn’t tell if I was a woman or man… I was no longer Nick. I was a shaman of sorts,’ he has said.
Soundsuits performance during the opening festivities of The Obama Presidential Center | image by Mitch Buss
When the body becomes architecture
Through the Soundsuit, Cave builds the stage onto the performer. The suit expands the body beyond its ordinary proportions. Strands of raffia extend into the surrounding air; beads and other elements move independently; rigid frames establish new silhouettes. When the wearer walks or dances, the sculpture alters the space around them, establishing a boundary between them and the outside world while simultaneously projecting outward into it.
Without a recognizable face or body, the viewer has fewer visual cues through which to categorize the person inside. Cave has explained that the suits ‘hide gender, race, class’ and force audiences to look at the work without judgment.
The anonymity is not neutral, however. It originates in a specific experience of racial vulnerability. Cave’s work does not erase that history so much as transform it into a question: what happens when the visual information through
which people are routinely judged disappears?
a form of armor that conceals the wearer’s race, gender, class, and other visible markers of identity | image by Elizabeth Corr
The stage moves into the crowd
For Heard NY in 2013, Cave worked with 30 dancers in horse-like Soundsuits who moved through Grand Central Terminal accompanied by live music. The performance interrupted the everyday routes of commuters. A building designed for circulation became, temporarily, a theater.
The same principle appears in Heard presented in Detroit, where a procession of horse-shaped Soundsuits and local dancers moved along Detroit’s riverfront, and in Up Right Chicago, presented during the Chicago Architecture Biennial. There, Soundsuit-clad performers were brought together with reflective ‘Stage Buoy’ sculptures designed by Studio Gang.
In these works, the distinction between performer and spectator becomes unstable. People stop, photograph, watch, and sometimes participate. The architecture does not disappear, but its function changes. A terminal becomes a parade route; a park becomes a performance ground; a monumental hall becomes a place for collective dancing.
Cave’s The Let Go, presented at the Park Avenue Armory in 2018, pushed this further. The large drill hall became a space for performance, music, dancing, and participation, with Soundsuit-clad dancers moving through crowds alongside live musicians, DJs, and singers.
20 Soundsuits were part of the performance | image by Elizabeth Corr
Sound turns sculpture into action
The first suit produced sound as Cave moved, and subsequent works have continued to incorporate materials capable of rattling, scraping, rustling, or colliding. Beads, shells, bells, buttons, and other loose components turn movement into percussion. This means that the suits cannot be understood entirely through photographs. Their sound and movement are structural parts of the work.
A static Soundsuit may initially read as an elaborate sculptural object. Once worn, its meaning changes. Walking activates the materials. Dancing amplifies them. The performer creates a sonic envelope that moves through the surrounding space.
The physical complexity of the Soundsuits also comes from their labor. Beading, stitching, weaving, binding, layering, and assembly are central to the practice. Cave’s use of found and discarded materials connects the works to a broader history of making through reuse and improvisation, while his interest in African ceremonial dress and African-American craft traditions informs the visual language.
image by Dayson Roa
From protest armor to collective spectacle
Cave has resisted the idea that the works should be understood only through their initial connection to racial violence. Their origins are personal and explicitly political, but their subsequent development has opened the work toward questions of identity, community, participation, joy, and collective experience.
That expansion is visible in the contrast between the first twig suit and the large public performances that followed. The original object was a private form of protection. Later, Soundsuits enter shared spaces and generate encounters between strangers.
This shift from armor to amplifier is perhaps the most useful way to understand the evolution of the work. The suit still protects by obscuring the individual, but it also amplifies movement, sound, color, and presence. What once functioned as a shield becomes a means of occupying space. Cave’s suits emerge from a ‘very dark place,’ as he has put it, yet their public manifestations can be exuberant, noisy, humorous, and communal.
image by James Prinz Photography, courtesy of the artist and Jack Shainman Gallery, New York
The garment is the architecture
The most compelling aspect of Cave’s Soundsuits is ultimately not their visual excess, but the way they reorganize the relationship between body and space. The suit hides the person while making the body more visible. It removes individual identity while giving the performer an amplified presence. It is both a protective shell and a public signal. It makes sound through movement and turns movement into a spatial event. Most importantly, it carries its own stage.
A Soundsuit does not need a theater, plinth, runway, or designated performance zone to become active. A railway terminal, a park, a gallery, or a street can become the setting. The architecture is temporarily reorganized around the moving figure, while spectators become part of the environment simply by stopping to watch.
In this sense, Cave’s work offers a different model of performance space: one that is portable, embodied, and activated through participation. The stage is no longer a fixed platform separating performer from audience. It is something worn, carried, sounded, and shared.
The Soundsuit began as armor. Over more than three decades, it has become something more expansive: a mobile architecture through which vulnerability can become visibility, individuality can become anonymity, and a single body can create a space for collective experience.
Soundsuits, Heard (detail), 2012 | image by James Prinz Photography
image by Elizabeth Corr

Russia And Ukraine Launch Attacks On Final Day Of Russian Parliamentary Vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:33:26 UTC
23:33:26 KST

There was no letup in fighting between Russia and Ukraine on September 20, as voters in Russia cast ballots on the final day of parliamentary elections from which a political party calling for peace was excluded.
Ukraine attacked Russia with drones and missiles overnight, launching what Moscow's mayor claimed was the "largest ever" barrage on the capital, while Ukraine reported Russian drone attacks on numerous targets nationwide.
As expected, the Kremlin-controlled United Russia party was set to be handed a big victory in the tightly controlled election -- the first vote to fill the State Duma, Russia's lower house of parliament, since President Vladimir Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Shortly after polls closed, the Central Election Commission claimed that with about 25 percent of the ballots counted in the nationwide voting by party list, United Russia had more than 57 percent.
In a highly managed process held September 18-20, voters could choose between United Russia and several parties in the "systemic opposition," which critics say provide a veneer pluralism but are largely loyal to the Kremlin.
"It gave Putin an opportunity to further promote war against Ukraine, for example, by glorifying veterans, many of whom ran for political office," Dominika Hajdu, director for policy and programming at GLOBSEC, a think tank, told RFE/RL on September 20.
Real political opposition is repressed in Russia, with even small acts of dissent -- online or in the real world -- often followed by stiff prison sentences, loss of employment, or other penalties.
Fighting Continues
As Russians voted, their country’s war on Ukraine continued unabated. Ukraine's military reported 138 Russian attack drones striking at 17 locations nationwide, and authorities said four people were killed in the Kyiv region, including three children, one of them four years old.
Kyiv officials said Russia continued to target the capital thoughout the day, with short breaks, and residents said loud explosions rang out overhead in the evening.
Ukrainian forces also struck in Russia, hitting the major Kapotnya refinery on the outskirts of Moscow. Officials in the region ringing the capital said two people were killed there, a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man, when drones hit their residential buildings.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed that Ukraine launched 1,600 Ukrainian drones at Russia overnight, including more than 400 targeting Moscow. He said one aprtment building in the city was hit and nobody in Moscow was killed.
Sobyanin's numbers were not confirmed by Ukrainian sources and could not be independently verified. The Russian military said its forces shot down more than 1,100 drones.
Ukrainian forces also fired domestically-produced Flamingo cruise missiles, according to both Russian authorities and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said Ukraine also used a new short-range ballistic missile, the Pelican, in the strikes.
Russian officials said the Ukrainian attacks were aimed at disrupting the election process. However, there were no reports of polling stations being hit and the strikes occurred overnight while they were closed.
Instead, the strikes appeared to be a continuation of a campaign that over several months has curtailed Russia’s capacity to refine and export oil products. The Ukrainian attacks have impacted an industry that is vital for bankrolling the Kremlin’s war effort while also bringing the war home to ordinary Russians in the form of fuel shortages and long lines of frustrated drivers at gasoline stations.
The Central Election Commission claimed turnout exceeded 56 percent -- about five percentage points higher than in the last Duma election, in 2021.
Since Putin came to power over a quarter-century ago, the Kremlin has increasingly stifled dissent, marginalized political opponents, and manipulated elections, leaving little room for surprises.
Over the three days of voting -- as well as earlier voting in some regions -- reports of alleged violations mounted.
Among other things, they included evidence pointing to ballot-box stuffing, pressure on state-sector workers to vote, and incidents in which observers from parties other than United Russia were obstructed from monitoring the balloting, including through physical force.
Past presidential and parliamentary elections have been marred by evidence of widespead fraud. Anger over alleged cheating in favor of United Russia in a December 2011 Duma vote led to a series of large demonstrations known as the Bolotnaya protests. The state cracked down hard.
United Russia was on track to maintain its dominance in the Duma, where it holds more than 300 of the 450 seats. The others with seats in the current Duma are the Communist Party, the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR), A Just Russia, and New People.
Yabloko, a liberal party that would have been the only party on the ballot calling for an end to the war on Ukraine, was disqualified in August on what its leaders said were "absurd" grounds.
Analysts said the Kremlin feared that Yabloko's message could have drawn a substantial number of voters and undermined the Kremlin's narrative of lockstep support for the war.
The ban showed Putin is "afraid of any kind of opposition," said Hajdu.
“If Yabloko had been allowed to run a more meaningful, full-fledged, and (maybe most importantly) legal anti-war campaign for 6-8 weeks, that could challenge the image of total consolidation around Putin and the war,” Mikhail Komin, a research fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), said before polling began. “This is the main reason why Yabloko was disqualified."
The elections came amid what appears to be rising frustration in Russia over the progress of the war, and opinion polls have shown falling approval ratings for Putin, who is widely believed to have expected Russia to subjugate Ukraine within weeks of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Urging Russians to vote in a speech released on September 16, Putin said the elections would "demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our troops, that we are a united people bound by shared values, historical memory, and love for the Motherland."
In addition to Russia, Putin's government was holding the balloting on Ukraine's Crimean Peninsula, which Russia has controlled since 2014, and in the Russian-occupied portions of four other Ukrainian regions that Moscow baselessly claims are part of Russia. Kyiv has denounced the effort.
Zelenskyy said late on September 20 that he had spoken to US President Donald Trump and that they agreed to meet in New York, where the annual UN General Assembly takes place September 22-28.
Trump made ending Russia's war against Ukraine a priority when he began his current term in January 2025, and in recent weeks his administration has sought to rveive diplomacy that had been largely dormant since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in late February of this year.

Yemeni forces target Houthis in Al-Bayda, down drone near Bab el-Mandeb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:30:44 UTC
23:30:44 KST

Mohammed Sameai and Mohammad Sio
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
Yemeni government forces said Sunday they targeted Houthi forces and equipment in the central province of Al-Bayda and shot down a drone belonging to the group near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in southwestern Taiz.
Military spokesman Majed al-Nazili said in a brief statement that government forces had “targeted personnel and equipment belonging to the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Al-Bayda province.”
Nazili also released a video that he said showed the moment Houthi positions were hit in Al-Bayda, without providing further details.
Separately, the government-aligned Nation’s Shield Forces said its 1st Brigade shot down a Houthi drone while it was flying over the Kahboub front near Bab el-Mandeb.
The force also released footage that it said showed parts of the downed drone.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the claim.
Several fronts in Taiz province saw clashes between government forces and the Houthis in recent hours, though neither side announced any territorial gains.
Meanwhile, relative calm prevailed Sunday in the central province of Marib and the northern province of Al-Jawf, with no major clashes reported, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
Several fronts across Yemen have seen renewed fighting between government forces and Houthi fighters, including Taiz, Marib, Al-Jawf, Al-Bayda and Lahj, in the worst escalation since a UN-brokered truce in April 2022.
Fighting escalated in September, allowing the Houthis to seize key locations in Al Hudaydah and Taiz, including the strategic city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s major shipping routes.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Foreign Minister Tsahkna on World Cleanup Day: Russia Must Be Held Accountable for the Environmental Damage It Has Caused in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:29:14 UTC
23:29:14 KST

According to Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna, an initiative that began in Estonia has, in less than two decades, grown into a global movement bringing together more than 100 million people with the shared goal of creating a cleaner environment. “This is not merely a clean-up campaign. It is an initiative that strengthens community cooperation, builds trust, and helps keep our planet sustainable,” said Tsahkna. He added that the movement is centred on the responsibility each person bears for their surroundings. The goal is to engage at least five per cent of the population in every country, turning local initiatives into lasting change and creating healthier, more sustainable, and waste-free communities.
The minister noted that World Cleanup Day also serves as a reminder that the environment is often a silent victim of war. “Through its war of aggression, Russia has caused an estimated €150 billion in environmental damage in Ukraine,” Tsahkna stressed. “The aggressor is using nature as a strategic weapon. In recent months, Russia has increasingly targeted civilian infrastructure, bombing fuel depots, railways, and ports. The resulting pollution, contamination, and fires are causing severe damage to Ukraine’s natural environment, water resources, air quality, and ecosystems.”
“Agriculture has suffered particularly heavily. Bombing, artillery fire, and destroyed military equipment have contaminated agricultural land, one of Ukraine’s most important economic resources, with toxic substances and heavy metals. Their impact on crops and ecosystems will be felt for decades. The deliberate destruction of the environment is a crime, and Russia must be held accountable.”
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, the war has generated an estimated 311 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions in Ukraine. Approximately 30 per cent of Ukraine’s territory is contaminated by landmines and unexploded ordnance. The cost of clearing the country of mines is estimated at USD 38 billion.
These figures reflect only part of the war’s impact. The long-term deterioration of ecological conditions, loss of biodiversity, and damage to ecosystems remain largely unmeasured and continue to worsen every day.
World Cleanup Day traces its origins to the first nationwide Teeme ära! clean-up campaign held in Estonia in 2008. Since 2018, more than 139 million people from 211 countries and territories have taken part in World Cleanup Day initiatives, collecting over 870,000 tonnes of waste. In 2023, the United Nations General Assembly officially designated 20 September as World Cleanup Day. The global headquarters of the movement, the NGO Let’s Do It World, is based in Estonia.

Israel in dark over Turkey fraud arrests as Jewish community says more Jews may be detained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:27:54 UTC
23:27:54 KST

In an unusual situation, Israeli officials still cannot say with certainty how many Israeli citizens have been arrested in connection with a massive fraud investigation in Turkey. Jerusalem does not even have an estimate of how many of the 201 detainees are Israeli, although Turkish authorities and media have reported that nine Israeli citizens were among those arrested. Turkey says the operation targeted an alleged international forex and cryptocurrency fraud network and involved 201 detainees, including nine people identified by authorities as Israeli nationals.
Sources in Turkey’s Jewish community, however, told ynet that eight of the nine are local Turkish Jews and that it is unclear how many of them also hold Israeli citizenship. The community also believes additional Jews were arrested in the case but do not appear on the list of nine people described in Turkish reports as Israelis.
Israel has contacted the Turkish authorities and requested an official answer on how many Israeli citizens were arrested and what allegations they face. The detainees themselves have not contacted Israel’s Foreign Ministry, nor have relatives approached the ministry on their behalf.
The Foreign Ministry said it had received reports that Israeli citizens had been detained in Turkey on suspicion of involvement in criminal activity and was “working to ensure that the rights of the Israeli citizens are protected.”
There is concern in Jerusalem that the handling of the case could be influenced by the severe political tensions between Israel and Turkey, particularly given Ankara’s increasingly hostile rhetoric toward Israel in recent years.
Israel expects it could take several days for Turkey to respond formally. Israel currently has no consul physically stationed in Turkey, with consular affairs handled from a third country, meaning communication between officials is largely conducted remotely.
So far, Jerusalem’s public response has been considerably more restrained than the tone of some Turkish coverage. The Foreign Ministry has neither confirmed nor denied the allegations against the suspects and has focused instead on ensuring their legal and consular rights.
The Turkish framing
The affair erupted Friday when Turkish authorities announced what they described as a major international investment fraud investigation and emphasized alleged Israeli links to the network.
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan subsequently lashed out at Israel in a post on X, accusing what he called the “Zionist massacre network” of seeking to undermine Turkey and declaring that his government would cut off the resources of what he described as enemies benefiting from the “terror industry.”
According to Turkish authorities, the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office, working with the National Intelligence Organization, or MIT, police and Interpol, carried out raids at hundreds of addresses in Istanbul and Muğla. The detention count later rose to 201. Turkish officials said the investigation focused on dozens of call centers and financial offices connected to companies allegedly offering fraudulent forex and cryptocurrency investments.
Turkish prosecutors allege that the operation lured victims through social media advertisements and websites promising high returns. Turkish reporting says the alleged scheme generated approximately 13 billion Turkish liras in transaction volume over two years, while prosecutors have also alleged that losses to victims worldwide exceeded $3 billion.
Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said Israeli-linked figures were prominent among the alleged owners and beneficiaries of the operation. Turkish media subsequently published names of nine people described as Israeli citizens.
But according to the Jewish community sources who spoke to ynet, at least some of those people are Turkish-born Jews, some of whom may hold dual citizenship while others may not be Israeli citizens at all.
That distinction complicates the national framing adopted by parts of the Turkish media, which have presented the investigation as an Israeli operation inside Turkey.
Yeni Şafak, a newspaper closely aligned with Erdogan’s government, went further, publishing a headline describing the alleged network as a “Mossad fraud ring” and asserting links to Israeli intelligence. The report did not publicly provide evidence establishing such a connection.
The uncertainty over the suspects’ citizenship also leaves Israel with little ability at this stage to determine who may be entitled to consular assistance.
Israeli officials are particularly concerned that the suspects’ Israeli or Jewish identities could become part of the political narrative surrounding the case. At present, however, there is no public evidence that Turkish courts have treated the detainees differently because of their nationality or religion.
The allegations in Turkey
According to Turkish reports, the alleged fraud network recruited potential clients through advertisements on social media and websites that promised high returns from foreign currency and cryptocurrency investments.
People who expressed interest were allegedly transferred to representatives who spoke their native languages and persuaded them to deposit relatively small amounts at first.
They were then shown purported profits on trading platforms and encouraged to transfer increasingly large sums.
When investors tried to withdraw their money, prosecutors allege, they were told that their accounts had been blocked and that they needed to pay additional amounts described as taxes, fees or payments to unlock the funds.
The money was allegedly never invested as promised and was instead transferred to bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets controlled by the network outside Turkey. Turkish officials say hundreds of complaints collected through international law enforcement channels formed part of the investigation.
Turkish prosecutors also claim that those running the operation instructed employees not to target Israeli or American citizens. According to findings attributed to MIT, Israeli-linked operators shifted activity abroad after Israel banned the sale of binary options to overseas customers in 2017.
Turkish authorities have not provided a detailed public breakdown establishing the individual roles of each foreign detainee.
The latest official figures cited by Turkey say nine detainees are Israeli citizens and 11 are Pakistani, alongside nationals of Azerbaijan, Syria, Jordan, Ukraine, Thailand, Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, the Philippines, Iran, China, Lebanon, the Palestinian territories, Mexico, Egypt, Mozambique, Argentina and Bangladesh.
For now, that leaves Jerusalem waiting for Ankara to answer the most basic questions: exactly who is being held, which of them are actually Israeli citizens and what each individual is suspected of doing.
