Meta launches legal challenge against UK media regulator over Online Safety Act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:24:33 UTC
23:24:33 KST

Meta has launched a fresh legal challenge against Britain’s media regulator in the latest of a slew of actions by social media companies who are accused of using the courts to slow down implementation of the Online Safety Act.
Lawyers for the parent company of Facebook served notice during the week in an appeal against placing WhatsApp and Instagram, which are also owned by Meta, in a category that subjects them to additional duties.
Those additional responsibilities include greater transparency, more user controls, measures to protect users from fraudulent advertising and increased recording of illegal content.
The move comes against the backdrop of hostility on the part of US tech corporations, and Donald Trump’s White House, over the fees and fines regime Ofcom is enforcing under landmark digital safety legislation.
Meta launched a legal challenge in London in May, claiming that Ofcom’s methodology for calculating the charges was flawed and should not be based on a company’s global revenue.
Breaches of the Online Safety Act can be punished by fines of up to 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue (QWR) or £18m – whichever is higher. Ofcom is funding the operating costs of carrying out its online safety work by drawing on a proportion of that revenue.
Other legal action is being taken by TikTok and X over how much information the companies need to give Ofcom to carry out its job of monitoring their services.
A senior director at the regulator told a committee in the House of Lords on Tuesday that Ofcom was “operating in a highly litigious environment”, including facing two actions by Meta and others from “a raft of services” bringing judicial reviews against the body for trying to collect data.
“We absolutely are looking to drive change in the best way we can,” Oliver Griffiths, the Ofcom group director for online safety, told peers hearing evidence about the Online Safety Act. “We have all come to work to make this happen, but, if we run unnecessary risks, we are going to get absolutely clobbered legally by deep-pocketed individuals and firms.”
Speaking about the latest legal challenge, a spokesperson for Meta said: “Like many others in the industry, including TikTok, Roblox, X and Quora, we are challenging specific aspects of implementation.
“These are not challenges to the law itself, but how Ofcom has interpreted it. This is a normal feature of any new regulatory regime being bedded in and ensures questions of process, scope and implementation get settled so the law is applied proportionately, accurately and consistently.”
Lisa Nandy, the secretary for digital, culture, media and sport, vowed last week to keep introducing legislation to govern the internet. “I think we’re going to have to start getting used to the idea, actually, that government is going to be far quicker, far more interventionist, and I think I’m going to have to see the law updated regularly because tech is changing so fast that we’ve got to be able to respond,” she told the Sky News Electoral Dysfunction podcast.

Russian exiles cast votes to voice dissent to Putin and Ukraine war
BERLIN/YEREVAN, Sept 20 - Russians living abroad cast their votes on Sunday, the final day of a parliamentary election, in what many described as a moral duty, if ultimately a futile act of protest against President Vladimir Putin and the war in Ukraine.
One exiled Muscovite, who gave her name as Olga, waiting in line to vote in the Armenian capital Yerevan, said she had no expectation her ballot would change anything inside Russia.
"It's about putting on a bit of a show," she said. "This is really more about symbolism, about bringing something positive, about solidarity."
The State Duma election, the first since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, is likely to be presented by the Kremlin as evidence of public support for Putin's policies and for a war that is now in its fifth year with no end in sight.
Most anti-war candidates were barred from the ballot and the other major parties have consistently voted in line with the ruling United Russia on major issues.
Hundreds of thousands of Russians, many of them young and well-educated, fled the country after the start of the war in Ukraine, settling in ex-Soviet countries like Georgia, Armenia and Kazakhstan, as well as across Europe and beyond.
After years outside their home country, several Russians who spoke to Reuters said they remained determined to see change come to Russia.
"We still have our whole lives ahead of us, and we really want to be in Russia one day and help build a new, democratic country," said 24-year-old Varvara from Moscow, who spoke to Reuters in Berlin.
Some protesters outside the Russian embassy in the German capital held up a placard reading, in Russian, "Putin is a murderer and a war criminal", and signs in support of Russian prisoners jailed for speaking out against the war.
Many voters expressed deep pessimism about Russia's future, even if the conflict ends soon. Others, including a man who gave his name as Valery, clung to the belief that casting a ballot still mattered.
"I want to believe, with every fibre of my being, that we can still make a difference and vote against the ruling authorities," he told Reuters in Yerevan. REUTERS

“Food, medicine, and other essentials have been blocked for the past month. Horrifying reports indicate that people are searching for scraps of food and gathering grass to survive,” Sybiha said.

“The only obstacle is Russia. Russia is deliberately preventing these efforts from reaching people who desperately need them, turning humanitarian access itself into an instrument of pressure,” Sybiha said.

Sybiha also said he intended to discuss these efforts with Mirjana Spoljaric, President of the International Committee of the Red Cross.
The international community must use its collective voice to break Russia’s humanitarian blockade, ensure immediate and unhindered access for humanitarian organizations, and enable the safe evacuation of civilians, Sybiha stressed.
“Moscow must not be allowed to turn occupation and isolation into a means of starving, terrorising, and trapping people beyond the reach of international assistance,” the Minister wrote.

South Korea held off Japan 67-57 to win the men's basketball final at the 2026 Asian Games on Sunday, while China finished fourth after losing 79-70 to Iran in the bronze-medal match.
Japan built a 16-12 advantage in the first quarter, but South Korea opened the second quarter with an 8-4 run to pull level, leaving the two sides deadlocked at 28 apiece at halftime.
South Korea seized control in the third quarter with a 17-8 surge, carrying an eight-point cushion into the final frame. Lee Hyun-jung reeled off five straight points early in the fourth quarter to stretch the lead to 13, putting the result beyond doubt.
Lee finished with a game-high 27 points, knocking down five of his eight 3-point attempts, and grabbed 18 rebounds. Lee Jung-hyun added 14 points and seven assists for the gold medalists.
For Japan, Ren Kanechika posted 13 points and six rebounds, while Atsuya Ogawa chipped in 12 points.
Iran took an early 8-2 lead before China responded with a 10-0 run to take the advantage in the first quarter. The two sides were tied at 42-42 with four minutes 30 seconds left in the third quarter, before Iran launched a 13-4 run to enter the final period with a nine-point lead.
Following a 3-pointer from Matin Aghajanpour, Iran extended its advantage to 13 points. 
Pang Zhenglin's driving layup and Li Hongquan's consecutive 3-pointers helped China close the gap to 62-63. However, led by Aghajanpour, Iran mounted another 16-8 run to secure the victory.
"It was an important game for us, especially for the young players. We put our heart out on the floor. We really wanted it more. We hustled really well. We dived for every loose ball and eventually we won the game," said Iran's Mohammad Jamshidi afterwards.
Only two China players scored in double digits. Pang scored a team-high 22 points, and Li contributed 12. Aghajanpour led Iran with 21 points, while Piter Girgoorian added 15.
"We didn't do well in defense and rebounding today, nor did we execute our pre-game tactics on the court. We controlled the tempo for a while in the second half, but failed to adjust after committing turnovers," said China captain Hu Mingxuan.
"Iran earned this win because they played harder than us, and they played tough. They had more energy than us, and they wanted this game. They played much better than us. That's why they beat us," China forward Cui Yongxi added. (Xinhua)

Russian Strikes Stop 90% of Ukraine’s Steel Output
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:16:00 UTC
23:16:00 KST

Russian ballistic missile bombardments have knocked out Ukraine’s three remaining large-scale metallurgical plants across the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, effectively halting 90 percent of the country’s domestic steel manufacturing.
Industry executives warned that the concentrated strikes on heavy industrial assets threaten the viability of the entire sector, according to the Financial Times.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In early September, coordinated ballistic barrages disabled blast furnaces across three major plants, killing 17 metallurgical workers.
Subsequent strikes have systematically targeted the damaged facilities to prevent repair efforts, including a dawn attack on Thursday, Sept. 17, when two Russian ballistic missiles struck the Zaporizhstal metallurgical complex in Zaporizhzhia, marking the fourth missile strike on that facility in five weeks.
“As of today, [Ukraine] no longer has a steel industry,” Oleksandr Vodoviz, head of the office of the chief executive at Metinvest, told the Financial Times. “They knew everything about the plant, they knew exactly where to hit.”
The precision strikes specifically targeted blast furnace infrastructure across two Metinvest enterprises alongside the ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih integrated steelworks in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
Metinvest and ArcelorMittal confirmed that the affected facilities, which collectively accounted for 90 percent of Ukraine’s national steel output, have suspended all production operations while technical teams attempt to assess whether damaged components can be restored.
Ukrainian Churches Urge Pope to Intervene Over Oleshky Starvation
Indeterminate repair timelines and
Engineers and operational specialists have been unable to establish definitive timelines for restoring blast furnace operations, with corporate officials noting that specialized replacement equipment and structural repairs could require extended schedules.
“Right now we do not understand how long repairs will take – days, weeks, months, or years,” Vodoviz stated.
Vodoviz emphasized that the indefinite idling of the three steel complexes directly imperils the livelihood of more than 15,000 employees.
The shutdown threatens severe macroeconomic repercussions for Ukraine’s wartime economy, depriving the state budget of essential corporate tax revenues and foreign currency earnings generated by industrial exports.
Prior to the full-scale invasion that began in 2022, Ukraine ranked among the world’s leading steel exporters. However, the sector has suffered compounding structural losses, beginning with the destruction and occupation of the Azovstal Iron and Steel Works and the Illich Iron and Steel Works in Mariupol, followed by recurrent power grid disruptions and logistical bottlenecks across Black Sea maritime corridors.
Repeated ballistic targeting of Zaporizhstal
The shutdown across the sector follows a systematic bombardment campaign directed against Zaporizhstal, one of Ukraine’s oldest and largest steel mills.
According to Metinvest, Russian forces have launched 17 ballistic missiles at the Zaporizhstal complex since August. The enterprise initially halted output on Aug. 11 after a strike killed eight employees and wounded 28 others while destroying core power distribution systems.
Subsequent missile impacts hit the site on Aug. 27 and Sept. 12, damaging blast furnace workshops, open-hearth facilities, internal electrical networks, and logistical transport links.
During the Sept. 17 dawn strike, two ballistic missiles struck production workshops and internal rail infrastructure, injuring one worker who was extracted from collapsed masonry.
Metinvest Chief Operating Officer Oleksandr Myronenko condemned the repeated attacks on the idled enterprise, characterizing them as a deliberate Russian strategy to prevent reconstruction and eliminate Ukraine’s basic industrial foundation.
Myronenko emphasized that the facility produced pig iron and rolled steel exclusively for civilian applications, rejecting any military utility.
The physical destruction has exacerbated severe financial strain across the metallurgical sector, with Zaporizhstal posting a net loss of Hr 1.06 billion ($23.7 million) in the first half of 2026, compared to a net profit of Hr 1.37 billion ($30.7 million) during the corresponding period in 2025.

Australians waiting years for dementia diagnoses, landmark survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:12:15 UTC
23:12:15 KST

First Australian dementia survey reveals long waits for diagnoses, overwhelmed carers
In short:
The first survey of Australians with dementia and their carers has revealed long wait times for diagnoses and mixed experiences with support.
Many carers reported low wellbeing and strained family relationships.
What's next?
Advocates say health professionals need to take the first signs of dementia seriously and refer more people to rehabilitation programs.
Less than half of Australians living with dementia received a diagnosis in the first year, with crucial early warning signs sometimes missed by health professionals, a landmark new survey has found.
The Living with Dementia report is the first time Australians with dementia and their carers have been surveyed, and experts have urged governments and healthcare professionals to pay close attention to the findings.
Dementia is considered by many to be the defining health crisis of the 21st century and is now the leading cause of death in Australia.
It is estimated one million Australians will be living with the condition over the next 35 years.
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare surveyed 266 people living with dementia in the community and over 1,600 carers between 2025 and January this year.
It found getting a diagnosis was often a complicated process and many carers were struggling.
There is no single test or pathway to obtain a dementia diagnosis, and around one third of people with dementia said they did not associate their symptoms with the condition.
"I didn't think I had a problem. I thought, you know, it's just, I'm forgetting things. I've got a lot on my mind. I was a busy man,"
— said one 68-year-old survey participant.
Seeking help did not always lead to a quick diagnosis, with people reporting delays accessing specialist appointments and tests, or GPs attributing symptoms to causes other than dementia.
Research has previously shown dementia patients, particularly women, are often misdiagnosed with depression or stress.
"I'd raised this with my GP, and I had the usual 'it's probably menopause or your chronic fatigue syndrome',"
— said one 59-year-old survey participant.
Dementia Australia's Kaele Stokes said too often healthcare professionals had a sense of "nihilism" and did not want to talk to their patient about dementia.
"There's a sense that dementia is an inevitable part of aging, which it isn't,"
Professor of healthy aging at the University of Sydney, Yun-Hee Jeon, said it was not acceptable that two in five people were waiting three years for a diagnosis.
"People are left in limbo and might miss out on accessing drugs that could help manage the symptoms of cognitive impairment or simply the opportunity to plan their future."
Many not receiving after-care information
About 40 per cent of survey respondents reported not receiving any information about support services after their diagnosis.
Although most said their diagnosis was a positive experience, some felt it was impersonal and lacked compassion.
"When we got the diagnosis, we got a couple of different brochures and things. Like, that was probably it. There was no referring back to the doctor. There was no, like, there was no 'these are the next steps',"
— daughter of someone living with dementia.
Dr Jeon said clinicians often did not know what services were available and people missed out on important rehabilitation.
Only 16 per cent of those surveyed took part in "re-ablement" programs, which involve goal setting, physical mobility and environmental adaptations so people can maintain independence.
"That's a really low figure when you think about it because it would be one of the best things for many people if they knew this type of program was available," Dr Jeon said.
Less than half of respondents had help from a care coordinator, and Dr Stokes said this showed the importance of embedding dementia care navigators in the system.
A dementia care navigator would provide a consistent point of contact throughout someone's dementia journey.
The federal government rejected Dementia Australia's proposal to fund these roles in the most recent federal budget.
"When someone has cancer or diabetes they are automatically connected to a diabetes or cancer nurse, and we just don't have the equivalent model for dementia," Dr Stokes said.
Despite the many challenges, nearly half of survey respondents living with dementia reported a high level of wellbeing.
Carers feel socially isolated
Most carers reported low wellbeing and said they felt overwhelmed by their responsibilities, with about 30 per cent spending 70 hours caring per week.
Most said they did not have enough time for their own self-care and felt lonely, and a third said old friends avoided spending time with them if the person living with dementia was present.
"I just had to stop my own personal things that I was doing so that I could be home to look after him. You know, I had to plan. Everything had to be planned,"
— said a spouse of a person living with dementia.
Half said relationships with some family members worsened since they began their caring role.
"This [tension] can come down to financial arrangements, different views about what's best for the person or getting different information from different sources," Dr Jeon said.
She said relationship counselling between family members could be beneficial, and respite care was also a critical tool but was often hard to access, especially in regional areas.
Most carers surveyed said the biggest challenge to accessing support, such as respite, was the complexity of application processes.
Many were also not aware of key supports such as the Dementia Behaviour Management Advisory Service, which can help manage psychological changes.
"If every single person living with dementia were requiring a more formal form of aged care or disability support, the system wouldn't be able to handle it," Dr Stokes said.
"So it is incredibly important that we provide support to carers."
Advocates hope bigger surveys can be done in the future and can include those living with dementia in residential aged care.
If you or someone you know has questions or concerns, contact the National Dementia Australia helpline on 1800 100 500.

Charles Spencer on the royal fallout following Princess Diana's death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:06:19 UTC
23:06:19 KST

Charles Spencer's striking claims about the royal fallout following Princess Diana's death
Charles Spencer is testing one of the lingering questions of our time: can the world ever get enough of his sister, Diana, Princess of Wales?
It turns out the controversy surrounding her life has not faded nearly 30 years after her tragic death.
In fact, Spencer's new book, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" (to be published Tuesday by Penguin Press), has pulled the scabs off some old wounds, especially when he recounts an unsettling conversion he says he had with Diana's ex-husband – now King Charles – shortly after she died: "He said about Diana, 'We'll forget her soon enough.' And he said it, I can't really recreate it, but it was said with a bit of a hiss, to be honest. And I said, 'I can't believe you said that.'"
You'd have to have been living under a rock not to know Diana's story … the daughter of one of England's grand aristocratic dynasties, chosen at just 19 to be the bride of the then-Prince Charles. Their seeming fairy-tale wedding, which turned into a rocky marriage, that ended in a bitter divorce. Her tragic early death in a Paris car crash. It was a riveting, if sad, real-life soap opera, with an apparently insatiable worldwide audience.
But why do a new book about such a well-known story?
"With the 30th anniversary of her death coming up next year, I was getting inundated with requests to be in somebody else's book or documentary," Spencer said. "And it suddenly occurred to me, well, if you're all so interested in hearing from me, I might just give you the definitive story."
Well, the Spencer version of the story.
Diana has always divided opinion. She was the modern breath of fresh air who blew the cobwebs out of the fusty royals – or she was the upstart whose popularity threatened the old ways and undermined an institution that had done very nicely, thank you, by maintaining its aloofness and its mystery.
Asked what he believes people have gotten wrong about Diana, Spencer replied, "I think people who picked at her and found fault with her did so without a true appreciation of the unique force that she was."
Was it malice? "I think a lot of people in the British establishment didn't know what to do with this totally rogue but brilliant force," Spencer said. "And there were a lot of attempts during her time on the public stage where they tried to suppress her. Diana would call them the 'men in gray suits' – people working for the royal family in particular."
Charles Spencer is the 9th Earl Spencer. His family has not endured near the top of the British aristocratic food chain by being critical of the royal household, but Diana's story has changed that.
Speaking at Althorp, his family's estate, Spencer said, "We're sitting in a house here, surrounded by portraits of my ancestors, all of whom served the crown very loyally. And there was probably a thought when Diana was plucked to become a royal bride that she would fit into the mold of the past, and she didn't. And so, I don't know about malice, but I do know about jealousy.
"She said it was very difficult, even from her first royal tour overseas, which was to Australia, how if she was on one side of the street with the public and [Charles] was on the other, the crowd on his side of the street were less thrilled, and that this was very difficult for him," Spencer said.
And, of course, Charles' continuing connection during the marriage to his old flame, now Queen Camilla, didn't help.
King Charles does not come off well in this book. So badly, in fact that the palace has responded, saying Spencer's recollections may be the result of "fraternal grief that can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory." Memories like the one of a call Spencer says he got from Charles soon after Diana's death: "He sounded excited in a sort of upbeat way," Spencer recalled. "And obviously I'm not justifying or criticizing, I'm reporting that's the fact."
Spencer has suggested that Charles may have felt "upbeat" because he finally felt free to pursue Camilla. "I said that that might've been it, yeah. But that's obviously, I can't say what he was thinking, but I'm trying to think why would somebody feel giddy at that time."
"I stand before you today the representative of a family in grief"
In his eulogy at Diana's funeral in September 1997, Spencer cast himself as protector of her legacy, and of her children, particularly after they were made to walk behind their mother's coffin. "I thought it was such an absurd idea that I just thought, well, that won't happen," he said.
Because he felt it would be too hard on the boys? "That, and I thought it was barbaric," he replied.
Spencer said he believes the idea of having them follow their mother's coffin through the streets of London was to protect Charles from the crowd's reaction. "That's what I heard from politicians who were involved at the time, yes," he said. "There was a concern that if he walked alone behind Diana's coffin, that he would be insulted by people in the crowd. That was the fear. And that that couldn't possibly happen if the boys walked behind. I was told they wanted to do it. And I was, I believe I was lied to."
Asked if he had talked about it with his nephews, Spencer said, "I never discuss what I've discussed with William and Harry, but I know the truth from all angles, I can put it that way."
It's been a long time since Diana was buried on an island on the family estate. But to Charles Spencer, what happened back then is still having an effect now.
Asked if he thinks Harry's current difficulty with the family and the press harkens back to his experience of the time his mother died, Spencer replied, "I do sometimes wonder with the situation, if I can call it that ..."
Between Harry and William? "I think the broader one of Harry's feelings, I wonder how much it is connected to this very sad time," Spencer said. "He was so young. And I just wonder if a gentler, more understanding treatment of his grief then might have helped him, and that everyone might have found a happier course ahead."
Asked what kind of queen Diana would have made if the marriage had lasted and she had lived, Spencer replied, "I think Diana would have been a really amazing queen. To have a sort of superstar in that role would have been very good for Britain."
WEB EXCLUSIVE: Watch an extended interview with Charles Spencer (Video)
Read the full statement from Buckingham Palace:
"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha LoP and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Sunday questioned the system over the Satya Niketan tragedy, asking who would take responsibility for the death of Arpit Jhaj and other students.In an X post, Gandhi said Arpit’s grieving family is seeking answers after his death, asking, “What was that innocent one’s fault?”

He questioned whether the tragedy could have been avoided had safety standards been properly followed.“The system’s irresponsibility and corruption have snatched away many lives full of dreams and devastated many families filled with hope,” Gandhi said.He said Arpit’s family, as well as the country, is demanding accountability and responsibility for students’ safety to be fixed so that no parent has to endure such a loss again.Gandhi also questioned why new and safe hostels were not being built and why students were being forced to live in unsafe PG accommodations.He further sought an update on the investigation into the Satya Niketan incident, asking: “How far has the investigation into the Satya Niketan incident progressed?”What's the Satya Niketan tragedy?The building at Satya Niketan, which housed a boys’ PG accommodation near Delhi University’s South Campus, collapsed on September 6.
The incident claimed lives of seven students. The tragedy renewed questions over the safety of private PGs and hostels, particularly those operating from old residential buildings.The Delhi High Court has also expressed concern over the safety of students living in PGs and private hostels and questioned the regulatory framework governing such establishments and ordered a high-level MCD inquiry.
It said the collapse of a multi-storey hostel building in Satya Niketan, which killed seven people including students, was "not an ordinary incident."“Four students lost their lives in the mishap...very tragic. It's not an ordinary incident of any mishap. These four students had come to the capital with a lot of hopes and dreams, coming from small towns. All of that was shattered by such callous and criminal conduct on the part of (certain persons),” the court said.

Choreographer bridges Chinese and Vietnamese cultures through dance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:02:43 CST
23:02:43 KST

Vu Minh Anh (L) practices dancing by a lake with a student in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Sept. 17, 2026.
For 30-year-old Vietnamese choreographer Vu Minh Anh, China is an important country in her dance career. Her connection with Chinese dance began in childhood. At 11, she came to Guangxi through a China-ASEAN arts cooperation program to study dance at a school.
After graduating in 2013, Vu returned to Vietnam and worked at a local theater. To pursue advanced professional training, she continued her studies at Guangxi Arts University in 2018, where she completed both her bachelor's and master's programs. She now teaches choreography at the university.
"My connection with China grew from Chinese dance shows I watched as a child," Vu said. "The refined grace of Chinese dance has always fascinated me."
Vu recalled arriving in China at a young age and feeling daunted by language barriers and unfamiliar daily routines. With help from her teachers and classmates, Vu quickly learned Chinese and adapted to campus life.
Years of working in Vietnam made Vu realize she still needed further artistic enrichment. "I chose to return to China, where my dance dream started. This place has always given me warmth and motivation," she shared.
Cultural integration defines Vu's choreographic style. As a teacher and creator, she seamlessly blends traditional Vietnamese aesthetics with Chinese dance. Her innovative works have won multiple awards at home and abroad.
Now settled in China, Vu actively explores new artistic inspirations and regularly visits China's ethnic minority areas to draw creative inspiration from local cultures. (Xinhua/Cao Yiming)

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- South Korea held off Japan 67-57 to win the men's basketball final at the 2026 Asian Games on Sunday, while China finished fourth after losing 79-70 to Iran in the bronze-medal match.
Japan built a 16-12 advantage in the first quarter, but South Korea opened the second period with an 8-4 run to pull level, leaving the two sides deadlocked at 28 apiece at halftime.
South Korea seized control in the third quarter with a 17-8 surge, carrying an eight-point cushion into the final frame. Lee Hyun-jung reeled off five straight points early in the fourth quarter to stretch the lead to 13, putting the result beyond doubt.
Lee finished with a game-high 27 points, knocking down five of his eight 3-point attempts, and grabbed 18 rebounds. Lee Jung-hyun added 14 points and seven assists for the gold medalists.
For Japan, Ren Kanechika posted 13 points and six rebounds, while Atsuya Ogawa chipped in 12 points.
Iran took an early 8-2 lead before China responded with a 10-0 run to take the advantage in the first period. The two sides were tied at 42-42 with four minutes 30 seconds left in the third quarter, before Iran launched a 13-4 run to enter the final period with a nine-point lead.
Following a 3-pointer from Matin Aghajanpour, Iran extended its advantage to 13 points. Pang Zhenglin's driving layup and Li Hongquan's consecutive 3-pointers helped China close the gap to 62-63. However, led by Aghajanpour, Iran mounted another 16-8 run to secure the victory.
"It was an important game for us, especially for the young players. We put our heart out on the floor. We really wanted it more. We hustled really well. We dived for every loose ball and eventually we won the game," said Iran's Mohammad Jamshidi afterwards.
Only two China players scored in double digits. Pang scored a team-high 22 points, and Li contributed 12. Aghajanpour led Iran with 21 points, while Piter Girgoorian added 15.
"We didn't do well in defense and rebounding today, nor did we execute our pre-game tactics on the court. We controlled the tempo for a while in the second half, but failed to adjust after committing turnovers," said China captain Hu Mingxuan.
"Iran earned this win because they played harder than us, and they played tough. They had more energy than us, and they wanted this game. They played much better than us. That's why they beat us," China forward Cui Yongxi added.
China head coach Guo Shiqiang expressed his regret over the defeat, admitting that his team was outplayed.
"We have many young players who lack experience in major tournaments, and we didn't perform well in crucial moments. The players were quite fatigued in the last two games. During the group stage, we only had a nine-man rotation at one point, and some players had heavy minutes, resulting in significant physical exhaustion," Guo said.
In women's basketball action, the Philippines defeated Hong Kong, China 90-73, and host Japan routed Kazakhstan 88-23. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: Pinglu Canal to boost China-ASEAN trade, upgrade regional logistics: Thai business expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:02:29 CST
23:02:29 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- The opening of the Pinglu Canal will not only significantly reduce logistics costs, but also provide a powerful boost to the flourishing trade and economic ties between China and ASEAN, Wichai Kinchong Choi, business development proficient at Kasikorn Bank, told Xinhua in a recent interview.
The Pinglu Canal, officially opened to navigation on Wednesday, links the Xijiang River shipping route with the Beibu Gulf, acting as a vital link connecting China's inland waterways with the sea.
China is Thailand's largest trading partner, Wichai said, noting that for years, the logistics industry has underpinned the prosperity of ASEAN-China cross-border trade. In addition to traditional road transport, the China-Laos Railway and the Lancang-Mekong shipping route have played pivotal roles in regional connectivity, he said.
"The opening of the Pinglu Canal -- a key component of China's Belt and Road Initiative -- will undoubtedly drive the upgrading of regional logistics and transportation," Wichai stressed.
According to official specifications, as the backbone project of the New Western Land-Sea Corridor, the Pinglu Canal is China's first national-level river-sea navigation waterway built since 1949. Spanning 134.2 km and designed for vessels up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal cuts the inland shipping distance to the sea for southwest-China-bound cargo by more than 560 km and reduces comprehensive logistics costs by 18-30 percent.
"Integrating the Pinglu Canal with the regional transport network will not only enhance logistics efficiency and lower costs but also spur economic development in the surrounding areas ... the canal will unlock new export shipping opportunities, foster mutually beneficial outcomes, and further strengthen the close economic and trade relations between China and ASEAN," said Wichai.
The project has overcome a total water level drop of 65 meters along the route via three major cascade hubs. Since construction commenced on Aug. 28, 2022, more than 20,000 builders have pushed forward intensive construction, achieving multiple breakthroughs in engineering technologies and construction progress.
Wichai said the canal represents a revolution in the regional shipping landscape. Its opening will help expand business opportunities in the region, promote the improvement of the China-ASEAN regional industrial chain, form a closer regional logistics network, and strengthen connectivity between western China and the ASEAN market.
Looking ahead, Wichai said, there is significant room for cooperation and exchanges between China and ASEAN in port construction and upgrading, including improving port management through artificial intelligence and digitalization, laying a more solid foundation for expanding import and export businesses in the region.
"The opening of the Pinglu Canal is not merely a one-way transportation channel benefiting only one country, but a friendly channel bringing broad benefits to cross-border trade between China and ASEAN countries, and will undoubtedly meet the rapidly growing demand for import and export goods in the region in the future," Wichai emphasized. ■

Economic Watch: German enterprises scale up investment in China amid market growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:02:14 CST
23:02:14 KST

QINGDAO, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- German companies are stepping up investment and expanding production in China, tapping into the country's growing market and emerging opportunities.
Weiss Group, a German "hidden champion" specializing in mechanical, mechatronic and digital solutions, has opened its first production base in China in Qingdao, east China's Shandong Province.
With an investment of 10 million U.S. dollars, the project will serve as the group's China headquarters for production, research and development (R&D) and trade. Its first phase is expected to generate annual sales of about 60 million yuan (about 8.89 million U.S. dollars) and annual imports and exports of around 35 million yuan once operational.
The Qingdao project is among a growing number of examples of German companies deepening their presence in China, with investment increasingly extending from production to localized R&D and supply chains.
ZF Group, a German automotive parts supplier and Fortune Global 500 company, delivered its advanced driver assistance system to Chinese customers in April, marking a further step in its "In China, For China" strategy.
The company has operated in Shandong since 1996, with operations in Jinan, Qingdao, Rizhao and Weihai.
Qian Xinmin, general manager of ZF Commercial Vehicle Systems (Qingdao) Co., Ltd., said three of four new production lines at the Qingdao plant had been put into operation this year, with the fourth undergoing testing and expected to come online by the end of the year.
The company is also considering investment in next-generation solenoid valves and sensors, Qian said.
"Eighty percent of our business comes from the domestic market, and we expect revenue growth of 15 percent to 20 percent this year. The outlook is very promising," he said.
The experience of LOGOMAT Automation (Qingdao) Co., Ltd. illustrates a broader shift: German companies in China are moving from importing and assembling products to localized production and, increasingly, supplying global markets.
Facing intensified competition in the automotive industry, the German manufacturer of industrial automated conveyor-line equipment is maintaining its competitiveness through localized R&D and cost-reduction measures, while expanding into emerging fields in China, including embodied robotics, energy storage systems and solid-state fuel cells, said General Manager David Huemmerich.
Since establishing its Qingdao plant in 2019, the company has become deeply integrated into LOGOMAT's global production network.
"We not only serve the Chinese market, but can also ship our products to Europe and the Americas," Huemmerich said.
Other German companies across China are also expanding their operations like LOGOMAT.
In March, BASF's integrated production site in south China's Guangdong Province became fully operational. With a total investment of about 8.7 billion euros, it is the largest single wholly foreign-owned project in China by a German company.
In northeast China, BMW has invested more than 120 billion yuan in its Shenyang production base since 2010.
Henkel, which is marking its 55th year in China, continues to invest in projects including an innovation center in Shanghai and a production base in Yantai, Shandong Province.
The trend is also reflected in the investment plans of German companies. A survey by the German Chamber of Commerce in China found that 61 percent of surveyed German companies planned to increase investment in China over the next two years, the highest level since 2023.
Germany's large community of "hidden champions," many of them small and medium-sized enterprises specializing in niche markets, has shown particular interest in China's expanding market and technological development, industry insiders said.
The investment trend comes as China continues to expand institutional opening-up and improve conditions for foreign investment.
In June, China's Ministry of Commerce, together with other government departments, released an action plan featuring 15 measures to stabilize and optimize foreign investment utilization. The plan calls for wider market access in the services sector, promotion of the "Invest China" initiative, and efforts to address foreign-funded enterprises' concerns over equal participation in government procurement and fair access to business operations.
China saw 35,000 newly established foreign-invested enterprises in the first half of 2026, up 7 percent year on year, the State Administration for Market Regulation said.
Separate data from the Ministry of Commerce showed that nearly 4,800 foreign-funded enterprises increased investment in China in the first half of 2026, while foreign direct investment in high-tech industries surged 33.2 percent year on year.
At the opening ceremony of the Weiss project, Michael Kern, executive director of the German Chamber of Commerce in China - East China, said the investment was not only an investment decision, but also an expression of confidence in China and in the opportunities created by combining German engineering and technology with China's economic dynamism.
"The relationship between German and Chinese companies is changing," Kern said, adding that it is no longer simply about bringing German products to China, but increasingly involves jointly conducted R&D, shared growth and benefiting other markets around the world. ■

Feature: Dance, volunteering weave a tighter bond in China's Inner Mongolia community
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:02:13 CST
23:02:13 KST

HOHHOT, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- As the music of the morin khuur, a traditional horsehead fiddle, fills the community center, Wang Jinrong rolls her shoulders, raises her arms and turns to the rhythm, leading her fellow dancers through the routine.
Wang, an ethnic Mongolian and retired resident of the Fu'an community in Xing'an League, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, has been a member of the community's dance group for more than two years.
The community is home to more than 9,000 residents, including people from Han, Mongolian and Hui ethnic groups.
Xing'an League is home to residents from 40 ethnic groups, with ethnic minorities accounting for about half of its permanent population of more than 1.3 million.
On May 1, 1947, the people of Inner Mongolia established the autonomous government of the region in Xing'an, which marked the founding of China's first provincial-level ethnic autonomous region under the leadership of the Communist Party of China.
In the run-up to this year's Mid-Autumn Festival, Wang and her teammates performed a Mongolian dance, made traditional Chinese mooncakes and took photos together at a celebration held in the community.
"Mongolian dance has a certain strength to it, and the rhythm is really strong," said Wang Liyan, a Han resident who has been part of the dance group. She added that they follow online videos to learn traditional dances of multiple ethnic groups, including Mongolian, Uyghur and Korean dances.
But the group does much more than dance.
"We travel together, join community activities and keep in touch through WeChat groups," Wang said. "We've been together for so many years that everyone has become really close."
For Zhang Ruixin, Party secretary of Fu'an community, a "complete community is a shared home for people of different ethnic groups," where everyone can participate, benefit and develop together.
That idea is reflected in the development of community spaces. "When we were developing the neighborhood activity center, we collected residents' suggestions through home visits and online, so as to decide on the layout and functions," Zhang said.
The community has built a "Pomegranate Red Square" that integrates functional areas such as the Tongxin Pavilion, an ethnic unity and progress corridor, and a themed plaza. China often likens all ethnic groups to pomegranate seeds holding tightly together as a metaphor for unity.
In 2025, the community partnered with China Sports Lottery to convert an idle building elsewhere in the neighborhood into a 300-square-meter activity center.
Equipped with table tennis tables, chess and card tables and a reading area, the center is free and open to all residents regardless of ethnicity, household registration or age.
Meanwhile, some community services, such as social security and medical assistance, have also been made available online.
Bringing services closer to residents' daily lives is also part of a broader effort in Chinese cities to build "complete communities." The push aims to make public and commercial services, elderly care and cultural and leisure facilities more accessible within neighborhoods.
More young people have also been getting involved in the community, finding their own ways to help others.
A youth environmental volunteer association in Xing'an League, registered in the Fu'an community in 2020, provides regular volunteer services in more than 30 communities across the league and runs care programs for children during summer and winter vacations, according to Du Tieyi, the association's head.
It now has more than 3,000 registered volunteers, including people from ethnic groups such as the Han, Manchu, Hui, Mongolian and Daur, said Du.
Zheng Qinghui, a student at Xing'an Polytechnic University who joined the association this month, has quickly built a rapport with the children.
"The children may be too young to fully understand environmental protection at first," Zheng said. "But through our discussions and activities, they may start thinking about it in their daily lives."
For Du, volunteering often shows up in small moments. At the end of a weeklong summer program, a rather shy child handed him a small note.
"I hope you're happy every day, and I hope to see you again during the winter vacation," it read. ■

TEHRAN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Iran's main military command, Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, on Sunday warned that if the United States and certain countries in the Middle East make any mistake, they will be targeted by "painful" strikes.
The headquarters said in a statement carried by Iranian media that it has intelligence indicating that Washington decided at a recent meeting in Europe to resume actions against Tehran with the backing of certain regional countries.
It warned that if the United States makes any mistake against Iran, all its bases and interests in the region would be targeted by "continuous, effective and painful strikes without any limitation or reservation."
The headquarters also warned that if regional states continue what it called their double-standard policy toward Iran and align themselves with the U.S. "aggression," they could "no longer expect restraint or forbearance from Iran's powerful armed forces."
The warning followed a reported meeting in Germany of top military commanders from the United States, Israel and several Arab states, including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt, to discuss the war with Iran and regional tensions.
Citing two Israeli officials, U.S. news outlet Axios reported on Tuesday that U.S. Central Command chief Brad Cooper, who convened the meeting, reassured the group that "the U.S. military would not withdraw from the region despite Iranian attacks on U.S. bases," and briefed them on plans to expand ship traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
Also on Sunday, Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said there would be no chance for a return to the previous state of negotiations on ending the war in the region or reopening the Strait of Hormuz unless Washington meets Tehran's conditions, recognizes the Iranian nation's "legitimate" rights, and fulfills its obligations.
Qalibaf said that Tehran's conditions had been conveyed to Washington through mediators.
On June 18, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on ending the war in the region on all fronts, including Lebanon. Under the MoU, they were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, a deadline that expired on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement, but the talks' fate remains unclear amid recent escalations.
Following U.S.-Israeli strikes, Tehran restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz, while U.S. forces imposed a naval blockade on vessels traveling to or from Iranian ports. ■

In the men's event, China, represented by Lin Shidong, Wen Ruibo and Huang Youzheng, swept past Macao, China 3-0 in its opening match.
In the afternoon, Wang Chuqin joined Lin and Xiang Peng to beat Qatar 3-0 without dropping a game in two matches.
"I was more excited than nervous during the matches, but I still need to adapt better to the venue. There are many opponents here that I have never faced before, which gives the competition a sense of the unknown," said Lin.
Japan also started perfectly with two 3-0 wins, beating the Maldives and Uzbekistan.
Group-stage matches will continue on Monday, when the women's doubles event will kick off its opening round. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China made a strong start to the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Sunday, claiming its first gold medal in the women's team modern pentathlon and setting a world record in shooting.
Chinese swimmers were particularly dominant in the pool, winning six of the seven gold medals on offer and helping China finish the opening day with 11 gold medals.
China successfully defended its women's team title in modern pentathlon to claim the delegation's first gold medal at the Asiad. The team event is decided by the combined scores of each team's top three finishers. China topped the women's team standings with 4,318 points, powered by solid performances from Zhang Mingyu, Wu Xiyao and Meng Xin. Zhang and Wu also took silver and bronze, respectively, in the individual event.
Later in the day, China's Li Liuchang won gold in the men's individual event.
The event marked modern pentathlon's Asian Games debut in its new format, with the obstacle discipline replacing equestrian and offering a preview of the sport's format for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Discussing the challenges she faced during the transition, Zhang said, "I had relatively little time to train for the obstacle event, so I had to put in extra effort. I'm also a little older than some of the other athletes, which can affect my physical condition."

China could have claimed its first gold earlier in the morning in the men's individual triathlon, but favorite Zhang Xirui had to settle for silver as Japan's Takumi Hojo won the first gold medal of the Games.
Zhang's silver was China's best-ever result in the men's individual triathlon at the Asian Games.
China continued its strong start in the shooting events, winning the women's 10-meter air rifle team title with a world-record score.
In the pool in Tokyo, Chinese swimmers, led by Olympic champions Pan Zhanle and Zhang Yufei, turned in a series of dominant performances on the opening day.

Yu had already gained international attention as the youngest swimmer to win a world championship medal, achieving the feat at the World Aquatics Championships last year at the age of 12.
The momentum continued as world record holder Pan Zhanle successfully defended his 100m freestyle title in 47.61 seconds, finishing ahead of South Korea's Kim Young-beom and Hwang Sun-woo, who took silver and bronze, respectively.
Veteran backstroke specialist Xu Jiayu retained his 100m backstroke title in 51.98 seconds, while distance specialist Li Bingjie won the women's 1,500m freestyle in 15:53.52.
In the sprint events, Tang Qianting successfully defended her women's 50m breaststroke title, clocking 29.45 seconds to lower the Games record of 29.50 she had set just hours earlier.
China also won the women's 4x100m freestyle relay, with Yu Yiting, Zhang Yufei, Cheng Yujie and Wu Qingfeng combining to claim another gold medal.
The only swimming gold China missed went to Japan in the men's 200m individual medley. Tomoyuki Matsushita edged teammate Yumeki Kojima to win the gold. China's veteran Wang Shun took bronze.
China's success continued on the wushu court, where Tong Xin retained her women's taijiquan and taijijian all-around title. In the men's events, athletes from Macao, China finished first and second in the changquan competition.
In table tennis, the tournament's top Chinese players also got their campaigns underway, with Sun Yingsha and Wang Chuqin helping the women's and men's teams advance to the knockout stages as group winners.
China had a tougher time in the men's team sports, with the football team playing to a 0-0 draw with Iran and the basketball team falling 79-70 to Iran to miss out on the bronze medal.

"The players were very tired in the last two games. We didn't have enough players to rotate, so some had to play heavy minutes and became very tired."
South Korea won the men's basketball gold medal, beating Japan 67-57 in the final.
China led the medal standings with 11 gold, six silver and three bronze medals, followed by host Japan (6-7-7) in second and South Korea (4-3-7) in third. ■

UNICEF official calls for sharing China's child health, development experience with developing countries
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:02:09 CST
23:02:09 KST

NANNING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's progress in child health, early childhood development, education, and child protection is generating experience that can be shared with other developing countries through South-South cooperation, said a United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) official.
Sanjay Wijesekera, UNICEF Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific, made the remarks during the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo, held from Sept. 17 to 21, in Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.
UNICEF welcomes China's policies and progress in supporting families, expanding childcare services, and building a child-friendly society, Wijesekera said, stressing that children's well-being depends not only on services for children but also on the environment, care and support around them.
He identified China's nationwide childcare subsidy and child-friendly city initiative as important examples.
"A key example is China's nationwide childcare subsidy program, announced by the government of China last year. This is expected to support early childhood development and ease the cost of raising children," he said.
China introduced a nationwide childcare subsidy program in 2025 as part of broader efforts to support families and encourage childbirth. The program will offer families 3,600 yuan (around 540 U.S. dollars) per year for each child under the age of three.
During a visit to UNICEF-supported projects in Liuzhou, Guangxi, Wijesekera said he saw programs covering social and emotional learning, maternal and newborn care, and child protection services.
"What struck me most was the commitment and passion of the people we met. Across different services and institutions, I saw officials and professionals who are deeply committed to improving outcomes for children," he said.
Wijesekera said China's experience in artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technology could also contribute to children's development, particularly through digital learning and skills development.
"China's experience in digital technology, AI, clean energy and public infrastructure is highly relevant to children because these areas shape how children learn, access services, stay safe and prepare for the future," he said.
"Sharing experience from China is why I am participating in the China-ASEAN Expo. South-South cooperation is a key method for sharing China's experience with ASEAN countries," he said.
He said that since 1979, UNICEF has been working closely with the Chinese government to improve the lives of children and their families in areas such as health, nutrition, education, child protection and emergency response.
This year marks the launch of the China-UNICEF Country Program for 2026-2030. Wijesekera said the new Country Program would place greater emphasis on government ownership and system strengthening, while continuing to work on child protection, climate action and social policy. Specific issues include children with disabilities, mental health and ending violence against children.
"We will also work with the government and Chinese institutions to enable other countries to learn from China's rapid development and how children can benefit," he said.
Since 2018, UNICEF and the Chinese government have worked together to reach vulnerable children in low- and middle-income countries, Wijesekera said.
He cited cooperation in Lao PDR as a practical example.
"In Lao PDR, cooperation between China, Lao PDR and UNICEF has contributed to combating acute malnutrition, improving child health outcomes and strengthening child protection services, with funding from the government of China," Wijesekera said.
Launched in October 2022 and concluding in December 2025, the Lao government and UNICEF jointly implemented a child nutrition program, funded by China's Ministry of Commerce and the China International Development Cooperation Agency. The program targeted 10 provinces with high rates of acute child malnutrition.
It has since treated more than 4,000 Lao children with severe acute malnutrition.
"Through South-South cooperation, countries can share practical solutions and innovation, helping accelerate progress for children across the region, especially the most vulnerable," he said. ■

The pro-Israel censors are starting to lose
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:00:32 UTC
23:00:32 KST

The pro-Israel censors are starting to lose
The Macklemore controversy demonstrates that the cost of speaking up for Palestine is diminishing.
For decades, Israel’s greatest advantage in the West was not simply military or political support. It was narrative power.
Israel and its supporters enjoyed enormous influence over the boundaries of acceptable discussion about Palestine: which violent incident received attention, whose security mattered the most, which historical context was relevant and, crucially, what criticism of Israel could be allowed in public.
That power has not disappeared. But the extraordinary controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from Ed Sheeran’s US tour shows how rapidly it is eroding.
The fact that the American rapper was dropped from the tour after he spoke about Palestine on stage meant that the old system worked. A powerful billionaire objected. Venues applied pressure. The artist disappeared from the stage.
What was different this time was the backlash.
In response to the censorship, every remaining support act on Sheeran’s tour walked away. Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga all withdrew. Meanwhile, ticket prices for Sheeran’s remaining concerts plunged, in some cases losing 50 percent of their value, as many fans felt outraged.
Macklemore stood his ground and pledged the $1m he had earned from his appearances to six organisations supporting Palestinians. Subsequently, the media reported Sheeran would donate $2m towards humanitarian relief in the region.
All of this has helped generate further donations and attention for Palestinian aid organisations, including a $1m pledge from children’s educator Ms Rachel.
Consider what happened.
An attempt to push “Free Palestine” off the stage resulted in Palestine receiving vastly more attention, artists abandoning one of the world’s biggest tours and more funds being donated to Palestinian organisations.
The attempt to control the message amplified the message itself. And that tells us something much bigger than how controversy is handled in the music industry.
Amid its genocide in Gaza, Israel is facing a crisis not simply of public opinion, but of narrative control.
For almost three years, the world has watched Palestinians killed, displaced and starved. It has seen neighbourhoods flattened, hospitals overwhelmed and families repeatedly driven from one place to another. A United Nations Commission of Inquiry has concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The old narrative increasingly struggles against a force Israel cannot easily control: people can see what is happening themselves.
Palestinian journalists, doctors, parents and ordinary citizens no longer depend entirely on Western governments or established media organisations to narrate their lives. Images, testimony and documentation travel directly from Gaza to millions of phones around the world.
There are limits to propaganda when people can witness the consequences of power for themselves. Public opinion increasingly reflects that rupture.
A Pew Research Center survey across 36 countries this year found a median of 67 percent of respondents held an unfavourable view of Israel. In the United Kingdom, it was 69 percent, Germany – 73 percent, Italy – 75 percent and Australia – 79 percent. Even in the United States, Israel’s most important ally, 60 percent viewed Israel unfavourably.
Among younger people, the transformation is more dramatic still. Seventy-four percent of Americans aged 18 to 34 surveyed by Pew viewed Israel unfavourably, as did 78 percent of young Britons and 87 percent of young Australians.
This does not mean everyone supports Palestine or agrees on what a political settlement should look like. It means that the cost of speaking up for Palestine is falling.
For years, the implied question confronting artists, academics and other public figures openly supporting Palestine was: what are you prepared to lose? Your booking? Your sponsorship? Your reputation? Your career?
The purpose of such consequences was larger than the individual. Punish one person publicly and hundreds of others would understand the warning and keep silent.
But deterrence only works when people are deterred.
This time, they weren’t. And that put pressure on the censors and those who complied.
The backlash forced Sheeran to speak up publicly about Palestine. On Saturday, during his concert in Philadelphia, where he had to play solo, he called what is happening in Gaza “unjustifiable”.
The equation has clearly changed.
Speaking for Palestine can still carry a professional cost. Macklemore has just demonstrated that. But increasingly, censors may discover that silencing pro-Palestine voices carries a cost, too.
That is why the Israeli narrative crisis runs deeper than falling approval ratings.
The old power was not merely the ability to silence Palestinians and those who stood with them. It was the ability to determine which account of Palestine the world would hear. That monopoly is breaking.
They succeeded in removing the man who said “Free Palestine” from the stage. But “Free Palestine” became louder.
And that may be the clearest indication yet that Israel is not simply losing an argument. It is losing its grip on the story.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

====================================================================================================

Bear-y good neighbors: humans and animals are learning to live together in an expanding LA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:00:17 UTC
23:00:17 KST

Every year, as summer draws to a close and fall begins, California’s bears get hungry.
Black bears have long roamed the state, hunting for acorns, ants and pine nuts by the bucketload to pack on calories before hibernation. But increasingly, for every berry and root, there’s an even greater temptation: our trash and the detritus of human existence.
That dynamic is playing out in perhaps a surprising place: Los Angeles. As communities on the outskirts of the metropolis grow, bears are butting up against humanity, drawn to residents’ pools, their chicken coops, their fruit trees and trashcans.
“Black bears are incredibly adaptable, versatile omnivores,” said Wilson Sherman, a PhD student at the University of California, Los Angeles, who studies human-wildlife interaction. “They can eat everything we can eat.”
Human-bear interactions have increased since the 1990s, Sherman said, which makes sense as communities expand and the state is now home to some 50,000 to 70,000 black bears. A few hundred of those live in the Angeles national forest, just north of the city and its millions of hungry households.
Brian Gordon and his partner moved to the state’s bear capital – Monrovia, California – four years ago. Their house is the last before the Angeles national forest begins, and as they were buying the home, a family of bears wandered through the back garden. It was the start of a new era of coexistence.
Now, the pair regularly share their pool with a family of bears and document their exploits on an Instagram account called PoolBearLife. Videos show bear cubs with their snouts bubbling in the water, climbing – and falling from – trees and causing adorable, young bear mayhem.
“I only had education up until I bought this house of bears from whatever I saw online. I actually thought people get eaten by bears a lot,” Gordon said. “But after we bought the house, we had bears walking through. That’s really all they’re doing. I realized, OK, I have an unnatural fear of these animals and we’ve kind of adapted to living around them.
“People will say ‘you guys are the bear experts,’” Gordon went on. “No, we’re city boys. We bought a house that happened to have bears.”
Gordon and his partner live amongst the bears, but they’re also vocal advocates for doing so safely. Trashcans are kept clean, temptations are removed and, despite the filming, they give the bears their space. Sometimes mistakes are made and a bear finds a case of beer in the garage.
But with consideration, bears don’t even stop to sniff the trash cans and will just pass through the backyard like it’s an extension of the forest nearby, the couple said.
In a perfect world, Sherman said, human dominated landscapes that buttress the natural world would take steps to minimize bear contact. That means making neighborhoods as unattractive to bears as possible.
“Pet food left outside, koi ponds, fruit trees with a lot of fruit on them, swimming pools, all these things can be attractive to bears,” he said.
It’s not that human food tastes better, it’s just much more calorie dense and therefore easier for bears to pack on the pounds. In fact, bears that live or forage near human environments tend to reproduce more often and at higher rates, likely due to the availability of our food.
“It takes a lot of work to get the calories from, say, a half eaten pizza in the trash in equivalent calories from acorns and ants,” he said. “It makes sense to get calories from human food.”
The other major factor is climate crisis. Warmer summers can alter the availability of natural food and force bears to expand their ranges. Major wildfires like the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires were also linked to a lack in natural food sources, prompting the bears near Los Angeles to search in neighborhoods instead.
Alex Heeran, a research scientist at the California department of fish and wildlife who studies the human dimensions of wildlife encounters, said human and bear interactions generally peak every year in late summer and early fall. September is often a really active month as black bears finish up their pre-hibernation hungry period, known as hyperphagia. 2026 is on track to be a record-setting year when it comes to reported bear encounters, Heeran said.
It’s also a time when humans are out in force around Labor Day for the year’s final picnics and camping excursions. Fish and wildlife officials will often get reports of bears creating a nuisance and occasionally damaging fences, getting into sheds and making a mess as they look for calories.
“The bear’s just looking for food, doing natural behavior, but it’s creating a situation that’s not ideal,” Heeran said. “A lot of the conflict can be prevented.”
Sometimes, however, that conflict can escalate, which can result in a bear being euthanized or relocated. It’s rare and wildlife officials try and prevent situations from escalating to that point, but it happens.
Earlier this year, the city of Monrovia erupted in fury after a mother bear known as “Blondie” was euthanized. Officials had determined she had swiped at local residents twice, causing minor injuries. She had two cubs at the time. They are now being raised in captivity until they can hopefully be released back into the wild.
Residents rallied for an alternative plan, but that effort ultimately turned into a memorial walk through the city in Blondie’s honor.
“The city was not a part of that conversation or decision,” Becky Shevlin, the mayor of the city, which is peppered with monuments to black bears, told the Los Angeles Times in March. “We were absolutely devastated, especially when you think about her having the two little cubs.”
Sherman said the spread of bear footage on social media, many of it captured by doorbell cameras that have exploded in the last decade, is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, people get to see bears being bears, doing cute things.
“Bears are really cute, and a lot of the things they do are really cute … This is a real way to build meaningful empathy for wildlife, and building empathy for wildlife is a powerful motivator for conservation actions,” he said. “There is this risk of … kind of Disney-fying them. Black bears are by nature not particularly aggressive unless they are put in a dangerous or threatening situation, but they can cause damage. It’s best to give them their space.”
As September draws to a close, interactions between bears and Angelenos will thin out for the season. But residents of the city will have to contend with their neighbors again come spring, alongside the mountain lions, deer and coyotes that call the city’s outskirts home.
“When people move to these foothill neighborhoods, a lot of people are moving in because they think it’s a suburb of LA. But they’re not necessarily thinking they’re going to have bears in their back yard,” Sherman said. “At first it can be really scary, but the people I’ve spoken to generally become accustomed to them.”
“Bears are super likable and this population of bears wouldn’t be there if people didn’t like bears so much.”

Autism is linked to a nearly 14-year shorter life expectancy among Medicaid beneficiaries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:00:02 UTC
23:00:02 KST

A new study indicates that autistic individuals enrolled in Medicaid have a life expectancy nearly 14 years shorter than the general United States population. The research highlights specific health conditions and accidents driving this gap, pointing to a need for better long-term healthcare for autistic adults. The findings were published in JAMA Network Open.
Autism is a lifelong developmental condition that affects how people communicate, learn, and interact with the world. Symptoms and support needs vary widely from person to person, ranging from mild social challenges to profound communication difficulties requiring full-time assistance. Because it is often diagnosed in childhood, much of the past research on autism has focused on its biological origins, early screening, and educational interventions. In recent years, public health experts have shifted more attention toward understanding the long-term physical health and quality of life of autistic adults.
This growing focus includes exploring how long autistic people live and what factors affect their mortality. For example, a 2023 systematic review suggested that autistic people face more than twice the risk of dying prematurely compared to the general population. In addition, research covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicates that autistic individuals tend to experience higher rates of chronic physical health disorders across almost all major organ systems.
While this elevated risk was already documented, the exact disparity in life expectancy measured in years remained unknown.
“It has been speculated since the late 1980s that autism might shorten life expectancy,” lead researcher Guohua Li, a professor of epidemiology and anesthesiology at the Columbia University Irving Medical Center, told PsyPost. “Due to inadequate sample sizes and age-specific mortality data, life expectancy for the autistic population remained unknown.”
“Life expectancy is the most important indicator of the overall health status for a defined population,” Li added. “Our study is the first in time to determine the life expectancy for the autistic population.”
To solve this problem, Li and his colleagues turned to Medicaid records. Medicaid is a public health insurance program in the United States that provides coverage for low-income individuals and people with disabilities.
To conduct the study, the research team analyzed nationwide data from the Transformed Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program Statistical Information System. They linked these detailed health records to the National Death Index, a centralized database of death record information on file in state vital statistics offices. The final dataset included all Medicaid beneficiaries across the 50 states and the District of Columbia between the years 2000 and 2020.
The study focused on a massive sample of 2,048,046 Medicaid beneficiaries diagnosed with autism. The group was predominantly male, making up about 76 percent of the sample, while females accounted for roughly 24 percent. The researchers used a statistical method called a life table, which calculates average life expectancy by looking at the death rates of a specific group at various ages. They also compared the specific causes of death among autistic individuals to the causes of death in the broader Medicaid population in 2010.
The team found that the average life expectancy at birth for Medicaid beneficiaries with autism was 64.9 years. This number is 5.6 years shorter than the life expectancy for the overall Medicaid population. When compared to the general population of the United States, the gap widened to 13.8 years.
“The COVID-19 pandemic cut the life expectancy in the US by 2.2 years,” Li explained. “The life expectancy deficit facing autistic people in the US is equivalent to the impact of six simultaneous COVID-19-like pandemics. Put it another way, autistic people in the US have the same life expectancy as the general population in Haiti or Angola.”
When breaking the data down by gender, life expectancy was similar for autistic men, who lived an average of 64.6 years, and autistic women, who lived an average of 65.0 years. However, because women in the general population tend to outlive men, the relative life expectancy deficit was larger for autistic women. Autistic women on Medicaid lost 16 years of life expectancy compared to the general United States female population, while autistic men lost 11.6 years compared to the general United States male population.
The researchers also observed changes over the two decades covered by the study. From the early 2000s to the late 2010s, life expectancy for autistic beneficiaries increased slightly, growing from 63.9 years to 65.6 years. In 2020, during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, life expectancy dropped across all demographics in the United States, reflecting the heavy toll of the virus. However, the autistic population on Medicaid experienced the largest drop, losing 4.1 years of life expectancy compared to the previous five-year period.
“The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on life expectancy for the autistic population was twice as much as for the general population, which underscores the exceptional vulnerability of this growing population group with special needs,” Li noted.
Beyond overall life expectancy, the researchers analyzed the specific health problems driving these early deaths. Autistic individuals on Medicaid had a 44 percent higher overall risk of death compared to the general Medicaid population. The excess mortality was driven by a variety of distinct illnesses and accidents rather than a single cause.
“Autistic people are at heightened risk of premature death due in large part to preventable causes such as influenza, malnutrition, pneumonia, and drowning,” Li said.
Some causes of death were heavily elevated compared to typical rates. Deaths from influenza were more than ten times higher than expected for the Medicaid population. Deaths linked to malnutrition were seven and a half times higher. Pneumonitis caused by inhaling food or liquid into the lungs occurred nearly seven times more often. Autistic beneficiaries also experienced elevated rates of fatal accidents, with deaths from accidental drowning occurring more than three times as often as expected.
“This finding is sadly surprising to me,” Li said of the elevated risk of dying from malnutrition. “Causes underlying this finding may include neglect, maltreatment, poverty, and impaired ability of selfcare.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Medicaid is a public program designed to help individuals with low incomes or qualifying disabilities. Because of this, autistic people enrolled in Medicaid tend to have fewer financial resources or more severe symptoms than autistic individuals covered by private insurance. The life expectancy calculated in this study might underestimate the true average life expectancy for the entire autistic population in the United States.
Another detail to consider is the demographic makeup of the Medicaid population. The autistic beneficiaries in the database were disproportionately children, young adults, and males when compared to the broader population. While the researchers adjusted their statistical models to account for age and sex, there may be other unmeasured factors related to these demographics that influenced the mortality rates.
Even with these limitations, the findings highlight a need for specialized medical support for autistic individuals across their lifespans. Providing better preventative care for infectious diseases like influenza, screening for nutritional issues, and taking safety precautions to prevent accidents could help narrow the life expectancy gap.
“Our long-term goal is to close the life expectancy gap facing autistic people by improving social support, home- and community-based services, and healthcare,” Li said.
The study, “Autism Spectrum Disorder and Life Expectancy Among Medicaid Beneficiaries,” was authored by Guohua Li, Carolyn G. DiGuiseppi, Ashley Blanchard, Matthew T. Russell, and Caleb Ing.
