Russians vote in final day of parliamentary elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:59:59 UTC
22:59:59 KST

The vote comes as the Russian capital was hit by what its governor described as the "largest-scale attack" on the city since the war in Ukraine began.
Russians are casting their ballots on Sunday in the final day of voting in parliamentary elections, with the pro-Putin United Russia party widely expected to emerge victorious.
United Russia has won every parliamentary election in the country since 2003.
The 2026 vote marks the first since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, meaning it could offer a slight hint at public sentiment towards the conflict, which has been increasingly impacting Russians at home.
However, in August, Russia's Supreme Court ordered the only party opposing the war - the Yabloko party - to be struck from the ballot. Its candidates are reportedly still able to run for individual seats in some districts.
In a statement at the time, Yabloko cofounder Grigory Yavlinsky hit out at the decision and said they would appeal.
"Barring Yabloko from the elections means refusing to engage in dialogue with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for the authorities," he said. "We stand for a ceasefire, diplomacy and peace, for the prevention of nuclear war".
On Saturday, the party reported that one of its election observers had "lost consciousness" while being "subjected to force" by police in St. Petersburg. It also complained that party observers were being "denied access to polling stations" and that their movement was being "restricted."
Russia reports cyberattacks
Ella Pamfilova, the chair of Russia's Central Election Commission, said on Sunday that Russia had recorded more than 1,000 waves of distributed denial-of-service attacks (DDoS) on election infrastructure over the last few days, per the Interfax news agency.
"The level of impact is assessed as very high," she said, adding that the attacks appeared to have been "carried out by highly professional, well-coordinated groups using artificial intelligence tools."
A DDoS attack involves hackers attempting to disrupt a targeted network, server, or service by attempting to overwhelm the system with a large volume of traffic.
Moscow hit by 'largest-scale attack'
The vote comes as the Russian capital was hit by what its governor described as the "largest-scale attack" on the city since the war in Ukraine began.
Sergey Sobyanin reported that Russian air defences had shot down more than 1,600 drones across the country since Saturday, 450 of which he said had been heading towards the capital.
"Several drones reached the territory of the Moscow refinery, and one struck a residential building. There were no fatalities," he wrote. Moscow Oblast governor Andrey Vorobyov said two people had been killed in attacks across the wider region.
Sobyanin also accused Ukraine of attempting to "disrupt" Russia's elections - which will determine the makeup of the 450-seat state Duma - with the attacks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine had targeted the Moscow region overnight, saying a "key" oil industry facility as well as a logistics facility were hit.
"Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night," he wrote in a post on X, adding that Russia had launched over 2,000 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 19 missiles against Ukraine this week.

Italy plans foreign student limits, burqa-hijab ban in schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:54:59 UTC
22:54:59 KST

Italy is preparing a measure that would introduce a legal limit on the number of foreign students in schools and ban the burqa and hijab there, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has said.
“Italian children cannot feel like a minority in the classroom,” Meloni said at Fenix, a national youth festival organised by her Brothers of Italy (FdI) party’s youth group.
“It’s unthinkable that in an Italian classroom, Italian children feel cornered because they’ve become the minority. It can’t be done,” she added, according to ANSA News Agency.
She further said her government would ban the burqa and hijab in schools.
Meloni said parents of foreign students struggling to integrate into the school system would also be required to learn Italian.
Meloni said the measure is expected to be submitted to the Council of Ministers soon.
Last year, Italy’s right-wing populist Lega party proposed a ban on veils that conceal the face in public spaces.
In 2023, the top European Union court ruled that public authorities in member states can prohibit employees from wearing signs of religious belief, such as a headscarf.
The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) said that a policy of strict neutrality that was intended to establish a neutral administrative environment may be regarded as being objectively justified by a legitimate aim.
It added that another public administration would also be justified if it decided to authorise, in a general and indiscriminate manner, the wearing of visible signs of belief.
The court said authorities in member states had a margin of discretion in designing the neutrality of public service they intended to promote.
However, this objective must be pursued in a consistent and systematic manner and measures must be limited to what is strictly necessary, the court said.

Naftogaz, MOL Partner to Build Fuel Storage Near Hungarian Border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:50:00 UTC
22:50:00 KST

Ukrainian national oil and gas company Naftogaz and Hungarian energy group MOL Downstream signed a memorandum of understanding on Sunday, Sept. 20, to construct refined petroleum storage facilities in Hungary near the Ukrainian border.
Finalized on the sidelines of the inaugural summit of the “Carpathian Eight” regional cooperation format, the agreement establishes a framework for the joint evaluation and development of dedicated fuel storage infrastructure engineered specifically to supply the Ukrainian domestic market.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Naftogaz Acting Chairman of the Board Serhiy Fedorenko stated that establishing strategic reserves outside Ukrainian territory is vital to insulating national fuel supplies from persistent Russian missile and drone bombardments.
“Under conditions of persistent Russian attacks on our fuel infrastructure, diversifying supply routes and creating additional storage capacities outside the bombardment zone is a matter of stability for the entire market,” Fedorenko said.
“The realization of this joint project will not only improve the reliability of fuel supplies for Ukrainian consumers in the long term, but also foster the mutually beneficial development of cross-border energy infrastructure between Ukraine and Hungary.”
Winter energy resilience
The cross-border storage project forms part of a broader Ukrainian strategy to reinforce national energy resilience ahead of the autumn and winter heating season.
First Batch of Polish City Buses Headed to Vinnytsia After Public Fundraise
Speaking at the 22nd Annual Meeting of the Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) in Kyiv, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi noted that while fully defending every individual asset remains unfeasible, Ukraine is considerably better positioned to endure winter attacks than in previous years.
Koretskyi emphasized that the government’s operational focus centers on the decentralization of critical energy, heating, and water supply networks across municipalities to prevent concentrated strikes from causing systemic power collapses.
The prime minister affirmed that Ukraine possesses the necessary reserves and contingency protocols to maintain stability despite escalating strikes.
Ukraine accumulated its baseline winter natural gas storage target a month ahead of schedule, with domestic underground storage facilities reaching 14.6 billion cubic meters by late August through coordinated operations involving Naftogaz, the Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine (GTSOU), and domestic extraction enterprises.
Concurrently, municipal utilities completed winterization procedures for roughly 100,000 residential buildings, 12,400 local boiler facilities, and 11,700 kilometers of district heating pipelines, supported by state allocations of Hr 6.8 billion ($152 million) for backup power generation and physical barrier defenses.

What’s behind Iranian authorities’ push for a mass mobilisation campaign?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:47:26 UTC
22:47:26 KST

What’s behind Iranian authorities’ push for a mass mobilisation campaign?
Iran has launched a major mobilisation drive, sparking fears of renewed conflict with the US.
“Do you know how to work with this?” reads the text on banners erected across Tehran, emblazened with the image of a rocket-propelled grenade, a sniper or assault rifle, or other military or communications equipment.
The Iranian authorities’ public messaging campaign is part of a push to train and arm volunteer civilians who would serve as part of state security under the Basij militia arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US-Iran talks in deadlock – what’s the latest?
- list 2 of 4Iran says Strait of Hormuz under its control, rejects Trump claims
- list 3 of 4Mahsa Amini death four years on: Iranians reflect on ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’
- list 4 of 4Iranians rally in biggest show of defiance against US since war began
The Islamic Republic first unveiled the messages as part of a major mobilisation drive – called Janfada or “those who sacrifice their life” – in late March at the peak of the war with the United States and Israel.
Janfada recruits held their first public “military exercise” on Friday in Tehran, where thousands of children, women and men – many masked and wearing shades – marched on downtown streets.
Prior to the event, the authorities called it a march of 313,000 people, although footage broadcast by state television did not appear to justify this claim. In Twelver Shia tradition, 313 is the number of the core companions of Mahdi, the messianic hidden imam who will reappear near the end times to establish justice.
Hassan Hassanzadeh, head of IRGC in Tehran, told state broadcaster IRIB that more than 600,000 people had heeded the call this week for the active mobilisation part of the campaign by registering on a website.
The authorities said more than one million people were expected to sign up, and that they had already formed an initial 1,000 units, described as “battalions”.
The Janfada campaign raised eyebrows just one month after its launch in late March when authorities claimed that more than 31 million people – which represents just over a third of Iran’s total population – had registered. It would also be more than half of the over-12 population, men and women.
Foreign-based activists accessed the website’s source code, which showed that fewer than four million people had registered. Only a phone number was required for registry, with no national identification number needed.
After the controversy, a ticker showing the number of recruits slowed down significantly, but then, the IRGC’s Hassanzadeh claimed on Friday that 33 million people are now registered. Authorities have not released documentation to back their figures.
The mobilisation effort is not exclusively military, as organisers said 26 percent of registrants selected military and security work, with other categories including rescue, social services, media, and financial support.
President Masoud Pezeshkian asked the volunteers during Friday’s parade to tangibly help his administration by consuming less fuel, electricity and other resources at a time when the country is challenged by energy imbalance and wider economic turmoil.
The government increased the price of fuel and limited petrol quotas allocated to personal vehicles earlier this month as it battles a budget crunch and fuel production shortfalls related to the war.
Iranian households and industries have also been afflicted, with intermittent power blackouts throughout the summer, with the upcoming cold season expected to bring more natural gas shortages in the resource-rich country.
Focus on children
The latest display of the “sacrifice” campaign in Tehran focused on children. Some teenagers were shown wielding assault rifles and other weapons during Friday’s military exercise, while others marched in the procession. Armed teenagers have been seen manning checkpoints and roadblocks on the streets of Tehran and other cities over recent months.
Sasan Zare, the spokesman of the Janfada campaign, told the state-linked Iranian Labour News Agency on Saturday that boys over 15 have been allowed to register for the campaign, but that there were also plans for under-15s to be recruited.
“Our effort concerning children and teenagers, first and foremost, is to introduce them to the culture of sacrifice and resistance,” Zare said.
“The stronger their value system is formed from childhood, and the more they become familiar with concepts like patriotism and self-sacrifice, the more significant the impact can be on their future.”
Women also featured heavily during Friday’s display, with many chador-clad volunteers wielding weapons on the streets.
Some of them were shown riding on motorcycles, despite women being officially banned from doing so in civilian life.
What’s the purpose?
During Friday’s parade, Iranian military hardware used in the war against the US and Israel went on public display.
The efforts come as Iran and the US clash over the future of the Strait of Hormuz and the outcome of the war. The US continues to impose a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports and has intensified its sanctions on the country.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera that seven conditions for negotiations had been relayed to Washington through intermediaries, but added that commanders were also prepared to resume the war.
The authorities have not elaborated on why they require hundreds of thousands of civilians to take up arms or engage in other security activities, considering that there are no prospects of a ground war with the US in the foreseeable future.
The campaign comes months after thousands were killed during nationwide protests in January, which Iranian authorities describe as a “coup” orchestrated by the US and Israel and armed agents acting in line with their interests.
A United Nations fact-finding mission alleged on Friday that the Islamic Republic committed crimes against humanity while cracking down on the protests. Amnesty International last week presented a lengthy report that identified dozens of senior authorities who engaged in crimes against humanity during the 2022-23 protests over Mahsa Amini, a young woman who died in Iranian police custody after being detained for wearing “improper hijab”.
Iranian authorities have repeatedly warned against more public protests in recent weeks, emphasising that any act perceived to be undermining national security and “social cohesion” is strictly forbidden.
Ali Alfoneh, a senior fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute, told Al Jazeera that he perceives the Janfada campaign as an effort to rebrand the Basij militia, which has become associated with the violent repression of protests.
He explained that following neighbouring Iraq’s invasion of Iran in 1980, hundreds of thousands of Iranians volunteered for front-line service out of a sense of religious or patriotic duty. These were mobilised through the Basij.
“Since the end of the war in 1988, however, the Basij has evolved into an instrument of domestic coercion and the suppression of dissent, severely damaging the organisation’s public image,” he said.
The public mobilisation campaign could thus be viewed as an attempt to restore the Basij’s former patriotic image in anticipation of future internal and external threats – “if not a US ground invasion of Iran, then the prospect of a US- and Israeli-instigated civil war in Iran’s peripheral regions, as well as large-scale popular uprisings driven by mounting economic pressure”, Alfoneh said.

Russia reports mass attacks on election systems amid Duma voting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:46:39 UTC
22:46:39 KST

Russia's electoral chief has said that there have been over 1,000 waves of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks targeting Russian election infrastructure in recent days.
The attacks appeared to have been carried out by "highly professional, well-coordinated groups using artificial intelligence tools", Ella Pamfilova, chair of Russia's Central Election Commission, said on Sunday.
DDoS attacks involve overwhelming a system with internet traffic so that it is unable to function normally.
"Over the past period, more than 1,000 waves of DDoS attacks have been recorded against infrastructure in Russia that is specifically involved in the electoral process," Pamfilova was quoted as saying by Russian news agencies.
Voting is currently under way in Russia to determine all 450 seats in the lower house, the State Duma.
The ruling United Russia party, which backs President Vladimir Putin and has won every parliamentary election in Russia since 2003, is widely expected to secure another victory.
Putin on Friday accused Ukraine of trying to interfere in the election, citing what he said was a Ukrainian strike on the home of an election official in the Russian-occupied part of Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region.
Putin told the nation in a televised address before the election that the vote would underline support for Russian troops fighting in Ukraine.
"Your choice, and your will, will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us," said Putin.
Initial results are expected to start emerging at around 1800 GMT on Sunday, with more complete results available on Monday.

Healthcare goes digital: When doctors go behind the app wall, who gets left behind?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:44:59 UTC
22:44:59 KST

Visuals of long queue at Delhi National Cancer Institute (pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)
What if your phone becomes the first thing you need to see a doctor?As healthcare increasingly moves from hospital counters and paper records to apps and online portals, access to care is becoming closely tied to access to technology.For many patients, digital healthcare can mean quicker consultations, easier access to medical records and fewer trips to hospitals. But for others, particularly older people, rural communities, low-income families and those with limited digital literacy, the shift can add another layer of difficulty.The problem is not simply whether a person owns a smartphone. Patients may struggle with internet connectivity, downloading and navigating apps, remembering passwords and OTPs, uploading documents or understanding information presented online.In many households, a single smartphone is shared by several family members, while caregivers often become the bridge between patients and digital health services.As government and private healthcare services increasingly encourage, and in some cases require, people to use digital platforms, a larger question is emerging: Is technology making healthcare more accessible, or creating a new barrier to accessing it?
Difficulties patients might face despite digital help
When the smartphone becomes the gateway to healthcare
Digital health has opened up several ways for patients to manage their care remotely.
People can consult doctors online, monitor blood sugar through connected devices, receive medication and appointment reminders, and access diet and educational resources without making frequent hospital visits.Telemedicine became particularly important during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns made physical consultations difficult. But the experience also exposed how uneven access to digital healthcare could be.A DIG-EQUITY study published in The Times of India, examining the experiences of people with diabetes, caregivers, healthcare providers, policymakers and community organisations in urban and rural Tamil Nadu, found significant differences in how people used digital health services.Younger patients were generally more comfortable with smartphones, health applications and teleconsultations, while many older people needed family members to book appointments, join consultations or access medical reports.For some, physical limitations added to the problem. Impaired vision or hearing, as well as difficulty handling smartphones, could make navigating digital platforms harder.Even among younger people, digital access did not automatically translate into a preference for online care. Some people with type 1 diabetes continued to prefer in-person consultations because of the need for physical examinations.The digital divide is also closely linked to where people live and what they can afford.Urban patients are more likely to have reliable internet connections, smartphones and access to digital services. A study published in Nature, examining barriers to digital health transformation in India, found that the challenges went beyond simply having a smartphone or internet connection.The study identified poor network coverage and inadequate IT infrastructure, the high cost of devices and digital systems, a lack of technical expertise, language and communication barriers, and difficulties faced by users among the major challenges.For patients, these barriers can have very practical consequences. The study noted that some had to rely on family members' smartphones to attend teleconsultations, while the cost of smart devices could limit access to mobile health applications.The findings suggest that digital access cannot be measured simply by whether someone owns a phone. Reliable connectivity, affordability, digital skills, language accessibility and the availability of human support all influence whether a patient can actually use digital healthcare.That distinction becomes particularly important as healthcare services increasingly move online. Putting a service on a digital platform does not automatically make it accessible to everyone.
Who gets left behind?
ABHA and the push towards connected healthcare
India's digital health infrastructure is expanding rapidly. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), through platforms such as ABHA, is aimed at creating a connected digital health ecosystem, while eSanjeevani has widened access to telemedicine.With hundreds of millions of ABHA IDs created and telemedicine consultations running into hundreds of millions, the scale of this shift is significant.But the benefits of digital healthcare are not evenly experienced.The gap becomes particularly visible when digital systems are introduced at the hospital level. For some patients, the shift has not removed queues; it has created an additional one.Rekha (name changed), a patient at the Delhi National Cancer Institute, said patients earlier had to wait in a single OPD queue, with doctors arriving around 8am. According to her, the process now involves generating a token through the ABHA app before reaching the hospital, followed by another number at the reception.“Earlier there used to be only one OPD line and the doctors used to arrive at 8am. Now they have made it mandatory to download the ABHA app and apply for a token number. Then we get another number from reception, and doctors arrive at 10am. Several patients need immediate care, but this extra queue has made life a bit more difficult,” she said.
Delhi National Cancer Institute (pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)
For those without a smartphone or reliable internet connection, Rekha said the process can begin hours before they reach the doctor. Some patients, she said, arrive around midnight or 1am and spend the night waiting because they cannot access the network or generate a digital token.Those with smartphones may apply through the ABHA app around 5am and reach the hospital by 7am, she said, only to wait again at reception before seeing a doctor later in the morning.Dr Manisha Arora, Director, Internal Medicine, CK Birla Hospital, Delhi, said ABHA should remain a facilitator rather than become a gateway to treatment.“A patient should never feel that access to technology determines access to healthcare,” she said, noting that patients without an ABHA ID, smartphone or internet connectivity should continue to be able to register physically and receive the same clinical care.She stressed that hospitals should adopt a digital-first, not digital-only, approach.“That means retaining manual registration counters, providing assisted kiosks and having dedicated digital-support personnel, particularly for elderly and first-time users.”
Insurance goes digital, but payment and paperwork remain a burden
Digital insurance processes are another area where patients can struggle. Families dealing with hospitalisation may simultaneously have to navigate e-KYC, pre-authorisation, co-payments, deductions and non-payable items.Manivannan Selvaraj, Founder and Managing Director, Kauvery Group of Hospitals, said translating a clinical treatment plan into a pre-authorisation submission, and then managing the queries and follow-ups that come back, involves a long chain of steps that a patient is neither equipped nor educated to handle, and should not have to handle while they or a family member is unwell.“Sometimes delays or claim issues arise because documentation is incomplete rather than because of a medical concern,” Arora said, stressing that hospital insurance desks need to act as patient counsellors, explaining the process rather than merely uploading documents.“True digital accessibility is when technology works in the background and the patient still experiences a human interface at the front,” she said.
What's the solution?
At 65, Amarnath (name changed) has an insurance policy but says managing it digitally has become difficult. He is often unsure about when he can claim, when premiums are due and how to complete the process online, leaving his son to handle the details for him.“I have an insurance policy, but I often don’t know when I can make a claim, when the premium is due or how to complete these processes online. My son manages it for me. At my age, it is not always easy to visit a centre every time I need to check my policy or make a claim. If healthcare is becoming digital, these services should also be made accessible to elderly people, so that we can manage them ourselves without having to depend on others,” he said.He also highlighted how the growing use of digital payments in hospitals can create another challenge for elderly patients unfamiliar with the technology. Having a UPI-enabled phone does not necessarily mean being comfortable using it, particularly during a medical emergency when payments may need to be made quickly.“I have UPI on my phone, but for people of our generation, it is difficult to become fully comfortable with the process and make an immediate payment, especially during a health emergency. This is something that should also be addressed,” he said.
Covid era showed that systems still struggle
The pandemic offered an early and stark example of how closely technology and healthcare had become intertwined.While telemedicine and digital systems helped patients access services during lockdowns, other parts of the healthcare chain showed that digitisation alone could not solve problems of capacity and access.As reported by The Times of India earlier, delays in Covid testing became a major concern during the second wave. Udham Singh, 22, developed high fever, severe cough, body ache and breathlessness after his sample was collected for an RT-PCR test. His report, which confirmed Covid infection, came several days after the sample was taken.“I would have landed in an ICU had I waited for some more time. The element of uncertainty due to delay also caused extreme mental trauma,” Singh said.For patients waiting at home, the delay was not merely an inconvenience. It affected decisions about treatment and isolation. Some families also faced difficulties maintaining quarantine while waiting for test results.Priya Jaiswal, a resident of Old Delhi, recalled how a network outage during the pandemic left her dependent on officials for essential medicines. With her internet connection down, she could not use UPI to make payments or order medicines online, leaving her waiting for officials to arrive at her home.“We had to wait for hours for officials to arrive and hand over the medicines while we were in quarantine. Even online consultations became difficult because of continuous power cuts at a time when we needed healthcare the most,” she said.The surge in demand for Covid testing also put pressure on government laboratories to issue digital reports on time, highlighting another challenge for digital healthcare: a digital interface is only as effective as the system supporting it.Covid-19 vaccination certificates also affected people's travel and employment plans.
Covid-19 highlights struggle
Varghese Thomas, a youth from the city, told TOI that five people in his group had taken their first vaccine dose around the same time, but only one had received the certificate nearly 40 days later.“When we applied for jobs, prospective employers were asking us about the vaccination. They wanted us to produce the certificate,” he said.Registering through Co-WIN was another difficulty for people in rural areas.As reported by The Times of India earlier, 68-year-old Adhi Kesavan from Gudiyattam in Tamil Nadu's Vellore district had to travel around 5-7 km with his wife to a common service centre to register for vaccination.Kesavan did not own a smartphone or know how to use one. He was directed to the centre by his panchayat head, who told him that his details could be registered there and that the hospital would contact him when a vaccine became available.“I heard from our panchayat head that we can get vaccinated if we register at the e-sevai maiyyam. Our number will be given to the hospitals nearby and we will get a call once the vaccine is ready,” Kesavan said.
Digital healthcare cannot mean digital-only healthcare
India's digital-health expansion will ultimately be measured not only by how many people are connected to the system, but also by whether those who are not can still access care with the same ease and dignity.The goal should not be to make healthcare digital at any cost. It should be to make healthcare more accessible, using technology when it helps, and providing human support when it doesn't.Because for a patient struggling to connect, navigate an app, remember an OTP or make a digital payment, the smartphone should never become another obstacle between them and a doctor.
Priyanka Jaiswal has four years of experience in digital journalism, news agency reporting and video production. Currently with The Times of India, she covers public policy, politics and global affairs. She is particularly drawn to human-interest stories that put people at the heart of an issue, spark awareness , and contribute to meaningful conversations.

Former Kremlin political prisoner Mykola Karpiuk killed in action
Former Kremlin political prisoner, public and political figure, and co-founder of Ukrainian National Assembly – Ukrainian People's Self-Defence (UNA-UPSO), Mykola Karpiuk has been killed in action.
Source: former MP Artur Palatnyi; Viktor Yahun, former deputy head of the Security Service of Ukraine

A storybook debut as Yam Madar begins his Maccabi Tel Aviv journey

22:39:46 KST

It was like something out of a movie. It was surreal.
It was a magical evening of basketball as Yam Madar returned to Yad Eliyahu, only this time wearing the yellow-and-blue of Maccabi Tel Aviv rather than the red of his former club, Hapoel Tel Aviv. Madar led his new team with an MVP performance as Maccabi captured the preseason Super Cup with a convincing 101-83 victory.
The last time we saw Madar was during last season’s championship series, when the two archrivals faced off in a series Maccabi eventually won 3-1. Madar played a leading role for Dimitrios Itoudis’ Hapoel squad. Now, remarkably, he was playing for the man who had been standing on the opposite sideline – Maccabi coach Oded Katash.
Only sports can provide such drama, theater and showmanship.
It’s not every day that a player who grew up through Hapoel’s youth system, before being selected by the Boston Celtics in the NBA Draft, decides to cross the street and join the other side. But there was Madar, trading red for yellow-and-blue and embracing a much bigger role than the one he had previously held.
Despite the pressure, Madar shows he's prepared
It takes a special kind of player to make such a move, knowing the pressure and criticism that will inevitably follow. Madar, however, showed that he was prepared to handle it and, ultimately, do what he believed was best for his career.
The Maccabi fans welcomed him with pomp and circumstance, song and dance, setting the stage for Madar’s coronation as a new Maccabi star.
Then he stepped onto the court, shook hands with his former teammates and got to work.
After an aggressive drive that didn’t quite go his way, Madar quickly settled in, drilling a three-pointer for his first points in yellow-and-blue before giving his patented gunshot salute. He then found Keaton Wallace in the corner with a perfect pass, allowing Wallace to knock down another three.
As the opening quarter wound down with the score fittingly tied at 26 – Madar’s jersey number – who else would get the ball? Madar received it inside the paint, faked, turned and knocked down a short jumper to give Maccabi a 28-26 lead after 10 minutes.
Madar was just getting started
Madar opened the second quarter by hounding Max Heidegger into a backcourt advantage and sending Madar into double figures.
Maccabi continued to pour on the offense after the break, with Iffe Lundberg, Roman Sorkin, Will Rayman, and Bonzie Colson all contributing while Madar took a breather. When he returned, he controlled the ball like a yo-yo, bouncing it up, down and around as Maccabi pulled away to a 79-56 lead after three quarters.
Madar returned to the scoresheet early in the final frame to the delight of the home crowd, while the anticipation grew as the Super Cup and MVP trophies appeared on the sidelines.
Maccabi continued to roll, with newcomer Armando Bacot finding his offense and TJ Leaf returning from a lengthy injury layoff to contribute. But this night belonged to Madar.
When the final buzzer sounded, the yellow-and-blue lifted the trophy high into the air.
For Madar, it was a storybook ending to his first game in a Maccabi uniform. His debut could hardly have gone better.
Now, however, the real challenge begins.
The EuroLeague awaits next week, and the preseason page has officially been turned. If this magical evening was any indication, Madar and Maccabi Tel Aviv appear ready for what comes next.

World Jewish Congress visits Slovenia after Israel opens first embassy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:39:45 UTC
22:39:45 KST

A senior World Jewish Congress delegation met Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša and senior government officials in Ljubljana on Thursday, becoming the first major international Jewish organization to visit Slovenia since Israel opened its first resident embassy in the country, the WJC said.
The visit followed the opening of Israel's first resident embassy in Slovenia on September 9, when Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar traveled to Ljubljana and inaugurated the mission alongside Slovenian Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer. The two countries also signed a cooperation program covering education, science, culture, youth, and sports through 2030.
Israel has also named Ruth Cohen-Dar as its first resident ambassador to Slovenia. Cohen-Dar had previously served as Israel's nonresident ambassador to Slovenia and Malta and headed the Foreign Ministry's department dealing with antisemitism and Holocaust remembrance.
The WJC delegation was led by Sara Friedman, CEO of the World Jewish Congress, Israel and North America, and Hadassa Getsztain, chair of WJC Israel. They were joined by Maya Samakovlija, WJC executive director of community relations, and Ernest Herzog, WJC executive director of operations and head of combating antisemitism, intelligence and security.
The organization, which represents Jewish communities in more than 100 countries, described the visit as part of an effort to strengthen engagement with Slovenia following a change in government and the renewed diplomatic contacts between Ljubljana and Jerusalem.
Janša returned to the Slovenian premiership in May for his fourth term in office. His government has since pursued closer relations with Israel after a period of strained ties under former prime minister Robert Golob. Slovenia's government has characterized the renewed relationship as a return to regular political and economic cooperation.
“There are moments in diplomacy when simply showing up carries meaning,” Friedman said. “The World Jewish Congress is here in Slovenia immediately following the opening of Israel’s first resident embassy because we believe this relationship matters, not only for Israel and Slovenia, but for Jewish communities around the world.”
Recent WJC-Slovenia meeting in contrast to atmosphere of April 2024 meeting
The WJC also presented Thursday's meeting as a contrast with a previous mission to Slovenia in April 2024. According to the organization, senior members of the previous government declined to meet Jewish leaders during that visit. The WJC said its representatives also walked out of a meeting with Slovenia's delegation to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance after a senior official attempted to hold the global Jewish community responsible for the war in Gaza.
The organization further said Slovenia's small Jewish community has faced vandalism, threats, and intimidation in recent years, including incidents directed at the Jewish Cultural Center and Jewish cemetery in Ljubljana and threats against community leaders after the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.
Members of Slovenia's Jewish community had expressed "cautious hope" about relations with the new government following Janša's return to office, while raising concerns about the community's security and its relationship with state institutions.
“Prime Minister Janša has demonstrated the importance of challenging anti-Israel bias and making clear that friendship with the only Jewish State should not be something governments are pressured to abandon. For Jewish people around the world, seeing a European leader stand with Israel, the historic homeland of the Jewish people, and recognize the importance of confronting antisemitism sends a message that extends far beyond Slovenia’s borders.”
During the talks, WJC representatives welcomed the renewed diplomatic engagement between Israel and Slovenia and called for the appointment of a formal special envoy for combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life.
“We are here to convey the message that when governments extend a hand of friendship to Israel and to the Jewish people, the global Jewish community is ready to extend its hand in return. We believe this is the beginning of an important new chapter between Slovenia, Israel and the Jewish world. It is also important for American Jewish business leaders and investors to come to Slovenia, experience the country firsthand and see why it is such a wonderful place to build partnerships and develop new opportunities.”

Russia or the US? Post-Assad Syria tries to keep both powers in play - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:39:32 UTC
22:39:32 KST

In the same week that Russian ships returned to Syria’s coast to resupply facilities still used by Moscow, representatives of around 50 American companies were sitting down with Syrian officials in Damascus to discuss investment, energy, telecommunications, and financial services.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
At first glance, the two scenes appear to represent competing directions in post-Bashar Assad Syria: Russia trying to preserve what remains of its military presence, while the United States moves in through investment, economic engagement, and Syria’s reintegration into Western markets and institutions.
But interviews conducted by The Media Line suggest a more complicated picture. Damascus does not appear intent on replacing Moscow with Washington overnight. Instead, it is trying to redefine its relationship with Russia on more limited terms while simultaneously building a broader relationship with the United States.
On September 7, a convoy of four Russian vessels arrived at the port of Tartus to resupply Russian facilities on the Syrian coast, the first such operation since Damascus and Moscow reached a new understanding in August over the future of Russia’s presence in Syria. Satellite imagery and accounts from the ground confirmed the ships’ presence, although neither Damascus nor Moscow officially disclosed the contents of the shipment.
The operation followed roughly 18 months of negotiations that ended with a memorandum of understanding redefining the status of Russian facilities in Tartus and Hmeimim. Under the arrangement, the Syrian state assumes control of civilian facilities, including civilian operations at Hmeimim airport and the commercial berth at Tartus port, while military facilities are transformed into joint training and capacity-building centers, with a continued Russian presence under the new arrangements.
For Professor Mahmoud Hamo al-Hamza, a Syrian mathematician, historian of science, and expert on Russian political affairs, the developments do not represent a return to the alliance that bound Moscow and Damascus during Assad’s rule.
“Today, it is certainly no longer a strategic relationship, but it has indeed become more pragmatic,” al-Hamza told The Media Line. “Both sides realized that it is necessary to preserve the relationship within certain limits, but on new foundations that guarantee the sovereignty of each state, especially Syria, and that the relationship should be one of equals and based on mutual interests.”
Syria's central role in Russian Middle East strategy under Assad regime
Under Assad, Russian-Syrian relations extended across arms sales, military training, energy, trade, education, and politics. Following Russia’s military intervention in Syria in 2015, Hmeimim and Tartus became central pillars of Moscow’s military presence in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Today, al-Hamza says many aspects of that relationship are “almost frozen,” and that Moscow and Damascus are trying to construct a new model that no longer gives Russia the freedom of movement it once enjoyed.
He says limited areas of military cooperation may remain, including training, arms imports, and security cooperation, but argues that the essential difference is that, if they continue, such activities will take place under independent Syrian decision-making.
“Russia is a major state, a permanent member of the UN Security Council, and possesses enormous military power,” al-Hamza said. “Russia is an important country that cannot simply be ignored, but Syria is not required to maintain the kind of excellent relations with Moscow that existed before. There can be commercial, military, or training interests, but all of it must be based on an independent Syrian decision.”
US delegation visits Syria to discuss investments, trade
At the same time, Syrian-American relations are expanding in a very different direction. This week, the first US Chamber of Commerce mission to Syria arrived in Damascus, bringing representatives from 50 companies and more than 80 participants from different sectors. The delegation held a series of meetings with government officials and business leaders to discuss investment, trade, and potential partnerships.
US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Jacob McGee said during the meetings that Washington is encouraging American companies to invest in Syria. He said firms including Chevron, HKN, Visa, and Mastercard had begun taking steps to enter the Syrian market or had signed agreements with Syrian entities.
The business mission comes as Washington dismantles many of the restrictions that once stood between Syria and the international economy. The United States ended its comprehensive sanctions program on Syria in 2025 while maintaining targeted sanctions on specific individuals and entities. On Aug. 24, Washington removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, eliminating another major obstacle to investment.
Can Syria open up to US while maintaining Russia ties?
The growing relationship raises a fundamental question: Can Syria open up to the United States on this scale while maintaining some form of military cooperation with Russia?
Political analyst Mohammad Alaa Ghanem believes Washington is, for now, approaching this equation with a high degree of pragmatism.
Ghanem told The Media Line that the continued presence of a “limited Russian military footprint” in Syria does not appear, by itself, to be an obstacle to improving Syrian-American relations.
He said Washington is more focused on “the nature, scale, and function of that Russian presence,” and on whether it gives Moscow broad influence over Syrian decision-making or allows Syrian territory to be used in support of wider Russian military objectives in the region.
According to Ghanem, US priorities are centered on security and stability, preventing the return of extremist groups, and opening the door to investment and Syria’s economic reintegration.
“Washington does not necessarily need to demand that Damascus cut ties with Russia,” he said. “Rather, it is seeking to reduce Syria’s dependence on it.”
Instead of asking whether Russia will remain in Syria or leave entirely, competition may increasingly revolve around the extent of Damascus’ dependence on Moscow and whether the United States and its partners can provide viable economic and commercial alternatives.
Damascus seeks alternatives to dependence on Russia
In August, Reuters reported that Damascus had expressed willingness during talks with Washington to sharply reduce imports of Russian oil. Sources said the United States had not made that step a formal condition for removing Syria from the state sponsors of terrorism list, but had encouraged Damascus to reduce its dependence on Moscow. At the time, Syria was importing around 60,000 barrels per day of Russian oil.
Ghanem says American and Western investment could give Damascus alternatives in energy, trade, finance, and reconstruction, gradually reducing Moscow’s ability to maintain its status as an indispensable partner.
The need for alternatives is not only geopolitical.
Syria witnessed widespread protests this month after fuel prices were raised, including road blockades, burning tires, and disruption of some tanker convoys. The Energy Ministry said the increases were linked to higher import costs and Syria’s heavy dependence on external supplies, as well as pressure on Russian deliveries and the closure of the Baniyas refinery for maintenance.
The government responded Thursday by announcing lower diesel prices for heating, agriculture, and industry, partially reversing the increases that helped trigger the protests.
Opening markets, attracting investment, and securing new energy sources are therefore domestic economic priorities as well as elements of Syria’s changing foreign relations.
Al-Hamza says Russia is uncomfortable with the speed at which relations between Damascus and Washington are developing, but he believes Moscow’s ability to influence Syrian choices is far weaker than it was during the Assad era.
“Russia is not comfortable with the American presence, the broad American role, and the good relations between the United States and the new Syria. There is no doubt about that,” he said.
Still, he added, Moscow is trying to preserve its channels with Damascus after losing much of the influence it once enjoyed.
Al-Hamza sees no benefit for Syria in replacing dependence on Russia with similar dependence on another power. He said the policy emerging in Damascus is based on “maintaining balanced relations with all countries of the world” and avoiding joining one alliance against another.
At the same time, he considers Syria’s current relationship with Washington far broader than its newly redefined relationship with Moscow, which is still in the early stages of being rebuilt. Ghanem agrees that Damascus can, for now, maintain relations with both sides, but he believes the hardest test has yet to come.
Conflicts between US, Russian interests could emerge in Syria
The more Syrian-American cooperation expands into security, intelligence, energy, and finance, and the more military cooperation with Moscow deepens in parallel, the greater the likelihood that areas of direct conflict between American and Russian interests will emerge.
Ghanem said maintaining the balance “will become more difficult as cooperation with both sides deepens in sensitive military, intelligence, and economic files.”
For that reason, he argues that the competition for influence in Syria will not necessarily revolve around expelling Russia entirely or replacing it with the United States. The issue, he said, will be “how much influence Moscow is able to retain, and how successful Washington is in building long-term political and economic influence inside the new Syria.”
This week offered an unusually clear illustration of that competition.
Russia is still able to send ships to Tartus and resupply its remaining presence, while dozens of American companies are arriving in Damascus in search of investment opportunities. Moscow retains military relationships built over decades; Washington is increasingly entering through markets, finance, and trade.
Damascus is trying to make use of both without returning to full dependence on either.
Whether it can maintain that balance when Russian and American interests collide will be a much harder test.

Writing on X, Sybiha emphasized that the cognitive domain of contemporary warfare represents a critical battleground, cautioning that Moscow continues to deploy multifaceted cultural and educational channels to advance its strategic interests abroad.

“The cognitive domain of modern warfare must not be underestimated,” Sybiha stated. “Russia is waging a global battle for the minds of people through a comprehensive network of tools and channels, including Rossotrudnichestvo and so-called Russkiy Dom (‘Russian House’) cultural centers. They in fact serve as tools for disinformation, destabilisation, and espionage.”
Sybiha commended European governments that have moved to dismantle the network, highlighting Germany’s decision on Friday to formally terminate operating agreements for the flagship Russian House in central Berlin following years of hybrid influence concerns.
“Our shared European home is not the place for ‘Russian houses’ promoting war propaganda and actively working to shatter peace in Europe,” Sybiha said.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Buk-M3, Nebo-U Radar, and Drone Site
Despite recent closures in several Western capitals, Sybiha noted that Russian cultural centers continue to operate in at least seven European nations, while maintaining an even broader presence across Africa, Central and Eastern Asia, the Asia-Pacific region, and South America.
In multiple jurisdictions, the centers remain formally integrated into Russian diplomatic infrastructure, granting staff diplomatic protections.
The foreign minister confirmed that Kyiv has transmitted formal diplomatic representations to foreign ministries worldwide, providing documentation detailing the national security threats posed by the facilities and presenting legal arguments for restricting their operations or shutting them down permanently.
The cognitive domain of modern warfare must not be underestimated.
Russia is waging a global battle for the minds of people through a comprehensive network of tools and channels, including Rossotrudnichestvo and so-called Russkiy Dom (“Russian House”) cultural centers. They in… pic.twitter.com/E5zLeOi7s5
The Berlin closure and intelligence footprint
Sybiha’s diplomatic appeal coincides with Germany’s move to shut down the Russian House on Friedrichstrasse in Berlin, traditionally the largest facility in the global network.
The German federal government ordered the facility closed after attributing an attempted drone sabotage plot at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 to Russian military intelligence (GRU).
In that incident, an explosive drone intended to target a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft failed to detonate due to a snapped wire, leaving 1.8 kilograms of Semtex intact inside a fuel-dense perimeter. In response, Berlin ordered the closure of the Russian House alongside the shuttering of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn.
The Russian House belongs to an institutional network managed by Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States Affairs, Compatriots Living Abroad, and International Humanitarian Cooperation, which functions under the jurisdiction of the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Rossotrudnichestvo maintains 87 foreign missions spanning 71 countries.
The EU imposed sanctions on Rossotrudnichestvo in 2022, identifying the agency as the Kremlin’s primary vehicle for projecting soft power and hybrid influence. EU findings stated that the organization coordinates networks of pro-Kremlin diaspora groups, finances propaganda operations, and disseminates revisionist historical narratives.
European intelligence assessments have linked the facilities to covert activities. Investigative findings published by German broadcasters WDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung revealed that French intelligence agencies formally categorized the Russian House network as an operational cover for Russian foreign intelligence services.
Security researchers have similarly identified the centers as espionage platforms. Nathalie Vogel, a research fellow at the Institute of World Politics in Washington, noted that the Berlin facility served as an operational instrument for establishing clandestine agent networks, while consular posts functioned as espionage hubs across Western Europe.

Uruguay’s governing Broad Front, known locally as the Frente Amplio, unanimously endorsed a pro-Palestinian march scheduled for Montevideo on October 8, calling on supporters to join the demonstration and urging President Yamandú Orsi’s government to pursue further international action on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
The coalition’s national political committee approved the decision on Monday. The march, organized by Coordinación por Palestina en Uruguay, is set to begin at 6:30 p.m. local time in central Montevideo and proceed toward Plaza Independencia, according to Uruguayan news outlet la diaria. Organizers are promoting the demonstration under the slogan “Free Palestine or barbarism.”
In its resolution, the Broad Front accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government of carrying out “genocide” in Gaza and said it was joining international demonstrations in solidarity with Palestinians. Israel has rejected accusations of genocide, saying its military campaign was directed against Hamas following the terrorist organization’s October 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel.
The October 8 demonstration comes almost three years after the Hamas-led massacre, in which terrorists killed some 1,200 people and took more than 250 hostages into Gaza. The Gaza war that followed continued until a ceasefire took effect in October 2025.
The Broad Front called for respect for international law and human rights across the region, specifically mentioning the West Bank and Lebanon, and reiterated its support for a two-state solution. It also urged Uruguay’s government to continue promoting initiatives in international forums aimed at reaching a lasting resolution to the conflict.
The party’s position reflects a more forceful line on Israel than the language generally adopted by Orsi’s government. Reports in Uruguay have described tensions within the governing coalition over foreign policy, with the Broad Front using the term “genocide” regarding Gaza while the government has stopped short of adopting the same characterization.
Orsi, who took office in 2025 after winning Uruguay’s presidential election as the Broad Front candidate, had previously been viewed as comparatively less hostile toward Israel than several other left-wing leaders in Latin America. Before becoming president, he visited Israel and Yad Vashem, and his election drew attention partly because of divisions over Israel within the Latin American left.
Uruguay suspended cooperation agreement with Hebrew University in 2025
Relations nevertheless faced new strains under his administration. In August 2025, Uruguay suspended a cooperation agreement with the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, citing Israel’s planned operations in Gaza City. Israel’s Embassy in Uruguay criticized the decision at the time.
Uruguay’s Foreign Ministry has continued to formally support a two-state solution and maintains diplomatic relations with both Israel and the Palestinians. The ministry describes Uruguay-Israel diplomatic relations as uninterrupted since 1948 and notes that Uruguay was among the first countries to recognize the newly established State of Israel.
Antisemitic incident in Montevideo concerns Uruguay’s Jewish community
Political debate over Israel has also coincided with concerns among Uruguay’s Jewish community. In November 2025, two Jewish teenagers were chased and threatened in Montevideo in an incident that Jewish community representatives described as antisemitic. A 2026 study of Spanish-language social media also found that antisemitic online content remained above pre-October 7 levels, with Uruguay among the countries highlighted in the findings.
The Broad Front previously backed a similar Palestinian solidarity mobilization in 2025. Its latest resolution calls on Uruguay’s national government to remain active in international forums while formally bringing the country’s dominant political coalition into the October 8 demonstration.

In a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it? | Steve Bloomfield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:38:46 UTC
22:38:46 KST

If all goes to plan, at some stage in the coming weeks 15 diplomats will emerge from a small sound-proofed room deep in the bowels of the United Nations headquarters in New York and announce the organisation’s next secretary-general.
The person they choose will face a combination of challenges unlike any that their predecessors have had to deal with. Two of the security council’s permanent members, the US and Russia, are engaged in wars of choice that have no end in sight. A UN commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, but the UN has effectively been reduced to the role of bystander, pushed out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. The climate crisis is creating a cascade of new humanitarian disasters, while every day now seems to bring a new security threat caused by the unregulated rise of AI.
All of this is happening in a world in which the very principles of the UN – multilateralism, a rules-based order and international law – are under threat.
Secretary-general elections have rarely been this consequential and conversations about who should win will dominate the sidelines of the UN general assembly this week and next, as world leaders gather for the annual summit.
The UN, and the world it speaks for, desperately needs a new leader who is both charismatic and competent. Yet the five permanent members of the security council – the US, UK, France, Russia and China – hold a veto. Anyone who wants the job will need the approval of Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and, most importantly, Trump.
It is not easy to argue you are best placed to save the UN when the man you need to persuade would rather it fails.
Three informal straw polls have taken place so far and no frontrunner has emerged, indeed opposition to the two leading candidates rose in last Friday’s vote. For the first time in the organisation’s 80-year history serious discussions are quietly taking place about what would happen if no secretary-general is chosen at all.
Ten years ago, the election of António Guterres of Portugal was widely welcomed as a shot in the arm for the UN after a decade of the low-energy leadership of the South Korean Ban Ki-moon. In his previous role as the UN’s refugee chief he had been an outspoken activist and had pledged to continue speaking up for the world’s most vulnerable people. Then, a month later, Trump took office as the US president.
Earlier this year, he announced the US’s withdrawal from 31 UN organisations, including the bodies responsible for dealing with climate change and women’s health, while in July his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced the administration’s desire to “dismantle” the international criminal court “brick by brick”. The abrupt closure of the US’s aid and development programme, USAID, led to deaths around the world.
Most controversially, the establishment of Trump’s Board of Peace sparked fears that it could be used to supplant the UN itself. The UN meanwhile is in the grip of a financial crisis, with Guterres warning during the summer that it faced “imminent financial collapse” due to unpaid dues, much of it owed by the US.
And yet, despite everything, the UN is still standing – and still matters. It is only the UN, through its Framework Convention on Climate Change, that manages to focus international attention on the greatest crisis the world is facing. Despite dramatic cuts in funding, there are still 11 peacekeeping missions staffed by more than 50,000 personnel in some of the most dangerous parts of the world. The UN’s office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs remains the best hope for negotiating access to deliver aid in war zones, including Sudan.
This year the general assembly passed two landmark resolutions: one recognising the transatlantic slave trade as a crime, another to adopt a new world map that correctly recognises Africa’s size.
We don’t know what the candidates think of these decisions, nor do we know where they stand on the war in Ukraine or what their stance is on Israel’s actions in Gaza. Despite the election’s importance – and despite the relatively recent transparency of “vision statements” and hustings – the candidates’ campaigns have been overwhelmingly cautious.
Part of the reason, of course, is that someone standing on an ambitious platform would stand no chance of getting the job.
UN experts believe there is a chance that the two current frontrunners, Guyana’s former foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Costa Rica’s ex vice-president Rebeca Grynspan, might become good secretary-generals. But no one is blown away by the choice on offer.
For Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband, both of whom will be in New York this week at the UN general assembly, there is a choice to be made. The UK is yet to express a preference, indeed the UK team at the UN is said to be unimpressed with all the candidates. So far, it’s understood, they have not voted in favour of anyone in the first three straw polls. The UK and France are both hoping another candidate will emerge.
Whether they will be any better is an open question. The New York Post reported in July that Trump wanted Fifa president Gianni Infantino to get the job. There is next to no chance that would happen, but European diplomats fear a Trump-backed dark horse – possibly one without a diplomatic background – may emerge in the coming weeks. This is, after all, the man who has outsourced his nation’s diplomacy to his son-in-law and a real estate investor. So far, Trump has said nothing in public, although that may change on Tuesday when he gives his speech at the general assembly. Or a social media post spat out at two in the morning could upend the race entirely.
The chances of the “Permanent Five” failing to agree on a name remain slim, but plans are already being drawn up in case the worst happens. Guterres may be asked to stay on, while another possibility is that a collection of senior UN officials is asked to serve in administrative roles until a candidate is found. Either way, it would leave the UN rudderless at a time it needs to be anything but.
No one is getting this job without Trump’s say so. But once the new general secretary is in office, the US president will have less sway on their actions. They will potentially serve for 10 years, eight of which will be without Trump in the White House.
But even without Trump, this will be an almost impossible job. The UN’s financial crisis is not going away. Severe cuts are coming. There will be no easy return to the 1990s and early 2000s, when the UN was at the heart of world events. A new leader will need to reinvent multilateralism in a world where it’s going out of favour.
Depending on the choice they make, we could look back at this decision as the moment that the crumbling international rules-based order began to be rebuilt – or when it slid irretrievably into irrelevance.
- 
  Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize

Polling stations for Russian State Duma elections open in Transnistria despite Moldova’s protest

The polling stations opened at 8:00 and will remain open until 20:00. The unrecognized leader of Transnistria, Vadim Krasnoselsky, also cast his ballot.

Digital Banking Shifts to Ecosystem Wars
Digital banking competition is transitioning from card visuals and gamification to integrated business ecosystems, where future market leadership belongs to platforms embedded in comprehensive economic value chains.
Early neobank models focused on customer acquisition through gamification and referral bonuses, but now face mounting user acquisition and retention costs. Similarly, models centered solely on corporate payroll remain vulnerable to institutional client concentration. Tobank represents the next stage by embedding digital banking into Tourism Financial Group’s broader ecosystem—spanning industries, hospitality, retail, and entertainment. Rather than dispersing funds via unguided cash loans, the platform prioritizes targeted credit lines for goods and services across merchant networks.
Highlighting this transition, Mohammad Bigdeli, CEO of Tourism Bank, remarked: "The next phase of digital banking is defined by targeted credit within active ecosystems, not plastic card features. Tobank links consumer financing directly to real economic activities, preserving retail purchasing power and ensuring continuous liquidity across the network."

Peter Thiel: Power, Palantir, and the antichrist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:29:00 UTC
22:29:00 KST

Peter Thiel: Power, Palantir, and the antichrist
September 20, 2026
He may not hog the limelight in the same way as Donald Trump, Elon Musk, or many of his other friends and associates, but Peter Thiel has a fair claim to be one of the world's most influential figures — as well as one of its richest.
Born in 1967 in Frankfurt am Main in what was then West Germany, the Thiel family moved to the US when Peter was just a year old. The family also spent six years in South-African occupied Namibia from 1971 to 1977.
Thiel's later rise to prominence came on the back of his tech firms and investments. His first major success was Paypal, a digital payments provider with which Musk was initially involved. Thiel then became the first outside investor in Facebook.
Today he also owns part of Musk's SpaceX, as well as OpenAI, and multiple other companies. Forbes puts his personal wealth at $35.7 billion (€31.1 billion).
But perhaps his most noteworthy company is Palantir. The surveillance, AI, and data-analytics company has won government contracts worth billions to create software for the Pentagon as well as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The company released a 22-point manifesto in April that critics said bore the imprint of "techno-fascism."
But Thiel could be considered as influential in politics as he is in business, and not just in the US.
Though several European countries, including the UK, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Spain are starting to reevaluate or end their governmental and military links with Palantir due to security concerns, the company is deeply embedded in security systems across the globe.
Thiel himself has recently moved to Argentina, where he has reportedly held talks with the country's right-wing president, Javier Milei, as the government proposes a series of regulations that include incentives for foreign companies and targets investments in AI data centers.
Early Trump support paid off
Thiel was an early backer, and later advisor, of Donald Trump, donating $1.25 million to Trump's 2016 election campaign and speaking at the Republican National Convention in the same year, at a time when Silicon Valley was broadly considered to be Democrat-leaning. Bar a hiatus between 2023 and 2025, he has been a generous donor to Republican campaigns and figures, including Vice President JD Vance.
Thiel's own political beliefs are not easy to pin down. He's been described as a libertarian nationalist and consistently expressed the belief that "technology is the alternative to politics."
He also shows a distrust of authorities, regulation, and liberal elites. This is partly born of a frustration with what Thiel considers inefficient decision-making by elected officials and voters.
"It's bordering on fascism," Max Chafkin, who wrote a 2021 biography of Thiel, told Time magazine. "He talks about how companies are better run than governments because they have a single decision-maker — a dictator, basically. He is hostile to the idea of democracy. That's pretty scary when you consider the role the companies that he's been involved in play."
These beliefs seemed to start to rise to the surface during his time at Stanford University in California. Thiel railed against the prevailing liberal campus ideology and founded the Stanford Review, a publication to express those contrary beliefs, something that would echo his current disdain for beliefs labeled as "woke."
Christianity, the antichrist, and AI
Thiel was raised in a strongly Christian household, and there is little doubt that his religion has colored his life and career. Thiel recently described himself as a "small 'o' orthodox Christian," something which seems to influence his conservative politics. His homosexuality, and marriage to American financier Matt Danzeisen, seem to many go against that grain. But paradox is not unusual for Thiel.
More recently, he has become preoccupied with the concept of the antichrist, touring with a series of lectures all over the world during the last few years. Rather than the figure depicted in the Bible, Thiel sees this as someone, or some group, who will deliver the apocalypse "by playing on our fears of technology and seducing us into decadence with the antichrist's slogan: Peace and safety."
Among those who have been, somewhat vaguely, cast in the role of soldiers of the antichrist have been environmental activist Greta Thunberg, whom he sees as a "Luddite who wants to stop all science," or governments that seek to regulate AI. He accused Pope Leo XIV of "working for the Chinese communists" in July after the pontiff warned about the "risk of dehumanization" by AI.
Despite his deep association with tech, Thiel also benefits from his relationships with powerful people, Musk, Trump, and Vance among them.
"I've built some great friendships over the years with people I've worked with," Thiel told the Washington Post in 2014. "And I think that's a really important part of what enables one to be successful in the long run in our society."
Using Vance to future-proof his interests?
Many observers think that Thiel may be using his relationship with Vance to help protect himself and his business interests in the future, with the vice presidentconsidered the most likely Republican to succeed Trump.
The pair met back in 2011 when Thiel gave a talk at Yale Law School. Vance, whose religious beliefs and politics have since shifted, wrote in Christian magazine The Lamp that Thiel "defied the social template I had constructed — that dumb people were Christians and smart ones atheists."
Thiel then reportedly became a mentor figure for Vance, before smoothing the relationship between Vance and Trump as Vance U-turned from previous opposition to the president to join his 2024 ticket. Most notably though, Thiel donated $15 million to Vance's Senate campaign in 2022, the largest amount ever donated to a single US Senate candidate.
The recent calls to slow the pace of AI, made in part by CEOs in similar positions to Thiel, may end up having an impact on Thiel's business interests. But his distinct character and connections have so far kept him a step ahead.

Trump claims triumphal arch will serve as a ‘top grade military complex’ to store weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:26:23 UTC
22:26:23 KST

Donald Trump is proffering a new argument for building his triumphal arch in Washington DC: it will be converted into a “top grade military complex” replete with drone and ammunition storage space and customised sniper facilities on the roof and plaza.
In a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning, Trump claimed that his new plan came at the “strong request” of the US military. He said the 250ft structure would be able to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage”.
With the hyperbole that is his trademark, the president added that the arch would be unique. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the world.”
The triumphal arch project has come under widespread criticism for its potential impact on the historic area of downtown Washington DC. Its intended location in a circle close to the Memorial Bridge could interrupt the sight lines of several of the most resonant structures, including the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery which would flank it.
The siting of the structure close to the Ronald Reagan Washington international airport has also prompted questions from Democratic Congress members.
Last week, the National Park Service warned that it could have “adverse effects to historic properties” and called for additional planning before the building work went ahead.
The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has initiated which he claims are necessary to elevate the visual greatness of the US capital but which critics have slammed as thinly veiled efforts to promote his own legacy. They include the creation of a White House ballroom, the refurbishment of the reflecting pool at the Lincoln Memorial and the renovation of the Kennedy Center.
All those projects have run into big problems, ranging from criticism of their aesthetic qualities, structural difficulties and legal challenges. In the case of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, one of the world’s pre-eminent cultural venues, Trump has hinted that he might demolish the property altogether in a fit of pique at the courts blocking the addition of his name to its title.
The White House ballroom, which Trump has also been calling a “military complex”, was beset by legal wrangling until the US supreme court last month said the project could go ahead.
The ground breaking that will kick off construction of the arch is expected to begin this month. Trump has linked it to the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, and said in Sunday’s post that it would be “by far the greatest” triumphal arch in any of the world’s top cities and capitals.
It will be clad in granite, with three golden statues on top.

Iran's family law framework can serve as model for Iraq, parliament official says
TEHRAN — Iran's legislative experience in supporting women and families, rooted in Islamic principles and Shia jurisprudence, can serve as a valuable comparative model for Iraq, a senior Iranian parliamentary official said.
Nader Nourouzi, deputy for legal affairs at the Iranian Parliament, made the remarks during a joint Iran-Iraq specialized meeting held in Tehran on transferring Iran's legislative experience in supporting women and families, with the participation of senior female lawmakers and officials from both countries.
Nourouzi said the shared cultural and religious foundations between Iran and Iraq create strong potential for comparative legal study, noting that Iran's constitution emphasizes the growth of women's personality and the restoration of their material and spiritual rights. He pointed to legal provisions covering maternity support, child custody, family protection, and special insurance for women — particularly widows and the elderly.
He highlighted Iran's 2013 Family Protection Law as addressing spousal relations, specialized family litigation, protection for women at risk of harm, and reconciliation and counseling mechanisms prior to court referral. Nourouzi added that laws on population and family have also created capacities in supporting childbearing, children, and working women, while the Civil Code outlines spousal duties and mechanisms for children without guardians or at risk, involving judicial, prosecutorial and welfare organization interventions.
He said Iran's parliamentary library and documentation center stand ready to provide Iraq with the necessary laws and records.
The meeting, held on September 15, was hosted by MP Somayeh Rafiei, a member of the Parliament Presiding Board, and brought together Zahra Khodadadi, head of the Women and Family Faction; Alieh Zamani Kiasari, head of the Population and Family Committee; Fatemeh Mohammadbeigi, deputy head of the Health Commission; and a delegation of Iraqi women officials and experts, including Hala Jaberi and Hoda Sajjad Mahmoud Shaker, a former Iraqi MP and deputy labor minister.
Rafiei proposed forming a joint Iran-Iraq working group on women and family affairs to exchange legislative experience, while Mohammadbeigi suggested holding quarterly joint sessions covering children, women, and social, cultural and economic affairs.
Participants also linked the discussion to regional developments, with several Iranian officials stressing that Iranian women and families played a key role in confronting recent pressures on the country and calling for continued Iran-Iraq cooperation against what they described as foreign interference in the region.
The session concluded with an agreement to continue exchanging legislative documentation and to move forward with establishing the proposed joint working group.
