During a trade mission organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), German companies advanced investment projects and explored new cooperation opportunities in Latvia in the fields of energy, defence technologies, autonomous mobility and space technologies. The combined planned value of the two most advanced investment projects exceeds EUR 600 million. The mission brought together 54 Latvian companies and organisations, which met with prospective clients, investors, banks, manufacturers, research centres and healthcare institutions.
The trade mission took place in Berlin from 14 to 17 September. Participating companies represented the information and communication technology, financial technology, life sciences, defence and dual-use technology sectors.
Summarising the results of the visit, Minister of Economics Viktors Valainis said: “Germany is Latvia’s largest export market outside the Baltic states and one of the world’s most important industrial and technology economies. Three years of focused work with German partners have already resulted in concrete investment projects worth more than EUR 600 million. In Berlin, we discussed the continued implementation of renewable energy projects with Notus Energy and the next steps concerning Dynamit Nobel Defence’s planned defence technology production facility in Latvia. Our meeting with Thomas Steffen, State Secretary at Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy, confirmed both countries’ interest in expanding economic cooperation. Our task is to ensure that investor interest translates into production facilities, technologies and jobs in Latvia, while Latvian companies secure increasingly strong positions in the German market.”
Sector-specific events and company visits were complemented by individual business and investment meetings.
“Latvia and Germany are united by successful economic cooperation and a shared vision of what must be done to promote economic growth in both countries and strengthen Europe’s competitiveness. The European Union’s single market is our greatest advantage, while establishing direct cooperation between companies is an essential prerequisite for successful development in the future,” emphasised German Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy Katherina Reiche and the ministry’s State Secretary Thomas Steffen.
From energy projects to autonomous vehicles
During a meeting with the management of Notus Energy, the parties discussed the continued implementation of two renewable energy projects in Latvia. Attention was given to practical matters affecting the projects’ progress, including the conditions for developing wind farms, connections to the electricity grid, permitting and access to financing.
Discussions with German defence technology company Dynamit Nobel Defence continued work on the company’s planned production facility in Latvia. The company and the State Defence Corporation signed a memorandum of understanding in February concerning the establishment of the facility. The Berlin meeting therefore focused on the project’s further development and opportunities to pursue other company initiatives in Latvia.
The Latvian delegation also met with HOLON, which develops fully electric autonomous passenger shuttles for public transport and mobility services. The discussions examined Latvia’s potential involvement in the company’s European development plans, including the production of vehicles and their components, the establishment of supply chains, autonomous mobility testing and technology development.
Berlin-based space technology company LiveEO, which uses satellite imagery and artificial intelligence to monitor power lines, railways, pipelines and other critical infrastructure, was invited to expand its operations in Daugavpils. The company’s Latvian subsidiary has been operating for four years. Opportunities for developing data centres in Latvia were also presented to German companies during a separate seminar.
In Berlin, the minister also met with German Federal Minister for Housing, Urban Development and Building Verena Hubertz, participated in a working lunch with investors and visited Microsoft’s office together with a delegation of Latvian information and communication technology companies.
Four sectors and different routes into the German market
Information and communication technology companies participated in events dedicated to German-Baltic digital cooperation and artificial intelligence, including the international Big Bang AI Festival. Latvian companies presented solutions in artificial intelligence, data processing, cybersecurity and process automation. At the Baltic-German Digital Summit, Viktors Valainis delivered a speech on Latvia’s transition from digital public administration to an economy prepared for the use of artificial intelligence.
Latvian financial technology companies entered the German market with considerable operational experience. Eight investment platforms regulated in Latvia serve more than 800,000 investors abroad, and the total amount invested through them exceeds EUR 13 billion. German investors account for approximately 30% of demand on Latvian investment platforms. In Berlin, Latvian companies met with 20 representatives of institutional investors, family offices and the financial sector to increase the amount of capital raised and expand cooperation with German banks and other financial market participants.
The life sciences delegation included companies alongside Latvian universities, hospitals and research organisations. The delegation visited the Berlin-Buch biotechnology ecosystem, the companies FyoniBio and BIOTRONIK, and Helios Klinikum Berlin-Buch. Latvian representatives approached prospective cooperation partners regarding joint product development, clinical research, technology testing and validation, certification, manufacturing and distribution.
Defence and dual-use technology companies represented a sector in which Latvia has already gained international recognition. Unmanned and counter-drone systems developed in Latvia are already being used in several NATO countries. In Berlin, Latvian companies met with the German Security and Defence Industry Association, a representative of the German Federal Ministry of Defence and German industrial companies. The discussions covered component supplies, supplier qualification, systems integration, electronic warfare, secure communications, counter-drone solutions and autonomous systems.
The delegation also visited Andres Industries AG, a manufacturer of thermal imaging and night-vision technologies. German companies participating in the in-depth industry discussions included Rheinmetall, HENSOLDT, Rohde & Schwarz and Quantum Systems.
Memorandum expands support available to exporters
In Berlin, LIAA, the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK) and the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce (AHK) signed a memorandum of understanding. It will provide Latvian companies with access to the expertise, contacts and services of the German Chambers of Commerce Abroad network at 150 locations in more than 90 countries.
The German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce will establish a dedicated contact point to support Latvian exports. Each year, LIAA and AHK will select two countries and two sectors in each country whose companies will receive particular attention in export development activities.
“This mission demonstrated the value of focused follow-up work after an initial meeting. For some investment projects, we are no longer discussing an initial contact — together with investors, we are advancing specific next steps so that, once the necessary preparatory work has been completed, negotiations can give way to construction machinery. For other Latvian companies, Berlin provided the first discussion with a prospective partner, and the key task now is to turn that contact into the next practical step — securing a technology trial, beginning supplier qualification or progressing towards a contract. Concluding an export deal can take several months, while complex or technologically advanced projects may require several years to implement. The agreement concluded in Berlin with German chamber of commerce organisations will expand the network of contacts and support available to companies. LIAA will continue supporting Latvian companies and advancing the projects discussed in Berlin towards concrete results after returning to Latvia,” said Vita Balode-Andrūsa, Director of LIAA’s Export and Innovation Services Department.
Germany is Latvia’s largest export market outside the Baltic states. Total trade in goods and services between Latvia and Germany reached EUR 5.5 billion in 2025, while Latvian exports to Germany amounted to EUR 2.09 billion.
“This was the third major trade mission by Latvian companies to Germany in recent years, this time bringing together 54 Latvian companies and organisations. Such continuity is important because one visit is not enough to enter the German market. Germany is Europe’s largest market and is located at the economic centre of the continent. Entering and establishing a strong position in this market often opens the way to other European regions as well. German companies are known for their demanding standards regarding quality, deadlines and supplier reliability, so successful cooperation with them significantly strengthens a Latvian company’s reputation and position in international markets. It is encouraging to see German investment projects worth more than EUR 600 million in green energy and defence technologies moving forward, with important implementation matters also addressed during this visit. This clearly demonstrates the scale and importance of the German market to Latvia’s economy,” said Līva Stūrmane, Head of the Latvian Exporters’ Association The Red Jackets.
LIAA organises participation in foreign trade missions under the European Union co-financed Innovative Business Development Programme for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises. The programme is supported by funding from the European Regional Development Fund and the Latvian state budget. Companies may participate in trade missions either for a fee or by receiving support to cover eligible costs.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine’s history as part of world history: What 200 researchers led by Timothy Snyder are creating
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:06:00 EEST
22:06:00 KST

Ukraine’s history as part of world history: What 200 researchers led by Timothy Snyder are creating
What does it take to tell the history of Ukraine to the world? For three days in Kyiv, 80 scholars, researchers, and other contributors gathered to work on that question, and to bring three years of collaborative research closer to publication.
The third annual conference of the Ukrainian History Global Initiative (UHGI), held from 14 to 16 September 2026, marked an important transition for the project. With its research programme moving towards completion, the Initiative is now preparing to transform years of academic work into books and an ambitious digital platform designed to make Ukraine's history accessible to audiences around the world.
Founded by businessman and philanthropist Victor Pinchuk in 2023 and led academically by world renown historian Timothy Snyder, UHGI brings together an international community of about 200 researchers to develop a comprehensive history of Ukraine, from prehistory to the present, placing the lands and peoples of Ukraine within the broader history of the world.
As Snyder explained in his opening remarks, the ambition is to produce a comprehensive history of Ukraine through the history of the world, and a comprehensive history of the world through the history of Ukraine.
A different kind of academic conference
Unlike conventional academic conferences, the Kyiv gathering was organised around collaborative work without formal presentations.
Over three days, participants discussed 58 research papers in 58 dedicated workshops. Each session brought together authors and fellow scholars to examine drafts, challenge interpretations, explore connections between different periods of history, and consider how complex academic research could be communicated to readers beyond academia.
There were no slideshow presentations and no hybrid online participation. The emphasis was on being together in the same room, reading one another's work, exchanging ideas, and building the intellectual relationships that make a project of this scale possible.
For many participants, the conference was also an opportunity to reconnect with colleagues who have been working together since the Initiative began, while welcoming new contributors who joined the project this year.
The discussions reflected one of UHGI's central ambitions: to produce history that meets rigorous scholarly standards while remaining engaging and accessible to a broad public.
That requires more than simplifying academic language. It means developing narratives that help readers understand why historical events matter, how different periods and places are connected, and how Ukraine's past forms part of a much larger human story.
Building a scholarly community in wartime
The decision to gather in Kyiv carried particular significance as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues.
For international participants, travelling to the conference meant experiencing some of the realities of wartime Ukraine firsthand. For Ukrainian researchers, it meant continuing their academic work amid the challenges and uncertainty of war.
Susan Bonner, a Canadian journalist and Senior Fellow at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, joined UHGI's Academic Council this year, bringing four decades of experience in journalism and public communication.
Her journey to Kyiv was disrupted by a Russian drone attack on railway infrastructure near the Ukrainian-Polish border. Travelling alongside other UHGI participants, she experienced lengthy delays and an evacuation to a railway station shelter before reaching the capital.
In an article published in Policy Magazine following the conference, Bonner reflected on the experience of travelling through a country at war to join an international project devoted to making Ukraine's past accessible to a global audience.
Her account illustrates a central idea behind the Initiative: understanding Ukraine's present requires a deeper understanding of its past and of the country's place in world history.
https://www.policymagazine.ca/letter-from-kyiv-riding-the-rails-in-putins-war/
For Timothy Snyder, the gathering also demonstrated the importance of scholarly collaboration at a time when isolation and intimidation threaten intellectual life.
In his closing remarks, he reflected on what participants had achieved together:
"We're certainly working against isolation. We're working against over-specialization. We're working against intimidation. We're working against demoralization and nihilism."
But the purpose of the gathering, he emphasised, was not simply to resist these pressures. It was also to build something together: a community founded on intellectual exchange, mutual support, and a shared commitment to historical truth.
"We're working towards community," he said, "but also affirmation of the principle that we can pursue scholarly truth and that you can do it together."
From academic research to books and a digital experience
The conference also marked the beginning of a new phase in UHGI's development.
Over the past three years, researchers have been investigating subjects spanning thousands of years of history. Their work encompasses archaeology, the movement of peoples, cultural and religious exchange, political developments, and the many connections between Ukraine and the wider world.
The discussions in Kyiv demonstrated the progress made in developing these individual studies into a coherent historical narrative.
Authors are now moving towards the next stage of their work: completing their research, responding to academic feedback, and preparing their texts for publication.
During the conference, researchers also met members of UHGI's editorial team led by Clive Priddle, which has begun working with authors to develop texts that combine academic rigour with clarity and accessibility.
The editorial process will be accompanied by the development of maps, illustrations, and other visual materials to help bring the research to life.
As Snyder explained in his closing remarks, the ambition extends beyond producing a conventional collection of academic publications.
"We're doing both scholarly and popular history," he said. "We're meant to be doing both written history and experienced history."
The Initiative plans to publish its research through books in English and Ukrainian, alongside an ambitious digital platform designed to bring Ukraine's history to a global audience.
The platform is intended to offer more than a digital library of academic texts. By combining historical narratives with visual materials and interactive ways of exploring the past, UHGI aims to create an experience that allows readers to discover Ukraine's history, understand its connections to world history, and explore subjects in greater depth according to their interests.
Snyder described the ambition as bringing scientific research to a very large audience in a way that respects readers' different backgrounds and empowers them to deepen their knowledge.
The next chapter: 2027 and 2028
Although the third annual conference has concluded, the work of the Initiative continues.
Further workshops are planned from October 2026 into 2027, allowing researchers to continue reviewing one another's work, strengthen connections between related subjects, and develop their manuscripts.
The coming year will focus on completing the remaining research and writing, alongside the continuing editorial process. Where necessary, additional focused studies will help address gaps in the research and strengthen connections across the broader historical narrative.
In parallel, UHGI will continue developing its publishing arrangements, visual materials, and digital platform.
The Initiative currently anticipates preparing its principal research outputs for public release in 2028, with the ambition of reaching audiences across Ukraine and internationally.
For Snyder, the opportunity offered to the researchers is an unusual one: to see their academic work become part of a much larger collective project, supported by extensive scholarly collaboration, professional editing, and new ways of reaching the public.
He encouraged participants to embrace that opportunity and to continue working together towards the project's completion.
The conference ended with a shared understanding that the work ahead extends beyond finishing individual manuscripts. It is about bringing together years of research into a history of Ukraine that can be read, explored, and experienced by people around the world.
And, as the gathering in Kyiv demonstrated, that work begins with the people willing to come together to make it possible.
Ruslan Kavatsiuk, Managing Director Ukrainian History Global Initiative

The All-Ukrainian Council of Churches and Religious Organizations (UCCRO) has appealed to Pope Leo XIV and international humanitarian leaders to use all available diplomatic means to prevent mass starvation in Russian-occupied Oleshky, the religious body announced.
The interfaith council, representing Ukraine’s primary Christian, Jewish, and Muslim communities, warned that the occupied city in the southern Kherson region has been placed under complete military blockade by Russian forces and stands on the precipice of a humanitarian catastrophe.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Religious leaders noted that confirmed commercial or humanitarian food deliveries have not reached the settlement since late May 2026, leaving thousands of civilians cut off from sustenance while Russian occupation troops actively block escape routes.
According to council estimates, more than 6,000 residents, including approximately 200 children, remain trapped across Oleshky and adjacent settlements on the occupied left bank of the Dnipro River. Trapped in a frontline grey zone directly opposite Ukrainian-controlled Kherson, residents face daily artillery shelling, unexploded ordnance, and loitering tactical drone strikes.
The UCCRO emphasized that the local populace confronts severe shortages of basic foodstuffs, potable drinking water, and essential medicines. The city’s municipal utility network has been almost completely destroyed, leaving districts without electricity, running water, or central gas supplies.
Ukraine Intel Tests Remote-Controlled Quad Bikes for Front Line
Religious leaders also pointed out that Oleshky suffered catastrophic flooding in June 2023 when Russian forces blew up the Nova Kakhovka hydroelectric dam, which heavily degraded local housing stock and municipal infrastructure.
The council addressed its humanitarian plea to Pope Leo XIV, the World Council of Churches, the World Evangelical Alliance, international human rights organizations, and member states of the United Nations, alongside the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), urging them to negotiate emergency humanitarian corridors and facilitate the evacuation of trapped non-combatants to government-controlled territory.
Complete blockade
The interfaith appeal follows warnings from local military administrators and international monitoring missions documenting the isolation of the frontline community.
According to Head of the Oleshky City Military Administration Tetiana Hasanenko, the final confirmed humanitarian resupply and evacuation run reached the municipality on May 26.
The United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) independently confirmed that zero food shipments reached the enclave between late May and late June, while local authorities verified that delivery routes remained severed through September.
Frontline geography has rendered escape virtually impossible. Although Oleshky sits only four kilometers across the Dnipro from liberated Kherson, destroyed bridges, intense frontline combat, dense minefields, and relentless drone surveillance prevent residents from crossing the river.
Local officials and evacuees report that physical money has effectively lost its utility inside Oleshky because retail stores and pharmacies have shuttered, leaving markets devoid of staple goods. While trapped civilians survived throughout the summer on home-grown garden produce such as zucchini, tomatoes, and eggplants, the transition into autumn has eliminated seasonal food sources.
Flour, sugar, cereals, and over-the-counter painkillers are largely unobtainable or traded exclusively through barter networks.
Witness testimonies gathered by human rights monitors and international news organizations indicate that Russian military checkpoints surrounding Oleshky systematically turn back civilian vehicles attempting to haul commercial freight or food into the city.
Cascading crisis
The humanitarian deterioration in Oleshky mirrors wider operational pressures across the lower Dnipro operational axis, where civilian survival remains complicated by persistent kinetic strikes.
Throughout the winter and spring, residents resorted to hunting wild birds, burning scrap wood for indoor heat, and rationing dried bread as municipal services ceased functioning.
Russian authorities conducted limited administrative aid distributions strictly conditioned on recipients holding Russian identity documents, leaving thousands of Ukrainian citizens without institutional relief.

Psilocybin and standard antidepressants both shift the brain away from negative biases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:00:56 UTC
22:00:56 KST

Psilocybin and standard antidepressants both reduce the brain’s tendency to view the world through a negative lens. The findings suggest both drugs might relieve depression by shifting how the brain processes emotional information, though they may achieve this through different timelines. The research was published in Translational Psychiatry.
Depression involves more than just a persistently low mood. It affects how people perceive reality on a subconscious level. People with major depressive disorder often exhibit a negative affective bias, meaning they tend to interpret ambiguous or even positive social cues as negative. They might look at a neutral facial expression and perceive anger or sadness.
According to cognitive models of depression, this skewed perception plays a fundamental role in maintaining the illness. When people constantly interpret their social environment as hostile or rejecting, it reinforces their depressed mood. Breaking this cycle is a primary goal of psychiatric intervention.
Traditional treatments like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, known as SSRIs, aim to correct this imbalance. Medications such as escitalopram often take several weeks to produce noticeable improvements in a patient’s mood. Researchers believe this delay happens because the drugs first shift the brain’s emotional processing bias. Patients then need time to interact with their environment and experience positive social feedback before their overall mood lifts.
In recent years, psychiatric researchers have explored psychedelic compounds as alternative treatments for depression. Psilocybin is the active hallucinogenic ingredient in magic mushrooms. Clinical trials indicate that psilocybin can alleviate depressive symptoms much faster than traditional daily pills, but it remains unknown exactly how the compound changes cognitive functions to achieve this rapid relief.
A team led by Marieke A. G. Martens, a psychiatry researcher at the University of Oxford, designed a study to compare the cognitive effects of both drugs. The team included Robin Carhart-Harris and Catherine J. Harmer, among other researchers. They wanted to see if psilocybin works through the same emotional processing pathways as conventional antidepressants.
The study involved 59 patients diagnosed with long-standing, moderate-to-severe depression. The researchers randomly assigned these participants into two separate groups for a six-week trial. They conducted the study under double-blind conditions, meaning neither the patients nor the clinicians knew which full treatment protocol any individual received.
The first group received two 25-milligram doses of psilocybin spaced three weeks apart. These patients also took an inactive placebo pill every day for the six weeks. The second group received a daily dose of the SSRI escitalopram for the entire six-week period. To maintain the blind design, this second group also received two tiny one-milligram doses of psilocybin, which acted as a placebo during the dosing sessions.
Medication was only one component of the treatment protocol. Both groups received identical psychological support throughout the trial. This included preparatory sessions before receiving the psychedelic doses. Therapists also provided integration sessions afterward to help patients process their hallucinogenic experiences.
To measure emotional processing, the researchers used a computer-based assessment called the Facial Expression Recognition Task. Participants completed this task at the beginning of the trial and again at the six-week mark. During the test, patients viewed images of human faces flashing on a screen for half a second.
The faces displayed one of six basic emotions: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, or surprise. The researchers morphed these images to display varying intensities of emotion, ranging from completely neutral to full intensity. Participants had to identify the emotion shown on each face as quickly and accurately as possible using a keyboard.
Before the treatments began, the participants displayed a measurable negative bias, accurately identifying negative emotions but struggling with positive ones. After six weeks, both treatment groups showed a reduction in this negative bias. The differences between the psilocybin and escitalopram groups were not statistically significant.
Across both groups, participants became less accurate at recognizing negative emotions compared to their baseline scores. They also made fewer errors misclassifying faces as negative. Reaction times for identifying negative and positive emotions improved after the treatments. The researchers noted that patients recognized positive emotions even faster than negative ones at the end of the trial.
Previous brain imaging studies on these same patients showed that the two drugs had different physical effects on the brain. Escitalopram reduced activity in the amygdala, an area involved in processing fear and emotion, when patients viewed faces. Psilocybin did not produce this same dampening effect on amygdala activity. Despite these neurological differences, the behavioral outcomes on the emotional recognition task were remarkably similar.
The researchers then looked for links between these cognitive changes and overall depression symptoms. They measured depression severity using a standard self-report questionnaire at the six-week mark. At this concurrent time point, the reduction in negative emotional bias did not correlate with a drop in depression scores for either group.
The team followed up with the patients one month after the trial ended, at the ten-week mark. For the patients who took escitalopram, a decrease in misclassifying positive faces as negative at six weeks predicted lower depression scores at ten weeks. This aligns with the theory that SSRIs slowly improve mood as patients experience the world through a less negative lens.
This longitudinal relationship did not appear in the psilocybin group. The reduction in negative bias at six weeks did not predict better depression scores at ten weeks for these patients. The lack of correlation suggests that while psilocybin does alter emotional processing, its fast-acting antidepressant effects might rely on other psychological or neurological mechanisms.
The researchers noted several limitations to their experimental design. The trial did not include a pure inactive placebo group that received no active medication at all. Without a strict control group, it is difficult to completely separate the chemical effects of the drugs from the psychological support provided during the trial.
There was likely an inadvertent sample bias among the volunteers. Patients who sign up for clinical trials involving psychedelics often hold a strong preference for receiving psilocybin over traditional daily medications. This preference could influence how they respond to the respective treatments and how they report their symptoms.
Future studies will need to incorporate active placebo groups to better manage the blinding process in psychedelic research. Researchers also plan to measure emotional processing much earlier in the treatment timeline. Assessing patients within days of taking psilocybin could reveal how quickly these cognitive shifts occur compared to traditional medications.
Both treatments successfully shifted how patients interpreted emotional information, highlighting a shared cognitive outcome. The exact pathway from altered perception to mood improvement remains an active area of investigation. The study, “Negative affective bias in depression following treatment with psilocybin or escitalopram – a secondary analysis from a randomized trial,” was authored by Marieke A. G. Martens, Bruna Giribaldi Cunha, David Erritzoe, David Nutt, Robin Carhart-Harris, and Catherine J. Harmer.

EU facing ‘worst energy crisis in history’ – Putin envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:58:14 UTC

EU facing ‘worst energy crisis in history’ – Putin envoy
Europe is facing “the worst energy crisis in history,” Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev has warned, describing the situation as a “self-made.” He has repeatedly blamed the EU’s decision to cut Russian energy imports as a key factor behind the crisis.
Dmitriev made the remarks after reports of worsening fuel shortages across the EU. Government data on Sunday showed that 15% of French gas stations were facing supply problems with at least one type of petrol or diesel.
German media also reported record fuel prices, with Super E10 gasoline reaching around €2.3 ($2.6) per liter and diesel averaging a record €2.45. Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% higher than a year ago, diesel is up 38%, and jet fuel costs more than double. Benchmark gas prices have surged 150% year-on-year to €81 per megawatt hour, with analysts warning they could reach €100.
“Europe finally understands it is facing the worst energy crisis in history,” Dmitriev wrote in a series of posts on X on Saturday, calling it “a self-made crisis with zero attempts to analyze root causes and adjust course.”
Self-made crisis with zero attempts to analyze root causes and adjust course. https://t.co/zvdb0RkYsE
— Kirill Dmitriev (@kadmitriev) September 20, 2026
The bloc this year has faced mounting supply pressures from the US-Israeli war on Iran, which disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and LNG.
Combined with Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping and Saudi energy infrastructure, the disruptions pushed crude benchmarks up around 50%, with prices hovering above $100 per barrel and driving fuel and gas costs higher. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen this week said the EU had spent more than €90 billion extra on fossil fuel imports since the war began. Much of the additional expense was passed on to households. Brussels also previously acknowledged that industrial gas and electricity prices remain two to four times higher than those of major trading partners.
The Middle East conflict, however, has further pressured energy markets already strained by Europe’s sharp reduction in Russian supplies following sanctions imposed after the 2022 escalation of the Ukraine conflict. Before then, Russia supplied around 45% of EU gas imports and 27% of crude oil. By 2025, its share had fallen to 12% of gas imports and around 2% of crude.
Even sanctions supporters, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, have linked Europe’s energy challenges to the loss of cheap Russian supplies. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned earlier this month that the EU cannot remain competitive while energy costs stay prohibitively high.
Meanwhile, the EU is entering the heating season with its lowest gas storage levels in 15 years. According to Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE), underground facilities were just 69.3% as of Saturday, below the 85% average for this time of the year over the last five years, prompting warnings of heightened price volatility and higher energy bills this winter.
Despite the dire situation, von der Leyen reaffirmed in her State of the Union address this week that the EU will continue with its REPowerEU plan to permanently end reliance on Russian energy, with Russian LNG set to leave the EU market completely by the end of 2026 and pipeline gas by autumn 2027.
Moscow has long criticized Western energy sanctions as illegal and counterproductive, arguing they have redirected Russian exports while forcing Europe toward more expensive supplies. Russia has offered to help fill oil shortages caused by the Middle East conflict and resume energy deliveries but says it has received no response. Earlier this year, Dmitriev said the EU would “inevitably beg” for Russian gas as energy prices continue rising.

Analysis: VW, Mercedes and BMW lose ground against global rivals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:57:20 UTC
21:57:20 KST

Germany’s three largest carmakers continued to lose ground against international rivals in the first half of the year, according to an analysis by consultancy EY.
The combined total revenues for Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW fell to around €284 billion ($325 billion) – a 2.9% decrease over the previous year, EY said.
By comparison, the 19 other international automotive groups examined by EY increased their revenues by 3.6% to just under €1.048 billion.
According to the data, this marks the third consecutive first-half revenue decline for the German manufacturers.
The lag becomes even more apparent in the corporate ranking: according to EY, 15 carmakers recorded a revenue increase – while the three German groups occupied places 16, 17 and 19. Tesla achieved the strongest growth, followed by Suzuki and Geely.
The weakness of the German automotive industry is also reflected in profits: earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) of the German carmakers fell by 19% to €13 billion in the first half of the year.
In absolute terms, VW, Mercedes and BMW remained well ahead of manufacturers from other countries. However, according to the analysis, this is the lowest figure since the pandemic year 2020.
Performance was also down for manufacturers from China (minus 21.9%) and Japan (minus 36.5%). Meanwhile, US manufacturers Ford, General Motors and Tesla grew by 32.9%.

The recent agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the US respects the kingdom's “red lines,” including its sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said on Sunday.
“It has been absolutely crucial for us, with a desire to strengthen security in the very troubled world we live in, that our red lines are respected,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.

“The Kingdom of Denmark is a sovereign state, and the Greenlanders' right to self-determination must be respected in the future. And what we call our territorial integrity. All of that is contained in this,” she added.
Frederiksen declined to discuss the specific content of the agreement before it is signed.

“But generally, I would not put my signature, and neither would Jens-Frederik Nielsen, on an agreement that was not good for Greenland and the kingdom,” Frederiksen said.

Asked whether she expected Trump to honor the agreement, she said she assumed all sides would do so.

German start-up DeepL offers translations in your own voice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:48:48 UTC
21:48:48 KST

German AI start-up DeepL is significantly expanding its real-time language translation technology with new language models for its DeepL Voice application.
The German AI pioneer aims to do more than translate spoken words — it also wants to preserve each speaker’s individual voice, tone, pace and emotions across language barriers.
The translation company has had increasingly tough competition from AI rivals like Microsoft, OpenAI and Google and has sought to hold an advantage with a suite of high-tech translation services.
The live translation service DeepL Voice launched just over a year ago, has until now focused primarily on providing subtitles in video conferences.
Direct voice-to-voice translation is now taking centre stage: a newly unveiled desktop app for Windows and Mac integrates seamlessly into platforms such as Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet. Speakers can be translated into more than 30 languages, while the Speaker Match feature preserves voice identity in 14 languages initially.
“Our voice shows who we are. It conveys far more than just words,” founder and chief executive Jarek Kutylowski told dpa. “The goal is that you can sit back and forget that an AI translation solution is involved at all,” he said.
If someone speaks in an excited or hurried manner, he added, that should also come through in the translated tone.
Kutylowski said DeepL is well placed to compete with tech giants such as Google and Microsoft partner OpenAI, which are also investing heavily in multimodal language processing.
The Cologne-based AI company is firmly focused on corporate clients. “For companies, it’s not just about translating an individual email or meeting,” Kutylowski said. “It’s about building a larger system that handles documents and speech consistently and applies company-specific terminology uniformly across all channels.”
DeepL made headlines most recently in May when it announced job cuts. Kutylowski said at the time that the workforce would be reduced by 250 positions — around a quarter of all staff – citing changes in workflows in the AI era.
“In a world where AI is playing an ever greater role, we also had to restructure our roles and our internal organisation,” he explained. Today he sees the company as far more strongly positioned: “I think we are now much better set up, both in Germany and in all the other countries where we are hiring again.”
Founded in 2017, DeepL says it currently employs around 900 people and has more than 200,000 business customers. Its backers include prominent venture capital firms such as Benchmark, IVP and Index Ventures.

Ed Sheeran doubles down on 'non-political' stance, says Palestine 'most complex political issue on the planet'
British musician Ed Sheeran took to the stage at his concert in Philadelphia on Saturday evening to address the Palestine-related controversy surrounding his tour, doubling down on not taking sides in "political" issues.
Sheeran appeared alone at the gig after all of his supporting acts had dropped out due to Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft's barring of rapper Macklemore from the lineup for saying "Free Palestine".
Sheeran appeared to read from a teleprompter as he opened the concert with a statement, saying this is not how he usually opens his performances.
"I don't want want to disappoint fans, and I've never wanted to be an activist musician, but this put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," he said.
"Now I want to address the question on where I stand on the situation in Israel and Palestine and whether my doing this concert tonight implies where I stand. I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division; about humanity, not politics," he added, appearing to double down on an earlier statement saying that he does not take sides in "political" issues.
"But, this is a humanitarian issue, and i cannot hide how i feel about it any more," he continued. "What happened in Israel and at the Nova music festival on October 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic, and unjustifiable and disproportionate. My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians' lives - of children's lives. Ukraine Intel Tests Remote-Controlled Quad Bikes for Front Line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:45:00 UTC
21:45:00 KST

Special operators from the Main Directorate of Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR) have conducted closed-door field trials of domestically manufactured quad bikes, focusing on platforms equipped with remote-control capabilities, the state defense technology cluster Brave1 reported.
The operational testing was carried out by combat operators from the 33 Group, a specialized detachment within the HUR’s Tymur Special Operations Unit. The reconnaissance personnel operated the vehicles directly across simulated tactical scenarios to evaluate handling, endurance, and field reliability, providing engineers with immediate technical feedback for modifications.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Brave1 stated that the evaluation was structured around operational criteria vital for autumn and winter frontline deployments, where unpaved terrain, mud, and intense drone surveillance complicate standard logistical operations.
The military requires versatile platforms that can transition between conventional driver operation and remote control to transport supplies, evacuate casualties, and conduct tactical resupply across contested sectors without exposing operators to direct enemy observation.
While the Armed Forces of Ukraine utilize foreign-manufactured all-terrain vehicles, cluster representatives noted that imported models carry high acquisition costs and lack organic remote-piloting capabilities. To address the gap, Brave1 has integrated unmanned quad bikes into a targeted grant program intended to foster an indigenous production ecosystem.
Russian Drone Strikes Ukrposhta Mobile Branch in Sumy
“Our goal is to build a fully-fledged Ukrainian buggy market,” Brave1 said, noting that the cluster has provided financial grants to developers representing more than half of the buggy designs currently operating domestically.
Following the trials, manufacturers began refining transmission, communications links, and control software based on operator assessments. The defense-tech cluster noted that subsequent phases will involve coordination with the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine to codify the vehicles and scale serial procurement for frontline units.
Scaling domestic defense tech and indigenous munitions
The development of automated all-terrain vehicles forms part of a broader drive by Ukraine’s defense-industrial base and the Brave1 innovation cluster to field cost-effective, indigenously designed military hardware to counter Russian numerical superiority.
The initiative follows the unveiling in early September of the RK-19, a domestically produced surface-to-air missile engineered to replace dwindling Soviet-era munitions for Ukraine’s Osa-AKM mobile air defense systems.
The RK-19 missile, developed by Ukrainian state defense enterprises and showcased at the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland, was designed to substitute for Soviet 9M33-series interceptors.
The missile is engineered to intercept low-altitude aerial targets at distances of up to 10 kilometers and altitudes reaching 5 kilometers, reaching a maximum speed of 600 meters per second using radio-command guidance.
Ukrainian defense planners have accelerated domestic substitution programs as international munitions deliveries fluctuate and existing Soviet stockpiles approach exhaustion.
In late summer, Ukrainian officials noted that deliveries of foreign air defense missiles had fallen threefold compared with 2025 levels, prompting domestic developers to prioritize cost-effective interceptors and decentralized tactical platforms.
Brave1 developers have also introduced asymmetric countermeasures against high-speed aerial threats, demonstrating low-cost interception technologies designed to counter Russian loitering munitions and hybrid drone-missiles at a fraction of the cost of conventional anti-aircraft missiles.

Caribbean nations considering legal strategies to bring UK to reparation negotiation table - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:44:20 UTC

Caribbean officials are considering legal strategies in an effort to get the United Kingdom into a negotiation for a reparations deal, The Guardian reported on Saturday.
The recent push came during the CARICOM Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place from Thursday to Saturday, the Guardian reported.
The conference was hosted by Barbados, and, according to its website, featured between 150-20 representatives from numerous Caribbean nations, including governmental officials, academics, activists, and cultural leaders.
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley compared slavery to the Holocaust during the conference, the Guardian cited, pointing out that the German government had repaid the Jewish community $95b.
She said that she did not want anybody to "diminish the fact that in this country here, which I have the honor to lead, that from settlement in 1627, 400 years ago next year, for 211 years, not six, people were treated as chattel.
“If they dared to speak or to do things that were displeasing, their lives and limbs were put at risk. The evidence is clear. What is absent is the will,” she said.
Repair Campaign adviser calls for multigenerational plan
“We need a concrete, multigenerational plan,” Ralph Gonsalves, former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines who now serves as an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, said.
According to the Guardian, Gonsalves challenged claims that Britain was not obligated to pay reparations due to it not having violated historical laws during the era of transatlantic slavery.
“The fact is that the consequences of slavery fall squarely under the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, which obliges states to help address the consequences of native genocide and slavery,” Gonsalves said.
Caribbean nations may go to ICJ for UK reparation negotiations
Among the legal strategies which may be employed by Caribbean nations is going to the International Court of Justice, David Comissiong, deputy chair of the Barbados National Task Force on Reparations, said.
Another option currently being employed by Jamaica, the Guardian cited Comissiong as saying, was "trying to engage with the national legal judicial system of the UK, the privy council."
The chair of the CARICOM Reparations Commission, Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, called reparations a matter of justice.
“When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write," he said. "After 300 years of British colonization, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?”

US House of Representatives passes act mandating free AM radio in every vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:44:18 UTC
21:44:18 KST

The US House of Representatives passed the bipartisan AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act by voice vote on September 15, 2026, moving forward legislation that would require automakers to provide AM broadcast radio at no additional cost in every new passenger vehicle manufactured or imported into the United States.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
H.R. 979 directs the Department of Transportation and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to establish a rule making AM radio standard equipment in new passenger vehicles. Automakers would be prohibited from charging additional fees or subscriptions for access to AM stations.
Supporters say preserving AM radio in vehicles is particularly important during emergencies when cellular networks, electricity, or internet services are unavailable. The technology also remains an important source of local news, weather, and agricultural information in rural communities.
“AM radio is a lifeline. When the power goes out, when the cell towers go down, and when the Internet cuts off during a storm or an emergency, AM radio is often the only way families can get the life-saving information they need,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5), who first announced and introduced the legislation in the 118th Congress.
National Religious Broadcasters (NRB), an international association of Christian communicators, welcomed the House vote.
“For Christian communicators, this vote stands as a major victory for radio and free broadcast distribution as a whole,” said Troy A. Miller, President and CEO of NRB.
Companion legislation, S.315, has more than 60 cosponsors and previously cleared the Senate Commerce Committee. The measure still requires approval by the full Senate before it can be sent to the president.
Trump tells NRB he supports AM radios in vehicles
US President Donald Trump has previously supported efforts to preserve AM radio in vehicles. Speaking at the NRB 2024 International Christian Media Convention, Trump said: “I will protect the content that is pro-God. To that end, at the request of the NRB, I will do my part to protect AM radio in our cars.”
NRB said it would continue working with the National Association of Broadcasters and other coalition partners as attention shifts to Senate action.

Ra’am, Joint List fight bids to bar them from Knesset election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:44:10 UTC
21:44:10 KST

Ra’am, the Joint List, Balad and two Joint List candidates have asked the Central Elections Committee to reject six challenges seeking to bar them from taking part in the election for the 26th Knesset.
Adalah filed responses on Friday on behalf of Ra’am, the Joint List, Balad, MK Ofer Cassif and former MK Sami Abu Shehadeh. No list, party or candidate has yet been disqualified; the committee must first hear the cases and vote on them.
The names reflect a decade of shifting alliances among four political organizations. Ra’am - the Hebrew acronym for the United Arab List - is running independently. The Joint List brings together Hadash, Ta’al and Balad.
All four formed the original Joint List before the 2015 election. Ra’am left in 2021, and the remaining alliance split in 2022, when Hadash and Ta’al ran together, and Balad ran alone. Balad returned for the 2026 election, creating the two lists now at issue: Ra’am and the reconstituted three-party Joint List.
One of the requests for removal came from the Orot Hashachar party, which has asked the committee to disqualify Balad itself, even though Balad is now part of the Joint List. Balad says Israeli election law allows the committee to bar an entire list or an individual candidate, but not one party from inside a joint slate.
If the committee agrees, it could reject the request without deciding whether the allegations against Balad are true.
The other requests invoke grounds set out in Basic Law: The Knesset. A list or candidate may be barred for rejecting Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, inciting racism, or supporting armed struggle against Israel by an enemy state or terrorist organization.
Supreme Court has set high bar for disqualifying Knesset candidates
The Supreme Court has set a high bar for doing so. Disqualification cannot rest on a stray quotation or isolated act; the evidence must clearly show that the prohibited position is central to the list or candidate.
The Central Elections Committee is chaired by Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg, but its members are representatives of the Knesset factions. They hear the arguments and vote. If they bar an individual candidate, that decision is not final unless the Supreme Court approves it. Decisions involving full candidate lists can also reach the court on appeal.
Three of the six requests target Ra’am. They were filed separately by Otzma Yehudit and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, Likud, and the Choosing Life forum.
The three requests overlap but are not identical. Together, they allege organizational or ideological links between Ra’am, the southern branch of the Islamic Movement and the Muslim Brotherhood, and refer to three nonprofit groups: Aid 48, the Humanitarian Deeds Association and the Al-Aqsa Association. Among the material cited is a July 2025 report by the Registrar of Associations, the Justice Ministry regulator responsible for overseeing nonprofit organizations, as well as court proceedings concerning bank accounts, which the applicants say show that donations promoted through Ra’am channels ultimately reached prohibited organizations or groups affiliated with Hamas.
Ra’am denies any formal or organizational relationship with the nonprofit groups, saying that the material concerns other bodies and does not show that Ra’am supported Hamas’s armed struggle or that of any other organization. It also says no officeholder in the associations was investigated for terror financing or another financial offense.
The party notes that similar claims were rejected in 2022, when the attorney-general submitted a position that included a Shin Bet review and the committee voted 14-0 against disqualification. The current applicants say information released since then changes the case; Ra’am says the new material still cannot be attributed to the party itself.
Islamist party Ra'am highlights chair Abbas's condemnation of October 7 massacre, work to secure hostage release
Ra’am also points to chairman Mansour Abbas’s condemnations of the October 7 attacks and his contacts with hostage families and efforts to secure the captives’ release.
Likud has asked the committee to bar both the Joint List and Cassif, relying on party platforms, proposed laws, public statements and Cassif’s political activity abroad. The Joint List says much of the material is old, distorted or already considered in earlier election cases, and that the Balad platform quoted by Likud is outdated.
Likud argues that Cassif’s criticism of Israel during the war and his activity overseas amount to support for the enemy’s armed struggle, describing his conduct as “assisting the enemy in wartime,” but Cassif has not been charged with that offense and no court has made such a finding. He says he condemned Hamas’s attack and opposes violence as a political tool.
Otzma Yehudit and Ben-Gvir have filed a separate request against Abu Shehadeh, Balad’s chairman and the third candidate on the Joint List. Their case centers on an Arabic-language article he published on October 8, 2023, describing the Hamas attack as an “important historic event” in military, political and strategic terms and saying others could learn from Gaza’s success in surprising Israel.
Abu Shehadeh says the article analyzed the attack’s political consequences and did not praise the killing of civilians. He said this weekend that he would not have published it had he known the full scale of the atrocities, and he denies supporting the massacre or political violence.
Ben-Gvir argues that the article shows support for Hamas’s attack and says Abu Shehadeh has no place in the Knesset.
The Joint List-Cassif and Balad proceedings are scheduled for Wednesday. The published election timetable sets October 2 as the deadline for the relevant appeals.

Only 17% of Israelis, 21% of Palestinians believe peaceful coexistence is possible, poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:44:03 UTC
21:44:03 KST

Only 17% of Israelis and 21% of Palestinians surveyed in the West Bank and east Jerusalem believe Israel and an independent Palestinian state can coexist peacefully, according to a Pew Research Center report published Tuesday.
A majority of Israelis, 56%, said such coexistence was not possible, while 68% of respondents in the West Bank and east Jerusalem gave the same answer. The survey did not include Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, where Pew said security conditions prevented it from conducting fieldwork.
The findings mark the first time since Pew began asking Israelis the question in 2013 that more than half have explicitly said peaceful coexistence between Israel and a Palestinian state is impossible. The share saying coexistence is possible was statistically unchanged from 2025, when Pew recorded its lowest level of Israeli optimism on the question.
Pew went beyond asking respondents whether they believed two states could coexist. Researchers also asked Israelis and Palestinians to explain their answers in their own words, revealing areas of both overlap and divergence in how the two populations viewed the conflict.
Among those who rejected the possibility of peaceful coexistence, respondents on both sides frequently pointed to disputes over the land, decades of violence, and deep distrust. Some Israelis and Palestinians described the two populations as competing over territory that they believed could not, or should not, be divided. Others cited religious or cultural divisions and said the history of violence had made trust difficult to rebuild.
The two groups differed, however, on some of the central obstacles they identified.
What are the biggest obstacles to peace between Israelis and Palestinians?
Israeli respondents who opposed a two-state solution frequently raised security concerns, including fears that an independent Palestinian state could become hostile to Israel, obtain weapons, or leave Israel with less territory from which to defend itself. Some said they believed Palestinian leaders or the Palestinian public ultimately sought Israel's destruction rather than coexistence.
Palestinian respondents in the West Bank and east Jerusalem, meanwhile, commonly cited Israeli control over the territory, settlements, checkpoints and restrictions on movement as reasons they did not believe peace was achievable. Some described Israeli settlement expansion as having made the creation of a viable Palestinian state increasingly difficult.
The findings come as other recent surveys have painted a complicated picture of Palestinian attitudes. An INSS poll published earlier in September found that 46% of West Bank Palestinians surveyed said Israel did not have a right to exist, while 52% said they preferred negotiations as a way of ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Separately, another Palestinian survey found that support for peaceful negotiations had risen while support for armed resistance declined. A Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research poll published in August similarly found support for a two-state formula rose when respondents were presented with a state based on the 1967 lines.
Small minorities still see a path to peace
Among Israelis and Palestinians who told Pew that peaceful coexistence was possible, some of the explanations were similar across the two populations.
Respondents spoke about a desire for peace, the need to avoid further bloodshed, and the belief that neither population would disappear, leaving coexistence as the eventual outcome of the conflict. Some also said clearly defined borders and political separation could provide a workable alternative to continued conflict.
Palestinian respondents who remained optimistic were more likely to emphasize the potential economic benefits of peace and the existing economic ties between Israelis and Palestinians. Some Israelis, by contrast, emphasized conditions that would have to be met before peace could succeed, including rebuilding trust, making political concessions and creating stronger political leadership.
Others on both sides said peaceful coexistence would depend on changes in education, attitudes and political leadership, while some respondents called for international involvement or security guarantees.
The Israeli figures also revealed differences within the country. Among Jewish Israelis, 16% said peaceful coexistence was possible, and 64% said it was not. Among Arab Israelis, 23% said it was possible, and 26% said it was not, but nearly half, 46%, declined to give a substantive answer.
Overall, one-fifth of Israeli respondents did not answer the coexistence question, twice the share that declined to answer in Pew's 2025 survey.
Pew surveyed 1,001 adults in Israel from April 5 to May 6 and 1,038 Palestinians in the West Bank and east Jerusalem from March 30 to April 28. The interviews were conducted face-to-face in Hebrew and Arabic during the Iran war, with fieldwork spanning both the fighting and the period following the initial ceasefire declared on April 7.

AI generated
MILAN – Italy is preparing to ban face coverings in schools and to cap the number of foreign students per class, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Sept 20 as she played up her right-wing credentials at a youth event organised by her party.
Italy is among the European countries most exposed to migrant arrivals because of its central Mediterranean location, making migration a hot-button issue and a major challenge for successive governments.
The integration of migrants, particularly those from Muslim-majority countries, remains contentious in Italian politics and society. Debates over religious symbols, cultural integration, citizenship rules and immigration policy frequently polarise public opinion.
“A measure will soon be presented to a Cabinet meeting to legally establish a maximum number of foreign students per class. It also requires parents of foreign students facing serious difficulties integrating into the school system to learn Italian and bans burqas and niqabs in schools,” Meloni told an annual gathering of the youth wing of her Brothers of Italy party.
“If there is only one child in a class who doesn’t understand Italian, that child will likely be able to learn the language and integrate quickly with the help of classmates and teachers. However, if the number of children who don’t understand the language becomes large – or even the majority – that is no longer integration; it is neglect,” she added.
Meloni did not specify what the maximum number of foreign students per class would be.
Students who are not Italian citizens account for 11.6 per cent of those enrolled in Italian schools – nearly 12 in every 100 students – according to Fondazione ISMU, a research institution.
“You must go to school with your face uncovered, and in Italy no one, in the name of a real or supposed tradition, can decide that a young woman must hide herself,” Meloni said. REUTERS

RNLI warns supporters their personal information may have been hacked

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:28:57 UTC
21:28:57 KST

Supporters of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution have been warned that their personal information may have been stolen by hackers amid targeting of the charity by far-right agitators.
In a letter accompanying the autumn copy of its Lifeboat magazine, the charity warned members that their “name, contact details and records of interactions with the RNLI” could have been breached in the raid on a company it uses for customer relationship management.
The Telegraph, which first reported the story, said the RNLI told its supporters that Beacon CRM advised the RNLI to “assume that data held within its systems was taken” in a cyber-attack that affected about 1,500 charities in late July.
The letter added there was no evidence to date that there had been misuse, sharing or publication of members’ personal data. But news of the breach comes after targeting of the RNLI by people who object to the charity going to the aid of people trying to reach the UK on small boats.
On Thursday, it emerged that a lifeboat station in Portsmouth, close to where far-right activists tried to stop asylum seekers landing, had been forced to temporarily shut.
On Sunday 6 September, activists tried to blockade the road leading to a landing spot where two RNLI crews helped bring a dinghy carrying 120 asylum seekers to Eastney in Portsmouth, a few hundred metres from the lifeboat station. Police officers were injured in clashes.
In the days after, lifeboat crew members were called traitors and protests took place against the charity, including at the RNLI headquarters in nearby Poole, where a museum telling the story of the RNLI closed temporarily.
Portsmouth lifeboat station took down its Facebook page and RNLI volunteers across the UK were told that they should consider not wearing the charity’s branded clothing if they felt it could put them at risk.
The RNLI vice-president, Sir Robin Knox-Johnston, condemned the intimidation aimed at staff and volunteers, including “online and physical abuse”, as “frankly quite disgraceful”. Far-right protesters had called for people to stop donating to the charity, but it reported that it had subsequently experienced a “significant” boost to its fundraising.
It has stressed that only 1.2% of its rescue work last year – 109 callouts out of 9,058 – was to small boats in the Channel.
A report on the hack published by Beacon CRM earlier this month said there was no evidence that it was a targeted attack on Beacon or any specific customer, and that the cyber-attacker had contacted it “only to indicate they would be deleting any data they have exfiltrated and no copy would be retained, sold or shared”.
A spokesperson for the RNLI said: “Beacon CRM works with many charities and organisations across the UK and Ireland, and while they cannot confirm exactly which records were accessed or downloaded, it advised all affected organisations, including the RNLI, to assume that data held within its systems was taken.
“At this stage, there is no evidence that information relating to RNLI supporters has been published, shared online or otherwise misused.”

Chilling pre-Oct. 7 photo: three soldiers salute Yom Kippur War fallen, only one survives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:28:03 UTC
21:28:03 KST

Between the days of Selichot and the sound of the shofar on the eve of Yom Kippur, there are images that refuse to leave the mind. One of them, taken on the eve of Yom Kippur 2023, less than two weeks before the October 7 attack and subsequent war, now looks like a chilling prophecy.
The photo shows three Armored Corps soldiers from the 401st Brigade standing at attention and saluting the graves of brigade soldiers who fell in the 1973 Yom Kippur War. The three had been sent by their unit as part of an IDF remembrance and commemoration project intended to connect generations, remember and honor the fallen.
They stood there, proud in uniform and black berets, with no way of knowing what fate awaited them only a short time later.
Of the three who stood that day before the row of cold marble headstones, Staff Sgt. Itay Saadon, 21, from Har Halutz, who served as a tank commander in the 52nd Battalion, was killed in battle in the northern Gaza Strip in November 2023.
Nearly a year later, in October 2024, his friend in the photograph, Staff Sgt. Ofir Berkovich, 20, from Modi’in-Maccabim-Reut, also of the 52nd Battalion, was also killed in the same sector.
The third soldier in the photograph, Staff Sgt. Gabriel, is the only one still alive.
“My memory of that day is very blurry,” Gabriel said in a special interview with Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. He remembers the special dynamic between himself, Itay and Ofir.
“Looking back, I understand just how chilling this picture is. I’m the only one left from it. The terrible news that Itay had fallen, during the first weeks of the ground operation in Gaza, was impossible to comprehend. I felt as though my world had collapsed. I didn’t know how to react, but I understood that I was in the middle of a war and that we had to keep going. To this day, it is hard for me to put into words what you feel in a situation like that. When Ofir was also killed, almost a year later, the feeling became even harder.”
“It’s a chilling coincidence. I’m the only one left alive from that picture,” Gabriel said. “If more people had been photographed there, it would not have felt like such a personal coincidence for me.
“On the one hand, you look at it and smile — what a beautiful picture of us standing there and saluting at the grave. On the other hand, it is very sad when you know what happened to the people in it.
“My message to anyone who has lost friends is that, no matter where you are, stay open and share what you are feeling, even when it is difficult. Whether it is now, in Gaza or in Lebanon — open up to the people around you. That is what helps you get through it more easily.”
The parents of Staff Sgt. Ofir Berkovich first saw the haunting photograph during the shiva mourning period for their son, when a casualty officer brought it to their home.
Ofir, whom his parents described as a child full of joy, tremendous energy and a love of extreme sports, summed up his outlook on life in a unit project called “Tankers’ Quirks” with a short sentence: “You have to collect as many experiences as possible and live.”
His father, Baruch, recalled the day he drove his son to the cemetery where the photograph was taken.
“Ofir emphasized that he had been specially chosen for this assignment and that he had prepared himself mentally for it,” he said. “He felt there was something honorable about visiting the grave of a fallen IDF soldier.”
His mother, Simona, described the painful emotions the photograph stirred.
“At first, I couldn’t bring myself to look at it. We are trying to hold on to life, and this picture is another tangible confirmation that your child is no longer here.
“This connection between past, present and future reflects our fate — apparently we are destined to live by the sword. What happened 50 years ago is continuing today, and all that remains is to hope for the best.”
The photograph also sends chills through the Saadon family.
Liat, Itay’s mother, recalled another picture he sent her that day, in which he stood alone in front of the grave.
“I remember the picture of him standing in front of the grave, and what I thought at the time — that I would have preferred him to visit wounded soldiers rather than graves. Today, when I am on the other side, I understand the profound meaning of that act.”
Itay, who dreamed of becoming a pilot when he was younger, found his place as a tank commander in the armored corps.
According to his mother, members of the company liked to joke about the special way he communicated with Ofir, whom he commanded, and how the two would sometimes communicate through notes.
“When I saw the picture with Gabriel standing alongside them, the only one who remained alive, I was very afraid for him. Those were days of fighting, and we were truly afraid that, God forbid, something might happen to him. It is important for me to tell Gabriel how happy I am that he is here with us,” Liat said emotionally.
She also stressed what she sees as an important point about Israeli society.
“At the military level, there is a deeply rooted tradition, and we are very much embraced. But in society as a whole, I sometimes feel that there is less attention being paid to bereavement," she said. “People want to return to routine, and that is natural and understandable in a society that has known so much loss. Still, I am certain that soldiers from the 401st Brigade will always come to Itay’s grave and that this bond will be preserved over the years.”
On this eve of Yom Kippur, the photograph of Ofir, Itay and Gabriel has become more than a chapter in a unit’s memory. It has become a symbol of Israeli society as a whole.
The IDF and the brigade’s investment in commemorating the soldiers who fell in 1973 brought the soldiers of 2023 to stand before their graves, without knowing that many of them would go on to write the next chapter in the book of remembrance with their own blood.
