Scientists discover a hidden “ID card” in cat urine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:24:21 UTC
21:24:21 KST

Scientists discover a hidden “ID card” in cat urine
Scientists have uncovered a hidden chemical “ID card” in cat urine that may let cats recognize one another long after a scent mark is left behind.
- Date:
- September 20, 2026
- Source:
- Iwate University, Japan
- Summary:
- Cats may identify one another through a surprisingly durable chemical “calling card” made from 13 unusual fatty acids in their urine. The compounds appear linked to mysterious fat droplets in the kidneys and may represent a scent-recognition system shared across the cat family.
- Share:
Cats rely heavily on scent to learn about one another, often gathering information from urine and other odor marks left behind in their surroundings. These chemical traces can continue communicating long after the animal that produced them has moved on.
That creates a puzzle. Many odor molecules evaporate, break down, or change with time. If a scent is constantly evolving, how can another animal still determine who originally left it?
Researchers from Japan, Germany, and Spain, led by Iwate University, may have found part of the answer in domestic cats. Their experiments point to a group of unusual fatty acids that could serve as a lasting chemical signature in cat urine.
The scientists identified 13 branched-chain fatty acids (BFAs). The particular mixture and proportions of these compounds varied from one cat to another, yet remained relatively consistent within the same animal. Behavioral tests also showed that cats could detect differences between BFA profiles when the researchers controlled for other lipids in the urine.
The findings suggest that BFAs could function as a durable chemical "calling card" that helps preserve information about individual identity. The study will be published in Current Biology.
Cats Remember Individual Urine Scents
Before searching for the chemicals involved, the researchers first needed to establish that cats could distinguish urine from different individuals.
When cats encountered the same urine sample repeatedly, they gradually spent less time investigating it. But when urine from a different cat was introduced, their interest rose again, and they spent more time sniffing.
Remarkably, cats continued to show reduced responses to previously encountered urine odors even after gaps lasting months. That pattern suggests that cats may retain long-term memories of particular urine scents.
Researchers also examined the flehmen response, the characteristic open-mouthed expression often seen when cats investigate certain odors. Cats displayed this response more often when smelling unfamiliar urine than when smelling their own.
As the same urine was presented again and again, the flehmen response became less frequent. When urine from another cat was introduced, however, the response increased once more.
"After confirming that cats can distinguish individual urine odors, we used the flehmen response as a clue to identify urinary molecules that may contribute to individual scent recognition," said Professor Masao Miyazaki of Iwate University, who led the research project.
13 Unusual Fatty Acids Form Distinctive Profiles
Using the cats' behavior as a guide, the scientists narrowed their search to a lipid fraction in urine containing unusual BFAs.
They ultimately identified 13 of these compounds. Based on a review of existing scientific literature, the researchers found no previous reports of the same BFAs occurring in mammalian excretions or secretions.
What stood out was not simply the presence of the compounds, but the pattern they formed. Each cat had a BFA profile defined by the combination and relative abundance of the different fatty acids.
Those profiles varied considerably between animals, while remaining comparatively stable when the same cats were sampled on different dates.
Genetics also appeared to play some role. Related cats generally had more similar BFA patterns, although each animal still maintained its own distinguishable profile even within the same family.
The compounds also proved relatively durable. Many volatile chemicals responsible for urine odor begin changing quickly once urine is deposited. BFAs, by contrast, are semi-volatile and evaporate more slowly.
In urine-soaked samples stored at 25°C, the distinctive BFA profiles associated with individual cats remained comparatively stable for at least 24 hours.
Cats Can Detect the Chemical Differences
The researchers then tested whether the cats themselves could actually distinguish these BFA patterns.
They controlled the other lipid components in the urine samples and changed only the donor-derived BFA-containing fraction. Cats that had already become accustomed to the original sample began sniffing more again when the BFA fraction was switched.
That behavioral change provided evidence that cats can perceive differences among individual BFA compositions.
The result strengthens the idea that these fatty acids may carry meaningful information about identity rather than simply being unusual chemical byproducts.
A Century-Old Cat Kidney Mystery
The investigation also produced an unexpected clue involving the kidneys.
Researchers detected BFAs in the kidney but not in the other tissues they examined. Lipids containing BFAs were also present among neutral lipids stored inside droplets in the renal cortex.
These kidney lipid droplets have puzzled scientists for more than a century. Cats are known to have large numbers of them, but their biological purpose has remained uncertain.
The new findings raise the possibility that the droplets act as a storage reservoir for lipids containing BFAs.
Such a reservoir could help keep a cat's chemical signature relatively steady even when diet or physiological conditions temporarily change. By buffering those short-term fluctuations, the kidney might help maintain a more consistent individual chemical profile in urine.
"Lipid droplets in the cat kidney have been known for more than a century, but why cats have so many of them has remained a mystery," Miyazaki said. "Our findings suggest that one of their functions may be to support a stable chemical signature in urine. How BFAs stored in renal lipids are ultimately released into urine is an important question for future research."
Similar Chemistry Appears Across the Cat Family
The researchers also looked beyond domestic cats to see whether the same traits appeared elsewhere in the cat family.
BFA-related compounds in urine and renal lipid droplets were detected in several felid species, including lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, lynxes, and the Iriomote cat.
However, the exact BFA profiles differed among species. Researchers also observed differences in both the amount and distribution of lipid droplets within the kidneys.
Differences were even seen between the Iriomote cat and the Tsushima leopard cat, two geographically isolated forms of the leopard cat found in Japan.
Together, these observations suggest that BFA-related chemistry and kidney physiology may be widespread across Felidae, while also having changed and diversified over the course of feline evolution.
Whether lions, tigers, and other wild felids actually use these compounds to recognize specific individuals has not yet been demonstrated.
How a Changing Odor Can Preserve Identity
The discovery also addresses a broader problem in animal communication.
Scent marks have to convey useful information even though their chemistry begins changing as soon as they are deposited. Understanding how an animal can leave behind a stable signal of identity despite that chemical change has long been a fundamental question.
Mice provide one known solution. In mice, major urinary proteins help preserve individual information in urine. But scientists have not established a similar protein-based identity system in many other mammals.
Cats may use a different strategy.
Instead of relying primarily on proteins, they may produce distinctive combinations of semi-volatile lipid-derived molecules. Because those compounds disappear more slowly and may be supported by a reservoir of lipids in the kidney, they could help preserve an individual's chemical identity over time.
Possible Uses for Cat Scent Chemistry
For now, the work is basic research and does not immediately produce a new product or technology. Still, the findings point toward several possible future applications.
A better understanding of BFAs could eventually contribute to methods for managing cat urine odor.
The kidney findings could also help researchers investigate why lipid accumulation is a normal physiological feature in some situations but is associated with disease in others.
There could even be implications for wildlife conservation. If researchers can show that BFA profiles reliably identify the same animal across multiple urine samples, urine collected from the environment could potentially offer a non-invasive way to monitor rare wild felids without having to capture or directly observe them.
What began as a search for the chemistry behind cat scent recognition may therefore help explain both a century-old mystery inside feline kidneys and a broader question about how animals leave recognizable identities behind in the environment.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Iwate University, Japan. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Shota Ichizawa, Jana Caspers, Reiko Uenoyama, Yuria Ito, Tamako Miyazaki, Mizuki Morisasa, Naoko Goto-Inoue, Yusuke Suzuki, Nozomi Nakanishi, Yasuyuki Endo, Masako Izawa, Tetsuro Yamashita, Beatriz Ortiz-Guisado, Elisa María Espinosa-López, Guadalupe Gómez-Baena, Stefan Schulz, Masao Miyazaki. Signatures of branched-chain fatty acids derived from a kidney reservoir confer stable chemical individuality on domestic cats. Current Biology, 2026; 36 (17): 4340 DOI: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.07.045

Estonia Ready to Close Russia Border if Moscow Declares General Mobilization. Here’s Why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:23:21 UTC
21:23:21 KST

- Category
- World
Estonia Ready to Close Russia Border if Moscow Declares General Mobilization. Here’s Why
Estonia is prepared to close its border crossings with Russia immediately if Moscow declares a general mobilization, according to Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, public broadcaster ERR reported on September 17.
Speaking after a government security cabinet meeting that assessed the impact of potential Russian mobilization scenarios, Michal emphasized that Tallinn monitors security developments continuously and has the infrastructure to shut border points on short notice, ERR wrote.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“There is nothing mysterious or extraordinary about this. It is no news to anyone that things are going very badly in Russia,” Michal said.
“There isn’t a single healthy part of their economy and 30,000 to 40,000 men are killed or wounded every month. At some point, they will have to take steps to keep the war going and NATO and European Union countries need to be prepared for those steps,” he continued.
Michal added that border operations can be terminated rapidly: “The border can also be closed immediately, as we have done on occasion when there have been troublemakers at border crossing points. The Police and Border Guard Board and the interior minister are aware of this, and we have the capability to close border crossing points very quickly,” according to ERR.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stated that a broad compulsory mobilization would heighten internal political friction within Russia, ERR reported.
“Everyone understands that if, for example, blanket compulsory mobilization is announced for a certain age group, it will significantly increase internal tensions in Russia,” Tsahkna noted.
Tsahkna highlighted that Schengen countries issued roughly 650,000 visas to Russian citizens last year, warning European partners that fleeing mobilization does not automatically grant eligibility for international protection or asylum, ERR wrote.
“A person in Russia may think that if they flee to Europe in the event of mobilization, it gives grounds for international protection,” Tsahkna stated. “It does not.”
It was previously reported that Russian conscripts face increasing restrictions when attempting to leave the country, with numerous documented cases where exit bans appeared in electronic registries without warning or immediately upon arrival at border control.
The tightening of border checks and real-time data sharing with Belarus coincide with escalating front-line losses, estimated at 1.4 million dead or severely injured, driving a surge in Russians attempting to flee abroad through land crossings into neighboring countries.

Italy 'not at war' as EU urged to strengthen Red Sea mission, foreign minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:21:58 UTC
21:21:58 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
Italy is “not at war” in the Red Sea, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said Sunday, urging the EU to strengthen its naval mission protecting merchant shipping in the strategic waterway.
“No, we are not at war,” Tajani told Italian daily Corriere della Sera when asked about a recent attack involving an Italian fighter jet and Houthi statements that they were not at war with Italy.
Tajani's comments follow a Houthi strike on the Taif airbase in Saudi Arabia, which reportedly damaged an Italian F-2000 (Eurofighter) aircraft on the ground.
Tajani said the European Aspides mission was created as a defensive operation to protect merchant ships transiting the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb from potential Houthi attacks.
He said Italy would continue supporting the mission “in the face of the worsening situation in the strait” and called for the EU to renew and strengthen it.
“We have a strong strategic interest: 40% of Italy's entire commercial maritime traffic and 60% of the goods we export to Asia pass through the Red Sea,” Tajani said.
Saudi Arabia has faced a series of missile and drone attacks attributed to the Houthis in recent days amid escalating regional tensions, with the group now controlling access to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Italy urges other countries to contribute to Aspides
For several months, Italy has been urging other countries to contribute to the mission, he said.
“I will do so again next week in New York, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly,” the foreign minister said.
Tajani said European countries should either provide additional naval units or contribute to the costs of the mission.
“Aspides absolutely must continue and be strengthened,” he said.
Tajani is due to discuss the mission at an EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting, the G7 foreign ministers' meeting and a meeting of the Rome Coalition for Food Security during the UN General Assembly in New York.
He said the coalition, launched by Italy and Croatia, would also discuss freedom and safety of navigation.
Potential meeting with Rubio on rare earth minerals
Tajani also said he would meet US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, with whom he plans to sign an agreement on raw materials aimed at securing supplies.
He said the agreement would include the “Pax Silica” initiative on critical minerals such as rare earths.
On the conflict in Iran, Tajani said Italy did not support it and favored peace.
“A conflict we didn't share and where we support peace,” he said.
He added that he would meet the Iranian foreign minister in New York despite Italy's critical stance toward Tehran, particularly over its nuclear program.
Tajani also backed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to make Canada an associated country of the EU, saying Canada is a strategic partner of Europe and a member of NATO and the G7.
He said his address to the UN General Assembly would focus on cybersecurity, hybrid threats and artificial intelligence.

‘You Can’t Live Underground’: Fatalism and Defiance Define Life in War-Battered Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:18:00 UTC
21:18:00 KST

Air raid warnings wail across Kyiv, and phone apps spark into life, telling people to proceed to the nearest shelter.
But on the streets of the Ukrainian capital on a warm Friday morning in early September people walk around untroubled by the alarms, enjoying the late summer sun. Sitting outside cafes, others chat over coffee as the warnings go unheeded.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Their lives and the city, in many ways, look at peace. But it is a beguiling appearance, hiding the pressure on a people desperate to maintain a semblance of normality amid the ferocity of war while refusing to be cowed by Russian aggression.
Kyiv’s residents are aware of the dangers. The incoming Russian jet-powered drones the Friday morning alarms warned of killed two and wounded 12 when they struck a filling station on the outskirts of the city. People know that death can come from the skies at any time.
Since late August a combination of Moscow’s increasing use of jet-powered drones and Ukraine’s shortage of interceptor missiles means that attack warnings in Kyiv now come around the clock. Daytime strikes, once a rarity, have become the norm.
What the people of Kyiv also know, and increasingly feel, is that the intensity and frequency of the Russian attacks would reduce their lives to nothing if they followed every warning and headed for the shelters.
“People have become very fatalistic,” says Kyiv resident Natalia, a television presenter and journalist who spends many nights sleeping in her bathroom, the one room in her flat with no exterior walls, rather than the safer basement. “They feel if their time comes, their time comes.”
Russia Fired 2,000 Drones and 19 Missiles This Week, Zelensky Says
This acceptance of whatever fate may bring is becoming increasingly widespread in the city, as people search for a way to cope with the tiredness, fear and anxiety caused by the constant attacks.
“I live close to an area the Russians like to target and the explosions make my building shake,” Andrii, a 35-year-old lorry driver sitting enjoying a cigarette with his friend Leonard in central Kyiv, tells TVP World. “But I stay, and I no longer go to the basement. You just have to say ‘Okay, this is life, you have to adapt.’ It’s not like you’re happy to live with it, but that is life.”
Leonard says he was more scared in 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, buts adds that the intensity of the attacks forces him to appreciate the time he has and embrace a carpe-diem approach to life.
“I’m happy that I wake up each morning,” he says. “I’m happy to enjoy the day, and that’s the main thing.”
Later the same day in a bar in the city center Alona and Vlad, a 30-something couple with children aged two and seven, queue to buy cocktails as they enjoy a night out with friends.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The bar, famed for its Latin American vibes and music, is packed despite the strong possibility of an air-raid alert sounding, and remains crowded until guests leave en-masse not long after 11 pm to comply with the 12 am curfew.
“We did have reservations about coming out tonight, it can be dangerous, but we can’t stay at home any longer,” says Alona as she waits to be served. “We’ve even had conversations about ‘not coming back’ if we go out. But you can’t live at home all the time. You can’t live underground. There has to be more to life than that.”
Both say they intend to stay in Kyiv over winter come what may, but for others the forthcoming season has become an ominous cloud on the horizon.
Russia is expected to launch an intensive blitz on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure that could exceed that of last winter’s campaign. Back then the attacks caused significant damage and led to lengthy power cuts that left people without electricity as the country endured weeks of sub-zero temperatures.
The prospect of something worse happening this winter could grind down the resolve of Kyiv’s residents. While Alona and Vlad plan to stay, other families might leave for another part of the country or a place close enough to Kyiv to commute but with its own sources of electricity and heat.
But winter remains months off, and for now Kyiv’s citizens appear intent of getting on with their lives as best they can; maintaining a normal existence, not just for their sanity but also as an act of defiance to Russian aggression.
“The more the genocidal approach Putin has towards Ukrainians, the more resilience we are showing,” says Natalia. “This is how it works. The dictator wants us to change our plans and behavior; to surrender. Nobody is going to give up. Nobody is going to take his terms and conditions. That’s it.”

NEW DELHI: BJP stalwart LK Advani and former Delhi deputy chief minister Manish Sisodia are among the prominent voters whose names figure in the list of 33 lakh people being issued notices over “logical discrepancies” in details furnished during the recent Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise in Delhi.“The notices arose from ‘logical discrepancies’ in the details furnished in their enumeration forms. Their names will be included in the final electoral rolls after due process of verification of facts and documents to be furnished by such voters,” a senior poll officer told PTI, confirming that notices had been issued to both Advani and Sisodia.
“The process of verification of facts and documents is underway and validation of entries is being done accordingly,” the officer added.The 98-year-old Advani, a former deputy prime minister, his daughter Pratibha and daughter-in-law Geetika also received notices after their names could not be mapped to the 2002 SIR electoral roll. From politicians to bureaucrats, thousands face verification over 'discrepancies' in SIR enumeration forms
Many prominent voters, including senior government functionaries, bureaucrats and politicians, have been issued notices as part of the SIR exercise in Delhi.Chief minister Rekha Gupta, AAP supremo Arvind Kejriwal and former Union minister Kapil Sibal have also received notices over similar discrepancies, officials said.Gupta’s entry was validated following verification of her documents, and her name has been cleared for inclusion in the final electoral roll of the Shalimar Bagh constituency, scheduled to be published on November 4.
According to the Delhi CEO’s office, notices are being issued to voters whose names could not be linked to the electoral roll prepared during the previous SIR, or whose details showed discrepancies when matched against the earlier roll.As part of the door-to-door verification exercise conducted between June 30 and August 17, every voter was required to submit an enumeration form.Of the around 97 lakh voters included in the draft electoral rolls, 33.13 lakh have been identified for notices over discrepancies in their enumeration forms. More than 31.63 lakh notices have been served so far.Most of the notices relate to the absence of corresponding records in the electoral roll prepared during the previous SIR in 2002.Voters have been asked to submit their replies along with supporting documents to the Electoral Registration Officers of their respective Assembly constituencies by October 29.

Matin Aghajanpour (R) of Iran celebrates with a teammate after the men's bronze medal match between China and Iran at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Luo Yuan)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's men's basketball team missed out on the bronze medal at the Asian Games after losing 79-70 to Iran in the third-place game here on Sunday.
Iran took an early 8-2 lead before China responded with a 10-0 run to take the advantage in the first period. The two sides were tied at 42-42 with four minutes 30 seconds left in the third quarter, before Iran launched a 13-4 run to enter the final period with a nine-point lead.
Following a 3-pointer from Matin Aghajanpour, Iran extended its advantage to 13 points. Pang Zhenglin's driving layup and Li Hongquan's consecutive 3-pointers helped China close the gap to 62-63. However, led by Aghajanpour, Iran mounted another 16-8 run to secure the victory.
"It was an important game for us, especially for the young players. We put our heart out on the floor. We really wanted it more. We hustled really well. We dived for every loose ball and eventually we won the game," said Iran's Mohammad Jamshidi afterwards.
Only two Chinese players scored in double digits. Pang scored a team-high 22 points, and Li contributed 12. Aghajanpour led Iran with a team-high 21 points, while Piter Girgoorian added 15.
"We didn't do well in defense and rebounding today, nor did we execute our pre-game tactics on the court. We controlled the tempo for a while in the second half, but failed to adjust after committing turnovers," said China captain Hu Mingxuan.
"Iran earned this win because they played harder than us, and they played tough. They had more energy than us, and they wanted this game. They played much better than us. That's why they beat us," China forward Cui Yongxi added.
China head coach Guo Shiqiang expressed his regret over the defeat, admitting that his team was outplayed on the court.
"We have many young players who lack experience in major tournaments, and we didn't perform well in crucial moments. The players were quite fatigued in the last two games. During the group stage, we only had a nine-man rotation at one point, and some players had heavy minutes, resulting in significant physical exhaustion," Guo said. ■

Economic Watch: China's power use surge spotlights industrial upgrading, emerging-sector momentum
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
20:13:08 CST
21:13:08 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's electricity consumption exceeded 1 trillion kilowatt-hours (kWh) again in August, with record peak load and much faster power demand growth in high-tech manufacturing and new-economy services, underscoring the economy's ongoing structural transformation.
Power use totaled 1.0332 trillion kWh in August, rising 1.7 percent year on year, the National Energy Administration (NEA) data showed on Sunday. Electricity load hit a record high of 1.56 billion kilowatts, 49.69 million kilowatts above the previous year's maximum, and exceeded that level on seven days in total during the month.
A breakdown of the August data revealed that power consumed by the primary industry rose 2.7 percent year on year to 16.9 billion kWh, while power consumed by the secondary industry increased 2.4 percent to 612.4 billion kWh. Power use by the tertiary industry reached 215.5 billion kWh, up 5.1 percent year on year.
"The secondary and tertiary industries are the main engines of electricity consumption growth," said Wu Liqiang, an official with the China Electricity Council.
"Within manufacturing, the pattern of 'new sectors rising and old sectors declining' continued. High-tech and equipment manufacturing maintained rapid growth, while consumer goods manufacturing was the second-largest positive contributor to manufacturing electricity demand after high-tech and equipment manufacturing."
Notably, electricity consumption by the high-tech and equipment manufacturing sector reached 122.2 billion kWh in August, an increase of 7.2 percent. Computer and communications equipment, automobile manufacturing, general equipment manufacturing, special equipment manufacturing and electrical machinery manufacturing saw power use rise 7.5 percent, 7.6 percent, 7.6 percent, 8.2 percent and 12.3 percent, respectively.
Within automobile manufacturing, power consumption for new energy vehicle (NEV) production jumped 22.2 percent year on year.
Wu added that electricity consumption in new business formats has become an important source of incremental demand for the tertiary industry and the economy as a whole.
The charging and battery swapping service sector and internet data services reported rapid growth in electricity consumption in August, rising 51.2 percent and 37.9 percent, to 17.2 billion and 10.2 billion kWh, respectively.
In contrast, residential electricity consumption dropped by 4 percent year-on-year to 188.3 billion kWh in August, as more frequent typhoons and heavier rainfall compared to last year significantly reduced air-conditioning demand.
In the first eight months of the year, China's total power use reached 7.17 trillion kWh, up 4.3 percent year on year, the NEA said. Power use by the primary, secondary and tertiary industries rose 3.3 percent, 4.4 percent and 7.1 percent, to 104.6 billion kWh, 4.53 trillion kWh and 1.43 trillion kWh, respectively.
During this period, high-tech and equipment manufacturing electricity consumption climbed 9.3 percent to 845.1 billion kWh. Electricity use by charging and battery swapping services and internet data services grew 55.1 percent to 114.7 billion kWh and 42.5 percent to 69.5 billion kWh, respectively. Residential power use rose 0.3 percent to 1.11 trillion kWh.
In recent years, China has made major strides in terms of its power infrastructure, helping ensure a stable electricity supply during peak periods and effectively supporting economic and social development as well as meeting people's basic needs, the National Development and Reform Commission said in July.
According to an annual development report of China's electric power industry released by the China Electricity Council in July, total electricity consumption nationwide in 2026 is expected to increase by 5 percent to 6 percent year on year.
The total newly installed power generation capacity for the year is estimated at approximately 400 million kilowatts, with new energy sources continuing to be the main contributors to the added capacity. The increase in conventional power sources is expected to be around 100 million kilowatts, roughly matching the growth in peak load, the report added. ■

KATHMANDU, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Nepal's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has established an environment diplomacy division under the ministry for the first time to strengthen diplomatic efforts on climate change and environmental issues amid the country's growing vulnerability to climate-induced disasters, the ministry said on Sunday.
The deadly mudslide of Aug. 26 has claimed at least 1,411 lives, while 5,875 people, including Nepali and foreign nationals, remained missing as of Saturday evening, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
A report by World Weather Attribution last week said that human-caused global warming had thinned glaciers and thawed mountain permafrost, which likely contributed to destabilizing a Himalayan slope that collapsed last month, triggering the disaster in Nepal.
Given Nepal's vulnerability to widespread destruction from the impacts of global warming in the Himalayas, the government decided to establish a separate division within the Foreign Ministry to carry out focused diplomacy on climate change and environmental issues.
"The ministry decided to establish the division in view of the growing impacts of climate change and the need to address emerging challenges through a dedicated institutional mechanism," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Nepal has been consistently participating in national, regional and international forums on climate change and environmental protection. "The new division has been established to advance these efforts in a more coordinated and institutionalized manner," the ministry said. "The division will facilitate international diplomatic initiatives related to climate and environmental issues and coordinate with relevant national agencies."
Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said in the statement that climate diplomacy should not be limited to participation in international conferences and events but should instead be pursued as a long-term institutional priority.
"Nepal has been continuously working on climate diplomacy at various international forums. Now, there is a need to institutionalize these efforts further," he said. ■

Feature: Chinese dance drama "Mulan" bridges cultures, resonates with New Yorkers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
20:13:07 CST
21:13:07 KST

by Vivien Liu
NEW YORK, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- A familiar Chinese heroine returned to the U.S. stage on Friday, as the award-winning dance drama "Mulan" made its New York debut at Lincoln Center, bringing a centuries-old Chinese legend to American audiences through dance, martial arts, music and visual art.
Presented at the David H. Koch Theater on Sept. 18-20, the production tells the story of Hua Mulan, who disguises herself as a man and takes her aging father's place in military service, embarking on a journey of courage, sacrifice and self-discovery.
For American audiences, Mulan is already a familiar figure. Through Disney's animated film and its live-action adaptation, Hollywood has brought the legendary Chinese heroine to the big screen, while other popular-culture portrayals have introduced the story to generations of international audiences. This long exposure has given American audiences a familiar entry point to a story rooted in Chinese culture.
"Mulan is a globally recognized cultural symbol," said Wang Lu, deputy general manager of China Arts and Entertainment Group. "When American audiences walk into the theater with their familiar impressions of Mulan, they will discover a richer image of her with a distinctive Eastern aesthetic."
Drawing on the spirit of the ancient Chinese folk poem "The Ballad of Mulan," the production presents the heroine through the aesthetics of contemporary Chinese performing arts.
A 15-meter revolving stage forms the centerpiece of the production, while classical Chinese dance, martial arts, traditional music, costumes and lighting create a theatrical world that moves between family life and scenes of war.
For Tang Xinyi, who plays Mulan, the character's humanity is central to the production.
"I hope she is a very three-dimensional character," Tang said. "She is strong and brave, but she also has a vulnerable side, a lonely side and moments when she feels sad."
Through movement, facial expressions and dance, she said, the production traces Mulan's growth from an ordinary daughter protecting her father to a woman discovering her own strength.
Wang Zheng, who plays General Wei, said martial arts training was incorporated into the choreography to create a physical language for combat.
"Because we do not share the same language, we can only use our performance and body movements to create resonance with the audience," he said.
The visual elements of the production captivated the audience.
"I'm loving the Mulan show. The art, scenery, the dancing, the music, the light, everything is amazing," said Alejandro Martin Rodriguez. "The costume design is very impressive, and the lighting. So it really takes you to that era and to that place in a way that is very transformative."
For the audience, the New York performance also offers a chance to see a familiar story from a new cultural perspective.
Keith Boyle, originally from Ireland, called the show "a great example of Chinese culture" and "a fantastic glimpse into ancient Chinese culture."
Laura and Cathy Traflet were particularly impressed by the music and the physical energy of the performance. Laura said her interest in the production was heightened by her familiarity with Mulan from the Disney film, her later exploration of the traditional legend and a trip to China last year.
"I was really excited to see this," she said. "We love the story too, the story of Mulan. So it's so special seeing it in real life."
Created by choreographers Zhou Liya and Han Zhen and produced by China Ningbo Performance & Arts Group, the production has won the China Dance Lotus Award, the highest honor in Chinese dance, and has been performed more than 100 times.
In September 2023, "Mulan" made its U.S. debut in Boston before moving on to Washington, D.C., where it received a warm response from American audiences.
"The positive response three years ago helped make it possible for us to bring Mulan to Lincoln Center in New York today," said Lin Hong, chairperson of China Ningbo Performance & Arts Group.
Lin said the production resonates across cultural boundaries because "the commonality of emotions and values has no borders." ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept 20 -- China's Tong Xin retained her women's taijiquan and taijijian all-around title on Sunday as wushu competition got under way at the 2026 Asian Games, while the top two spots in the men's changquan event went to athletes from Macao, China.
Tong finished with a combined score of 19.553 points, adding another Asian Games title after winning the event in Hangzhou three years ago.
She topped the standings in the morning taijiquan competition with 9.770 points before again finishing first in the afternoon taijijian event.
"I am very excited and happy," Tong said after the competition.
Tong's victory delivered China's third gold medal of the Games but she said she had tried not to think about the pressure of defending her title.
"As long as I fully prepared myself beforehand and showed the best of myself, that was enough. I didn't really think about the pressure when I was competing," she said.
Tong said greater experience had made her more composed than when she made her Asian Games debut in Hangzhou.
"At the previous Asian Games, it was my first time competing and I was relatively inexperienced. After several years of training and experience, I feel much more composed now," she said.
"In the past, I focused more on how the movements looked, such as whether a posture was correct or where the hands should be placed," she added.

Israeli forces kill Palestinian near Jenin in occupied West Bank
Israeli forces have killed a Palestinian man near Jenin, and an Israeli settler was fatally shot in a separate incident in the central West Bank.
Israeli forces have killed a Palestinian man near the city of Jenin in the northern occupied West Bank after he “attempted to carry out a vehicular attack” near an illegal settlement.
An army spokesperson said on Sunday that Israeli forces shot the man near the illegal settlement of Ganim, east of the Palestinian city of Jenin. The spokesperson said there were no casualties among Israeli forces.

The Palestine Red Crescent Society said Israeli forces prevented their medical team from reaching the victim, the Wafa news agency reported.
In a separate incident, an Israeli settler was fatally shot in an attack near the illegal settlement of Halamish in the central West Bank.
The 30-year-old man was taken to a hospital where he died of his wounds, police said.
The military said it the suspect opened fire from a vehicle and left the scene on foot. After a search by security forces, the military said the man, who was injured while fleeing, was detained at a hospital where he had sought care.
Minister calls for death penalty
Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir demanded on Sunday that the suspect face the death penalty. He said in a post on X that this is the “first case that meets the criteria of the Death Penalty Law” since the Knesset – Israel’s parliament – adopted the law in March this year.
The death penalty law allows military courts to impose the death penalty on Palestinians convicted of killing Israelis, but does not impose the same penalty on Israelis convicted of killing Palestinians.
Ben-Gvir was a strident campaigner for the law before it was adopted. In May, he shared an AI-generated video on TikTok, saying he “dreams” of nooses.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he ordered the military and security agencies to increase their forces and carry out arrests and offensive activities in the area. He also said he ordered the demolition of the suspected attacker’s home.
After the shooting, Israeli forces closed all entry and exit points to Ramallah and el-Bireh cities, Wafa reported.
Escalation in the occupied West Bank
Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has been steadily growing since the eruption of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, but the pogroms intensified significantly this year.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recorded more than 1,330 settler-related attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank from January to late July, averaging six a day and marking the fastest pace in about 20 years.
Various settler groups, often supported or protected by Israeli soldiers, have attacked Palestinians in several ways, including shootings, besieging homes and engaging in other forms of communal violence that experts have described as “pogroms“.
In July, Israeli forces shot dead four Palestinians in the town of Tal, near Nablus, during a settler incursion on their land. Two Israelis were also killed in the incident, which triggered a violent “rampage” by Israeli settlers.
Rights groups warn that settlers are increasingly armed with military-issued weaponry and wear military uniforms during attacks, blurring the line between settler and soldier.

====================================================================================================

BBC bias helped pave way for UK sanctions on Israel, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:08:08 UTC
21:08:08 KST

Trevor Asserson spent years trying to document what he says was systematic anti-Israel bias at the BBC. Now, the British lawyer argues that the consequences have moved beyond journalism and into government policy — with potentially significant implications for Israeli companies, banks and exporters.
Asserson, senior partner at British law firm Asserson, whose largest office is in Tel Aviv, led a 2024 study examining BBC coverage of the Israel-Hamas war. The report analyzed the broadcaster’s English- and Arabic-language output between Oct. 7, 2023, and Feb. 7, 2024, and accused it of repeatedly violating its own editorial standards.
“The BBC was a problem because the reputation of Israel was being undermined by the world's most well-respected media organization, the BBC, and it had a huge influence,” Asserson told ynet Global. “So I needed to demonstrate in a proper legal way that it was breaking its own rules and was entirely biased, unfortunately, in its reporting.”
The Asserson Report said it identified 1,553 alleged breaches of BBC editorial guidelines and was particularly critical of BBC Arabic. Its analysis claimed that more than 90% of the Arabic service material it assessed reflected pro-Palestinian or anti-Israel sentiment. The BBC rejected allegations that its reporting was biased and said it would consider the research, while maintaining that its coverage sought to meet its standards of accuracy and due impartiality.
For Asserson, however, the problem was not confined to individual errors.
“The level of anti-Israel feeling within the BBC is such that we, for instance, have been representing employees in the BBC who have been literally persecuted for expressing a view that something was not accurate,” he said. “So it's really become an institutional problem.”
He described BBC Arabic in still harsher terms, saying his research found its performance comparable to Al Jazeera on the measurements used by his team.
“BBC Arabic is essentially the same as Al Jazeera,” he said. “They're both about the same level on an international measure.”
The BBC has faced criticism of its Middle East coverage from opposing directions. Jewish organizations and pro-Israel critics have accused it of hostility toward Israel, while more than 100 BBC employees were among signatories to a 2024 letter alleging that the broadcaster’s Gaza coverage favored Israel. The corporation has repeatedly said it is committed to accurate and impartial reporting.
Resignations and a wider BBC crisis
Asserson believes the debate that followed his report contributed to broader scrutiny of the broadcaster. He pointed to the eventual departures of BBC Director-General Tim Davie and BBC News chief Deborah Turness.
“So the report had some effect,” he said.
Davie and Turness resigned in November 2025 amid a separate controversy over the editing of a Donald Trump speech in a BBC Panorama documentary and broader allegations concerning the corporation’s impartiality, including its reporting on Gaza and transgender issues. Turness rejected claims that BBC News was institutionally biased, while Davie said mistakes had been made and that he had to take ultimate responsibility.
Asserson argued that the Trump controversy reinforced his broader criticism of the broadcaster.
“It literally fakes news in order to try and make Trump look bad, to say things that he didn't say,” he said, referring to the disputed Panorama edit.
BBC Chairman Samir Shah later apologized for what he called an “error of judgment” in the editing of the Trump speech.
‘We have to move on’
Asserson said his attention is now shifting away from the BBC itself toward what he sees as the political consequences of years of damaging coverage of Israel.
“I think that Israel has to move on from the BBC coverage and media coverage,” he said.
He pointed in particular to Britain’s increasingly restrictive policy toward Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank.
The British government announced another package of measures on Sept. 8, including plans to ban imports from Israeli settlements it considers illegal and sanction individuals and companies that support, facilitate or benefit from settlement activity. Earlier in June, London coordinated sanctions with several other governments against individuals and organizations accused of financing or enabling settler violence.
Asserson acknowledged allegations of violence in the West Bank and criticized Israel’s handling of the issue.
“What’s happened, the recent decision by the British government to impose sanctions on Israel is obviously to some extent the result of things which were going on in the West Bank, which clearly are, where the government is failing to deal with it, you know, shameful,” he said.
But he argued that British policy cannot be separated from a broader deterioration in Israel’s public standing.
“What has happened is the reputation of Israel has been so undermined and so damaged by the media coverage for such a long time that you've reached a stage where there's a very general mood within the Labour Party to impose sanctions on Israel,” he said.
Could sanctions spread beyond the settlements?
Although Britain has said its measures are directed at settlement activity rather than Israel as a whole, Asserson warned that the practical distinction could prove difficult to maintain.
“The UK has expressly announced that its sanctions will be aimed at the ‘settlements,’ but not against Israel,” he said. “It remains to be seen if that division will stick.”
He said Israeli businesses that could potentially be affected should begin reviewing their operations before the final rules are published.
Companies, he said, should conduct audits to determine whether any part of their business could fall within the measures and seek legal advice where necessary. Once the precise language is published, which Asserson expects could take several months, companies should reassess any steps they have taken to reduce their exposure.
His firm is already advising some Israeli companies that have been sanctioned, he said.
“We believe that steps to mitigate the dangers can and should be taken,” Asserson said.
He also warned companies against viewing the issue as exclusively British, arguing that they should prepare for the possibility that other European governments and Canada could adopt similar measures.
“That considerably widens the threat Israel faces,” he said.
Could companies inside Israel also be affected?
Asserson said businesses operating within Israel’s pre-1967 boundaries could also face consequences, even if they have no direct activity in West Bank settlements.
He described one danger as “contagion”: Foreign companies, he said, may find it difficult or costly to verify whether an Israeli supplier has any connection to settlement activity and could decide that doing business elsewhere is easier.
“They will go elsewhere for their dates, avocados or semiconductors,” he said. “The fear of a fine imposed by the regulator will have a chilling effect on trade with Israel.”
A second potential problem, he said, stems from modern supply chains. Depending on how the British rules are ultimately drafted and interpreted, questions could arise over products that receive only a small portion of their added value in the West Bank.
“The risk lies, one, with the wording of the sanctions when drafted, and, two, with how the regulators and ultimately the courts choose to interpret those rules,” Asserson said.
He warned that a broad interpretation by regulators or courts could expand the practical reach of the measures beyond what the British government says it intends.
Asserson also expressed concern that officials’ personal views of Israel could influence how discretion is exercised, though he offered no evidence that British regulators had done so.
How would Britain determine where a product comes from?
Much will depend on the final wording of the measures, Asserson said. He expects authorities to draw on existing British or European rules governing the origin of goods, including customs frameworks and principles already used in trade.
Exporters generally certify the origin of their products and make declarations to British customs authorities under rules that vary by category of goods. Customs officials can accept those declarations but also retain the power to investigate them.
For Asserson, the greater concern is what happens when questions arise.
An intensive customs inspection could lead to lengthy delays even if the Israeli exporter ultimately establishes that its goods are not covered by the measures, he said. A foreign customer could decide that waiting is not worth the trouble and turn to another supplier.
“The fact that the product might eventually be given a green light could be academic if the ultimate customer has lost interest in the meanwhile,” he said.
That, he argued, is another way measures intended to target settlements could have wider effects on Israeli trade.
‘Support, facilitate or profit’ could have broad reach
Asserson said the principal risk is not necessarily limited to physical goods produced in settlements.
He pointed to language targeting companies or individuals that “support, facilitate or profit from settlement activity,” which he said could potentially encompass financial institutions and other service providers depending on how the final measures are written and enforced.
Asserson offered deliberately broad examples to illustrate his concern: an international accounting firm preparing year-end accounts for a grocery store in a West Bank settlement, a plumber providing services in East Jerusalem or a supermarket chain with one outlet in a settlement.
Whether such examples would actually fall within the British measures would depend on their final wording and subsequent regulatory or judicial interpretation.
For Asserson, however, the uncertainty itself presents a commercial risk.
“Rather than supply an Israeli company, a UK manufacturer might be overwhelmed by the risk that the Israeli purchaser might have some minor relationship with the West Bank,” he said. “The UK supplier might choose to find customers elsewhere.”
Why Israeli banks are a particular concern
Asserson sees the banking sector as the most serious potential vulnerability because international commerce depends on access to financial institutions.
“If Israeli banks are frozen out of international banking, the effect could be catastrophic,” he said.
He outlined a worst-case scenario in which Israeli companies could struggle to receive payments from foreign customers, Israeli banks could encounter difficulty borrowing on international markets and routine transactions involving Israeli accounts could become harder to process.
Britain has said it does not intend to isolate Israel’s banking system, but Asserson worries that a bank could potentially expose itself to sanctions through even limited business connected to settlements.
He cited the hypothetical example of an Israeli bank changing the interest rate on a mortgage for a West Bank household. If regulators interpreted such an action as prohibited support for settlement activity and sanctioned the bank, he argued, other financial institutions could become reluctant to deal with it.
“The danger is acute,” he said.
What is driving Britain’s tougher approach?
Asserson attributes the British government’s policy partly to domestic politics, an interpretation that reflects his own political assessment.
He pointed to Labour’s losses in recent local elections to the Green Party and independent pro-Palestinian candidates and argued that taking a tougher line toward Israel offers the government an electoral incentive.
“Hitting Israel hard is a cheap electoral card for Labour to play,” he said.
Asserson also accused Labour’s progressive wing of longstanding hostility toward Israel and invoked the antisemitism crisis under former party leader Jeremy Corbyn. His firm represented a principal complainant in proceedings involving the Equality and Human Rights Commission, which found in 2020 that Labour had committed unlawful acts of harassment and discrimination related to antisemitism.
But Asserson said responsibility did not lie solely with Britain.
He argued that the Israeli government had provided London and other governments with an opening through its policies in the West Bank, including plans for construction in the E1 area.
“The Israeli government gave the UK, and the other 11 countries that moved with it, a gift,” he said.
He also sharply criticized Israel’s response to settler violence against Palestinians and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s handling of statements and actions by far-right members of his government.
“By appearing to condone, and possibly even support, settler violence, including murder, against Palestinians, Israel was placed in a morally indefensible position,” Asserson said.
He characterized the British sanctions as an “overreaction,” but said they represented “the culmination of years of growing frustration with Israeli conduct.”
‘The problem has now arrived’
Asserson also accused successive Israeli officials of underestimating how deteriorating perceptions abroad could eventually translate into political and economic measures.
“I don't think that the Israeli government has dealt in an adequate way in dealing with that problem,” he said. “It's a problem which we've seen coming over the hill for many years. It's now arrived in a material way.”
For Asserson, the dispute over BBC coverage is therefore no longer primarily about winning an argument over individual reports.
“The BBC and other media organizations have created an atmosphere in which what has just happened has been possible,” he said.
“We need a government that will actually recognize the danger and deal with it.”
Could Israel’s election change the picture?
Asserson argued that the outcome of Israel’s upcoming election could affect how the country is received internationally, though his assessment is necessarily speculative.
If Netanyahu returns as prime minister, Asserson said, he believes the result would further damage Israel’s standing among governments and institutions already highly critical of him.
If Israelis elect a different government, he argued, foreign governments could be more willing to reassess their approach. But he cautioned that repairing Israel’s international standing would not happen quickly.
“Immense damage has been done to Israel’s standing,” he said, adding that any future prime minister would also inherit Israel’s continuing military and security challenges.
Even if repairing relations with the international community became a priority, Asserson said, “it will still be a long and painful climb back.”
He said responding to the threat of international sanctions should therefore rank high among the next government’s priorities.
‘The sanctions point a dagger at Israel’s commercial heart’
Despite his warnings, Asserson said he does not regard the broader economic consequences he described as inevitable.
“The sanctions point a dagger at Israel’s commercial heart,” he said. “But the concerns I have outlined are by no means inevitable.”
He noted that Britain has said it wants to avoid broader spillover and limit the impact of its measures to settlements and settlement-related activity.
Asserson believes Israeli businesses and the government can substantially reduce the risks if they prepare for the rules, scrutinize supply chains and financial relationships and engage seriously with the potential consequences.
“If an Israeli government grapples intelligently and sensibly with this threat, I believe it can be materially mitigated,” he said. “But if this threat is met with hollow bravura, I fear for the future.”
Trevor Asserson is the founder of Asserson, an international English law firm with its largest office in Israel. The firm advises clients on commercial matters, including British sanctions law. The views expressed by Asserson are his own.

Iran’s military warned Sunday that it will launch "continuous, effective, and painful attacks" against American bases and interests across the Middle East if the U.S. resumes offensive military actions, claiming Washington has decided to launch new strikes with the backing of regional allies.
The fresh warnings from Tehran’s Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters came as senior Iranian leadership signaled a willingness to return to a June framework agreement with Washington.
Top Iranian officials confirmed Sunday that they have conveyed specific conditions to the U.S. through diplomatic mediators for ending the war and reopening the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a vital maritime choke-point for global oil and gas exports.
In a statement broadcast on state-run television network IRIB, Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya central military command claimed that Tehran had received intelligence pointing toward an imminent resumption of U.S. military operations.
"According to the information received, the criminal America, has once again decided to resume measures against Iran, with the green light of some regional countries, at a joint meeting in a European country," the military command declared.
The Iranian armed forces threatened widespread retaliation against American military assets and cautioned neighboring countries against assisting U.S. operations.
"We warn that if the countries of the region – by continuing their dual policy toward the Islamic Republic of Iran – align with the Great Devil's aggression against a powerful and sovereign Iran they will all be considered complicit in this evil and can no longer expect restraint or decency from Iran's powerful armed forces," it said.
Regional stability has deteriorated since Feb. 28, when the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran. Tehran responded with retaliatory strikes against regional installations hosting American military assets and instituted a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Despite the heightened military rhetoric, Iranian officials indicated that a diplomatic resolution remains possible if the U.S. honors commitments established in earlier negotiations.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, acting as chief negotiator, confirmed that Iran’s terms for ending the conflict had been delivered to Washington via diplomatic intermediaries.
"Our messages and the explanation of our conditions have been clearly conveyed to the other party through mediators," Ghalibaf said, according to Iranian state television.
"As long as the conditions are not met ... and the U.S. commitments are not honored, it will be impossible to return to the situation from before the negotiations and to an open strait," he added.
Clarifying those demands, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary-general of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera that Tehran’s conditions mirror the terms outlined in the 14-point framework agreement signed by Washington and Tehran in mid-June.
"Our conditions are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade," Rezaei said, adding that Iran is also seeking a formal end to fighting between the Houthi movement in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
Diplomatic efforts are set to continue in Tehran Sunday with the arrival of Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who is traveling to the Iranian capital for bilateral talks in his country's role as a mediator. Qatar has also served as a primary channel for conveying proposals to the U.S. government.
The diplomatic initiative follows the collapse of the June framework agreement, which called for a 60-day negotiation period to secure a permanent end to hostilities.
Under that agreement, Iran committed to ensuring the safe, toll-free passage of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while the U.S. agreed to lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and unfreeze Iranian financial assets.
The temporary accord broke down following sharp disagreements over navigation rights in the Strait of Hormuz and the technical procedures for releasing frozen funds. The initial 60-day timeline expired without an extension or a finalized permanent treaty.
Independent analysts observe that Iran is eager to conclude the conflict, provided it can secure strategic concessions.
"Iran has no interest in an endless war. There is a clear understanding in Tehran of the importance of bringing the conflict to an end, but only through an agreement that changes the strategic reality in Iran's favour," wrote Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli Iran analyst, in an assessment posted on X.
Citrinowicz said that Tehran remains unwilling to restart diplomatic talks from scratch or offer new concessions beyond the June memorandum.
"What Tehran is not prepared to do is renegotiate the agreement from scratch. Iran will not negotiate new terms for the Memorandum of understanding. It will not reopen nuclear negotiations before the memorandum is restored. And it will not offer additional concessions beyond those it already made during its negotiations with Washington," Citrinowicz noted, adding that any progress requires Washington to fulfill its pledges regarding frozen funds and Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz.

Australia begins campaign for seat at world's most powerful table
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:02:49 UTC

Australia launches campaign for two-year seat on UN Security Council
In short:
Anthony Albanese says Australia is in a "pretty strong" position to join the UN Security Council, with Finland the only other nominee for the two non-permanent seats.
The council has faced criticism about its ability to handle global crises, in part because Russia and China both have veto rights.
What's next?
A secret ballot will take place in mid-2028, and Australia will need a two-thirds majority of UN General Assembly members to succeed.
Anthony Albanese has officially launched Australia's campaign for a two-year term on the powerful United Nations Security Council (UNSC), insisting Australia "punches above its weight" and wants to help shape the global response to issues including the rapid rise of AI.
Declaring Australia was "in a pretty strong position" to nab one of the two spots available, the prime minister released a slick video to accompany the campaign in New York on Sunday, local time, where dozens of world leaders were gathering for this year's UN General Assembly.
While launching the bid, Mr Albanese named former News Corp executive Siobhan McKenna as Australia's next consul-general in New York, one of the country's most sought-after postings.
"Siobhan McKenna is a professional, and she will do an outstanding job representing Australia and the Australian government here in New York," Mr Albanese said.
Ms McKenna — a former top lieutenant of Lachlan Murdoch — is currently the Australia Post chair and will succeed businesswomen Heather Ridout, whose term expires in December.
Campaigning under the banner "We listen. We partner. We protect" for the UNSC seat, Australia plans to leverage its position as a first mover when it comes to online safety and tech regulation, as well as its leadership on climate change, as this year's COP31 president of negotiations.
Speaking to reporters at the UN headquarters, Mr Albanese said having a seat at the table would enable Australia to influence the way the world responded to emerging challenges, including AI.
"Australia's voice on the council matters, so we can be a part of shaping some of these biggest issues which are facing the world and our nation," Mr Albanese said.
"Australia punches above our weight … and we can have an impact on the world, and that's what I want to see Australia do."
On Sunday, Mr Albanese urged the "two giants", the US and China, to cooperate when it came to AI, as US Donald Trump again dismissed calls to regulate the increasingly powerful technology.
Pre-empting critics at home, Mr Albanese said the campaign would be "very modest" and sought to remind voters that Australia was not immune to global crises, including the conflict in the Middle East, which is hammering Australia's economy and sending fuel prices soaring.
"That's why engagement with the world matters. It matters because it makes a difference to the cost of living, to inflation, to Australians' way of life," he said.
"And that is why we can't afford to not be engaged with the world, because it has a direct impact on the quality of life of Australians on a day-to-day basis."
So far, only Australia and Finland have nominated for the two non-permanent positions on the 15-member council from 2029.
A secret ballot will take place in mid-2028. To succeed, a country must secure a two-thirds majority of UN General Assembly members, or at least 128 votes if all 193 members vote.
"We're in a pretty strong position. We're well regarded around the world," Mr Albanese told Insiders on Sunday.
Australia last held a non-permanent spot in 2014 and used the position to push for an international inquiry into the downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 over Ukraine, in which 298 passengers and crew were killed, including 38 Australians.
The UNSC is responsible for maintaining international peace and security and seeks to mediate disputes using peaceful methods.
But it persistently faces criticism of its ability to handle global crises, particularly because Russia and China both have veto rights along with the other permanent members.
Mr Albanese acknowledged it was an institution that needed reform and to be made more effective.
But with ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, and rising strategic competition, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said having a seat at the table would give Australia the chance to advocate for a world governed by rules, not by force.
"A safer world is one governed by rules, not power and force alone. Australia's vision is a world where all countries have the freedom to decide their own future," Senator Wong said in a statement.
"As an active and ambitious middle power, we have a practical contribution to make to international peace and security."
"There's a need for middle powers such as Australia to exercise the influence that we have."

‘I have nothing in the UK at all’: British man torn from his Swedish wife and home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:02:43 UTC
21:02:43 KST

Doubled over a Heathrow baggage trolley, the former British business director is sobbing uncontrollably, exhausted emotionally and physically after being deported from Sweden.
Hours earlier the 65-year-old had been marched on to a plane in Stockholm, separated from his home and his Swedish wife after a five-year battle to stay in the country after Brexit came to an end.
An only child with no children and no property in the UK, Charles has in effect been made homeless. He was last in the UK in 2022 for one week, and before that not since 2017 when he emigrated.
“I have nothing, nothing in the UK at all,” says Charles as he shows a text from the British consulate explaining where in Heathrow those suddenly left homeless can get help.
“All I want is to return to my wife, my home and my friends in Sweden and to live a quiet, peaceful life,” adds Charles, who does not want to publicly share his full identity.
His forced flight on Tuesday shows that deportations of British citizens who lived in Sweden before Brexit are continuing. Stockholm has already deported 458 British people after rejected residency applications, a higher proportion in terms of its population than any EU member state.
The situation persists despite promises from opposition parties now on track to form a government that they will introduce urgent laws to give Britons a second chance to apply for residency.
“I’ve done nothing wrong but feel I’ve been treated like a criminal,” Charles says.
“Since arriving in Sweden nearly nine years ago, I’ve done everything I can to integrate myself into Swedish society. I’ve learned some basic Swedish, contributed to Swedish society and the Swedish economy, and for that, I’m being punished. Why are they doing this to good, honest, hard-working people like me and my wife?”
Shortly after disembarking in London, he is sitting down in an airport cafe processing what has just happened.
Pointing to a small holdall and a large reusable shopping bag, he says: “All I have is what my wife packed in my bag here with clothes and my little bag” – in which he has belongings handed back to him by the captain as he got off the plane.
The bag includes a plastic envelope sealed and emblazoned with the words Kriminalvården, the Swedish Prison and Probation Service, containing meagre belongings.
In it is a miniature tube of toothpaste, a toothbrush and earplugs given to him in the detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks.
A bright yellow envelope was also handed to him by the captain before disembarking, which he opens for the first time.
Inside is a police document saying he does not need to be “escorted”. Another says he is being deported over a failed residency application under the Aliens Act – his latest legal attempt to stay in Sweden after a pre-Brexit residency application, made on time, was rejected.
Charles’s plight started just over two weeks ago when he and his wife received a text requesting that they come to their local police station to discuss their migration case. They thought it was to discuss their five-year battle to persuade authorities they were in the country lawfully before Brexit. But he was immediately detained and told he would be deported.
“It was an incredible shock. I was distraught. This is not about leaving Sweden, this is about me being forced to leave my wife and my house. They are separating me from my wife,” he said. “They said we think that if we don’t detain you, you will abscond from Sweden because you are not cooperating.
“For the last nine years, all we’ve done is cooperate with them.”
He said he begged authorities not to detain him, telling them he would go of his own accord but they said no. He asked if he could drive back to Britain “so at least I could take some belongings with me because I have nothing in the UK, and they said: ‘No, the decision has been made.’”
Before Brexit, British citizens could live, work, study or retire in any other member state. Under EU law deportation was reserved for exceptional cases of criminality such as terrorism.
After Brexit, Britons and EU citizens who had exercised those free movement rights were told their rights to remain in their host country would be guaranteed in the legally binding withdrawal agreement.
The campaign group British in Europe has raised concerns about the hardline treatment in Sweden for years but this summer it became an election issue after a series of controversial cases emerged, including a removal order issued to a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, who had been in the country for 21 years.
A 74-year-old British man with dementia in full-time care was also ordered to leave after 25 years while another British man, 34, in the country since he was 10 years old, was deported in January.
The cases raised questions about whether Sweden’s hardline immigration position had infected decision-making relating to Britons there before Brexit, a cohort with special protection.
Charles says the experience has been humiliating, particularly as he spent a career in public service helping prisoners and unemployed people to start up businesses.
“When I first moved to Sweden, I thought it was a wonderful place to live. Clean air. We were very close to the sea. Forests, nature, the people that I met when I first moved there were all generally very nice people. That did change,” he said.
“Only two friends know what’s happened in the last couple of weeks. And they’re disgusted by it. One of them said, ‘I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed of what we’ve done to you’.”
Jane Golding, the chair of British in Europe, says “it is another case that raises the question of whether Swedish implementation is in line with the spirit of the withdrawal agreement,” referring to the legally binding treaty that Michel Barnier, then the EU’s chief negotiator on Britain’s exit from the EU, and Boris Johnson, the then prime minister, promised would protect EU citizens in the UK and British citizens in the EU.
“This British man who has sufficient means and a home and a Swedish wife in Sweden now faces homelessness in the UK where he has nothing,” she says. “This wasn’t the intention of the EU and UK negotiators of the agreement who said that citizens should broadly be able to continue their lives as before,” she adds.
She points out that, unlike the UK, there is no statutory body in any member state to oversee correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. “Monitoring and support resources for UK citizens in the EU trying to enforce their rights are not commensurate with those in the UK, where there is a dedicated independent monitoring authority. Unfunded volunteers trying to help are overwhelmed,” says Golding.

Charuhov said in the same post that some of the casualties his unit evacuated by UGV would likely not have survived evacuation by any other method, and that each mission is planned around factors including the severity of the injury, the terrain and conditions at the site.

Kostyantyn Hushcha, the company’s CEO, said on LinkedIn that the trip marked MAUL’s first trip outside Ukraine, and that Swedish personnel used the visit to learn about the platform’s role in casualty evacuation and the broader experience of using ground robots in combat conditions.
