Guatemala’s Democracy Dilemma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:01:58 UTC
20:01:58 KST

Guatemala’s Democracy Dilemma
A reformist president weighs the pressure to move fast against the imperative to restore institutions his people can trust.
Just over three years ago in Guatemala, a coalition of young and Indigenous voters helped propel Bernardo Arévalo, a reformer who campaigned against corruption, to an astounding presidential win. Guatemala had not only refused the global trend toward populist authoritarianism; it had also defied what its citizens called “the pact of the corrupt,” a loose alliance of politicians, judges, criminal networks, and crony capitalists that had gained control of the country’s institutions.
Today the mood in Guatemala is less hopeful. Some of Arévalo’s former allies, and many of those who voted for him, are dejected, convinced that the president missed a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform the country. When I met with Arévalo in Guatemala City in May, he defended the pace of his administration’s progress and suggested that the alternative would have been to abuse the powers of a government he was elected to reform.
In Latin America, “we never truly got used to understanding that the rule of law is fundamental,” he told me. “Rule of law is not the same as rule by law. Rule of law is when we all accept that we are subject to the law and we operate within that framework to solve problems. Rule by law is when I use the law that’s at my disposal as part of my political arsenal.”
Had he crossed that line, Arévalo insisted, he would have risked being ousted by his opponents and replaced by someone willing to do much worse. His critics disagree.
Arévalo’s personal integrity is undisputed. But some of the reformers who helped elect him now argue that he may be too scrupulously rules-respecting to deal effectively with the “pact of the corrupt” and the institutions it captured—too much of a liberal democrat to save democracy. When he leaves office in 2028, they fear that the pact will quickly retake control of the few institutions it has lost, or that voters will choose an autocrat who promises to crush crime without concern for legality.
Guatemala’s predicament points to a more universal problem. Can liberal reformers unwind authoritarian state capture without, themselves, engaging in at least a little bit of illiberalism? The dilemma is not Guatemala’s alone. Move too aggressively, and you risk being branded an autocrat, or even becoming one. Move too cautiously, and you risk obstruction, sabotage, and ineffectuality. South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa chose a gradualist approach to reversing Jacob Zuma’s state capture and disappointed many of his supporters. Placing the opposite bet, Poland’s Donald Tusk bent rules to try to undo the damage done by the right-populist Law and Justice party—and stood accused of undermining the rule of law. Hungary’s post-Orbán leader, Péter Magyar, seems to be following Tusk’s example.
In a way, both Arévalo and his critics are right. Guatemala has avoided a democratic breakdown. But the president’s rules-bound approach has also left many Guatemalans feeling that he has not fought for them forcefully enough. The question now is whether Arévalo has preserved democracy as an ideal that Guatemalans believe in and, if necessary, will defend.
In Guatemala City, I watched as hundreds of people gathered outside the country’s public prosecutor’s office, a bunker-like building ringed by a huge black-steel fence put up three years before, allegedly to shield the occupants from nonviolent democracy protesters. The crowd had come to celebrate the long-awaited end to the term of María Consuelo Porras, the country’s attorney general and, to many citizens, the personification of the pact of the corrupt.
For the past eight years, Porras had been a figure of fear. She used the power of her position to investigate and jail critics of state corruption. When Arévalo was elected in 2023, her office tried to overturn the results, alleging irregularities that international observers found baseless. That effort looked likely to succeed—until indigenous Maya communities organized peaceful demonstrations that lasted 106 days and drew the participation of nearly 2 million Guatemalans. Arévalo was inaugurated.
That he did not take extralegal action to remove Porras from her post has given rise to some of the fiercest criticism against him. She opened an investigation into Arévalo’s party, the Seed Movement, for relatively minor party-registration irregularities. Although the probe did not produce formal charges, it led to the party’s dissolution and thus thwarted any hope of its controlling Congress. Porras also brought more than 75 legal cases or complaints against the president and his supporters, including the arrests of two of the Indigenous leaders behind the 2023 protests, and even a cabinet minister. Now Porras was finally leaving, and a new attorney general was taking over.
The Guatemalans gathered outside the office had waited for this moment. What they had not anticipated was how long Porras’s departure would take, and how few people would come out to celebrate it. Thousands had massed in the same street just a few years before.
When I met Arévalo a few days later, he justified the delay by explaining that his government had arrived “with an enormous level of public legitimacy, but without control of the Congress, and with the justice system positioned against us.”
Legally, he had no authority to simply eject the attorney general. He sent a bill to Congress to grant him that power, but the opposition blocked it. “If, in that scenario, I make a political miscalculation, the result isn’t that I go with a hundred people to pull Consuelo Porras out of that building and that this is sustainable and produces results,” he said. It was that “I go to prison or into exile, and someone else comes in, one of them, to take power.”
Like much else in Guatemala, the colossal, mint-green presidential palace where Arévalo sat down with me is a holdover from a bygone era of authoritarianism. It was built by Guatemala’s Hitler-admiring, yet U.S.-backed dictator, Jorge Ubico, who rose to power in 1931 and was forced to resign amid mass protests in 1944.
Arévalo, before winning the presidency, was best known as the son of the man who succeeded Ubico, in Guatemala’s first truly free elections. Juan José Arévalo, an educator and a social democrat, returned to Guatemala from exile in 1944 to run for president against the ex-dictator’s favored candidate. As his son would later, he won by a landslide, and Guatemala’s “democratic spring” began, a time of expanded rights and education. But after his freely and fairly elected successor, Jacobo Arbenz, went further, carrying out a land reform that threatened the interests of wealthy families and the powerful U.S.-based United Fruit Company, the United States organized a coup that put the military in power in 1954. Nine years later, a guerrilla leader asked Arévalo to help spearhead armed resistance to the regime, and the former president refused, saying that confronting the military head-on would turn Guatemala “into a lake of blood.”
He was right. In the name of crushing the greatly outnumbered guerrillas, the military and its allies killed or disappeared more than 100,000 Guatemalans over the next three decades. It massacred leftists, labor leaders, and residents of more than 400 Maya villages suspected of supporting insurgents. Guatemalan courts eventually deemed the latter crime a genocide.
Bernardo Arévalo, born in exile in Uruguay, returned with his family in the middle of the dictatorship period, and he began a career as a diplomat at its tail end, as the country formally returned to elections and civilian rule in 1985. He later left the diplomatic service, earned a Ph.D., and worked in international peace-building.
The wood-paneled presidential office where we met was decorated only with two portraits: his father’s, in black-and-white, and his own, beside it, in color. Arévalo’s demeanor was professorial.
“We are in a process of recovery,” he said. “Democracy doesn’t develop in a linear, unidirectional way; it has leaps and twists, not only here, but everywhere in the world.” For much of the 1990s and 2000s, Guatemala had been twisting its way toward democracy, but corruption networks and drug traffickers had insinuated themselves into the country’s institutions. “Part of what we set out to do is to recognize the serious damage this had caused the country—this corrosion, this penetration of political-criminal networks” that served no “ideological interest,” Arévalo said, but rather “the highest bidder: whoever could pay for impunity.”
Dislodging these forces from the machinery of the state has been neither swift nor straightforward, and even those most anxious for change are hard-pressed to offer practical solutions. The president told me that some supporters had asked him to use the military to remove Porras. He found the suggestion unsettling: “Are you really asking us to go back to the years of military dictatorships of the 1970s, when armies were the only solution?”
I asked Arévalo about the Indigenous protest leaders, Luis Pacheco and Hector Chaclán, who had then been imprisoned for more than a year while under investigation on terrorism charges. “I would like the people who say ‘But the government could have done something else’ to tell me what,” Arévalo replied, exasperated. “What they’re venting is the frustration we all feel.”
He assured me that the pact of the corrupt was weakening incrementally as its networks lost access to the state: first the executive branch, then the public-works contracting system, now the prosecutor’s office. “Without tools, they aren’t powerful. And our task is to keep removing those tools from them.”
Arévalo can point to some successes. Young lawyers have worked to clean up corruption in the judicial selection process. Appointed in March, the new bench of the Constitutional Court, which rules on the constitutionality of laws and policies, is more favorable to reformers than the one it replaced, as is the new electoral tribunal, which oversees elections. I spoke with the new attorney general a few days after he assumed his post: He was so busy firing Porras’s apparatchiks and preparing for the institution to resume serious criminal investigations that he was sleeping only four or five hours a night. An anti-corruption commission that Arévalo formed early on has already filed more than 200 criminal complaints against former officials.
Arévalo was tasked with not only freeing a state captured by kleptocrats, but also strengthening one that was fundamentally weak. The bureaucracy he inherited had little capacity to provide public services, reduce poverty, or fight organized crime. In this, too, his administration has made some progress. It has hired more than 15,000 new teachers, and built or refurbished more than 150 rural-health clinics (his predecessor built just six in four years, Arévalo said). The government has also replaced dirt floors with cement in more than 75,000 households in the country’s poorest rural municipalities, and has distributed water filters and cleaner-burning stoves.
Still, much else that Guatemalans had hoped for has failed to materialize. Congress, which remains dominated by the old-guard pact forces, has blocked or stalled bills aimed at curbing corruption—for example, bills to modernize public-works contracting, require shell companies to disclose who owns them, and protect whistleblowers. Partly because the contracting system remains dysfunctional, the government has made little visible progress toward repairing the country’s crumbling highways. And, unwilling to buy votes in Congress outright, as his predecessors did, Arévalo has resorted to pork-barrel spending and raising congressional salaries to win legislative support. Such tactics are deeply unpopular with the public.
Another limiting factor has been the Trump administration. Although Arévalo’s cooperation on crime and drugs has kept the relationship cordial, his opponents have courted President Trump to try to tip the scales against reformers. In April, the U.S. ambassador to Guatemala personally called reluctant Guatemalan lawmakers to pressure them to approve a Constitutional Court judge favored by pact elites and conservatives, a top lawmaker, Luis Aguirre, told me. This tied the court between reformers and their opponents, leaving Arévalo without a reliable majority.
The young reformers who campaigned with Arévalo knew that he would face constraints, but some wish that he had more often tested those limits.
Samuel Pérez, 34, is a member of Congress; he was also the head of the Seed Movement bloc in Congress before it was dissolved. I went to see him in a building plastered with missing-persons flyers for those who were disappeared during the military dictatorship decades ago. The flyers are a common sight in Guatemala City, posted and reposted by the victims’ families.
Pérez told me that Arévalo was elected not only “to overthrow the regime, but also to construct something new, and that isn’t happening.” Now Pérez was creating a party, called Raíces, to which most of the lawmakers formerly associated with the Seed Movement had defected. They would still support Arévalo, but they would advocate for a more confrontational approach. “The president interprets power and good government as doing things a little better and a little more than what already existed. For me, no. You don’t use power to administrate what’s already there, but to transform what isn’t working,” Pérez explained.
I’d last seen Pérez during Arévalo’s presidential campaign in 2023. He’d told me then that if the Seed Movement won, the government’s greatest difficulty would be managing popular expectations. But he hadn’t predicted that he himself would be among the disappointed. Arévalo should have rallied the public to pressure Congress to pass the law removing Porras, Pérez said. He should have conceded less to business elites, and done more to free Pacheco and Chaclán. Pérez was particularly upset that the police had come to arrest the two men in a white van with tinted windows—a symbol of the dictatorship, which used such vehicles to disappear its victims—and that the government had not stopped this.
Several young Guatemalans in the reform movement suggested to me that the political caution of their parents’ generation was a product of the fear instilled in them during the years of military rule and internal armed conflict. Some speculated that Arévalo’s aversion to escalation emanates from that experience, too, given his youth in exile and the persecution of many of his father’s supporters in the years after the 1954 coup. “I think he is a son of his circumstances,” said Andrea Reyes, a young lawmaker helping Raíces organize.
Arévalo readily locates his most formative influences in that era—as a source not of fear, but of strengthened conviction. He spoke to me of his father’s refusal to abandon democratic principles: “Even when the world began to change around him, he kept his convictions, which today we see were the correct convictions, after all, 80 years later.”
Arévalo, too, has found his convictions under pressure—not only from former allies who worry that his reforms have gone too slowly, but also from constituents and conservative politicians who want a government that will ignore constitutional limits in cracking down on crime. In this they compare him unfavorably with the autocrat next door: Many Guatemalans who live in daily fear of extortion and kidnapping see gangs, not illiberal state capture, as the biggest threat to their basic freedoms, and they see President Nayib Bukele’s El Salvador as a beacon of safety.
Bukele, first elected in 2019, took an almost opposite approach from Arévalo’s to governing. He purged institutions of his political rivals, packed them with loyalists, and then cut secret deals with gang leaders before cracking down on their followers. His mass roundups virtually eliminated violent crime in his country, by jailing more than 90,000 people suspected of gang ties, many without due process. Arévalo is unwilling to pursue such methods. He has, however, seized record quantities of cocaine, extradited crime bosses, hired thousands of new police officers, and begun building the country’s first new maximum-security prison in 40 years. But murder and extortion rates have proved stubborn, and many are now demanding more-radical methods.
“Guatemalans are searching for their Bukele,” said Alvaro Arzú Escobar, a conservative lawmaker sanctioned by the Biden administration for allegedly trying to undermine Arévalo’s inauguration. Arévalo “isn’t radical in his ideas or his actions,” Arzú told me. But, he added, “the country’s biggest problem right now is a lack of authority. As president, he doesn’t exercise the power he holds. There is a lot of rhetoric, but little action.”
The Mariscal Zavala military prison sits on a pine-covered ridge on the outskirts of Guatemala City. A former army base, it houses the state’s highest-profile prisoners. I went there to meet Pacheco and Chaclán, the Indigenous leaders who’d played such an instrumental role in safeguarding the 2023 presidential election. Both had been on the board of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán—one of the country’s oldest Indigenous self-governing bodies, in rural western Guatemala—when the attorney general’s office had moved to annul the vote. Pacheco and Chaclán canvassed rural villages on foot, helping gather some 50,000 signatures calling for Porras’s resignation. Later they helped organize protests in the capital.
“The 48 Cantones is also a democracy, with elected leaders and term limits,” Chaclán told me. “For us, democracy is sacred, and although Guatemala often doesn’t reflect it much, we must respect it.”
In April 2025, Porras ordered him and Pacheco into pretrial detention. After that, their court hearings were repeatedly delayed, seemingly intentionally, and when I met them in May, they had no idea when the next one would be.
I asked them whether they believed Arévalo should have rallied protesters or found some other tool to remove Porras, and thus to free them. Pacheco responded, “I would have liked it at first, but later I realized it would have only changed the person, not the form of doing justice.” Chaclán added, “This is nothing simple, and surely he is doing what is best for the country. We have faith we have already passed the majority of our time here.”
Chaclán was right. On August 5, a judge released Pacheco and Chaclán to house arrest, reuniting them with their families. Around the same time, the prison-like, black-steel fence was taken down from around the public prosecutor’s office.
Guatemala’s next presidential election is just nine months away. Right-wing candidates are beginning to emerge, some imitating Bukele, and many sure to court the White House, in the hope that Trump will try to tip the scales. Arévalo’s and Pérez’s reformists claim that they will join forces behind a unity candidate, but such a figure has not yet surfaced. Democracy is twisting its way forward, in Arévalo’s words. No one thinks it is leaping.
But the passage of time may provide a different perspective. On one of my last days in Guatemala City, I walked by a cathedral I had passed dozens of times before. I had never previously noticed the tiny engraved names of more than 13,000 victims of the internal armed conflict, so small as to be illegible from even a short distance, on its stone columns.
For much of the 20th century, Guatemalans who advocated for self-government, equality before the law, and the welfare of the majority—that is, social democrats—knew that the state might try to kill them. Today, social democrats govern. Reformers may disagree as to whether Bernardo Arévalo made the most of the opportunity he was given. But that such an opportunity could ever arise is more than many members of his father’s generation likely thought possible.

Maladaptive daydreaming is linked to social media addiction and hypersexuality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:00:40 UTC
20:00:40 KST

Individuals who spend excessive amounts of time lost in vivid, immersive fantasies also tend to report higher rates of problematic social media use and hypersexual behavior. A recent study suggests that narcissistic personality traits, which involve a deep need to regulate self-esteem, may act as a psychological bridge connecting these behavioral addictions. The research was published in Psychology of Consciousness: Theory, Research, and Practice.
Most people daydream to pass the time, process recent events, or regulate their emotions. The mind naturally wanders. Some individuals, however, develop a rigid reliance on fantasy. They spend hours each day absorbed in complex, lifelike imagined worlds.
These individuals often experience vivid sensory details during their fantasies while maintaining a dual awareness that keeps them partially anchored to reality. When this behavior begins to interfere with work, school, or relationships, psychologists refer to it as maladaptive daydreaming.
While not yet an official psychiatric diagnosis, maladaptive daydreaming shares characteristics with behavioral addictions, obsessive-compulsive traits, and dissociative disorders. Psychologists Alessia Renzi and Rachele Mariani of Sapienza University of Rome, along with Filippo Maria Nimbi of eCampus Telematics University, wanted to understand how this intense daydreaming relates to other compulsive behaviors.
The research team focused on two specific issues: problematic social media use and hypersexuality. Problematic social media use involves a loss of control over digital habits, leading to conflicts and emotional dependence. Hypersexuality is characterized by persistent, unsuccessful attempts to manage intense sexual impulses and behaviors, often using sexual fantasies to cope with difficult feelings.
The researchers also looked at pathological narcissism as a potential connecting factor. In clinical psychology, narcissism is not simply about vanity or self-absorption. It involves an inflated self-concept that acts as a shield, masking deep-seated feelings of inferiority, shame, or fragility.
Narcissism generally presents in two forms. Grandiose narcissists exhibit a sense of entitlement and rely on fantasy to sustain an elevated self-image. Vulnerable narcissists are highly sensitive to criticism and retreat into imagination to manage pervasive shame. The researchers suspected that people with high levels of narcissism might use compulsive daydreaming, endless social media scrolling, and hypersexual behavior as quick ways to gain emotional relief and regulate their fragile self-esteem.
To test these associations, the researchers recruited 559 adults for an online survey. The participants had an average age of 27, and 68 percent were women. Most respondents lived in European countries, including Italy, Greece, Turkey, and Spain.
Participants completed a series of standardized psychological questionnaires. One survey measured the frequency and intensity of their maladaptive daydreaming, asking about their urge to daydream and how much it impaired their daily life. Nearly 29 percent of the study participants scored above the suggested clinical threshold for maladaptive daydreaming.
Another questionnaire evaluated social media addiction by asking about symptoms like withdrawal, mood changes, and conflicts arising from internet use. A third questionnaire screened for hypersexual behavior. This test focused on recurrent sexual fantasies, the urge to engage in sexual behavior as a coping mechanism, and the distress these experiences cause.
The researchers noted that questions asking if participants used sexual fantasies to avoid difficult problems perfectly mirror the psychological functions of maladaptive daydreaming. A final survey measured both grandiose and vulnerable narcissistic traits.
The researchers found that higher levels of maladaptive daydreaming were moderately associated with both social media addiction and hypersexual behavior. People who reported more intense daydreaming symptoms were also more likely to report higher levels of pathological narcissism.
Using statistical models, the team examined whether narcissism acts as a mediator. A mediator is a variable that helps explain the relationship between two other conditions. For example, if variable A affects variable B, a mediator is the stepping stone in the middle that explains how or why that effect happens.
The analysis showed that narcissism partially accounted for the connection between social media addiction and maladaptive daydreaming. It also partially explained the link between hypersexuality and maladaptive daydreaming. In both cases, the presence of narcissistic traits seemed to reinforce the relationship between the behavioral addiction and the urge to retreat into fantasy.
Together, these variables accounted for roughly 20 to 24 percent of the variance in maladaptive daydreaming scores. This indicates that while self-esteem regulation plays a large role, other psychological factors are also at play.
These results point to a shared underlying mechanism. Individuals who struggle to maintain a stable sense of self-worth may turn to various compensatory behaviors to manage their frustration and negative emotions. Social media offers indirect feedback, a curated presentation, and a way to capture attention.
Sexual fantasies provide a sense of control and sensation. Maladaptive daydreaming offers an escape into a customized reality where the individual can experience power, validation, or comfort. The researchers also observed specific patterns depending on the type of narcissism.
Grandiose narcissistic traits were more strongly linked to hypersexuality. The authors suggest that grandiose narcissists might use sexual thoughts and behaviors to assert dominance or fulfill a heightened sense of entitlement. Vulnerable narcissistic traits were more closely associated with problematic social media use.
This aligns with the idea that highly sensitive individuals might prefer asynchronous digital communication, where they can control their image and avoid direct, face-to-face rejection. Younger participants tended to report more severe symptoms across all these categories. This observation aligns with the idea that young adults often face greater challenges with emotional regulation.
Because the study relied on a survey conducted at a single point in time, the results cannot prove that one behavior causes another. The findings only show that these traits tend to appear together. Future research tracking individuals over months or years would be required to understand exactly how these habits develop and influence one another.
The data collection method also presents some limitations. The survey was distributed online and relied on self-reported answers. This approach can sometimes be inaccurate if participants misjudge their own behavior or try to present themselves in a favorable light.
The study sample included a vast majority of women, meaning the results might not fully capture how these dynamics operate in men. The survey was also conducted in English, which was not the native language for many of the European participants. This language barrier could have introduced minor misunderstandings in how questions were interpreted.
Despite these limitations, the results suggest that treating behavioral addictions might require a deeper look at a person’s self-esteem. Interventions that help young people manage frustration, process shame, and build strong real-world relationships could prevent the development of overlapping compulsive habits. Therapies focused on underlying narcissistic vulnerabilities might be more effective than simply trying to stop the addictive behaviors on the surface.
The study, “Maladaptive Daydreaming, Hypersexuality, and Social Media Use: Testing Narcissism as a Mediator in a Young Adult Online Sample,” was authored by Alessia Renzi, Filippo Maria Nimbi, and Rachele Mariani.

Dining across the divide: ‘He suggested the Clacton byelection was a vanity project. Obviously I disagree’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:00:15 UTC
20:00:15 KST

Chris, 42, London
Occupation Electrical supervisor of the maintenance team at an NHS hospital
Voting record Labour
Amuse bouche He used to play and referee mid-level community rugby until he got “too old and unfit”
Alex, 42, London
Occupation London Assembly member
Voting record Conservative for most of his life, then during the pandemic he moved to Reform (in a move his still-Tory husband characterised as “throwing a strop”) because he didn’t agree with lockdown, masks or banning social gatherings of more than six people
Amuse bouche He has two Brittany dogs, and one won a class at Crufts
For starters
Alex I didn’t know what to expect, though part of my job is talking to people with different views. Chris was really friendly.
Chris We got on well. Alex is a really nice, personable guy, and it’s quite hard to question somebody belligerently when they’re so easy to talk to.
Alex I had calamari to start, which was lovely. For the main course, I had fettuccine with lamb ragu and a glass of montepulciano, and for dessert I had my go-to: tiramisu. It was great.
Chris I had the calamari to start, with a minty tartare dip. Then I had a spicy pepperoni pizza, a couple of bottles of beer, and for dessert a really nice lemon tart.
The big beef
Alex He suggested the Clacton byelection was a vanity project. Obviously I disagree, but it’s a perfectly understandable position. Nigel Farage clearly believes (and I support him) that ultimately his constituents should be the judge – and they gave him a resounding vote of confidence.
Chris If constituents could be the judge, then why would there be another byelection later if he’s found to have breached parliament’s rules? In Clacton, you’d only need about 8,000 people to sign a petition to recall him, which seems likely because almost 10,000 people voted for a man with a bin on his head.
Alex It was a lot easier canvassing for Reform in Clacton than in the local elections earlier this year in London. I got more abuse during that campaign than I had had in 27 years of politics.
Chris I said, imagine how it is now for a canvasser who isn’t a middle-aged, white, Anglo-Saxon male. If you’re a woman, or from an ethnic minority, or if you’ve got a disability, you’re probably going to get a lot more abuse.
Sharing plate
Alex Hurtling towards an artificial target of net zero is counterproductive. We’re doing self-inflicted damage to the economy for what’s largely virtue signalling, in my view, because of the 1% of emissions we’re responsible for. Fundamentally, we need to keep the lights on and food on the table. I support more efficient use of our own natural resources, including oil and gas.
Chris I’m in favour of investing in renewable energy; he’s more in favour of bringing energy costs down by extracting more fossil fuels. I said we can do that, but it’s going to make global warming worse. At our NHS hospital, we’re pretty much at maximum electrical capacity, and if we were to install loads of extra air-conditioning units, as people think we should, that would overload our electrical system.
For afters
Alex Andy Burnham is not willing to make tough decisions on things like welfare spending. My view would be that we need to look very seriously at things like Pip [personal independence payment] and foreign-born residents being able to claim universal credit.
Chris He was all for shrinking the state a bit, but he didn’t really go into much detail on how he would do that. I think we should try to raise revenue in other ways, such as bringing capital gains tax in line with income tax, going after big corporations because they’re not paying proper tax, and reforming other taxes like VAT and council tax, because I believe those are regressive taxes that hit the people in the lowest income brackets the hardest.
Takeaways
Alex I think that just by having an interest in politics you’ve got more in common with someone else, even if they’re taking a contrary view. Even though we disagreed, we had that shared interest.
Chris We swapped numbers. He was nice, personable and easy to get on with. I imagine he’ll stand as an MP in the next general election, so I’ll probably text him around then and see how he’s doing.

‘You could absolutely rip your bloody hand off’: competitors gather for England oyster shucking championship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:00:15 UTC
20:00:15 KST

Beneath bunting in the middle of Mayfair, there was a feverish atmosphere as the finals of potentially the poshest sport in England began: oyster shucking, judged by actor Stanley Tucci.
“The secret is not being scared of stabbing yourself in the hand,” says Quincy Coulter Young from Rocks Oysters, one of the fastest oyster shuckers in the country.
He was taking part in the Speed Shucking Oyster Open, during which competitors battle through a series of heats before a grand final, with shuckers racing against the clock to see who can open oysters the fastest without maiming the mollusc. The winner will go on to represent England at the World Oyster Opening Championship next weekend in Galway, Ireland.
Coulter Young said “repetition” was the key to having become so fast. “It’s the only job I’ve ever had. I hope I am good at it, as oyster shucking isn’t exactly a transferrable skill. My uncle was the head chef for Wright Brothers seafood bar in Borough Market, so he taught me from a very young age.”
Tucci looked happy to judge the taste and quality of the shucked oysters, despite apparently not knowing what he had got himself in for. “I thought this was going to be a wine tasting,” he joked, “but I am glad there’s food”. He was drinking from a huge goblet of white wine, eating his oysters with some trepidation, delicately using a fork rather than shooting them into his mouth.
During the first round, 16 competitors from restaurants around England were timed to see who could open twelve giant native oysters the fastest. The bivalves were then inspected by a panel of expert judges and points were lost for broken shells, damaged oyster meat and grit. Then, the fastest and most precise shuckers gathered for the final, during which they had to open thirty under the same conditions.
The winner was Fredrik Linifors a serious-looking shucker from Notting Hill Fish Shop. He was expressionless as he effortlessly prised open shells with a very steady hand.
English people have been eating oysters for more than two thousand years. The Romans loved the flat, elliptical mollusks found on our coasts, the prized delicacy known as a native oyster. In the 19th century, they were cheap and plentiful, so eaten by the poor as a source of protein.
Now, they are served by smiling, suited oystermen in upscale bars like Bentley’s, a century-old restaurant in Mayfair which serves 10,000 oysters a week, and was hosting the competition.
Two hundred spectators crammed into a tent to sip champagne and watch the shucking from the terrace which, on a Friday afternoon, is usually full of bankers and tourists enjoying bottles of champagne and seafood platters.
Helming the restaurant, and supervising the competition, is celebrated Irish chef Richard Corrigan, who bought Bentley’s in 2005. A good oyster shucker needs charm, wit – and strong arms, he says: “You don’t find oyster shuckers; you make oyster shuckers, and they need to have a smiley face and a warm heart and strong hands. It’s a completely social job. And it’s great for the biceps; don’t go to the gym, come to Bentley’s and open oysters for me!”
It’s also more perilous than it looks; the oyster shells, and the knife used to prise them open, are both very sharp.
“It’s likely you could absolutely rip your bloody hand off,” Corrigan says. He has been a victim of an oyster injury: “During the opening week of Bentley’s 22 years ago, I had a hospital bandage wrapped around my my hand. After a day of opening oysters, I was shattered and the knife slipped.”
Oysters are an important indicator of the marine environment, and they filter toxins from the water. “A native oyster is a great sign of how well our coastal waters are doing,” says Corrigan.
He has had to change where he sources his oysters, out of caution. This is because water companies in England spew sewage through pipes into the sea, which, if the pipes are too close to the oyster beds, can pollute the bivalves. “We get our oysters from Loch Ryan in Scotland, the west coast of Ireland [and] Jersey. We moved away from the Mersea, Colchester area, the south coast of England.”
Presenting me with a big, round oyster, he says: “Just chew this oyster. You’re tasting a bit of sea. This is Mother Nature.” Eating one himself, he closes his eyes and goes: “Jesus. A very mineral flavour, and you see this is not about how clever a chef is or a cook is, but about the sacrosanct respect we have for nature.”
Corrigan hopes the competition will get restaurants to “be more confident about putting oysters on the menu”. He added: “Knowing what part of Britain, where the waters are blue flag and where they’re not blue flag, that is where the best place is to get oysters from, you know. This is what it’s about. This is as good as any environmental contest.”

China’s stranglehold on rare earths must be ended, says hopeful supplier to EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:00:14 UTC
20:00:14 KST

The head of a mining company hoping to supply the EU with rare earths in two years’ time has said it is “paramount” to end China’s stranglehold on the supply of the raw materials used in everything from cars to wind turbines and military jets.
As Donald Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, prepare to meet on Thursday in their second summit of the year, Rafael Moreno said it was also “imperative” that they do a deal for Beijing to ease up, once again, on its threat to ban exports of rare earths.
“The market is nervous,” said Moreno, the managing director of the Australia-listed Viridis Mining and Minerals, which has assets in Brazil, Australia and Canada.
China first brought in controls on rare earth exports in April 2025, hitting the auto industries in the EU, UK, US and Japan hard.
After a summit last October with Trump in South Korea, Xi agreed to suspend the introduction of even stricter global restrictions, but only for 12 months.
Industry leaders had hoped Trump would have sealed a deal to extend the suspension at the two leaders’ last summit in May but the question remains hanging over next week’s summit.
“It cannot not be extended if they are to continue to have these presidents’ meetings regularly,” said Kurt Tong, a managing partner of the Asia Group, a Washington strategic advisory and public policy firm.
But he said a suspension deal could be delayed until November, when Trump is expected to travel to China again to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) governmental forum of 21 countries.
Viridis is already attracting attention in Brussels, where diversification of supply chains away from China is a top priority of Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president.
It has opened a demonstration plant to scrape the surface of its mine in Minas Gerais, Brazil, and produce a crumbly powder, which will then be further separated, potentially in France, to isolate the rare earths.
The EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, will travel to Beijing for his own summit with China’s commerce minister, Wang Wentao, on 8 October to try to avoid a trade war.
The EU is deeply concerned about what Šefčovič has said is the “unsustainable” deficit with China, now running at €1bn a day, with the scale of exports of electric vehicles, cars and renewable energy machinery as well as components deep in supply chains causing alarm.
While Šefčovič heads up the urgent trade mission, senior EU politicians and officials are scrambling to find alternative supplies of critical raw materials and rare earths.
But their challenge is long-term, as China controls between 80% and 90% of the world’s raw materials and processed end products, giving it powerful leverage over global manufacturing. The Chinese exchange rate is also driving down the cost of imports from China.
Eurometal, a trade group representing buyers of steel products, protests that Brussels does not fully appreciate the pressures industries are under, saying component buyers or original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) are under pressure each day to opt for Chinese goods, which can sometimes be 30% cheaper than domestic alternatives.
The EU’s international partnership commissioner, the Czech politician Jozef Síkela, visited Viridis’s Colossus demonstrating plant this year in Brazil to hear how the company hopes to win 5% of the rare earths market, with production starting at the end of 2028.
Moreno said: “It is natural for a company or OEM to want to buy the cheapest product, but then, you know, the impact of them not supporting a domestic supply chain means that the domestic supply chain just never gets off the ground.”
He is working with the French chemical company Solvay to process the rare earths. “We are looking forward to keep moving forward with our strategic partnership with Solvay to start to supply all the OEMs, car manufacturers, you know, wind turbine manufacturers like Siemens Gamesa, for example, all that sort of stuff here in Europe,” he said.
“What we’ve started to design and build now, is around 5% of the world’s rare earths market share in terms of those precious magnets. So that’s that’s where we’re starting. So this is not a small project, as you can imagine.”

‘It’s transformed the village’: the volunteers greening up Britain’s train stations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:00:13 UTC
20:00:13 KST

Every year since 1964, towns across the UK have bloomed with hanging baskets and brightly coloured flowerbeds planted by residents.
They wield their trowels in aid of the Royal Horticultural Society’s Britain in Bloom competition, a coveted accolade for the 1,600 communities that enter each year.
Now, the charity is launching a new award for railway stations to honour the volunteers who keep platforms planted with cheerful flowers and pretty shrubs.
Five of the best have been shortlisted for the RHS Railway Stations in Bloom competition, marked for their beauty but also for how well they welcome wildlife and withstand changing climate conditions.
The winner, announced this week, was the Cardross Community Organic Garden in Scotland. The RHS said: “The judges were especially impressed by how active the group was in including different members of the community in the station’s activities, from school children, Brownies to other volunteering and gardening groups”. But all of the railway gardens are impressive.
It has been an extremely hot and dry summer in Alresford, Essex, but the gardeners were prepared. Working hard to cut through asphalt to create flowerbeds, they have planted a “dry garden” inspired by the horticultural pioneer Beth Chatto, who died in 2018. Also from Essex, she managed to grow plants in dry ground that had never been cultivated.
“It’s transformed the centre of the village,” said the lead volunteer, Frank Belgrave. Ten years ago the station was described in the local paper as “rundown”. Now, the planting beds rival any at Chelsea flower show.
Belgrave said residents were very pleased their station had received the spruce-up: “It’s wonderful. People sometimes stop by with plants and compost to help us, and we are very lucky to have some lovely volunteers as the garden requires constant maintenance.
“We used to spend all our time watering. So we decided to seek advice and build a dry garden with drought-resistant plants.”
At a windswept station on the west coast of Scotland, commuters may be surprised to find trees heaving with fruit and a thriving vegetable patch. But Jane Connolly, who heads the Cardross station volunteer group, has found a way to create such bounty.
“Since March 2022, every bit of the station that can be changed, has been changed,” she said. “We do have harsh winters – we don’t take summer bedding plants as we don’t get enough out of them – we choose hardy shrubs. We put up windproofing on the shore side to protect the plants but in general we have had very few failures.”
Connolly and her fellow volunteers filled the station with plants from their own gardens and visit most days to tend to them.
Having a pretty, flower-filled rail station rather than a neglected one makes a huge difference to the village, she said: “Every time we are down there, somebody will come along and peruse it and say how grateful they are with what we have done. I notice stations now wherever I go, even if it’s a window box. People come to our station just to see our gardens.”
Other shortlisted stations include Maghull in Merseyside, where the ticket office’s window boxes are full of pretty flowers and volunteers have planted a woodland. At Wylde Green in Birmingham, overgrown areas were cleared and replaced with pollinator-friendly plants, creating a “bee corridor”. The volunteers carry out an annual butterfly count and have seen numbers increasing.
Keynsham station in Somerset on a hot day looks especially exotic because volunteers have filled it with a remarkable array of succulents, of all shapes and sizes. Like the Essex gardeners, they have selected plants that will withstand hot summers.
The volunteers at the stations have spoken of how social the job is and many have made friends. It also gives commuters a chance to chat. Belgrave said: “It’s very rewarding. Lots of people come and chat, they talk about plants, it gives them a social thing.”
He hopes to get funding for a community hub and coffee shop. “On the platform there is a very ancient station house, to the back of that there was an area which was neglected and used as a community rubbish dump. We have turned that into a garden. Now, we hope we can open a coffee shop on the site.”
In Cardross, the gardeners have become fast friends. Connolly said: “We garden together and there is always laughing and joking and there is often more joking than working! We go out socialising together now as well. It is a very social thing.”
Wildlife has returned to Alresford station, according to Belgrave. “We have noticed incredible amounts of wildlife, bees particularly. Honeybees, solitary bees, butterflies. That has changed a lot, we have seen the return of hedgehogs, we have slowworms.”
The gardeners hope their example will encourage others to get involved.
Belgrave said: “There are lots of stations which aren’t in the scheme, so if people do get involved it would be really good. It would be nice to see more stations planted up.”

A guide to Hong Kong’s bitter herbal teas and how Gen Z is reviving the health tradition
These century-old ‘leung cha’ cooling teas for ailments such as excess internal heat are finding new fans among health-conscious Gen Z
In the first instalment of a four-part Health Matters series on traditional Chinese medicine, Lisa Cam and Ashlyn Chak explore how a new generation of health-conscious youth is discovering century-old leung cha and helping neighbourhood tea shop owners safeguard a dying trade.
Long before modern chain pharmacies and over-the-counter painkillers were readily available in Hong Kong, there were leung cha: intensely bitter herbal “cooling teas” brewed in massive brass cauldrons in traditional open-front shops.
To the uninitiated, these dark, earthy, grassy decoctions served in ceramic bowls are an acquired taste at best. For generations of local workers, though, these century-old remedies have been consumed to ease sore throats, flush out seasonal “dampness” and reset bodies run down by urban stress.

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire on Arc, the Future of Quantum and the Agentic Economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

Circle is known to many as the issuer of the $74 billion digital currency USD Coin, or USDC. But co-founder and CEO Jeremy Allaire believes the company’s latest launch may be the “most consequential major platform launch” in its history.
“Arc is built from the ground up for what the financial system needs: fees paid in dollars, settlement that is final in under a second, confidentiality with compliance built in, and operators that boards and regulators can trust,” Allaire wrote in a recent email.
Allaire likens the Arc blockchain and full-stack platform, launched on Sept. 16, to an Android operating system for the global economy, facilitating payments, lending, trading, and even, one day, commerce between AI agents. “Humans tolerated money that sleeps on weekends; machines will not,” he says.
The platform has more than 100 institutional and ecosystem builders including global banks, asset management firms, payment networks, exchanges, and AI platforms. Its founding validators include BlackRock, Standard Chartered, Mastercard, Visa and Intercontinental Exchange.
Allaire, who co-founded Circle 13 years ago, is a serial entrepreneur. Before his work on stablecoins, he founded cloud-based online video platform Brightcove, and before that, software company Allaire Corporation with his brother, which was acquired by Macromedia in the early aughts. He spoke with TIME in June, ahead of the launch of Arc.
How are you thinking about the different regulatory environments in all the markets that you're operating in?
Blockchain networks are just technology services. They're soft, open software protocols that run on the internet. They're general purpose computers, and so general purpose computers and network protocols are themselves not regulated activities. It's what people do on top of it. It's a little bit like the internet itself. The internet is unregulated, but the activities on the internet become regulated, whether it's privacy, data, or financial activity.
But one of the biggest challenges of actually [having] what we think of as the core of the financial system run on public internet infrastructure like this, has been that the major regulators have had concerns about [whether] this infrastructure [is] too decentralized, where it's a bunch of unknown actors and therefore, even though it's meant to be trustless, it's sort of not trustworthy, or you could have the commingling of bad actors and good actors. The other is slightly more technical, but important, which is: central banks, for example, care about that. When a transaction happens, it's a final transaction, and the way a lot of these networks have worked in the past is there's what’s called probabilistic finality. And so if you're building a system where I bought or sold a stock or I made a transfer of value from one point to another point, you need to know that it actually happened. That has to be final. So regulators have a framework for that that is applied to the infrastructure that runs the existing financial system, and what we've done with Arc is we've designed Arc specifically to meet those standards, so that from a central bank perspective, or from the [perspectives of the] regulators that oversee, for example, the guts of the stock market, essentially think of it as the service guarantees that are required in the traditional financial system.
So, in that sense, we do think about the regulatory environment. Does this technology stand up to the demands of that? Even though it's a general purpose technology that can be used for thousands of different use cases, it needs to stand up to that scrutiny, and so, in that way, it's not so much we're worried about people regulating Arc; it's more [for] Arc and the people who want to use Arc, can it meet the regulatory expectations?
What does this mean for the future of trading desks, and how will that look in the future? Presumably, fewer people, more agents?
There's several things all happening. One is getting this general purpose economic infrastructure out there, where machine software can deploy and run and intermediate value all programmatically. The second is taking existing financial contracts, and digitizing those onto these networks—tokenization. An equity is a contract. It conveys governance. It conveys a waterfall of economic participation. Taking the financial contract itself and the instrument itself, and digitizing those fully, that whole process of tokenization is going to take years, but it's already begun. Once that happens, then all of these become themselves programmable. Just like we have with things like USDC, we now have programmable money, and that's really powerful. The second piece is basically the development of agentic infrastructure. There's the development of the agentic infrastructure from an AI platform perspective, and then there's this convergence of agentic infrastructure and economic infrastructure. I call it the agentic economy, and this convergence of those will, I believe, completely reconstitute the way every firm in the world operates.
Yes, the job of trading, essentially will be increasingly driven by AI agents, and whether they're operating on behalf of a treasurer in a company, they're operating on behalf of a household, or they're operating on behalf of a financial institution or a financial intermediary, a trading firm, etc. All of these will increasingly be executed agentically, and that's happening quite fast. Things are happening on exponentials, and it's very hard for humans to think in exponentials.
You have said that you consider Circle to be in the very early stages of what it could be, even though you are already a very big business. Where do you see the future of Circle going?
When I founded the company, I was thinking about it over a multi-decade timeframe, and we're broadly a decade into this, and the first thing that we wanted to achieve was this idea of programmable money, open protocols for dollar digital currency on the internet, and getting that into a place where it could scale. It took around 10 years or so to get there. We're now there, but the adoption of that is still at the very start. So there's $360 billion of stablecoin money in circulation. There's a lot of transaction volume, but if you look at the total supply of electronic money in the world, roughly $120 trillion of electronic money in the world, there's an enormous amount of growth to happen, and I believe that this kind of money is a superior form of money and will eat into the electronic money base over time. It's at the front end of penetrating all these different areas of markets and commerce and the financial system.
At the same time, I have a bigger thesis, which is these economic operating systems that are emerging, whether it would be like the mobile operating systems or the cloud platforms, they're emergent environments that will take 10 or 15 years to really mature. But what they portend is a world where more and more of what a corporation is will become transformed into being pure software—and that's not like we have SaaS applications or software that we interact with. The nature of the firm itself will become software, the economic activity of the firm—so that's the money, the contracts, the governance that is there, the coordination mechanisms that are part of the firm—will become run by software machines, and then the actual work of the firm, which for many companies is basically cognitive work, will be decomposed into agentic work, and will get reconstituted as agentic infrastructure with a mix of AI and humans, all of this being run on these new operating systems. That's a transformation of the very basis of the economic system, it's a transformation in the nature of the firm. It's a transformation in the way economic coordination and governance and contracts and other things work, and I think we're at the very beginning of that. I view Circle's opportunity as being a company that provides the platforms to help make that happen, that provides the infrastructure to the agentic economy that builds and issues money for that system, and that builds applications that support that change. So, we're going from, “we did the digital dollar” to “let's build the comprehensive platforms to think about this complete upgrade to the economic system that's going to take place over 10 or 15 years.”
How are your efforts around building quantum resilience going? Has AI overtaken those concerns?
There's the countdown to quantum, sort of like Y2K. It's very clear quantum is coming, and for us there's two things that we have to be thinking about. One is we have an existing financial infrastructure which runs on 35 different blockchain networks, which is USDC, and there's money issued on all of these, and those networks themselves are going to be vulnerable to quantum. So we have to track all the existing infrastructure and the progress that they're making, and if they're not making progress, we have to think about how do we help those people safely get somewhere else. The other is, we're building de novo—from scratch—new infrastructure, and we have the benefit of building that new infrastructure at a moment in time where post-quantum cryptography is beginning to be available, and so I think we're going to be the very first public blockchain network with Arc that has post-quantum features from day one when we launch, and so that's a piece of the puzzle. And then there's a whole roadmap for every layer of what we do in this infrastructure to be post-quantum prepared. My view is this is coming. AI may accelerate the timeline to quantum coming, because AI is just assisting with advancements in technology design in general. So it may continue to solve essentially scientific problems that are needed to solve quantum. So in some ways, AI accelerates the need to figure this out, but we do have the benefit of building now in a moment where there has been enough progress and an understanding of what that first wave of quantum might look like. That kind of quantum cryptography is something that we can apply in our own infrastructure.
You're a serial entrepreneur. What skills do you think are required to be a successful founder?
There are many pathways to being successful as a founder and an entrepreneur, but I'll describe what I've experienced at least in my in my realm. There are some founders who are, let's just say, really difficult, and who drive people extremely hard and have huge success, and then there are founders that are demanding, but also operate with more human compassion. So I'm more of the latter. What I'd say is, it’s critical that founders have to really have deep conviction about what it is that they're trying to accomplish, a belief of some significant change that you can bring to the world—and it doesn't have to all be rosy sunshine. Without that core, it's very difficult to be successful because the reality is that the odds are so against you. One of the hardest parts of being a founder is you're envisioning something that doesn't exist, and so inherently the world is skeptical. Inherently you're going to be told over and over again why you're wrong, why it's not going to work, why the existing world already solves the problem. It's endless. And if you go back and read through media coverage of Circle from 13 years, you'll see for probably about 10 years it was all skepticism, and still. And so, whether it's hiring people, retaining people, people have to feel like they believe in the founder, the mission, and even when you're slapped in the face or you have a huge setback and a huge failure—which you're going to—you're going to have endless failures. Failures happen every day; they happen every month. There's small scale failures and there's large scale failures. You have to have that perseverance.
Are there things that you've learned about leadership over the course of your career that you come back to?
There are a variety of things. I believe in openness and transparency. I believe it's really important for everyone to understand what the strategy is, and communicate and overcommunicate about those things. That openness and transparency is extremely critical during the early stages of a business as well, and that includes total transparency about your financial circumstances.
I've learned a lot from a talent perspective. There are phases that you go through in terms of of scaling, and the people who are willing to be joining you when you found a company are not necessarily the people who are going to be the right people for leading during the bigger commercialization phase, and those may not be the right people for being a public company. There's a constant organizational evolution. There's lots of smaller lessons like hire slow, fire fast. It's like a motto I have. When I was a young entrepreneur in my 20s, I was very skeptical about the importance of culture and values. That has really evolved for me a lot and so I really got religious about mission, values, culture, and overcommunicating about it, interviewing for it, performance managing around it, making it central because a company is an organism, and you want a healthy organism. Results really comes from that.
There's a lot of consternation about what AI means for young people entering the workforce. What would your advice be to someone early career in the age of AI?
I'll give you a real-world example. I have two sons who both graduated college in the last two years, and they're entering the workforce. One of my sons studied finance and marketing, and he wanted to get into business development. He went to a startup, and he got a job but [became] frustrated. But he got AI-pilled in January of this year, and he does not have a background in technology in any explicit way, but he just poured himself into learning these agentic systems, and he came to me and he said, "I'm going to quit my job and I want to master these skills. I want to build things. I want to create things.” I'm like, “OK, go do that.” And it is essentially my advice for anyone who is at any stage in their career, but I'll say for young people who are coming in, the opportunity right now is incredible. If you're a generally good thinker, you can become a master of literally hundreds of different domains, and you can learn how to create and orchestrate and build things that it was impossible to do before, and so it's one of the greatest periods ever in human history for individuals and individual agency, and that's why we're seeing a huge surge in solo founders. That's why we're actually seeing record numbers of new business creation that are happening in the U.S. Agents give agency. So, my recommendation is that people should dive in whatever their domain interest is and master these tools, because it effectively is going to give you superpowers. And that’s the exact message I've given every single employee at Circle. I’ve said everyone's jobs are going to be transformed. We are going to reconstitute this company. We're going to reorganize this company around the capabilities of agentic [AI], and it's the greatest career opportunity you're ever going to have. Take as much time as you want to master this, because you're going to be more valuable in Circle, or if you choose to go do something else as well.

Welcome to Dogs Anonymous, the Online Support Group for People With Difficult Dogs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Just past 6 pm on a recent Wednesday night, half a dozen pet owners logged into a Zoom meeting to confess something they’re afraid to talk about in public: They’re fed up with their dogs.
Before discussion began, Louise Crane, the president and cofounder of Dogs Anonymous, the organization hosting the meeting, recited the seven acknowledgements participants must agree to, the first being, “I admit that life with my dog is not what I imagined.” Crane wore a black T-shirt exclaiming “Abolish ICE” in thick white lettering.
“I may need to be talked off a ledge,” one attendee said as conversation kicked off, mentioning that she wasn’t sure how to handle her dog’s mood swings. Her family had been through a series of new changes: Their other dog died and they were also fostering one, and now their boxer was “unsettled” and “grumpy” to the point he was doing more “demand barking, which has never been like him.”
Other attendees confessed their private shames: a shepherd mix had started engaging in more intense “resource guarding” when around other dogs—the term for when dogs aggressively protect something they value. “He got into it with my sister’s little weiner dog the other day because they both were begging for food.” One woman, who lives in a busy apartment complex, needed advice on how to better handle her dachshund’s constant barking at strangers. (In the spirit of anonymity, Dogs Anonymous asked WIRED to leave out the names and identifying characteristics of its participants.)
Shame is the emotion attendees struggle with the most in these meetings. “The embarrassment of having a dog that’s losing its shit, especially as a woman,” is difficult for some people, Crane tells me when we speak a few days before.
Crane launched Dogs Anonymous, a nonprofit focused on training and emotional support by animal behavior experts, in 2025 in an attempt to help people vocalize their shame.
“We wanted to give people not just a space they could trust for advice on behavior issues or if they are having a crisis with their dog, but also a place where they don’t feel judged to ask questions and admit that maybe it’s a little bit too much for them,” Daphne Mendoza-Tervanis, a cofounder, says.
Sessions are held weekly and span first-time and experienced dog owners, adopters, foster caregivers, and occasionally trainers seeking tips on how to work aggression cases. The meetings are primarily attended by US residents, though previous sessions have attracted dog owners from Singapore, Costa Rica, and beyond.
Jerri Scherff, a cofounder who is 13 years sober, had first-hand experience with recovery programs, and it was important to her that Dogs Anonymous also include some of the same traditions as Alcoholics Anonymous. “We wanted to create something that was repeatable, sustainable, and eventually autonomous, which is the way that recovery groups work,” she says. The most important one was anonymity—what is discussed in the group stays in the group.
The founders say the effectiveness of the group doesn’t necessarily stem from the advice they impart during meetings but comes from members bonding over shared struggles. “The magic of AA the community is that you are going through something that somebody else has either been through or they’re going through the same thing,” Crane adds. This approach, called “sharing your experience, strength and hope,” is a core part of the 12-step recovery program and encourages members to analyze their experience in a way that makes them feel less alone.
According to a survey published in the scientific journal Pets in June examining guilt, burden, and wellbeing among owners of dogs with behavior problems, 53 percent of respondents reported feeling alone, and 78 percent reported “elevated caregiver burden,” a term for the emotional and financial strain of being a caregiver.
During a meeting in August, the group took a beat to dig into the particulars of why shame was the first emotion owners often experience when their dog reacts aggressively. One attendee said it threatened their sense of belonging in a neighborhood they already felt out of place in. Another mentioned how it made them feel judged because others wouldn’t think they were a capable owner. “There’s so much shame when you don’t get Lassie,” Crane says of the fictional TV dog that, for many Gen Xers and millennials, represented the ideal companion.
“I just broke down crying on the way home from my dog’s reactivity training,” one owner in New Orleans posted on Threads last month, writing that she signed up for classes after a woman threw coffee at her “anxious pit” for reacting badly. Dog reactivity is the number one issue most owners deal with. A 2026 study by researchers at the University of Lincoln shows that behaviors group into three main categories—oral attacks, frustration, and posturing—with lunging and barking reported as the most frequent symptoms.
“After three sessions it seems like the main lessons are to avoid triggers and anticipate my dog’s reactions,” the New Orleans owner continued. “As someone who has spent my entire life anticipating human volatility, I’m exhausted. Is there no other way?”
Another Threads user suggested she attend Dogs Anonymous, replying, “Part of what you’ll do here is grieve the dog you thought you would have as you grow closer to the one you have.”
No Dogs Anonymous meeting is the same. Some weeks attendees might discuss what it’s like dealing with their dog’s anxiety issues or ask for advice about going through the euthanasia process. Other weeks, they might vent about life. “The other day we were talking about random things that our dogs had pooped,” Mendoza-Tervanis says. “It was a lot of money and tampons.”
Unlike other support groups for owners of dogs with behavioral challenges, DA prioritizes the owner first. “Why we’re in the problem that we are right now is because we are putting dogs before people,” says Mendoza-Tervanis, who has worked in pet care for 15 years. According to the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, 2 million dogs were adopted from shelters in 2025, but Mendoza-Tervanis believes the problem is that most owners do not have the actual support they need, especially when the dog doesn’t meet their expectations. “A lot of services are becoming financially inaccessible”—hourly rates for private dog trainers in Los Angeles, for example, can cost up to $300 an hour—“so when someone comes to us the question is not, how much can you pay, but how are you feeling about what happened.”
Social media has also warped the expectations people have around dogs, where colorfully-curated pages of petfluencers @_violasnow, the Husky with 5.8 million Instagram followers, and @tikatheiggy, the Italian greyhound Vogue once called “a new fashion it girl,” can often make owners feel like they are not doing enough. It’s why organizations like DA have become a refuge.
In March, after Scherff’s American bulldog passed, weekly meetings became her safe space to process what happened away from the judgments of social media. Scherff has 283,000 Instagram followers “but with the group, I knew that whatever I said, it was going to stay there and they weren’t going to think anything of me.”
Before Wednesday’s session wrapped, one attendee in Puerto Rico expressed gratitude for the gathering. “I’m just glad we all ended up here through the magic of the internet. It can be such a dark place sometimes. It’s just nice to hear these conversations.”
More than anything, the founders want the weekly Zoom meetings to be a forum that keeps the “toxic outside noise out,” Crane says. “This is a place where you can come and say, I fucking hate my dog today. And there are people who are going to be like, yeah, that was me last Tuesday. Sometimes they drive us crazy and that’s OK.”

Munich’s Oktoberfest roars to life as the mayor taps first keg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:59:38 UTC
19:59:38 KST

AFP Photo
Munich’s Oktoberfest kicked off on Sept. 19 with the city’s mayor tapping the first keg of beer and opening the 191st edition of the world’s largest folk festival.
Mayor Dominik Krause put the first keg on tap with only two strokes and the traditional cry of “O’zapft is” — or “It’s been tapped.”
Thousands of revelers — the women dressed in Bavarian dirndls, the men in lederhosen — stormed the beer tents on Munich’s Theresienwiese fairground in the morning to get a good spot on the benches. To the sounds of brass music and the taste of freshly tapped beer, they soon started singing, dancing and swaying.
Besides beer, pretzels, pork roast and sausages were also sought-after delicacies.
Over the course of 16 days, through Oct. 4, some 6 million visitors are expected at the Oktoberfest. The majority of them come from Munich and southern Germany. However, millions of guests also travel from other parts of Germany and from around the world.
German authorities tightened security measures, after the festival last year had to close temporarily due to overcrowding. AI-powered cameras were installed for this year’s fest to detect large crowds early on, the German news agency dpa reported.
A ban on knives and flying objects — especially drones — was also in effect. There are entry checks, large bags are prohibited — and smoking marijuana is not allowed. About 600 police officers are on duty around the festival in addition to Bavarian riot police, specialized pickpocket investigators, and international task forces from eight countries, dpa reported.

Iran putting Caspian Sea back at center of regional cooperation with COP7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:51:42 UTC
19:51:42 KST

Iran putting Caspian Sea back at center of regional cooperation with COP7
TEHRAN – Iran is once again bringing the Caspian Sea to the forefront of regional cooperation by hosting COP7 of the Tehran Convention, with officials describing the meeting as an important opportunity to strengthen international efforts to protect the shared marine environment.
The seventh meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP7) to the Tehran Convention on the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Caspian Sea is being held in Tehran from September 20 to October 1.
Shina Ansari, head of the Department of Environment, said the conference, being held in Tehran after a three-year hiatus, provides an important opportunity to strengthen international cooperation on protecting the Caspian Sea.
Shina Ansari, head of the Department of Environment
Speaking about the international event, Ansari said the meeting is being hosted by the Department of Environment to revive the regional mechanism for cooperation on Caspian Sea protection.
She noted that expert-level meetings of COP7 have begun in Tehran, bringing together representatives of the Caspian littoral states and international organizations. The expert sessions will continue through Tuesday, followed by a high-level meeting on Wednesday.
Ansari said Iran has sought to provide a platform in the capital for the environmental challenges facing the Caspian Sea to be addressed and followed up within a regional and international framework.
During the four-day meeting, participants will discuss key issues concerning the protection of the Caspian Sea environment, regional cooperation, common challenges, and ways to strengthen collaboration among the littoral states. Decisions will also be made on relevant documents and issues agreed upon by the participating countries.
The environment chief stressed that hosting the meeting in Tehran is the result of continued efforts by Iran and the Department of Environment to keep regional mechanisms for Caspian Sea protection active.
She added that Iran’s hosting of the international gathering provides a valuable opportunity to place Caspian Sea issues higher on the regional agenda and pave the way for more effective cooperation among the littoral states.
Ansari said Iran will seek to make full use of regional and international dialogue to pursue key shared concerns related to the Caspian Sea and lay the groundwork for joint decisions and practical measures to protect the body of water.
At the conclusion, the views and discussions of participating countries will be summarized in a conference statement, reflecting the member states’ positions and areas of agreement on the most important environmental issues facing the Caspian Sea.
For Iran, Ansari noted, the Caspian Sea is a shared natural heritage and a valuable asset for present and future generations. She said holding COP7 of the Tehran Convention in Tehran, under Iran’s hosting and with the efforts of the Department of Environment, represents an important step toward strengthening regional and international cooperation to protect the Caspian Sea.
The Tehran Convention, which provides the main framework for cooperation among Caspian littoral states on environmental protection, marks its 20th anniversary of entry into force this year. The Islamic Republic of Iran will assume the rotating presidency of the Tehran Convention for the upcoming term.
Tehran Convention
The need for joint protection and management of the Caspian environment and its resources has been a long-standing concern for the Caspian littoral states. In 1998, the Caspian Environment Programme (CEP) was established as a regional initiative aimed at stopping the deterioration of the Caspian Sea’s environmental conditions of and promoting sustainable development for the long-term benefit of the Caspian population.
Since its inception, the CEP has tackled various environmental issues by developing a coordinated management structure, creating Strategic and National Action Plans, and implementing transnational measures to address imminent threats to the Caspian environment. Funded by the littoral states, the European Union, and the international community through the Global Environment Facility (GEF), the CEP has worked to formalize its structure and activities by concluding the Tehran Convention.
In 2003, the Caspian littoral states: Republic of Azerbaijan, Islamic Republic of Iran, Republic of Kazakhstan, Russian Federation, and Turkmenistan, signed the Framework Convention for the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Caspian Sea (Tehran Convention). After the ratification by all the five Governments, the Tehran Convention entered into force on August 12, 2006.
The Tehran Convention serves as an overarching legal framework that establishes general requirements and an institutional mechanism for environmental protection in the Caspian Sea region. It is based on principles such as the precautionary principle, the polluter pays principle, and the principle of access to and exchange of information. The two major areas of focus are (i) prevention, reduction, and control of pollution, and (ii) protection, preservation, and restoration of the marine environment. The Convention includes provisions on environmental impact assessment as well as general obligations related to environmental monitoring, research and development.
