Foreign representatives warn of growing maritime, energy risks for Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
09:30:11 UTC
18:30:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Foreign representatives warned at a resilience forum in Taipei on Saturday that growing Chinese maritime activity could alter the operating environment around Taiwan and urged the country to strengthen its energy and critical infrastructure resilience, per Nikkei Asia.
Speaking at the 2026 Resilient Taiwan for Sustainable Democracy International Forum, British Office Taipei Representative Ruth Bradley-Jones, European Economic and Trade Office Head Lutz Gullner, and American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene discussed Taiwan’s vulnerability to gray-zone pressure, supply disruptions, and energy shortages.
The forum, organized by the Presidential Office’s Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee, brought together more than 500 experts and guests from Taiwan and overseas to discuss climate change, gray-zone activities, geopolitical risks, and societal resilience, per a press release.
Bradley-Jones warned that the challenge around Taiwan was not simply the growing number of Chinese vessels operating in nearby waters. She said maritime activity had risen significantly compared with last year, describing the increase as “double or triple,” per Nikkei Asia.
She also pointed to a shift toward what Beijing describes as “law enforcement” activity, saying this could change perceptions of who controls the waters around Taiwan. She added that the use of commercial vessels could serve as a “force multiplier.”
Gullner similarly warned of an “erosion of the rules of the game” in waters around Taiwan. He said developments around Taiwan had parallels elsewhere in the world and underscored the need for stronger safeguards for critical infrastructure, including undersea telecommunications cables.
The officials also discussed possible disruptions to Taiwan’s maritime supply lines. A blockade or quarantine could affect the country’s access to fuel and other essential commodities, highlighting the importance of maintaining sufficient reserves and alternative supply arrangements.
Greene said the US wants to work with Taiwan to strengthen its ability to maintain reliable power supplies. “One is the base load, ensuring that Taiwan has the energy supplies to continue its amazing economic growth,” he said, per Nikkei Asia.
Taiwan’s semiconductor industry and rapidly expanding AI data center sector are particularly energy-intensive, Greene said. US companies including GE Vernova and Bechtel are working with Taiwan on projects involving power generation, liquefied natural gas storage, fuel cells, battery storage, geothermal energy, and nuclear power, he added.
Greene said Taiwan has made progress in developing multiple energy sources to improve resilience. In a major energy crisis, Taiwan could introduce rationing before relying more heavily on renewable energy and existing coal reserves, he said.
He added that a serious disruption would have consequences beyond Taiwan because of its role in global manufacturing and trade. A major interruption to shipping through the Taiwan Strait could force vessels to take longer routes and cause wider economic disruption.
Gullner warned that Taiwan remains heavily dependent on imported energy and other resources. “There needs to be a lot done in terms of diversification, in terms of strategic orientation as well, to get away from this vulnerability,” he said.
The forum covered civil-military cooperation, psychological defense, maritime resilience, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure, and responses to gray-zone activities, per the press release.

====================================================================================================

Beyond Europe’s fence: Ceuta, Melilla, and unfinished decolonization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
09:30:09 UTC
18:30:09 KST

From Phoenicians to Franco: Why are these African cities Spanish at all?
Amid the migration crisis in Ceuta that erupted in late July, the dispute between Rabat and Madrid over two Spanish semi-exclaves on Africa’s Mediterranean coast once again came to the forefront. Spain called the mass border crossing by over 70,000 illegal migrants a violation of its territorial integrity. For its part, Morocco, which does not recognize Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla or the small adjacent uninhabited islands, once again raised the issue of their “occupation” by Spain and asserted its own historical right to them.
The dispute has a long history. Ceuta and Melilla did not become Spanish territories because they had once belonged to Spain; neither did Morocco’s borders as we know them today exist in the 15th century. Rather, Ceuta and Melilla came under the control of Spain as a result of the later Crusaders’ expansion in the Mediterranean and the early modern-period wars, events that later gave rise to European colonialism.
The standoff between Rabat and Madrid
Since Morocco gained independence in 1956, Rabat has regularly raised the question of the status of the enclaves, seeking to have them brought back under its own control by means of dialogue. In 1975, Rabat unsuccessfully attempted to bring the matter before the UN; in 1987, King Hassan II officially proposed establishing a joint “célula de reflexión,” reflection cell, with Spain to negotiate the future status and eventual handover of the two cities. Unsurprisingly, Spain rejected this proposal.
In the early 2000s, diplomatic demands even escalated into a brief military standoff. On July 11, 2002, a Spanish Civil Guard patrol boat discovered a Moroccan flag and a group of gendarmes on Perejil, a tiny islet located near Ceuta which is also claimed by Rabat.
After Morocco rejected Madrid’s demand to immediately remove both the flag and the armed personnel from the island, Spanish special forces landed there by helicopter on July 17. The Moroccan troops were disarmed without a shot being fired and were subsequently returned to their country, restoring the status quo.
In 2007, Morocco officially recalled its ambassador for consultations following a historic state visit by Spain’s King Juan Carlos I and Queen Sophia to both enclaves.
The dispute over the status of the enclaves reignited in 2021, when Rabat recalled its ambassador from Madrid after Spain secretly admitted Brahim Ghali – leader of the POLISARIO Front, which fights for Western Sahara’s independence from Morocco – to a hospital for treatment. Diplomatic relations were restored in March 2022, when Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez sent a letter to the King of Morocco endorsing the Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara.
“They are super-Spanish”
The current events in Ceuta have once again stirred up the dispute surrounding the two enclaves, despite the strong partnership between Madrid and Rabat and their commitment to cooperation in resolving the migration crisis. Moroccan Minister of Justice Abdellatif Ouahbi spoke on the matter.
In an interview with Arab media on August 11, he stated that his country had consistently raised the issue of the status of the cities, seeking a long-term solution through dialogue. In response, Spanish authorities stated that they had always considered both cities an integral part of their territory.
“Ceuta and Melilla aren’t just Spanish; they’re super-Spanish and cannot be touched,” said Defense Minister Margarita Robles when asked to comment on Ouahbi’s remarks.
No further official statements were issued by Moroccan officials; however, a noteworthy event took place on August 24. During the Eid al-Mawlid (Prophet Muhammad’s birthday) ceremony held in the presence of King Mohammed VI, Moroccan Minister of Islamic Affairs Ahmed Toufiq mentioned ancient Sufi prayers and texts from the 7th and 15th centuries.
He claimed that they had served as a rallying cry for Moroccans during past battles to liberate occupied territories, such as the Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla. He also noted that Ceuta had given Morocco two prominent religious figures: Qadi Ayyad, author of ‘Al-Shifa’, and Abu al-Abbas al-Azafi, author of ‘Al-Durr al-Munazzam’. Although these remarks were not official, the fact that they were spoken before the Moroccan monarch sparked intense media discussions.
In Morocco, where the words of officials spoken in the king’s presence are carefully weighed and politics is steeped in symbolism, such a historical reference is no minor detail, especially when it concerns a topic as sensitive as “occupied cities” and is voiced just weeks after a crisis that has once again thrust Ceuta and Melilla to the forefront of the debate between Morocco and Spain.
The population of the enclaves
An uninitiated observer glancing at a map of Morocco might be surprised to find two cities on its coastline belonging to a state located on another continent. Geographically, Ceuta and Melilla are situated in Africa and surrounded by Moroccan territory; yet politically and administratively, they belong to Spain.
Such ‘patches’ on the world’s political map are often the result of colonial expansion, wars, unequal treaties, and established historical borders. Many of them retain conflict potential and ignite diplomatic disputes. Examples include French Overseas Territories such as Mayotte (claimed by the Comoros) and the Scattered Islands in the Indian Ocean (disputed by Madagascar) – as well as the Chagos Archipelago, which the UK never transferred to Mauritius.
Spain considers Ceuta, Melilla, and the nearby small islands to be its territory and has secured their inclusion within the EU, thereby establishing the EU’s southern frontier in Africa. Today, the two cities have a combined population of approximately 170,000 people, the majority of whom are of Moroccan origin.
A Spanish report titled ‘The Demography of the Canary Islands, Ceuta, and Melilla’ and published by the Center for Studies, Training, and Social Analysis (CEU CEFAS) in July 2028, stated that native Moroccans with Arabic surnames account for 53.5% of the population in Ceuta and 56.4% in Melilla. Among newborn boys, the proportion of Arabic names stands at 81.1% and 93% respectively, whereas 50 years ago this figure ranged from 22% to 23%.
For decades, Moroccans and Spaniards have coexisted peacefully in these two enclaves. The countries coordinated operations at border crossings and erected long walls separating both cities from Moroccan territory—structures that, in a sense, resemble the walls built by Israel in the West Bank. Spain constructed these barriers years ago with EU support and in coordination with Morocco to prevent illegal migration into Ceuta and Melilla, which are part of the Schengen Area.
Phoenician, Roman, Byzantine, Arab, and Portuguese Ceuta
Historically, both cities date back to antiquity and were founded by the Phoenicians. Over the centuries, they came under the rule of various empires and dynasties. Spain claims the enclaves as its own on the grounds that they were incorporated into its territory long before the formation of an independent Morocco in 1956.
Morocco, however, maintains that the cities, which are located on the African continent and directly off the country’s coast, are part of its indivisible territory, insisting that dynastic changes did not sever the close ties of Ceuta and Melilla with the surrounding region.
Ceuta is situated at the point where the Mediterranean Sea connects to the Atlantic Ocean, directly opposite Gibraltar. Historically, it has served as a transit point for ships, goods, armies, and religious missions.
The city experienced Phoenician, Roman, and Byzantine periods; in the 8th century, following extensive Islamic conquests, it passed into Arab hands and was subsequently ruled for centuries by Arab and Berber dynasties of the Maghreb and Al-Andalus. Throughout this time, Ceuta remained an important city of the western Islamic world.
Notably, the Portuguese, not the Spanish, captured Ceuta in 1415, when the forces of King John I seized the city from the Marinid Sultanate.
This campaign, imbued with the spirit of the Crusades, is generally regarded as the beginning of the Portuguese Empire (Europe’s first colonial empire). The major overseas stronghold ushered in an era of Portuguese expansion along the African coast and, subsequently, toward India, Brazil, and the Atlantic.
Transfer of Ceuta to the Spanish Crown
Ceuta was the only territory of the Portuguese Empire to remain loyal to the Spanish Crown after Spain and Portugal, which formed the Iberian union in 1580, dissolved it in 1640. Its transfer to Spanish sovereignty was formalized by the Treaty of Lisbon: on January 1, 1668, King Afonso VI of Portugal officially ceded Ceuta to Charles II of Spain.
Therefore, Ceuta came under the control of Spain not through a Spanish conquest of Morocco, but as a result of the dissolution of the dynastic union between the two Iberian monarchies; the city’s fate was determined not by its inhabitants, but by local elites and monarchs. In this context, it is difficult to assert with certainty that Ceuta is an integral part of Spain based on its historical affiliation.
The conquest of Melilla and the status of free ports
The story of Melilla is somewhat different. Located further east than Ceuta, the city also boasts a long history. By the time of its conquest by the Spanish in 1497, Morocco was undergoing a period of political fragmentation and a weakening of central authority, coinciding with the onset of active expansion by European invaders hardened by the wars of the Reconquista.
The capture of the city was almost bloodless: Melilla had been weakened by regional conflicts and could not defend itself properly. The Spanish quickly transformed the city into a military and trading stronghold on the opposite shore of the Mediterranean.
Melilla and Ceuta were not the only ports and territories in Morocco conquered by the Spanish at the dawn of the modern era. While many territories were subsequently lost, these two enclaves, administered directly from Madrid, remained under Spanish sovereignty due to their strategic and military value.
Ceuta and Melilla were repeatedly besieged by Moroccan forces. The Hispano-Moroccan War of 1859–1860 significantly strengthened Spain’s position in North Africa.
Following the Treaty of Fes in 1912, France and Spain established a protectorate over Morocco, while Ceuta and Melilla were granted the status of free ports.
The Francoist position: ‘Ancestral Spanish lands’
Melilla went down in history as the starting point of the Francoist uprising in 1936. When Morocco gained independence in 1956, Ceuta and Melilla were not included in the agreements governing the transfer of sovereignty to the new state. The fact that Spain retained control over these cities is often linked to the foreign policy of the Francisco Franco regime.
Spain maintained that these cities had never been part of the protectorate established in 1912. Francoist diplomacy drew a sharp distinction between “protectorate territories” (which were returned to Morocco) and “ancestral Spanish lands”
Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla has been enshrined in the country’s constitutions: first, the Constitution of 1812 and then the current Constitution of 1978. In 1995, both territories were granted autonomous status and officially designated as autonomous cities of Spain.
Unfinished decolonization
Morocco calls Ceuta and Melilla occupied cities and views them within the context of an unfinished decolonization process. Politically, this stance is understandable. Morocco gained independence in 1956, yet the Spanish territories on its northern coast remained outside the new state.
Rabat is highly sensitive to any issue concerning national borders and regards Spanish sovereignty over the two enclaves as a violation of its territorial integrity, much like the dispute over Western Sahara.
One of Spain’s arguments is that Ceuta and Melilla are not on the UN list of Non-Self-Governing Territories, to which the decolonization framework of Chapter XI of the UN Charter applies. That list includes territories whose peoples have “not yet attained a full measure of self-government.”
In 1975, Morocco attempted to place the inclusion of Ceuta, Melilla, and other Spanish possessions in North Africa on the UN’s decolonization agenda, but the initiative was unsuccessful. Spain also emphasizes that both cities are not overseas territories with a separate colonial status but rather integrated parts of the state: they possess elected institutions, representation within the Spanish political system, and the status of autonomous cities.
Gateway to Europe: painful colonial legacy
The current crisis has brought this longstanding dispute back into sharp focus, demonstrating that migration has once again become a tool of diplomatic leverage. Both Spain and the EU rely heavily on Morocco to police coastal routes and the land borders around the enclaves.
For its part, Morocco gains significant leverage: the loosening or tightening of border control immediately becomes the EU’s problem. For example, in May 2021, about 8,000 people crossed the border into Ceuta over the course of two days; many of them swam from Morocco. At that time, amidst a cooling of Spanish-Moroccan relations, border management was used as an instrument in the diplomatic conflict.
The dispute over Ceuta and Melilla remains a painful legacy of the colonial era when the fate of territories and peoples was determined by the will of European powers rather than by their own right to self-determination. The fact that the issue remains unresolved serves as a reminder that colonialism left behind not only political borders but also enduring conflicts.

What ChatGPT Thinks It Knows About You Is Affecting Its Answers. Here’s How to Change That
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

A memory of some kind is now a standard feature for an AI chatbot. The chatbot stores all of your interactions in its memory, enabling you to refer back to previous conversations, and giving the tool some useful context to frame its answers with. For example, if you tell it you're vegetarian, it won't recommend recipes with meat in them.
This comes with privacy considerations as more of us share more of our lives with these apps. But it also has the potential to affect the responses you get from the AI in ways that you don't necessarily want.
Perhaps you've spent a week researching how to replace a light switch and ChatGPT thinks you're a DIY enthusiast. Or you've been looking up places around a certain location that you're heading to for vacation, and the AI thinks you live there. All the bot's answers come with memory context now. Here's how it works, and what you can do about it.
How ChatGPT Memory Works
When ChatGPT first introduced a memory feature back in April 2024, you had to be very specific about what you wanted it to remember: You had to explicitly say to the bot "remember this" about something, otherwise it would be lost in the flow of conversation. You could then refer back to it as needed.
It was a start, but not a very good one. These memories were very fixed—so if you mentioned an upcoming party, ChatGPT would always assume it was still in the future, even after the date had passed. Until you told the AI bot otherwise, it would always be referring to an upcoming event.
After an update in June, ChatGPT now does something called dreaming, as explained on the OpenAI blog. Memories are now flexible, and are now built up and edited over time—so ChatGPT knows the party is in the past, not the future. What's more, memories are saved and sifted through automatically, so you don't have to make manual requests any more.
Essentially, it's now down to the chatbot rather than you to decide what's important enough to be remembered—and while that's certainly more convenient for users, it can come with its own problems. ChatGPT is continually refining what it thinks it knows about you every time you interact with it, and it won't always make the right assessments.
OpenAI says the three main aims of memory (or dreaming) are to carry forward useful context, to follow preferences and constraints, and to stay current over time. Ideally, that should mean responses that are tuned and personalized in helpful ways, but you don't get as much control over this as you might expect.
You Can Edit ChatGPT’s Memory
To find out what ChatGPT has remembered about you in the web app, click your profile icon (bottom left), then choose Personalization and scroll down to the Memory section. In the mobile apps, tap the menu button (top left), then your profile icon, then Memory.
The first thing you'll see is a toggle switch for enabling the memory feature. You can turn this off to stop ChatGPT from remembering anything you say, but this won't wipe out existing memories—the AI won't refer to them, but it will hang on to them in case you decide to use memory again.
Choose Manage next to Memory summaries to take a closer look at the AI's profile of you. This will cover topics like your interests and how you prefer answers to be delivered: You can highlight anything here, and then choose Make a correction or Don't mention this again to make changes. You can also use the prompt box at the bottom to issue commands like "forget that I'm a journalist."
To wipe everything, select the three dots at the top, then choose Delete and turn off memory. Once you've confirmed your choice, you and ChatGPT will be starting again from scratch, memory-wise—although your past conversations don't go anywhere, and if you turn memory back on, these chats will be indexed all over again as ChatGPT tries to figure out who you are.
Of course another way to manage memory is to not tell ChatGPT anything you don't want remembered. There's also a temporary chat feature available: Nothing in temporary chats is committed to memory, and they're forgotten as soon as they're closed. On the web, click the dotted speech bubble (top right) to start a temporary chat.

Israeli president pardons soldier who killed wounded Palestinian

Breadcrumb
Israeli president pardons soldier who killed wounded Palestinian
Israel's President granted a pardon Saturday to a former soldier who gunned down a badly wounded Palestinian man in 2016 after he had already been incapacitated by troops in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron.
Elor Azaria had been freed from prison in May 2018 after serving nine months behind bars, half his original sentence, for the manslaughter of Abdul Fatah al-Sharif.
His conviction and his release drew enormous attention in Israel. In his first interview after his release, Azaria said that “I would act exactly the same, because that’s how I needed to act.”
Azaria had approached Abdel Fattah al-Sharif as he lay on the ground, unarmed and badly hurt, after stabbing a soldier in the city of Hebron. A cellphone video captured Azaria shooting al-Sharif in the head.
Al-Sharif had lain on the ground for about 11 minutes before Azaria shot him. The soldier had said in his trial that he feared Sharif was wearing an explosive belt and could blow himself up, a claim judges rejected.
Palestinians and human rights groups had described Azaria's sentence as far too lenient. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of three to five years.
After the sentencing, the Palestinian government minister in charge of prisoner affairs, Issa Karaka, called it a “joke.”
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he "decided to grant the request of Elor Azaria to erase the remaining period of his criminal record and continue with his life."
"President Herzog has decided that the circumstances, the length of time passed, and the sorrow Azaria expressed justify enabling him to be allowed to begin a new chapter in his life," a statement from Herzog's office read, though the military countered the claim.
The statement claimed the decision had been made in the spirit of Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement that begins on Sunday evening.
At the time of the case, many right-wing Israeli politicians including current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that the shooting was justified, calling for Azaria to be released or pardoned. However, senior Israeli army officers denounced the shooting.
Israel has illegally occupied the West Bank since 1967 and frequently carries out attacks on Palestinian communities.
In July, Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir addressed a letter to Herzog saying the army opposed Azaria's request to expunge his criminal record.
"The position is based on several considerations, including the fact that the applicant has refrained from expressing remorse and taking responsibility for his actions, even a decade after his conviction," Zamir wrote.
Israel's extremists National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir welcomed the pardon Saturday. "As someone who demonstrated a decade ago for Elor Azaria, the cancellation of the criminal record of someone who eliminated a terrorist is deeply moving and joyful for me," he wrote on X.
Ben-Gvir also urged President Herzog to also grant a pardon to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who is standing trial for corruption.

Czech Republic receives all four Israeli Rafael SPYDER air defense systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
09:08:17 UTC
18:08:17 KST

The Czech Republic has received all four SPYDER air defense systems it purchased from Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, the country’s Defense Minister Jaromír Zuna announced.
"I am pleased to be able to present the complete SPYDER system batteries to the general public on this occasion,” Zuna said during NATO Days, one of Europe’s largest defense and security events, held in the Czech city of Ostrava.
“The introduction of this system represents a significant technological and qualitative shift in the field of air defense and an important step in building modern, layered airspace protection for our republic," Zuna continued.
The delivery of the system is part of a 2021 government-to-government (G2G) agreement by Israel’s Defense Ministry and the Czech Republic. Production of all batteries has been completed with adaptations to the country’s military requirements and NATO standards.
The Czech Defense Ministry said the system is fully integrated into the NATO air defense alliance system and that all maintenance and service are provided entirely in the Czech Republic.
“The program, which is evolving into a comprehensive and integrated air defense capability for Czech skies, reflects the ministry’s strategy, which views defense exports as a central pillar in strengthening the IDF's force build-up, advancing foreign policy objectives, and driving growth in the defense industries and the Israeli economy,” Israel’s Defense Ministry said in a statement.
The SPYDER system is a mobile, quick‑reaction air‑defense solution designed to protect against a wide spectrum of aerial threats.
SPYDER will project stationary, maneuvering ground forces on battlefield, Czech Def. Min. says
According to the Czech Defense Ministry, the SPYDER will protect stationary objects as well as maneuvering ground forces on the battlefield.
Rafael’s SPYDER family of short- to long-range mobile, quick-reaction, combat-proven Air Defense Systems includes the SPYDER SR, SPYDER MR, SPYDER LR, SPYDER ER, and the SPYDER All-in-One.
It is built around the Python‑5 and Derby missiles, adapted from air‑to‑air use for ground launch and designed to counter aircraft, helicopters, UAVs, and precision‑guided munitions. The system uses an electro-optical observation payload and wireless data-link communication and can engage multiple threats simultaneously up to 160 kilometers away in all weather conditions.
The EL/M 2106 radar, manufactured by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) subsidiary, Elta, can track up to 500 targets simultaneously in all weather conditions while on the move.
Its modular architecture allows for both stationary and mobile deployment, and its rapid response time is intended to provide effective protection of strategic assets in complex air environments.
SPYDER has been operational for more than 15 years. Several militaries worldwide use it, including Romania, the United Arab Emirates, Morocco, India, the Philippines, Vietnam, and Singapore.

The outlet described the statement as rejecting recent claims that a direct warning had been conveyed to Netanyahu.
The statement is the clearest response from the UAE to date to the controversy sparked by an investigation published by Haaretz, which claimed that about a week and a half before the Hamas attack, MBZ called Netanyahu and warned him that Yahya Sinwar, then-leader of Hamas in the Gaza Strip, was planning a significant move against Israel.
According to the investigation, the call lasted approximately 45 minutes, and the information was not subsequently passed on to the heads of Israel’s security establishment.
The Prime Minister’s Office denied the report from the outset, saying that no conversation between Netanyahu and MBZ had taken place during the period in question and that the prime minister had not received any warning from him.
Netanyahu also announced that he intended to file a libel lawsuit against Haaretz and the authors of the investigation.
New response follows cautious, noncommittal statement from UAE
The new response from Abu Dhabi comes after the UAE Foreign Ministry issued a more cautious statement on September 8.
At the time, the ministry declined to confirm or deny that the conversation had taken place, saying that the government does not comment on “reports or speculation” regarding conversations between leaders. At the same time, it emphasized that direct lines of communication exist between Israeli and Emirati authorities, and that relevant intelligence is shared, when necessary, between the appropriate bodies.
In recent weeks, the issue has become a major focus of Israel’s political debate ahead of the elections, particularly over which warnings reached the political leadership before the October 7 attack, who was exposed to them, and whether they were passed on to security officials.
The National also noted in its latest report that the affair has taken on particular significance against the backdrop of the election campaign and the parties’ focus on security issues.

Türkiye's Erdogan heads to UN as leaders gather amid Middle East, Russia-Ukraine wars and AI risks

World leaders gather in New York this week for the UN General Assembly, bracing for US President Donald Trump's return to the rostrum for a second year running, with talks centring on the widening conflicts in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war and the risks of artificial intelligence.
Nearly 130 heads of state meet with the post-World War II order under strain and with the UN itself struggling to remain relevant.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan will travel to the United States from September 20 to 23 for high-level engagements and make a speech at the "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All" session.
He is set to join the general debates of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, according to an announcement by Türkiye’s Head of Communications Burhanettin Duran on his social media account.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping will skip New York in favour of one-on-one talks with Trump in Washington on Thursday, fueling debate about the UN's relevance in addressing global crises.
Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organisation.
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres completes his term at the end of 2026, with no clear frontrunner in the race to replace him.
The 15-member UN Security Council may hold high-level meetings on Russia-Ukraine war, AI and the conflicts in the Middle East, including talks with Arab leaders, diplomats said.
More than a year into Trump's second term, "we would no longer say that the UN is in freefall, but we would say that it's stuck in an open-ended crisis," said Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group.
"The UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it seems to be trapped in a trauma centre for the foreseeable future," Gowan said.
The US avoided losing its vote at the assembly by paying $725 million in contributions to the regular budget this week, but it still owes the organisation more than a billion dollars and makes ongoing demands for cuts and reforms.
Growing AI risks
The assembly meets shortly after several artificial intelligence industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and escape human control.
Guterres has said that AI will be a major topic, adding that countries pushing its frontiers should set up "common guardrails in order to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level."
The secretary-general has long proposed global governance of AI.
In 2023, the UN created an advisory body on the technology, with members including tech executives, government officials and academics.
Middle East tensions
The Middle East will again be a focus of discussions, as the US-Israeli war on Iran continues to drive global inflation and destabilise the region. Recent attacks by Yemen’s Houthis threaten shipping in the vital Bab al Mandab Strait and could further spike energy prices.
"It's very difficult to have a military solution for that problem, and the experience of fighting in Yemen demonstrated how complicated it is to have successful interventions," said Guterres, adding that the UN's envoy on Yemen was making a "huge effort" to advance talks.
Peace talks remain stalled, however, as Iran and the US continue to exchange strikes and Trump threatens a major escalation of the war.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the assembly on Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – wanted by the International Criminal Court over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza – is to speak on Thursday.
For the second year in a row, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will not be able to attend the gathering in person. The US, an Israeli ally, denied him a visa again —leading the General Assembly to vote on Thursday to allow Abbas to address the meeting via video.
There is likely to be a high-level meeting on the conflict in Sudan on the sidelines, diplomats said, although a diplomatic breakthrough is unlikely.
Russia-Ukraine war, food security
Also on the agenda is Russia and Ukraine's more than four-year-old war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will address the General Assembly.
Zelenskyy will likely seek to shore up Ukraine's position ahead of what is expected to be another tough winter, diplomats said.
The Security Council has been unable to take action to end the conflict because permanent member Russia holds a veto.
Trump has at times appeared frustrated that he has been unable to broker an end to the war, a goal he declared a priority when he began his second term in January last year.
The US president spoke with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin earlier this month, but it was unclear whether he plans to meet Zelenskyy in New York.
Guterres highlighted the impact the war was having on civilians but also on food security and energy prices.
"The effective blockade existing in the Black Sea is creating enormous problems that add to the problems generated by the Middle East crisis, and I think it would be very important to find a way to allow Ukrainian exports and Russian exports of food, fertilisers and energy to take place in a safe way through the Black Sea," he said.

Dead engines and planes that flew themselves: 10 aviation stories so bizarre they sound fake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
09:06:38 UTC
18:06:38 KST

Aviation is built around strict procedures, redundant systems and layer upon layer of safety. Yet over the decades, there have been moments when reality proved stranger than anything a screenwriter could invent. 
Human error, rare mechanical failures, unexpected decisions and almost impossible coincidences have produced incidents that continued to fascinate investigators, aircrews and aviation enthusiasts for years. Here are 10 of the strangest, most surprising and unforgettable.
Flying without a roof
On April 28, 1988, Aloha Airlines Flight 243 took off from Hilo, Hawaii, bound for Honolulu. About 20 minutes after departure, as the Boeing 737 flew at roughly 24,000 feet, it suffered a catastrophic structural failure: a large section of the upper fuselage tore away in flight, leaving an entire stretch of the passenger cabin completely open to the sky. 
Passengers sitting in the area suddenly found themselves inside what looked almost like a flying convertible, exposed to violent winds, deafening noise and rapid decompression.
Flight attendant Clarabelle Lansing, who was standing in the aisle at the time, was swept from the aircraft and her body was never found. Despite the extreme damage and fears that the plane could break apart, the flight crew managed to retain control and land safely at Kahului Airport on Maui. Everyone else aboard survived, although dozens were injured.
Investigators concluded that metal fatigue and accumulated damage to the fuselage, partly linked to the aircraft’s enormous number of takeoff-and-landing cycles in a marine environment, contributed to the extraordinary rupture.
The captain sucked out of the plane, and survived
On the morning of June 10, 1990, British Airways Flight 5390 departed Birmingham for Malaga with 81 passengers and six crew members aboard. About 13 minutes after takeoff, as the aircraft climbed through roughly 17,300 feet, a deafening bang erupted in the cockpit.
One of the front windshields, on Captain Tim Lancaster’s side, had blown out because of the pressure difference. The explosive decompression ripped Lancaster from his seat and pulled his upper body outside the aircraft, while his legs remained inside the cockpit.
Flight attendant Nigel Ogden lunged forward and grabbed him, with other crew members later joining the effort to hold Lancaster against the tremendous airflow and freezing temperatures. For portions of the roughly 20-minute ordeal, they believed the captain might already be dead, but refused to let go.
First Officer Alastair Atchison, meanwhile, took sole control of the aircraft and made an emergency landing at Southampton. Lancaster survived with fractures, bruising and frostbite.
The investigation revealed how the extraordinary incident began. The windshield had been replaced shortly before the flight, and 84 of the 90 bolts securing it were smaller in diameter than required. The remaining six were also the wrong size.
The plane that landed itself
On February 2, 1970, a U.S. Air Force F-106 Delta Dart interceptor took off from Montana on a training flight. During an air-combat exercise, the aircraft entered a flat spin, rotating almost horizontally while losing altitude, and the pilot was unable to recover.
After every attempt to regain control failed, he made the obvious decision and ejected, leaving behind a fighter jet that appeared certain to crash within minutes.
Instead, the opposite happened. The change in weight and balance caused by the pilot’s ejection altered the aircraft’s behavior, and the F-106 recovered from the spin on its own.
With nobody in the cockpit, it continued descending, stabilized and eventually made an astonishingly gentle belly landing in a snow-covered field near Big Sandy, Montana.
The damage was relatively minor. The aircraft was recovered, repaired and even returned to operational service. The incident earned it the famous nickname "Cornfield Bomber," although it was neither a bomber nor, at the time, sitting in an active cornfield. The aircraft survives to this day and is displayed at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force.
All four engines died, then came back to life
On June 24, 1982, British Airways Flight 9 was flying from London to Auckland, with stops in Asia and Australia. As the Boeing 747 cruised at night at around 37,000 feet over Indonesia, the crew began noticing strange phenomena: a bluish glow around the windows, a sharp smell of smoke and what appeared to be dust flowing over the wings.
Within minutes, one engine began losing power, followed by another, then a third and finally the fourth. All four engines had shut down.
Without the crew realizing it, the aircraft had flown into a cloud of volcanic ash from Mount Galunggung.
The 747 became a giant glider and began losing altitude as the crew repeatedly attempted to restart the engines and prepared passengers for the possibility of ditching in the sea.
After several long minutes of gliding, the aircraft emerged from the ash cloud. The pilots were then able to restart the engines gradually.
Even then, the ordeal was not over. The ash had sandblasted the cockpit windows until visibility through them was severely reduced. Despite that, the crew managed to land safely in Jakarta. There were no fatalities.
The airship that came home without its crew
On the morning of August 16, 1942, the U.S. Navy airship L-8 departed Treasure Island in San Francisco Bay on a routine anti-submarine patrol. Only two crew members were aboard, Ernest Cody and Charles Adams.
Some time after takeoff, they radioed that they had spotted what appeared to be an oil slick at sea and intended to investigate. It was effectively their final meaningful communication.
Hours later, residents around Daly City were stunned to see the airship returning from the ocean alone, losing altitude before eventually crashing to the ground.
When Navy personnel examined the aircraft, the truly strange part of the story emerged. The crew compartment was empty, yet investigators found no obvious evidence of a struggle or disaster that could explain how both men had disappeared in flight.
They were never found.
The L-8 itself already had a notable history. Months earlier, it had delivered critical equipment to the aircraft carrier USS Hornet ahead of the Doolittle Raid on Japan. But what happened to Cody and Adams remains one of the strangest mysteries in World War II military aviation.
The teenager who embarrassed the Soviet Union
On May 28, 1987, Mathias Rust, a 19-year-old amateur West German pilot with only a few dozen hours of flying experience, took off from Helsinki in a rented Cessna 172. His real destination was not listed in his flight plan: Moscow.
At the height of the Cold War, Rust penetrated Soviet airspace and flew hundreds of miles through one of the world’s most formidable air-defense systems.
Contrary to the myth that later developed around the incident, the Cessna was not invisible. Soviet radar detected it at several points, but a chain of identification, coordination and decision-making failures allowed it to continue.
After nearly five and a half hours, Rust reached central Moscow, searched for somewhere to land near the Kremlin, brought the Cessna down on a bridge over the Moskva River and then taxied toward Red Square, near St. Basil’s Cathedral.
Stunned bystanders surrounded the aircraft before Rust was arrested.
The humiliation for the Soviet military was immense. The penetration exposed serious weaknesses in a system considered nearly impenetrable, and senior defense officials were dismissed in the aftermath.
Rust, who said he had wanted to create a "bridge" of peace between East and West, was sentenced to four years in prison.
The ground worker who stole an airliner and went stunt flying
On the evening of August 10, 2018, something that initially seemed almost impossible unfolded at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Richard Russell, a 28-year-old Horizon Air ground employee, entered an empty Bombardier Q400 passenger aircraft alone, started it, taxied to a runway and simply took off.
Russell did not have a pilot’s license, and investigators found no evidence that he had received formal flight training. Through his work, however, he was familiar with some aircraft systems, knew how to operate its auxiliary power unit and had experience moving planes on the ground. The FBI also found that he had watched flight-instruction videos online.
For more than an hour, Russell flew over the Puget Sound area, performed unusual maneuvers and held lengthy, at times strikingly calm, conversations with air traffic controllers who tried to persuade him to land.
At 8:46 p.m., the flight ended when the aircraft crashed on Ketron Island. Russell was the only person aboard. The FBI investigation found no accomplices, terrorist motive or broader plot. Analysis of the flight data showed that the final descent toward the ground was deliberate. The medical examiner ruled his death a suicide.
Passengers watched their own emergency landing on live TV
On September 21, 2005, JetBlue Flight 292 took off from Burbank, California, bound for New York. Shortly after departure, the pilots discovered an unusual problem. The Airbus A320’s nose landing gear had remained extended, with its two wheels turned sideways and locked at a 90-degree angle to the direction of travel.
The crew decided to divert to Los Angeles and remain in the air for hours to reduce the aircraft’s weight before attempting a landing.
But the passengers had something few people aboard an emergency flight ever experience: live television on JetBlue’s seatback screens.
News networks soon began broadcasting live footage of the aircraft circling Los Angeles. The people sitting inside it could watch anchors and aviation experts discussing, in real time, the chances that their own flight would land safely.
Passengers later said watching the coverage only heightened their anxiety. The live feed was switched off before the landing itself.
The pilot touched down first on the main landing gear and kept the nose in the air as long as possible before finally lowering the damaged gear onto the runway. Its tires shredded, sparks flew and flames appeared beneath the nose, but the aircraft came to a safe stop. Nobody was injured.
The pilot who let his son fly the plane, with catastrophic consequences
On March 23, 1994, Aeroflot Flight 593 was flying from Moscow to Hong Kong when something happened in the cockpit of the Airbus A310 that should never have happened.
During cruise, the relief captain brought his two children into the cockpit and allowed them, one at a time, to sit in the pilot’s seat and touch the controls while the aircraft was being flown by autopilot.
When his 15-year-old son applied sustained pressure to the control column, the force was sufficient to partially override the autopilot on the roll axis. The entire system did not disengage at once, meaning the developing situation was not immediately obvious to the crew.
Gradually, the aircraft began banking, with the angle becoming increasingly severe. By the time the crew realized something was wrong, they were facing a rapidly developing sequence of altitude and speed changes and a loss of control.
At one stage, the pilots almost managed to stabilize the aircraft, but the correction that followed caused a loss of speed and created another dangerous situation. There was not enough altitude left for a complete recovery. The A310 crashed in the Kemerovo region of Siberia, killing all 75 people aboard.
The investigation concluded that the central cause was the partial, unintentional disengagement of the autopilot after an unauthorized person had been allowed to occupy the pilot’s position.
The airliner that became a glider
On July 23, 1983, Air Canada Flight 143 was flying from Montreal to Edmonton via Ottawa. The Boeing 767 was still relatively new to the airline’s fleet, and Air Canada was in the process of switching from imperial measurements to the metric system.
The aircraft’s fuel quantity indication system was not functioning properly, meaning crews had to manually calculate how much fuel was in the tanks and how much needed to be added.
That was where the critical error occurred. The calculation used a fuel-density figure measured in pounds per liter instead of kilograms per liter. As a result, the crew believed the aircraft was carrying far more fuel than it actually had. At 41,000 feet over Canada, one engine shut down. Soon afterward, the second engine failed as well.
Suddenly, a wide-body passenger jet weighing tens of tons had become a glider. Captain Bob Pearson and First Officer Maurice Quintal realized they would not reach their planned airport and instead chose a former military base at Gimli.
There was another complication. One of the old runways had been converted into a motor-racing track, and people were on it that day. Pearson managed to land the 767 without engine power. The nose landing gear collapsed as the aircraft slowed, but nobody was killed.
The plane was repaired and returned to service, earning a nickname that has followed it ever since: the "Gimli Glider."

Tiny Hairs That Help Corals Breathe May Malfunction in Warming Oceans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
At first glance, corals present as little more than colorful rocks—piles of lobes, stalagmites, and branches poking out from the seafloor.
They are anything but. Corals are complex creatures that form enduring colonies, and just like other animals they need oxygen to live. Across the living surface of coral, a frantic dance of survival takes place, invisible to our eyes and unknown to science before 2014. The tiny dancers are hairlike cilia, and new research into these microscopic structures is revealing just how active corals are in determining their own fate.
Corals aren’t fortunate enough to have a consistent supply of oxygen, and they can’t change location to seek it out. During the day, the tiny polyps that make up a coral colony get plenty of oxygen from the symbiotic algae that photosynthesize within their tissues. But at night that process stops, and a coral polyp’s only source of oxygen is the water around it. Then it’s do or die for the cilia. Using mechanisms scientists are still trying to understand, the cilia wave around to generate fast-moving vortices of water that circulate oxygen to the coral’s outer tissues, in addition to helping keep the colonies free of sediment.
A study published in Science in May 2026 provides new insight into how organisms with no brain or musculoskeletal system can generate and regulate this process—and what happens when the water around them warms up. Warmer water naturally carries less oxygen, which prompts corals to move their cilia faster and faster, as if gasping for breath. Above a certain temperature, the system starts to work against itself; the furious beating of cilia uses up any oxygen the coral’s tissues can absorb, and then the polyps can suffocate in the less oxygenated water. Biophysicists, marine biologists, mathematicians, and modelers are now collaborating to better understand the physiological and hydrodynamic forces at work, and how they correlate with bleaching patterns, coral disease, and mass die-offs.
This dynamic picture is somewhat new to scientists, who have long used corals’ symbiotic algal partners as indicators of their health. Cilia may serve as a more direct signal, said Rachel Alderdice, a marine biologist who studies coral stress biomarkers and genomics at the University of Konstanz in Germany and was not involved in the research. “It’s these finer details that could help us understand why some corals bleach and others don’t, [even when] they sit right beside each other.”
Every coral colony is cushioned by a thin boundary layer of water whose movement is slowed by friction at the coral’s surface. Researchers assumed that corals were passive with respect to the slow-moving boundary layer, simply relying on natural diffusion through it to provide nutrients and oxygen.
Then, in 2014, a team from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Weizmann Institute of Science published a groundbreaking study showing that coral cilia interact with the boundary layer by rapidly whipping about to generate swirls of fresh, oxygenated seawater. Until a decade ago, scientists thought of these cilia merely as brooms that move mucus and sweep away waste particles and other debris. The research not only modeled the tiny vortices created by the cilia for the first time, but also revealed the cilia’s importance for survival and metabolism.
At first, the microbiologist and environmental engineer Orr Shapiro, who led the 2014 work at MIT as a postdoctoral fellow, was interested in how microbes that infect corals and cause disease follow concentration gradients, a process called chemotaxis. Under the microscope, he noticed something weird: In the boundary layer, particles were swirling around and mixing together—not at all like the passive diffusion he had been expecting.
“That was to me, and I think later on to the entire field, sort of a paradigm shift,” said Shapiro, now a researcher at the Volcani Institute in Israel. It became clear that the boundary layer wasn’t static, but rather a dynamic zone, and one where cilia were creating their own turbulence. The realization inspired Shapiro’s team to go off on a tangent, mapping the flow of oxygen to coral tissues via cilia. “It really transformed how we understand this [micro]environment, because suddenly the diffusion is no longer really important,” Shapiro said.
Diffusion is the default route for nutrients traveling through water, but it’s painfully slow. It can take as long as four minutes for oxygen to travel just 1 millimeter. That’s why the fast-moving flows created by cilia are so important: because naturally flowing water slows down near the coral’s surface, and corals consume oxygen faster than diffusion can supply it.
It is a system that delivers enough oxygen, despite the cilia’s energy consumption. But there’s a downside: Oxygen dwindles as temperature climbs. That’s when corals run into trouble.
Scientists have a clear understanding of one thing that happens to corals when water gets too hot: bleaching. As water temperatures rise, a coral’s symbiotic algae become stressed and release molecules that are toxic to the coral in large quantities. To protect itself, the coral expels its own algae—a primary food, energy, and oxygen source—and soon loses its color. It’s a slow death and an increasingly common occurrence as heat waves sweep across the world’s reefs.
But sometimes, some corals on a reef bleach while others don’t, and in other cases corals under heat stress die without expelling their algae. An international team of microbiologists, engineers, and physiologists was eager to understand how heat affects cilia, and whether this could explain different types of coral death.
“We’re living in a world right now of extreme scenarios,” said Cesar Pacherres, a co-author of the new study and a marine biologist at the University of Copenhagen who studies fluid dynamics. As marine heat waves become more common, and as a particularly strong El Niño year threatens to catalyze a fifth global bleaching event in late 2026, “corals can experience an increase in temperature of several degrees in a time frame of a few hours,” Pacherres said.
To explore heat’s impact on cilia, the team ran a series of 24-hour experiments. They exposed aquarium-raised stony coral called Porites lutea to incrementally higher water temperatures up to 39 degrees Celsius (more than 102 degrees Fahrenheit)—an extreme scenario, but one that could occur. They kept the tanks dark to better observe how cilia transport oxygen when algae aren’t producing any.
Every hour, the researchers recorded the microscopic cilia with a high-speed camera to capture how frequently they moved as they were exposed to warmer and warmer water. The team also used a technology called SensPIV to track oxygen flow. Fluorescent, oxygen-reactive nanoparticles “traced” the water swirls, creating a vivid map of how oxygen concentrations corresponded to the cilia’s vortices.
Visualizing the movement of oxygen was key to the team’s findings. In warmer water, corals burned energy faster, which increased their demand for oxygen—prompting the cilia to dance faster. But there’s only so much dissolved oxygen available in the surrounding water, and as temperatures climbed, the cilia started to send oxygen-deficient water toward the coral in their frenzy. “The oxygen demand of the coral increased faster than the increased swirling of the water,” said co-author Michael Kühl, a marine microbiologist at the University of Copenhagen.
When the water approached 37 degrees Celsius (the temperature of the human body), the cilia started to slow down. Past 39 degrees Celsius, they shut down altogether, and the coral died. These were the findings they reported in Science in May 2026.
Pacherres cautioned against interpreting these temperature limits as a standard threshold; each species of coral is adapted to its own range of daily temperature fluctuations. Even so, climate change has started to push many corals toward their respective limits, with record-high surface water temperatures nearing 38 degrees Celsius in places such as Florida.
Why the cilia move faster in hotter water remains a mystery. Perhaps seawater’s viscosity—which decreases as temperature increases, making the water thinner—affects ciliary movements, Shapiro said. Corals lack a central nervous system and brain, but they do have neurons—inside what’s called a nerve net—to process sensory information. Perhaps the coral senses heat or lack of oxygen, and some biological mechanism then triggers the faster beating. “It’s physics, biology, engineering, all mixed up together, which is what makes it really interesting,” he said.
Scientists are now investigating cilia physiology and the boundary layer as a whole. “It’s much more complex than we thought,” Shapiro said.
In another paper co-authored by Pacherres and Kühl in May 2026, they found that cilia’s vortices resemble corkscrews. The turbulence pushes unwanted particles away from the coral’s surface while redirecting nutrients toward polyps’ mouths.
The cilia on each polyp, they found, are arranged in hexagonal units that keep ciliary movement streamlined, which helps explain how cilia can coordinate their movement to produce predictable swirls. “It demonstrates that coral skeletal architecture and living tissue are functionally integrated,” Pacherres said.
Combined, the studies recontextualize how ciliary movement, previously overlooked, gives corals some stability and buffers them against environmental change, he said.
The relationship between cilia and bleaching remains ambiguous, said Alderdice, who was not involved in the studies. But testing cilia under bleaching conditions without heat—by using red light, for example, which can also trigger bleaching—would help answer this question.
Scientists knew from the 2014 work that cilia help corals self-ventilate when water flow is low, said David Suggett, a marine biologist at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology who wasn’t involved in the research. “But until this point, we had been focusing on molecular and metabolic machinery” to understand how corals evolved to deal with low-oxygen conditions, he said. “We hadn’t really appreciated that there are these behavioral-physiological mechanisms at play.”
For Suggett, the research raises a critical question: What does this say about how corals will deal with future climates?
Sometimes, corals of a single reef don’t bleach evenly, with some individuals dying off while their neighbors persist. In new research led by Suggett’s colleague Tadd Truscott, marine biologists are finding that these patchy bleaching patterns are correlated with areas of reduced water flow—areas therefore receiving less oxygen.
Next, Kühl and Pacherres’ team wants to test corals under different conditions—especially under normal light-dark cycles—and to better understand the mechanism driving ciliary beating. Is it a molecular process that activates their movement? The physics of warmer seawater? A bit of both, or something else?
It’s only in the past decade that scientists have realized the role of deoxygenation in coral health, Suggett said. Ocean acidification took center stage as the primary concern for corals in the early 2000s. In hindsight, deoxygenation was a much bigger issue, he said. The new research suggests that deoxygenation, not just bleaching, is a fatal threat to corals resulting from a hotter climate.
“We’re playing massive catch-up,” Suggett said. “The amount of information we’re gathering quickly is demonstrating just what a problem for corals it is—so much so that we’re starting to really revisit long-standing paradigms of the role of other environmental factors, like temperature and light, where in fact, it could be oxygen that’s been the smoking gun all along.”
Original story reprinted with permission from Quanta Magazine, an editorially independent publication of the Simons Foundation whose mission is to enhance public understanding of science by covering research developments and trends in mathematics and the physical and life sciences.

ISLAMABAD, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Pakistan's Senate Deputy Chairman Syedaal Khan has underscored the enduring Pakistan-China partnership and expressed readiness to deepen bilateral cooperation and share in development opportunities.
While addressing a seminar on Friday in Islamabad organized by the Diplomatic Focus, an Islamabad-based media organization, to celebrate 75 years of diplomatic relations, Khan said Pakistan and China have stood by each other through difficult times, demonstrating the strength, depth and resilience of their longstanding friendship.
Over the decades, China has played an important role in supporting Pakistan's development and economic growth, particularly through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), he said, adding that the flagship project has contributed to infrastructure development, connectivity, energy and employment opportunities.
Talking about China's remarkable growth over the years, the deputy senate chairman said Pakistan greatly values China's experience and achievements in areas including economic development, governance, education, technology, agriculture and social development.
"There is considerable scope for Pakistan to benefit from China's experience while adapting relevant practices to its own national circumstances. Increased exchanges between institutions, businesses, universities and people can further strengthen cooperation and promote the sharing of knowledge, skills and expertise," he added.

Greater collaboration in these sectors can create new opportunities for investment, employment, innovation and sustainable economic growth, he said, adding that the historic Pakistan-China friendship, built over 75 years of diplomatic ties, provides a strong foundation for expanding this partnership and further strengthening the bonds between the two peoples.
In his speech, Shi Yuanqiang, charge d'affaires of the Chinese embassy in Pakistan, said that, as a flagship project of the Belt and Road Initiative, the CPEC has always adhered to the principle of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, achieving remarkable results that have attracted worldwide attention.

Explainer: How will China's Pinglu Canal chart new economic tides for ASEAN
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:59:13 CST
17:59:13 KST

HONG KONG, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- The Pinglu Canal, China's first national-level river-sea navigation waterway built since 1949, officially opened to traffic Wednesday, marking another milestone in the country's infrastructure development for opening up.
Spanning 134.2 km and designed for vessels up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal runs from Hengzhou, a county-level city in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, to the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China.
The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets.
Functioning as an open regional public good rooted in development-oriented cooperation, the canal underpins the physical conditions for the upgraded China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 and is expected to reinforce broader regional economic integration in various ways.
EASIER MARKET ACCESS TO CHINA
The Pinglu Canal cuts the inland shipping distance for southwest-China-bound cargo to the sea by more than 560 km and reduces comprehensive logistics costs by 18-30 percent.
The canal delivers a cost-competitive river-sea intermodal shortcut connecting ASEAN producers with the vast consumer market in southwest China. Tropical fruits, aquatic products, grain, rubber, minerals and other bulk commodities from ASEAN can reach Guangxi and China's inland southwest via Beibu Gulf ports and the canal network at lower freight costs and with greater delivery reliability.
"The canal becomes the region's shortest and most economical sea-access corridor," Vietnam's Danang News observed in its online report, adding that it will create new impetus for freight transport and trade with ASEAN.
For maritime-reliant economies including Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia, the waterway offers an additional viable logistics option for their export-oriented goods, according to Zhang Hongshi, president of the Guangxi Academy of Social Sciences, who added that for land-locked ASEAN member Laos, the canal complements the China-Laos Railway and New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor block trains to expand its connectivity to regional and global markets.
Liu Yingkui, researcher at the Academy of China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, noted that ASEAN small-and medium-sized trading enterprises also stand to benefit from new avenues to tap China's inland consumption base.
DEEPER CROSS-BORDER INDUSTRIAL COOPERATION
Beyond facilitating commodity trade, reduced logistics costs drive shifts in bilateral trade patterns and foster more integrated regional supply chains.
ASEAN mineral resources, agricultural produce and seafood can be transported efficiently to southwest China for deep-processing. In return, Chinese manufactured products such as new-energy vehicles, power batteries, photovoltaic equipment and engineering machinery flow to Southeast Asia along the same route, noted Yu Hong, senior research fellow at the East Asian Institute, National University of Singapore.
This will boost growth in intermediate-goods trade and closer upstream-downstream industrial collaboration, Yu said.
"Large-scale circulation of capital, technology, talent and labor will spur new cross-border investment and industrial-cooperation projects and enable more efficient integration of regional industrial and supply chains," said Lu Xinning, vice chairperson of the regional government of Guangxi.
Meanwhile, enhanced connectivity is expected to support the expansion of port-side processing and cross-border logistics services across ASEAN, generating local jobs and enabling fuller participation in RCEP-led labor division, Liu added.
CATALYZING INSTITUTIONAL UPGRADES, BROADER OPENING-UP
Infrastructure alone cannot automatically deliver full economic dividends, as realising the canal's potential hinges on effective "soft connectivity," Yu said, citing the importance of alignment on customs clearance procedures, mutual recognition of inspection and quarantine results, seamless river-sea intermodal transfer and digital logistics platforms.
Yu pointed out that the Pinglu Canal's operational experience in multi-modal transport coordination, standardized vessel specifications and smart customs clearance offers referable practices for ASEAN countries building their own inland-coastal transport systems.
Wilson Lee Flores, a columnist for The Philippine Star, believed the canal's significance goes beyond cargo. "Ultimately, infrastructure such as the Pinglu Canal can turn geographic proximity into practical economic opportunity."
"If efficiently operated and complemented by good trade policies and sustainable development, it can become an important new link in the ASEAN-China economic relationship, a potential win-win corridor for entrepreneurs, traders, investors, workers, students, farmers, scientists, artists and consumers on both sides," said Flores.
Lu said the canal will help build a global hub for opening up.
"It will not only greatly elevate China-ASEAN regional cooperation, but also connect China-ASEAN ties with the Belt and Road Initiative by reaching north toward Eurasia, expanding regional opening-up and bringing benefits to ports and transport corridors along its route," Lu said. ■

Feature: Fighting way out of favela, young Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu coaches head for China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:59:13 CST
17:59:13 KST

A Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu coach trains at a gym in Shanghai, east China, Sept. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/You Zhixin)
by Xinhua writer Lu Junyu, You Zhixin and Zhou Yongsui
RIO DE JANEIRO/SHANGHAI, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- The rain in Sao Goncalo falls with a rattle, punching through the rusted tin roof of a 10-square-meter shack in the favela, or slum. Inside, the air is thick with humidity and sweat. A dozen children in frayed kimonos bow silently, drop into ground guards, and trade submission holds.
Outside lies one of Brazil's municipalities with the highest crime rate. These children are training to escape street poverty, and their ticket out is Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, which takes them to an unexpected destination, China.
For Rogerio Moura, 48, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu offered a lifeline. In 2008, Moura launched the project "Vencedores em Cristo," a grassroots social initiative to pull vulnerable kids in the favela off the streets.
"We now run three locations, guiding around 300 students as they progress from white belts to black belts," Moura said. "First, I want them to become good, law-abiding citizens. I also want to prove that Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu can be a tool to earn a living."
While many of the project's alumni now coach across Brazil and worldwide, a new and remarkable gateway has opened thousands of miles away in the East.
Fueled by global Ultimate Fighting Championship hype and homegrown stars like Zhang Weili, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu has exploded into a mainstream fitness trend across China's megacities. The boom resulted in a shortage of qualified black-belt instructors.
Saulo Melo, a Brazilian entrepreneur who has spent 14 years building a network of 22 Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu academies in China, saw a chance to bridge both worlds. Over the past two years, he has systematically recruited top talents from Moura's project.
"The moment you step onto a mat, you share knowledge and express yourself," Melo noted. "Our coaches teach Chinese students the value of resilience, and in return, China offers these young athletes a safe, dignified platform to turn a decade of grit into a career."
No story illustrates this journey better than that of 25-year-old Vieira.
Fifteen years ago, Vieira was a withdrawn boy in Sao Goncalo, grief-stricken after his father's death. With his mother working round-the-clock shifts, Vieira was left exposed to the streets until he joined the project.
"At first, we couldn't even afford uniforms, and three or four kids shared just one," Vieira recalled. "I went to training so that I could eat dinner at the project and spare my mother that burden."
The mat became his sanctuary. Vieira threw himself into the sport, eventually earning his black belt, capturing three Brazilian National Championship titles under the Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Confederation, and taking silver at the International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation European Championship. Two months ago, he moved to China's eastern metropolis Shanghai to coach full-time at Melo's BUSHIDO Gym.
"Now, I can walk down a Shanghai street at night without fear. I get to do what I love every single day," Vieira said.
For Maxsuell da Silva, 28, who grew up with the project and now balances a full-time job with volunteer coaching, Vieira's path serves as a clear blueprint. Preparing to join him in Shanghai, da Silva sees the move as a purpose, not just a career step. "I don't just want to teach flashy techniques or help kids chase belts," he said, watching the youngsters train. "I want to teach them character, kindness, and self-discipline -- how to be a good person both on and off the mat."
The project is also trying to break gender barriers in a traditionally male-dominated sport. For years, Kettly Viviane, 23, was the only female practitioner on the mat. Today, she is surrounded by young girls watching her every move with eager eyes.
"I used to be the only girl here, but now they see me coaching, and they know there's room for them too," she said, watching two young girls lock guards across the room. "Seeing my friends make it to China gives us all permission to dream bigger. It proves that no matter where you start, if you work hard, the world is open."
Back in the cramped room in Sao Goncalo, the rain drums in a steady rhythm against the tin roof. A new group of children tie their frayed belts, bow, and slap hands. In the dim light, they drop onto their knees to lock guards, their knuckles pressing firmly into the mat, fighting for every inch of leverage in a room that no longer feels quite so small. ■

Asian Games | China breaks world record to win women's 10m air rifle team gold
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:59:03 CST
17:59:03 KST

Du Yuchen (L), Han Jiayu (C) and Wang Zifei of team China pose for a group photo during the awarding ceremony of the 10m air rifle women team final of shooting at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Toyota of Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Sept. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Liu Lei)
TOYOTA, Japan, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China claimed the women's 10m air rifle team title with a new world record at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Sunday.
Wang Zifei, Han Jiayu and Du Yuchen all delivered strong performances in an event in which China has traditionally been strong, with each scoring more than 633 points.
The trio combined for 1,904.2 points to take the gold medal, breaking the previous world record of 1,902.0.
The women's 10m air rifle field is particularly competitive in Asia, with seven of the world's top 10 shooters coming from the continent. China, South Korea, India and Japan all fielded strong lineups at the Asian Games.
In the qualification stage, China's Wang Zifei maintained steady form throughout, consistently posting high scores to top the qualification standings with 636.8 points, just 1.1 points short of her own qualification world record in the event. Han scored 633.8 points, while young shooter Du Yuchen, competing in the second group, registered 633.6. Han and Du finished fifth and sixth respectively in qualification.
The team standings were determined by the combined qualification scores of each team's three shooters. China totaled 1,904.2 points to win gold and set a new world record, while India took silver with 1,898.0 and Japan bronze with 1,897.1.
All three Chinese shooters finished in the top eight in qualification, but with each team allowed a maximum of two places in the final, Du missed out by a narrow margin.
The Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya marked 16-year-old Du's first appearance at the continental event. Despite missing out on the individual final, she was "very excited" to have helped China win the gold and break the world record.
"This has given me valuable experience in major competitions. Having competed at a multi-sport event like the Asian Games, I feel more prepared for future events such as the Olympics," Du said.
In the final, Japan's Taichi Hinata won the individual gold with 253.0 points, while India's Elavenil Valarivan and South Korea's Ban Hyo-jin took silver and bronze respectively. Wang and Han finished fifth and seventh respectively. ■

Swiss to vote on referendum against new nuclear power plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Swiss to vote on referendum against new nuclear power plants
The Swiss are set to vote against the possibility of building new nuclear power stations. In a span of three months, more than 125,000 people signed the referendum petition against the government proposal that was approved by parliament in June.
“The success of this petition shows that the public rejects a return to nuclear power, a costly and dangerous technology that increases our dependence on uranium imports, particularly from Russia,” wrote the “No to New Nuclear Power Stations” coalition in a press release.
During the summer session, parliament had approved the government’s indirect counter-proposal to the “Stop the Blackout” (Electricity for All at All Times) popular initiative. The proposal aims to lift the ban on building new nuclear power stations in Switzerland.
More
Nuclear power in Switzerland: ‘The most sensible policy is to keep the existing plants running’
With this proposal, the government and parliament are “ignoring the will of the people”, the coalition for the referendum protested. It points out that the public has “clearly” spoken out three times in favour of a future based on renewable energy: through the adoption of the Energy Strategy 2050 in 2017, the Climate Protection Act in 2023 and the Electricity Act in 2024.
For the referendum committee, “this approach is bearing fruit: Switzerland is increasingly meeting its energy needs through locally produced solar, wind and hydro power.” Conversely, the costs and risks associated with nuclear power are considered “too high”.
The “No to New Nuclear Power Stations” coalition brings together the Greens, the Social Democrats, the Green Liberals, part of the Centre Party and around thirty organisations such as WWF, Greenpeace, Pro Natura and Swissolar.
