Delhi pollution crackdown: Hotspots to be mapped, pending road works get Oct 31 deadline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:22:53 UTC
17:22:53 KST

A thick layer of smog engulfs the India Gate and Kartavya Path as pollution level deteriorates, in New Delhi.
NEW DELHI: The Delhi government has stepped up its crackdown on air pollution, directing district administrations to map pollution hotspots, identify sources within a three-kilometre radius and assign agencies specific corrective measures and deadlines. The government has also set October 31 as the target for completing pending road and civil works, wherever feasible. It ordered tighter action against road dust, construction pollution, waste burning, illegal parking and traffic congestion.The directions were issued during district-level review meetings chaired by Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa for East, North-East, South-East and South Delhi. Officials were told to use AQI monitoring data to identify problem areas, assess the sources driving pollution and take immediate action at the ground level.
Hotspots to get source-specific action plans
District administrations will map pollution hotspots based on data from AQI monitoring stations. Each hotspot will then be assessed for sources such as road dust, traffic congestion, vehicular emissions, construction and demolition activity, unauthorised parking, open or uncovered areas and biomass or waste burning.
Where applicable, pollution-generating activities within a three-kilometre radius of each hotspot will also be examined.Authorities will prepare source-wise action plans setting out the remedial measure, the agency responsible and the timeline for implementation.Locations recording high levels of PM10 and PM2.5 will receive focused attention, particularly areas with heavy traffic, heavy-vehicle parking, significant road dust and congestion. Such locations will be inspected for their pollution sources and immediate remedial action will be taken.
October 31 target for pending road works
The government has directed agencies to complete pending civil works on priority and by October 31, wherever feasible.These include pothole repairs, treatment and development of brown areas and other road and roadside works. Officials have also been told to maintain completed works properly to reduce road-dust generation.Where essential works cannot be completed because other projects are still underway, agencies will have to continue water sprinkling and other dust-suppression measures until the road surface is restored.
Construction, waste burning face tighter action
The government has directed agencies to strictly enforce dust-control norms at construction and demolition sites. Violations will attract stringent action under applicable rules.The ban on biomass burning will also be enforced without exception. Preventive measures will be strengthened against the open burning of garbage, plastic and rubber waste, textile and fibre waste, industrial and organic residues, scrap and other combustible material.
Illegal parking and encroachments targeted
Officials were also directed to remove illegal encroachments from roads and public spaces where they contribute to congestion and obstruct traffic movement.The move is aimed at improving traffic flow and reducing pollution caused by idling vehicles and prolonged traffic movement.At Anand Vihar Bus Terminal, agencies have been directed to step up enforcement against unauthorised parking of buses and heavy vehicles. Cranes will be deployed wherever required to remove or tow such vehicles.
Patparganj gets special focus
Patparganj Industrial Area was identified for area-specific measures targeting road dust, traffic congestion and vehicular emissions.Agencies have been directed to maintain continuous water sprinkling and dust-control measures at vulnerable locations, particularly where road or allied works are underway.
Future roads to minimise exposed soil
For future applicable works, departments have been directed to incorporate end-to-end carpeting or paving of roads and relevant roadside areas wherever technically feasible and in accordance with applicable specifications.The aim is to reduce exposed soil and unpaved surfaces that can contribute to road dust.
The government has stressed closer coordination between departments and agencies, with responsibility for individual pollution-control measures clearly assigned.The meetings involved area MLAs, district magistrates, deputy commissioners of police, MCD deputy commissioners and senior officials from various departments.Officials from the Revenue Department, DPCC, PWD, MCD, Traffic Police, DSIIDC, I&FC, DJB, DMRC, NHAI and other agencies were involved in the coordinated effort.The minister also directed ground teams to maintain regular vigilance at vulnerable locations and take immediate action against violations. DPCC and enforcement agencies were asked to impose stringent penalties, including heavy challans wherever applicable.Officials were further told to ensure prompt resolution of citizen complaints, particularly those received through Helpline 311.

Far from the Holy of Holies: How did ancient Jews observe Yom Kippur 2,000 years ago?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:13:44 UTC
17:13:44 KST

Two thousand years ago, as the high priest entered the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur, Jews throughout the Land of Israel and across the Diaspora were fasting. But what else were they doing?
The Yom Kippur rituals and observances practiced in the Temple thousands of years ago are clearly enumerated in the Bible (Leviticus 16), the Mishnah (Yoma), and the Talmud.
During the Yom Kippur Service, the high priest (kohen gadol) offered a bull as a sin offering for himself and his household, and confessed his own sins and those of his household and the other kohanim.
Two identical goats were placed before him, and lots were drawn: one “for the Lord” and one “for azazel.”
The first would be sacrificed; the second became the famous se’ir la’azazel, often translated as the “scapegoat,” which was sent into the wilderness. The Mishnah describes it being taken to a cliff and pushed to its death.
The day’s special status was highlighted by the high priest’s entry into the Holy of Holies, where he offered incense.
While many people undoubtedly came to Jerusalem to see the Temple Service, Yom Kippur is not one of the three pilgrimage festivals, like Sukkot, Passover, and Shavuot, and there was no special mitzvah to go to Jerusalem.
How did Jews living in Beit Shemesh, the Galilee, or Beersheba observe Yom Kippur? What did the Jews in Alexandria, Rome, and Babylonia do on that day?
While the biblical rules of fasting and the prohibition of labor applied to everyone, the major prayers of Yom Kippur that we are so familiar with today – Kol Nidrei, “Avinu Malkenu,” “Unetaneh Tokef” – had not yet been composed.
Did they pray at home? Did they hold prayer assemblies? Did they attend a synagogue? If they prayed, what did they say?
The American writer and humorist James Thurber (1894-1961) once observed, “It is better to know some of the questions than all of the answers.” When it comes to reconstructing Yom Kippur as it was experienced by ordinary Jews 2,000 years ago, Thurber’s observation is particularly apt.
How Jews observed Yom Kippur outside Jerusalem
TO BETTER understand what Jews outside Jerusalem and in the Diaspora did on Yom Kippur during Temple times, I spoke with Prof. Yair Furstenberg of the Talmud department at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
Furstenberg suggests that the primary source that sheds light on what Jews outside the Temple did on Yom Kippur comes from the writings of Philo, the Jewish philosopher who lived in Alexandria, 20 BCE-50 CE, while the Second Temple was still standing. Alexandria was one of the most important Jewish communities in the ancient world.
In his work The Special Laws, Philo discusses Yom Kippur and notes that even less religiously observant Jews took the day seriously, a pattern echoed in many parts of the Jewish world today.
In section 186, he writes, “On the 10th day the fast takes place, which they take seriously – not only those who are zealous about piety and holiness, but even those who do nothing religious the rest of the time. For all are astounded, overcome with the sacredness of it; in fact, at that time the wicked compete with the righteous in self-control and virtue.”
Adds Furstenberg dryly, “The commentator here writes, ‘There is nothing new under the sun.’”
Beyond fasting, how did the people observe Yom Kippur?
Furstenberg again cites Philo (ibid. section B193), who writes, “From morning until evening, the people spend their time doing nothing else but offering fervent prayers, seeking to appeal to God and asking forgiveness for their sins, both intentional and unintentional, and hoping for His favor – not because of their own merit, but because of His merciful nature.”
Where and how did they pray?
While Talmudic sources attribute the origins of organized prayer to the time of Ezra, Furstenberg says that the idea of fixed prayer – the formal prayers with which we are familiar – was unknown in Judaism during the Second Temple period.
“We assume that synagogues are made for prayer,” he says, “but Second Temple sources associate synagogues with Torah study.”
Taking the question further, he asks, “Philo says that we’re asking for forgiveness and praying; who knows if there is someone who leads the prayer. Does one pray personally? How do you do it? It’s hard to say.”
If one accepts the Talmudic concept of fixed prayer during the Second Temple period, one could imagine Jews gathering to recite the Shema and the Amida and read the Torah on Yom Kippur.
If, however, Furstenberg’s theory is correct, then the question remains – what did they pray and how did they pray?
While Furstenberg says the standard format of fixed prayer we are familiar with did not exist at that time, the Qumran sect, which existed during the Second Temple period, from the second century BCE until 68 CE, had created its own set of fixed prayers.
The Dead Sea Scrolls, found in caves near Qumran on the northwestern shore of the Dead Sea about 35-40 km. east of Jerusalem, preserve prayers and liturgy from Jews who lived during this period and separated themselves from the religious establishment in Jerusalem.
One of the Yom Kippur prayers found in the Dead Sea Scrolls reads, “Remember, O Lord, the appointed time of Your mercy, and establish it for us – the appointed time of fasting, an everlasting statute.
“You know the hidden things and the revealed things, and You know our nature, our rising and our lying down. We live with sorrow in our hearts by day, and we have no confidence in our lives. Remember our sorrow and our weeping.”
Yom Kippur was not always a day of joy
Interestingly, the sect used the terms “sorrow” and “weeping” (Hebrew: yagon and bechi), which suggests a markedly somber understanding of the day, emphasizing sorrow and weeping with fasting and supplication.
While the Torah states that on Yom Kippur “you shall afflict yourselves” (Leviticus 23:27), Yom Kippur, according to most sources, is not considered a day of mourning.
Furstenberg adds that the Karaites, who appeared many years later, in the ninth century, also adopted the idea of affliction and sadness on Yom Kippur.
In one of their writings, it was stated that on Yom Kippur, one should “stand on one’s feet in prolonged prayer, again and again, to the point of afflicting oneself; deprive one’s eyes of sleep; change one’s clothes and dress in sackcloth and ashes; and weep with a loud voice until one’s strength is exhausted” (Jewish Festivals in the Time of the Mishnah and Talmud, by Joseph Tabory).
This approach sharply contrasts with a Mishnah at the end of Ta’anit (4:8), which states: “Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: There were no days as joyous for the Jewish people as the 15th of Av and as Yom Kippur…”
On those two days – Yom Kippur and the 15th of Av – the Mishnah continues, the daughters of Jerusalem would dress in borrowed white garments, so that poorer women would not be embarrassed, and dance in the vineyards. At the same time, young men sought wives, emphasizing character and family over beauty.
The Talmud connects the joy of Yom Kippur with the giving of the Second Tablets on that day, symbolizing reconciliation between God and Israel after the sin of the Golden Calf.
Furstenberg notes that this passage portrays Yom Kippur as a day of rejoicing. Why did the people of Jerusalem celebrate?
Beyond the Talmudic explanation, Furstenberg suggests that this celebratory spirit was connected to the release of tension surrounding the Temple Service, as the people waited for the high priest to emerge from the Holy of Holies.
Another source of tension surrounded the sending of the goat to Azazel, which symbolized the removal of the people’s sins.
What did Jews pray on Yom Kippur?
WHAT DOES all of this leave us with? How did the people outside the Temple, both in the Land of Israel and the Diaspora, pray on Yom Kippur? Did they have fixed prayers or informal prayers?
Even if they had a set prayer format, there is little reason to assume that they sat in a synagogue all day, listening to prayer leaders chant complicated liturgical poems as many do today.
For many, Yom Kippur may therefore have included far more private prayer and introspection than the synagogue-centered observance familiar to us today.
Furstenberg suggests that for many, the Temple was the focal point of worship that day, and those who were not there had to wait for the results. Something larger than them was happening. “I think that makes sense in an ancient mindset,” he concludes.
We may never know precisely what a Jew in Alexandria, the Galilee, or Babylonia said to God on Yom Kippur 2,000 years ago. Ironically, even today, with hundreds of pages of carefully ordered prayers before us, we can sometimes find ourselves facing the same problem: What do we say?
Prayer throughout the year, and especially on Yom Kippur, can be difficult, and the combination of ritual and introspection can be especially challenging.
Perhaps the challenge of Yom Kippur prayer is not simply finding the right words, but the sincerity behind them.
A story attributed to the Baal Shem Tov (1700-1760) tells of an uneducated man who could not recite the High Holy Day prayers. Knowing only part of the Hebrew alphabet, he repeatedly recited its letters and told God: “Please, Master of the Universe, take my letters and form them into words that will please You.”
His simple prayer embodied the principle of Rahmana liba ba’i – “The Merciful One desires the heart.”

Pahlavi: Iran regime continues to erode from within as defections grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:13:33 UTC
17:13:33 KST

Iran’s exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi said Saturday that members of the Islamic Republic’s military and civilian establishment were already quietly breaking with the regime, describing Iran as having entered an “active defection” phase in the struggle to overthrow the country’s rulers.
Addressing thousands of supporters at the "Cyrus the Great II" gathering in Toronto over the weekend, Pahlavi outlined how in the months since the bloody January uprising, when over 40,000 Iranians were killed on the streets, the opposition had regrouped, adapted its tactics and expanded networks inside Iran, even as the regime sought to convince Iranians that the protest movement had been defeated.
“We are more experienced, more cohesive and more determined today than ever before,” he told the gathering. “Our objective is clear: the overthrow of the Islamic Republic and achieving a free and prosperous Iran.”
Central to his speech was the claim that erosion within the regime itself is continuing. For months, Pahlavi has said that officials from within the Islamic Republic’s apparatus have been quietly reaching out to him to signal their clandestine opposition to the regime.
These members of Iran’s civilian and military structures have used secure channels to distance themselves from the Islamic Republic and side with the opposition. For now, Pahlavi argued, many remain outwardly within the system, retaining their positions while gradually ceasing to perform the functions expected of them.
“They remain within the structure outwardly, but they no longer perform their former functions for the regime,” he said. “Quietly, but decisively, they are eroding the pillars of repression from within.”
Open defections, including soldiers publicly laying down their weapons, would represent a later stage reached once the balance of power had shifted decisively toward the opposition.
Pahlavi placed January's anti-regime protests within cycle of longer period of Iran unrest
During his Toronto address, Pahlavi also placed January’s uprising within a much longer period of unrest in Iran, dating back through several protest cycles.
Rather than portraying December-January’s demonstrations as an isolated explosion of anger, he traced their origins through a decade of growing opposition, from the large Cyrus Day gatherings of 2016, through the protests of 2017-18 and November 2019, to the nationwide uprising that followed Mahsa Amini's death in 2022. Saturday also saw global marches across the Iranian diaspora to mark four years since Amini’s death in the custody of the Iranian regime.
“The great uprising of Dey was not the product of a fleeting burst of emotion,” he said. “Behind it lay a long, difficult and costly road.”
The events of January 8 and 9, when the Islamic Republic launched a massive crackdown as demonstrations spread across the country, had nevertheless changed the circumstances confronting the opposition.
The scale of the killing, Pahlavi said, required changes in how the opposition operated, although not in what it ultimately sought to achieve.
“A change in tactics does not mean a change in objectives. It means adapting our methods to new circumstances.”
Saturday’s gathering was held at Meridian Hall as part of "Cyrus the Great II: From a Great Civilization to a Greater Future," organized by the Cyrus the Great Cultural & Humanity Organization. Organizers had said ahead of the event that more than 3,000 Iranian Canadians and supporters were expected.
The event brought Pahlavi together with Canadian political and civic figures, most prominently Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre, who used his appearance to call for stronger Canadian action against individuals linked to the Islamic Republic.
Canada's Poilievre calls for scrutiny on IRGC-linked actors entering country
Poilievre called for greater scrutiny of those connected to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps entering Canada, continued targeted sanctions, and measures to prevent regime-linked assets from being moved into the country.
Canada severed diplomatic relations with Tehran in 2012 and designated the IRGC as a terrorist entity in 2024.
Poilievre also spoke of Iran beyond the Islamic Republic, invoking Cyrus the Great and the country’s pre-Islamic history while expressing hope that Iranians would one day be able to return freely to their country and see the Lion and Sun flag raised there again.
For Pahlavi, much of Saturday’s address focused on another battle between the opposition and Tehran: the competing picture each presents of the state of resistance inside Iran. He accused the regime of promoting two central claims – that Iran’s opposition remains hopelessly divided and that no meaningful organization exists inside the country.
On the first, Pahlavi argued that agreement over Iran’s eventual form of government was not a prerequisite for cooperation against the Islamic Republic.
Republicans and monarchists, as well as those on the political left and right, could work together around four principles: Iran’s territorial integrity; separation of religion and government; individual freedoms and equality before the law; and Iranians' right to determine their future system of government through free and fair elections.
“The embrace of Iran’s Lion and Sun Revolution is open to every Iranian who accepts these four principles,” he said.
The second claim – that the opposition lacks organization – brought Pahlavi back to the networks he says now operate beneath the surface inside Iran.
If no organization existed, he asked, how could millions of Iranians inside and outside the country act together at critical moments?
According to Pahlavi, the answer lies in decentralized networks embedded in Iranian society, beyond the regime’s ability to easily dismantle. He claimed Tehran’s intelligence and security apparatus was itself increasingly concerned by their development.
The Iranian opposition leader nevertheless cautioned his supporters against assuming the Islamic Republic’s collapse was inevitable or imminent.
“We must be realistic. The work is not yet finished,” he said. “Overthrowing this criminal sect that has occupied our country is a complex, multi-stage process.”
But the central message of the Toronto speech was that Pahlavi believes that process has moved into a different stage – one increasingly focused on weakening the machinery of the Islamic Republic from within.
“The enemy is decaying from within and is hollow,” he told the crowd. “We are more determined and more organized than ever. Believe that the dawn of freedom is near.”

Russia is Attacking Europe: Let’s Stop Calling it ‘Hybrid’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:13:00 UTC
17:13:00 KST

Let’s stop calling Russian attacks against Europe hybrid attacks. The phrase has become a political sedative. It allows governments to acknowledge Russian aggression while placing it in a category that sits safely below war, Article 5 and any meaningful retaliation.
Let’s call them what they are: acoordinated Russian campaign of covert, warlike attacks, designed to discover how much violence Europe will absorb without imposing a price.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The problem is that each attack is treated as a separate incident against a separate country. The evidence is investigated nationally, the condemnation is issued nationally and any response is left to the country attacked. The campaign against Europe is broken into isolated cases, making a collective response politically much harder.
And it is a collective response that is the best way to respond to these attacks and force Russia into some kind of restraint. Europe should treat every confidently attributed Russian operation as part of an attack on European security, then select a collective and proportionate response from an agreed ladder of measures.
Europe is hardly out of options. It can tighten sanctions, freeze more assets, expel Russian operatives, launch cyber operations and put pressure on the countries helping Moscow, especially China. Further up the ladder come intercepting Russian drones and missiles, protecting western Ukraine from the air and, in the gravest circumstances, direct NATO action.
Largest Drone Strike on Moscow Hits Oil Refinery and Logistics Hub
Most attacks would be answered far below the top rung. A no-fly zone or direct military action would remain emergency options. Keeping them on the table does not mean reaching for them now.
Europe sees incidents but for Russia it’s a campaign
The term “hybrid” once described a useful fact. Russia mixes sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, political interference and deniable kinetic attacks. Sure, the mix is hybrid but the political effect of the label has changed.
It makes acts of violence sound ambiguous, manageable and somehow less real. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys put it plainly: “Russia’s attacks against us are no longer hybrid. They are very kinetic.”
Radosław Sikorski, the Polish foreign minister, spoke in a similar vein, saying on Thursday that “Russia’s hybrid war against Europe has already taken on a ‘kinetic’ dimension” and that these are “on the border between hybrid warfare and outright aggression.”
It’s almost war
The evidence is accumulating. Germany has attributed the explosive-drone attack at Leipzig-Halle airport to Russia. European authorities have investigated suspected Russian sabotage against defense companies and infrastructure in Poland, Estonia and Slovakia. Russia has also been linked to cyberattacks, interference with railways and energy systems, threats to undersea infrastructure and repeated violations of NATO airspace.
The Institute for the Study of War, a US based think-tank, says: “The Kremlin is conducting these actions against Europe as part of a series of mutually supporting kinetic and cognitive campaigns.”
Each attack is also as if the Kremlin is checking the cost it has to pay for each provocation. The results have been encouraging for Russia. Poland responded to the Russian-directed railway bombing by closing Moscow’s last consulate in Gdańsk. Germany answered the Leipzig attack by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin. Russia retaliated by closing Germany’s consulate in St Petersburg and its Goethe-Institut centers.
These actions imposed some cost. They were still national and easy for Moscow to absorb. Neither attack automatically brought an EU-wide sanctions package, coordinated expulsions or additional weapons for Ukraine. The extra European cost was effectively zero.
The real target is collective defense
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that Russia could strike NATO territory and then present the incident as “accidental”. The official story, he said, would be that there was no reason to consider a NATO response.
That’s the point. Russia wants Article 5 to appear, in Tusk’s words, “more theoretical than practical”. The immediate target may be a train, factory, airport or undersea cable but the strategic target is the credibility of collective defense. The Kremlin also wants to break European unity and wear down support for Ukraine.
NATO already accepts that a hybrid operation could, in some circumstances, trigger Article 5. The obstacle is political. Allies examine each incident separately, so almost every operation appears too small to justify a collective response.
Europe must reverse that calculation. An attack intended to divide European countries should bring them closer together. An operation designed to weaken Ukraine support should automatically produce more weapons, funding or air defense for Ukraine. Every Russian attempt to frighten one country should trigger a visible response from all.
That would send Moscow a message it could understand. These attacks are failing. They are strengthening European unity, increasing the cost to Russia and delivering more support to the country the Kremlin is trying to destroy.
Russia may be ready before Europe
The danger extends beyond sabotage. “According to all our sources, late autumn and winter will be the most critical moment so far in the Russian-Ukrainian war,” Donald Tusk told parliament. He warned that Russia could extend the pressure to NATO’s eastern flank through supposedly “accidental” drone or missile strikes designed to paralyze the alliance’s response.
Europe is rearming, but many of its new forces, factories and air-defense systems will not be ready until 2029. Meanwhile, Washington wants Europe to take greater responsibility for conventional defense, and the Pentagon is considering a substantial reduction in US forces on the continent, even by as much as 50%, according to the latest reports from NBC.
Russia also retains an effective army despite its slow progress in Ukraine. It has battle-hardened troops, a wartime arms industry and growing experience with drones, missiles and infiltration tactics.
Russia would not need the strength to conquer Europe. A limited incursion, drone strike or missile attack could be enough to test whether NATO could agree on an Article 5 response.
NATO provides the shield. The EU sets the price
NATO remains Europe’s main instrument for military deterrence and defense. The EU controls many of the economic tools most useful after sabotage or a cyberattack, including sanctions, asset freezes, export controls and defense financing.
The problem is that these powers are divided. NATO cannot impose sanctions, the EU cannot command NATO forces, and security powers such as Britain and Norway sit outside the EU.
Ursula von der Leyen has proposed three ways to connect them. A counter-hybrid playbook would list the available responses. An Emergency Security Protocol could be triggered by one EU member and force all 27 to consult. A European Security Council would bring key non-EU partners, including Britain, Norway, Ukraine and Canada, into the political discussion.
The playbook would provide the options, the protocol would trigger the process and the Security Council would build the coalition. The council could still become another talking shop. Its value would depend on governments agreeing the response ladder in advance and arriving ready to act.

Economic Watch: China's five-year plan to elevate electronic information manufacturing sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:07:54 CST
17:07:54 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- As artificial intelligence (AI) plays an increasingly significant role in reshaping the global industrial landscape, China has recently unveiled a plan to advance its electronic information manufacturing sector, a critical foundation for AI development, over the next five years.
The development plan for the electronic information manufacturing industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and the National Development and Reform Commission, aims to further consolidate the pillar role of the industry by 2030.
Industrial firms in the sector with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan (about 2.96 million U.S. dollars) are expected to see their combined revenue surpass 30 trillion yuan, and R&D investment intensity of the sector will rise to 3.5 percent, according to the plan.
TO ENHANCE INDUSTRIAL BASE
The electronic information manufacturing industry is a major force in the new industrialization drive. By the end of 2025, China's electronic information manufacturing industry had led the country's 41 major industrial sectors in terms of revenue for 13 consecutive years.
Building on that foundation, the plan presents a systemic framework to strengthen the industrial base, spanning integrated circuits, electronic components and materials, intelligent sensors, specialized electronic equipment and measuring instruments, and the photonics industry.
The framework aims to tackle bottlenecks in key areas and build an independent and controllable industrial base, said Liu Bin, an official with the MIIT.
Liu pointed to photonics as an example, noting that advancing breakthroughs in core technologies and establishing pilot testing platforms for key areas and shared needs will strengthen the sector from the ground up. These efforts, he said, will lay a solid foundation for development and accelerate both technological innovation and industrialization process.
As a representative sector of the electronic information manufacturing industry, China's integrated circuit industry is entering a new phase of rapid growth, driven by the explosive global demand for high-end computing and memory chips brought about by the AI revolution.
Customs data shows that in the first seven months, the country's integrated circuit exports reached 216 billion U.S. dollars, up 99.5 percent year on year, already surpassing the full-year total of 2025.
A semiconductor technology company in southwest China's Sichuan Province has already completed its first half-year production targets, and aims to double its output value from last year, according to its general manager.
TO STRENGTHEN COMPETITIVENESS
While strengthening the industrial base, the plan also sets out strategies to boost the competitiveness of whole devices and systems. This includes enhancing industrial chain resilience in key areas, developing a robust computing ecosystem, and promoting innovation in consumer electronics, among other initiatives.
Terminals form the basic foundation of industrial scale and serve as the gateway through which smart technologies reach hundreds of millions of users, said Liang Linjun, a researcher at China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT).
The plan outlines a dedicated push for innovation in key consumer electronics products, ranging from high-end mobile phones and personal computers to virtual reality devices. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), China's output of core consumer electronics, including mobile phones and computers, maintained a top global ranking.
The accelerating evolution of a new generation of AI is bringing new demand, new product forms, and new ways of development to the electronic information manufacturing industry, while raising higher requirements for basic hardware supply and system coordination, said Liang.
Liang called for efforts to open up typical application scenarios, develop standards for agent collaboration, high-speed computing interconnect, and hardware-software compatibility, increase long-term capital supply that matches innovation cycles, and train more talent with expertise in both AI and electronics manufacturing.
The plan also addresses rising concerns over cutthroat competition in the industry. It calls for timely revisions to industry norms, coordinated planning and early-warning systems for capacity across subsectors, and a comprehensive effort to curb cutthroat competition.
As the "hardware foundation" of the digital world, the electronic information manufacturing industry is undergoing profound changes in its strategic position, competitive logic, and growth model, said Ao Li, vice president of the CAICT.
Turning scale into systemic strength, as well as moving from leading in volume to winning on quality, will be a major task for China's electronic information manufacturing industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, Ao said.
Industry insiders say government, industry, academia, research institutions, and users need to work together to translate the plan into results by strengthening the industrial foundation and making the supply chain more resilient.
Such a collective push is expected to put China's electronic information manufacturing sector on firmer footing, with a more complete chain and more active innovation, and to lay a solid base for the country's goals of building itself into a manufacturing powerhouse and a cyber powerhouse, they said. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- The World Organization for Science Literacy made its debut in Beijing on Sunday.

China's August power use tops 1 trillion kWh again, load hits record high
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:07:16 CST
17:07:16 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's electricity consumption, a key barometer of economic activity, topped 1 trillion kilowatt-hours (kWh) again in August, while the electricity load hit a record high last month, official data showed on Sunday.
Power use totaled 1.03 trillion kWh in August, rising 1.7 percent year on year, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA). Electricity load hit a record high of 1.56 billion kilowatts, 49.69 million kilowatts higher than the previous year's peak.
A breakdown of the August data revealed that power consumed by the primary industry rose 2.7 percent year on year to 16.9 billion kWh, while power consumed by the secondary industry increased 2.4 percent to 612.4 billion kWh. Power use by the tertiary industry reached 215.5 billion kWh, up 5.1 percent year on year.
Notably, electricity consumption by the high-tech and equipment manufacturing sector reached 122.2 billion kWh in August, an increase of 7.2 percent. Computer and communications equipment, automobile manufacturing, general equipment manufacturing, special equipment manufacturing and electrical machinery manufacturing saw power use rise 7.5 percent, 7.6 percent, 7.6 percent, 8.2 percent and 12.3 percent, respectively.
The charging and battery swapping service sector and internet data services reported rapid growth in electricity consumption in August, rising 51.2 percent and 37.9 percent, to 17.2 billion and 10.2 billion kWh, respectively.
In the first eight months of the year, China's total power use reached 7.17 trillion kWh, up 4.3 percent year on year, the NEA said. Power use by the primary, secondary and tertiary industries rose 3.3 percent, 4.4 percent and 7.1 percent, to 104.6 billion kWh, 4.53 trillion kWh and 1.43 trillion kWh, respectively.
During this period, high-tech and equipment manufacturing electricity consumption climbed 9.3 percent to 845.1 billion kWh. Electricity use by charging and battery swapping services and internet data services grew 55.1 percent to 114.7 billion kWh and 42.5 percent to 69.5 billion kWh, respectively. Residential power use rose 0.3 percent to 1.11 trillion kWh.
In recent years, China has made major strides in terms of its power infrastructure, helping ensure a stable electricity supply during peak periods and effectively supporting economic and social development as well as meeting people's basic needs, the National Development and Reform Commission said in July. ■

China launches new group of satellites

A Lijian-1 Y18 carrier rocket carrying nine satellites blasts off from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China, Sept. 20, 2026. China successfully launched nine satellites into space from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China at 12:03 p.m. Sunday (Beijing Time). The satellites were carried by a Lijian-1 Y18 carrier rocket and have entered their planned orbits. The launch mission was a complete success. (Photo by Wang Jiangbo/Xinhua)
JIUQUAN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China successfully launched nine satellites into space from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China at 12:03 p.m. Sunday (Beijing Time).
The satellites were carried by a Lijian-1 Y18 carrier rocket and have entered their planned orbits.
They will mainly be used for space environment monitoring, disaster prevention and mitigation and scientific experiments.
The launch mission was a complete success.
This was the 17th flight mission conducted by the Lijian carrier rocket series, which were developed by commercial spaceflight company CAS Space. The Lijian series have so far successfully sent one spacecraft and 121 satellites into space, with a total payload mass in orbit exceeding 21 tonnes, according to the company.
The launch schedule for Lijian-1 carrier rocket has been set through the second half of 2027.
CAS Space is China's commercial space company that has launched the largest number of satellites and the heaviest payloads in the country's private space sector, the Science and Technology Daily reported Sunday. ■

US State Department Approves $2.68 Billion Air Defense Sale to Ukraine
The US Department of State has approved a potential Foreign Military Sale to the Government of Ukraine for Air Defense Development Upgrades and associated equipment valued at an estimated $2.68 billion, the US Bureau of Political-Military Affairs announced on September 18.
If finalized, Ukraine will fund the purchase through a combination of European financial contributions and US Foreign Military Financing (FMF) appropriated during the prior administration. The FMF funds will be credited as a US capital contribution to the Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund via a 1:1 reimbursement framework.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine remains heavily dependent on constant replenishments of air defense interceptors to shield its cities and critical energy infrastructure from sustained Russian long-range missile and drone strikes. With Russian forces launching thousands of aerial weapons every month, securing a multi-layered defensive shield is essential to prevent widespread destruction of key civilian facilities and maintain the country’s operational stability.
The requested procurement package includes non-major defense equipment, specifically S-300 Clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, and Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, the US Department of State wrote.
Kyiv also requested Improvised Transporter Erector Launcher 1.5 units, mobile launching system modification kits, RPS 202 counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) radars, erectable mast trailers, major modifications, and maintenance support.
Additional elements of the potential sale encompass spare parts, consumables, accessories, repair and return support, software, technical publications, transportation support, and engineering and logistics services provided by the US Government and contractors.
“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic progress in Europe,” the Department of State said in a statement.
The statement also noted that the sale will enhance Ukraine’s ability to conduct self-defense and regional security missions while maintaining that the equipment will not alter the basic military balance in the region or adversely affect US defense readiness.
Principal contractors will be selected through competitive procurements under the Federal Acquisition Regulation.
The European Union had previously approved $7.1 billion for Ukraine under the Ukraine Support Loan framework, clearing the way for Kyiv to purchase American PAC-3 Patriot interceptor missiles via NATO's PURL mechanism . The funding allocation includes specific exceptions to standard conditions to accommodate high-value Ukrainian-made drones as well as critical US-manufactured air defense systems.

Trump Signs Sweeping “Sanctions From Hell” Bill Against Russia Into Law
US President Donald Trump signed sweeping legislation into law targeting Russia’s energy, defense, and maritime sectors, the White House announced on September 18.
Formally designated as the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” often referred to as the “sanctions bill from hell,” the law was named in honor of the South Carolina Republican Senator who died in July after being a long-standing advocate for aggressive economic measures against Moscow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The bill gained final congressional approval after passing the House of Representatives on Wednesday following its passage in the Senate last month.
The landmark legislation specifically targets Russia’s primary revenue streams by imposing secondary economic measures on third-party entities and allowing the president to levy tariffs on foreign nations that continue to purchase Russian energy exports, Reuters wrote.
It also targets Russia’s defense industrial base, major financial institutions, and the illicit “shadow fleet” of tankers used to circumvent international oil price caps.
Critics and foreign policy analysts noted that the legislation grants the executive branch broad discretionary authority, enabling the president to impose secondary tariffs that could remain in place far beyond his administration. Despite these concerns, supporters emphasized that restricting Kremlin revenues is essential to weakening Russia’s war economy as the invasion of Ukraine continues, according to Reuters.
The Russia sanctions bill was previously stalled in the US House of Representatives due to opposition from corporate lobbying groups and concerns regarding expanded tariff powers.
After overwhelmingly clearing the Senate with an 86–11 bipartisan vote, the bill encountered significant resistance from corporate giants—including ExxonMobil, General Electric, Ford, and Pfizer—over potential tariff impacts on American consumers.

Jairam Ramesh attacks Union home minister Amit Shah.
NEW DELHI: Congress on Sunday took a swipe at Union home minister Amit Shah over the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleging that it was a "Shah Instigated Removal" of voters.Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh said the Election Commission began Phase 1 of the SIR process in Bihar in June 2025, followed by Phase 2 in November 2025 across nine states and three Union Territories.According to Jairam Ramesh, 7.8 crore names were deleted during the first two phases, amounting to 13% of the pre-SIR electoral roll.
Jairam said Phase 3 began in 16 states and three Union Territories in mid-2026. Citing data from 12 states and two UTs, he claimed that 6.18 crore names had been deleted from a total of 36.06 crore voters."The deletion rate works out to over 17% 2. An additional 5.43 crore voters have been issued notices demanding additional documentation to have their names retained on the electoral roll. The risk of deletion rate works to another 15%. This is an unusually high proportion that reflects structural flaws in the entire SIR process," Jairam said.
He questioned how such a large number of voters could still be required to undergo verification after the deletion of millions of names."Thus, a staggering 32% (or about one in three) of voters have had their names deleted or face risk of deletion," Jairam added.
He cited Delhi, Chandigarh, Jharkhand, Uttarakhand, Meghalaya, Maharashtra, Telangana, Karnataka, Haryana, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Punjab as states and UTs where he claimed a significant proportion of voters had either been deleted or faced the risk of deletion.The Congress leader also alleged that large-scale deletions were disproportionately affecting voters from economically and socially disadvantaged sections. He further claimed that, in most major states, more women than men had been removed from electoral rolls during the SIR process.Jairam said the exercise had shifted the burden of verification from the state to citizens, who were being asked to produce documents that they may never have been issued. "A test that the overwhelming majority of citizens cannot pass is just a 'machine for exclusion'," he said."SIR is actually a massive Shah Instigated Removal of voters. It is an assault on our Constitution," he added.Tagging his statement on X, he wrote, "SIR is actually a Shah Instigated Removal of voters on a massive scale. Here is a statement on this brazen assault on our Constitution itself."
Jairam also said voter lists facing deletion risks had been made publicly available in Karnataka, Telangana and Jharkhand, allowing voters to check their names. He claimed Delhi made its list public only on September 19, 2026, following public pressure, while other BJP-ruled states and Punjab had not done so.The Election Commission has maintained that the SIR, being conducted after 22 years, is aimed at cleaning electoral rolls by removing ineligible and duplicate entries while ensuring that all eligible citizens are included in the rolls.Opposition parties have alleged that the exercise could target voters who do not support the BJP and its allies. The allegations have been rejected by the Election Commission, which has defended the revision as an exercise to ensure accurate and legally eligible electoral rolls.

Victims say Home Office attempt to curtail spycops inquiry will result in a ‘cover-up’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:00:10 UTC
17:00:10 KST

Victims of intrusive police surveillance have accused the government of seeking to cut short the spycops public inquiry that has been examining widespread misconduct committed by undercover officers.
The independent judge-led inquiry is scrutinising how officers, who spied on tens of thousands of political activists over more than four decades, carried out abuses such as deceiving women into sexual relationships and fathering children.
The inquiry has been running for more than a decade, and is expected to last another two years.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has said she is concerned about the length and cost of the process. It was set up in 2015 and was supposed to have been completed within three years. Latest figures show the inquiry, which has been led by retired judge Sir John Mitting, has so far cost £144m.
Mahmood initiated a public consultation, which closes on Sunday, that she said would help determine whether the inquiry should continue in a different format.
However, those who were spied on say that the Home Office is looking to severely limit or scrap the later stages, leaving the full extent of wrongdoing by the police hidden. They say more than 2,000 people have objected to what they believe would be a cover-up.
The spycops inquiry is one of the longest-running public inquiries. According to the House of Commons, the longest in modern times was an inquiry into a sectarian murder in Northern Ireland which reported last week, 22 years after being commissioned.
It has so far been investigating the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), a Metropolitan police unit that infiltrated political groups between 1968 and 2008.
The inquiry has heard how the SDS officers formed long-term relationships with women without disclosing to them their true identity, spied on grieving families such as the parents of murdered teenager Stephen Lawrence, stole the identities of dead children and lied in court hearings.
It is due to examine a second undercover squad, the National Public Order Intelligence Unit, which infiltrated political groups between 1999 and 2011.
One of the unit’s key undercover officers was Mark Kennedy who infiltrated environmental and left-wing groups for six years. He deceived a large, but unknown, number of women into intimate relationships.
Environmental campaigners had their criminal convictions overturned because crucial evidence gathered by Kennedy was withheld from their trials.
The inquiry is also scheduled to look at the case of an undercover police officer who used his fake identity while infiltrating serious crime to deceive a woman into a 19-year relationship during which they had a child together.
Victims of the surveillance say that the consultation is phoney and rigged as it only offers three alternatives: an inquiry with a narrower remit, one that would not have legal powers to force reluctant witnesses to testify or asking the police to disclose documents to victims without any type of inquiry.
Kate Wilson, who was deceived into a two-year relationship by Kennedy, said: “Whatever the intentions of the Home Office in doing this, the practical effect of them curtailing the inquiry or reducing its powers to compel evidence will be a cover-up, and we may never understand the full extent of the misconduct that has occurred in undercover policing.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “The historic failings in undercover policing continue to shock the public. We are determined to get justice and hold those responsible to account.
“However, the undercover policing inquiry was established more than a decade ago, and is yet to deliver justice for those affected, at significant cost to the taxpayer. It’s only right that we ask those affected themselves about the future of the inquiry.”

Ed Sheeran speaks on Gaza after Macklemore controversy
September 20, 2026
British pop star Ed Sheeran has addressed the Israel-Palestine conflict, following a row over Macklemore's removal as a supporting act on the tour after the US rapper made pro-Palestinian comments on stage.
Performing in Philadelphia on Saturday night, the first concert since the controversy erupted, Sheeran said the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, which killed around 1,200 people and saw dozens taken hostage, was "horrific."
He also described Israel's subsequent war in Gaza, which killed more than 70,000 people, as "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate."
Sheeran also condemned the "systemic injustice" in the occupied West Bank, where the Israeli government is pushing to expand Jewish settlements, which the United Nations has called a "flagrant violation of international law."
"I don't want to disappoint fans, and I've never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," Sheeran said.
"I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so, so sorry," he said.
Sheeran's latest statement was a reversal from his earlier stance on Instagram, when he said that his concert audiences "do not expect a political forum."
How did the controversy occur?
The pop singer's tour faced controversy after rapper Macklemore was dropped as a supporting act after he said "Free Palestine" at the opening of Sheeran's US Loop Tour in New Jersey in early September.
Sheeran has denied being responsible, saying venues had threatened to cancel shows if Macklemore remained on the tour.
Macklemore posted on Instagram that billionaire Robert Kraft had told Sheeran that the rapper would not be allowed to perform at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, which he owns.
Several supporting acts subsequently withdrew in solidarity with Macklemore, including musician Finneas, Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe, as well as Sheeran's backing band — leaving one of the best-selling musical artists of all time without an opening act.
Pro-Palestinian demonstrators protest outside concert venue
Dozens of pro-Palestinian protesters rallied peacefully outside Philadelphia's Lincoln Financial Field before Sheeran's concert, waving Palestinian flags and chanting "Free, free Palestine."
Among the demonstrators was 18-year-old Brandon Ateke, who accused Sheeran of "complicity" with Kraft and others in silencing Macklemore.
"I decided to not attend the concert and instead attend the protest to bring light to the genocide going on in Gaza today," Ateke told AFP news agency.
The Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI), a pro-Palestinian group, has called for a boycott of Sheeran's world tour.

The UK suspiciously reeks of the late-stage USSR
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:58:00 UTC
16:58:00 KST

The UK suspiciously reeks of the late-stage USSR
“The era of Westminster is coming to an end!” the nationalist leaders of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland declared this week.
John Swinney, Rhun ap Iorwerth, and Michelle O’Neill gathered in Cardiff to sign an agreement asserting their nations’ right to self-determination, as they called on London not to obstruct referendums and outlined their preferred futures beyond the UK, including EU membership for an independent Scotland and Wales, and Irish reunification for Northern Ireland.
In Russia, the meeting has already been dubbed Britain’s version of the Belovezha Accords, and the comparison is tempting because, as in 1991, political leaders from three of a state’s constituent parts gathered around a table to discuss a civilized divorce.
But the resemblance largely ends there, given the driving force behind the Soviet Union’s dissolution was its largest republic, Russia, represented by Boris Yeltsin. He joined his counterparts in dismantling the state that Moscow built, but no representative of England attended the Cardiff gathering, and Westminster has shown little enthusiasm for presiding over its own retreat.
The participants were also considerably more cautious than their Soviet predecessors, so they signed as party leaders, making the declaration a joint political initiative rather than an agreement binding their governments to secession.
This distinction exposes the central weakness of the Cardiff Pact. Its signatories want to leave the UK while remaining within the constitutional framework that holds it together. Their ambitions therefore depend on political and legal processes they don’t control.
Ireland’s experience offers an uncomfortable historical comparison, as the settlement that opened the way to independence followed two years of guerrilla warfare. Today’s nationalist leaders are pursuing an entirely peaceful route, through negotiations, elections, and referendums, but whether London will accommodate them is another matter.
Scotland has already encountered this obstacle. In 2022, the UK Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament couldn’t legislate for an independence referendum without Westminster’s consent, and after the close vote in 2014, London has little appetite for another.
Public opinion presents a further difficulty. Scotland remains divided down the middle, whereas in Northern Ireland, the figure cited for support for Irish unity is around 36% and Welsh independence remains a minority position, however much its advocates have gained politically.
Swinney wants another Scottish referendum by 2031, but his counterparts have offered no comparable timetable and their agreement establishes a direction of travel, but supplies neither a departure date nor a convincing explanation of how they will get there.
Britain’s dissolution is therefore hardly imminent, but nevertheless, London would be foolish to dismiss Cardiff as an exercise in nationalist theater.
Some British coverage attributed the meeting to an ill-judged intervention by Prime Minister Andy Burnham when he suggested that referendums in Scotland and Northern Ireland might be considered if there is broad public consensus, before attempting to narrow the implications of his remarks.
Qualifications rarely travel as far as the original statement and nationalists heard an opening and acted accordingly.
Yet an unfortunate choice of words can’t explain the forces behind this gathering. The more immediate political background was Labour’s local elections defeat in May, which strengthened nationalist parties and created favorable conditions for cooperation and Cardiff gave that cooperation a common platform.
However, the deeper problem is the condition of the British state itself. In 2014, many Scots supported independence because they believed London ignored their interests and governed badly – and since then, Westminster has supplied little reason for them to reconsider, as economic stagnation and trained public services have steadily eroded confidence in the established order.
Conservatives and Labour have each promised renewal, only to leave voters wondering whether either possesses a credible plan, while Reform and nationalist parties have moved into the space created by that failure. Their proposed remedies differ, but their appeal rests on a shared conviction that the old arrangements no longer work.
Brexit sharpened this argument, as Britain’s departure from the EU in 2020 changed the calculation for those considering a future outside the UK. Previously, independence meant leaving a state that already offered access to the EU, but now nationalists can present separation as a route back into it.
The choice, as they frame it, is between joining a larger, more successful economic and political community and remaining attached to a declining imperial center, still occasionally tempted to compensate for its weakening position with displays of former grandeur.
This argument doesn’t remove the economic risks of independence, nor does it guarantee EU membership, but it gives separatists something more persuasive than a historical grievance: A competing account of where prosperity and security might lie.
Cardiff matters principally for this reason. It did not produce a mechanism for dismantling the UK, but it brought together politicians willing to imagine what might follow it and an alternative once discussed separately in Edinburgh, Cardiff, and Belfast has acquired a shared political expression.
It’s far too early to suggest that Burnham will be Britain’s last prime minister, as states can survive years of disillusionment, and nationalist declarations are easier to sign than to implement.
But Westminster’s problem is that preserving the union requires more than obstructing its opponents, and it also requires giving people a convincing reason to stay.

Did Ukraine Use Pelican Ballistic Missile to Strike Moscow?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:58:00 UTC
16:58:00 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Sept. 20, that Ukrainian forces deployed an array of domestically developed long-range strike systems against strategic targets in Russia overnight, including a ballistic missile designated “Pelican.”
Writing on social media, Zelensky confirmed strikes on critical oil refining and logistics facilities supporting the Russian war effort across the Moscow region and an industrial enterprise in the Voronezh region.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The president specifically listed the weapons deployed by Ukrainian intelligence and military units, identifying the FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sichnevyi, and Pelican.
“In the Moscow region tonight, our long-range responses worked very noticeably,” Zelensky stated. “Key oil industry and logistics facilities supporting the aggressor’s war machine were hit. These represent billions of dollars sustaining the war effort.”
The public inclusion of Pelican among the strike assets ignited widespread technical debate among military observers regarding whether Ukraine has deployed its newly developed FP-7 short-range ballistic missile in combat, and whether it could physically reach the Russian capital.
Range limitations, operational role of the FP-7
Multiple reports have linked the Pelican to Ukrainian arms maker Fire Point’s FP-7, though it’s not entirely clear whether they’re one and the same.
Fico Claims West Seeks NATO-Russia War After ‘Failed’ Ukraine Plan
In September 2025, Ukrainian arms maker Fire Point revealed the development of the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile and the larger FP-9, positioning them as sovereign strike alternatives to foreign systems such as the US-supplied ATACMS – but they were never given a name, save for the model number.
Fire Point previously designated its FP-5 cruise missile as the “Flamingo,” though the name “Pelican” has never been mentioned until Sunday by Zelensky.
Defense analysts caution that the FP-7’s technical specifications make a direct ballistic strike on Moscow highly improbable.
Radio NV military analyst Vasyl Pekhno noted that the FP-7 has an engineered operational range of 200-350 kilometers (124-217 miles), whereas Moscow sits approximately 450-500 kilometers (280-311 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
“There are great doubts that it could fly that far, because its design range is only 350 kilometers,” Pekhno explained. “It cannot reach Moscow directly.”
Pekhno suggested that the ballistic weapon may have played an integral role within a coordinated, multi-axis combined strike.
Under such an operational design, short-range ballistic missiles could engage Russian air defense batteries, such as S-400 radar and launcher sites deployed in border regions like Bryansk or Voronezh, creating localized air defense gaps that allowed slower long-range drones and Flamingo cruise missiles to penetrate deep into metropolitan Moscow.
“If we consider that ballistics were an element of the broader operation, the puzzle comes together,” Pekhno added. “For instance, ballistic missiles could strike S-400 deployment sites while other systems saturated the air defense network, enabling Flamingo missiles to reach their designated targets.”
Development of the FP-7 and long-range FP-9
The FP-7 can be seen as a tactical ballistic missile, while the FP-9 is reserved for deeper strikes.
In February 2026, Fire Point released footage demonstrating the initial test launch of the FP-7. According to technical specifications published by the manufacturer, the ground-launched missile carries a 150-kilogram (331-lb) warhead, has a maximum speed of 1,500 meters per second (3,355 mph), and achieves a reported terminal accuracy deviation of roughly 14 meters (46 feet).
Earlier in September, Fire Point Chief Executive Officer Iryna Terekh announced at the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland that the FP-7 had concluded two phases of operational testing and was preparing for immediate frontline combat deployment within weeks rather than months.
Concurrently, Fire Point has been developing the larger FP-9 ballistic missile, engineered to achieve a reported range of up to 850 kilometers (528 miles).
Fire Point chief designer Denys Shtilerman noted during the summer that flight trials for the 850-kilometer system could involve test trajectories directed toward symbolic Russian targets, given that testing an 850-kilometer missile within Ukrainian airspace is geographically unfeasible.
Both the FP-7 and FP-9 systems were known to be advancing through rapid development and testing cycles over recent months.
While specific technical parameters regarding the Pelican missile mentioned in Zelensky’s statement remain classified, defense assessments indicate that the missile directly impacting metropolitan Moscow is unlikely to be the baseline FP-7 given its 200-300-kilometer range.
At the same time, it remains unconfirmed whether Fire Point has expedited combat trials of the heavier 850-kilometer FP-9 platform, or whether the Pelican designation was applied to an intermediate ballistic variant tailored to strike Russian air defense corridors.
Capital refinery damage and multi-drone saturation
The overnight attack inflicted structural damage on key Russian industrial infrastructure. The General Staff of the Ukrainian military confirmed hits on the Gazprom Neft Moscow Oil Refinery in Moscow’s southeastern Kapotnya district, approximately 15 kilometers (9 miles) from the Kremlin.
According to military authorities, long-range drones operated by the Security Service of Ukraine’s (SBU) “Alpha” Special Operations Center flew over 500 kilometers to breach dense capital air defenses, striking the refinery’s AVT-6 primary crude distillation unit, an integrated refining facility, and an isomerization unit. Geolocation analysis of footage published by metropolitan residents confirmed large fires at the refining site.
The Moscow Oil Refinery processes approximately 11.6 million metric tons of crude oil annually, supplying roughly 40 percent of the fuel requirements for the capital and 70 percent of gasoline and aviation kerosene consumed across the wider Moscow region.
Simultaneously, Fire Point confirmed that its FP-1 attack drones struck and destroyed commercial storage complexes operated by Modern Warehouse Technologies in Sofyino, within the Ramensky district of Moscow region.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that Russian air defenses intercepted more than 1,600 drones across all defensive echelons since Saturday, including 450 downed on approach to the capital, calling the barrage the largest drone assault on Moscow to date.
Moscow Region Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported at least two civilians killed and six injured across the surrounding province.

Foreign Minister: Russia's State Duma elections a 'political performance'
Estonia's assessment of Russia's State Duma elections remains unchanged, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said.
Tsahkna said the ongoing elections have been neither free nor fair and had the sole purpose of consolidating Vladimir Putin's grip on power.
"The Kremlin imposed particularly severe restrictions on the opposition and its supporters ahead of these elections," Tsahkna noted. He said candidates deemed unacceptable by the regime, and critics of Russia's war against Ukraine, were excluded from political competition, with distorted registration requirements, administrative measures and criminal prosecutions used to that end.
Tsahkna cited the banning from running of Yabloko, the only registered party running on a peace platform, as "a telling example of the Kremlin's determination to cling to its monopoly on power."
The minister said the absence of independent international observers, alongside growing repression and systematic suppression of the opposition, meant "this political performance orchestrated by Putin bears no resemblance to free elections." He described it as "yet another ritual intended to reaffirm and prolong Putin's rule."
Tsahkna also condemned the holding of elections in Ukrainian territories illegally occupied by Russia: Crimea and the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts. The minister noted this constitutes a clear violation of international law and of Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
"Through these so-called elections, Russia seeks to legitimize its illegal occupation policy and create a legal basis for extending its jurisdiction in Ukraine," Tsahkna said. He said Estonia unequivocally condemns this and is working to ensure the organization of elections in occupied Ukrainian territory is met with clear international consequences.
Tsahkna reiterated Estonia's support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Ukraine launched what Moscow's mayor called the biggest ever drone attack on the Russian capital on Sunday, but the Kremlin said the attempt to disrupt the final day of a parliamentary election had failed. The State Duma vote, the first since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine started in 2022, is expected to see Putin's party, United Russia ,retain its dominance in a system critics say does not tolerate dissent, with most anti-war candidates barred from the ballot. Putin has cast the election as a test of public support for the war, and is likely to present the outcome as evidence of national unity.

NATO military chiefs tell industry they are ready to buy
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:57:42 BST
16:57:42 KST

Allied chiefs of defence have sent what NATO describes as a direct and united message to the defence industry that allies are ready to buy at scale, and that industry must be able to deliver with speed, scale and predictability, the alliance stated.
The message came from the annual Military Committee Conference, held in Copenhagen on 18 and 19 September, bringing together the 32 allied chiefs of defence with the two strategic commanders, General Alexus Grynkewich as Supreme Allied Commander Europe and Admiral Pierre Vandier as Supreme Allied Commander Transformation.
Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, Chair of the Military Committee, set out the purpose of the meeting as moving from commitments to delivery. He said: “We, the NATO Chiefs of Defence, together with SACEUR and SACT, will do the work that follows from the Ankara Summit, as we shift focus from committing budgets to delivering on capabilities that will enable NATO to deter adversaries and defend the Euro-Atlantic area.”
He added that the conference would address “collective deterrence and defence, innovation and technology, and accelerated adoption of new defence capabilities”.
His language on Russian activity over recent months was considerably blunter than the rest of his remarks. “Over recent weeks and months, we have seen once again the reckless behaviour of Russia, including airspace violations, drone incidents, hybrid activities and attempts to test Allied resolve,” he said. “Let me commend Allied forces for their swift, professional and effective responses to these incidents. NATO remains vigilant. NATO remains ready. And NATO will do what is necessary to defend every inch of Allied territory.”
General Michael Wiggers Hyldgaard, Chief of Defence of Denmark, said: “Today, in Copenhagen, NATO Allies once again show their commitments to strengthening the Alliance, bolstering our innovation and technology and our support for Ukraine. We will do what it takes to defend our common freedom and transatlantic security.”
Alongside the industry message, the conference covered implementation of the summit decisions and capability targets, and the acceleration of allied readiness and the ability to operate across multiple domains.
Allied nations also elected General Carsten Breuer, Chief of Defence of Germany, as the next Chair of the Military Committee. He takes up the post in summer 2027 for a three-year mandate, succeeding Admiral Cavo Dragone.
The line to industry echoes the commitments made at the Ankara Summit in July, where allies pledged to strengthen industrial resilience by expanding manufacturing capacity and removing barriers to defence trade within the alliance, launching the NATO Front Door for Industry and agreeing a Strategy for Industry-NATO Cooperation.
The Military Committee meets in Chiefs of Defence Session twice a year at NATO headquarters in Brussels, and once a year holds a conference hosted by a member state, with the next plenary meeting due in Brussels in January 2027.

German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:57:32 BST
16:57:32 KST

German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz
- Published
Local elections are taking place in two German states on Sunday which could increase the political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Opinion polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern suggest Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is at risk of damaging defeats, which would raise further questions about the chancellor's future.
These latest elections come after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, while the CDU saw its vote halved.
There has been speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced as chancellor mid-term unless the CDU's political fortunes improve.
He has said he will carry on but is facing poor approval ratings amid rumours of a so-called chancellor swap, though his challengers are "still hesitating", writes German news site Tagesschau, external.
According to the polls, Merz's conservatives could lose power in Berlin as it tussles with Die Linke (The Left) over first place.
Meanwhile in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU has only just been hovering above the 5% threshold needed for a party to enter the state parliament. It could spell their worst ever result in a state election.
How did it come to this after just 16 months in power? Friedrich Merz is having to answer for the tumbling popularity of his own party, while the political force that he aimed to counter - the AfD - continues its rise.
Some branches of the AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.
But its anti-immigration, Russian-friendly, Germany-first agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.
The AfD is hoping to build on its recent landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt by topping the polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
However, the centre-left SPD has staged a late comeback to be in contention for the top spot through its lead candidate, Manuela Schwesig.
Currently the state premier, Schwesig is trying to sweep up the anti-AfD vote as she bills herself as the "Die Frau gegen Blau" - "Woman against Blue", the AfD's party colours.
But her local popularity belies the far poorer fortunes of her national party which is locked in a loveless coalition with Merz's CDU.
In a queue for a campaign event in the city of Neubrandenburg, AfD supporter Reinhart tells us that the traditional parties are being washed away.
"Not only in Germany. In Italy, in France, in Great Britain. Everywhere the traditional parties go down."
He smiles when asked what he thinks of Merz, saying: "Oh well everyone thinks the same about him.
"He is arrogant, out of touch, not on the same level as the general public."
Merz's backers argue that the chancellor has had a tough time with global events and that a lot of the problems the nation faces are ones he has inherited.
But whatever faith people had in his ability to fix those problems, it is apparently ebbing away - and, the brutal truth is, it can be hard to find voters who like him.
The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left.
His blunt communication style has also caused irritation, such as his dismissal of "work-life balance", telling Germans they need to work more and take less sick leave.
Supporters would argue he is a man who is ready to administer the medicine the nation needs, even if people do not like the taste of it.
But the country's long-stuttering economy, high energy costs and fraught debates about immigration are feeding a sense of national gloom.
Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz and said restoring trust in the CDU lay in "listening and taking political action, not in debates over personnel".
But while no one within his party has openly challenged Merz for the top job, murmurings of discontent have grown louder.
Martin Rohloff, the CDU candidate for Neubrandenburg, thinks Merz does not have the "Fingerspitzengefühl, the feeling for the small persons".
"Maybe he wants the right things," muses Rohloff, but "he cannot communicate well".
Asked if Merz should go, he says it is not an easy question but: "If I have to answer yes or no, I would say yes. There are other people who maybe have better feelings for the public."
Merz has vowed to carry on as his coalition government aims to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms that are finally due before parliament this autumn.
But Sunday's vote brings a danger for the chancellor - that he is already out of time.
The chancellor is reportedly due to meet senior party figures in Berlin on Sunday evening having already cancelled a planned trip next week to New York, in an apparent effort to contain the crisis.
A staunch backer of Ukraine, the fall of Friedrich Merz would trigger further instability in a continent already rocked by warnings of increased Russian aggression.

In response to the claims made in the memoir, a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said on Wednesday: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”

Asked whether he had evidence of the king’s comments, he told the BBC: “I told friends and family straight away, close friends and family, about what had been said, because it was so monstrous.”
The Sussexes, who returned to the UK from the US on 26 August, have long been critical of their treatment by the media, with Harry in 2021 telling Oprah Winfrey the tabloid press had created a “toxic environment”.

Turkish universities to adress ‘terror-free Türkiye’ goal in first lessons

Turkish universities will address the government’s “terror-free Türkiye” goal in opening ceremonies and first lessons of the 2026-2027 academic year, under a directive issued by the Higher Education Board (YÖK).
In a letter signed by YÖK President Erol Özvar and sent to universities across the country, the board said Türkiye is undergoing an important process aimed at strengthening peace and security, national unity and social cohesion.
