Reform UK has committed to a more hardline immigration policy than proposed by other mainstream parties, promising mass deportations of people who have entered the country illegally and deployment of the Royal Navy to intercept small boats in the Channel.
The party did not respond to a request for comment on whether it would seek to emulate Trump’s style of immigration enforcement under ICE which has been criticised for its brutality.
Farage interviewed Homan for his GB News show last year, describing him as uncompromising and saying he had achieved remarkable results on deportations, while acknowledging there had been “some backlash”.
On Trump in general, Farage said at the event that it was “important that our country, and Europe too, get a better, more sensible view of America than it gets of the Trump administration through traditional mainstream media who frankly paint the whole project out to be villainous”.
Farage’s positive remarks towards Trump and his administration come after the Reform UK leader appeared to distance himself from the president, saying in April they had not spoken for many months and questioning his judgment on the Iran war.
His latest trip to the US comes at a time when relations between the White House and Downing Street are under strain over Iran and policy towards Israel since Andy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer.
Burnham will have his first meeting with Trump in New York next week, with the US president having previously described him as “extremely liberal” but also having praised him for potentially opening up the North Sea to further drilling.
Farage did, however, depart from Trump’s views again earlier this week after the US president said he would love to see a united Ireland.
“Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom,” Farage said. “The people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum nor unification.”

====================================================================================================

10 of the best mountain huts in Europe: bunkrooms, bothies and bonhomie
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:08 UTC
15:00:08 KST

Cabaña Verónica, Spain
A good mountain hut, I reckon, should be small and only accessible on foot after considerable effort. Throw in a bit of historical interest and I’m bound to be happy. In which case, Cabaña Verónica in the Picos de Europa is a fine start to this list. It sleeps six, and at 2,325 metres requires a two-hour trek from the nearest cable car station, never mind road. It has incredible views and a friendly custodian who keeps things in good order. Yet the real attraction is that this place was formerly a gun turret of a US navy battleship that was scrapped in Bilbao in 1960. An enterprising engineer, Conrado Senties, had it carried up on horseback and reassembled on a plug of rock in the middle of nowhere. Don’t ask why, just enjoy the eccentricity.
€15, reservarefugios.com
Låktatjåkko, Sweden
An absolute gem just over 100 miles north of the Arctic Circle and 1,228 metres up a mountain, Låktatjåkko is well placed to deliver that other essential experience of a decent hut: cosy conviviality while surrounded by frequently hostile conditions. When I visited, it was hard to find the hut because it was coated in thick ice and half-buried in snow. The snug timber-clad lounge is the perfect spot to sit in front of the fire and read old accounts of Arctic explorers such as Fridtjof Nansen (there is no phone coverage). The kitchen bangs out endless plates of waffles with cloudberry jam and cream as well as more substantial fare. Be warned, however: in winter the chances of being marooned are quite high and the skiing can be a serious challenge due to extreme cold and fast-changing mountain weather.
From 515 Swedish kronor (£40), laktatjakko.se
Gaustatoppen, Norway
Like many other huts belonging to the wonderful Norwegian Trekking Association, this place is small, well-run and traditional. It’s the route up to it that is astounding. You enter a mountainside, take a thundering old-school funicular railway one kilometre inside the granite, then wander through tunnels of military-grade concrete, before exiting through a blast-proof steel door and climbing down a short way to the hut. All that startling infrastructure is the cold war relic of a Nato communications station now doubling up as a museum and underground route to the hut, which dates back to 1893. This unique means of access gives the hut an advantage: you can stay in winter (weekends only) on the summit of the highest peak in Telemark province, Gaustatoppen, a popular ski resort, and then ski down. When I was there, the view was about 10 metres into thick mist. On a clear day, however, they say you can see one-sixth of Norway.
From 1,550 Norwegian kroner (£122), dnt.no
Chata pod Rysmi, Slovakia
The Tatra mountains have some excellent huts, but this is my pick. Close enough to the summit of Rysy (2,501 metres) for an early start to catch dawn on the top, it is traditional, well-run and basic. The weather here can take a brutal turn at any time of year and, like all the best huts, this is in precisely the right position to be a genuine bolthole. If it looks younger than its 1933 start date, that is because it has been destroyed several times by avalanches and rock falls, which is also why it only opens 1 June to 31 October.
€65, chatapodrysmi.kst.sk
Kredarica on Triglav, Slovenia
This is, in many ways, a standard, old-fashioned mountain refuge, but Kredarica has the great advantage of being the last potential stop en route to the summit of Slovenia’s highest peak, Triglav (2,864 metres). Given that every Slovene feels compelled to visit the summit at least once in their lifetime, this can be a busy place in summer, especially as the views are magnificent. The hardcore, however, savour its spartan winter comforts, when the dormitories are unheated bunkholes for those about to tackle the final, rather tricky ascent to the top (ice axe and crampons essential).
€30 half-board, triglavskidom.si
Le Refuge de Ciottulu di Mori, Corsica
One of the attractions of Corsica’s epic GR20 long-distance footpath is its unapologetically old-fashioned mountain huts. No emergency helicopters swooping in when the G&Ts run out: this is gruff, mule-supplied, mountain hospitality. Ciottulu is a good example of the genre: bare bones dining room and a dormitory with communal sleeping benches for 26. Its ambience is more like a bothy set at 2,000 metres in a vast stony panorama with a slightly unpredictable caretaker. 
€15, le-gr20.fr
Breiðuvik, Iceland
The east of Iceland is home to a scattering of superb huts like this one. Breiðvik is actually on the coast and has the usual bunk rooms and well-appointed kitchen. The location is the big attraction: a wild, desolate coastline of volcanic sand beaches and abandoned villages. Together with 39 other locations, Brieðvik is part of a useful network run by the Icelandic Touring Association.
11,500 Icelandic kronur (£70), ferdaf.is
Scotland’s mountain bothies
The UK has always remained aloof from the continental urge to build something cosy on a mountain top. We are much happier sitting inside our leaky waterproofs eating soggy sandwiches. The Mountain Bothy Association is doing a little to encourage us away from such Spartanism, but not too much. Most are former cottages for miners or shepherds; many now have a fireplace or even a wood burner. In some, there are a few supplies left on a shelf by previous guests. I have a soft spot for the hard charms of the least comfortable, where you may find only a stone bench and an open doorway. A few have become over-used and afflicted by visitors who don’t understand the ethos of mucking in, sharing out and cleaning up. For that reason, I’m not sure it’s worthwhile picking out any particular bothy (pictured is the Elphin Bothy in the Assynt region of Sutherland), suffice to say that the roster contains some absolute classics. Go and find them.
mountainbothies.org.uk
Rifugio Nuvolau, Italy
The Dolomites are so blessed with exceptional huts and Nuvolau is one of the best. Only accessible on foot, it was originally built in 1883 as a bequest from the Baron Richard von Meerheimb, the man who coined the term “psychodrama”, something he may have dreamed up while watching a Nuvolau sunset. The impeccable location is famous for its stunning shifts in light and colour. Inside is a dining room that serves excellent food, including a three-course dinner; upstairs is a small dormitory.
€51 B&B, rifugionuvolau.it
Rifugio Lagazuoi, Italy
Many huts in the Dolomites have learned that economic survival is via tourists rather than hikers and climbers. Lagazuoi is one of them. Built as a climbers’ refuge, it has expanded over the years and been connected to the road by cable car, which enables coach parties to stay. And yet, it remains magnificent. The south-facing terrace is lovely and there are fantastic walks all around, not least through the tunnels and terraces of the first world war frontline that lie on the cliff face below. Mount Lagazuoi (2,835 metres) was one location where the Austro-Hungarian empire faced off against Italians. Many years later, in 1965, Ugo Pompanin, a local Alpine guide and rock-climbing pioneer, recognised the potential and built the first hut, which, several additions later, is still run in great style by his son Guido.
From €85 with breakfast, rifugiolagazuoi.com

Chinese firms keen on investing in Oman’s International Financial Centre: official

‘Flip the table and rise up’: Lib Dems’ president in combative mood as party gathers in Brighton
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:07 UTC
15:00:07 KST

Standing outside Toynbee Hall in the East End of London, Josh Babarinde doesn’t exactly look like a rabble-rouser. But despite the well-cut suit and disarmingly large smile, the president of the Liberal Democrats is, apparently, up for a fight.
“There are big modern giants that are getting in the way of people’s ability to thrive, and it is the job of Liberal Democrats to address that,” says the 33-year-old. “How are we going to do that? Well, first of all, we’ve got to flip the table over and rise up.”
Flipping over tables is not behaviour normally associated with Liberal Democrat members, about 5,000 of whom are in Brighton for its annual conference this weekend.
But Babarinde, frequently described as a rising star in the party’s ranks, wants his comrades to channel the spirit of the great Liberal thinker William Beveridge, who finessed his radical ideas on social reform in the 141-year-old Whitechapel building.
Beveridge decried the five evils of want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. However, Babarinde, the Eastbourne MP, is taking aim at targets from big tech to crypto billionaires. “People are looking for a force to help break some of those giants and give power and cash back to people who this country is meant to be working for,” he says.
That people are seeking alternatives to the status quo is undeniable, but whether they are looking at the Liberal Democrats is a matter of debate.
The historic 2024 election result gave the party 71 MPs, yet it has been stuck at about 11% in polls for months.
The Lib Dems gained 153 councillors in England in May and six seats in the Scottish parliament, although the party’s advances were more modest than those of the Greens and Reform UK. The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, also struggles to command attention. Lib Dem MPs grumble that Nigel Farage only has to sneeze to attract media coverage, while Davey has to resort to bungee jumping.
“You’ve got a very crowded multiparty system. You’ve got Reform saying any old shit in the media and getting coverage for it with no plan for delivering,” says Babarinde. “As Liberal Democrats, we’re not going to fall into that trap. But what we have got to be clear about is the diagnosis of the problem, who it is standing in the way and what needs to be done.”
He dismisses the idea that the party is yet to produce eye-catching retail policies – “There’s oodles and oodles of it!” – but says it needs to reach beyond its middle England strongholds with digital campaigning that is as strong as its much-envied ground game.
Babarinde, who has spoken about his mother being subjected to domestic abuse and how it shaped his politics, has experience engaging with hard-to-reach communities. He set up a social enterprise smartphone repair service staffed by former offenders and at-risk youth more than a decade ago, which earned him an OBE.
After a stroll through the East End, he points to the stand in Spitalfields market where they had pinned up sheets of A4 paper with “Cracked It” written across them in felt-tip, and laughs. “I would never have got my phone repaired there,” he says. “But when people were giving their money over … I was seeing these guys think: ‘Oh my God, wow! Someone wants my skills. They want what I can offer.’”
Do the Lib Dems want what the ambitious Babarinde has to offer? Despite being elected in 2024, he was elevated to the role of president in November, giving him a vital say in strategy and organisation. He bats away the inevitable question about whether he would like the top job – but when asked if he is a natural leader, he smiles.
“I roll up my sleeves and get stuck in,” he says. “When I saw those young people in the East End prolifically involved in crime amid a lack of opportunities. I wasn’t waiting for someone to swoop in to come to address that issue. I decided to come up with a solution.”
So if the problem is that the Liberal Democrats – despite a seemingly advantageous political backdrop – are stuck on 11% in the polls, what does he see as the answer? “The solution is exactly what is in the strategy we’re talking about this week,” Babarinde says.
“I stood to be party president because I thought I had something to offer: to help develop a new strategy for the party so we can reach new heights.”

Reαd carefully: how to spot – and avoid – a homoglyph attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:07 UTC
15:00:07 KST

You’ve read the email carefully and it looks legitimate. The link it asks you to click on has none of the usual red flags: there are no weird numbers or extra parts to the URL. You feel safe to proceed.
But if you had looked slightly closer you may have noticed something slightly wrong with one of the characters. Just as in the headline of this piece where instead of “a” we used the Cyrillic “α”.
Fraudsters can use letters from different alphabets to create URLs and email addresses that look almost identical to the real thing, but in reality send anyone who clicks on them to a spoof website or inbox. From there they can harvest personal details to use in their scams.
There are other letters and symbols that are easily switched. Last year tech experts spotted fraudsters using the Japanese hiragana character ん to look like a / in an address designed to look as though it was on Booking.com’s website.
Jake Moore, global security adviser at cybersecurity company ESET, says the fraudsters “love Microsoft” as a company identity to spoof. “A fake site might use the Cyrillic “с” instead of the Latin “c” (miсrosoft v microsoft),” he says.
Moore says this type of fraud – known as a homoglyph attack – is becoming increasingly popular. A homoglyph is a character that looks very similar, or even identical, to another one.
“Most phishing attacks are designed to point people to links these days instead of downloading attachments. Attachments can easily be scanned and caught by security software if malicious,” he says.
“Therefore, criminals need to design their websites where the links look genuine and casually request people to click on them without thinking.”
Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN, says homoglyph attacks “are really more of a psychological trick than a technical one”, because the fraudsters are typically trying to panic you into responding quickly, rather than taking time to check things out.
“The goal is to create a sense of panic so you don’t look too closely at the URL. They’re betting that when we’re in a rush, our brains see what we expect to see,” Briedis says.
 It just goes to show that the split-second decision you make when clicking a link is often the most vulnerable part of the whole security chain.”
What it looks like
The real thing. Until you look closely.
You will receive an email or text message suggesting you need to click on a URL or email to sort something out.
Some fonts make substitutions almost impossible to detect. In an email address given in comic sans , for example, the Cyrillic a does not look at all out of place.
“We’ve spent years telling people to check the website before trusting it but the problem with this technique is that you can do exactly that and still be fooled as it can look as it should,” says Moore.
If it’s a URL, Moore says typically it will lead to a site that encourages you to enter your credentials for the real site, including your username, password and even a one-time passcode.
What to do
If you are sent a link, take a moment to think rather than reacting immediately.
“If any text, WhatsApp or email is asking you to log in anywhere, it is vital that you independently visit the genuine website rather than trusting the link in front of you to save a few seconds,” says Moore.
And apply the same thinking to email addresses. Type in the address you know to be correct, rather than clicking on a link.
Keep your browser updated. It will flag up suspicious websites, and by keeping it updated it will catch the criminals’ latest workarounds.
Put in place two-factor authentication, or multifactor authentication (2FA or MFA), which means you have two steps to log into a site.
If you find that your details have been compromised, change your passwords immediately. Contact your bank and report the phishing attack to Report Fraud.

Germany: Polls open in two key state elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Germany: AfD wins in northeastern state, Left in Berlin
Published September 20, 2026last updated September 21, 2026
What you need to know
- 
	The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, narrowly ahead of the center-left Social Democratic Party
- 
	Chancellor Friedrich Merz 's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) failed to enter the state parliament
- 
	Merz strikes defiant tone, pledging to 'get down to business' with reforming Germany after 'disaster' state election
- The socialist Left Party has finished first in Berlin with roughly 25% of the vote, ahead of CDU
- Smaller parties hovering around the 5% threshold could still have a major impact on the final balance of seats
- The outcome of the elections could determine the political future of Merz, whose approval rating is at a record low
- For the first time, 16- and 17-year-olds are eligible to vote in both states
Follow along here for all the highs and lows today:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
AfD wins election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — election commission
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) failed to secure any parliamentary seats.
According to the preliminary results announced by the election commission early Monday morning, the AfD secured 38.2% of the vote on Sunday. The Social Democratic Party (SPD), which is led by state premier Manuela Schwesig, garnered 35.5% of the vote.
The socialist Left Party (6.5%) and the environmentalist Green Party (5.7%) were the only other parties to make it into the state parliament.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU suffered disastrous losses, failing to secure a seat in parliament with only 4.9% of the vote.
The populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which combines left-leaning economic, conservative migration and pro-Russian foreign policy initiatives, also fell short of entering the state parliament with 4.8%.
The business-focused Free Democratic Party (FDP) failed to regain a seat, securing only 1.0%.
The AfD will therefore hold 32 seats in the new state parliament, while the SPD will hold 29. The Left Party and the Greens will each hold five seats.
The previous SPD-Left Party coalition no longer has a majority, but a three-party alliance with the Greens would have one. All three parties have ruled out forming coalitions with the AfD.
BSW admits failure to enter parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
The left-wing populist BSW has acknowledged it would not be represented in the next state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, as it failed to secure the legal minimum of 5% of the votes.
"We didn't make it," BSW's top candidate Peter Schabbel told the DPA news agency late on Sunday. This marks a contrast with his comments hours before, when he said the party was "very confident" about entering parliament.
In his latest remarks, Schabbel said his party failed to qualify due to the polarizing battle between the AfD and the SPD, which harmed smaller parties. He also said the BSW wants to overcome this polarization and would continue to work towards this goal.
Another senior BSW representative in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Sabine Firnhaber, also said the BSW will continue its work in the northeastern state.
"We have a state association, we have regional groups, we have active members," she said. "And we represent goals that would also be worth fighting for in four or five years."
READ: German elections deal a blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz
Elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have dealt the CDU a historic defeat while the AfD saw a massive gain.
Just minutes after the first projections were released, Merz made a statement: "We can't sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — it was a disaster." As for the heavy losses in Berlin, he described the outcome there as "reasonable."
Read the election night analysis by DW's Marcel Fürstenau here.
Will SPD Premier Manuela Schwesig hold on to power in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania?
The center-left SPD placed second in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, securing around 35,4% of the votes compared to the AfD's 38.3%.
However, the current head of the state government, Manuela Schwesig, might still keep herself and her SPD party in power.
With the center-right CDU and the leftist populist BSW both projected to stay out of parliament, the assembly is likely to be comprised out of only four parties: the AfD, the SPD, the Left Party and the Green Party.
Schwesig's current administration is backed by the Left Party. According to projected results, a new alliance between the Left Party and the SPD would fall short of a majority, but a three-way coalition involving the Greens would form a ruling bloc of 39 seats, enough for a majority in the 71-seat assembly.
While other coalitions are theoretically possible, it appears unlikely that any of the other parties will enter a coalition with the AfD, despite its success at the ballot box.
Other German political parties rule out working with the AfD in a strategy known as the "firewall" against the far right.
WATCH: AfD's Alice Weidel says Merz 'can no longer stay in office'
Berlin: Left Party's top candidate celebrates victory in German and Turkish
With the socialist Left Party securing the largest share of the state parliamentary vote in Berlin, the party's mayoral candidate Elif Eralp celebrated the victory of "love and justice over hate."
"Starting today, we are changing Berlin together and make it a better place," said Eralp, who hopes to become the first female mayor of Berlin with immigration background.
Eralp was born in Munich in 1981 to a family of Turkish refugees. While her victory speech was mostly in German, she also shouted out "We wrote history, friends" in Turkish during her address.
The Left Party has big plans for Berlin, including tackling its housing crisis by expropriating real estate own by large corporations. In order for Eralp to become the mayor of Berlin and the head of its state government, however, her party would need to form a coalition, with the center-left SPD and the environmentally friendly Green Party being the most likely contenders for a power-sharing deal.
CDU slips under 5% parliament threshold in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — projections
Germany's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) will not enter the next parliament in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, according to projections published by Germany's top public broadcasters.
The latest predictions published by public broadcaster ARD put the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz at 4.9%, cementing its worst-ever defeat in a state election of this kind. Another German public broadcaster, ZDF, initially maintained its 5% projection before also adjusting its estimates to 4.9%.
The conservative party is not the only one in danger of falling below the legal limit, with the leftist populist Sahra Wagenknech Alliance (BSW) also seemingly just below the threshold.
If both of these factions are kept out of the next parliament, the new assembly would have only four parties: the far-right AfD, the center-left SPD, the socialist Left Party, and the environmentally friendly Greens.
The AfD would still require a coalition partner to form a majority.
CDU faces its worst-ever state election defeat in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is fighting to stay in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament, with its result hovering around the 5% mark.
However, even if the conservatives are represented in the next state parliament, the Sunday election already marks their worst ever election defeat in the state parliamentary votes held anywhere in Germany. The party, founded in 1945, was traditionally considered one of the country's "big tent" political factions seeking to accommodate a wide spectrum of voters.
Its previous worst score was 9% of the vote they secured in Bremen in 1951, according to a report published by NDR, the public broadcaster covering Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
How did Berlin's young people vote?
German citizens in Berlin aged 16 and 17 were able to cast their ballots in the state election for the first time on Sunday — and they were among a group that voted overwhelmingly for progressive parties.
According to results on Sunday evening, some 43% of voters aged 16-24 voted for the socialist Left Party. Another 12% voted for the Greens, while 7% voted for the Social Democrats (SPD).
Meanwhile, around 12% of voters aged 16-24 for the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD).
It was voters in the 25 to 34 age group who were the biggest bloc to have supported the Left Party, with 48% casting their ballots for the far-left party.
Support for the Left Party dims as the age groups grow older, with voters around 33% of voters above 70 having voted for the incumbent Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
Berlin bishops say city voted for democracy, diversity
Commenting on the Berlin state election, the city's Protestant Bishop Christian Stäblein said the majority of the voters endorsed "liberal democracy."
"We are a church bound by the Christian view of humanity and by the dignity of every person," he said.
His Catholic colleague, Heiner Koch, said his church would "continue to critically observe politics, and warn against the supposedly easy solutions, and speak up for those, who are insufficiently seen or heard in the political debate."
Berlin "is and stays diverse," the Catholic bishop said.
Verdi chief urges Merz to rethink reforms
The head of Germany's Verditrade union has called on Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government to change course on planned reforms following the elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
"I hope Mr Merz realizes that he has screwed up," Verdi chairman Frank Werneke told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper.
Werneke called on the government to abandon plans requiring employees to provide a doctor's note from the first day of illness and ending full retirement benefits after 45 years of contributions.
"Many people reject abolishing the full pension after 45 years of contributions. That is an important reason for the CDU's poor performance in the recent elections," Werneke said. "People are worn out and exhausted. They want to stop working, and they need to."
Werneke also described the recent electoral gains of the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) as "extremely threatening."
"An AfD federal government would be a catastrophe," he said, arguing that leaving the euro and European Union would be economically disastrous and that Germany needed immigration.
"Everything must be done to ensure that the AfD does not enter government," Werneke said.
Verdi and other trade unions plan a nationwide day of protest on Saturday, with demonstrations expected in 15 cities.
Berlin: SPD's Krach refuses to discuss new coalitions
The top candidate for the center-left SPD in Berlin, Steffen Krach, refused to discuss cooperation with other parties in the city's Senate.
"It's too early to talk about coalition options," he said, when asked if his party would prefer to rule with the Left Party or the CDU conservatives.
Talking to state broadcaster ARD, Krach noted that the incumbent CDU-SPD coalition was clearly defeated at the polls, and that future steps will be decided within the party committees in the following weeks.
Meanwhile, the Green party indicated they were ready to rule together with the Left Party and the SPD.
"We want to take responsibility and forge a progressive alliance for Berlin together with the SPD and the Left," said senior Green representatives Nina Stahr and Philmon Ghirmai, saying that Berliners voted in favor of political change.
Populist BSW projected to fall short, stay out of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament
According to incomplete projections published by German media, the leftist populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) will not be entering the state legislature of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, depriving them of the kingmaker role they had previously secured in Saxony-Anhalt.
The estimates published by German state broadcasters ARD and ZDF just after 8 p.m. on Sunday show BSW at 4.9% of the votes, just shy of the 5% threshold they need to secure in order to be represented in the state parliament.
Moreover, the latest available numbers show Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) hovering around 5%, also putting it at risk of not having a parliamentary presence. A failure by the center-right CDU to enter the chamber would ramp up pressure on the chancellor, whose power is already shaken by the Saxony-Anhalt vote and his party's already staggeringly low result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The numbers are subject to change as the official count continues.
Populist BSW rejects AfD coalition in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
With the far-right populist AfD leading the pack in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but still projected to fall well short of the parliamentary majority, the leftist populist BSW rejected the possibility of officially joining forces.
BSW's top candidate Peter Schabbel said there would be no coalition with the AfD.
"We are sticking to it," he said.
However, he noted that cooperation between the two parties was still possible, including voting together.
This language reflects BSW's attitude following the Saxony-Anhalt election two weeks ago. With the AfD also falling short of a parliamentary majority in this German state, the BSW said it would "decide on the substance" when it comes to supporting them in parliament.
On Sunday, Schabbel also sought to dispel doubts that BSW would clear the 5% hurdle to enter the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament, despite the projections showing them at the very edge of the required percentage of the vote.
"We are very confident that we will get into the state assembly," Schabbel said.
Leading CDU figure blames party firewall critics for voter uncertainty
Senior Christian Democratic Union (CDU) politician Philipp Amthor has blamed members of his own party who questioned its firewall against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) for contributing to the CDU's poor showing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Amthor, a minister of state in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Chancellery, told public broadcaster ZDF that there was a "very clear position" across the state CDU on maintaining its distance from the AfD.
He said individual party figures had tried to soften that position, but that this had instead contributed to "even greater uncertainty among our voters here in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania."
"I am very grateful that everyone kept their nerve and did not draw the wrong conclusions," Amthor, who himself hails from the state, said.
The CDU is hovering around the 5% threshold in the latest projections, a big drop from the 13.3% it won in 2021.
Amthor described the CDU's result as a "historic defeat" and a "tectonic shift" for a party that governed Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania from 1990 to 1998.

A few years ago, the architects began collaborating with Jirka Vávra and Katka Jiroutová, who took over management of the successful family business VAVI, founded by Věra Vávrová. The brand outfits entire corporate teams, including international ones, from management to operations, with production largely concentrated in Vimperk and supplemented by facilities in Prague and elsewhere, all under a long-term emphasis on quality and craftsmanship.

How did Berlin's young people vote?
German citizens in Berlin aged 16 and 17 were able to cast their ballots in the state election for the first time on Sunday — and they were among a group that voted overwhelmingly for progressive parties.
According to results on Sunday evening, some 43% of voters aged 16-24 voted for the socialist Left Party. Another 12% voted for the Greens, while 7% voted for the Social Democrats (SPD).
Meanwhile, around 12% of voters aged 16-24 for the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD).
It was voters in the 25 to 34 age group who were the biggest bloc to have supported the Left Party, with 48% casting their ballots for the far-left party.
Support for the Left Party dims as the age groups grow older, with voters around 33% of voters above 70 having voted for the incumbent Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
Berlin bishops say city voted for democracy, diversity
Commenting on the Berlin state election, the city's Protestant Bishop Christian Stäblein said the majority of the voters endorsed "liberal democracy."
"We are a church bound by the Christian view of humanity and by the dignity of every person," he said.
His Catholic colleague, Heiner Koch, said his church would "continue to critically observe politics, and warn against the supposedly easy solutions, and speak up for those, who are insufficiently seen or heard in the political debate."
Berlin "is and stays diverse," the Catholic bishop said.
Verdi chief urges Merz to rethink reforms
The head of Germany's Verditrade union has called on Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government to change course on planned reforms following the elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
"I hope Mr Merz realizes that he has screwed up," Verdi chairman Frank Werneke told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper.
Werneke called on the government to abandon plans requiring employees to provide a doctor's note from the first day of illness and ending full retirement benefits after 45 years of contributions.
"Many people reject abolishing the full pension after 45 years of contributions. That is an important reason for the CDU's poor performance in the recent elections," Werneke said. "People are worn out and exhausted. They want to stop working, and they need to."
Werneke also described the recent electoral gains of the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) as "extremely threatening."
"An AfD federal government would be a catastrophe," he said, arguing that leaving the euro and European Union would be economically disastrous and that Germany needed immigration.
"Everything must be done to ensure that the AfD does not enter government," Werneke said.
Verdi and other trade unions plan a nationwide day of protest on Saturday, with demonstrations expected in 15 cities.
Berlin: SPD's Krach refuses to discuss new coalitions
The top candidate for the center-left SPD in Berlin, Steffen Krach, refused to discuss cooperation with other parties in the city's Senate.
"It's too early to talk about coalition options," he said, when asked if his party would prefer to rule with the Left Party or the CDU conservatives.
Talking to state broadcaster ARD, Krach noted that the incumbent CDU-SPD coalition was clearly defeated at the polls, and that future steps will be decided within the party committees in the following weeks.
Meanwhile, the Green party indicated they were ready to rule together with the Left Party and the SPD.
"We want to take responsibility and forge a progressive alliance for Berlin together with the SPD and the Left," said senior Green representatives Nina Stahr and Philmon Ghirmai, saying that Berliners voted in favor of political change.
Populist BSW projected to fall short, stay out of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament
According to incomplete projections published by German media, the leftist populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) will not be entering the state legislature of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, depriving them of the kingmaker role they had previously secured in Saxony-Anhalt.
The estimates published by German state broadcasters ARD and ZDF just after 8 p.m. on Sunday show BSW at 4.9% of the votes, just shy of the 5% threshold they need to secure in order to be represented in the state parliament.
Moreover, the latest available numbers show Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) hovering around 5%, also putting it at risk of not having a parliamentary presence. A failure by the center-right CDU to enter the chamber would ramp up pressure on the chancellor, whose power is already shaken by the Saxony-Anhalt vote and his party's already staggeringly low result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The numbers are subject to change as the official count continues.
Populist BSW rejects AfD coalition in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
With the far-right populist AfD leading the pack in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but still projected to fall well short of the parliamentary majority, the leftist populist BSW rejected the possibility of officially joining forces.
BSW's top candidate Peter Schabbel said there would be no coalition with the AfD.
"We are sticking to it," he said.
However, he noted that cooperation between the two parties was still possible, including voting together.
This language reflects BSW's attitude following the Saxony-Anhalt election two weeks ago. With the AfD also falling short of a parliamentary majority in this German state, the BSW said it would "decide on the substance" when it comes to supporting them in parliament.
On Sunday, Schabbel also sought to dispel doubts that BSW would clear the 5% hurdle to enter the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament, despite the projections showing them at the very edge of the required percentage of the vote.
"We are very confident that we will get into the state assembly," Schabbel said.
Leading CDU figure blames party firewall critics for voter uncertainty
Senior Christian Democratic Union (CDU) politician Philipp Amthor has blamed members of his own party who questioned its firewall against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) for contributing to the CDU's poor showing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Amthor, a minister of state in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Chancellery, told public broadcaster ZDF that there was a "very clear position" across the state CDU on maintaining its distance from the AfD.
He said individual party figures had tried to soften that position, but that this had instead contributed to "even greater uncertainty among our voters here in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania."
"I am very grateful that everyone kept their nerve and did not draw the wrong conclusions," Amthor, who himself hails from the state, said.
The CDU is hovering around the 5% threshold in the latest projections, a big drop from the 13.3% it won in 2021.
Amthor described the CDU's result as a "historic defeat" and a "tectonic shift" for a party that governed Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania from 1990 to 1998.

AfD wins election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — election commission
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) failed to secure any parliamentary seats.
According to the preliminary results announced by the election commission early Monday morning, the AfD secured 38.2% of the vote on Sunday. The Social Democratic Party (SPD), which is led by state premier Manuela Schwesig, garnered 35.5% of the vote.
The socialist Left Party (6.5%) and the environmentalist Green Party (5.7%) were the only other parties to make it into the state parliament.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU suffered disastrous losses, failing to secure a seat in parliament with only 4.9% of the vote.
The populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which combines left-leaning economic, conservative migration and pro-Russian foreign policy initiatives, also fell short of entering the state parliament with 4.8%.
The business-focused Free Democratic Party (FDP) failed to regain a seat, securing only 1.0%.
The AfD will therefore hold 32 seats in the new state parliament, while the SPD will hold 29. The Left Party and the Greens will each hold five seats.
The previous SPD-Left Party coalition no longer has a majority, but a three-party alliance with the Greens would have one. All three parties have ruled out forming coalitions with the AfD.
BSW admits failure to enter parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
The left-wing populist BSW has acknowledged it would not be represented in the next state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, as it failed to secure the legal minimum of 5% of the votes.
"We didn't make it," BSW's top candidate Peter Schabbel told the DPA news agency late on Sunday. This marks a contrast with his comments hours before, when he said the party was "very confident" about entering parliament.
In his latest remarks, Schabbel said his party failed to qualify due to the polarizing battle between the AfD and the SPD, which harmed smaller parties. He also said the BSW wants to overcome this polarization and would continue to work towards this goal.
Another senior BSW representative in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Sabine Firnhaber, also said the BSW will continue its work in the northeastern state.
"We have a state association, we have regional groups, we have active members," she said. "And we represent goals that would also be worth fighting for in four or five years."
READ: German elections deal a blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz
Elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have dealt the CDU a historic defeat while the AfD saw a massive gain.
Just minutes after the first projections were released, Merz made a statement: "We can't sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — it was a disaster." As for the heavy losses in Berlin, he described the outcome there as "reasonable."
Read the election night analysis by DW's Marcel Fürstenau here.
Will SPD Premier Manuela Schwesig hold on to power in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania?
The center-left SPD placed second in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, securing around 35,4% of the votes compared to the AfD's 38.3%.
However, the current head of the state government, Manuela Schwesig, might still keep herself and her SPD party in power.
With the center-right CDU and the leftist populist BSW both projected to stay out of parliament, the assembly is likely to be comprised out of only four parties: the AfD, the SPD, the Left Party and the Green Party.
Schwesig's current administration is backed by the Left Party. According to projected results, a new alliance between the Left Party and the SPD would fall short of a majority, but a three-way coalition involving the Greens would form a ruling bloc of 39 seats, enough for a majority in the 71-seat assembly.
While other coalitions are theoretically possible, it appears unlikely that any of the other parties will enter a coalition with the AfD, despite its success at the ballot box.
Other German political parties rule out working with the AfD in a strategy known as the "firewall" against the far right.

Berlin: Left Party's top candidate celebrates victory in German and Turkish
With the socialist Left Party securing the largest share of the state parliamentary vote in Berlin, the party's mayoral candidate Elif Eralp celebrated the victory of "love and justice over hate."
"Starting today, we are changing Berlin together and make it a better place," said Eralp, who hopes to become the first female mayor of Berlin with immigration background.
Eralp was born in Munich in 1981 to a family of Turkish refugees. While her victory speech was mostly in German, she also shouted out "We wrote history, friends" in Turkish during her address.
The Left Party has big plans for Berlin, including tackling its housing crisis by expropriating real estate own by large corporations. In order for Eralp to become the mayor of Berlin and the head of its state government, however, her party would need to form a coalition, with the center-left SPD and the environmentally friendly Green Party being the most likely contenders for a power-sharing deal.

According to incomplete projections published by German media, the leftist populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) will not be entering the state legislature of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, depriving them of the kingmaker role they had previously secured in Saxony-Anhalt.
The estimates published by German state broadcasters ARD and ZDF just after 8 p.m. on Sunday show BSW at 4.9% of the votes, just shy of the 5% threshold they need to secure in order to be represented in the state parliament.
Moreover, the latest available numbers show Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) hovering around 5%, also putting it at risk of not having a parliamentary presence. A failure by the center-right CDU to enter the chamber would ramp up pressure on the chancellor, whose power is already shaken by the Saxony-Anhalt vote and his party's already staggeringly low result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The numbers are subject to change as the official count continues.
Populist BSW rejects AfD coalition in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
With the far-right populist AfD leading the pack in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but still projected to fall well short of the parliamentary majority, the leftist populist BSW rejected the possibility of officially joining forces.
BSW's top candidate Peter Schabbel said there would be no coalition with the AfD.
"We are sticking to it," he said.
However, he noted that cooperation between the two parties was still possible, including voting together.
This language reflects BSW's attitude following the Saxony-Anhalt election two weeks ago. With the AfD also falling short of a parliamentary majority in this German state, the BSW said it would "decide on the substance" when it comes to supporting them in parliament.
On Sunday, Schabbel also sought to dispel doubts that BSW would clear the 5% hurdle to enter the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament, despite the projections showing them at the very edge of the required percentage of the vote.
"We are very confident that we will get into the state assembly," Schabbel said.
Leading CDU figure blames party firewall critics for voter uncertainty
Senior Christian Democratic Union (CDU) politician Philipp Amthor has blamed members of his own party who questioned its firewall against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) for contributing to the CDU's poor showing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Amthor, a minister of state in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Chancellery, told public broadcaster ZDF that there was a "very clear position" across the state CDU on maintaining its distance from the AfD.
He said individual party figures had tried to soften that position, but that this had instead contributed to "even greater uncertainty among our voters here in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania."
"I am very grateful that everyone kept their nerve and did not draw the wrong conclusions," Amthor, who himself hails from the state, said.
The CDU is hovering around the 5% threshold in the latest projections, a big drop from the 13.3% it won in 2021.
Amthor described the CDU's result as a "historic defeat" and a "tectonic shift" for a party that governed Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania from 1990 to 1998.

A 66-million-year-old tooth reveals T. rex was nearly as warm as a human
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:56:26 UTC
14:56:26 KST

A 66-million-year-old tooth reveals T. rex was nearly as warm as a human
Fossilized teeth reveal that T. rex ran at about 97 degrees Fahrenheit, giving scientists their first direct evidence of just how warm-blooded the giant predator really was.
- Date:
- September 20, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Los Angeles
- Summary:
- Chemical clues preserved inside fossilized T. rex teeth reveal that the dinosaur maintained a body temperature of about 97 degrees Fahrenheit, almost identical to humans. The finding provides direct evidence that the giant predator was warm-blooded, helping explain how it stayed active and survived in chilly environments as far north as Alaska.
- Share:
For more than a century, scientists have tried to reconstruct the biology of Tyrannosaurus rex from bones, teeth, footprints, and other traces left behind more than 60 million years ago. Fossils discovered as far north as Alaska have suggested that T. rex could tolerate cold conditions, adding to evidence that the giant dinosaur was moving away from the cold-blooded physiology of many reptiles and toward the warm-blooded metabolism seen in birds.
Now scientists have done something that once seemed impossible: they have effectively taken T. rex's temperature.
Researchers at UCLA developed a method for estimating body temperature from fossilized teeth and applied it to specimens held by the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County. Their results indicate that T. rex maintained a body temperature of about 97 degrees Fahrenheit, remarkably close to that of humans.
The finding supports the picture of T. rex as an active predator or scavenger with a relatively fast metabolism rather than a sluggish animal that depended heavily on basking in the sun. Its ability to generate and regulate internal heat may also help explain how tyrannosaurs survived in colder regions that were inhospitable to many other reptiles.
A Fossil Thermometer Refined Over a Decade
UCLA researchers first developed their prehistoric thermometer method about a decade ago. The technique used skeletal material to investigate whether extinct animals were warm-blooded or cold-blooded.
Applying it to T. rex initially posed a major problem. The early version of the method required more fossil material than a museum would reasonably sacrifice from such an important and irreplaceable specimen.
Over the following decade, however, the UCLA team dramatically improved the technique. Researchers reduced the amount of material needed for testing ancient teeth by roughly 90%.
That improvement persuaded L.A.'s Natural History Museum to provide tiny portions of two teeth belonging to Thomas the T. rex, the most complete of the towering tyrannosaur skeletons displayed in the museum's dinosaur hall.
Although other lines of evidence have increasingly suggested that T. rex was warm-blooded, the study, published Sept. 16 in Science Advances, provides the first actual temperature measurement for the animal.
"No one's been able to make a temperature measurement like this before," UCLA geobiologist and study co-author Robert Eagle said. "We found T. rex was 36 Celsius (97 Fahrenheit), about the same as humans. The temperature is about what I would have guessed -- higher than a reptile or a slow mammal like a sloth, but lower than an avian."
T. rex was still a scaly, egg-laying reptile, but its 36 C body temperature was much closer to that of a warm-blooded mammal than a modern reptile.
Modern cold-blooded reptiles typically maintain temperatures around 28-30 °C (82-86 °F), while most birds, the evolutionary descendants of dinosaurs, often have considerably higher body temperatures of 40-43 °C (104-109 °F), according to Eagle.
How Scientists Took T. Rex's Temperature
The secret is hidden in microscopic chemical bonds preserved inside tooth enamel.
Rare isotopes of carbon and oxygen can bond together within enamel. How frequently those bonds form depends partly on temperature. More of the bonds form under cooler conditions, while fewer form at warmer temperatures.
That relationship allows researchers to use the chemical signature preserved in fossil teeth as a kind of ancient thermometer. A warm-blooded animal should leave behind fewer of these isotope bonds than a cold-blooded animal.
"That's the basis of using the isotopes as a thermometer," Eagle said. "In theory, we can make measurements using any part of the skeleton, but the bones in our body are constantly being remodeled and dissolved and replaced. Tooth enamel has large crystalline structures that are extremely durable, making it the part of the skeleton that most resists chemical alteration by the environment over the eons."
To make the measurement, Eagle and lead author Randy Flores used a dental drill to collect enamel from the fossil teeth. They then dissolved the powdered enamel in phosphoric acid, releasing carbon dioxide gas that contained the isotope bonds they wanted to study.
A mass spectrometer was used to measure the isotope ratios in that gas. The researchers also pressurized the gas to create a denser stream of CO2, allowing the instrument to obtain usable measurements from much smaller quantities of fossil material.
A Warm-Blooded T. Rex Was Built for an Active Life
The 97-degree reading adds physical evidence to the idea that tyrannosaurs were energetic animals with relatively high metabolisms.
Maintaining their own body heat would have helped T. rex remain active while hunting or scavenging enough food to support such a metabolism, Eagle said. It also helps scientists place the dinosaur along the evolutionary path that ultimately produced modern birds, whose body temperatures are generally even higher.
Warm-bloodedness may have given T. rex another important advantage: access to colder environments.
Study co-author Alessandro Chiarenza, a paleontologist at University College London, said an internally regulated body temperature could have allowed tyrannosaurs to live in regions where cold-blooded reptiles struggled to survive.
T. rex lived during the Cretaceous Period, when Earth's climate was much warmer than today. Global conditions were approximately 11-25 °F warmer than modern temperatures, and dinosaurs had millions of years to adapt to that hot-house world.
Yet even under those generally warmer conditions, winters in ancient Alaska would have been extremely challenging for a cold-blooded dinosaur.
That pattern is reflected in the fossil record. Paleontologists have not found fossils of lizards, turtles, crocodiles, or other reptiles from Cretaceous Alaska, Chiarenza said. Tyrannosaurus fossils, however, have been discovered there.
"Now we have empirical evidence using this geologic thermometer," Chiarenza said. "Using paleoclimate models of the past, we were able to reconstruct a range in North America 66 million years ago that stretched from Mexico to Alaska, based on where T. rex could have survived with a 97 °F body temperature."
Why Scientists Were Finally Allowed to Test T. Rex Teeth
Obtaining material from a famous fossil is not a simple decision. Any analysis that requires drilling or removing part of a specimen permanently alters an object that cannot be replaced.
After years of working with Eagle and UCLA, the Natural History Museum concluded that the improved technology could produce valuable results while requiring only very small samples.
The museum therefore allowed researchers to take portions of two Thomas the T. rex teeth that were not on public display, according to Luis Chiappe, curator of the museum's Dinosaur Institute and head of NHM research and collections.
"We're asked for fossils for use in destructive analysis all the time," Chiappe said. "The museum contains tens of millions of specimens of minerals, animals and fossils that are irreplaceable. We have to make decisions that balance the damage to the specimen against gaining knowledge about the natural world. Sacrificing small portions of two teeth to learn about T. rex's body temperature is definitely worth the trade-off."
An Ancient Crocodilian Provided an Important Check
Thomas the T. rex was excavated from Hell Creek in Montana, a site that also produced ancient crocodilian fossils analyzed by the researchers.
Those crocodilian remains provided an important comparison. The team measured a body temperature of 30 °C (86 °F) for the crocodilian, substantially lower than the 36 °C (97 °F) reading from T. rex.
That difference helped rule out the possibility that geological processes at the fossil site had altered the chemical signatures in both animals in the same way. If the surrounding geology had been responsible for changing their molecular composition, the two species would have been expected to produce similar temperature readings, Eagle said.
Instead, their sharply different temperatures support the conclusion that the chemical signals preserved in the fossils reflect genuine differences in the animals' biology.
The research was supported in part by grants from the National Science Foundation.

Germans vote in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, pitting SPD against AfD as Merz faces leadership test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:50:01 UTC
14:50:01 KST

Voters across the eastern German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern cast ballots on Sunday to elect a new state parliament in a tense race.
Premier Manuela Schwesig's centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the far-right Alternative for Germany, known as the AfD, were running neck and neck throughout the campaign.
Polling stations open at 8 a.m. and close at 6 p.m. local time, with about 1.3 million residents eligible to cast a vote.
The electorate included 16- and 17-year-olds voting in a state election there for the very first time this year.
The contest followed the AfD's record 43.8 percent showing in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks earlier, its strongest result yet in any German state.
A final public broadcaster ZDF poll put the Social Democrats (SPD) narrowly ahead at 37 percent, with the AfD trailing just one point behind at 36 percent.
The socialist Left Party polled at 9 percent, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative CDU hovered close to the 5 percent entry threshold, at 6 percent.
The Greens stood at 5 percent, the left-wing Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) trailed at 4 percent, and 21 percent of respondents remained undecided before the vote.
What’s at stake
Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is a thinly populated state on the Baltic Sea, with Schwerin as its capital. The SPD has governed there since 1998 with changing partners.
Schwesig, premier since 2017, won 39.6 percent in the 2021 election and has since governed alongside the Left Party.
A recent ZDF survey found 61 percent would back Schwesig in a direct vote, against just 30 percent for her AfD rival.
Her AfD challenger, federal lawmaker Leif-Erik Holm, campaigned on economic grievances and a pledge to end 28 years of Social Democratic rule.
Possible coalition scenarios
Neither the SPD nor the AfD is expected to win an outright majority in the state parliament, meaning both would need partners to form a government.
Analysts said the likeliest outcome remained a three-way alliance of the Social Democrats, the Left Party and the Greens.
Every mainstream party ruled out governing alongside the AfD, leaving its path to power unclear even in victory.
Beyond Schwerin, the vote doubled as a referendum on Merz, who cancelled a UN trip to New York to stay in Berlin.
Test for Merz
In Berlin, Sunday's election served as a barometer of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's standing, whose support has slid to historic lows.
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU polled around 6 percent, risking a fall below the 5 percent threshold for parliament entry, a result that would leave it without seats in Schwerin for the first time since reunification.
Merz cancelled a UN trip to New York to stay in Berlin, meeting senior CDU leaders late Sunday, with further talks continuing on Monday and a CDU-CSU lawmakers' gathering two days later.
Leadership speculation has built for weeks, though all 8 CDU state premiers backed Merz on Wednesday.
Observers said a strong AfD result paired with another CDU defeat could still spark a leadership fight.

Discrediting the army or spreading what the authorities regard as fake news are punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
In a small act of defiance, Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoilt his ballot paper, writing his party’s name and the slogan “For peace”.

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico accused Western politicians of seeking to provoke a conflict between NATO and Russia. He stated that Slovakia would not take part in such a war.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said that some Western politicians allegedly seek to provoke a conflict between NATO and Russia. He also criticized support for Ukraine and stated that under his government, Slovak soldiers would not fight against Russia. Dennik N reports, according to UNN.
Details
The Slovak prime minister believes that Western politicians seek to provoke a NATO–Russia conflict if Ukraine is defeated on the battlefield.
The failure of the strategy to destroy Russia through the war in Ukraine is forcing many Western politicians to conclude that if this cannot be achieved with the help of the Ukrainian army and its full support, then everything must be done to provoke a conflict between NATO and Russia

If anyone is interested in provoking a military conflict between NATO and Russia in order to satisfy their own national-state interests, they must bear responsibility for such a step themselves and not shift it onto other NATO member states
Fico assured that Slovakia would not participate in such a "conflict," despite Article 5 of NATO.

Germany’s Berlin, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania states head to polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:42:50 UTC
14:42:50 KST

Far left wins in Berlin, far right in Germany’s northeast vote: Exit polls
Far-right AfD defeated German chancellor’s CDU in recent Saxony-Anhalt state election, casting doubt on his future.
Germany’s far-left party Die Linke (the Left) has been projected to win the most votes in a state election in Berlin, exit polls show, though it would need allies to take control of the mayor’s office in the German capital for the first time since reunification in 1990.
An exit poll for public broadcaster ARD showed Die Linke at 24.5 percent, the incumbent conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz at 20 percent, and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) at 16 percent.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Tens of thousands march across Germany to protest against far-right AfD
- list 2 of 3AfD is rising, but it can still be stopped
- list 3 of 3Germany’s AfD wins in key state: Is far-right on cusp of national rule?
In the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, however, the AfD is projected to win the elections, polling at 37 percent, just above the centre-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), which is expected to secure 36 percent.
Merz said the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania were a “disaster”.
Speaking at a crisis meeting of the CDU leadership, the German chancellor told reporters he promised to stay on, after recent speculation he may soon be ousted by his party.
“What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience,” the 70-year-old said at the Berlin headquarters of his centre-right CDU. “The reforms have to come. I am taking on this responsibility because I want to move our country forward.”
AfD, Die Linke react
Following the results, the AfD’s national co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, called on the German chanceller to resign.
Chrupalla told ZDF television that “the chancellor’s statement today really was more than feeble – he announced that he’d carry on as before, instead of finally drawing the consequences and resigning”.
Meanwhile, Elif Eralp, Die Linke’s lead candidate, who is the daughter of Turkish immigrants, celebrated her party’s triumph over the anti-immigration AfD.
“In our city, love and justice have triumphed over hatred,” she said.
About 2.5 million people were eligible to vote in the city-state of Berlin, Germany’s capital, and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday. Polling booths in both states – traditionally seen as left-leaning – opened at 8am local time (06:00 GMT) and closed at 6pm (16:00 GMT).
Pressure on Merz has been mounting after the far-right AfD delivered a significant defeat to his CDU party two weeks ago in the key state of Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD fell just short of an absolute majority, which would have allowed it to govern on its own.
After just 16 months in power, Merz’s approval ratings have plunged to about 14 percent, the latest polls suggest, as he struggles to push through promised economic and social welfare reforms with his centre-left coalition partners, the SPD, raising doubts among fellow party members about whether he can continue to lead.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU was an onlooker to the main battle between the SPD’s popular state premier Manuela Schwesig and the AfD’s lead candidate, former radio presenter Leif-Erik Holm.
Reporting from Schwerin in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane said that “when he [Merz] speaks of disaster, from his perspective that is what this result is”, as he outlined that Merz’s party has received its worst result in this state since any state election following the formation of Germany after World War II.
“But there is nuance to what he had to say,” Kane said. “His party got 20 percent in Berlin, and that is not disastrous from his perspective. Though the AfD is clearly the strongest party in the old East Germany, outside Berlin, they are not so in western Germany, and that is where the vast majority of the German population lives, and where elections matter the most.”
“As far as where Germany goes next,” Kane added, “Merz wants to stay on, but will his party let him?”
AfD’s previous victory
Regional elections would not usually draw much interest outside Germany, but the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt, which it sees as the first step towards winning federal elections due in 2029, has sent shock waves through Europe.
“Saxony-Anhalt was certainly a revolution for the German party system,” Florian Hartleb, a professor of international relations at Modul University in Vienna and expert on far-right movements, told Al Jazeera.
Hartleb said the AfD had been “fundamentally excluded” from the power system, with the other political parties trying “everything” against it in recent years. “But it didn’t work out,” he said, citing voters’ dissatisfaction over migration, the economy and social inequality.

RIYADH – The United States warned on Sept 19 that hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthis could “escalate rapidly” after a missile attack targeted Riyadh for the first time since the Yemen conflict resumed.
US President Donald Trump cut short a weekend at Camp David, a secluded presidential complex in rural Maryland, to return unexpectedly to the White House on Sept 19.
The White House gave no explanation for the early return, which comes as a new threshold was crossed in the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who control a large part of Yemen and are fighting government forces backed by a coalition led by Riyadh.
Loud explosions rang out twice on Sept 19 in the Saudi capital, where AFP journalists saw a fuel tank bearing the logo of oil giant Aramco on fire near the airport.
“This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly,” the US State Department warned, adding that American citizens outside the Middle East should “seriously reconsider travel to and through the region”.
The Houthis’ lightning offensive seizing swathes of Yemeni territory in recent weeks has left hundreds dead and, according to the UN, displaced more than 110,000 people.
‘Thwarted’
The clashes and subsequent hostilities with the kingdom have already disrupted exports from Saudi Arabia – the world’s leading supplier of crude oil – as well as maritime traffic.
The Riyadh-led coalition confirmed on Sept 19 on X that a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the capital was “successfully intercepted and destroyed”.
The coalition added that the pro-Iranian fighters had tried to target “civilians and civilian infrastructure” in several cities, including the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, an important export hub for Saudi oil.
It said the attacks were “thwarted by the Gulf monarchy’s air defences”.
Saudi Arabia has responded with scores of air strikes on Houthi-held areas but failed to stop the advance. The Houthis said they responded to recent Saudi attacks by carrying out “two successful military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones”, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement on Telegram.
“The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu.”
Saudi authorities had earlier issued an overnight air raid alert.
Hours after the early morning alert, residents said they heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.
Lightning offensive
This is the first time since Yemen’s civil war resumed that strikes have threatened the Saudi capital, piling further pressure on a global economy already rocked by seven months of war between the US and Iran.
“The area is under a hostile aerial threat,” according to a message received just before 3am by Riyadh residents, urging them to stay indoors.
AFP journalists then heard two explosions, before the Saudi civil defence agency lifted the alert half an hour later.
“I heard the alarm, then my windows shook,” said a Riyadh resident. Another resident described the attack as “terrifying”.
The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca on Sept 16, denouncing it as a “cowardly terrorist attack” on Islam’s holy city, which welcomes millions of pilgrims each year. The Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a “worn-out lie”.
The Houthis have reported scores of retaliatory strikes carried out daily by Riyadh since their offensive in September to take over the country’s entire Red Sea coast, giving them control over the vital Bab al-Mandab strait.
The United States, according to US news platform Axios, last week refused a Saudi request to strike the Houthis.
Washington approved a US$24.3 billion (S$31 billion) sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets on Sept 17 to help Riyadh “deter current and future threats”, the State Department said.
War in Yemen broke out in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the capital Sanaa and other regions, triggering a military intervention led by Saudi Arabia in March 2015.
A fragile truce reached in 2022 between the warring parties collapsed in July, when the Houthis defied Riyadh’s control of Yemeni airspace by allowing an Iranian aircraft to land in Yemen.
