Why has Pauline Hanson joined forces with Muslim and Vietnamese-born MPs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:31:40 UTC
14:31:40 KST

In brief
- Pauline Hanson, Fatima Payman and Dai Le have united to argue parliamentary staffing allocations are unfair.
- The prime minister has significant discretion over personal staff, but the trio wants an independent system instead.
Pauline Hanson and Fatima Payman have clashed over race, religion and politics.
But this week, the One Nation leader and Muslim independent senator stood together, alongside Vietnamese-born independent MP Dai Le.
At the centre of their unlikely alliance is a fight over parliamentary staffing, with the three accusing Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of unfairly determining who gets additional staff and calling for the system to be taken out of the prime minister's hands.
The unlikely trio appeared together at Parliament House on Thursday, arguing the way personal staff are allocated to politicians is unfair and lacks transparency.
Their grievance centres on an unusual feature of Australia's parliamentary system: while MPs and senators employ their own staff, the prime minister has significant discretion over the allocation of additional personal staff.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
That discretion has previously faced scrutiny in parliament.
Why did Hanson, Payman and Le join forces?
Despite their political differences, all three say they are being denied the staffing resources they need to do adequately their jobs.
Payman, who left Labor in 2024 after crossing the Senate floor over Palestinian statehood, currently has no additional personal staff allocated to her.
Le, who defeated Labor to win the western Sydney seat of Fowler as an independent in 2022, has one.
One Nation, meanwhile, increased its representation at the 2025 election but says its staffing allocation did not increase accordingly.
According to AAP, modelling puts One Nation's allocation at 0.83 personal staff per parliamentarian, compared with 4.09 for Labor and 1.47 for the Coalition.
Those figures include different categories of parliamentarians and office-holders, so they are not a direct like-for-like comparison of backbench MPs.
Hanson, Payman and Le argue the differences demonstrate the need for a more transparent and independent system.
According to The Conversation, Le told reporters on Thursday there were "no published criteria, no explanation, no appeal" for staffing decisions.
The three have threatened to pursue legislation changes when parliament returns in October to remove the prime minister's power over non-government personal staff allocations and give the responsibility to an independent authority.
Who actually decides how many staff politicians get?
Parliamentary staffing is divided into different categories, with different rules governing how positions are allocated.
Politicians generally have two broad categories of staff: electorate employees and personal employees.
Electorate staff perform work such as assisting constituents and supporting MPs and senators in their parliamentary duties.
Personal staff can perform different roles, including providing policy advice, research, communications and support for a parliamentarian's work in Canberra.
They are employed under the Members of Parliament (Staff) Act, commonly known as the MOP(S) Act, and cannot legally be employed for party-political purposes.
But additional personal staff are not distributed to every politician according to a single automatic formula.
The Department of Finance says the prime minister determines the number of personal employee positions allocated to ministers and assistant ministers, as well as the allocation given to the opposition.
The prime minister also determines the allocation given to the leader of a minority party, who can then distribute those positions among their party's MPs, and may allocate personal employees to independent parliamentarians.
That means gaining another MP or senator does not necessarily translate into an increase in personal staff members.
Albanese's power over staff members is not unique. The system has given successive prime ministers significant control over personal staffing allocations
Why do extra staff matter?
Additional personal staff provide support across a range of parliamentary duties, and can affect their capacity to carry out parliamentary and electorate work.
They can research legislation, prepare MPs and senators for parliamentary debates and committee hearings, develop policy advice, deal with media and stakeholders and help offices manage correspondence and constituent issues.
Crossbenchers and smaller parties also have fewer parliamentary colleagues and party resources to draw on than the major parties.
The Parliamentary Library has previously noted that staffing levels for crossbenchers have varied significantly over time, and have sometimes changed depending on the political circumstances of the parliament.
When independents held the balance of power following the 2010 election, for example, additional staff were allocated to crossbench MPs. Those arrangements changed after the 2013 election.
Additional personal staff can assist parliamentarians with work including scrutinising legislation, preparing for parliamentary debates and participating in committee work.
Has this fight happened before?
The allocation of personal staff to crossbench parliamentarians has previously been contested, including since the Albanese government took office in 2022.
After Labor took office four years ago, Albanese reduced the number of additional personal staff allocated to crossbench parliamentarians, prompting significant criticism from independents.
A Parliamentary Library research paper subsequently noted that while the overall number of personal staff had increased substantially over the longer term, allocations to crossbenchers and former leaders had not increased in the same way.
The issue returned to parliament in 2025, when senators sought to change how personal staff were allocated to non-government parliamentarians and reduce the prime minister's discretion over the process.
A bill co-sponsored by Coalition and crossbench senators, including Hanson and Payman, proposed guaranteeing minimum personal staffing levels for non-government parliamentarians.
It also sought to limit the prime minister's discretion over those minimum allocations.
The bill passed its second reading in the Senate but was ultimately defeated at the third-reading stage in September 2025.
The Senate nevertheless backed an amendment calling for the government to work with elected groups and independents to develop a "fair and independent staffing model" that accounted for representation, staff wellbeing and workloads.
Reviews of parliamentary workplaces have also previously recommended greater transparency around staffing allocations and an evidence-based examination of workloads.
Why is their alliance so unusual?
Hanson and Payman, in particular, have a long history of clashing politically.
In 2024, Hanson sought to have Payman's eligibility to sit in parliament investigated over questions surrounding her Afghan citizenship.
Payman responded with a fierce attack on Hanson in the Senate, comments she was subsequently required to withdraw.
The political tensions between them remained.
Payman told reporters on Thursday however that politicians should be capable of putting those disagreements aside when they find a common cause, according to a by The Guardian.

California governor signs 13 bills to protect elections from federal interference
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:31:27 CST
14:31:27 KST

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- California Governor Gavin Newsom on Saturday signed a package of 13 bills aimed at protecting the state's November midterm elections from interference, including measures concerning mail voting and demands for voter data, according to his office.
Midterms are congressional elections held midway between presidential elections. In the United States, state law primarily governs election procedures, while federal law sets nationwide standards, according to the Election Assistance Commission.
Among the measures, Assembly Bill 282 makes it a felony to seize ballots, election records or certified voting technology before election results are certified, while Senate Bill 259 makes it a felony for an authority figure to direct someone to interfere with the delivery or return of a mail-in ballot. Assembly Bill 1664 requires local agencies and election officials to promptly notify the state of specified law-enforcement actions involving election records or certified voting technology.
The legislation comes amid a dispute between California and the Trump administration over federal election policies. Trump issued an executive order in March directing federal agencies to provide states with lists of confirmed citizens of voting age and directing the U.S. Postal Service to begin rule-making on standards for mail-in and absentee ballots. California and other states challenged the order in federal court.
The Supreme Court later rejected the request and blocked it from enforcing new restrictions on mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterm elections. California has also resisted federal demands for statewide voter-registration data.
Newsom, Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Attorney General Rob Bonta said the package would protect against federal interference in state election administration.
"This legislative package ensures that California voters will not be silenced or intimidated," Weber said in a statement. Newsom also noted that "These bills today build upon the wall California has built to safeguard our electoral process." ■

TEHRAN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Saturday that participation in the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York is Iran's "legal right."
"Being present in New York holds absolutely no appeal for Iran's representatives. However, it is a stronghold that must not be abandoned. Iran's participation in the UNGA's session is a legal right, not a favor to be granted to us by someone. Iran is one of the UN's 50 founding members," Baghaei said in an interview with state-run IRIB TV.
"It is our duty as the Iranian nation's representatives to attend this major international event to make the world hear the Iranian people's rightfulness," he said, accusing "the other side" of employing every available tool to prevent the Iranian delegation's participation.
Such "obstructionism and negative propaganda" will never make Iran back down from its legitimate right to participate in the session and articulate its positions, he said.

"Peace Train-2026" medical team conducts academic exchanges in Laos
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:30:55 CST
14:30:55 KST

VIENTIANE, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- The China-Laos "Peace Train-2026" medical team has conducted simultaneous academic exchanges and medical service activities at multiple locations across Laos, including Vientiane, Pakse, Savannakhet, and Attapeu province.
The academic exchanges from Sept. 16 to 18 focused on common and prevalent diseases in Laos, as well as practical needs related to medical support. Renowned Chinese medical experts delivered specialized lectures on topics such as emergency cardiac surgery, emergency medical rescue for mass-casualty incidents, and the treatment of degenerative scoliosis.
The experts also shared the experiences of Chinese military medical personnel in disaster medical rescue and grassroots operational support, promoting deeper exchanges and cooperation between the two militaries in the field of medical support.
The academic exchange activities attracted more than 1,600 participants, including key clinical personnel from medical institutions of the Lao People's Army and cadets from the Military Medical Academy of Laos.
Savaengxay Dalasath, director of the Lao Military Hospital 103, said that the arrival of the Chinese medical team had greatly benefited Lao medical personnel, allowing them not only to learn advanced medical concepts and clinical techniques but also to build lasting friendships.
The medical service campaign is scheduled to continue until late September. Since its launch in 2017, the "Peace Train" series of events has consistently provided specialized medical services and treatment for patients with rare and complex conditions. ■

Interview: China's Global Development Initiative gives Global South stronger voice, opportunities: former Egyptian PM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:30:42 CST
14:30:42 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's Global Development Initiative (GDI) helps give developing countries, especially those in the Global South, a stronger voice in global governance while creating broader opportunities for development, former Egyptian Prime Minister Essam Sharaf has said.
"After decades of major economic and social transformation, China has accumulated considerable development experience and become more willing to share this experience and its capabilities with other countries, especially those of the Global South," Sharaf, founder and chairman of the Sharaf Foundation for Sustainable Development, told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Sharaf said one of the GDI's most important contributions over the past five years has been to bring development back to "the heart of global attention" at a time of geopolitical conflicts, economic competition and successive crises.
"Development should not become a victim of these conflicts, but should remain a shared priority for the international community," he stressed, noting that peace and development are closely intertwined.
Sharaf said sustainable peace is difficult to build in a world where development gaps are widening, just as real development is difficult to achieve amid conflict and instability.
"One of the most important lessons reinforced by the initiative is that investing in development is, at the same time, an investment in stability, peace and the future," he said.
Sharaf said the GDI also reflects a broader understanding of development that goes beyond economic growth and new projects to improve people's livelihood, reduce poverty, ensure access to food and energy, and strengthen health, education and resilience to crises.
Turning to global governance, Sharaf said the GDI contributes to strengthening multilateralism by promoting greater participation of developing countries in international decision-making.
"From this perspective, I believe the GDI makes an important contribution to shifting from the concept of governance for countries to a broader concept of governance with the participation of countries," Sharaf said.
He said that the GDI's emphasis on participation is particularly important because major global challenges, from climate change and food security to energy and digital transformation, cannot be addressed by any single country alone.
"Ultimately, true multilateralism is not simply about having a large number of countries around one table; it is about ensuring that everyone feels they have a voice, and that their interests and needs are part of the process of shaping a shared future," Sharaf said.
He expected the digital sphere to be one of the most important areas for the GDI's future development, as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly central to one of the fastest technological transformations in human history.
Sharaf warned that if advanced technologies are available only to wealthier countries and societies, the world could move from the traditional development gap to an even more dangerous digital divide.
He said supporting the "Digital South" should go beyond expanding internet access and digital infrastructure to include building human capacity, transferring knowledge, strengthening digital education and scientific research, and ensuring equitable access to technology.
Sharaf said the GDI can play an important role in linking digital development with equitable development, while helping ensure that developing countries benefit from advances in artificial intelligence.
He also pointed to the China-led establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, saying it aims to strengthen international cooperation and global AI governance while promoting the safe, equitable and inclusive development and use of artificial intelligence.
"I believe the GDI has a major opportunity to help shape an important principle for the next phase: the future of technology should not be a future for a limited number of countries, but a shared future for humanity," he said. ■

Between 3:00 a.m. and 5:00 a.m. Moscow time (midnight and 2:00 a.m. GMT) on Sunday, at least 249 drones were jammed and destroyed in 17 municipalities of the Moscow Region.
"The attack is ongoing," the governor wrote.
In his words, damage to private houses and apartment blocks have been reported in a number of the region’s municipalities.
In the Ramenskoye district, the roof of a 21-storey apartment block caught fire after being hit by a drone, prompting the evacuation of around 400 people, including 70 children. In addition, 20 cars were damaged there, the governor said.
In Sofyino in the Ramenskoye district, a warehouse was set ablaze. Another serious fire was reported in the city of Kotelniki on Moscow’s southeastern outskirts, where a drone hit an apartment building, setting fire to apartments on three floors.
"Casualty reports are being verified," the governor said. "Firefighters and emergency services are working at the scene."
Later, the governor said three apartment blocks in the Novye Kotelniki residential complex in the city were damaged. It was not immediately clear whether he earlier referred to one of these buildings.

Spokespersons for Moscow’s main airports told TASS over 30 flights have been unable to land in Moscow on Sunday for security reasons.
About 25 planes bound for Sheremetyevo Airport were diverted to Nizhny Novgorod, Kazan, Cheboksary, St. Petersburg, Samara and Nizhnekamsk.
About 10 flights, namely from Hurghada (Egypt), Tashkent and Fergana (Uzbekistan), Istanbul and Dalaman (Turkey), Dubai (UAE), as well as Russia’s Novosibirsk, Yekaterinburg and Chelyabinsk, were unable to land at Vnukovo Airport.

====================================================================================================

Einstein’s “spooky action” just survived one of physics’ most extreme tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:16:00 UTC
14:16:00 KST

Einstein’s “spooky action” just survived one of physics’ most extreme tests
- Date:
- September 20, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Physicists have detected strong evidence that heavy, fleeting Z bosons can become quantum entangled during Higgs boson decays at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider. The result shows that Einstein’s “spooky action at a distance” survives even under some of the most extreme conditions ever created in a laboratory.
- Share:
Physicists at the University of Oxford have helped demonstrate that one of quantum physics' strangest phenomena, quantum entanglement, can persist even among some of the heaviest and shortest-lived particles ever produced. The finding, made with CERN's powerful Large Hadron Collider, has been published in Physical Review Letters.
Quantum entanglement occurs when two particles share properties in such a way that measurements of one can reveal information about the other, even when the particles are separated. The connection is one of the most counterintuitive features of quantum mechanics and has challenged physicists' understanding of reality for decades.
Albert Einstein famously called entanglement "spooky action at a distance," and scientists have previously observed the effect in systems involving photons, electrons and trapped ions. Entanglement has also become central to several emerging technologies, including quantum computers, ultra-secure quantum communication networks and advanced sensors. In quantum computing, for example, entanglement allows multiple qubits to be manipulated together rather than one at a time, making it possible to carry out multiple calculations simultaneously.
Testing Quantum Entanglement at Extreme Energies
What remained less clear was whether entanglement could survive under far more extreme conditions, including the violent, high-energy particle collisions produced at CERN.
To investigate that question, an international team used the ATLAS experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC) near Geneva, Switzerland. Instead of studying photons or other relatively long-lived quantum systems, the researchers searched for entanglement between pairs of Z bosons, massive particles that exist for only a tiny fraction of a second before decaying.
The Z bosons examined in the experiment came from the decay of a Higgs boson, the particle discovered at the LHC in 2012. A Higgs boson can briefly decay into two Z bosons, which then decay into pairs of electrons or muons. The Higgs bosons themselves are produced when protons traveling at 99.99% the speed of light collide at energies reaching thirteen trillion electron volts.
Fleeting Z Bosons Leave Quantum Clues Behind
Although Z bosons disappear almost immediately after they are created, the ATLAS detector can accurately measure the electrons and muons produced by their decay.
Researchers analyzed the angles at which those particles emerged and used that information to reconstruct the spins of the original Z bosons. That allowed the team to determine whether the two Z bosons displayed the correlations expected from quantum entanglement.
The measurements provided strong evidence that they did. The result represents one of the highest energy confirmations of quantum entanglement ever achieved.
Study co-author Professor Alan Barr, at Oxford's Department of Physics, was among the first researchers to suggest that particle colliders could be used to investigate quantum entanglement at energies far beyond those used in traditional quantum experiments.
Barr, who was involved in building the LHC, recognized that the enormous collider could serve purposes beyond the search for new particles. His ideas helped inspire a 2023 ATLAS experiment that demonstrated entanglement between pairs of top quarks, the heaviest known elementary particle.
Professor Barr said: "We're used to thinking of entanglement as something delicate, seen in laboratory experiments with single photons. Finding it alive and well among particles as heavy and short-lived as Z bosons, created in some of the most violent collisions we can produce on Earth, shows just how fundamental and robust this quantum effect really is. It's a nice reminder that the same strange rules of quantum mechanics that may one day power quantum computers are at work everywhere in nature, even at the extreme energies of the Large Hadron Collider."
Quantum Computing Ideas Meet Particle Physics
The work is also part of a broader effort to bring concepts from quantum information science (the field behind quantum computing) into high-energy particle physics.
By applying ideas developed for quantum systems to the enormous data sets produced by particle colliders, researchers hope to create more sensitive ways of detecting subtle patterns. Those techniques could eventually reveal effects that do not fit within physicists' current understanding of the universe and potentially offer clues about physics beyond existing theories.
At Oxford University, Professor Barr co-leads a major interdisciplinary project focused on the foundations of quantum mechanics at high energies. The project is testing quantum behavior at extremely small scales and very high energies while also examining the philosophical questions raised by such experiments, including what they may reveal about the underlying nature of reality.
Project co-PI Professor Chris Timpson (Faculty of Philosophy) said: "Entanglement is both the most promising and the most puzzling aspect of quantum reality; these collider experiments detecting entanglement present a new frontier in investigations of the foundations of quantum mechanics."
CERN Prepares for Even Deeper Quantum Tests
Oxford University scientists are also contributing to the ongoing upgrade of the ATLAS detector. Together with the upgraded High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, these improvements are expected to provide vastly larger data sets and give physicists new opportunities to investigate quantum phenomena at extreme energies.
The additional data could also allow researchers to apply more sophisticated quantum information techniques to particle physics, potentially increasing the sensitivity of future searches for previously unknown phenomena.
Professor Daniela Bortoletto (Department of Physics, University of Oxford), who is the UK coordinator for producing the modules for the upgraded ATLAS detector's pixel system, said: "This measurement demonstrates the scientific power of the ATLAS collaboration and the unique capabilities of CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Oxford researchers have played a leading role in developing these new approaches to studying quantum phenomena at the highest energies, and we are proud to contribute to an international effort that is opening new ways to explore the fundamental laws of nature."
The study "Measurements of Z-boson pair entanglement in decays of Higgs bosons at the ATLAS experiment" has been published in Physical Review Letters.

Forestry agency uses drones to reforest Hualien
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:14:00 UTC
14:14:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency said Saturday that it is using drones to reforest landslide areas upstream of the Mataian River.
Heavy rain from Typhoon Wipha caused landslides near the river and formed a barrier lake in July 2025. Two months later, heavy rain from Typhoon Ragasa caused the lake to overflow and fail, flooding central Guangfu Township, per UDN.
The steep upstream terrain makes reforestation on foot dangerous. The forestry agency’s Hualien branch has therefore used drones to drop seeds and seedlings in materials developed with National Ilan University, per CNA.
The agency conducted its first two rounds of airdrops from December 2025 to January. The third took place from Sept. 5–7, covering about 20 hectares across 67 drop sites and bringing the total area covered to 40.2 hectares.
The latest mission featured three methods:
- Seeds encased in moist gel granules that supply water and protection.
- Germinated seedlings, growing medium, and seeds secured in water-soluble netting.
- Seeds and growing material enclosed in water-soluble capsules.
The agency said drones are also being used to monitor plant growth. Once root systems and ground vegetation become established, they are expected to reduce erosion and the amount of sediment flowing downstream, lowering the risk of river siltation and blockages.

In the Kherson region, Russians struck a monastery with a drone; one priest was killed and four were injured

China has reiterated its opposition to the unilateral sanctions imposed without the United Nations authorization after US President Donald Trump signed into law legislation expanding coercive measures targeting Russia and extending existing ones against Iran.
A Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson made the remarks on Saturday in response to the US passage of the Russia sanctions bill, saying Beijing opposed unilateral sanctions lacking a basis in international law and would reserve the right to take measures to protect its development interests.
"We have noted the relevant developments. China has always opposed unilateral sanctions that lack authorization from the United Nations and a basis in international law, and opposes so-called secondary sanctions measures taken against other countries on the pretext of involving third parties,” the official said.

The legislation authorizes and expands sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions targeting Russia, while extending existing illegal sanctions against Iran.
Among its provisions, the law allows the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas. It also provides for sanctions against Russian officials, banks, and vessels involved in transporting Russian energy.
The legislation further extends sanctions against Iran's energy and defense sectors that were due to expire after the end of 2026.
The bill passed the US House of Representatives on Wednesday by a vote of 262-159, after previously receiving Senate approval in an 86-11 vote, according to Press TV.

Pledges, timed visits and taxes: The strategies diverting tourists from hotspots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:09:20 UTC
14:09:20 KST

Timed visits, taxes and pledges: The strategies diverting tourists from hotspots
For many people, a holiday in a beautiful destination far from home is the perfect way to relax and leave behind the daily grind.
For those who live in tourist destinations, travellers bring business and work opportunities.
But when more and more people flock to the same places, the pressure on locals and their environment can become destructive.
The city of Amsterdam, known worldwide for its picturesque canals, red light district and bike lanes, has stopped investing in traditional marketing altogether.
"Amsterdam is not trying to grow tourism. Amsterdam is trying to manage tourism," Amsterdam & Partners corporate communications specialist Mila de Heer says.
"Our aim is a visitor economy that contributes to the city, respects residents and strengthens Amsterdam's cultural, social and economic fabric.
"Visitors are welcome, but not at any cost."
The Dutch city is not alone.
In destinations around the world, over-tourism has aggravated residents who say they no longer benefit from an industry that is overtaking their infrastructure and contributing to a lack of affordable housing.
Now many of the world's most desirable destinations are saying no to unrestrained mass tourism — but finding the antidote is not simple.
Different strategies are being tested to limit the influx of tourists, including taxes, access restrictions and the closure of hotspots.
Not just 'a lot of tourists'
In 2025, the travel and tourism sector generated $US11 trillion ($15 trillion) and accounted for nearly 10 per cent of the global economy, according to research by the World Travel and Tourism Council.
Western Sydney University sustainable tourism professor Joseph Cheer says it is important to understand that over-tourism means more than just "a lot of tourists".
"At its most basic, over-tourism is when tourism growth starts to create problems at a local level," he says.
Over-tourism manifests as overcrowding, loss of amenities, rapid development that communities cannot keep up with, noise, pollution, waste management issues and increased housing costs, Dr Cheer says.
He says housing in popular destinations often gets used to accommodate tourists because it is more profitable.
"In a situation where we have a housing crisis or housing affordability crisis, this locks out locals from the housing that they would otherwise have had access to," Dr Cheer says.
Accommodation and cruise ship bans
In Barcelona, Spain's most visited city by foreign tourists, authorities announced a moratorium on short-term rentals such as Airbnb to help make the city more affordable for residents.
Mayor Jaume Collboni said the city would scrap the licences of more than 10,000 apartments approved as short-term rentals by November 2028.
Housing is a pain point in Barcelona, where demonstrators have hit the streets the past two summers with water pistols to protest tourism.
Regulation of platforms such as Airbnb has proven successful, according to Dr Cheer.
"It's been able to put limits around the extent to which tourism takes place in local areas. Airbnb had a slogan: 'to live like a local'. The trouble is, no-one asked the locals whether they wanted people to live like them," he says.
The ban is part of Barcelona's wider plan to cut off tourism growth.
"The demand can't grow if there's no accommodation for [tourists]. Already this summer we're seeing that there are people who can't come because they can't find a place to stay. We're not going to respond to growing demand," the city's new sustainable tourism commissioner José Antonio Donaire told The New York Times.
The Italian city of Venice banned large cruise ships from entering its historic centre in 2021, following years of protests by locals.
The community group No Grandi Navi (No Big Ships) attracted media attention for protesting on water, waving flags from small boats.
When a cruise ship full of passengers descends upon a city, facilities and infrastructure can be put under pressure without much economic benefit, Dr Cheer says.
University of Adelaide tourism management senior lecturer Freya Higgins-Desbiolles says the cruise ship ban is a good example of a community being centred in decision-making.
"The local communities should be setting a vision of what they want for tourism in their place," she says.
Tourist taxes and minimum spends
Japan, a favourite destination for Australians, has increased a number of fees aimed at tourists and immigrants amid fears of over-tourism and a surge in anti-immigration sentiment.
This includes the tripling of Japan's international tourist tax, which is attached to airfares departing Japan.
According to the Japan National Tourism Organisation, the fee will "support the maintenance of public works, critical infrastructure at airports and tourist sites, restoration of historic assets, and the creation of online tourist resources".
Closer to home, the Balinese have watched their island completely transform, with its rice paddies and agricultural land turned into villas for tourists.
Foreign visitors have almost tripled in the past 15 years. Almost seven million foreign tourists visited the island last year, more than 1.5 million of them Australian.
But the infrastructure has not kept up with the pace. The island is grappling with a waste crisis, and frustrated locals blamed overdevelopment after the island was hit with deadly floods.
In 2024, Bali implemented a tourist tax. The 150,000 rupiah ($15) payment is collected at the airport, but some visitors have found its implementation confusing.
The charge goes toward conserving ecology and culture while offsetting some of the environmental damage caused by tourism.
Dr Cheer says the effectiveness of tourist taxes is debatable because they do not address the root cause of problems, and it is not always clear whether they will be used to solve the problems created by tourism.
"Tourist taxes are a very blunt instrument that doesn't really change what's happening in the tourism system," he says.
"A 5 euro tax is not going to stop someone from wanting to go to Venice. A $50 Bali entry tax is not going to deter people from going to Bali.
"It's a small drop in the pond when it comes to what they are spending overall."
The Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan has been wary of tourism ever since it opened to visitors in 1974.
The country imposes strict parameters on international travellers, including a ban on mountaineering to preserve its peaks.
Before 2020, a minimum spend of $US200 ($299) per day was required of foreign nationals, as well as a $US65 ($90) daily fee.
Bhutan's reopening to the world after the pandemic saw the minimum spend requirement scrapped in favour of raising the daily "sustainable development fee" (SDF), which the government says is used to offset carbon generated by visitors, to $US200.
In Bhutan, the government can control "who comes in and how much they spend and where they go," Dr Cheer says.
"It might work in Bhutan, but it doesn't necessarily work everywhere else."
In September 2023, in the wake of declining visitor numbers, the country cut the SDF to US$100 per day for the next four years.
Pledges and regeneration closures
In Thailand, the government closes Maya Bay, popularised by the 2000 movie The Beach, for two months every year.
The Phi Phi Islands beach was reopened in 2022 after a nearly four-year closure due to damage to its ecosystem.
The reopening has come with strict rules, including a ban on swimming, and the tourists who have attempted to wade into the turquoise waters have been fined for doing so.
Boats can no longer enter the bay; there is a daily visitor cap and a one-hour time limit for visits.
A similar approach was taken in the Philippines in 2018, when authorities closed the paradisiacal island of Boracay for six months to clean up its shores.
Results from the closure were contentious, but locals say they saw the restoration of the island to its former glory during COVID-19 lockdowns.
From an ecological point of view, closures such as that of Maya Bay and Boracay have been successful, Dr Cheer says, but some outcomes remain to be seen.
"The question remains, if you close and then when you reopen [and] it's business as usual, have you really made any progress? Are you just going one step forward and one step back constantly?" he says.
It can also be difficult for authorities to stick with closures that create ripple effects in the economy.
Even the limited return of tourists to Maya Bay has come with setbacks to the environment, leaving authorities struggling to strike a balance between preserving its ecosystem and sustaining livelihoods.
The Pacific island nation of Palau asks each tourist presenting at immigration to sign a passport pledge to act in an ecologically and culturally responsible way.
"I vow to tread lightly, act kindly and explore mindfully," the pledge reads.
"The only footprints I shall leave are those that will wash away."
Pledges can be helpful in influencing tourists to be more careful about how they visit a place, Dr Higgins-Desbiolles says, but the effect may be limited in an industry as complex as tourism.
"When we shift the focus to the tourist as the consumer, you're not actually getting to the heart of the problem, and you're not making the tourism industry take responsibility," she says.
"I don't think consumer choice is actually going to have the impact that we need, because, of course, it's only the sensitive type of tourists that will be moved by that and engage in that."
The tourism industry's 'growth fetish'
In 2025, international tourist arrivals grew by four per cent, with an estimated 1.52 billion international tourists recorded globally, according to the UN World Tourism Barometer.
That growth has continued but slowed down in 2026 amid the conflict in the Middle East.
Dr Higgins-Desbiolles says the industry must deal with its "growth fetish" if it is to address problems with over-tourism.
"Endless growth is not possible without damaging societies and ecology, so it's got to be managed," she says.
But Dr Higgins-Desbiolles says the industry itself should not be "at the forefront of decision-making".
"They should be a voice in it, but my view is the local people are the ones that have to live with the consequences of tourism, so it's them that should have a strong seat at the table, and often they're not represented," she says.
Amsterdam has put in place a formal "Tourism in Balance" framework, which includes a cap on overnight stays per year.
If overnight stays approach 18 million, the municipal executive must propose measures to prevent the 20 million cap from being exceeded.
The city has made progress in positioning itself as "a place of culture, creativity, neighbourhoods, innovation and local life, rather than as a permissive playground," Ms de Heer says.
"The goal is not more tourists, but better balance. Visitors who behave respectfully, spread across the city and region where appropriate, contribute to culture and local businesses, and do not add disproportionate pressure to already crowded areas."

World leaders return to UN amid wars in Middle East and Ukraine

World leaders return to UN amid wars in Middle East and Ukraine
- World leaders gather at the UN General Assembly to address conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, AI risks, and UN challenges amid US funding cuts and leadership uncertainties.
- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urges global AI governance to prevent disaster, contrasting with US President Trump's dismissal of AI risks as a "hoax."
- The Assembly focuses on Middle East tensions, stalled peace talks, and Ukraine's war impact on food security and energy, with key speeches from leaders including Zelensky and Netanyahu.
AI generated
UNITED NATIONS – World leaders gather in New York this week for the UN General Assembly, bracing themselves for US President Donald Trump’s return to the rostrum for a second year running, with talks centring on the widening conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine and the risks of artificial intelligence.
Nearly 130 heads of state meet with the post-World War II order under strain and with the UN itself struggling to remain relevant and weathering attacks from Trump, who has slashed America’s contributions and withdrawn from dozens of UN bodies.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping, who last addressed the diplomatic jamboree via video in 2021, will skip New York in favour of one-on-one talks with Trump in Washington on Sept 24, fuelling debate about the UN’s relevance in addressing global crises.
Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organisation: Secretary-General Antonio Guterres completes his term at the end of 2026, with no clear frontrunner in the race to replace him.
The 15-member UN Security Council may hold high-level meetings on Ukraine, AI and the Middle East, including talks with Arab leaders, diplomats said.
More than a year into Trump’s second term, “we would no longer say that the UN is in free fall, but we would say that it’s stuck in an open-ended crisis,” said Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group.
“The UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it seems to be trapped in a trauma centre for the foreseeable future,” Gowan said.
The US avoided losing its vote at the assembly by paying US$725 million (S$925 million) in contributions to the regular budget this week, but it still owes the organisation more than a billion dollars and makes ongoing demands for cuts and reforms.
Growing AI risks
The assembly meets shortly after several artificial intelligence industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and escape human control.
Guterres has said that AI will be a major topic, adding that countries pushing its frontiers should set up “common guardrails in order to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level.”
The secretary-general has long proposed global governance of AI. In 2023, the UN created an advisory body on the technology, with members including tech executives, government officials and academics.
The warning has put Guterres at odds with Trump, who dismissed AI risks as a “hoax”, saying there is a “sick conspiracy” against it and that China would benefit from the doubt being cast on its development.
Middle East escalation
The Middle East will again be a focus of discussions, as the US-Israeli war on Iran continues to drive global inflation and destabilise the region. Recent gains by Houthi militants threaten shipping in the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and could further spike energy prices.
“It’s very difficult to have a military solution for that problem, and the experience of fighting in Yemen demonstrated how complicated it is to have successful interventions,” said Guterres, adding that the UN’s envoy on Yemen was making a “huge effort” to advance talks.
Peace talks remain stalled, however, as Iran and the US continue to exchange strikes and Trump threatens a major escalation of the war.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the assembly on Sept 23.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza that Israel denies – is to speak on Sept 24.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will for the second year running not be at the gathering in person. The US, a close Israeli ally, again denied him a visa. On Sept 17, the General Assembly voted to allow Abbas to appear via video.
There is likely to be a high-level meeting on the conflict in Sudan on the sidelines, diplomats said, although a diplomatic breakthrough is unlikely.
Ukraine, food security
Also on the agenda is Russia’s more than four-year-old war in Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will address the General Assembly. Zelensky will likely seek to shore up Ukraine’s position ahead of what is expected to be another tough winter, diplomats said.
The Security Council has been unable to take action to end the conflict because permanent member Russia holds a veto.
Trump has at times appeared frustrated that he has been unable to broker an end to the war, a goal he declared a priority when he began his second term in January 2025. The US president spoke with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin earlier in September, but it was unclear whether he plans to meet Zelensky in New York.
Guterres highlighted the impact the war was having on civilians but also on food security and energy prices.
“The effective blockade existing in the Black Sea is creating enormous problems that add to the problems generated by the Middle East crisis, and I think it would be very important to find a way to allow Ukrainian exports and Russian exports of food, fertilisers and energy to take place in a safe way through the Black Sea,” he said. From fashion forward to failure: What went wrong for Cue?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:05:20 UTC
14:05:20 KST

Claudia Schiffer was once the face of Cue. Now it and Veronika Maine have 'lost relevance'
It was a modern-day success story, an idea sparked by Beatlemania that became deeply woven into the fabric of Australia's identity.
Long a cornerstone of Australian fashion, Cue repeatedly reinvented itself to outlast the times, with the proof hanging in the wardrobes of generations of women.
Its success was a far cry from its humble beginnings as a business that started by selling T-shirts.
Now, Cue and sister label Veronika Maine have become the latest casualties in Australian retail, with a team of experts last week rallying in an effort to stop the company from being consigned to history.
But what inspired the start of the clothing brand in 1968 ultimately became its downfall.
'On the ball'
It was during a holiday to London in 1964 that Rod Levis, a young Australian law student, found himself swept up by the youth culture that was taking England by storm.
Levis knew nothing about fashion but saw an opportunity for an Australian brand to sell clothing that appealed to young people.
He opened Levis's in Sydney's Strand Arcade, selling clothes that capitalised on the popularity of The Beatles and stocking items created by cutting-edge designers.
The success of the business allowed Levis to expand into designing and manufacturing, and he launched Cue in 1968.
"Back then the clothing choices were mumsy and dowdy or too sophisticated," Levis told Marie Claire in 2018.
"Cue made way for a new wave of young fashion inspired by what was going on in London and Paris.
"The name says it all: it means to be on target, on the ball, ready for the next thing."
By the 1970s, Cue was stocked in Myer stores across Australia and the company began opening standalone stores as demand grew.
The 1980s was transformative for Cue, with the brand creating its signature tailored suits that became a staple for working women.
With the dawn of the 1990s, Cue was an unstoppable force. Supermodel Claudia Schiffer became the face of its 1997 campaign, and in 1998 the more contemporary brand, Veronika Maine, was launched.
'Really iconic company'
When the new millennium arrived the company had fully cemented itself as an Australian fashion juggernaut, with stores around the country and its clothes stocked by both Myer and David Jones.
But wholesale was a key area for the company too, and the popularity of the brands was so great that it allowed Kristen Tassone to start her own business onselling the clothes 26 years ago.
"They were the biggest brands on a wholesale level," she recalled.
"They knew what they were doing. It was quality craftsmanship, it was super commercial price points and really comprehensive collections that people enjoyed.
"They were just a really iconic company to work with, and it shaped the rest of my 26 years and counting in the fashion wholesale industry."
Tassone spent 10 years selling Cue and Veronika Maine to her clients before the company shifted its focus to direct-to-consumer channels.
"It was greatly missed when they pulled back from wholesale," she said.
"I'm just really grateful that I was able to start a successful business with Cue and Veronika Maine as my kickstart."
The Cue and Veronika Maine labels were removed from wholesaling entirely by 2008, before the economic shockwaves of the global financial crisis rippled through Australia's retail sector as consumer spending plummeted.
It took years for confidence to return to the retail sector, and when it did, it coincided with the rise of online shopping, fast fashion, and more competition.
By 2017, Marcs and David Lawrence — two of Cue's direct competitors — had collapsed, before being purchased by Myer.
Australian luxury retailer Oroton went bust later that same year but was rescued at the last minute by major shareholder Will Vicars.
In November 2018, Cue marked 50 years in business, and the following year announced an exhibition at the Powerhouse Museum in Sydney.
But within months of it opening, the COVID-19 pandemic hit.
'Losing touch'
The pandemic fundamentally changed Australian retail. The rise of working from home saw people swapping corporate for comfort, a reliance on online shopping, and more competition from retailers overseas — particularly on price.
When people did return to the office, they favoured a more casual approach to workwear and that, along with cost-of-living pressures restricting consumer spending, and a lack of aspirational brand identity curated on social media, created a perfect storm that Cue and Veronika Maine could not navigate.
For a company that was once at the forefront of what consumers wanted, the labels had lost their way.
It's a scenario that seasoned retail analyst and restructure expert James Stewart has seen play out repeatedly during his 40 years in the industry.
"The single biggest reason, in my view, that mid-market apparel brands end up in trouble is because of the product, because they end up losing touch with their target market, and their target market just doesn't see their product proposition at their price points as value anymore," he said.
"When you lose relevance to your target customer, then they start shopping somewhere else.
"You can blame it on Shein, you can blame it on the resale market, you can blame it on consumer sentiment, all of which will have some impact … but at its core, what's in your control is product, range architecture, price point, and brand proposition.
"Every apparel retailer that I've dealt with, almost all of them have had exactly the same problem. They lose relevance.
"Your job as a retailer is to read your target market and pivot your product proposition accordingly."
Levis's son Justin had tried to do just that as the executive director of Cue and Veronika Maine, until his departure in 2024.
Two weeks after his exit, the eponymous label of young Australian designer Dion Lee collapsed. Cue had acquired a stake in 2013. Lee's brand has since been acquired by US retail group Revolve.
Selling up shop
Behind the scenes, Cue was struggling financially.
Filings lodged with ASIC for the 2024 financial year saw the company record a $14.1 million loss — six times greater than the $2.3 million loss from the previous year — and its total liabilities outweighed its assets by $3.3 million.
Despite that, the financial report noted Cue had "received assurance from the shareholders … to continue its operations" for 12 months.
By April 2025, Rod Levis sold Cue to Hilco Capital, a British company that specialises in turning around troubled businesses.
Shortly after acquiring Cue, Hilco appointed retail veteran Eric Morris as chairman, installed Melanie Remai as its CEO and recruited Josephine Barbaro as its chief financial officer.
Despite the appointments, the company remained in distress. Online shoppers have complained about not receiving their orders, and landlords and suppliers have not been paid.
Morris stepped down as chairman in June, and Hilco put Cue up for sale in August.
Stewart, who has a longstanding working relationship with Hilco but is not involved in the current process, said its decision to purchase and sell Cue within 16 months indicated that all was not well.
"Hilco's acquired this business from a distressed seller … with a view that if they can turn it around and make it work, that's great and that creates value," he said.
"But you've got a buyer of last resort trying to sell something that they couldn't fix."
Within a month of putting the business up for sale, Barbaro and Remai announced their exits.
Days later, Hilco called in the receivers. It couldn't save Cue.
Restructure, rebuild, regrow
The future is still uncertain, but it's still early days in its receivership.
FTI Consulting said the decision to put the company into receivership was because its operating costs were outweighing its sales, even though they had improved.
Cue's latest financial report lodged with ASIC at the end of May showed it had incurred a net loss of $5 million, while its liabilities outweighed its assets by more than $3 million.
The report highlighted that its forecasts were dependent on Cue "meeting a number of operational and financial assumptions that are subject to uncertainty".
"If [Cue] is unable to achieve these assumptions, there is a material uncertainty that may cast significant doubt on [Cue's] ability to continue as a going concern," it stated.
While receivers are now tasked with working out what the future of Cue and Veronika Maine may look like, the company made the "difficult" decision on Friday to close five of its 51 stores, saying it was in the "best interest of the business".
Its department store footprint will remain unchanged for now, but Stewart said he expected any rebuilt version of the business would be significantly scaled back.
"It's a bit like pruning a tree, so you decide what's my strongest channel to market, where are my customers buying, where am I getting the most margin out of it and what's sustainable in the long term?" he said.
"Some of the restructuring I've seen, often they don't cut hard enough … they're actually better ripping the whole band-aid off, letting the whole thing breathe a bit, and then coming back and rebuilding over time."
There remains the possibility that Cue might become a receivership success story, much like Marcs, David Lawrence and Oroton.
"There has been good initial interest from potential buyers in the sale process, highlighting the strong brand recognition and positive sentiment for Cue and Veronika Maine," the receivers said.
Those potential buyers could be businesses that have been in Cue's position, including Myer and Oroton Group. Initial offers by any prospective bidders are expected to be made in early October.
Any offer will inch Cue closer to achieving 60 years in business — the same decade that inspired its creation.

Are global stock markets heading for a crash?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

At the height of the summer, the mood was optimistic in the world’s financial capitals. Powered by the AI revolution, the US stock market had rallied to a fresh all-time high, as investors bet the multitrillion-dollar investment spree would overshadow the hit from the Iran war.
Now the warning lights are flashing red. As the fighting in the Middle East intensifies without clear sign of a resolution, financial markets have been thrown into renewed turmoil. A slowdown looms in the AI arms race, and tinderbox conditions in the market for government debt are fuelling alarm.
In the past week the US government’s borrowing costs climbed to the highest level since 2007, with knock-on consequences for the finances of households, businesses, and other governments worldwide. The fear is that Donald Trump’s war is igniting higher levels of inflation. The president’s tax and spending plans – driving Washington’s debt levels above $40tn (£29.9tn) – also have investors worried.
But as the soaring global oil price to above $100 a barrel stokes heavy selling pressure in the bond market, could shares be the next in line for a crash?
With the S&P 500 index of leading US companies 3% below an all-time high, and a combined value of more than $20tn for the “magnificent seven” tech stocks – Nvidia, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Tesla – the concern is that markets are overextended just as the storm clouds gather for the world economy.
“These are febrile times,” Albert Edwards, a senior analyst at the French investment bank Société Générale, wrote in a note to clients. “The key worry for investors and policymakers alike is the extent to which the current oil price ‘shock’ will ripple through the global economy and whether it will necessitate sharply higher, recession-inducing, interest rates.”
Famed for his gloomy predictions, Edwards thinks the ingredients for a financial crisis could be coming together.
Such is the worry over the Iran war stoking inflation that the US Federal Reserve defied Trump this week with its first interest rate rise since 2023. As households and businesses come under pressure from rising energy bills and surging fuel prices, central banks elsewhere are also taking action.
Financial markets suggest the Bank of England will raise interest rates four times before the end of next year, even after it kept borrowing costs on hold this week. The European Central Bank raised rates last week, highlighting the hit to the eurozone from the escalating conflict, and the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to a 31-year high on Friday.
The rationale is that adding to the cost of borrowing will weigh on the economy – limiting the potential for short-term higher rates of inflation from becoming entrenched. However, it will hit households and businesses already struggling with a cost of living crisis. Job losses will probably rise, in-turn compounding the challenges facing governments swimming in debt.
A US recession has historically followed about three to 3.5 years after the first rate rise, on average, Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid has calculated. Markets have a habit of falling, or even crashing, before a recession begins, and often start to recover before the economy does.
However, the big concern among investors is that the main hope of economic redemption – AI – could also turn out to be a dud, amid fears it has fuelled an almighty bubble in the US stock market.
One popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE ratio – or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio – has risen to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market is unusually highly valued compared with its profits.
The CAPE ratio for the S&P 500 share index is almost 41 points, more than double its long-term average of about 17 points, and approaching the record high of 44.19 points in December 1999, just before the dotcom crash.
Highlighting the challenge, research by Fathom Consulting shows that for the multitrillion-dollar AI boom to turn a profit, it would need the AI-related sales of the tech companies involved to rise by between $600 and $800bn within two years.
Against a febrile backdrop as investor patience is increasingly tested, the consultancy gives a 30% chance that the AI bubble pops next year.
Brian Davidson, an economist at the consultancy, said: “For all the impressive advances in AI technologies in recent years, the economics behind the current capex boom do not work.
“Yes, recent AI advances could yet unlock huge productivity gains; but sales of AI models need to increase by hundreds of billions of dollars per year over the next two years to justify the current spend. Such growth appears unlikely.”
Investors are clearly worried. More than 1,000 investors registered for an analyst call conducted by Jefferies this week into “AI Extinction Warnings”, after the bosses of the world’s top tech companies called for a slowdown in “reckless” development.
The situation has parallels with the dotcom crash of the year 2000, when many internet companies that had been billed as the next big thing dramatically tumbled in value. That was a reminder that even if a technology is going to be revolutionary, investors can still lose their money if they finance too much infrastructure too early.
“It took a decade or more for demand to catch up with the infrastructure laid down in the British canal and railway and US telecoms and fibre booms – and many investors never recovered their capital,” points out Adrian Cox of the Deutsche Bank research team.
There are also sobering comparisons with the buildup to the great crash of 1929. A hundred years ago, many small US investors were buying stocks “on margin” – acquiring them with borrowed money. They blew up in the market turmoil that preceded the Great Depression.
This year, South Korea’s army of traders have been buying shares in AI-linked chip makers on margin – doubling the value of the blue-chip Kospi index. But once the market started to fall, they were hit by a massive wave of margin calls – when investors are told to stump up more cash to keep borrowing. Many were forced to sell their shares. According to Goldman Sachs, 1.2 million South Korean retail investors were hit by margin calls – which is the equivalent of one in 30 adults getting a nasty call from their broker asking them to hand over more money.
The huge spending plans announced by AI companies are causing concerns that they may simply borrow too much.
One firm with ambitious AI plans is Oracle, the database software vendor. Oracle’s shares surged a year ago after it announced a cloud computing deal with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.
However, they have halved since, as investors have fretted that Oracle could be borrowing too much to fund datacentres.
There are other signs of rising stress in the credit markets. The Bank of England reported this summer that the spread between the riskiest and safest high-yielding debt has widened since the Iran war began, showing that investors are warier of holding risky debt.
Government bonds have been sold off in recent weeks, and that fall in prices pushes up the yield (or rate of the return) on sovereign debt. Those higher bond yields make owning shares less attractive – an investor has less incentive to buy equities (which are riskier) than bonds, which are seen as safer.
For the US this week the rise in borrowing costs involved the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year bonds, known as Treasuries, climbing above the psychologically key threshold of 5%.
That level is “seen by some as a threshold above which financial markets might go into meltdown,” said John Higgins, the chief economic adviser at Capital Economics.
“While we aren’t convinced that 5% is that ‘magic’ number, higher Treasury yields would certainly pose a risk to the sustainability of the US public finances as well as threaten equities,” Higgins told clients.
Bloomberg macro strategist Simon White argues that trouble would really start if the US 10-year Treasury yield rose above 5.25%. He has calculated that this is the “inflection point” where, historically, stocks and bonds have reinforced losses in one another.
Despite the turbulence there are still hopes that a crash can be avoided, including optimism that markets are overestimating the inflation risk from the Iran war.
“A major downturn would need a trigger. Further geopolitical instability could be the catalyst, but we’ve long argued that the impact of geopolitical shocks on economic activity is overstated,” analysts at Oxford Economics wrote in a note to clients.
“Resurgent inflation and policy rate hikes by the Fed and other central banks are another candidate. However, our view on inflation is less alarmist – we think market expectations overstate the risk of further policy tightening.”
For many investors a slowdown in feverish AI investment will guard against the danger of a bubble.
There are signs that AI is beginning to power economic growth. The US economy has recorded a rise in productivity growth, while AI is also among reasons the UK economy has beaten expectations to grow at the fastest rate in the G7 in the first half of this year.
Such a turnaround in productivity could help the companies with sky-high share prices to begin justifying their valuations. However, it is a high-stakes play at a time of intense global volatility.
“Do I think there’s a significant dose of reality though in that productivity miracle in AI? Yes,” Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, told LBC this week. Still, he warned the situation is fragile.
“I don’t think outright collapse in a dotcom bubble type fashion. But could I see a slow release of air that doesn’t collapse the world economy, but slows it down? Yes, I could.”

Kid, London W1: ‘Fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

Earlier this month, a kind-of Turkish ocakbaşı opened on a corner in London’s Soho. The brains behind Kid are chef Sertaç Dirik and restaurateur David Carter, and I say “kind-of” because, yes, while it has a Turkish-influenced menu – sucuk with grilled peach, pide, börek, hummus, içli köfte with aged beef – and the whiff of live fire, nothing either of them does is ever remotely straightforward, hence the buzz around their new place.
Carter founded Smokestak a decade ago in Shoreditch, a wild, Americana-tinged barbecue joint where, somehow, he made brisket in buns and peach cobbler old fashioneds London’s hottest ticket. Five years later, he opened Manteca, also in Shoreditch, a reimagining of the Italian trattoria for the 2020s, followed by Oma, his Greek-influenced Michelin-starred venture in Borough, and its little sister Agora, and all of them remain dependable places where you get serious bang for your buck. All of those influences – American smoke, Italian flair and Greek boldness – are present and correct at Kid. Dirik’s story, meanwhile, has about it elements of TV’s The Bear: a Copenhagen-trained chef cajoled home to bolster the family business and going on to create the hugely loved Mangal 2 in Dalston. What Dirik and Carter have in common, aside from reputation, is a love of setting fire to stuff, in a culinary sense rather than in a Prodigy’s Twisted Firestarter sense. Kid’s Galata mackerel is testament to this: it’s almost completely blackened and has an incredible hit of smoke in its flesh.
Kid’s website says it’s on Frith Street, but the entrance is actually on Bateman Street, thanks to an aggressively discreet front door that will have you wandering around the glass-fronted corner like some confused visitor at Sea Life, pressing their nose against the tank looking for jellyfish and turtles. Here, however, there are diners beyond that glass, and you may cry when you see them inside sipping their gemlik martinis (black olive, black pepper, white vermouth, frozen gin). Warning: do not accidentally wander into Regulation, a boutique emporium of a very different persuasion just 10 metres away and where a very different type of lubrication is on offer. And of stuffing, for that matter. I shall leave the parallels there.
 Kid, as its name suggests, favours the use of kid goat, which will either delight or unsettle the British diner, because as a nation we still quibble about goat meat but for some reason raise no such objection to lamb. They have much in common taste-wise, and Kid’s signature dish – a £65 kid with fig leaf and freekeh for two – comes in an earthenware pot looking very much like a plump lamb shank just waiting for all that flesh to be pulled through the cooked grains beneath. The dish arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely clean, as did the pickles alongside: fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance.
The room is a rhapsody of browns, with an industrial feel and wilfully uncosy, a design movement that I’m calling “sumptuous sackcloth and ashes”, and there’s a long counter that focuses on a central grill. We visited on day four, and the place was already packed with Smokestak cultists, Mangal 2 zealots and assorted food writers, all of them gazing at the fire and tearing at blistered, kaymak-slicked grilled pide, as well as seeded ramazan pide as fluffy as a Turkish morning after too many rakis.
 We began with courgette flowers, which at £7 each will make some people reach for the smelling salts. But these are not those flaccid petals draped over unseasoned ricotta with which Brits habitually offend the French. Here, the batter is intensely crisp, the goat’s cheese insides rich, with atom honey to cut through: it’s a crunchy, sticky, oozing delight. A round of bluefin tuna ezme, a fine, fresh tartare in the Turkish style, comes on what can only be described as a poppadom-like cracker – fried, decadent and completely naughty.
The mackerel, however, is when you understand the point of all this live-fire hoopla. A huge butterflied fish with blackened skin comes crisp from the grill, its flesh all soft and meaty, and stuffed with a carrot-based slaw cooked in what tastes like rich, deep shellfish liquor. It’s the undoubted star of this show.
 We end with mountain tea rice pudding infused with sideritis, a wild Anatolian herb that’s warm and vaguely honeyed, and finished with a crunchy, brulee top; it’s also one of the finest desserts I’ve eaten all year. Don’t skimp on the mint oil-topped mastic ice-cream, either: it tastes exactly like toothpaste, and I mean that as a compliment.
 A very long lunch closed with shots of Turkish coffee that even Carter admitted tastes “slightly muddy”. That coffee sent me blinking into the daylight and I was still wired six hours later. Much as Kid did itself: distinctive, delicious and thoroughly making its mark.
- 
  Kid 53-55 Frith Street, London W1 (no phone). Open Mon-Sat, lunch noon-3pm, dinner 5.30-10pm. From about £45 a head à la carte, plus drinks and service

Fritz Hansen Sound Club invites visitors to enjoy music in Bauhaus-inspired listening spaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

Fritz Hansen Sound Club invites visitors to enjoy music in Bauhaus-inspired listening spaces
Danish design brand Fritz Hansen has teamed up with audio specialist Technics to transform its Farringdon showroom into a series of domestic listening scenes for London Design Festival.
As part of the Fritz Hansen Sound Club, the showroom has been organised into four domestic scenes where guests are invited to listen to a curated selection of vinyl records.
The installation combines Fritz Hansen's furniture and lighting products with turntables, headphones and speakers from Japanese firm Technics.
A 90th anniversary limited edition of the Kaiser Idell Luxus table lamp and Technics' SL 40CBT turntable form the centrepiece of the various settings, both reimagined in a matching burgundy hue.
In reference to the table lamp's modernist origins, the interior styling evokes the Bauhaus movement and combines 1930s furniture with pieces from Fritz Hansen's catalogue.
Fritz Hansen Sound Club originally debuted during 3 Days of Design in Copenhagen, with the aim to explore how sound informs the way users experience interior settings.
,"Sound plays a direct role in how we experience space," said Fritz Hansen creative director, Els Van Hoorebeeck. "It shapes how we move, where we pause, and how we relate to furniture, light and materials."
"With Fritz Hansen Sound Club, we explore how these elements work together to define the character of a space, and how this way of thinking continues to shape our design today."
The Study area pairs steel-framed desks with Arne Jacobsen's Ant Chair in a cherry veneer finish, while the designer's iconic Egg Chair provides a cosy spot for relaxing in the nearby Reading Corner.
Downstairs, the Living Room provides a setting for socialising, with a turntable and speakers oriented towards the guests.
Furniture including Poul Kjærholm's PK31 sofa and PK80 daybed creates a relaxed, lounge-like feel, while a 1930s drinks trolley and PK61 coffee tables encourage conversation and interaction.
Fritz Hansen was founded in 1872 and is known for working with famous architects and designers, including Jacobsen and Kjærholm, as well as Hans J Wegner, Børge Mogensen and Verner Panton.
More recently, the brand has collaborated with contemporary talents such as Piero Lissoni, Jamie Hayon and Cecilie Manz, who created a compact and comfortable plywood chair that can be used in a variety of contexts.
A new version of Manz's Monolit chair forms part of the presentation, alongside a more compact, wall-mounted take on the Kaiser Idell lamp and an upholstered version of Japanese studio Nendo's N02 Recycle chair.
Other highlights from this year's London Design Festival include the debut show of design platform Collate Lobby and a bamboo pavilion covered in traditional Indian police shields.
Fritz Hansen Sound Club is open daily to the public until 20 September at 78 Cowcross Street as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

NRL finals: Newcastle Knights defeat New Zealand Warriors 12-10, projectiles thrown at refs
Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.
Newcastle, last season's wooden spooners, silenced the huge 48,511-strong crowd at Auckland's Eden Park to secure a nail-biting 12-10 win, advancing to the NRL preliminary finals for the first time in 13 years.
Some in that large Eden Park crowd hurled projectiles at referee Ashley Klein and his team, while Warriors coach Andrew Webster described three late decisions that went against his side as "frustrating".
Warriors centre Leka Halasima was knocked to the ground before he could contest a high kick in the 79th minute, with Klein clearing the contact made by Knights prop Tyson Frizell and not giving the home side a chance to send the match into extra time with a penalty goal.
Frizell had his eyes on the ball, but did appear to cut across Halasima's line, allowing Fletcher Sharpe to leap high and catch the ball for Newcastle.
Minutes earlier, the Warriors were left fuming when Bunker official Chris Butler overturned a Knights knock-on but did not overturn a strip penalty against them, with the home side believing the ball was dropped because of a loose carry.
"It was frustrating. I feel like they were trying to find ways to take it off us," Webster said in reference to the two Bunker reviews.
"The last one, and two points would have drawn the game, he's [Tyson Frizell] going across Leka [Halasima], pretending to try and catch the ball, which they [NRL] have told us you can't do."
Webster made it clear those decisions were not the reason his side will not be facing Penrith next Sunday in Sydney, while Knights coach Justin Holbrook said he thought the officials made the right calls late.

Knights stun Warriors, set up prelim date with Panthers
— reporting by AAP
Newcastle's fairytale finals run has claimed another scalp as the Knights toppled the Warriors 12-10 to set up a preliminary final showdown with Penrith.
In front of a heavily pro-Warriors crowd at Auckland's Eden Park on Sunday, the undermanned Knights celebrated one of their most famous victories with tries from Fletcher Sharpe and Dominic Young.
The Knights will play the Panthers at Stadium Australia on Sunday in their first preliminary final since 2013, which further underlines the club's incredible revival under coach Justin Holbrook after they finished with the 2025 wooden spoon.
Holbrook, who guided the Knights to seventh at the end of the regular season, is the strongest candidate to be crowned Dally M coach of the year after his troops battled to finals wins over South Sydney and the Warriors without their first-choice front row and prized playmaker Dylan Brown.
From the kick-off, the Knights — led by captain Kalyn Ponga and the electrifying Sharpe — chanced their arm and were unlucky to have not scored twice in the opening 10 minutes of the semifinal.
Dane Gagai threw a forward pass to Young after a blistering break from five-eighth Sharpe, before the number six had his only try chalked off because of a Francis Manuleleua knock-on in the lead-up.
The Warriors could also count themselves lucky that Ali Leiataua was only placed on report after collecting Ponga high with no intent to wrap his arms.
Centre Leka Halasima crossed soon after Sharpe's try was ruled out to give the Warriors a 12th-minute lead.
The home side enjoyed a bounty of possession and territory for the next 15 minutes, but a combination of poor last-tackle options and courageous Newcastle defending meant the Warriors came up empty-handed.
The Knights have made a habit of striking from distance this season and a break down the left through Bradman Best levelled the game.
Best burst through the Warriors' right edge in the 29th minute and found Sharpe on his inside, the five-eighth juggling the infield pass to race 30 metres to score.
Sandon Smith had no issue with the conversion to make it 6-6 at half-time and Newcastle didn't take long to hit the front.
Manuleleua jolted the ball loose from Dallin Watene-Zelezniak and on the first tackle the Knights spread the ball to the right where Gagai unleashed Young with a flick pass and the towering Englishman touched down.
Smith again made the conversion to open up a six-point buffer with 35 minutes to go and it felt as if the Warriors were running out of chances as winger Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad failed a head injury assessment and Leiataua had a try ruled out for obstruction.
Halasima scored with an incredible 70th-minute finish to give the Warriors hope but Taine Tuaupiki missed the sideline conversion.
Both Tuaupiki and Ponga went off for head injury assessments in a nail-biting final 10 minutes, but the Knights held firm to win.

BEIJING, September 20. /TASS/. China has increased its imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) by 28.2%, to 5.15 million metric tons year-on-year in January-August, the General Administration of Customs of China reported.
According to the statistics, Russian LNG supplies to China grew by 13.2% in value terms in the reported period, reaching $2.66 billion. Russia is in the top three of China’s LNG suppliers, after Australia and Malaysia.

According to figures released, Russian oil deliveries to the country grew by 33.3% in value terms in the reporting period, to $44.84 billion. This makes Russia the largest supplier of oil to China.
