Trump Is Now Invoking National Security for Both Triumphal Arch and White House Ballroom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
19:13:43 UTC
04:13:43 KST

President Donald Trump announced Sunday that his proposed “triumphal arch”—which is planned for Memorial Circle near the Virginia end of Arlington Memorial Bridge in Washington, D.C.—will serve as a military complex with drones, ammunition storage, and sniper facilities.
“There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World,” he wrote on Truth Social, adding that the arch would “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones” and that there would be snipers “on both the roof and plaza areas.”
The announcement comes almost a year after he debuted a model of the 250-foot arch in the Oval Office on Oct. 15, 2025. In his initial proposal, Trump said that the arch was meant to commemorate America’s 250th anniversary.
Trump has also argued the arch is significant because it brings the United States on par with other world capitals featuring similar monuments. He emphasized that point again on Sunday, writing: “Out of the 59 top cities and Capitals, Washington, D.C., IS THE ONLY ONE IN THE WORLD THAT DOES NOT HAVE A TRIUMPHAL ARCH, but it will now and, by far, the greatest of them all.”
Trump did not identify the 59 cities he was referring to or explain the basis for the comparison. He appeared to mean that Washington was the only one among a group of leading world cities and capitals that lacked a triumphal arch.
His post said that the changes to the plan for the arch came “at the strong request of the United States Military” and had been made “for National Security purposes.”
The President’s post did not elaborate on the security role that a militarized arch would play in Washington, and Trump has not made public any revised proposal, model, or mockup of what changes that might entail.
TIME has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment.
Trump’s new description of the arch echoes the Administration’s defense of another signature construction project: the White House ballroom.
How Trump’s White House ballroom project became a ‘military complex’
The White House ballroom was initially presented as a privately funded venue for state dinners and other large events. In subsequent litigation, however, the Administration argued that the ballroom and the underground military facility beneath it constituted a single, integrated project.
That argument emerged amid legal challenges to construction already underway at the site of the former East Wing. On March 31, a judge ordered the ballroom project halted unless authorized by Congress, while leaving open an exception for work necessary to ensure the safety and security of the White House. The Administration subsequently argued that the security exception allowed the entire project to continue—claiming that it is one “massive” military complex that is “vital” to national security.
Prior to litigation, Trump had called the $400 million ballroom a social and diplomatic space to “host major functions honoring world leaders.” But in court documents filed last month, Solicitor General John Sauer raised the stakes, writing: “Every day the President does not have access to the vital security features of the military complex presents unacceptable risk.”
On Aug. 31, the Supreme Court stayed the injunction, allowing construction to continue while the government seeks further review. The Court did not rule on the project’s legality.
Much like the ballroom project, the triumphal arch has been the subject of legal and political scrutiny since it was announced in 2025.
The U.S. Commission of Fine Arts—whose members were all appointed by Trump—approved the project’s design in May. House Democrats called it a “vanity” project and introduced a bill to Congress to block its construction, along with the construction of any triumphal arch exceeding 50 feet on any National Park Service (NPS) lands in Washington “except by express authorization of Congress.” Democrats also argued that the arch was an unnecessary expenditure amid the affordability crisis affecting Americans.
“As President Trump strips away the necessary safety nets from Americans who are struggling to afford their basic needs like groceries and healthcare, he builds his unauthorized, grandiose Triumphal Arch,” Rep. Dina Titus of Nevada, one of the representatives who introduced the bill, said in a statement in May.
A group of Vietnam War veterans and a historian have jointly sued to block construction, arguing in Lemmon v. Trump that the monument would disrupt historic sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. The group has also argued that the plan requires congressional authorization.
“The President’s new justification for this wildly unpopular construction does nothing to cure its fundamental illegality,” Nicolas Sansone, the plaintiffs’ lead attorney, said in a statement Sunday. “Congress has not authorized the arch, and unless and until Congress does so, building the arch on Memorial Circle is unlawful.”
How national security matters can expand presidential power
The difference between a construction project that is a matter of national security and one that is not can inform the role of Congress, according to Kimberly Wehle, a professor at the University of Baltimore School of Law.
Wehle tells TIME that Administrations have, for decades, used this understanding to expand presidential powers. There has been a “lot of deference” given to Presidents in the past when they invoke such reasoning, she says, pointing to the example of the Bush Administration’s warrantless wiretapping and torture efforts after 9/11. At the time, the Justice Department argued that Congress cannot limit a President’s core military and national security decisions during a time of war.
Although the Supreme Court ruled in 2006 that President George W. Bush’s military commissions had to comply with restrictions imposed by Congress, the decision did not foreclose broader claims of presidential power over national security. Successive administrations continued to invoke those claims—or expansive congressional authorizations—to defend actions including surveillance, targeted killings, and military operations undertaken without a formal declaration of war.
Wehle says that decades-long accumulation of authority has brought the Executive Branch close to treating the President as “above the law.”
“Trump’s authority is at its apex when it can be tied to the Commander-in-Chief power,” Wehle says.
Republicans control both the House and Senate, she says, and Trump could have attempted to get Congressional approval for both the ballroom and arch projects by rallying his own party’s support—but he didn’t.
Instead, the Administration has opted to add military justification to its efforts, she says, which “makes it more convenient for the court to reinterpret the Constitution around unaccountable, unlimited, concentrated power in one person.”
Can Trump’s triumphal arch also function as a military site?
Trump has not given much information regarding what military use the arch would have, but George Washington University law professor Sara Bronin, who is also an architect, tells TIME that she is not aware of any other structures that double as commemorative monuments and military infrastructure.
“It seems crazy to include national security infrastructure in a site that is intended to be used by the general public and is intended to be a tourist attraction,” Bronin says, calling the two intentions “fundamentally incompatible.”
“Take the Pentagon, for example. Obviously, that is a site of national security importance, but that is not a site where members of the public are generally welcome,” she adds.
Bronin also points out that the National Park Service prepared a 22-page memorandum of agreement last week, acknowledging that the arch will unavoidably harm historic sites in the capital. The document sets out measures intended to mitigate those effects.
“NPS recognizes that Memorial Circle is located within a highly sensitive historic and commemorative landscape and that the undertaking’s location contributes to adverse effects to historic properties whose significance is associated with setting, design, feeling, association, spatial organization, circulation, and contributing views and vistas,” the agreement said.
It concluded, however, that the project cannot be located anywhere else since erecting it at Memorial Circle is “central to the undertaking.” To mitigate any adverse impacts, NPS said officials would create interpretive signs, webpages, and other materials documenting the site, its history, and the views affected by the project.
That document did not take into account any proposed military infrastructure.
“If this type of use and these physical improvements will be incorporated into the memorial arch, the memorandum of agreement will have to be completely redrafted,” Bronin says.
Judge Tanya Chutkan, who is presiding over Lemmon v. Trump, has not ruled on the central question of whether the arch can be built without Congressional authorization. On Sept. 4, she ordered the Trump Administration to provide 48 hours’ notice before undertaking arch-related activity other than specified archaeological work. She also reminded the government of an earlier consent order requiring final NPS authorization and 14 days’ notice before construction or demolition. Last week, she denied the Justice Department’s request to dissolve the 48-hour requirement.
The Administration has not yet presented the arch’s new military rationale to the court or released plans showing how the proposed military infrastructure would be incorporated into the monument. That leaves the legal significance of Trump’s remarks unresolved.
But the claim places the arch on a path already taken by the ballroom. Both were introduced to the public principally as civic or ceremonial projects; both are now being described in military terms amid disputes over whether Trump can build them without Congress. Together, the projects may test how much additional authority a President gains by recasting a building project as military infrastructure.

Christine Taylor revealed how she was robbed at gunpoint in the '90s
Kyiv • UNN
In the early 1990s, an armed man stole Christine Taylor's car and purse. The aftermath of the attack haunted the actress for years.
American actress Christine Taylor revealed that in the early 1990s in Los Angeles, an armed man carjacked her at gunpoint. The star spoke about the attack and its aftermath on the podcast "We're Still Here, Honey," E! News reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the 55-year-old actress, she was with her friend and neighbor David Pressman. The attack took place at around 3 p.m. near their apartment.
It was three in the afternoon. Detroit Street, near Beverly Boulevard—we lived in an apartment there, and we were robbed at gunpoint
The attack lasted only a few minutes
The actress said that she parked the car and got out with her friend. Another car stopped nearby, and an armed man got out. He ordered Pressman to stay where he was and Taylor to hand over the keys.
Because of the anti-theft steering-wheel lock, the attackers had to call her back so that she could remove it. After that, they also took the actress's bag.
It probably all happened within a minute and a half to two minutes, but it felt as though time had stopped. It was so frightening
Taylor admitted that she did not see a psychotherapist at the time, and that friends and family helped her cope with what had happened. A few days after the attack, the actress landed a role in the 1994 horror film "Night of the Demons 2."
According to her, filming unexpectedly became a kind of therapy for her. At the same time, the effects of what she had experienced stayed with her for years: whenever Taylor saw someone approaching a car, she could freeze out of fear that the attack might happen again.

Record on Indigenous kids in jail overshadows Australia's UN Security Council bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:43:58 UTC
07:43:58 KST

ON BRIEF
- Australia's overincarceration of Indigenous children could hinder it's chances on the UN's Security Council.
- Indigenous young people between 10 and 17 years old made up 60 per cent of the youth detention population.
Australia is seeking international backing for a seat at the United Nation’s highest table, but the federal government has recently been the subject of an urgent UN plea to address the overrepresentation of Indigenous children behind bars.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese launched the campaign for a two-year stint on the UN Security Council overnight in New York with a promotional video that begins with the Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy speaking in her traditional Yanyuwa language.
She goes on to appeal for support for Australia’s bid saying "we are home to the oldest continuous culture on the planet".
But the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination issued an "early warning and urgent action procedure” earlier this year, expressing grave concerns about racial discrimination against Indigenous children through education, healthcare and housing conditions — a "key factor contributing to their heightened vulnerability to arrest, incarceration and re-offending.”
The committee went on to criticise the states and territories where the age of criminal responsibility is 10 years of age and where children face adult penalties for their crimes, including life in prison.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The United Nations committee also raised a red flag about the “limited progress” on the Closing the Gap measures which are at the heart of the federal government’s Indigenous Affairs policy.
It followed an investigation by the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention into Indigenous youth incarceration in Australia.
Last year the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare found across the country Indigenous young people between 10 and 17 years old made up 60 per cent of the youth detention population, that’s despite making up only 6.6 per cent of the general population.
Indigenous young people were 21 times more likely than non-Indigenous youth to be in detention, and the numbers were increasing.
When pressed by SBS News in New York to explain what he would do to address concerns that the federal government is not showing enough leadership, the Prime Minister said he would discuss the issues with Indigenous leaders when he returns to Australia.
"Indigenous disadvantage is a fact in Australia," Albanese said.
"My government continues to work on Closing the Gap in a range of areas in Australia."
The prime minister also responded to questions about an investigation by The Australian newspaper into the Indigenous child protection system in Western Australia, despite yesterday dodging similar questions by saying he would not address domestic issues while abroad.
"We're not about to intervene against the Western Australian government," he said.
"This is a Western Australian issue, and, you know, I will refer you once again to Malarndirri McCarthy, our minister in Australia. It is impossible to follow, on an hour-by-hour basis, what is happening in Australia from New York."
Albanese said it was right to highlight the importance of Australia's Indigenous culture in the United Nations Security Council bid, to secure a non-permanent seat for two years in 2029 and 2030.
"Indigenous disadvantage is something that, of course, I’m always concerned with ... we have in having the oldest continuous culture on Earth, and that needs to be a source of pride. It certainly is for myself as Australia's prime minister."
Albanese went on to outline the government’s efforts to address a chronic shortage of housing in remote Indigenous communities.
"That is a multi-billion-dollar program being rolled out."
He also said the government's public education funding deal was assisting young Indigenous students to access school, and the federal government was assisting in healthcare, including providing financial support for dialysis treatment in remote communities.
Further, he defended the measures the government has taken to support more job opportunities and said the Indigenous ranger program was raised during his trip to Apple headquarters in Silicon Valley, being partly funded by the company.
"You don’t overcome intergenerational disadvantage in a year, or indeed in a term," he said.
"If there were easy answers, someone would have done it. The truth is, it hasn’t happened. The truth is, all governments in Australia need to do better, and that is one of the priorities that my government has.”
Australia and Finland are the only countries that have so far nominated for the two seats allocated for their geographic area, if no other countries nominate and they are accepted they would be assured to secure the coveted positions.
Albanese said elevation to the council would ensure Australia has a voice on the future of Artificial Intelligence, climate action and dealing with international conflicts, arguing that would also mean being able to make a difference to domestic cost of living issues like inflation and fuel prices.
He said it would be a "modest" campaign in terms of the cost to taxpayers.

Far-right AfD wins state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, CDU fails to enter parliament

Germany: AfD wins in northeastern state, Left in Berlin
Published September 20, 2026last updated September 21, 2026
What you need to know
- 
	The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, narrowly ahead of the center-left Social Democratic Party
- 
	Chancellor Friedrich Merz 's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) failed to enter the state parliament
- 
	Merz strikes defiant tone, pledging to 'get down to business' with reforming Germany after 'disaster' state election
- The socialist Left Party has finished first in Berlin with roughly 25% of the vote, ahead of CDU
- Smaller parties hovering around the 5% threshold could still have a major impact on the final balance of seats
- The outcome of the elections could determine the political future of Merz, whose approval rating is at a record low
- For the first time, 16- and 17-year-olds are eligible to vote in both states

AfD wins election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — election commission
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) failed to secure any parliamentary seats.
According to the preliminary results announced by the election commission early Monday morning, the AfD secured 38.2% of the vote on Sunday. The Social Democratic Party (SPD), which is led by state premier Manuela Schwesig, garnered 35.5% of the vote.
The socialist Left Party (6.5%) and the environmentalist Green Party (5.7%) were the only other parties to make it into the state parliament.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU suffered disastrous losses, failing to secure a seat in parliament with only 4.9% of the vote.
The populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which combines left-leaning economic, conservative migration and pro-Russian foreign policy initiatives, also fell short of entering the state parliament with 4.8%.
The business-focused Free Democratic Party (FDP) failed to regain a seat, securing only 1.0%.
The AfD will therefore hold 32 seats in the new state parliament, while the SPD will hold 29. The Left Party and the Greens will each hold five seats.
The previous SPD-Left Party coalition no longer has a majority, but a three-party alliance with the Greens would have one. All three parties have ruled out forming coalitions with the AfD.
BSW admits failure to enter parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
The left-wing populist BSW has acknowledged it would not be represented in the next state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, as it failed to secure the legal minimum of 5% of the votes.
"We didn't make it," BSW's top candidate Peter Schabbel told the DPA news agency late on Sunday. This marks a contrast with his comments hours before, when he said the party was "very confident" about entering parliament.
In his latest remarks, Schabbel said his party failed to qualify due to the polarizing battle between the AfD and the SPD, which harmed smaller parties. He also said the BSW wants to overcome this polarization and would continue to work towards this goal.
Another senior BSW representative in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Sabine Firnhaber, also said the BSW will continue its work in the northeastern state.
"We have a state association, we have regional groups, we have active members," she said. "And we represent goals that would also be worth fighting for in four or five years."
READ: German elections deal a blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz
Elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have dealt the CDU a historic defeat while the AfD saw a massive gain.
Just minutes after the first projections were released, Merz made a statement: "We can't sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — it was a disaster." As for the heavy losses in Berlin, he described the outcome there as "reasonable."
Read the election night analysis by DW's Marcel Fürstenau here.
Will SPD Premier Manuela Schwesig hold on to power in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania?
The center-left SPD placed second in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, securing around 35,4% of the votes compared to the AfD's 38.3%.
However, the current head of the state government, Manuela Schwesig, might still keep herself and her SPD party in power.
With the center-right CDU and the leftist populist BSW both projected to stay out of parliament, the assembly is likely to be comprised out of only four parties: the AfD, the SPD, the Left Party and the Green Party.
Schwesig's current administration is backed by the Left Party. According to projected results, a new alliance between the Left Party and the SPD would fall short of a majority, but a three-way coalition involving the Greens would form a ruling bloc of 39 seats, enough for a majority in the 71-seat assembly.
While other coalitions are theoretically possible, it appears unlikely that any of the other parties will enter a coalition with the AfD, despite its success at the ballot box.
Other German political parties rule out working with the AfD in a strategy known as the "firewall" against the far right.
WATCH: AfD's Alice Weidel says Merz 'can no longer stay in office'
Berlin: Left Party's top candidate celebrates victory in German and Turkish
With the socialist Left Party securing the largest share of the state parliamentary vote in Berlin, the party's mayoral candidate Elif Eralp celebrated the victory of "love and justice over hate."
"Starting today, we are changing Berlin together and make it a better place," said Eralp, who hopes to become the first female mayor of Berlin with immigration background.
Eralp was born in Munich in 1981 to a family of Turkish refugees. While her victory speech was mostly in German, she also shouted out "We wrote history, friends" in Turkish during her address.
The Left Party has big plans for Berlin, including tackling its housing crisis by expropriating real estate own by large corporations. In order for Eralp to become the mayor of Berlin and the head of its state government, however, her party would need to form a coalition, with the center-left SPD and the environmentally friendly Green Party being the most likely contenders for a power-sharing deal.
CDU slips under 5% parliament threshold in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — projections
Germany's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) will not enter the next parliament in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, according to projections published by Germany's top public broadcasters.
The latest predictions published by public broadcaster ARD put the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz at 4.9%, cementing its worst-ever defeat in a state election of this kind. Another German public broadcaster, ZDF, initially maintained its 5% projection before also adjusting its estimates to 4.9%.
The conservative party is not the only one in danger of falling below the legal limit, with the leftist populist Sahra Wagenknech Alliance (BSW) also seemingly just below the threshold.
If both of these factions are kept out of the next parliament, the new assembly would have only four parties: the far-right AfD, the center-left SPD, the socialist Left Party, and the environmentally friendly Greens.
The AfD would still require a coalition partner to form a majority.
CDU faces its worst-ever state election defeat in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is fighting to stay in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament, with its result hovering around the 5% mark.
However, even if the conservatives are represented in the next state parliament, the Sunday election already marks their worst ever election defeat in the state parliamentary votes held anywhere in Germany. The party, founded in 1945, was traditionally considered one of the country's "big tent" political factions seeking to accommodate a wide spectrum of voters.
Its previous worst score was 9% of the vote they secured in Bremen in 1951, according to a report published by NDR, the public broadcaster covering Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
How did Berlin's young people vote?
German citizens in Berlin aged 16 and 17 were able to cast their ballots in the state election for the first time on Sunday — and they were among a group that voted overwhelmingly for progressive parties.
According to results on Sunday evening, some 43% of voters aged 16-24 voted for the socialist Left Party. Another 12% voted for the Greens, while 7% voted for the Social Democrats (SPD).
Meanwhile, around 12% of voters aged 16-24 for the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD).
It was voters in the 25 to 34 age group who were the biggest bloc to have supported the Left Party, with 48% casting their ballots for the far-left party.
Support for the Left Party dims as the age groups grow older, with voters around 33% of voters above 70 having voted for the incumbent Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
Berlin bishops say city voted for democracy, diversity
Commenting on the Berlin state election, the city's Protestant Bishop Christian Stäblein said the majority of the voters endorsed "liberal democracy."
"We are a church bound by the Christian view of humanity and by the dignity of every person," he said.
His Catholic colleague, Heiner Koch, said his church would "continue to critically observe politics, and warn against the supposedly easy solutions, and speak up for those, who are insufficiently seen or heard in the political debate."
Berlin "is and stays diverse," the Catholic bishop said.
Verdi chief urges Merz to rethink reforms
The head of Germany's Verditrade union has called on Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government to change course on planned reforms following the elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
"I hope Mr Merz realizes that he has screwed up," Verdi chairman Frank Werneke told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper.
Werneke called on the government to abandon plans requiring employees to provide a doctor's note from the first day of illness and ending full retirement benefits after 45 years of contributions.
"Many people reject abolishing the full pension after 45 years of contributions. That is an important reason for the CDU's poor performance in the recent elections," Werneke said. "People are worn out and exhausted. They want to stop working, and they need to."
Werneke also described the recent electoral gains of the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) as "extremely threatening."
"An AfD federal government would be a catastrophe," he said, arguing that leaving the euro and European Union would be economically disastrous and that Germany needed immigration.
"Everything must be done to ensure that the AfD does not enter government," Werneke said.
Verdi and other trade unions plan a nationwide day of protest on Saturday, with demonstrations expected in 15 cities.
Berlin: SPD's Krach refuses to discuss new coalitions
The top candidate for the center-left SPD in Berlin, Steffen Krach, refused to discuss cooperation with other parties in the city's Senate.
"It's too early to talk about coalition options," he said, when asked if his party would prefer to rule with the Left Party or the CDU conservatives.
Talking to state broadcaster ARD, Krach noted that the incumbent CDU-SPD coalition was clearly defeated at the polls, and that future steps will be decided within the party committees in the following weeks.
Meanwhile, the Green party indicated they were ready to rule together with the Left Party and the SPD.
"We want to take responsibility and forge a progressive alliance for Berlin together with the SPD and the Left," said senior Green representatives Nina Stahr and Philmon Ghirmai, saying that Berliners voted in favor of political change.
Populist BSW projected to fall short, stay out of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament
According to incomplete projections published by German media, the leftist populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) will not be entering the state legislature of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, depriving them of the kingmaker role they had previously secured in Saxony-Anhalt.
The estimates published by German state broadcasters ARD and ZDF just after 8 p.m. on Sunday show BSW at 4.9% of the votes, just shy of the 5% threshold they need to secure in order to be represented in the state parliament.
Moreover, the latest available numbers show Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) hovering around 5%, also putting it at risk of not having a parliamentary presence. A failure by the center-right CDU to enter the chamber would ramp up pressure on the chancellor, whose power is already shaken by the Saxony-Anhalt vote and his party's already staggeringly low result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The numbers are subject to change as the official count continues.
Populist BSW rejects AfD coalition in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
With the far-right populist AfD leading the pack in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but still projected to fall well short of the parliamentary majority, the leftist populist BSW rejected the possibility of officially joining forces.
BSW's top candidate Peter Schabbel said there would be no coalition with the AfD.
"We are sticking to it," he said.
However, he noted that cooperation between the two parties was still possible, including voting together.
This language reflects BSW's attitude following the Saxony-Anhalt election two weeks ago. With the AfD also falling short of a parliamentary majority in this German state, the BSW said it would "decide on the substance" when it comes to supporting them in parliament.
On Sunday, Schabbel also sought to dispel doubts that BSW would clear the 5% hurdle to enter the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament, despite the projections showing them at the very edge of the required percentage of the vote.
"We are very confident that we will get into the state assembly," Schabbel said.
Leading CDU figure blames party firewall critics for voter uncertainty
Senior Christian Democratic Union (CDU) politician Philipp Amthor has blamed members of his own party who questioned its firewall against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) for contributing to the CDU's poor showing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Amthor, a minister of state in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Chancellery, told public broadcaster ZDF that there was a "very clear position" across the state CDU on maintaining its distance from the AfD.
He said individual party figures had tried to soften that position, but that this had instead contributed to "even greater uncertainty among our voters here in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania."
"I am very grateful that everyone kept their nerve and did not draw the wrong conclusions," Amthor, who himself hails from the state, said.
The CDU is hovering around the 5% threshold in the latest projections, a big drop from the 13.3% it won in 2021.
Amthor described the CDU's result as a "historic defeat" and a "tectonic shift" for a party that governed Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania from 1990 to 1998.
